  worker's. Rows the report takes from aterm's record of rows that scrolled off still carry the
  panel's edge and text: that record does not say which rows were drawn beside the panel, so a
  table's own `│` there could be taken for the panel's edge. A turn you sent that wraps onto a
  second row beside the panel is found as the report's start, on the screen or in that record,
  also once the panel has closed or its edge has moved, and the ledger finds it there to size its
  reply: the panel's edge on its first row hid it, so the report said it found no start and ran
  from the top, and the ledger said the turn's row was not found. A change in the panel's own
  text, such as its list of changed files, no longer reads as the agent moving on: it read as a
  new point in the turn, a sent message's turn drawn, a conversation that moved, and new words
  from an agent held busy by background work, which started over aterm's count of how long that
  agent had been stuck.

## [0.155.0] - 2026-11-05

### Changed

- **Land waits for the processes an agent left running.** Under Autopilot Land, a `Nothing
  left:` reply now lands only once each process the session's agent started and left running
  (the ones `aterm ctl @self sys left` offers it) has been ended with `aterm ctl end <token>`, or
  kept with a `keep <token>` line under `Nothing left:`, for one the person asked it to run.
  Until then Land's prompt says how many still run and how to end or keep them, and `status
  land_held=` says `left`; after three such holds in one landing Land stops holding on them. A
  partial or missing process reading never holds a landing. The worker's `done` record says what
  was left: `left=0`, `left=kept:<n>`, `left=<n>`, or `left=unchecked`. Cruise's done check names
  the count too and holds nothing, and `aterm ctl harness policy` lists `land_checks=git,left`
  for a harness that supervises itself.

- **The harness approves more read-only Bash commands under zsh.** `git show HEAD^`,
  `git diff HEAD^^ HEAD` and `grep -n ^fn src` are approved as reads when your shell startup
  cannot turn zsh's `EXTENDED_GLOB` on. Without that option zsh reads `^` and `#` as plain text.
  `cat *.json` is no longer refused as a possible read of a dotfile such as `.credentials.json`,
  because neither bash nor zsh expands `*` to a leading dot by default. If your startup may turn
  either option on, or sets anything the harness cannot read, these commands still come to you.
  A `git grep` pathspec is read the way git matches it, where `*` also matches dotfiles and other
  directories: `git grep token -- '*.yml'` run in your home, an exclusion alone (`':!x'`) there,
  and a pathspec from the repository's top (`':/'`) come to you.

- **Harness versions since v0.154.0: `alab claude harness 0.12`, `alab agy harness 0.10`, `alab grok harness 0.12`, `alab muse harness 0.11`.** Each harness's minor moves once per release in which it changed.

- **`sys` says the Mac's own thermal word.** `aterm ctl sys` prints macOS's thermal state as
  it names it, "thermal nominal", "fair", "serious" or "critical", where it printed "throttled:
  light" at fair. `sys why` names the `throttled` cause only at serious or above, in Low Power
  Mode, or where Linux counts throttling, so a Mac at fair is calm. `await sys` waits on
  `thermal` (`thermal<serious`) in place of `throttle`. `await sys quiet` waits out a thermal
  level that claims throttling (serious or above, or Linux's counted throttling) and no longer
  fair, so a Mac at fair can read quiet; it timed out there before. The JSON `throttle` keys and
  the `throttle` event are now `thermal`.

- **Under Autopilot Land, a question dialog is answered with Land's words.** Its free-text
  row gets: take the option that lands all of this work on remote main soonest and start no
  new work, and never force push or delete work. Where that text cannot go in, or the dialog
  does not take it, its Recommended option is taken instead, and the dialog is handed to you
  only where you typed into it yourself or no option can safely be picked for you. A session
  set to ask you, or with question answers turned off, still leaves its questions to you.
  Before, a dialog under Land took its Recommended option as under Cruise, which could start
  new work while Land was landing.

- **aterm decides each NEEDS YOU need once, across restarts and the fleet.** aterm posts no
  desktop notifications of its own (they went with the other automatic alerts), but with
  `desktop_alerts = true` in `aterm.toml` it still decides, and records in `aterm.log`, which needs
  it would tell you of: each need an agent's NEEDS YOU line names once, until you press Return in
  its tab or the agent takes the need down. A named need that comes back in the same words after
  another report pushed it aside, or a list of named needs that is only re-ordered or loses one, is
  recorded as `not queued: told once`; a new need beside one you were told of is decided once, by
  its own words. Needs aterm sees only as a count (`(+2 more)`), an approval box, a question or a
  stop are decided each time they come. That memory now survives a quit and restart (closing the
  last window included), a crash and an update, though a Return you pressed before it still lets
  a need be told again after it. Another Mac of your fleet whose survey shares content names its
  needs (`need_ids=` in `aterm ctl survey`), so its needs are decided once here too. The menu bar
  and `aterm ctl survey` keep showing every need until the agent clears it.

- **Quitting asks a plain native "Quit aterm?".** On a Mac the quit question, and the question
  before closing a window whose process is still running, is a standard macOS sheet on the window
  again, with Quit and Cancel buttons and one short line saying what ends, instead of the text band
  across the top of the window. Return quits and Escape cancels, as before.

- **The tab where you type setup's one Mac password is titled Mac Setup.** It was titled
  Command Line Tools even on a Mac that already had them, where the same password only turns
  developer mode on and does setup's other owed steps. System State's headline and notes name
  the Mac Setup tab.

### Added

- **An agent can see what it left running.** `aterm ctl @self status` now says `left=<n>:<oldest_ms>`
  beside `program_check=`: how many processes this session's agent started that still run (those
  `aterm ctl @self sys left` offers to end, including those of a dead verify run it started), and
  how long the oldest has run; `left=0:-` with none, and `left=-` with no whole, current
  reading. `sys left` marks each of them `left_of=<sid>`. A process started while an agent ran in
  the tab counts, even from a short call the jobs view never saw; one you start yourself after
  the agent has exited does not. An agent aterm supervises is also told once per episode, on a
  prompt aterm types anyway: "2 processes this session started still run, the oldest for 20 m;
  `aterm ctl @self sys left` lists them", each re-checked as it is told. The words carry counts
  and an age only, never a program's name or path.

- **An agent hears when another session changes the same files.** When another agent
  session of the same aterm, in the same repository, changes a file the agent's branch
  also changes (CHANGELOG.md counts), aterm adds one line to the next prompt it types
  the agent anyway, such as its continuation or Land's instruction: `(aterm: 1 file this
  branch changes is also changed by s-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718293)`. It carries only the count
  and the other sessions' ids, never a file name, a path or a branch, and is told once
  for each set of sessions: more shared files with the same sessions say nothing new,
  another set (one more session, or one fewer) does. It goes by each session's work
  record, read at its turn ends, and leaves out a record read more than 10 minutes ago.
  It never rides an answer or a line typed at a break, refuses nothing and leases
  nothing, and `[harness] facts = false` turns it off with the other facts. A session
  that lands stops counting. `lab work-overlap` checks it with two real Claude Code
  workers against the lab's stub.

- **The fleet survey says where each Mac keeps its work, and `--host any` can require it.**
  A content survey (`aterm ctl survey`, `survey --fleet`, `--json`) now names each
  instance's home, the free space on its volume, and each checkout aterm's setup cloned
  there (`~/<name>`, a clone of `github.com/<owner>/<name>`): its HEAD and branch, how far
  behind `origin/main` it was at its last fetch and how old that fetch is, and whether it
  has uncommitted changes. aterm reads these offline, at most every 10 minutes, and never
  fetches. An older aterm, or one that has not read them yet, reports them as unknown
  (`"repos":null`), never as none. `aterm ctl --host any spawn … need=repo:trust,free:150g`
  places the worker only on a Mac whose read from the last 30 minutes lists that checkout
  and that much free space. A Mac that cannot say is never chosen, and a refusal counts the
  members that lack the checkout, lack the room, or cannot say. A fleet spawn also takes
  `'cwd=~/<path>'`, resolved against the chosen Mac's own home (quoted: bash turns an
  unquoted `cwd=~/…` into this Mac's own home first). aterm refuses one that leaves the
  home, reaches a folder macOS guards, or does not exist (`aterm help workers`,
  `aterm ctl help spawn`).
- **The messages page lists processes that outlived their tab or run.** An hour after a tab
  closed or a verify run died, the messages page lists, for whenever you look, what it left
  running that you may want to end (a record, never an alert, badge or banner): "Processes
  outlived their tab or run", with up to three lines naming them by program and where they
  came from ("ugrep ×2 from Tab 2, 3 h"). A dead verify run's
  leftovers are always listed (they are aterm's own leak); a closed tab's only when they cost
  something (at least one second of CPU for each hour they have run, or a binary from a build
  folder the disk watch must keep), since a program you `nohup`ed may be wanted. It names
  nothing a tab that is still open left, and ends nothing: end the ones you do not want with
  `aterm ctl end`, naming each token from `aterm ctl sys left`. It clears itself once none is
  left.
- **`aterm doctor`'s `leftovers:` row.** It says how many processes outlived a closed tab or
  a dead verify run and how long the oldest has run, how many dangling build links the disk
  watch found, and to look at `aterm ctl sys left scope=aterm`; it warns once one of them is
  one the message above names. With no aterm running it counts what dead verify runs left
  from their records alone. While macOS's program check is at its thread limit the row is
  not read.
- **`aterm ctl exits` says what each closed tab left running.** Each row ends `left=<n>`, the
  processes that tab left that `aterm ctl end` can take, or `left=-` where aterm keeps no
  record of the close.
- **An agent is told of every held program its tab started.** The one `aterm:` line an agent
  gets while macOS's program check holds its programs now counts a program its tab started
  that is in no job (started and orphaned between two readings), as `status program_check=`
  already did, beside the programs of its calls.
- **Dangling build links are named, never touched.** When the disk watch searches a checkout
  and finds its `target` link pointing at a folder that is gone (or on a volume that is not
  mounted), `aterm ctl sys left scope=aterm` lists it as a `link` row and the message log
  records it once. aterm does not delete, retarget or repair the link. A lab run that refuses
  a link in what it left in its scratch records that too, once per path.
- **A fleet task board: every worker a Mac started, and a resume that needs no sid.** `aterm
  ctl spawn` takes `label=<word>` (it stays on this Mac), and every worker this Mac starts,
  here or with `--host <h>` or `--host any`, gets a row on this Mac's board: its Mac (by node),
  program, model, account, Autopilot, working folder and a SHA-256 of its task (never the
  task's text), then its state, rev, conclusion, why, `checked=` and landing commit, which
  this Mac's aterm keeps current while the workers move, whether or not a window is open.
  `aterm ctl board [--json] [from=<sid>] [label=<word>]` reads it, and `aterm ctl --host <h>
  board` reads another Mac's where that Mac lets this one drive it. `aterm ctl [--host <h>]
  await task board since=0` waits on every open row, each where its worker runs, so a
  dispatcher restarted, or started on another Mac, resumes its workers without knowing their
  sids; one Mac that does not answer ends only its own workers' part of the wait. `aterm ctl
  board accept <@sid|label> <word>` records a package's accept result on its row. The board
  replaces `driven-any-hosts.tsv`: `--host any @<sid>` follows a worker by its row.
- **A recording can keep keys aterm cannot see echoed, by your yes, for that one recording.**
  On macOS, View ▸ Record Keys Not Echoed… asks you in aterm's alert whether the front window's
  `aos` recording may also keep the keys you type into a program that does not show them (a
  remote shell's editor through ssh or tmux, a TUI that draws its own input), which otherwise
  stop the recording. A yes lasts until that recording ends or the program leaves the front of
  its tab, and the same row stops it sooner. Such keys are kept as how many keys each burst
  held and one instant per burst, marked unseen: `aos status` says `unseen=on`, and `aos trace`,
  `aos export` and `aos check` say how many keys the trace holds unseen. A password prompt aterm
  can see still stops the recording: a local one, one that shows `*` or `•` as you type, and
  Secure Keyboard Entry. Nothing else turns it on: no setting, no `aterm ctl` verb or invoke,
  and an update does not carry it.
- **A vault's other addresses.** `aterm secrets mirrors add <url>` lists another address of
  this Mac's vault in its `source.toml` (`mirrors`), such as the server's IP beside its
  `.local` name, and `aterm secrets mirrors remove <url>` takes one off. When the vault's
  `url` does not answer or brings nothing newer, a sync reads each mirror too, and takes
  what one serves only when it verifies under the vault's pin and is newer than the version
  this Mac holds, so a mirror never rolls a Mac back. Nothing is ever written to a mirror,
  no join, request or admin publish goes to one, and a mirror is not told which Mac reads.
  Because nothing keeps a mirror current, a mirror alone never lets a removed Mac back in by
  proof: that check still needs the vault's url or one of its servers. A bad entry costs
  that address only: `aterm secrets status` names it and why, and the vault still reads. An
  aterm before this one reads the file as its `url` alone.

### Removed

- **System State no longer asks for debugger access on its own.** Setup's one Mac password
  already turns developer mode on, so the Debugger row has no Turn On… button, System State
  raises no SamplingTools dialog of its own, and the permission walk has no debugger page
  (`aterm ctl permissions walk now debugger` is a usage error). Settings ▸ Security still turns
  debugger access on or off, and `aterm doctor` still reads it.
  While developer mode is off, the Debugger row reads Waiting and names the ways on: the Mac
  Setup tab's password, `aterm init --only base.clt`, or Settings ▸ Security. A Mac Setup tab
  that did not finish now says `Running aterm init in a terminal tries again.`, true with the
  tools in place too. A relaunch mid-setup no longer offers its plan back to System State.

### Fixed

- **An update no longer waits on a window that holds only a Workers list.** An aterm opened from the
  Dock whose only windows held a Workers list with no worker in it kept its update until you opened a
  tab or quit. It now hands itself over to the new build, which reopens each list where it was, with no
  shell you never had. Finished rows leave the page, as across any update, and `aterm ctl @<sid> result`
  still answers for them. This needs both builds to have the change, so the first update to it still
  waits for the next launch on such a desk.
- **A new build that fails to start no longer deletes closed workers' results.** Ending before it
  took over, it removed the result files of the rows it had been handed, so the running aterm's
  `aterm ctl @<sid> result` had nothing to answer with. It now leaves them.
- **Allocation opens as its own tab when a Workers list is in front.** It used to split the list's
  tab, and that pane could not be brought back across a relaunch or an update.
- **Account reports stop promising a sign-in that will not happen.** A row no session on this Mac runs on now says it waits for `aterm harness accounts renew <label>`, in `aterm harness accounts`, limits and a sync's receipt, and the settings help says when aterm signs a login in by itself: a login that ends under a session here, or comes due after a session here used it within a week. A second account still takes a person's first sign-in, so a report no longer reads as if one is on its way.
- **Reports stop asking you to sign in accounts your sheet gives to other Macs.** A row with no login on this Mac, whose account the sheet, fleet file or pool file names only for other Macs, now reads as that Mac's: `aterm harness accounts` says whose it is rather than asking for a sign-in, and `aterm ai login` leaves it alone, including when it runs with nobody at the Mac. `accounts renew <label>` still signs it in for anyone who means to borrow it, and a row you pinned stays yours. An older build gave some Macs another Mac's rows.

- **`targo` builds a project kept in Documents, Desktop, Downloads or Library into a target you
  name.** A Rust build of a project in a folder of your home that aterm never looks into, with a
  `--target-dir` or `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` anywhere in your home, was refused with `atpkg: build
  cache ownership refused`, and no other target in your home got past it. Such a build now runs,
  as a build of a project outside your home does. A project aterm does manage still needs a
  target it can keep.
- **A Claude Code tab whose own background job runs at its limit moves once the job ends.** The
  move onto another account would end that job, so the relaunch refused it, and each refusal woke
  the tab to ask again at once: one run asked 371 times in under five minutes, each ask taking the
  row through the rotation and back. The move now waits for the job, the tab reads `held: jobs`
  in `aterm harness accounts`, and the move is made about two seconds after the job ends.
- **A limit met under an account's own login is booked to that account.** Claude Code names the
  default login's address in a conversation's transcript even when aterm runs it under another
  account's login, so the transcript scan also booked that limit to the default account, and with
  both walled nothing was left to move to. aterm now records when each conversation runs under an
  account's own login, and the scan books none of those rows by the address they name.
- **An account written over by `/login` no longer reads as usable.** When Claude Code's own
  `/login` replaced the account on the default login, the row it replaced was recorded as signed
  out, but that word could be hidden by an older retired word or by the same sync's change to the
  row, and the row then read `limited` or `usable`, so a Mac could rotate onto an account with no
  login. It reads signed out until a sign-in or a working session says otherwise, or the sheet
  names another account on the row. A record already in that state (m8's) keeps reading as it does
  until something next says otherwise.
- **`aterm fleet census` says whether accounts can rotate and whether they have.** It printed
  `short by 0 accounts (0h lost to shortfall)` of a fleet with Macs at their walls and nothing to
  move to: its supply counted accounts nobody had signed in to, it counted nothing with no pool
  file, and its hours were the account count under another name. It now names each Mac and CLI whose
  every signed-in account is at a wall, from what the Macs report, and a `rotation:` line says how
  many Macs with sessions hold two signed-in accounts of one CLI and how many moved in seven days. A
  move counts once a session proves the row it chose; one tried with no proof is counted apart. Macs
  report `moves_7d=`, `move_tries_7d=` and `last_move=` on `survey`, from their ledgers; a build that
  does not, or a ledger it cannot read, is unknown, never no moves. The hours are gone until
  something measures them (`ATERM-KI-1104-14`).

- **An idle Mac no longer spends cores re-checking vault peers that are already in sync.** Each
  vault repair round with a peer re-reads the membership records about 200 times, and on a Mac
  whose records file had grown past 1 MB every read hashed the whole file again, so an idle aterm
  on a lab of 50 Macs used two to four cores. A read of the file as it was last read now takes the
  records already checked, and a file that has changed is still read and checked in full.

- **A resting window no longer slows Tab Control or Allocation.** With `idle_rest_secs`
  set, a window nobody touched for that long slowed the one stream of readings that every
  reader in aterm shares, to a reading every 5 seconds, so a Tab Control page or an Allocation
  view a person watched without touching, beside that window or in it, refreshed five times
  slower. The rest now slows the shared readings only while no page reads them: while aterm is
  in front, a page on screen keeps its reading a second, as an open stats lens keeps its two a
  second. Each of those readings redraws the page and every window that shows the deck, so the
  rest is expected to save less GPU memory while a page or a lens shows (not measured). A page
  in a tab behind another is not on screen and keeps nothing.

- **A restart or a worker no longer turns a Claude Code yolo that nobody asked to be.** A relaunch
  onto a newer build with nothing on its line (a new tab with no conversation, whose permission
  mode could not be read), and a worker started from outside a session whose parent lends it no
  permission flags, reached atpkg's managed `claude`, which adds `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.
  Each now runs that build directly and lands in Claude Code's own settings. Such a worker starts
  without the usage tap until its first relaunch, as a worker a session started does.

- **A program in a tab can no longer change aterm.toml's owner keys by posting keys or clicks
  into aterm's window.** Every program in a tab can post keyboard and mouse events with aterm's
  own Accessibility access (`CGEventPost`, System Events' `keystroke` and `click`), and those
  reached aterm as your own typing. aterm now reads which process each key, click and scroll came
  from. An edit another process's input made to the aterm.toml in force, including text an
  input method composed from its keys or a Paste its click chose from the menu, marks the buffer:
  a Save that would change `[harness]`'s `occupancy`, `occupancy_source` or `occupancy_rule` is
  refused until Discard Changes and Reload from Disk, and so is such a Save that input chose.
  Such input also no longer presses Settings ▸ Harness's Owner rules or Settings ▸ Security's
  macOS access buttons, or lets a recording keep keys aterm cannot see echoed. Everywhere else
  that input is still yours, so Screen Sharing, the on-screen Accessibility Keyboard and
  remappers that post events keep copying, pasting and answering confirmations.

- **A busy Mac no longer keeps `aterm fleet` waiting on its secrets sync.** The background
  job that keeps this Mac's secrets in step starts a sync that can update the list of fleet
  members, and every thread of that sync ran at the lowest priority, which macOS would not let it
  leave, so a loaded Mac could stall it for seconds while `aterm fleet` waited on the list. The
  sync and the helpers it starts still run at the lowest priority, and only the one thread
  updating the list runs at normal priority until it is done. While this Mac waits to be let into
  a fleet, the job's repeated checks no longer make `aterm fleet` wait once this Mac has its node
  key (the first check creates it). A sync a window or the first launch starts now runs every
  thread at low priority, where only its first thread did.

- **A Mac with no aterm window open updates itself.** aterm's background service now checks for
  and downloads updates whether or not a window is open. With no window, it restarts onto the new
  build, installing it before it serves the fleet again; with a window open, the window updates
  as before. With `[update] auto_apply = false`, the install still waits for you.
- **`aterm-lab tape promote` and `rerecord` work on a Mac whose host name is under three bytes.**
  The tape scrub refused a host name such as `m8` (taken alone, it would rewrite text like `m80`),
  so building the machine's scrub failed and neither verb could run. A short host name is now
  taken only where the Mac writes it joined to another name, as `user@m8` and `m8.local`; a host
  name of three bytes or more is taken as a word, as before.
- **Quitting right after answering an alert no longer crashes aterm on macOS 27.** On the way
  out, aterm closed every window the app had, including the hidden glass window macOS 27 puts
  behind each alert. macOS freed that window while the alert still used it, and aterm crashed as
  the alert went away. aterm now closes only its own windows when it quits.

- **A session's posts stay single and in order through a crash.** If the Mac lost power soon
  after aterm quit with a post still unanswered, the next start could put that post on the bus a
  second time. And a session that posted to a person and then to another session could see the
  second land first, if the broker refused the first and the bridge died before reading the
  answer. The stop now saves what the next start needs to find the post, and the second post now
  waits for the answer to the first.
- **A symlinked `aterm.toml` is read again everywhere.** Where the file is a link (a dotfiles
  checkout, home-manager), aterm 0.154 stopped serving this Mac to the fleet, turned
  disk cleanup off, ran `aterm harness` and `aterm drive` on default settings, read `[fabric]` as
  broken and ignored `windowing_behavior`. A link whose target is gone counts as unread settings,
  never as no file. A linked `rules_file` keeps its standing rules too.
- **`brew bundle add` no longer erases a Brewfile it could not read.** A symlinked Brewfile, or one
  over 4 MiB, was overwritten with only the new entry. Brewfile links are followed again, and any
  other unreadable Brewfile now fails and is left alone. `brew deps --brewfile=-` reads stdin again.

- **On Linux a helper a window ties to itself is tied to the whole window.** Linux ends such a
  helper when the thread that started it ends, so one started from a short-lived part of the
  window could end with that part. Each now starts from a thread that lasts as long as the
  window, so it ends when the window does, killed outright or crashed included, or when an
  update restarts the window in its own place.

- **At an expired Claude Code login whose settings pin the sign-in method, aterm no longer types
  `/login`.** With `forceLoginMethod` set (to `claudeai` or `console`, in any settings file Claude
  Code reads: the user's, the project's, the managed file or the cached server-managed
  `remote-settings.json`), Claude Code's `/login` draws no method picker and opens the browser one
  tick after its Enter, over the person's work. aterm now reads the agent's settings at the lost
  login, whether or not the login's notice is still on screen, and, where a method is pinned, a
  gateway signs in (`forceLoginMethod` `gateway` or `forceLoginGatewayUrl`), the settings cannot
  be read or name a policy helper whose output aterm cannot see, or the agent was started on a
  cloud session (`--cloud`, `--remote`, `--teleport`, `--attach-serve`), types nothing and raises
  one quiet need (`login-not-run`, saying why), so the person types `/login` when they are ready.
  A managed folder or server-managed copy that the agent's environment names in place of the
  usual ones is read too. The model's `NoBrowserOpenedByAterm` law now covers a pinned method.

- **A need beside a Land rest or a stop says `waits on you` on every surface.** The needs entry's
  tail now says `waits on you` wherever the loop will not type again (Land resting or landed, and
  the stop on replies that repeat, under any mode), not only beside Land's rest; the chip's
  screen-reader description, the menu bar's tip and the tab's hover speak the entry's own tail
  where they said `carrying on` whatever the entry said.

- **An outage that resumed on a witness stays latched whatever the resume typed.** A witnessed
  resume typed as Land's instruction or sent as the person's draft now latches the outage as the
  measured line does, so a later witness does not resume the same wall again, and the latch rides
  the retry mark (`witnessed=yes`) into the loop that follows.

- **A `NEEDS YOU: nothing` in the middle of a turn no longer takes down the agent's real need.**
  The agent's own none (not quoted, not fenced) retracts the needs named before it in the same
  message, and only the turn's last message retracts the needs of its earlier messages and of the
  turn's earlier points. A none quoted or fenced (a worker's reply relayed) retracts nothing, and
  one said in an earlier message retracts nothing beyond that message, so a lead that quotes a
  worker's `NEEDS YOU: nothing` keeps its own need on the menu bar.

- **`aterm db alab import --apply` finishes on a busy Mac, and says when it did not.** Each of its
  passes held a product open's 2 s budget, which a loaded Mac overran, and a seed pass that failed
  still exited 0 with the rows written and the providers they name missing. Each pass now has a
  minute, and a failed seed pass exits 1 and says how to fill them.
- **A Claude Code row a page stopped is left alone for the six hours the help promises.** A
  background sign-in that met Cloudflare's bot check came back after as little as 15 minutes, at
  once when any file in `~/.secrets` changed, and after any restart of aterm. It now waits six
  hours from its last try, unless a person signs its browser in. A network move no longer ends
  that wait: macOS's Local Network answer counted as one and came soon after most launches.
- **A row whose last try met a bot check no longer promises a sign-in by itself.** `aterm harness
  accounts --cli codex` and `--cli kimi` said aterm signs it in by itself beside a ledger of tries
  that ended at that check, and so did Claude Code's `accounts sync`. They now name what a person
  runs. `accounts sync --cli agy` likewise names only `renew`, since no upkeep tries those rows and
  a browser window leaves them no route.
- **A Kimi Code CLI row with no route no longer claims aterm signs it in by itself.** Unless a
  person's browser sign-in of that row is on record, `aterm harness accounts --cli kimi` and
  `accounts sync --cli kimi` say nothing signs it in unattended and name `accounts browser`,
  which gives it a route.
- **Claude crash recovery rechecks the account before planning a new command.** A held,
  retired or unavailable managed account keeps the conversation waiting; a renewed account
  uses its current login directory. Clean exits still end normally, and an already recorded
  restart keeps its existing command.

- **A Mac another vault let go can join a new one with `aterm members join`.** On a Mac that had
  been in one vault, the vault it was let into next stayed unreadable: with the new vault's log
  handed over, every read said `membership history awaits its first durable acknowledgement`, and
  with its files handed over, the new vault's first version was refused as a rollback or a fork
  of the version this Mac held of the old one, so `aterm secrets get` read nothing. Joining
  another vault this way now starts it afresh, as `aterm secrets join` already did: its records
  count as this Mac's first history of it and its versions apply, so its secrets read as on any
  Mac that joined it, at once where the member handed its log.
  Joining the same vault again keeps what this Mac holds of it, so an older version of that vault
  does not apply and an older copy of its records put back is still refused. A member's bundle
  that names this Mac's own vault under another vault's name is refused before anything is
  written: it used to save that name first, and every vault read on this Mac failed from then on.
- **A proof lets a Mac back only into its own vault.** A Mac that waits to be let in, or that its
  vault let go, proves itself with nobody's Allow to the members it finds on the network and on
  its fleet, when its vault subscriber asks them and when `aterm members join` runs with no
  phrase. Any member that let it in by that proof handed it its own vault, and the Mac moved
  there: a member of another vault included, such as one in which this Mac had a seat before.
  Now a bundle of another vault than the one this Mac is configured for is refused before
  anything is written; a person's phrase, or `aterm secrets join`, still moves a Mac.
- **A Mac that cannot read its vault right now no longer lets in Macs on its book's word alone.**
  Fleet admission took a vault it could not read for no vault at all and fell back to the book.
  That happened while a vault sync held its lock, after an older copy of the vault was put back,
  when a records layout change was cut short or its data file was missing, and in an older aterm
  still running after an update had raised the store's capacity. A Mac the vault removed or denied
  then showed in the census, and `aterm fleet peers rm` said it might still drive this Mac. At the
  fleet listener, a member's retired node key could drive this Mac or get its book entry merged,
  and also once the records file itself went missing. Now a reader that has read a verdict before
  keeps it while the same vault stays configured, through a records file gone too, and through a
  mirror added, a host renamed or a signer rotation. Once this Mac joins another vault, or its
  vault is replaced, it keeps none: a read that fails then admits no key. Once this Mac has
  applied a version written at its vault's membership log (its locker for this Mac names the
  log's heads), it admits no key until that log's records arrive, so right after `aterm secrets
  join` of such a vault the Macs of the vault it left do not drive it on its book's word until
  then. Once they arrive, a Mac of the vault it left that the new log does not bind, one that
  vault held out included, drives this Mac again by its book entry and its drive grant where it
  holds this Mac's fleet secret, until a fleet sync moves this Mac to the new vault's fleet
  (`docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`, ATERM-KI-1105-10). While a join still waits to be let in (the version
  applied holds no locker for this Mac yet), or after a version whose locker names no heads (one
  a writer with no seat in the log published), this Mac admits by its book, as a Mac whose log
  has no genesis yet does.
  One with no earlier verdict admits no key: the listener turns away every Mac that dials, as it
  does before reading its deny list, its heartbeat and its survey facts go to no one, and
  `aterm fleet join`, `aterm fleet allow drive --from` and `aterm ctl --host` ask you to try
  again. `aterm fleet peers rm` says when it cannot tell whether a Mac still drives this one.
  Nothing is deleted because of
  this. Stored survey facts, book entries and drive grants stay, the census counts no Mac denied
  that the vault does not deny, this Mac signs no record for itself, and its census does not count
  this Mac out. A Mac with no vault, or one whose store holds no log while the version it applied
  names none, still admits by its book.
  An aterm process that first reads its log after the records file went missing no longer does:
  the history this Mac keeps of its vault's log says the vault exists, so that process admits no
  key until the records are back, as `aterm secrets sync` brings them. Records a vault write saved
  before it was cut short of acknowledging them count the safe way round: a Mac they remove, or a
  node key they retire, is turned away at once, and a key they add gets in once the next vault
  write acknowledges them.
- **Autopilot no longer sends a command a person left in the prompt.** Since Autopilot began
  sending a draft a person left unsent once their two minutes had passed, it sent any draft,
  commands included: `/clear`, `/exit`, `/logout`, `/compact`, a `!` shell line or `exit`, even
  through Claude Code's command menu. It now sends a person's draft only where the agent would
  take it as a prompt. A draft the agent would run as a command (a line starting with `/` or `!`
  in agy, Muse Code, codex-alab, Grok Build and Kimi Code; in Claude Code a `/` and a command
  name, such as `/clear`, but not a file path such as `/tmp/build.log explain`, and the bare
  `exit`, `quit`, `:q`, `:q!`, `:wq` and `:wq!`) stays exactly as it was left: nothing is typed
  over it or cleared, the harness journal notes once that the tab is waiting on it, and nothing
  is shown on screen. Send it or clear it, and Autopilot goes on. A `/usage` Autopilot finds
  standing after a restart is sent and its panel closed only where aterm's own record shows it
  typed that `/usage` in that window with no typing of a person's since; any other `/usage` is
  the person's and stays as they left it.

- **A member that lost Commons control lets Macs into ALab again.** A Mac is an ALab member for
  as long as the vault's membership log seats it, but its members desk and its automatic home-LAN
  admission also needed it to hold Commons control. Most members no longer hold that control, so
  each of them refused every Mac that asked it to join (`aterm members requests` answered `this
  Mac is not an ALab member yet`), and only the two or three Macs that still held control could
  let a new Mac in. A member the membership log seats now keeps its desk whatever Commons control
  says: a Mac on its home ALab LAN that proves itself gets in, and a Mac a person allows on it gets
  the membership log, as on any other member. Commons control itself is unchanged: such a member
  still holds none, and it hands a new Mac none.

- **A harness note reaches Messages whole.** A note an agent harness sends with `aterm ctl
  appnotice harness` was cut to 120 characters, its first 119 and an ellipsis. A note whose
  cut matched the last one recorded was not written. Each of codex-alab's continuations starts
  with the same words, so its acts collapsed into a single entry, and the note of a stuck
  background command at the end of one was lost. The entry's title is still the cut note, its
  details now hold the whole note, and a note is left out only when its whole text matches the
  last one recorded.

- **A finished workflow whose title runs onto a second row is read as finished.**
  Claude Code draws a long workflow title over two rows. Where no turn-time line followed the
  workflow's completion, its "Waiting for … dynamic workflows to finish" line was read as work for
  as long as it stood: a line the agent dropped was never restarted for, and a move onto a fallback
  model, back from one or onto another account waited the same way. A completion whose title wraps
  now counts.

- **Background work Claude Code counts only in its bottom line holds a restart in place.** Claude
  Code's bottom line counts the background work still running (`1 MCP task`, `2 background
  tasks`, `◇ 1 cloud session`). Where that count was the only place the work showed, as with turn
  durations turned off, a question or a usage limit drawn over it read as a turn at rest: a line
  the agent dropped was restarted for over the running work, and a move onto a fallback model,
  back from one or onto another account could restart over it too. Every count of work there now
  holds those restarts, as a count of shells or monitors already did. A pending Claude Code
  upgrade waits for that work too: at its last rung it restarted the agent over work only that
  count showed.

- **A shell or a monitor a turn left running is read as running wherever Claude Code shows it.**
  0.153.0 stopped a finished workflow's progress row, which Claude Code leaves drawn, hiding a
  monitor still running under it from the restart for a line the agent dropped. The row no longer
  hides such a monitor from the ask to free disk space made while it runs, or from a stalled tab's
  record of what it waits on, either. A shell and a monitor Claude Code counts together in its
  bottom line (`· 1 shell, 1 monitor`) are each read as running: where that line was the only
  place they showed, as after Claude Code compacted an idle conversation, the turn read as having
  left nothing running.

- **Text in Claude Code's side panel is no longer read as the conversation's.** Claude Code
  2.1.310 and later can draw a panel beside the conversation. Panel text beside the status line
  was read as part of that line: text saying a shell or a workflow still runs read as the agent's
  work, which holds a dropped line's restart, an ellipsis read as a turn still running, and an
  ellipsis beside a wait for workflows hid that wait. The status line is now read up to the
  panel's edge. So is Claude Code's network retry row, which beside the panel was never read as
  one: a turn the Mac slept through in that retry now gets aterm's Esc with the panel open too.
  Panel text that said `Still working` beside a row under the status line no longer reads as
  Claude Code's hint of a turn still running, which kept a finished turn from being continued.
  Nor does panel text beside a workflow's end row count that workflow as completed, which could
  read the work an earlier wait still waited for as ended. A status line too long for the space
  beside the panel, which Claude Code wraps onto a second row, is read whole: its first row alone
  could hide work still running that it names at its end. Where Claude Code compacted an idle
  conversation beside the panel, the line that ended the turn above that compaction is now read
  as it is with no panel: background agents it named as still running had read as no work, so a
  line the agent dropped could be restarted over them. A question the agent asks beside the panel
  now reads as a question: the row's padding and the panel's edge after its `?` read it as a
  finished turn, and with the panel's divider beside it an earlier row read as the agent's last
  words. The agent's last words aterm reads, the prompt a turn answered and the turn's line in
  aterm's journal no longer carry the panel's edge or its text, and a finished `/login` beside
  the panel reads as finished. A usage-limit or error notice a turn ended on beside the panel is
  read as its own words: its message took in the padding, the panel's edge and the panel's text,
  though its kind and reset read right. A hint Claude Code draws over the composer beside the
  panel (the goal mark, the critical-memory warning, usage credits in use, a login about to
  expire) is read against the panel's edge: it went unread there (the goal mark was read only
  where the panel's own text ran its row out to the window's edge), and panel text reaching that
  edge read as such a hint. A question you declined with Esc beside the panel is read as your
  stop, not as a turn that ended by itself. A row holding an emoji such as ✅ or 🚀 is read up to
  the panel's edge too: aterm counted such an emoji one column wide where it draws two, so it
  missed the edge on that row and a question there read as a finished turn. So is a row holding
  an emoji written with its variation selector (✅️), joined to others (👩‍💻), with a skin tone
  (👍🏽), a flag (🇯🇵), a keycap (1️⃣) or a letter with a combining accent: aterm counted the
  selector, the joined emoji, the skin tone, the flag's second half or the accent as columns of
  their own, where its grid draws each in the columns of the character before it, and now counts
  a row as its grid lays it out. So is a row holding an emoji or a CJK character whose
  text-style selector narrows it to one column (✅︎): aterm's grid reads the column it leaves
  blank back as a space, which aterm counted on top of the two columns the character took. The
  usage limit a cancelled auto-continue leaves beside the panel now reads the same kind, reset
  and place as with no panel: a limit notice in the panel's text, or Claude Code's word there
  that it continued by itself, read as the newest limit or as the auto-continue's end, so the
  cancel was read as leaving no limit. Its message there can still take in the notice's
  `/upgrade` line after it, as it does in a window that narrow with no panel. Where no status
  line shows over the composer, the conversation is read as ending above the rows blank up to
  the panel's edge: they read as conversation, so the report of a worker's turn ran on through
  those rows of padding and edge. Claude Code's rating cards, its drafted bug-report card, its
  transcript-share ask and a rating's thanks are read as cards beside the panel too: the
  conversation was read as running on through them, so an Esc you pressed above one read as a
  turn that ended by itself, and an open rating card read as none.

- **A restart put off while a dropped line is held is asked afresh after aterm's other steps.**
  While aterm held a line Claude Code had read and not shown, a restart it put off (for the
  agent's memory, say) kept its first ask past every other step aterm took, so asked again later
  it could be answered from that first ask's record with nothing restarted. Only the dropped
  line's own restart, a move onto a fallback model or back whose relaunch is under way or done,
  and a move onto another account ahead of a limit put off to a quiet moment (below), keep their
  ask past other steps now.

- **A restart asked in the agent an earlier one had just started is made, also within the same
  second.** 0.153.0 made a restart for Claude Code's critical-memory warning, or onto a fallback
  model and back, asked in the agent an earlier such restart had just started, restart that agent
  instead of being answered by the earlier one. Where both were first asked in the same second,
  the later one was still answered by the earlier one; it now restarts that agent too.

- **A restart asked just after a native restart landed is no longer recorded as made without
  happening.** When the harness had restarted Claude Code through aterm's native restart and was
  then asked for another restart in place of the agent it started (for Claude Code's
  critical-memory warning, or onto a fallback model and back), finishing the native restart
  answered for the new one: nothing was restarted, and the harness recorded the new restart as
  made. It now finishes the native restart, waits, and asks the new restart again.

- **A restart aterm already made is not made again when it is asked once more.** Where the
  relaunched Claude Code took longer to register than aterm waited, aterm asks for the same
  restart again later. If aterm had resumed the relaunched agent by then, that ask ended it and
  relaunched it a second time. The restart now counts as made, and nothing is ended. This does
  not change a move onto another account.

- **A move back to a model restarts Claude Code once.** aterm puts the move back off to a quiet
  moment when the relaunch it asked for has to wait (the relaunched Claude Code not yet
  registered, say), and asks it again at a later turn end. The turn ends in between asked it as a
  new move, so the relaunch the first ask had made was restarted a second time. The move now
  keeps its first ask until it is made or refused, unless another restart is asked in between. A
  move onto another account ahead of a limit put off the same way keeps its first ask too, which
  does not change how its relaunch is answered.

- **A move back to a model is still made once when aterm's harness for the tab starts again.**
  Where the harness restarted (aterm itself restarting, say) while a move back to a model was put
  off, it asked the move as a new one, and the relaunch the first ask had made could be restarted
  a second time. The harness now asks it as the same move. A move onto another account ahead of a
  limit put off the same way keeps its first ask too, which does not change how its relaunch is
  answered.

- **A move onto a fallback model restarts Claude Code once, whatever aterm does in between.**
  Where the relaunch onto the fallback had to wait (the relaunched Claude Code not yet
  registered, say), aterm asks the move again later. The steps aterm took meanwhile made that ask
  a new move, which ended the relaunched agent and relaunched it a second time, and a harness
  that started again in between did the same after its first step. A move onto a fallback model
  or back now keeps its first ask while its relaunch is under way or done, until it is made or
  refused or another restart is asked in between, also across a restart of the harness. A move
  whose ask restarted nothing (a person's hand was on the tab, say), or whose relaunch stopped
  without making it, is asked as a new move after aterm's next step, and the fallback counts from
  when the relaunch that made the move was started. A finished relaunch counts as the move made
  only for the Claude Code it started, not for one started later in the same shell. A move
  already started by an older aterm when this one takes over can still be restarted once more.

- **A failed codex-alab command is a failed step.** On a measured codex-alab build, a
  command that exits non-zero before its call returns, or one that was declined, closes its
  step `out=error` in the session log and counts in its turn's `errs=`. Every codex step used
  to read `out=ok`. A command still running when its call returns (one that outlives its
  `exec_command` yield, 10 s by default) still reads `out=ok`, since codex writes its exit
  after its step closed.

- **A recording no longer lets a chord that types text slip past it, or stops at Shift-Enter.** A
  `[key_sequences]` chord that sends text (`"alt+3" = "#"`) now counts as that typed text: an
  `aterm ctl aos attach` recording holds it for the program's own echo, or stops before
  recording it, as it does a typed key. Before, the chord's moment could reach the recording
  with the screen's next frame. Shift-Enter in a full-screen program (a composer's new line)
  types no character, so it no longer stops a recording unless keys are still waiting for
  their echo.

- **A test, a lab instance or any other private aterm no longer reaches your toolset sharing
  port.** A private aterm kept off your fleet port could still listen on or dial port 7487,
  where your aterm shares this Mac's toolset archives with your fleet: its own sharing could
  listen there beside its fleet listener (on macOS a listen on the loopback takes that address's
  connections from your aterm's), and its downloads dialed it at each fleet member and at each
  `[packages] peers` entry that names no other port. It now listens on and dials neither of your
  two ports, by the one rule your fleet port already had.

- **bash with bash-preexec (atuin, bash-it) reports each command, once.** A `.bashrc` that loads
  bash-preexec used to cost aterm's command marks: depending on the bash and bash-preexec versions,
  every line after the first was reported as `__bp_interactive_mode`, or no line was, and each prompt
  installed bash-preexec again, so hooks ran one more time per prompt. aterm now leaves bash-preexec
  in charge of the prompt and takes its marks from bash-preexec's own hook lists. Measured against
  the real 0.4.1, 0.5.0, 0.6.0 and master on bash 3.2, 5.2 and 5.3.

- **The rainbow trail no longer ends in a hard vertical cut when a frame runs out of budget.** A
  frame with more trail than it may draw (several full rows on a large window) stopped the oldest
  light dead in one column. It now thins away over six cells, as the trail's own tail does.

- **A restored agent that did not come back is said as soon as that is known.** After aterm
  reopened your tabs, the `Couldn't resume` row waited until every tab had been tried, which can
  take minutes, and quitting in that time lost it: the tab then reopened bare on the next launch
  with nothing said. Each miss now updates the one row at once, naming every tab missed so far.

- **`resizes` says who repaired a tab.** After aterm's repaint nudge gave up on a program, or a real
  resize replaced the attempt, a later repaint of the program's own was reported as `healed
  by=nudge`. It now reads `by=app`, and a repair the nudge did make still reads `by=nudge` when it
  is first seen at the next resize.

- **The installer no longer promises a toolset you turned off.** With `[packages] auto_install =
  false`, which `--no-toolchain` saves and later runs keep, or after `aterm pkg uninstall --all`
  declined it, `--dry-run` and the run itself still said the 4.4 GiB toolset would install, and that
  aterm would edit your shell profile for it. atpkg was right to install nothing; every line now says
  so and why, and the profile line only promises what will happen.

- **Uninstalling one aterm no longer sweeps what a damaged one still uses.** A scoped
  `install.sh --uninstall` took an `aterm.app` outside its scope with a lost or garbled `Info.plist`
  for another app, and removed the toolchain store and `PATH` links it runs on. Only a readable
  identifier naming another app now proves that.

- **Clicks, drags and the wheel no longer queue behind a flooding program.** A mouse or wheel event
  over a tab printing as fast as it can waited for the terminal without telling the output reader,
  so the reader kept the terminal and each report landed late. These waits now register as the
  keyboard's and the redraw's do, and `metrics percentiles` books them as `term_wait_mouse`.

- **A stopped or stalled aterm keeps its control socket and its tabs' discovery entries.** An
  aterm that stops accepting (stopped, under a debugger, or not being scheduled) fills its queue,
  and a full queue refuses a connect just as a dead socket does. Another launch used to read that
  as dead: it deleted the instance's discovery entries, so `aterm ctl` in its tabs could drive a
  different window, and a launch with the same `--control-sock` replaced its socket and token,
  leaving it running but unreachable. Each instance now holds a lock on its socket's token file
  while it serves, which the system lets go when the process ends, and that lock decides. On
  Windows a refused connect still reads as dead.

- **aterm no longer kills a shell 250 ms into its last work.** A shell still running its
  `trap ... HUP`, `zshexit` or EXIT trap was killed about 250 ms after its hang-up, so that work
  could stop halfway. It now gets about 1.5 s; only a shell that already ignored the hang-up is
  still killed at 250 ms. Quitting aterm gives all of these their time. Closing a tab or window
  does for a `trap ... HUP`, but a `zshexit` or bash EXIT trap can still be cut there, because the
  terminal closing hangs the shell up again. A program that catches the hang-up and carries on now
  holds Quit about 1.5 s.

- **A Claude Code that dies as an upgrade or restart brings it back is now said.** When the new
  process registered its conversation and exited before it came up, aterm counted the move as
  landed and left the tab at a shell with nothing said. It now takes a failed move back onto the
  build the agent ran where it can, and otherwise tells you the agent is not running.

- **A renamed tab now gets its stall warnings.** The harness judged a stalled Claude Code tab by
  the name the tab showed, so a tab you had renamed could miss its `STUCK` or `STALLED` notes and
  its exception, and a busy terminal could withdraw a warning already given and start it over. It
  now reads Claude Code's own title, and a look that gets no answer changes nothing.

- **A damaged Trust install no longer takes rustup's working `trust` toolchain with it.** When the
  store's current Trust build had been removed, or had lost a tool or its sysroot, a package pass or
  `aterm pkg repair` could delete the `lib/` and other folders of rustup's `trust` copy, leaving a
  `trustc` with no sysroot and at most a bare `No such file or directory`. rustup's copy now stays
  as it was, and the pass names the build and what brings it back: `aterm pkg install trust`, or,
  for a build that still reads as installed (one that lost only its sysroot), `aterm pkg uninstall
  trust` and then `aterm pkg install --default-set`.

- **A wait for free space now says when the disk watch is stuck.** A wait's own requests to the
  watch counted as progress, which could hide a stuck look from `aterm ctl @self await sys
  'free>=room'`. It now answers `why=watch-stalled` once a look has made no progress for two
  minutes. Long steps of a look (process scans, comparing build artifacts, removals) report their
  progress by time, so a slow look is not taken for a stuck one. A wait whose first request lost to
  a look running for a smaller request, or for none, now asks again rather than waiting for the next
  look.

- **A recording no longer logs a space it never saw echoed.** Since 0.148.0 `aterm ctl aos
  attach` holds a key typed into a program that reads keys raw until the program shows that key.
  A space typed right after an echoed word was taken as shown once the caret had moved past its
  cell and anything was printed anywhere, though a blank cell looks the same whether or not the
  program printed the space, so a program that only moved the caret (a password reader among
  them) had that space's timing recorded. A space is now recorded only once a typed character
  after it shows. A space followed by a key that types no character (Enter, Tab completion, an
  arrow) stops the recording within a second, as any key the program does not show does: over
  ssh, `cd` then a space then Tab stops it.

- **The typing glow holds still while a recording waits for a key's echo.** The 0.148.0 notes
  said it did, but the glow went dark the moment the program echoed the key, until a second key
  showed, and for a whole second after a lone key. It now stays lit at the brightness it had, on
  the caret, until the keys are recorded or the recording stops.

## [0.154.0] - 2026-11-04

### Changed

- **A codex tab's session log records its approval boxes and questions.** Each box or
  question a status sweep shows from a codex program's own report (OSC 7501) is a claimed
  step in its session log (`open p<n> approval box=other src=engine conf=claim`, `open p<n>
  question …`), one per box: two stacked boxes of one kind whose report stays `blocked`
  share one, and a box shown and answered between two sweeps, or one whose `blocked`
  coalesced past the bucket, has none. The step closes when the box goes, attributed only
  to an input that dismissed it (the harness's bound approve `out=approved by=harness`, a
  person's key or a `send` `out=passed`), else `out=passed`, and `out=gone` when the program
  or its turn went. The tab's turns and runs count these steps in `appr=` and `qs=`, and
  `brief` lists them. While one stands, `status`'s `step=` names it and `need=` and
  `need_since_ms=` its claim need (unless an observed need outranks it), and `await log
  need` answers on its open; the tab's tooltip and menu clause names it as it names a
  Claude Code box. `agent=`, survey, NEEDS YOU, banners and notifications do not move.

- **Harness versions since v0.153.0: `alab claude harness 0.11`, `alab grok harness 0.11`, `alab kimi harness 0.10`, `alab muse harness 0.10`.** Each harness's minor moves once per release in which it changed.

- **A session's queued messages can travel with several in flight.** The message bus fences
  writes after a refusal, letting the link send several posts before waiting for their answers
  while preserving order. Against a broker without that guarantee, posts still go one at a
  time. The link asks the broker for the fence, so the broker serves an older aterm's link as it
  always did. The link rechecks that aterm is alive after waiting, before sending another post.

### Added

- **Codex tabs hear about a stuck background command.** When an updated codex-alab
  supervises a tab, the continuation, done check or Land prompt it types can end with
  aterm's measured note that one of the agent's background commands has made no progress,
  once per stall, as Claude Code tabs already do. Settings ▸ Harness counts these notes
  under codex-alab. `[harness] facts = false` turns them off for both.

- **Compare membership records across machines.** `aterm db commons-status` reports
  `complete_inventory_sha256`, a fingerprint of the complete signed membership records.
  Matching fingerprints mean the observed record sets match, even if the records arrived in
  different orders. Waiting records are counted separately; a matching history does not by
  itself prove current connectivity or access to shared tables.

- **`aterm ctl survey` counts a codex-alab tab's terminals.** A codex-alab that reports them in
  its session record shows `bg=<n>` where every codex tab said `bg=-`. The number is the
  terminals its own footer and `/ps` count for the thread it shows, a command a running tool
  call is still waiting on included, so it is not only background work. The text form shows
  ` bg=2` as it does for Claude Code's background shells. The count is codex-alab's own claim,
  read while its proven claim stands (or, read only, while a released claim's process runs on
  in front), and it goes when codex-alab leaves the front. aterm reads it again two seconds
  after the tab's screen last moved, so a terminal that ends while the tab rests leaves the
  count within about two seconds. An older codex-alab still says `bg=-`.

### Fixed

- **A step that a report, `aterm ai` or a refused launch names can be taken.** Where Codex's own
  login moved to another account, every surface now gives the same next step, and it is one that
  works here: `aterm harness accounts sync --cli codex` where a sync moves the login to the row
  that holds it, a sign-in of the row where it does not, and a word about why (the row's directory
  holds another account's login, keeps its logins in the keyring, or holds other files). `aterm ai
  login codex` follows the row that account is on, and no longer offers a sign-in that it would
  only refuse. A build that cannot read a row's login is told to update, not to sign in. Sign-in
  steps no longer name a command with a wrong flag.
- **A sync that added rows and then refused to move the default login says no row moved.** It said
  nothing was written, though the new rows were in the file. A sync with nothing to read now counts
  and wakes on a move it did make, and `--json` names the row that took the login.
- **A Codex row a person renamed keeps following the default login.** A renamed row, or the row on
  the default login under a new name, took the wrong directory when discovery listed the account
  under its old label.
- **A Codex session at a weekly limit hands off from the default login, and only to a row with
  room.** A session on this Mac's own login never handed off; a fresh read that finds a row low now
  keeps that row out and is recorded; and a later wall that names no reset keeps the one a read
  gave. `codex exec` is told at once when no handoff is coming, where it used to wait.
- **A fabric bridge whose aterm has quit sends no more of its sessions' posts.** When aterm quit,
  or gave way to an updated aterm, while its bridge was still sending posts its sessions had
  queued, the old bridge could send one more of them after aterm was gone, while the new aterm's
  bridge waited to take over the node; and if the connection to the broker dropped at that
  moment too, the new aterm's bridge could send that post itself. The old bridge now looks again
  just before each send and sends nothing once aterm is gone, and a post it never sent is no
  longer left for the new bridge to send.

- **A codex-alab that crashed or was restarted comes back on an account that can serve it.**
  Its relaunch used to type its old line on the Codex account it ran on, even when that
  account had reached its limit or was signed out. It now moves to the account a new Codex
  worker would start on, as a Codex tab aterm reopens after it restarts already did, and both
  read the old account's usage first when their reading is over five minutes old, so a limit
  met since then counts. `[harness] accounts = "off"` keeps the old line.

- **A Kimi Code account at its limit is passed over.** When `aterm harness accounts refresh
  --cli kimi` reads a full window on Kimi's `/usage` panel, its five-hour or its monthly one,
  that account is held until the window resets, so a launch picks another.

- **A busy Mac no longer keeps `aterm fleet` waiting on its own background job.** The job that
  answers other Macs ran every thread at a low priority macOS would not let any of them leave, so
  while it updated this Mac's list of fleet members a loaded Mac could stall it for seconds, and
  an `aterm fleet` command waiting on that list gave up after 2 seconds. Its own threads still run
  at the same low priority, and the one thread updating the list now runs at normal priority until
  it is done; a few small helper processes it starts (its Bonjour advert) now run at normal
  priority. The job's settings are rewritten on the next sync.

- **`aterm fleet leave` with `CI` set no longer deletes your node job's file and leaves the job
  running.** Where `CI` was set and `HOME` named your own home by any path (a self-hosted runner
  on a fleet Mac), a leave deleted `~/Library/LaunchAgents/systems.alab.aterm-node.plist` without
  stopping the job, which ran on, and said it removed the node job. There it now keeps the file
  and says it stopped no job; `aterm node off` says the same, and `aterm node on` changes nothing
  and says why.

- **After a restart, Cruise and Land read the agent's quick reply to the restart prompt at
  once.** When Claude Code answered aterm's restart prompt within a second, before aterm saw it
  working, aterm waited 30 seconds for the agent to take the prompt before it read the reply.
  It now reads the reply as soon as the screen shows the restart prompt answered. The 30-second
  wait remains for a reply the screen never shows, and for a restart prompt in the same words as
  the one the agent answered last, which the screen cannot tell apart.

- **System State's own Local Network step now goes on once you answer its alert, even where no
  ALab vault can hear the answer.** When System State's Local Network step asked macOS "Allow
  aterm to find devices on local networks?", its re-probe of the network let System State go on
  to Full Disk Access once it heard your answer: Don't Allow, or Allow on a network where an
  ALab vault answered. An Allow it could not hear (no vault on your network) held System State
  until you had been at the Mac 30 seconds since your first touch after the question, and every
  other answer held it until the re-probe heard it. On macOS 26 and 27, aterm now also ends the
  hold on an Allow the re-probe cannot hear, and on any answer before the re-probe hears it: it
  watches, from a background thread, which windows UserNotificationCenter (the process that
  draws that alert) has, reading only window owners and numbers and whether each is on screen,
  so it needs no Screen Recording permission. Once the alert it saw come is gone and
  UserNotificationCenter has no window left, on screen or off, at a read made while you are at
  the Mac, System State goes on at that read. The watch reads every quarter second for the first
  half minute after the question, so an alert you answer at once is still seen. A read made while
  you are away never counts: after that first half minute the watch reads every 5 seconds while
  you are away, and a quarter second after each read once you are back. When it sees no alert
  come (macOS asked aterm before, or the alert came and went between two reads) or another
  UserNotificationCenter window is still up, aterm still waits your 30 seconds at the Mac. The
  question macOS asks at aterm's first local-network use outside System State's step is the next
  entry's. aterm never presses the alert's buttons.

- **System State also goes on once you answer the Local Network question a first local-network
  use asked in its step's place.** After you press Turn On macOS Access…, aterm's first uses of
  the local network (the Commons service, System State's vault look or join, Tab Control's sweep,
  the ALab network browse, the fleet's reads) wait for System State's Local Network step to ask
  macOS. The step asks only while System State is in front, so once you have been at the Mac a
  minute without it, the next such use goes at a quiet moment and macOS asks "Allow aterm to find
  devices on local networks?" itself. aterm then held its next macOS question or System Settings
  page, Full Disk Access's among them, however soon you answered: until you had been at the Mac 30
  seconds with that question, or for 30 seconds from the use where the Commons service asked. On
  macOS 26 and 27 the window now watches that question as it watches the step's own: the use waits
  up to a second for the watch's first look before it goes (past that, or where the window list
  cannot be read, it goes unwatched), and once the alert the watch saw come is gone and
  UserNotificationCenter has no window left, at a read made while you are at the Mac, the hold
  ends. On any macOS the hold also ends as soon as System State's local-network check hears your
  answer (Don't Allow, or Allow where an ALab vault answers), once its Local Network step has read
  that question as its own. Where the Commons service asked, the hold now counts your 30 seconds
  at the Mac, as the other uses' hold does, rather than 30 seconds of the clock. The question the
  Commons service asks under its own gate for another reason (where System State takes no Local
  Network step, as before you press Turn On macOS Access…, where aterm's records say macOS asked
  or answered aterm before, or where an earlier aterm used the local network on this Mac) is not
  watched: it still holds aterm's next question for 30 seconds from that use.

- **A full ALab membership history no longer keeps new Macs out.** A vault's membership
  history held at most 4,096 records of every kind, and ALab's had reached that limit. So no
  Mac on the home network could be admitted, no Mac removed, and no key rotated. It now holds
  16,384 records: up to 4,096 that admit and remove Macs, and 12,288 for the keys, secrets and
  names it hands out. Macs on your home network are admitted again once they and the Macs
  already in the vault run this release.
  A Mac on an older release is refused before it could receive a history longer than 4,096
  records, rather than given part of one, and needs this release to follow the vault again.

## [0.153.0] - 2026-11-04

### Changed

- **Harness versions since v0.152.0: `alab claude harness 0.10`, `alab grok harness 0.10`, `alab kimi harness 0.9`.** Each harness's minor moves once per release in which it changed.

### Fixed

- **A restart onto another model or account no longer ends the agent's own background work.**
  When Claude Code moves to a fallback model, back to its own at the reset, or onto another of
  your accounts, the harness restarts it in place; that restart now waits, as the restart for a
  line the agent dropped does, while the screen shows a background agent or workflow of the
  agent's still running. The restart for Claude Code's critical-memory warning still goes at once.
  A finished workflow's progress row, which Claude Code leaves drawn, no longer holds a dropped
  line's restart for as long as it stands, nor hides a monitor still running under it; and a
  "Waiting for 1 dynamic workflow" line no longer counts as work once that workflow's completion is
  shown under it, where no turn-time line followed.

- **A line the agent dropped is no longer typed twice after a restart that was put off.** When
  the harness restarts Claude Code in place for a line it read and never showed, and that restart
  was put off before it began (another sweep busy, or work still on the screen), asking it again
  could take an earlier line's finished restart for its own: nothing was restarted, and the line
  was typed again to the agent that still held it. Each line's restart now knows its own record.
  The same holds for a restart for Claude Code's critical-memory warning, or onto a fallback model
  and back: asked in the agent an earlier such restart had just started, it restarts that agent
  instead of being answered by the earlier one.

- **One account listed twice beside this machine's own login is merged or named.** A sync that
  would list the default login's account under a row of its own now folds that row into the
  default login's row, keeping the label you gave it, where the other row holds nothing that would
  be lost; otherwise the sync and the report say the two rows are one account (`one account: ...`).
  Either way, `at a weekly limit:` no longer offers to move a session from one to the other. The
  report names the sync that folds them only where a source is there to read and the sync would.

- **A Codex default login moved to another account and back no longer strands a Mac.** A row takes
  back a login directory it left when that directory's login still names its address, so moving
  the default login there and back keeps syncing; before, every sync after the second move refused,
  and launches and reviews on that row with it. A directory holding anything else still refuses,
  now with the step that clears it, and a sync that writes rows before such a refusal prints the
  receipt of what it wrote. After such a move, the handoff `at a weekly limit:` promises also runs:
  it refused, retrying, where a row had left the login another row now holds.

- **The accounts report and `accounts sync` say when the default Codex login names another account
  than its row.** The report lists that row under `not next:` and the sync's receipt and `--json`
  (`default_login_names`, always; `default_login_moved_off`, `default_login_refused`) say what it
  names; they said `login: ok` and nothing else. A sync with no source to read now follows that
  login to the row of its address too, and succeeds, instead of stopping at `nothing to read`.

- **`aterm secrets create` keeps the rows of a Claude Code roster you made.** Finding the accounts
  on this Mac relabelled every row from the machine's name and minted two more rows where a login
  named another address than its row. It now keeps each row's label, directory and order, the rows'
  sequence in the file and a row you renamed, adds only an account no row holds, and records such a
  login as a wrong-account login, as a renewal does.

- **A lab sync says what it changed on rows it kept.** A first lab sync clears every row's `held_by`
  and sets each row's order from the lab, as it did, and now names each hold cleared and order
  changed in its receipt and in `holds_changed` and `orders_changed` in `--json`. An account the lab
  prefers here whose label a row of another account holds is no longer left out silently: the
  receipt and `label_clashes` in `--json` name the label and the account. Claude Code's lab sync says
  `N the lab prefers here` and no longer names a fleet file it did not write; its `fleet_roster` is
  null in `--json`.

- **The accounts report and `accounts use` name the step that works.** "Renew by" now means one date
  on every surface, the day a login is forecast to end; the start of the window it comes due in is
  `due_from` in the report's `--json`. A row in shared custody names its `shared-renew` in the
  report, as `accounts use` does. With Codex CLI not installed, both lead with that, rather than
  with a build's fault or a sign-in aterm would run by itself. A row a sign-in stopped names a
  renewal carrying the row's `--cli`.

- **`aterm ai` says more of a refused roster, and its review follows rotation off.** The doctor
  prints a refused roster's fix whether or not you asked for that CLI, and says its reason whole
  rather than cut at 120 characters. An `aterm ai review` of Claude Code under `[harness] accounts =
  "off"` starts on the login a new session starts on, not the pool's pick. `accounts sync` with
  nothing to read names `ai-pool.toml` among the files it looked for.

- **`--admit now` no longer refuses work because another admission was deciding at that
  moment.** A run started with `--admit now` (`targo --unverified verify --admit now`,
  `ATERM_ADMIT=now`, the lab's and the Trust lane's `--admit now`) skips the wait for room, but
  it still takes its turn at the capacity ledger's lock, which each admission holds only while
  it decides. When another admission held that lock, it used to be refused at once: a verify
  run, which admits several stages at the same moment, reported the stages that met the lock as
  NOT RUN with "pid N holds the ledger's lock", N being verify's own pid, a build was refused, and
  a Trust lane check started without its claim. It now waits for its turn, as `--admit wait`
  does, and is admitted as soon as the lock is free; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM still ends that wait, and
  the Trust lane's other checks run on meanwhile. A `targo` build started inside another build
  whose lock it cannot prove its own, which makes one admission look, was refused as a wait
  that "could cycle" when that look met another admission deciding; it now waits its turn too.

- **A fabric state folder on a disk other than your startup disk now also lets go of the
  sessions a restart of your Mac ended.** The first start after a restart removes the small
  files and the message reservations those sessions left, but it skipped a state folder off
  the startup disk (a home folder on an external disk, or on Linux a `/home` on its own
  filesystem): there the record of each connection named no restart, so a leftover
  reservation kept its session's names counted against the node's budget on the bus, restart
  after restart. That record now names the restart on every disk, and the first start after a
  restart removes them there too. A record an older aterm wrote there still names none, so
  that folder is cleared at the restart after this aterm first connects. The bridge still
  skips its disk write at a connection only on the startup disk.

- **System State's own Local Network step now goes on once you answer its alert, even where no
  ALab vault can hear the answer.** When System State's Local Network step asked macOS "Allow
  aterm to find devices on local networks?", its re-probe of the network let System State go on
  to Full Disk Access once it heard your answer: Don't Allow, or Allow on a network where an
  ALab vault answered. An Allow it could not hear (no vault on your network) held System State
