  into a tab (the agent gave the same reply twice with no work) and you switch it to
  Land, your switch counts as your turn: Land types its instruction once, opened by
  one sentence that quotes where the agent stopped and says you switched the tab to
  Land, so it lands what it can and names in a `NEEDS YOU:` line only what a person
  must give. Settings ▸ Harness's state line says so until the answer comes
  (`status land_asked=switch`). If the agent answers the same again, the tab stops
  again with no second prompt, and switching away and back over that same answer
  asks nothing more. Only your own switch counts (the chip, the Autopilot menu or a
  Settings ▸ Harness row): one by `aterm ctl meta set`, a Land timer or the harness
  types nothing, nor does a switch to Cruise. Under Cruise, where your switch would
  ask, the stop's words now say it types again at your turn, your switch to Land,
  or once the agent works.

- **Autopilot Land lands on the agent's own answer, not on how its report is worded.**
  Land used to decide that a task had landed by reading the agent's `Nothing left:`
  report for words that mean work is left. On reports nobody had read, that reading
  landed about one in six that named a leftover, and nudged about two in five honest
  ones at every free moment. Now, when a report defends that nothing is left and `git`
  finds nothing left to push, Land types one short land check (`⤓ land check`): what
  counts as not landed (a change not on the remote main branch; a check skipped, flaky,
  failing or not run; work deferred, partial, or on another branch or repository;
  something only a person can give) and to reply with only `LANDED` when none of it
  applies. `LANDED` lands the task, and takes down a need the report named, since the
  check counts a need as not landed; where `git` by then finds work left, it lands nothing
  and the need stays, and a check's turn you stopped lands nothing. A reply of only
  `NEEDS YOU:` lines puts the need on the menu bar, and Land types nothing more until
  someone else's turn, except where the need is a go-ahead for the agent's own reversible
  work, which Land gives as it does after any reply. Any other
  reply is the agent's own list of what is left: Land's next prompt quotes it (`You said
  this is left: “…”`), and the same list given again holds, quoted. When a sentence of
  the report reads as open work, the check quotes it first, so the agent looks at it.
  Land types one check per defense; another needs real work (two minutes of it, not a
  quick `git status`) or a new reply in between, and a check the agent never took leaves
  its defense owed one. The check's own turn is not counted as the task's work, so it
  never makes a short task read as ended. A worker spawned under Land is told that its
  work ends at the check's `LANDED`.
  Claude Code, agy and Muse Code get the check from aterm; codex-alab, which lands by its
  own check, is served its text as `land_check_text=` by `aterm ctl harness policy`. A
  landed task's words (the chip's `✓ landed` title and the `Autopilot landed` record) and
  its journal's `RECEIPT` line say that the land check was answered, read from the one fact
  the receipt keeps; a landing with no receipt saying so (one an older build noted, before
  the check) says only that the agent said nothing is left.
- **On a Retina display the palette, the Overview and the build badge keep their
  1× look.** Their corner radius cap, drop shadow, border, row insets and selection
  ring, and the badge's type floor and corner cap, are now points, so at 2× they are
  the 1× card at twice the pixels instead of thinner and squarer. The palette's filter
  field keeps its lines as before, clear of `type to filter`. At 1× every shape is
  drawn exactly as before. A rounded border or ring is now drawn by weighing
  only its sides' line and its corners, not a band as deep as its corner radius, so a
  card redraws faster than before at both scales, its larger 2× corners included.
- **System State and Settings wear your Mac's accent colour.** Their switches are drawn as
  macOS draws them: on in the accent colour you chose in System Settings ▸ Appearance (blue
  where you chose none), off in macOS's grey, with a white knob, and they follow a change of
  accent at once. On System State the working line's spinner and band wear it too, and green
  means done and nothing else. What needs you is ringed in macOS's orange and what failed in
  its red, with no tinted card behind them; in light mode the lines sit on white cards over a
  grey page; a line's opener points right and turns down when the line is open, with no grey
  band behind an open line, and every mark stays readable under the pointer; and a card's
  titles line up with the lines'. The lockup's rainbow is the brand's dim trail again, rising
  toward the caret, and starts only once the caret has left the words. Under High Contrast and
  Serious Mode the lockup shows one progress, a bar that fills to its end.

- **A helper a window ties to itself gets a chance to finish.** When a window dies, killed
  outright or crashed included, the helpers it tied to itself (the consent observer's `log
  stream`, the Settings machine read, the harness screen's `dns-sd` browse, the fleet
  advertiser's `dns-sd`, the capped `aterm` runs and the login shell's PATH probe) now get
  `SIGTERM` first instead of `SIGKILL`. On macOS aterm checks that each is still the same process
  before every signal, and sends `SIGKILL` only to one still there 10 seconds later; a helper
  macOS's program check is still holding gets no signal. On Linux one that ignores `SIGTERM` runs
  on. On macOS the process that watches each helper now runs on its own, outside the helper's
  process group, so a kill of that group or a hangup of its terminal no longer reaches it.

- **Settings ▸ Harness calls them Forced continues.** In WHAT THE HARNESS DID, the row
  under `Kept going` that read `past “done”` reads `Forced continues  3 today · 3 in 7
  days`, and one quiet line under it says what it counts: "The agent said it was done;
  the harness had it check its work and keep going." VoiceOver reads the line right
  after the row. No other row's words change.

- **`aterm ctl instances` and `aterm doctor` no longer print a `kill <pid>` for an instance
  whose launcher exited.** They point at `aterm ctl sys left scope=aterm`, which lists it with
  its proof and, where the proof holds, the token `aterm ctl end` takes: a pid typed later can
  name another process by then. Doctor's `instances:` row names a link broker launchd adopted
  that is not the one serving the fabric's socket as unsupervised, and when a dead verify run's
  record proves it that run's, says to end it with `aterm ctl end <token>`.
- **System State is redesigned.** The setup screen leads with a headline that says where
  setup stands and the aterm lockup, whose rainbow ribbon and kitty move along as steps
  finish (`❯ aterm · ALab` on an ALab Mac, `❯ aterm` elsewhere). Anything that needs you
  sits in one card pinned under it (the permission walk's current page, macOS's local
  network question, the Command Line Tools password, the Allow from another ALab Mac, a code
  to approve on an admin Mac with Copy Command, a step that failed with what aterm does
  next), and nothing else asks. Five lines (Mac settings, Permissions, Secrets & identity,
  Developer, Sign out of Messages & FaceTime) each have one switch and say what is true now
  and, where setup changes it, now → wanted; open one to see its rows. On a Mac outside
  ALab the sign-outs' line says aterm leaves Messages and FaceTime alone, and its switch
  cannot be turned on. Joining ALab waits quietly for 30 seconds
  before asking you to press Allow on another Mac, in the window and in `aterm init`. The
  village scene stays in Settings.

- **System State says where each step stands, in its own words.** A step aterm stopped in
  twice, or that ran over an hour, reads Waiting on its rows with why, and the headline names
  it; one that ran over an hour is checked again by itself, and one aterm stopped in twice
  waits for Check again, so it cannot stop aterm again on its own; a step resumed after aterm
  stopped says so on its rows while it goes. A Mac asking to join ALab's vault takes the phrase a member shows in System State's
  own field, with Join, and never sends you to a terminal; a vault try that
  aterm repeats by itself waits calmly. A refused GitHub token says only a vault admin can
  save a new one, with Copy Command for the line they run. The Command Line Tools row says
  what needs them, and its button reads Install Command Line Tools… where it fits. A note is
  never cut mid-sentence or said twice, and a settled System State page no longer wakes aterm
  every second.
- **System State asks nothing aterm can do itself.** Changes to make start by themselves
  ("Setting up your Mac"), with no Set up now to press; a step that did not take, a Check
  that failed and a row it could not confirm are tried again after 1, 2, 4, 8, then every
  15 minutes. Set up now stays only at the foot of the page after you press Stop. Before
  anything is read the page claims no count and no progress, each line shows what it
  covers, and the footer waits for the first readings; Restore shows once aterm has saved
  preferences to put back. The headline counts in numerals ("1 thing needs you",
  "1 step failed"), the progress counts only what is done, a step that failed is said once,
  by its card item, and a Mac in no vault never reads its secrets as done. The permission walk is one card item with what comes next under its
  button, and keeps its page while its helper panel is up. Joining ALab's quiet 30 seconds
  run whether or not the page is shown, and a relaunch picks them up where they were.
  VoiceOver hears the headline first, a live region that never repeats it or a count and
  names what the card asks, each line's name and state once, and each card reason once;
  Return in the vault's address or password field joins, as Join does.
- **Closing System State never holds setup.** Closing its tab before setup started used to
  leave setup for the next launch, with `Setup has not started` and Set up now; setup now goes
  on in the same launch, behind your tab. When aterm learns this Mac is an ALab Mac after its
  own plan has run, it adds the ALab profile's groups at once, with nothing to answer.
- **Muse Code sessions aterm starts run Muse Wonder Full at xhigh, with contributor
  mode off.** A worker (`spawn agent=muse`) that names no `model=`, a fresh relaunch and
  an `aterm ai review` run `muse-wonder-full-1.0` at `xhigh`; every relaunch — and the
  resume line aterm tells you to type — carries `--contributor-mode off`, replacing the
  launch's own word on it. A named `model=` still wins, and a resumed session keeps the
  model and effort it already runs.
- **Harness versions since v0.147.0: `alab codex harness 0.7`, `alab claude harness 0.7`, `alab agy harness 0.7`, `alab grok harness 0.7`, `alab kimi harness 0.7`, `alab muse harness 0.7`.** Each harness's minor moves once per release in which it changed.
- **A go-ahead aterm answers no longer goes on your menu bar.** A `NEEDS YOU:` line that only
  asks you to say go for the agent's own build, test, commit, or push or merge of its own branch
  now stays off the menu bar, the window border and the tab's hover, with no notification, once
  Cruise or Land answers it with your standing go-ahead, or Land with its instruction to land
  the work, which the go-ahead follows. It used to stay there after the agent went on. Your
  other `NEEDS YOU` lines still show. The line does show when aterm does not
  answer it: answers off, within an hour of your typing in the tab, beside an irreversible ask,
  or once the agent has refused three times or for an hour, together with that alert. At a
  pause of the agent's own background work the go-ahead now goes within 15 minutes of aterm's
  last line to it, as it does when the agent stops, not up to an hour later.
- **Cruise's done check says it too.** When an agent says it is done, Cruise's check now tells it,
  as Cruise's usual prompt does, that its own reversible work needs no one's go-ahead and is never
  a `NEEDS YOU` line, and that a hold you gave still stands. Within an hour of your typing in the
  tab it leaves that sentence out, and so does the check typed after `aterm harness upgrade`
  restarts an agent that had said it was done. When the check also carries the reminder to
  approve nothing irreversible and the acknowledgment of `NEEDS YOU` lines, and the repository
  holds unlanded work, there is not always room for both: the request to land the agent's own
  work then replaces that sentence.
- **`aterm init` sets up what this Mac's scope takes, and keeps what you turned off.** On an
  ALab Mac (one the ALab vault has let in) it sets up everything, the clones and the Messages
  and FaceTime sign-outs included, and `--no-profile`, `--no-sign-out` and `--no-clone` leave
  one out; on any other Mac it sets up aterm's permissions, the secrets vault and Rust in
  Spotlight, and `--profile`, `--sign-out` and `--clone` add one. A group you turned to Leave
  as is in System State, or every group while you stopped setup there, stays as it is for
  `aterm init` and `aterm doctor --apply`; each says so in one line and names how to set it
  up anyway. `aterm doctor --check` reads such a group as off, and the ALab profile on a Mac
  that is not ALab's as not in scope, never as a failure.
- **`aterm init` joins ALab's open vault without a question,** at the console and from an
  agent's tab, a script or an SSH shell alike, and shows no pairing code away from the
  console. In the console's own session it first waits for macOS's Local Network answer,
  which System State asks for. GitHub waiting for the vault now reads deferred and exits 0:
  the vault's sync clones your repositories once its token lands, with no second
  `aterm init`.
- **The converge pass keeps your choices.** While System State leaves the vault off or your
  Stop holds setup, no Sync row acts on the vault and the sync process is not reinstalled;
  `sync.identity` keeps an `[ai]` or `[fleet] machine` name you set, and honours
  `[identity] name`.
- **System State starts setup at once, whether or not you are at your Mac.** Setup used to wait
  for a key, click or trackpad touch within the last minute before it began. Now the vault,
  Rust in Spotlight, the workstation preferences and repositories start the moment aterm opens.
  Only the steps that put something in front of you wait for you: the permission pages, the
  debugger question, the Command Line Tools password and the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs.
  They pause while the screen is locked or you are away, and go on when you come back.
- **An update no longer holds back setup that had not started.** The aterm an update started
  used to leave a setup that had not begun waiting for the next launch, with a note saying so.
  Now it starts that setup at once, as every launch does.
- **A Mac an older aterm set up with permissions alone now gets the vault and Rust in
  Spotlight.** Every Mac now syncs the vault and keeps Rust out of Spotlight. A setup an older
  aterm began with only aterm's permissions gains those two by itself, and System State says
  so in one line. A setup you shaped, stopped, turned off or restored stays as you left it.
- **`aterm ctl aos attach` keeps recording through keys a program echoes for itself.** A
  recording used to stop at the first key typed into a program that reads keys raw (a shell
  without aterm's integration, a REPL, vim's insert mode), because such a key could be a
  password. Now the key is held until the program shows that very key on screen, visibly and
  where it was typed, and is recorded at that moment. A key that is not shown, shown as `*` or
  `•`, hidden, shown only by aterm's own predicted echo, or typed where its character already
  shows still stops the recording within a second, and nothing of it is recorded. While keys
  wait for their echo the typing glow holds still: up to a second per key, and through a whole
  burst typed faster than the link echoes. Keys relayed by ssh, mosh or tmux should behave the
  same, but that is not yet measured.
- **A setting you changed yourself is no longer counted as a change to make.** System State's
  headline and Set up now leave out a row that reads Changed by you.

### Fixed

- **Asking to join no longer puts anything on screen.** A Mac that asks to join ALab
  and that nothing let in is now one quiet entry in the exceptions list ("New Mac calling
  itself m20"), with Allow (or, on an admin Mac, Approve) beside it, instead of a banner
  that waits for you. Four or more asking Macs are one entry. The name a device chose is
  shown cleaned and cut, so a made-up name cannot hide its entry, and two devices with
  one name are told as two. An entry follows its Mac: it goes about half an hour after
  the Mac stops asking (not a day later), as soon as any member or admin lets the Mac in,
  and when this Mac moves to another network. A Mac the vault let go that asks again
  shows the same way on an admin Mac, with Approve, for you to compare its code.

- **The ALab vault no longer lets in a device just because it shares a network with an
  admin.** The open ALab vault let any device with a private address in by itself, so a
  phone hotspot, a café, a hotel or a travel router that an admin's Mac joined counted as
  "the LAN", and a stranger's laptop there could get every shared secret and the fleet code.
  Now a new Mac joins by itself only on your home ALab LAN: the Ethernet or Wi-Fi network
  the Mac's internet traffic takes (never a VPN, a virtual machine's network or cellular),
  where at least three fleet members proved themselves to the vault server's Mac in the
  last ten minutes, behind the same router, never a phone hotspot or a network macOS
  calls expensive, and with the approving admin reaching that vault server on that network
  too. A new Mac that asks a member Mac on that home network joins the same way, with no
  entry filed: the member passes its ask on to the vault, but only from another Mac on its
  own home network, never from a hotspot, a virtual machine's network or a second network it
  also reaches. Anywhere else it waits for an Allow on a member. The vault now marks itself open in a
  way older aterms read as closed, so an admin still on an older aterm lets nothing in by
  the old rule once any updated admin has run; a new Mac on the home network then waits for
  an updated admin.

- **Your Macs already in ALab get back into the vault by themselves when their keys
  change.** A Mac whose vault key changed (a reinstall, a reset vault folder, a restore)
  had to ask to join again like a stranger and wait for someone to press Allow. Now it
  proves to a member that it is the same Mac, and the member lets it back in under its old
  name, with nobody pressing anything; nothing pops up. A new Mac on your home network
  still joins with nobody pressing Allow, and on a hotspot or café network no new Mac is
  admitted. A Mac you removed stays out: removing any Mac now changes the fleet code too
  (before, only `--stolen` did), so its old copy proves nothing, and the member first reads
  the vault's newest records so it cannot miss a removal. A Mac takes its old seat back only
  once that seat has been quiet for a day and no other Mac answers with its identity, so a
  copied identity (Migration Assistant, a restore, a cloned disk) never takes a seat from a
  Mac that still runs, and two copies never trade one seat: it moves by itself at most once a
  day and four times in all, then a person decides. The whole vault lets at most eight Macs
  in by proof or Allow a day. Seats wait for a person until every Mac the fleet heard from
  in the last two weeks runs this aterm or later, because an older one would leave the
  returned Mac out of the vault's newer keys. A Mac whose old seat no record ties to its
  fleet identity (a founding Mac that never published it) comes back under a new name, and
  only while it holds the current fleet code.

- **Rust build caches keep their cleanup ownership through interrupted setup.** On macOS,
  atpkg stages and records a new explicit target before the compiler can use it. A managed
  build that names an existing unregistered target now stops with a reason and a fresh-target
  remedy, rather than quietly losing automatic cleanup. Existing targets keep their contents.

- **aCaffeine keeps this Mac awake after a restart.** A window's launch started aCaffeine but
  never turned its Enable at Startup on, so after a restart nothing kept this Mac awake until
  a window opened. Every ordinary aterm window, at launch and every five minutes, and the
  vault subscriber's converge pass now turn the installed app's Enable at Startup on (in
  `/Applications` or `~/Applications`) and start the mug where none runs, each unless you
  turned it off.

- **An aterm launch keeps your aCaffeine off.** A window you launch and the converge pass no
  longer turn aCaffeine back on, or its Enable at Startup, once you turned it off (an update's
  relaunch already kept the mode as saved), and an off you chose lasts through a restart too;
  with Enable at Startup off by your choice, the vault subscriber's pass at login leaves
  aCaffeine to a window.

- **aCaffeine's timed spans end.** Activate for 1, 8 or 24 hours turns aCaffeine off at the
  end of the span, so the Mac may sleep again: the checked row reads `… 52 min left` and the
  tooltip `keeping this Mac awake for 52 min more`, with no `then forever`. An ended span had
  gone back to keeping the Mac awake forever.

- **A quit from outside aCaffeine's menu no longer turns it off for good.** A SIGTERM from
  another program or Activity Monitor's Quit stops the mug and keeps its mode, so the next
  window, converge pass or login starts it again; only a click on the mug, Quit in the menu,
  `off`, `quit` and the end of a span turn it off.

- **aCaffeine starts again when it could not keep the Mac awake.** A mug that could not
  start ended for good; one stopped by something that can clear up (a full disk) now exits
  for launchd to start it again about a minute later, from the copy of the app it already
  made, and one whose reason lasts (a refused menu bar, a lock path that is a directory)
  ends without a start a minute, for the next window or pass to try again. One whose
  keep-awake activity macOS refused turned itself off; it now keeps your choice, shows its
  tooltip saying so and asks macOS again every minute. A trouble that lasts ten minutes is
  an exceptions entry, cleared once it is gone even across a relaunch, and `aterm doctor`'s
  new `awake:` row says whether macOS actually holds aCaffeine's assertion.

- **An old Caffeine login item whose aterm cannot retire it is removed.** A window removed a
  login item left under aCaffeine's old name, `aterm caffeine`, only when its aterm was gone
  or was the window's own, so one whose aterm is a 0.145.0 still installed (a second install,
  say), whose run only fails, started it every 10 seconds all session. Every ordinary window,
  and the vault subscriber's pass when it starts the mug, now also removes an item whose
  aterm answers no to `aterm help caffeine`; one whose aterm answers yes, 0.144.0 or before,
  is that aterm's own mug and stays. ATERM-KI-1027-7 names the case left: after a restart
  that started the mug at login, such an item fails every 10 seconds until a window opens.

- **Every build-cache removal the disk ledger says has started now says how it ended.** The
  sweep writes its intent (`removing`) before it moves a build directory or tool aside. When the
  move was then refused (a flag, an ACL entry or a folder mode set after the check, or a volume
  mounted there), or a process came to use the entry first, nothing closed that row, and the
  ledger showed a removal in flight that never started, every pass. Each such entry is now
  returned and journalled as `kept`, with 0 bytes and the refusal's one-word reason in `error`
  (`PermissionDenied`, `CrossesDevices`, `Stopped`), and the next pass judges it again. One
  stopped after it was already moved aside is kept under its stage's name (`Staged`), and the
  next pass finishes that stage. A kept entry is not counted as freed. `aterm harness disk` gives
  `sweep_in_flight`, the intents no outcome followed. `aterm pkg machine cache clean` and a run's
  disk relief name what was kept. On Linux, a build directory that is immutable or append-only
  (`chattr +i`, `+a`) is now neither planned nor asked for; and off macOS, neither is one in a
  sticky folder when neither the folder nor the build directory is yours.

- **An asked restart or signal no longer reads as a crash, and pages nothing.** `aterm ctl
  restart`, the tab's restart pill and `aterm ctl signal term|kill|int|quit|hup` now write
  `act word=restart` (or `word=signal`) with `by=` the asker into the session log just before
  they signal. The program's and agent's runs they end close `out=signal by=<asker>`, and so
  does a command that ends nonzero, keeping its `code=` (one that exits 0 stays `ok`), even
  when the signal reaches a command the session log has yet to see running. Before, the
  command closed `out=fail code=143`, the session read `need=failure` for about a second, and
  `aterm link notify --on need` paged a failure for every self-restart. An end more than 35
  seconds after the ask (or after the restart's `SIGKILL`, when one follows), or of another
  program, still reads as that program's own. `signal cont` and `signal tstp` ask for no end.
- **A program's or agent's run that held the front until its command ended now takes that
  command's end.** A clean `/exit` closed the agent's run `out=unknown`, and a killed program
  read the same. Now the run reads `ok` when its command succeeded, `signal` when aterm was
  asked to end it, and `gone` when its command failed (only the command carries `code=` and
  the one `failure`, so a harness relaunch still lifts it). When the run closed before its
  command's end was read (the shell's prompt came back, the program could no longer be named,
  or the screen stopped showing the agent), it closes `unknown` as before and an `amend` with
  its end follows at the command's end, or `signal` at once when aterm was asked to end it.

- **A restarted agent starts working again.** A restart of a Claude Code, agy or Muse Code under
  Autopilot `cruise` or `land` now ends with one prompt, typed at the relaunched agent's first
  rest: it says the agent was restarted, that work it ran inside its own process (subagents,
  workflows, background shells) ended with it, and to read its handoff and carry on; codex-alab
  carries itself on. An agent that restarted itself from a running tool call used to sit waiting
  for a person: Claude Code restores the cut call as `Interrupted · What should Claude do
  instead?`, and the harness read that as a question and as a person's Esc. The prompt also waits
  behind a draft in the composer where it used to give up, however long the draft stands, comes
  under `land` as under `cruise`, comes ahead of Autopilot's own prompts, and is never typed under
  `off`, after a person's own message (a key or a click is not one), or into work Land finished
  or the agent defended as landed. The relaunch is seen at rest as soon as it is, where a restored
  row cost it 15 seconds.
- **An agy turn end is read once, however often a person types into its composer, pastes into it
  or clears it.** The harness named agy's points by rows that reached its composer and footer, so
  each draft a read found, typed or cleared, journaled a new point (`EVENT idle`) and was decided
  again, where Claude Code and Muse Code read none. A point is now the turn above the program's own
  composer on agy and Kimi Code, at any pane width; at a limit wall agy's point still moves when
  the model its footer names changes, so a `/model` switch there is weighed at once. A draft
  cleared under a reply agy keeps giving now starts that reply's count again, as on Claude Code. A
  line whose Enter a person's key blocked now gets that Enter alone once their grace is out, never
  a second write; with their words joined to it, it is sent as neither's and stands badged as
  aterm's own until they send or clear it. A decision due as a frame drawn for one read shows is
  taken at the next look instead of dropped. `docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` ATERM-KI-1101-3 and
  ATERM-KI-1101-5 say what is left.
- **A person's sign-in waits for one already running.** An automatic sign-in can hold this Mac's
  sign-in lock for up to 15 minutes, and `accounts renew`, `login`, `browser` and `shared-renew`
  gave up after 2 seconds with `held`, so on a Mac that kept retrying a stopped sign-in they often
  did nothing. At your own terminal they now say so and wait, about 16 minutes at most, then go by
  what that sign-in left, and stop if it already renewed the row. An agent or a script is still
  refused at once.
- **A Mac that logs out, restarts or shuts down frees the AI accounts it was using.** Each Mac
  claims the shared Claude Code accounts it uses, and a claim on a Mac's home account kept that
  account from every other Mac for up to a day after the Mac went off. Now, once a log out,
  restart or shut down goes ahead, aterm gives up every claim on that Mac and hands the change to
  the other Macs before it goes, so they can use those accounts. The window does this, also when
  a shut-down command or (on Linux) the system ends it, or the background job does when no window
  is open. A log out that you or aterm's quit dialog cancel keeps the claims, so the sessions that
  go on running keep their accounts. The note a Mac makes as it goes to sleep, which lets its
  accounts go two hours later, now reaches the other Macs before it sleeps too; before, it
  reached them only if they happened to fetch it before the network went down. Each waits at
  most 5 seconds for another Mac to take the change; where none does in time, the accounts stay
  held as before. After a restart, an account another Mac took in the meantime stays with that
  Mac, and the restarted Mac's sessions move to another account. A Mac that loses power still
  holds its home account until its claim lapses, up to a day, or until it starts again and its
  sessions have been idle two hours; one that sleeps after leaving the network holds it until the
  claim lapses, since the other Macs cannot tell it from one still working elsewhere.

- **The vault's log says why it moved a job onto this aterm.** When aterm moved the vault's
  server, approver or subscriber off another copy of aterm, or installed a missing subscriber, its
  log said only that the job moved. It now names why: an ALab server older than 0.146 (which
  neither pulls from the other servers nor hands the shared name on), an ALab approver older than
  0.146 (which let every Mac in), an older copy of aterm (ALab's jobs follow the installed
  release), a copy that cannot read the admin locker, or a subscriber job that was missing.

- **Macs keep answering each other as the fleet grows.** On a busy Mac with dozens of
  members, `aterm fleet peers` showed peers as `connected, but no fleet handshake within
  3.0s` (and the Mac itself as taking a connection but finishing no handshake), because the
  node job took one connection at a time and decrypted the vault's roster for each one before
  reading a byte from it, and again two or three times for each one it served. Every other
  connection waited behind that check, and one whose peer had already given up cost as much
  as a live one, so the job fell behind and every peer it did reach had already given up.
  Each connection is now checked on its own, so a slow check no longer holds up the ones
  behind it. The job checks the deny list only for a peer that has proved the fleet secret,
  and reads it again only when one of the vault files it comes from changes, so a removed Mac
  is still refused at once. A connect that proves nothing no longer makes the node touch the
  vault at all.

- **A sign-in Cloudflare stops now says so.** When Cloudflare's bot check on claude.ai
  stopped an automatic Claude sign-in, `accounts` said only "the sign-in did not finish",
  and the next line said aterm would sign the row in by itself. The row now reads `blocked`,
  names the bot check, and `sign-in needed:` gives the step to take: run
  `aterm harness accounts renew <label>` in a terminal on that Mac, which now opens the row's
  own browser profile, or your default browser if it names none, instead of meeting the same
  check again. `aterm ai` names that step too, and an agent's `aterm ai login` leaves the row
  to you, as an agent's `accounts renew` now leaves any row it would need a browser window for.
- **`accounts --help` says what a label is.** A label such as `m2-3` is one more account on
  Mac `m2`, not a Mac.
- **A sign-in Cloudflare stopped waits out its backoff.** A fleet's peers coming and going
  counted as this Mac's network moving, about 110 times an hour on 40 Macs, so a sign-in that
  failed ran again seconds later. A Commons beacon now counts only after every peer went quiet,
  or from a peer never heard before, and a heard peer no longer ends the wait of a row
  Cloudflare stopped; a real network change still does.
- **`aterm link notify --on need` pages a need whose raising record the bus lost.** A need
  that rose while a follower watched its session, but whose own record never reached the
  follower (a record the bus dropped, or one the bridge could not publish), was named only by
  the session's next snapshot, and a need only a snapshot named never paged, so nobody was
  told. Such a need now pages once, at the first whole snapshot that names it with nothing
  lost after it, when the follower read the session whole before the need was raised, even
  while an older need of the same word stands (a second failed command whose close was lost).
  When that page's command fails, or any need's page is owed, it pages again at the session's
  next record that still shows the need, in the same run or after a restart, however that
  record knows it. A need that stood before the follower started still never pages, nor does
  one only a short snapshot names until a whole one does. The closing line's `standing=`
  counts the records this run found already standing, and `--help` now says so: a `--once`
  run that reads no new record says `standing=0` whatever stands.

- **The harness types only into an agent the kernel confirms; a program merely named like one is
  observed.** A tab's program named `claude` (or `agy`, `muse`) was driven on its name alone, so
  a link, a copy, an `exec -a claude` of any program got the harness's keys, answers, turns,
  `/compact` and `/login`. Now every input the harness sends goes through one gate that asks
  what the kernel says of the running image, compared by file identity: its vendor's install
  (Claude Code's versions directory, a registered atpkg build, a codex-alab package), its
  vendor's Developer ID signature, held to its certificate (macOS), or, in a development
  build, a lab stand-in. Anything else is observed: its boxes are read, logged and raised for
  you, nothing is typed into it, and the harness does not restart it.
  `ctl status` says which (`supervisor_act=on|observe|-`), the session log marks each change
  (`meta field=supervisor … why=confirmed|unconfirmed`), and a later confirmation, such as an
  exec into the real install, lifts it. An npm install that runs `node … cli.js` is observed
  for now: nothing confirms such a script by identity yet.

- (developer tool) **`lab swarm partition` checks a fleet larger than one heartbeat round,
  from every Mac.** It ran 5 fleet Macs, every one registered at the minter, and surveyed only
  from a1 and b1, so it would have passed with either of F17's review fixes undone (every Mac
  merging what it hears, and heartbeats that rotate past the same three members). It now runs
  seven fleet Macs, three of them joined at a member other than the minter (a4 at a2, b4 at b2,
  and b3 at b1 during the cut). Before the cut, and again after the heal, it reads whom each
  Mac's heartbeat reached from that Mac's own answer stamps, before any Mac surveys (a survey
  stamps who answered it too), and marks each member whose last dial missed. After the heal it
  also surveys from every Mac and drives every Mac from every other. The judge wants every
  heartbeat to reach every member, every survey to hear every Mac and every drive admitted. The
  heartbeats back at the minter come from the same stamps. The lane used to read them from the
  minter's book, where a member's entry moves whenever the minter reads another member's book,
  so "whole again" passed on heartbeats that had never reached the minter. `--minter-away`
  stops a1's aterm instance (its fleet listener and heartbeat) before the heal, so whatever
  spreads after it spreads with no minter. `--label WORD` names a record without replacing
  another. Every lab Mac registers from 127.0.0.1, so the instances raise the four members a
  book records from one address through a new debug-only seam,
  `ATERM_DEBUG_FLEET_JOINED_PER_ADDRESS`, which a release build never reads. With the old
  issuer-only merge put back, the lane failed 5 of its 19 checks of the time, and 24 of 42
  drives were admitted. With the old fixed three-member heartbeat order put back, it fails 3 of
  22; the one main passes is the reach before the cut, where each Mac reached only three of its
  five others. Built from main, it fails 2 of 22, both from one defect the design doc keeps
  open: after a cut heals, a Mac's heartbeat does not reach a member whose dial missed during
  the cut while three other members answer.

- **Account rotation reads each CLI's own switches.** Switching Claude Code off
  (`[harness.claude] enabled = false`) no longer stops the window's account bookkeeping for
  Grok Build and Kimi Code sessions, and a worker's launch and a Codex tab's cold relaunch or
  resume line read the switches the window does: rotation is off at launch where the harness or
  that CLI is switched off, not only under `[harness] accounts = "off"`. Automatic sign-ins stop
  for the CLI you switch off (`[harness.claude]` or `[harness.codex]` `enabled = false`) and
  only for it, and `aterm ai` names that switch as the reason.

- **A Claude Code worker spawned from a tab at its limit starts on another account.** It starts
  where the window would move that tab next: onto the account you pinned, or the active one
  while it is fresh, and past a limit onto the account a move would take, instead of on the same
  limit. Where the window would keep the tab (an account still proving itself, too many moves
  in the last hour, a tab short of its limit under `[harness] accounts = "wall"`), on a home of
  its own, or with rotation off, the worker keeps the tab's own login.

- **One conflicting row in the account sheet no longer stops every account's sync.** Rows that
  give one address two machines, slots, sign-in flows or regions, or a member row beside one
  that disqualifies it, add that address to no pool (a Mac that already lists it keeps its row
  as it is where one of those rows names that Mac or none; where every one names another Mac,
  the row drops, as for one row naming another Mac), the rest of the sheet is read, and
  `aterm harness accounts sync` (also when it syncs nothing), `aterm init`, the window's log and
  its digest name the CLI and the sheet rows (never the address) until they agree. A sheet that
  is gone or refused is not logged as rows that agree.

- **A Claude Code account move that cannot be judged says why in the log.** When the window
  has no accounts' state folder, cannot read a session's process login (or the process changed
  while it was read), or cannot read the accounts' state, it logs which once, instead of keeping
  the session's account without a word.

- **ALab's network is now fixed by its genesis.** m22 signed ALab's founding membership
  record (Genesis v2, listing the vault's 40 machines) with the released 0.146.0, and this
  build checks ALab's genesis by that record's digest alone: any other genesis for ALab is
  refused, including one signed with the vault's own key.

- **A lost login's need always says how to sign in again.** When an agent's login was gone, the
  quiet need aterm raised quoted the program's error first and then how to sign in again, and the
  need keeps only the first 120 characters of that text, and no more than its 200 bytes leave
  beside the error it names: agy's 401 (Google's whole message), Muse Code's rejected key and any
  long error of Claude Code's pushed the sign-in step (quit agy and run it again, or give it a
  valid Gemini API key; Muse Code's own remedy; `/login`) off the end. On every program the
  sign-in step now comes first wherever the error would push it off, with retries off and over a
  draft too; a short error still reads first.

- **Two Macs whose membership records are both full stop re-sending records the other
  refuses.** A Mac keeps at most 4,096 membership records. Two Macs that each reached that
  bound with records the other lacks (after a key flooded its own branch of the log, or a long
  partition) offered each other 16 records a round over Commons repair, in up to three rounds a
  pass, and each refused every one, so about 48 records crossed each way again on every pass,
  every few seconds, for good. A Mac now stops offering a peer records once the peer has
  refused all it could offer: one round from a peer that holds 4,096 records, otherwise every
  record the peer lacks, offered once each. It offers one round again a minute later, and at
  once when either Mac's records change. A peer that refused a round only because its disk was
  busy, or that set aside records whose parents it lacked, is still offered the rest straight
  away.

- **A session on an AI account this Mac cannot claim leaves it at its next turn end, and its tab
  says why it waits.** When a Mac could not record its account claims (its Commons control
  history split in two, or it is not a Commons Writer) and its own claim on a Claude Code account
  that is not one of its home accounts had lapsed, its session kept using that account, though
  another Mac could start on it unseen. Under `[harness] accounts = "wall"` it stayed outright;
  under `"early"` it stayed whenever none of its home accounts was free. Now, under `"early"` and
  `"wall"`, it moves at its turn end to one of its home accounts, or one it still holds a claim
  on. With none free, or with its account pinned (`aterm harness accounts use`), it waits: the
  harness types nothing into it and asks again every few minutes, until the Mac can record its
  claims again, one of those accounts opens or the pin is lifted. With no home account free, that
  wait lasts until someone restores the Mac's Commons access. The tab's account line shows the
  wait: `Waiting`, then why the session cannot keep its account (this Mac cannot record account
  claims, or another Mac's claim holds it and until when), naming a pin that keeps it there, and
  when it asks again. A launch already kept off such an account. `accounts = "off"` still moves
  nothing.

- **An agy session at a subscription quota wall (`Individual quota reached`) no longer gets
  spammed with continuation prompts, and rotates even after `/model` or past a 32 MiB
  transcript.** When agy stopped at a quota wall while a background task ran, after `/model`
  switched models inside the session, or once `transcript.jsonl` grew past 32 MiB, the harness's
  quota reset check could overwrite the wall's `Resets in …` notice with a past timestamp and
  type `continue` into the wall, while live rotation waited on `log-unproved` or read only the
  launch's `--model`. aterm now keeps a wall's future reset unless the session's pool was first
  observed blocked and then refilled, reads the active model from the agy footer when `/model`
  changed pools, skips notice cards over `Error ID:` rows, and streams `transcript.jsonl` up to
  1 GiB without loading the file into memory.

- **An agy session whose model calls fail in words aterm does not know is tried again, not
  left idle.** The window stops typing to an agent that gives the same reply twice. A turn
  where agy says nothing (a failed model call aterm cannot name yet) counted as that, so a
  session stayed idle until someone typed, two days in one case. Now the window waits an hour
  and types again, then two hours, doubling up to eight. A reply with words is held as before.

- **A person's Esc in Claude Code no longer reads as the agent asking.** After a declined
  approval box or an interrupted reply, Claude Code writes `Interrupted · What should Claude do
  instead?` and returns to its prompt. aterm read that line as the agent asking in prose, so the
  tab showed a question that needed a decision and the session log closed the turn as `asked`.
  The vendor's question to the person is no longer read as the agent's, so the turn reads as the
  person's, as an interrupted turn. An approval box the person stopped the turn under now closes
  `out=declined` in the session log, where it closed `out=passed`.

- **`aterm fabric brief` shows a session that died without its close reaching the bus as
  closed.** After an aterm crash, the dead session's close never reached the bus, so the brief
  showed its run open forever. The brief now shows it closed (`out=gone`, every open run, turn
  and step closed, need `exited`), still marked partial, once a successor's restore names it
  after its aterm died, or a later incarnation of its node retires its row; it works the close
  out at each read and publishes nothing. `aterm link notify --on need` pages its exit
  (`exited`, detail `gone`) once, at that restore; the retired row alone pages nothing. A
  restore after a clean quit's relaunch, or a reopened tab's, says nothing died: the quit
  withdrew its sessions, and a reopened tab's session pages its own exit.

- **A Mac where Claude Code cannot start no longer collects a stuck disk worker every six hours.**
  When the disk filled, aterm started a background Claude Code tab to free space. On a Mac where
  Claude Code stopped before its composer (a sign-in or first-run screen), that tab stayed open
  there, and six hours later the next one did the same, so one Mac had six such tabs. aterm now
  starts no other disk worker while one it started earlier still runs or stands stopped, whether
  at a sign-in screen or before Claude Code could start: the one tab keeps asking for a person,
  and if the disk is still filling, the disk alert comes to you as it does whenever no worker can
  start. Once that tab finishes, exits, is closed or has its Autopilot switched Off, the next can
  start.

- **A vault server reads at most two large vault versions from other servers at once.** On each
  check a vault server asks every other server it hears of on the network (up to 16) for a
  newer vault version, all at once, and it read each answer whole, up to 16 MiB. A device on
  the network that advertised 16 servers and answered each with 16 MiB could make it hold about
  256 MiB at once on each check. A server now reads each answer only up to 256 KiB at first,
  and asks again for a longer one and reads it whole at most two at a time, without the extra
  copy it made of each answer. It still asks every server it hears of on each check; with
  many large answers that check can take longer.

- **A second login's vault server on the same Mac no longer restarts every 10 seconds.** When
  two logins on one Mac are both ALab members, each runs a vault server on the same network
  port. The second found the port taken by the first, exited, and macOS started it again every
  10 seconds for good, adding to its log each time. It now waits, tries the port again every
  minute and serves once the port is free, while the first login's server serves the same
  vault to both. It still stops when asked and when an update replaces its program.

- **The Mac serving the vault as `alab-secrets.local` takes the name again after macOS's
  network naming service restarts.** When mDNSResponder restarted (after a crash or an OS
  update), every network advertisement on the Mac ended, the vault server's `alab-secrets`
  among them, and the server took that for the name lost to another device: it stopped
  advertising the name, and nothing answered at `alab-secrets.local` until some Mac took it
  over 90 to 120 seconds later. New Macs and older clients, which reach the vault only there,
  could not reach it in that time. The server now looks whether another device answers to the
  name, and when none does it advertises the name again on its next check, about 30 seconds
  later; it still leaves the name to a device that answers.

- **The Mac serving the vault as `alab-secrets.local` keeps the name when its server restarts.**
  When the vault server that held the `alab-secrets` name stopped for an update (its program
  replaced) or a move of its background job, the server started in its place took the name
  again only after 90 seconds in which no vault answered there. New Macs and older clients,
  which reach the vault only at `alab-secrets.local`, could not reach it for 90 to 120 seconds
  on each such restart. A server that stops while it holds the name now notes so in its store,
  and the server started in its place takes the name back at once when its first check comes
  within 45 seconds of the stop, the Mac has not slept since, and it holds a vault version at
  least as new. A server that crashed, or one whose first check came later than that, still
  waits the 90 seconds.

- **A tab running a program says what it runs.** While a command's program ran long enough for
  aterm to see it (`sleep 9`, a build), the tab's tooltip and menu lost their `now:` line; a
  shell builtin kept it. They now say `now: sleep · 40s`, naming the program as they name the
  command.

- **`aterm ctl brief` counts a shell session's commands.** A session of shell commands briefed
  only its session line and marks and ended `more=-`, as if nothing was left out, while no
  command it ran had a line or a count. It now prints `runs <n> · fail <k>`, the closed commands
  and how many failed (under a shell aterm does not integrate, such as `/bin/sh`, each program it
  ran), and once a tight budget sheds that line `more=` names `runs:<n>`. `help brief` now names
  all four count lines, and says that a budget below the one-line floor gets the floor, with
  `used=` over the budget.

- **An `aterm.toml` that aterm makes is no longer refused on a Linux with umask 002.**
  aterm reads `aterm.toml` only when no other user can write it. On Ubuntu and other
  systems that give each user a group of their own, new files are group-writable by
  default, so the first Open aterm.toml, the first Settings change and
  `aterm --window --write-config` each made a file that aterm then refused to read ("mode
  664 lets other users write it"). aterm now makes that file without the group and other
  write bits, whatever the umask. A file you make yourself is still held to the same rule,
  and the refusal still says `chmod 600`.
- **A spare shell no longer outlives an aterm that was killed.** aterm keeps a shell
  started ahead for your next tab. When aterm was force-quit or crashed, that waiting shell
  could stay behind for good, holding nothing anyone could see. The waiting shell now reads
  its go-ahead from a channel aterm hands it, and exits as soon as aterm is gone, whether it
  was still waiting to start, running your startup files, or about to show its first prompt.
  A zsh or bash tab closes that channel as it opens, so nothing you run there inherits it.
  A program your startup files start in a shell started ahead, and a fish tab, keep a copy
  of its read end, which carries nothing more once the tab is open.

- **`sys jobs` says when its job readings were taken.** A reading that does not look at jobs
  again (a pull, or one inside the jobs cadence) carries the last look's rows and findings, but
  the header named the new reading's time, so a held program's `for_ms` stood still under a
  fresh `as_of=` while `status program_check=` grew. The header's `as_of=` and `age_ms=` (and
  `--json`'s `as_of`) now name the look the rows come from.

- **`sys jobs` is as fresh as it says.** Its freshness was judged by the reading that carried
  the job rows, not by the look they came from, so with no window open a reply could carry a
  look 30 s old without saying `state=stale`, and `fresh=0` never got a newer look. `fresh=`
  (2 s by default) now judges the look itself: an older one makes the reply ask the jobs engine
  to look again, and a look that does not come in time is answered `state=stale`.

- **`sys left` and `privacy` tell a held program's wait in full.** Each read the age of a
  program macOS's program check holds as of the last jobs look, under the time of a newer
  reading, so `check_ms=`, `program_check_oldest_ms=` and `privacy`'s `program_check=` fell up
  to 30 s short of `status program_check=`. They now count from the look the age came from.

- **A job reads its next wait as soon as macOS's program check lets its program go.** The
  first reading after the hold ended kept `wait=program-check` for one more reading: with no
  window open, about 30 s more after a hold seen at two readings or more, and, after a hold
  seen at one reading alone, until something else read the job. It now shows the wait the
  program is in at that reading.

- **A job that polled before its program was held reads as waiting at once.** A job whose
  polling or CPU use had been read just before its program waited at macOS's program check, or
  for Rosetta, read `polling`, `busy` or `thrashing` for a reading or two more, counting toward
  `quiet`. It now reads as waiting from the reading that names the hold, and none of that earlier
  polling carries into what the program does once it starts.

- **An x86_64 program Rosetta is translating is work in line, not a quiet job.** A tool call
  whose only program had not started because Rosetta was still translating it read `quiet`
  beside its own `translating` finding. It now reads `wait=translating`, fine however long,
  never quiet or stuck, as a program macOS's program check holds does, and `sys jobs` no longer
  also names it `probably-program-check`, a guess meant for programs that started.

- **What stays of a build-cache stage is named with its reason, and forecast before a pass.**
  `aterm pkg machine cache` now says, of a stage an earlier pass left, which entries its
  removal will leave and why (another user's, on another volume, one whose ACL denies reading
  its attributes, or a stage that will not open; for a retired registered cache, a stage that
  holds what its removal was never given, or a payload whose `Cargo.toml` stops its removal),
  read by the rules of the removal that takes it and changing nothing. Unread folder contents
  make the forecast incomplete; a forecast that reaches its entry limit also says how far it
  was read (`not forecast past 100000 entries`). After a
  pass, the disk relief line, `aterm pkg machine cache clean` and the window's disk ledger name
  each entry that stayed as the removal counted it, with the reason it gave: an entry deeper
  than the system's path limit is named itself, not the folder above it, and nothing inside a
  folder the removal never entered is named. For an entry whose ACL denies reading its
  attributes, which the removal never acts on, the words name the `chmod -N <path>` that
  clears it.

- **Cache cleanup retains an inaccessible folder when it cannot safely change it without
  following links.** An unsupported `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW` on any Unix remains a refusal;
  cleanup never retries that chmod with following enabled. This includes Linux without
  `/proc` or older glibc where the flag is unavailable. Another process of the same user can
  replace a name even inside an owner-only folder, so a raced link must never change a target
  outside the stage. The retained entry is counted and named with its refusal reason.

- aterm-dirfd's Trust floor is re-based onto the store's default prover (20565c325: 97/259),
  so `ship trust run -p aterm-dirfd` no longer reports a ratchet regression against a count the
  old prover (321aaeda7) recorded.

- **`aterm fabric tail --bodies` shows a presence row's fields.** A record with no `text=`, such
  as a presence row, tailed as `len=0` with an empty body. Its body is now its whole first line,
  and `len` its bytes; nothing past a record's first line is ever shown, so a terminal input
  record's keystrokes stay hidden.

- **`aterm link notify` says a standing condition once.** A follower printed its wait for a
  durable record on every record, and `could not subscribe` on every retry while the broker was
  gone. It now says the wait once per broker log, a hold past its size cap once until the
  broker says the held records are durable, an outage once with how often it retries, each
  other error once more however the errors alternate, and once how many tries failed when it
  subscribes again.

- **An amend with nothing the bus may carry no longer crosses as an empty record.** A Claude
  Code turn's transcript match crossed the bus as a turn amend with no field, which a reader
  folds as nothing. It now stays in the local log and takes no place in the mirror's count.

- **A broker that nothing supervises says how to start it again when its build is replaced.**
  Its exit line said a supervisor would start the new build even when none runs it; it now gives
  the command to run, as its exit for a damaged log already did.

- **Land's rest on a need survives a restart.** An agent that answered Land's land check with
  only `NEEDS YOU:` lines rests until the person answers. A loop that followed (an update, a
  crash restore, a re-hosted tab) forgot that rest and nudged the agent at the same screen. It
  now reads the reply again as the check's answer, so the rest, the listed answer and the
  defenses the check already audited carry over: no defense is checked twice.

- **A need stands until the agent takes it back.** A one-word `LANDED` no longer takes down a
  `NEEDS YOU:` the agent did not retract. An earlier need in the check's turn that the agent
  later cleared with `NEEDS YOU: nothing` no longer stops the landing or stays up, whether the
  retraction came in a later message or a later paragraph. The agent's last word on its needs
  wins, and a go-ahead or a blocked reply no longer answers a need the agent took back.

- **Only the person's own switch lifts a hold.** An Off set by `aterm ctl`, a timer or a lead
  (not `autopilot_by=human:…`) no longer forgets the replies that held, or Land's rest on a need,
  so Off and then Land over a held or resting tab types nothing and the need stays on the menu
  bar. The person's own Land after such an Off is their turn, as their switch from Cruise is.
  The switch's one ask stays spent across a restart, and a land check typed again after
  `/compact` keeps the defense it audits.

- **The land check's turn is never counted as the task's work.** A permission box, its approval,
  a dropped phase read or a wall's resume inside the check's turn no longer counts the rest of the
  turn as work, so a quick task gets no false end mark or cheer. A busy run already open when the
  check's act arrives is left out from its start, and a go-ahead aterm types past the check
  counts as work again.

- **A need beside a landing says the work waits on you.** Where Land rests on a `NEEDS YOU:`
  line, or landed beside one, the menu bar, the border and the Harness page now say `waits on
  you` after the need, not `carrying on`: nothing is typed until you answer.

- **A codex-alab worker's task file no longer promises a land check.** The fact line names the
  land check only for Claude Code, agy and Muse Code, which aterm's loop types it into.

- **`checked=` is aterm's alone.** A hand `task mark … checked=` from the owner socket is
  refused. The help, the manual and the supervise skill now say a missing `checked=` means aterm
  has no record of checking that landing, in words the help and the manual take from one source,
  and `aterm ctl help status` lists `land_asked=`.

- **A long session's log keeps which vendor turn each turn is.** A turn's `vref=` (the
  transcript's message the turn answers) and `cont=` (the earlier turn it continues) come in an
  `amend` record once the transcript is read. A busy session's log could evict that amend, and a
  seamless update or a later journal segment could leave it out, while keeping the turn's
  `open`, so `aterm ctl log` showed the turn unnamed while the session's state named it. The
  amend now goes with its turn's `open`, as a command's program and an agent's model already
  did: it is kept while the turn is open, and evicted, carried and restated in a journal segment
  together with the open after that. When one turn is named more than once, only the name the
  session's state keeps goes with the open; the older ones are evicted first, as detail.

- **A Claude Code session with a running `/goal` no longer reads as resting, and an upgrade
  no longer restarts the agent over work Claude Code says is still pending.** Where Claude
  Code draws its `◎ /goal active` mark at the end of another row (`✔ Update installed ·
  Restart to update◎ /goal active (1d)`, or the right end of its footer), aterm missed the
  goal, so a turn waiting on its own workflows under that goal published `idle` and cruise
  could type into the running goal. The mark now counts wherever Claude Code draws it as its
  row's last item. A pending Claude Code upgrade also took only the first busy sign on the
  screen: a workflow's progress row under the footer could hide a `Waiting for …` that Claude
  Code carried above a later message, or a done row's `… still running`, and at its last rung
  the upgrade could restart the agent over that work. It now waits for that work whatever
  else the screen shows. A done row drawn beside Claude Code's side panel (2.1.310 and later)
  was read past the panel's edge, so its `2 agents still running` went unseen; it is now read
  up to that edge. A workflow shown only by its progress row under the footer still holds
  nothing, because Claude Code leaves that row drawn after the workflow ends.

- **A system message over a prompt the API never answered is now waited out, not answered.**
  When the API or the connection failed before the model answered (Claude Code's transcript
  ending on your prompt or a tool's result, under `API Error: Can't reach the API server — check
  your internet or DNS (ENOTFOUND)`; an overload's 529 takes the same rule, though no screen
  has shown Claude Code leaving one out of its transcript yet), the harness read the turn end as
  the model's and could type Cruise's or Land's prompt into the error screen. It now waits as it
  does at any outage (`waiting: API overload`, `waiting: connection error`) and resumes once
  when it clears. A tool's own output that quotes such an error is still the tool's. An outage
  that names no clearing is still tried on its back-off (2 minutes doubling to 60), one
  `may have cleared` line a rung, into the outage if it still stands: about 2, 6, 14, 30 and 62
  minutes in, then hourly (13 lines over a 9-hour outage).
  The resume is not typed in a dark wake on a Mac really sleeping (the lid closed, the Mac awake
  only for seconds in each minute): it waits, deciding again on a step that doubles from 20 s to
  about 5 minutes, and is typed in the next full wake, once the Mac has spent most of its last few
  minutes awake, or at its first decision past an hour. A Mac whose wakes are too short to decide
  anything goes on waiting for a full wake. A Mac kept running with its lid closed, which never
  reads a full wake but stays mostly awake, types it as an awake Mac does. An answer that says it
  needs you (`NEEDS YOU:`) after running tools is now
  kept, so the same words again are held quietly instead of drawing another prompt; a new count
  beside the same need is work done, and the prompts go on. Muse Code's `model failed after N
  attempts: …` is read as the API error it is (a transport error as the connection's), so Muse
  Code waits there too. On 2026-10-25 the lid was closed and Claude Code met `ENOTFOUND` only in
  dark wakes: no prompt went into the screen under either rule as the day ran; on a Mac awake
  the old rule would have typed two, the new one none, and the one resume moves from a dark
  wake the Mac slept 26 s into to the evening's full wake.

- **The harness no longer opens your browser to sign Claude Code in.** At an expired login it
  still types `/login`, but it leaves the method picker to you (one quiet `NEEDS YOU:` line) and
  never presses the pick that opens the browser sign-in, which brought a browser window forward
  over your work.

- **A Claude Code turn that ends while its own background work runs now counts as ended.**
  When Claude Code stops with background agents, dynamic workflows or shells it started
  still running (`Waiting for 3 dynamic workflows to finish` over a composer that takes your
  next message), aterm read the session as busy for as long as that work ran: `agent=busy`
  for 19 hours on one Mac, and its session log kept one turn open for 70 hours, folding every
  later turn into it. The session now reads `idle` there (`question` when its last words ask
  one), and each such turn, and each turn a finished task wakes it for, closes in the session
  log. A live turn over the same work still reads busy, an agents panel holding the cursor
  keeps the session busy, and `aterm drive phase` prints the turn's rest after the busy
  reason. A pending Claude Code upgrade never restarts the agent over workflows or background
  agents its screen shows running, at any rung; it waits for a turn end with none running.
- (developer) **`aterm-lab autopilot-captures` measures a hovered title beside the agent's
  other chips, and leaves another run's lab up.** Its `the hovered title cut short` finding
  read 0 cells for every title, because it counted from the chip's own end while the rule draws
  the title past the block's other chips (`─ auto` beside Claude Code's); it now counts from
  where the title begins, so a lean fit shows as a finding and a whole title as whole. A
  capture run whose lab name (harness, look and scale) is held by a lab whose aterm still runs
  (another run, of another `LAB_ATERM`) now refuses with exit 3 instead of taking that lab down
  under it; a lab left by a run that died is still taken down.

- **On Linux, a command that prints nothing is named.** With no process watch (Linux, and a
  Mac session whose watch could not open), `sleep 2`, a quiet `python3` or `perl -e 'sleep 1'`
  and a linked program showed no detail in `aterm ctl status`, `survey` or the session log:
  aterm saw a program only when its output did. aterm now looks at which program holds the
  terminal a couple of milliseconds after each batch of output, and then at doubling intervals
  up to once a second while a command runs, so a command that holds the terminal for a moment
  is named, and the program an alias or a function runs stands in for a word that is no
  program (`sleep` for a function that sleeps). Still not named there: a command that ends
  within a few milliseconds or prints without pausing, unless it printed while it held the
  terminal and the word you typed is its own program. On a Mac with no watch, `ls` is named,
  an alias of `ls` is not, `/usr/bin/true` shows nothing, and `env X=1 ls` shows the wrapper,
  `env`. On Linux, a command as quick as `ls`, `date` or `env X=1 ls` (a millisecond or two)
  shows nothing, while `seq 1 200000`, which prints for longer, is named. Also not named:
  a stopped or background job you bring back with `%1` or `%vim`, which starts no program
  (`fg` shows `fg`); pwsh's commands, which run in pwsh's own process group; and a program
  aterm may not read (`sudo`).

- **`aterm harness usage` no longer shows a bare `?` for Claude Code's 5-hour window.**
  Claude Code 2.1.316 reports a window only while Anthropic's replies carry it, and on some
  logins they carry only the week. aterm now fills the 5-hour figure from what it already
  holds for that account: another session on the same login, or the cached `/usage`. When
  nothing holds it, the line reads `opus –/5h · 1%/7d · …`, and the next line says why: `5h –:
  not reported: Claude Code reports this login's week but no 5-hour window …`. `--json` adds
  `missing: {"five_hour": "not-reported"}`. `aterm harness accounts stats` says `not
  reported` for the 5-hour window where it used to say `no reading yet`, and so does Settings ▸
  Lab's CLAUDE ACCOUNTS card (`Not reported; Claude Code's usage reading of <time> carried the
  week but no 5-hour window …`) where it said `Unknown; no retained quota reading`. The
  accounts ledger's usage-tap row reads `tap: session – (not reported by Claude Code) week 1%`
  instead of `session ?%` (a `/usage` panel's row, `– (not on the panel)`), and no longer
  books a closed window's old figure as current. Where the two windows come from different
  sources, the line names each one's age (`5h tap 5s · 7d store 5d`), so a week held for days
  never looks fresh; the reason line says which of the accounts store and the `/usage` cache
  aterm read; the cache is taken only for a session on the default login's own account; and
  `resets` reads `–` where neither window has a figure. No other usage output shows a bare `?`
  either: `aterm harness accounts report` reads `week – (no reading yet)` (or `window reset, no
  reading since`, `usage tap off`, `not reported by Claude Code`), `accounts stats --cli` rows
  read `week – (not in its newest reading)` and `monthly – (no reading yet)`, a `/usage`
  probe's review line reads `week=– (not on the panel)`, `aterm harness agy` reads
  `5h – (no figure given)`, and the Claude Code account's hover title and Accounts menu read
  `weekly – · until relaunch` (and the other reasons) instead of `weekly ? · …`. aterm never
  makes up a figure, and it does not poll Anthropic's usage endpoint for one.

- **A headless aterm at `--scale 2` draws every window at 2×.** A window it opened
  after its first (a new window, a tab torn into its own window, a restored window)
  kept a scale of 1 under 2× cells, so its palette and Overview were half as wide in
  columns as at 1× and cut their rows short. Every window a headless aterm makes now
  takes its `--scale`.
- **A panic in an update check no longer puts its message in `aterm.log`.** The update
  checker's line for a check that panicked quoted the panic's message, which can hold what the
  check was reading. It now names the panic by its kind and length (`other panic (37B)`), as
  aterm's other lines do; the message stays on stderr and in the crash report.

- **An idle aterm no longer wakes every 2 seconds while a tab runs a command.** With no window
  showing the stats bars, a command left running in any tab (a `sleep`, a build, a server, `tail
  -f`) made aterm read every process again every 2 s for as long as it ran, or every 30 s for a
  command waiting on the network or a timer: 10 timer wakes every 20 s, all of them `system_vitals`.
  Such a command is now read when it starts and ends, when its output moves its screen, at the
  harness's minute disk look, and when `aterm ctl sys` asks, so an idle aterm is back to zero
  wakes; `status job=` still names its job, with its quiet time counted to now. An agent's call
  that may hang, a program macOS has not let start, and a process a closed tab left running that
  aterm offers to end are still watched on their own timers.

- **A codex-alab landing under Autopilot Land gets its Done for you row.** aterm reads no
  working state from codex-alab's screen, so the work behind a landing counted as none, and no
  codex-alab landing ever reached Done for you in the menu bar. aterm now counts the turns
  codex-alab reports itself, so a landing after 30 seconds of its work is listed there, as a
  Claude Code landing is. With it, a codex-alab tab's working and waiting time now counts in
  Settings ▸ Harness's numbers, and its landing marks the tab with `•` and gets the cursor
  pet's cheer, as a Claude Code landing does. A turn codex-alab ends on an API or connection
  error counts as a wait, not as time at its prompt.

- **An idle codex-alab tab no longer wakes aterm every second.** aterm re-read codex-alab's
  session record a second after each look, even with nothing new on its screen; it now does so
  only after the program wrote, or just after a burst of its output.
- **An agy session that runs out of its Antigravity quota picks up again once the quota
  resets.** agy 1.4.12 reports a signed-in account's quota at once (`Individual quota reached.
  … Resets in 4h29m33s.`), in words aterm did not recognise as a limit. The window took each
  such turn for the agent's own reply, and after the same reply twice it stopped typing, so the
  session stayed idle long after the quota came back: two days on one Mac. aterm now reads it as
  a usage limit, waits until the reset it names and types again there. Any other failure of
  agy's model call that aterm does not recognise is waited out and tried again, never taken for
  a reply.
- **Setup's first network uses go on as soon as the network opens, and your join phrase is
  kept safe.** A Secrets join waiting on the Local Network step now goes on the moment that
  step asks or its minute runs out, whatever window is in front, instead of waiting for
  something else to wake it, and it no longer cuts short the 30 seconds macOS's question is
  given. Only the time you are at the Mac counts toward those waits. A terminal session's
  first network use waits, as a window's does, for a quiet moment with you there, and once
  the vault's background service has made macOS ask, System State counts the question as
  asked rather than raising it again. A join phrase that never reached a Mac in ALab, or whose
  try stopped part way, stays in the field and is still good; if macOS's Local Network
  switch for aterm is off, System State says where to turn it on. A phrase typed after
  System State was closed and opened again during an earlier try is no longer wiped when
  that earlier try ends. The phrase field is now
  a secret: assistive tools read bullets, and the words are wiped from memory once used,
  when the field goes away and when the page closes. With sharing off (`[swarm] enabled =
  false`) aterm also stops advertising its vault and browsing for others, and atpkg stops
  dialling other Macs. A settings file another user can change is no longer read by any of
  these.
- **Asking macOS about aterm again no longer gives up when macOS's queue is backed up.**
  After you switch aterm on in Developer Tools, aterm starts one new program so macOS asks
  about it again. When macOS's program check was too backed up for that program to finish,
  `aterm doctor` said it "could not make macOS ask about aterm again", and the window asked no
  more. Doctor now says "asking macOS about aterm again has not settled: macOS's queue is
  backed up" (with where the prime's copy was kept), and the window asks once more once the
  check catches up.
- **`aterm doctor` no longer asks macOS about aterm again into a backed-up queue.** Once your
  switch reads on, doctor counts again the programs macOS's program check holds, and while
  three or more wait, or one waited when the report counted and one waits now, it starts no
  new program of its own, which would only wait behind them. It says so: "did not ask macOS
  about aterm again: now 3 programs of this user wait for macOS's program check, the oldest
  started 21 m ago, and that ask is a new program that would wait behind them; macOS asks again
  when aterm next starts". The window already waited for the queue to drain.
- **`aterm fabric` lists only an instance's own bridges, and reads no other program's command
  line for them.** Its BRIDGES column named any child of an instance whose command line read
  `aterm link serve`, from a list of every program's command line (`ps` on Linux); it now
  names only children that run aterm itself, whose command line is read only then. On Linux
  the broker is found from the kernel's own list of listening sockets, so a socket whose name
  holds a line break can no longer pass for the broker's socket, and where that list cannot be
  read `aterm fabric` names no broker rather than guess. Also on Linux, a program whose name
  is not UTF-8 is read like any other: one such program on the machine no longer stops aterm
  from keeping a shell ready for your next tab, and one in a tab is still seen when it stops
  (Ctrl-Z), named, and ended with its tab.

- Harness upgrades keep a continuation pending when its conversation ledger cannot
  be read, including when it grows past the read limit. A person's own exchange
  and a continuation already typed by the supervisor are no longer treated as
  absent when that evidence is unreadable.

- Mailbox and sign-in curl requests finish when the direct child exits, even if a
  descendant keeps its pipes open. Config input and complete output share a
  deadline, and the owned config buffer is scrubbed when the request stops.

- A fleet leave finishing after a new join keeps the node job that join needs,
  instead of stopping it. Membership that cannot be read also keeps the job.
- The Land person-exchange lab matches journal and ledger records by act sequence
  and order, so independently sampled timestamps do not fail a valid first instruction.
- **Removing an agent build no longer risks hanging every new program on your Mac.** After
  an update lands a Claude Code or Codex build, `aterm pkg` runs it once in the background,
  and a toolchain install checks each new program with `--version`. When that run did not
  end on its own (stopped after 30 seconds, ended by a signal, or `aterm pkg` itself quit
  first), macOS could still be checking the program. An `uninstall` or a clean-up of old
  builds could then delete it mid-check, and on macOS 27.0.1 that leaves every program you
  start afterwards hanging until a restart. The build is now marked before the program
  starts, the mark goes once the program ends on its own, and while it stands for up to ten
  minutes `uninstall` asks you to try again in a few minutes and clean-ups leave the build.
- **Freeing disk space no longer risks hanging every new program on your Mac.** The harness
  checks a new Claude Code version by running it with `--version` or `--help`, and stops it
  after a few seconds when it does not answer; `aterm harness disk` removes the Claude Code
  versions nothing uses. A version stopped that way could still be under macOS's check of its
  first start when the clean-up removed it, and on macOS 27.0.1 that leaves every program you
  start afterwards hanging until a restart. A version the harness started now stays until it
  has answered, or for up to ten minutes, and `aterm harness disk` lists it as kept and says
  why.

- **Commons repair that keeps being refused stops retrying at once, and says why.** When this
