  Mac's own vault or trust state refused Commons repair, an aterm window retried every fifth of a
  second (`aterm node serve` every 2 s), and its log said only "refused local configuration or
  trust state". The line now names the step that refused (`custody`, `owner lease`,
  `log witness`, …), and in a window each refusal in a row waits twice as long, up to 30 s;
  `aterm node serve` keeps its 2 s, so it still hands Commons to a window that opens. A fleet peer
  that does not answer, or whose answer this Mac refuses, is dialled again after 5 s, then 10, 20
  and so on up to 2 minutes, where it was every 3 to 5 s. A peer busy with another round, one that
  has not yet approved this Mac, or one that refuses it is still dialled every 3 to 5 s: each
  closes before it answers, and this Mac cannot tell them apart. A member with more than 16 peers
  also decodes each peer's membership log once, not on every round. An idle member whose peers all
  answer still runs repair rounds back to back, about 2 cores on a 30-member fleet:
  `docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` ATERM-KI-1030-2 says what is left.

- **The Command Line Tools tab starts every time.** Its program could miss the line the
  window types to start it, when that line arrived before the program was ready, and then
  sat there doing nothing. It now keeps a line typed early. It also no longer waits for
  another install of aterm's tools to finish before it asks for your password: it never
  needed that install.

- **Shells opened during the Command Line Tools install get the shim, and it goes when it
  should.** A tab opened after setup started waiting on the tools used to run Apple's `git`
  stub, which raised Apple's install dialog. Every shell aterm opens while the tools are
  awaited now gets the shim, in windows already open too, and keeps it ahead of `/usr/bin`
  after a login profile's `path_helper` (zsh, bash, fish and PowerShell). The shim used to
  stay after you pressed Stop, after the tools arrived, and even into later launches. New
  shells now stop getting it the moment you stop setup, turn the Workspace group off, or the
  tools arrive; its folder stays until aterm next launches, so a shell that already ran `git`
  keeps working instead of failing with "No such file or directory".

- **The shim never runs one of Apple's install stubs while aterm installs the tools.** Once
  the tools arrive it hands each command to Apple's own `/usr/bin` program, `xcrun`
  included, which runs the tools' own with the SDK set, so `cc hello.c` builds in a shell
  that had the shim as it does anywhere else. A name the tools do not include (`pagestuff`,
  say) prints one line and stops, instead of raising Apple's dialog. After you press Stop
  with the tools still missing, it hands the command to Apple's own, as you chose. The shim
  finds its folder from where it runs, so a shell that changed `HOME` still gets it right.

- **A login shell an agent starts inside a tab keeps the shim during the install.** A
  `bash -lc` (or a script) started in an aterm tab ran its profile after aterm placed the
  shim, put `/usr/bin` first again, and raised Apple's dialog on its first `git`. While aterm
  installs the tools, `BASH_ENV` now points at a small aterm hook that runs your own
  `BASH_ENV` first and puts the shim back after the profile; your own comes back once the
  install ends. A `fish -l` started in a fish tab does the same. A `zsh -lc` has no such hook
  (only `ZDOTDIR` reaches it, and that would send your own startup files' writes to aterm),
  nor do an interactive `bash -l`, `sh -l` or `pwsh -Login`: those still get Apple's `git`.

- **The shim says the tools are on their way only while something installs them.** An
  install that ended unfinished (closed, failed, or on an account that may not install
  them), or an earlier launch's tab that never finished, used to leave every new shell told
  the tools were coming. New shells now get Apple's own route then, and a shell that already
  had the shim hands its commands there too, until an install starts again. A shell started
  under one that had the shim no longer puts it back once nothing wants it.

- **An update that keeps your shells keeps their shim working.** A launch that adopted live
  shells removed the shim's folder they still had on PATH, so a `git` those shells had run
  before failed with "No such file or directory". The folder now stays for them; only a
  launch with no live shells removes it. An install those shells carry on with gets the shim
  on new shells again.

- **Ctrl-C during your own `aterm init` no longer leaves `sudo` holding your password.** The
  stop waits until `sudo -K` has run, then ends the run.

- **Low Data Mode no longer ends the Command Line Tools tab on "something unexpected went
  wrong".** The tab now says `Low Data Mode is on, so the download waits. Turn it off in
  System Settings › Network, then press Install… again.` System State waits calmly, keeps the
  one tab it opens by itself for later, and opens it once Low Data Mode is off.

- **An account that is not an administrator is told so.** Only an administrator of the Mac
  can install the Command Line Tools. The tab now says so before asking for any password, and
  the GitHub repositories row says it in place of an Install… that could only fail again.

- **`aterm init` asks for your Mac password only when it should.** It used to ask in an
  agent's tab, run with no terminal and fail, or ask while the tools were already installing
  and then fail. In each of these cases it now leaves the tools waiting and exits 0. Once the
  install starts, a Ctrl-C waits for it, so the tab's last line says what really happened.
  The password is forgotten as soon as the install ends (`sudo -K`), in your own terminal as
  well as in the tab. The root step reads no file you could change, and System State,
  `aterm init` and the install agree on whether an install is running. A second `aterm init`
  run while the first still waits on Apple's installer window now leaves that install alone
  instead of taking over its marker.

- **The agent harness never raises Apple's install dialog.** On a Mac without the Command
  Line Tools, its look at a session's repository used to run Apple's `git` stub, even when it
  had checked another `git` earlier on PATH. It now runs exactly the `git` it checked, and
  finds no `git` where there is only the stub.

- Repository checks follow executable PATH lookup, including relative entries
  and aliases, before deciding whether Apple's Git stub can run quietly.
- Warm-shell eligibility records preserve files and links that already occupy
  a temporary staging name.
- Command Line Tools cleanup keeps an installation marker when process readings
  cannot establish that no installer holds it.
- AGY upgrades keep background work open when transcript payloads quote message
  headers or a kill result cannot be matched to one call.
- System State runs an observation retry or token check when it is due, even
  while the page's next refresh is still ahead.
- A permission walkthrough keeps its page when the first presence observation
  arrives late, without counting the unobserved interval as time at the Mac.
- The Local Network setup step refreshes its state after subscribing and after
  coalesced network changes, keeping Offline and No LAN rows current.
- Shared build caches keep verified ownership after more than 64 workspaces use
  them, so eligible generations can still retire under the disk budget.
- The Autopilot test driver checks the full received go-ahead against the intended
  command, catching an answer whose middle was lost.
- `aterm fleet` commands on a busy Mac whose aterm window keeps it in the fleet are less
  often refused with "another aterm is writing the book; run this again": that window's
  fleet heartbeat now makes its short update of the book at normal priority instead of its
  background one, at which a loaded Mac held that update past the two seconds a command
  waits for it. The node job's heartbeat still runs at background priority. `aterm fleet
  leave` stops the node job only once it has let the book go.
- Autopilot preserves another person's ownership when their name appears in
  uppercase, so it leaves those requests for their owner.
- Nested package-lock updates refuse linked or unreadable files before staging
  changes, and preserve earlier files when repository discovery cannot be read.
- **A setup step that crashes aterm twice now waits for you, even after a refused update.**
  An update that did not go ahead used to leave the step marked as quit, so a crash after it
  resumed the step again. Another aterm or `aterm doctor` holding setup's records no longer
  makes a step aterm stopped in look alive, so it resumes at the next launch by itself.
- **A Mac that slept no longer makes a setup step look stuck.** The hour a step may run
  before it waits for Check again now counts only time the Mac was awake.
- **Setup a newer aterm saved is no longer damaged by an older one.** A setting the older
  aterm does not know is left alone and the rest are honoured, and a crash loop is still
  broken when a newer aterm left records of an earlier run.
- **An update no longer cuts a setup step in half.** It never relaunches aterm in the middle of
  a Messages or FaceTime sign-out, the last step of a repository clone, or the install of the
  vault's sync process: it waits up to 10 seconds for the step to finish, and otherwise tries
  again at its next check. A step that waited for an update checks again before it runs, so a
  sign-out that finds you gone waits for your return, a clone whose vault changed meanwhile is
  not published, and a sync process turned off meanwhile is not installed.
- **The Messages and FaceTime sign-outs check you are still there right before each one.** If
  you walk away after Messages signs out, FaceTime waits for your return instead of being
  clicked with nobody there. System State in front no longer wakes every second while a
  sign-out waits for Check again, for Accessibility, or after a failure: it looks for your
  return only while the sign-outs wait for you.
- **System State keeps showing a setup step as running until that step ends.** When the vault's
  step finished first, the workstation rows still being set up used to read as idle.
- Automatic identity setup preserves configuration choices changed after its
  initial read instead of overwriting them with the resolved machine label.
- Release measurements preserve unrelated temporary files and leave existing
  measurements intact when a staging write fails.
- **`aterm init` never signs out of Messages or FaceTime with nobody there.** It signs out
  only while you are at the screen when the sign-outs start, after every other step, in a
  terminal or not; if you have gone by then they wait for the next run, and `--sign-out`
  with no terminal is refused while nobody is there. Its wait for
  another setup ends after 10 minutes (at once with `--no-wait`): its preferences and
  sign-outs are left as they are, and the rest of the run is still reported, exit 75.
- **`aterm init` keeps your choices made while it runs.** A Stop, or a group turned off in
  System State while init waits or runs, holds what it has not reached, a clone not yet
  started included, even in a group a flag named; a flag sets only a group already left as
  is when init began. A group you left as is stays off in System State's plan, and a run
  that sets no Mac setting saves no plan; init no longer holds System State waiting while it
  clones your repositories; and a setting you changed after aterm set it, a sign-out you
  undid included, stays as you set it, with a line naming it as System State does and Set up
  now or `aterm doctor --apply` to set it again. A clone you named over your Leave as is is
  kept until the token lands, and one that waited for Apple's Command Line Tools runs once
  they arrive.
- **The first `aterm init` or `aterm doctor --apply` on a Mac aterm.app never set up** keeps
  the secrets vault, Rust in Spotlight and (on an ALab Mac) GitHub repositories running
  afterwards, and the vault in sync; neither turns aterm's permissions back on after you
  turned them off.
- **`aterm doctor --apply` takes only this Mac's scope:** it no longer signs a Mac outside
  ALab out of Messages and FaceTime, and `--check` no longer calls an ALab Mac's profile out
  of scope. The line about held groups names only a way back that runs where it is printed,
  `aterm init --only` with the group's word (`dock`, `scrolling`, `github`, ...) to set it
  alone, and says plainly when a newer aterm set this Mac up. `--apply` while your Stop or an
  earlier aterm's Cancel holds every group changes and saves nothing, and its plan keeps
  aterm's permissions where an older aterm's plan left them out; `--check` reads each group
  a Stop holds as off and a setting you changed as yours, never as drift.
- **The vault's sync holds at your Stop and your switches:** a Stop pressed mid-pass holds
  each vault step not yet started (the message bus is this Mac's alone and goes on) and a
  clone about to begin, which stays owed for Set up now; GitHub repositories left as they
  are since the run that owed the clone began (or `[github] enabled = false`) drop it; a
  clone only you can finish is not run again until the token, init.toml or Apple's git
  changes, and a token file aterm cannot use says what is wrong with it. A machine name an
  earlier aterm wrote is no longer read as yours, one you set back stays yours, and an
  unrecorded pair of names counts as aterm's only where the vault's roster gives it to this
  Mac.
- **`aterm doctor --apply` refused while System State sets up this Mac says so,** instead of
  naming a doctor pass nobody ran.
- Shared native API-key preparation holds when local settings cannot be read or
  parsed, and rechecks Off before observing a queued credential. Explicit local
  profiles and provider environments keep their own credential route.
- Release-cache cleanup honors explicit configured executables and retains
  artifacts whose first-run evidence cannot be read safely.

- Package preparation preserves primary and unrelated files when rebuilding hard
  links, including filenames that resemble temporary files.
- Seamless updates preserve legacy input pauses and keep newer builds' mouse-only
  activity separate from typing.
- Package maintenance preserves large removal and shell-wiring histories, holds
  changes when their evidence is unreadable, and keeps complete builds for other
  architectures intact.
- Package progress and generated-file updates recover from occupied old
  temporary files without changing those files or their link targets.
- Command recovery accepts valid relative build selections and contained staged
  aliases. Store discovery reads the same supported configuration size as the
  package loader.
- Build wrappers that never start a build preserve queued signal exit outcomes.

- Release-cache cleanup keeps bundles that running processes or configured services
  still use, including when their release journal has moved on.

- Release preparation refuses linked publication sources and linked token files
  before accepting their contents or changing their permissions.

- System monitoring shows a build's memory wait immediately and clears earlier polling,
  busy or stuck reports, including when the build is admitted.
- System State recognizes Apple's command-line installer while the Command Line Tools
  install marker is held, keeping the installation status calm.

- The Linux VM cache keeps helper copies whose first run is unconfirmed, and
  refuses to replace incomplete copies while a helper still uses them.

- **A `NEEDS YOU` line from an agent's background work survives a dropped call.** When an
  agent's turn ended with its own background work running and named something only you can
  give, a control call left unanswered at that pause, or the menu bar's own update, could keep
  the line off the menu bar and the window border until the agent next stopped. aterm now puts
  it up at that pause whatever else failed, and tries again at the background work's pauses if
  the update itself went unanswered.
- **The standing go-ahead keeps every safeguard, says its own limits, and waits an hour after
  you type.** The go-ahead (`go-ahead@v1`) now says itself that it covers only the agent's own
  reversible work and that a hold you gave still stands. A reply that asks for an irreversible
  act gets exactly the answer it got before the go-ahead existed, or reaches you with answers
  off, whatever the tab's width. The one exception is a `NEEDS YOU` line the tab wrapped whose
  only such act is the agent's own cleanup, such as removing its own worktree. The go-ahead is
  no longer typed over a tag, a rollout to your hosts, someone else's pull request, a review you
  said you would do first, a job the turn says publishes or deletes by itself (`CI releases
  every green build`), git's short force-push forms (`push -uf`, `push origin main -f`, `push
  origin +main`), an act on another session's build or cache, the files a worktree holds, or a
  push to another repository's main. Your words are not read for a hold: for an hour after you
  type in the tab (or after the turn your message opened ends, if later), aterm types no
  go-ahead, whatever you wrote and however the turn ends, at a pause of the agent's background
  work too and after a restart, and nothing the harness types starts that hour again. An agent
  left waiting through that hour gets the go-ahead when it ends, though its screen has not
  changed, and scrolling or clicking in the tab does not count as typing. It gets it then even
  when it woke itself and asked again within the hour, not up to an hour later. Under Land, one
  that asked within that hour, before Land's instruction, gets the instruction and then the
  go-ahead when the hour ends, instead of waiting for you for good. The hour counts the time
  your Mac slept. Another person driving the tab starts that hour as your typing does, and it
  runs on after they let go. Past it, the go-ahead and every line the harness types or installs
  about it say a hold you gave still
  stands, and an agent that still waits after three of them, whatever word it asks you to say,
  or an hour after the first with no work, usage limit, outage or sleep of your Mac since, is
  shown on the menu
  bar as waiting on a person, perhaps on a hold you gave. An agent that worked past the hour
  on the go-ahead and asks again gets it again, not that alert. A switch to Land onto a waiting
  agent types Land's instruction first, so the go-ahead follows it. Whether a
  reply waits on the go-ahead no longer depends on the tab's width or on code an earlier message
  names (`for_launch`, a file's path), and an agent waiting for memory or disk room as told
  (`waiting until memory frees up`, `waiting for memory, not for a go-ahead`) is not counted as
  refusing it. An agent already held on one reply it keeps repeating gets the go-ahead once
  before that hold applies, and Land gives it to an agent waiting to merge or push its own work
  even when the folder shows nothing unlanded.
- Repository setup can use verified GitHub credentials when a legacy SSH URL
  rewrite is present, without changing Git settings or existing worktrees.

- The Linux VM helper refuses a linked run directory without changing the
  linked directory's permissions. Its own plain run directory still becomes
  private, including repair of an unreadable owned directory on macOS.

- System State's Command Line Tools tab is titled Command Line Tools and speaks in plain
  words: no command line on its screen, one line before macOS asks for your Mac password
  (`Mac password:`), and one last line that says the tools are installed and you can close
  the tab, or why the install did not finish and that Install… on System State tries again.
  The password headline's Go to tab brings that tab to the front.
- Once that tab installs the tools, System State reads GitHub repositories again at once and
  stays calm meanwhile, instead of saying it needs you.
- System State asks you to finish in Apple's installer window while that window waits for your
  press. A placeholder an ended install left behind no longer reads as an install, and the next
  install replaces it.
- A press of Install… whose tab could not open says why: on the row, with Install… there again,
  or in a message when the tab could not start. A press waiting for a macOS dialog lets go once
  the tools arrive meanwhile. While Install… shows, the row says why the tools are needed.
- While a newer aterm manages the setup, the vault's address reads as plain words, with nothing
  to type into or press. The ALab profile aterm adds by itself waits for another setup as
  `Waiting to add this Mac's ALab profile…`, never as your choice.

- **System State's first-launch steps wait for you.** macOS's Local Network question asked
  while you were away still keeps System Settings back when you return: the first-launch walk
  opens its pages only once macOS has your answer, or once you have been at the Mac for 30
  seconds since your first touch after the question. A walk page left up behind a lock, or
  while nobody touches the Mac, is still there when you come back: its ten minutes count only
  your time, and it checks nothing meanwhile. A page you leave unanswered for ten minutes of
  your time closes and does not come back by itself; the pages after it come at the next quiet
  moment.
- macOS's administrator password dialog for debugger access also waits until you have not
  typed into aterm for 10 seconds, so a key you are typing does not land in it.
- aterm's first use of the local network no longer waits for good on System State's Local
  Network step while System State sits behind a terminal tab: after a minute of your time at
  the Mac it goes ahead, and macOS asks once, only while you are there, not typing into
  aterm, and with no other macOS question of aterm's on screen. Time away from the Mac does
  not count, and once one use asked, the others follow your answer.
- System State asks macOS's Local Network question on every network: on a campus network
  that hands out public addresses it names a host there, and on an IPv6-only network it asks
  through a short Bonjour look of its own. Its row reads "Nothing to ask yet" only on a Mac
  with no network at all, and aterm looks again when the network changes, not every minute.
- With sharing off (`[swarm] enabled = false`), aterm makes no local network use by itself:
  its Bonjour browse stops, and starts again when you turn sharing on, and Tab Control says
  sharing is off instead of looking for computers. A phrase you type, or `aterm members
  join`, still goes.
- aterm reads `[swarm] enabled` through a symlinked `aterm.toml` (a dotfiles link) as the
  window does, and where it cannot read the file it says so plainly, once, instead of in
  every log line.
- A phrase you type on System State's Secrets row that reaches no Mac in ALab (none answered
  on this network) is no longer read as a wrong phrase: the words stay in the field, and the
  page says the phrase is still good and that the Mac that showed it must be awake and on
  this network. A phrase that was used is wiped from memory, its edit history included.
- Waking on the same network no longer makes this Mac ask ALab's members again from the
  start, nor ends a paused Secrets try early: a route read before the router's address
  resolves counts as the network aterm knew.
- An aterm that opens into an update gives a Mac that never had its first-launch walk that walk,
  and goes on with the pages left when System Settings' Quit & Reopen opened it.
- A walk that `aterm doctor`, `aterm init` or `aterm ctl permissions walk now` starts opens no
  System Settings page while System Settings shows a sheet of its own.
- When a newer aterm saved this Mac's setup, this aterm's first use of the local network no
  longer waits for a System State Local Network step it will not take.

- An enabled ALab vault now restores its missing subscriber after setup has
  finished, including unattended launches, while preserving explicit Off,
  pinned programs and foreign service definitions.

- **System State's ALab widen ends when it cannot finish.** On an ALab Mac, the widen of
  aterm's own setup could find that a newer aterm had saved this Mac's setup meanwhile, or
  could fail to read back what its own save wrote. It was then kept and tried again at every
  look, and the page could keep showing a run that was not happening. Now a newer aterm's setup
  ends the widen, and System State says a newer aterm manages this Mac's setup. A save aterm
  cannot read back is left for the next launch to settle, and a Stop still covers what it
  wrote. Only a save that stopped part-way, or one waiting for another setup to finish, is
  tried again.

- The Command Line Tools tab that System State opens by itself, once per Mac, no longer opens
  again after a power loss right after it opened: its mark now reaches the disk before aterm
  goes on.

- Build-memory record updates preserve an oversized or unreadable file and report
  the refusal. Oversized writes leave the previous readable records intact.

- **Sharing off reads as your choice.** With sharing with your other Macs turned off in
  `aterm.toml` (`[swarm] enabled = false`), System State's vault row reads Sharing off, calmly,
  instead of a change to make. The Permissions stage no longer waits for a Local Network step
  that sharing off never takes, so System State no longer reopens at every launch, and GitHub
  repositories set up from this Mac's own sign-in instead of waiting for a vault. A vault service
  already running stops asking ALab's Macs, waiting on the vault and applying its changes until
  sharing is on again, and aterm starts its shared-data service only once sharing is on.
- **A Mac waiting to join ALab asks less often.** It asks ALab's Macs again after 1, 2, 4 and 8
  minutes and then every 15 minutes, not every minute. Moving to another network or pressing
  Join asks at once. Each Mac in ALab still shows one request for it.
- **A vault that does not answer is tried less often, calmly.** Setup tries the ALab vault again
  after 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 minutes and then once an hour, never as a failure, and at once when
  this Mac moves to another network (another router, Wi-Fi network or interface). AirDrop, VPN
  and temporary IPv6 addresses coming and going no longer wake it.
- **aterm's background service waits for System State's Local Network step.** `aterm node
  serve`, a window's fleet heartbeat and its fleet readings make no use of the local network
  before System State asks macOS for Local Network access, so that step's question comes first.

- Shared account sign-in can use approved mailbox information for Claude as
  well as Codex and Kimi, without falling back to another mailbox on an error.

- A copied or moved Commons table can recover automatically into a newly
  admitted local writer. Existing files and unconfirmed crash tails stay intact;
  verified committed operations keep their IDs and canonical table identities.

- Shared application tables replicate with older fleet versions while retaining
  current membership and per-record authorization checks.

- Files named like Cargo locks no longer bypass build memory admission. Verified covering
  claims keep nested builds running; an unclaimed nested build that could wait in a cycle
  refuses with guidance to enter the outer build through the admission shim.

- Automatic signing setup can use an existing local certificate and key when both
  exactly match the authorized shared copy, without replacing them or taking ownership.

- Release signing keeps the authorized shared certificate selected after routine
  keychain maintenance. Readiness still requires a current signing proof.

- **Cruise no longer stops for good while the agent's own background work runs.** A turn
  that ends while a dev server, a monitor or a long workflow of the agent's runs is carried
  at that break, and four causes held the carry there long after they had passed. A Mac
  wake's settle never ran out at such a break. A usage limit stayed open after the agent
  resumed and worked past its reset. A context wall compacted while the work ran left its
  continuation owed, with no point to type it. A sign-in wall a supervisor told the disk-free
  ask stayed told after that supervisor ended, so the ask waited on a sign-in long gone. Now
  the wake's settle holds the carry only until it runs out, a limit closes at the break the
  agent's own turn reaches once it works past the limit (and a limit past its reset and grace
  holds nothing), the compaction's continuation is typed at the break in the carry's place,
  and a new supervisor's first turn end tells the window what holds the session now. A cause
  that still stands still holds.

- Shared tables can preserve custody across a later macOS device-number change by
  recording the persistent volume identity. Valid existing stores add this evidence
  automatically while their previous directory binding still matches.

- **A session on an AI account another Mac holds pauses even while a new account is being
  tried.** After another session on the same Mac had just moved to a different account, a
  session whose own account another Mac's claim held kept working on it until that new account
  first answered, up to ten minutes and longer when the new account was low, so both Macs used
  the account. It now pauses at its turn end until the trial ends, then moves to the new account.
  A second such session that another beat to the trial pauses too, instead of working on the
  account for one more turn. So does one whose move to another account must wait for a
  background job it runs, a tab someone holds or a missing socket: it pauses until the move can
  be made, instead of working on the account at every turn end while it waits. So does one
  whose move was refused, or that has used its four account moves for the hour: it pauses as one
  with no account to move to does, instead of working on the account for up to an hour. A
  session whose own account this Mac had just moved to, before the other Mac's claim on it
  arrived, moves to a free account, instead of pausing for as long as the other Mac keeps its
  claim (`F19`).

- **The harness waits for a Claude Code reply to finish before it acts on the turn's end.**
  In a Claude Code session with a status line (aterm's usage tap or your own), Claude Code
  shows no busy sign while it draws a reply: the footer drops `esc to interrupt`, and the
  spinner goes once the reply's first line is on screen. The harness could take a reply
  that was still being drawn for the end of the turn. Under Land it could then judge a
  `Nothing left:` reply before its `NEEDS YOU` lines were drawn, and under Cruise type into a
  reply still streaming. Where the turn's closing timing line (`✻ Brewed for 6s`) is drawn,
  the turn has ended. Otherwise the harness now waits until Claude Code's own window title
  says the turn is over and, if it saw the reply still running, reads the screen once more
  after that, so the reply's last line is on it. Where Claude Code shows no status in its
  title (`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE`, or a static title under a terminal
  multiplexer), the title cannot say the turn still runs, and the harness reads the screen as
  before, at most once more after it saw the reply running.

- Autopilot Land carries the work on after a person's mid-job question that was answered
  while the session was Off. Switching back to Land used to leave that reply to the person,
  so nothing was typed until someone typed. It also keeps carrying it past a usage wall's
  retry and a relaunch, which used to hand the reply back as the session's opening message.
  The session's opening message stays theirs.

- After a network outage held a turn end, the harness no longer holds Cruise's keep-going
  prompt and its other lines at later background waits once the connection is back. The
  outage measured at that turn end could hold them for up to an hour from when it began,
  after you or the agent had already moved on; now only what the connection measures at the
  wait itself holds them.

- **An API error with no status no longer gets a resume typed into a connection aterm measured
  down.** When Claude Code's `/goal` line said the API was unavailable with its error row out of
  sight, the harness typed "the API error may have cleared" on its back-off while aterm measured
  the connection down. Such an error now waits in silence while the connection is measured down,
  for up to an hour from when it went down, and is resumed once when it comes back, as a
  connection error is. Past that hour it is tried on its back-off again, so a connection check
  that is wrong about the route (a firewall that blocks aterm's check but not the agent) costs
  the session one hour, not a stop. Where aterm has not measured the connection down (the Mac's
  network stayed up and no check was running), the error is tried on its back-off as before.
  Errors with a status, and overloads, are still tried on their back-off.

- **Cruise and Land no longer give your go-ahead for someone else's approval.** An agent that
  ended its turn waiting for another person's approval to merge its own branch (`Waiting for
  Alice's approval`, `NEEDS YOU: a reviewer's approval on PR 812`, `approval from @alice`,
  `until the reviewer gives the go-ahead`) was answered with your standing go-ahead to merge,
  and a `NEEDS YOU` line was told to go. Now an approval the agent waits on that someone else
  gives keeps the turn's usual prompt and its `NEEDS YOU` line on the menu bar. Your own
  go-ahead still gets the standing answer when a deadline or a channel follows it (`your
  go-ahead by Friday`), or when the reply also says a reviewer has already approved.

- **Cruise and Land no longer tell an agent to drop a `NEEDS YOU` line whose work waits on
  your password.** A reply that said `The rebuild needs your GitHub password, which I don't
  have.` above `NEEDS YOU: say "go" so I can rebuild the branch` was answered with your
  standing go-ahead and `Drop that NEEDS YOU line now`, which took the only notice of the
  password off the menu bar. Now a sentence of the turn that says the line's own work needs or
  lacks what only you can give (`needs your GitHub token`, `I don't have push access`, `I can't
  log in`, `the token expired`) keeps the line, and the turn keeps its usual prompt. A sentence
  that only mentions a token, or says the work doesn't need one, changes nothing.

## [0.147.0] - 2026-10-29

### Added

- Macs on the local network join the default open ALab vault automatically and receive
  shared secrets, Commons access and fleet membership without a per-machine approval.
- Fleet peers with drive access can send messages directly to a session's inbox and read
  its replies without typing into its terminal. Arrivals appear in normal mail notifications
  and subscriptions, and messages survive session handoff and application updates.

- **Shared AI account lists.** The dashboard and command-line lists now show shared account
  descriptions and imported spreadsheet candidates, including providers without a local
  adapter. Source rows and true, false or missing provider markers are preserved, while
  missing sign-in details remain pending.

- `aterm secrets need peek --all --json` reads credential requests without posting,
  sweeping or advancing their state. It reports offers, current-member sweep coverage
  and custodian decisions retained on this Mac, so account sign-in waits can be inspected.

### Changed

- **The vault stops writing the copy only 0.145 Macs read once none is left.** An admin Mac
  kept every change made in the membership log mirrored into the old vault file, for Macs on
  0.145 that cannot read the log. It now asks the vault's servers which Macs subscribed in the
  last 14 days, and copies a change of a secret only while one of them has not yet proven its key
  in the log. A Mac still on 0.145, or one whose server answers no such question, keeps it on,
  and a removal always reaches that copy, so a removed Mac never keeps reading it. Every asked
  server must supply a complete history: new, interrupted or unreadable histories keep the copy
  running for a fresh 14-day window, while clean server updates preserve that coverage.
  Plain legacy reads without an identity also keep it running; explicit background observer
  probes do not count as a Mac consuming the copy.

- **Updated the bundled Astream libraries.** Aterm follows the current event-store,
  capability and wire implementations and terminal conformance reference, while its
  application dependency set stays the same.

### Fixed

- Managed ALab background services follow the installed release automatically, including
  services still running an older copy. Explicit service pins remain respected.
- A fleet request that races a session handoff keeps its caller's permissions: it retries
  safely instead of forwarding with the receiving Mac's owner access.

- **Shared release signing sets itself up on each enrolled Mac.** A matching signed release
  ring and delivered Developer ID pair now prepare a private keychain, repair unattended key
  access, and prove a real signature during ordinary sync. Lost keychain passwords are
  recovered while preserving the old files. Status distinguishes delivered files from a
  successful signing proof.

- **Missing notarization credentials can be requested from the lab.** Publishing asks for
  the credential the current release subscriber reads, and waits for Apple's live sign-in
  check before considering the request fulfilled. Older Macs leave these requests for an
  updated member to handle.

- **Many shared application tables no longer stop a Mac's account claims.** Every Commons table
  a Mac keeps, one per resource window included, took one of 63 storage slots, and each day's
  account-claims table needed one too. Once applications had taken them all, the Mac recorded no
  account claim, so it kept to its home accounts, and exchanged none with other Macs, for good.
  Eight of the slots are now kept for the claims tables, so applications can take 55. A Mac
  whose applications already took more than 55 keeps those tables, and its account claims stay
  stopped (`F19`).

- **A Mac whose clock ran ahead and was put right sees the other Macs' account claims again at
  once.** After its clock ran two or more days ahead and came back, a Mac kept to the claim
  tables of the days it had jumped to until real time caught up: it saw none of the other Macs'
  account claims and they saw none of its own, so two Macs could use the same account. It now
  reads today's claims at once. It records no account claim of its own, keeping to its home
  accounts, until its clock reaches the days it had jumped to: one day fewer than its clock ran
  ahead, however far that was. A Mac cannot tell a clock put right from one set back, and a
  Mac whose clock was set back two days would otherwise claim accounts without seeing the
  other Macs' claims of the day (`F19`).

- **A Mac whose account-claims state is lost or damaged no longer keeps old claim tables for
  good, or takes one it deleted back up on a clock set back a day.** Rebuilding that state
  looked only 400 days either side of the clock and kept no record of the oldest day still
  allowed, and a deleted state was not rebuilt at all. A Mac back after a long absence, or whose
  state was deleted, kept its old day tables' storage for good, each taking one of the 63 table
  slots, and one rebuilt while its clock was set back a day could take up again a day table it
  had already deleted. A rebuild now finds every day table the Mac holds, however old, and
  deletes those whose rows have lapsed, and the oldest allowed day comes back from a second copy
  kept beside the state (`F19`).

- **A folder in place of a Mac's account-claims state no longer stops its claims.** Where a
  folder stood where the claims ring keeps its state (`ring-accounts-claims.state` in the Commons
  folder), that Mac recorded no account claim, so it kept to its home accounts, and exchanged no
  claim rows with other Macs until a person removed the folder. The Mac now moves the folder
  aside as `ring-accounts-claims.state.damaged-1` (it is never deleted) and writes a fresh state
  in its place, so its claims and their exchange go on (`F19`).

- Package builders can bound newly created disposable Rust build targets automatically.
  Idle whole generations retire above a 64 GiB soft budget or below 20 GiB free space;
  a large first successful build learns enough room for reuse. Guardian and Cargo
  locks, running images and mapped readers retain a generation, and interrupted
  retirement resumes before another generation is admitted. Existing unmarked or
  older registered targets keep their previous behavior.

- **Future-dated mailbox inputs do not restart automatic sign-ins.** A mail message,
  configuration file or secret dated after the current read no longer clears an account's
  retry hold or hides newer mail that has already arrived. Valid input changes still allow
  one new attempt, and an explicit account choice keeps its existing behavior.

- Disk cleanup keeps a build cache while a process on macOS or Linux still maps a file
  from it, even after closing the file descriptor. An incomplete or refused mapping
  scan keeps the cache for a later look.

- **A Claude Code session that never stops working is told an update waits, instead of
  waiting on it silently.** The live upgrade moves a session onto a newer Claude Code only
  when none of its own work is running, so a session under Autopilot Cruise or Land whose
  workflows and background shells outlived every turn could stay on an old build for hours.
  Once its own work has held the move for an hour, aterm now types one line telling the
  agent which build waits, that it moves when none of its work is running and, where the
  tab offers it and the build is proved to start, that `aterm ctl @self restart` moves it
  sooner. It asks nothing and ends nothing. It is said at most three times per build in
  one run of the agent, two hours apart, and never while a person is at the tab, at a usage
  limit, after a task landed, about a build that failed to start, or where aterm could not
  relaunch the session. Outside Cruise, a manager's wait holds it too. `aterm harness
  upgrade --status` shows it as `agent_told=`.

- **A Mac serving the vault as `alab-secrets.local` gives the name up as it goes to sleep.**
  When macOS says it is about to sleep, the vault server now stops its network advertisements
  (the `alab-secrets` name and its own name) and lets the Mac sleep once the programs that
  made them have ended, or after 2 seconds at most. Before, macOS could hand them to a Bonjour
  Sleep Proxy on the network (an Apple TV or HomePod), which then answered for
  `alab-secrets.local` while nothing served the vault there, or woke the Mac for each request,
  and kept every other member from taking the name over. macOS starts its own hand-over to such
  a proxy at the same moment, so this narrows that window rather than closing it: whether a
  proxy still answers for the name while the holder sleeps has not been measured on a real
  sleep. On wake the server advertises its own name again at once. A member that had taken
  `alab-secrets` over takes it back the way any other member does, after 90 seconds in which no
  vault answers there; a server started with `--advertise alab-secrets` and no member name of
  its own advertises it again at once, as before. A server that macOS starts while the Mac is
  in a dark wake (during Power Nap) may not hear the sleep that follows, and then keeps its
  advertisements through it as before. A server that stops cleanly gives both names up at once,
  as before.

- **A vault server no longer copies and rewrites its whole records store for each post.** Each
  post of membership records to a vault server, which any Mac on the network may send, copied
  the server's whole store (up to about 64 MiB) to check it, and each post that added a record
  rewrote the whole records file. A copy of the store now shares its records instead of
  copying them, and new records go on the end of the file. The file is still written whole on
  the first write, when an append fails, when the store let a record waiting on a missing
  parent go to make room, and when the file holds other than the store's records. A server
  that restarts after a power loss cut a write short keeps the records written before it. Where a removed
  Mac filled a server's store to its limit with records waiting on missing parents, each
  record a member then adds still rewrites the whole file.

- **A vault server that never answers a publish no longer stalls every secrets command on the
  admin's Mac.** A publish sends the new vault version to every server it knows of, including
  servers found on the network that nothing has checked. One that took the upload and never
  answered held the admin Mac's secrets lock until the upload's 120-second deadline, so every
  other secrets command there (a sync, the next Allow or edit) waited that long. The lock is
  now held only to check that the vault configuration has not changed; publishes from one Mac
  still reach the servers one after another, under a lock of their own that nothing else
  takes. A server that never answers still holds that publish, and the next one from that
  Mac, for the deadline.

- **A Mac asking to join keeps its row on a member's desk through a flood of new requests.**
  A member shows at most 64 join requests. Once full, with none settled, each new request took
  the place of the oldest one still asking, so a host with many addresses that sent fresh
  requests pushed out every other Mac's row, the one that had waited longest first, and the
  person found no row to Allow. A new request now takes the place of a request from the
  addresses that hold the most, so a host sending from fewer addresses than the desk holds
  requests never pushes out a Mac asking from its own address, one that has just asked
  included. Among those, a Mac still waiting to join goes last: one that asked again at least
  30 seconds after its first ask and within the last 3 minutes (a waiting Mac's subscriber
  asks once a minute, and `aterm members join` every 3 seconds while it runs). A host that
  sends from 63 or more addresses and asks its own requests again can still push out a Mac
  that has just asked.

- **A vault server keeps no membership records a LAN host sends before the vault's genesis.**
  Any Mac on the network may post membership records to a vault server, and while a vault had
  no genesis yet (ALab's case until Genesis v2) the server kept records anyone signed, up to
  about 63 MiB, rewrote the whole file on each post that added one and read it back at every
  start, though no member is ever sent such records. A server now takes records into a store
  with no genesis only together with the genesis that roots them, and answers other posts
  with a refusal; a records file an earlier build filled that way reads as empty, and the
  vault's next records replace it. A server that refuses a member's new records this way
  fills its store from the genesis by pulling from the other servers, as one with an empty
  store already did, and a member sends it its whole store the first time it posts to that
  server and again an hour after its last whole post.

- **No `aterm ctl hwkey` key answers a confirmation, whatever window it names.** A posted key
  was dropped only when it named the confirmation's own window, but `hwkey … shape=press` keys
  name none (macOS hands them to the front sheet), and keys posted while a Quit or Close
  question was up named the terminal window, so `hwkey return shape=press` could still press
  Paste on the person's multi-line paste. Now a posted key that could reach a confirmation is
  dropped, and `hwkey` refuses to start, and stops a running burst, while a paste, Quit or
  Close question is on screen. Opening any of these questions, or an owner's question in
  Settings ▸ Security or Stop Worker, also clears the keys already queued, so a burst's key
  that was on its way can no longer answer it either; a stopped burst says how many keys it
  posted, and a paste whose sheet cannot be guarded is dropped rather than shown unguarded.

## [0.146.0] - 2026-10-29

### Added

- **Any member removes a Mac, and the Macs a hostile member removed can undo it.** Where
  the vault has a membership log, `aterm members remove <name or join code>` (or `aterm
  secrets revoke`) works on any member, not only an admin. It takes the Mac out, makes new
  keys for everything it could read, puts every value again under them, and prints what the
  Mac could read; `--stolen` also bars its labels and fleet key and changes the fleet code.
  Two removals on the two sides of a split end in one new key with nobody acting. A removed
  Mac that asks to join again shows as "m40 was removed by m7 on Oct 30. Allow again?", not as
  a new Mac, and only "Allow again" (`aterm members allow --again`) lets it back in. If one
  Mac removes the others, each Mac it removed shows "m7 removed this Mac and 3 others. Undo
  m7's removals?", and a person's press signs that Mac's share (`aterm members undo` lists
  the rows and signs none). Once more than half of the Macs that were members before m7's
  removals, and at least two, have signed, its removals are void, they are back in with a new
  key it does not hold, and it stays out. Only the Macs it removed see the row, so the Undo
  answers a removal of most of the lab; a removal of a few Macs is answered by Allow again, or
  by removing m7. `aterm members list` shows who is in and who removed whom. On a vault with
  no log yet (ALab until its Genesis v2 ships), for a Mac the log does not seat, and for
  another admin of the vault 0.145 Macs read, the admin's `aterm secrets revoke` stays the
  way and says so (`F16`).
- **The native Commons startup lab uses the ordinary executable hosts.**
  `lab commons-startup` requires automatic enrollment, exact signed application values
  in both directions and recovery after a window restart, using private custody and
  loopback transport. Its private-socket negative control must fail the observer check.
- **A codex-alab tab can carry the Autopilot chip.** Where codex-alab leaves its composer's top
  line to aterm and carries itself under aterm's Autopilot word (its own proven claim), the tab
  shows its Autopilot chip right after the `codex-alab` label, before the harness switch, with
  Claude Code's faces: `∞` cruise, `⤓ land`, `✓ landed`, `⤓ quiet`, `○ off` (until codex-alab
  gives its claim back for Off) and a timed word. A click moves Autopilot to its next mode and
  types nothing into codex-alab, a right-click (control-click on a Mac) opens the Autopilot
  menu, its hover title reads beside it, and a screen reader reads its word
  (`Autopilot: cruise.`). It takes only the line's own blank cells: an active goal is laid after
  it, the label and the switch never move, nothing re-grids, and a pane too narrow for it shows
  the switch alone. No codex-alab build shows it yet. With its ALab interface on (the default)
  codex-alab draws that line itself, its own `[Cruise]`, `[Land]` and `[Off]` among it, and
  aterm draws nothing over it; with it off (`[tui] alab_interface = false`, its vanilla mode)
  codex-alab takes no claim and follows no Autopilot word, so the line keeps its label and
  switch and lays no chip, as under an off switch, and `aterm ctl chrome` says
  `why=switch-only`. A vendor `codex` shows nothing new. Before, `aterm ctl chrome` said
  `why=no-footer` for a codex-alab tab.
- **A program can open aterm's Autopilot menu at its own Autopilot face.**
  `aterm ctl @<sid> open autopilot-menu at=<row>,<col> [by=pointer|keys]` opens that session's
  Autopilot menu at a 0-based cell of its own screen, for a program such as codex-alab that
  draws its own Autopilot face where aterm shows no chip. It opens only where the session is the
  front window's focused one, is the owner's alone as the bare form is, types nothing into the
  session, and `by=keys` lights its first choice. It closes when the focus moves, the pane
  scrolls back, is rewound or re-grids, or the program leaves (another job in front, or its
  screen flips between main and alternate), since aterm cannot tell where the program draws its
  line then; the program asks again. Unaimed or malformed it answers
  `ERR usage: @<sid> open autopilot-menu at=<row>,<col> [by=pointer|keys]`, and under a hold
  `ERR halted`. The bare `open autopilot-menu` is unchanged. Before, the verb ignored its aim and
  opened only at aterm's own chip, so a program with its own face could not open it.
- **Commons reads membership, device bindings, and epoch keys from the signed membership log.** Once Genesis v2 seeds `EpochAudience::Commons`, Commons control v2 derives active and historical roster views from `<name>.records` instead of the authority-signed control journal: any bound member's `Admit` enrolls a newcomer (even without an admin-signed `0.145` envelope), any `Remove` retires the device and rotates `Commons` and `Everyone` epochs, unproved founders enroll over `ACE1` / `ACW2` against any active member, and `ACX2` control repair reconciles split-island wrap gaps and concurrent `Commons` epochs before table sync without authority-journal `Conflict` forks blocking admissions or table writes (`F18`).
- **A new Mac joins ALab with one Allow and a three-word phrase.** On the new Mac,
  `aterm members join` finds ALab on the network by itself (no account, no password) and
  asks every member at once. Every member's window shows "<name> wants to join ALab" with
  Allow and Ignore. Press Allow on any one of them: that Mac shows a short phrase in a sheet
  on its own screen, for 5 minutes, and you type it into the new Mac. The new Mac gets
  GitHub, publishing and AI-account credentials right away, from the member you allowed it
  on, and follows every later vault change once an admin Mac is reachable. No member is a
  leader. Allow takes only your own click: `aterm ctl`, a fleet drive and a harness answer
  are refused, and `aterm members allow <name>` or `aterm members invite` in a terminal
  print only that the phrase is on that Mac's screen. A wrong phrase burns it, as does a
  sheet that fails to open, and each Mac gets 3 tries a minute. Only the Mac that asked can
  use the phrase shown for it: another device on the network that copied its request cannot
  spend it, and a flood of requests from one cannot push a request you allowed off a member.
  A Mac that leaves the vault stops showing the rows and answering new Macs. `aterm members
  join` asks every member of a lab of up to 64 Macs, and when more than one shows a phrase it
  names each by the address `--at` takes. On the new Mac, the join System State and
  `aterm init` make asks every member it hears itself, so the row shows on a member with
  nothing run here, and asks again each minute while it waits, so a member that wakes up or
  restarts shows it too; `aterm init` then says to press Allow and type the phrase, or, with
  no member on the network, to run `aterm members join`. System State's Secrets row says to
  run `aterm members join` and press Allow, and once a member let the Mac in it says so.
  Neither names an admin.
  `install.sh` with no window now runs `aterm members join --no-wait`, which asks and
  returns. `aterm help members` explains it.
- **Once a vault has a membership log, any member lets a new Mac in by itself.** Pressing
  Allow on any member that holds a seat in the log signs the new Mac in there and hands it the
  keys to every shared entry, including ones sealed before the last key rotation, so it reads
  GitHub, publishing and AI-account credentials from the log and follows later changes with no
  admin Mac reachable. The Mac it gets is named `m<N>` by the member that allowed it. A Mac let
  in on one side of a network split reads values written on the other side once the two meet
  again: the first member that notices hands it the missing key, with nobody acting, and a
  member let in that way can already let the next Mac in. An Allow never lets back in a Mac the
  vault removed (the run ends saying so), and a value removed from the shared section stays
  closed to every Mac that joins after. The new Mac keeps asking an admin Mac to record it until
  one does, so a laptop that allowed it away from the LAN loses nothing. Until ALab has its log
  (its Genesis v2 is signed with a released build), joining works as before: the member hands
  its own files and an admin Mac records the admission; once the log arrives, a Mac still
  waiting that way asks the members again.
- (developer tool) **`lab mac nux --scenario vault-phrase` rehearses the new-Mac acceptance
  test in one command.** In a fresh macOS guest, a seed identity founds a vault on the guest's
  loopback holding a synthetic GitHub token, publish token and AI accounts list. A second
  identity, an existing member that is no admin, presses Allow, so the vault's admin admits an
  Allow another Mac signed. A third identity joins through the build's own CLI:
  `aterm members join --no-wait`, then the phrase the member shows typed at
  `aterm members join`'s prompt, then its own vault subscriber. The row times the ask to each file
  on disk and to `aterm members status` reading In. It fails unless the phrase came from that
  member, every file holds the seed's value, the Mac is In, every aterm listener is on loopback,
  and every `_alab-vault._tcp` and `_alab._tcp` browse in the guest and on this Mac ran and heard
  no guest advert. Nothing leaves the guest. It is not the acceptance test itself: the joiner
  dials the member at its loopback address (`--at`) instead of browsing the LAN, Allow is pressed
  by the lab rather than in a window, and no website install, bridged network or real credential
  is involved.
- **`aterm fleet peers` says since when this Mac has been away from every member.** Each time
  a member answers this Mac (a `peers` check, an `aterm ctl survey --fleet`, a fleet
  heartbeat), the time is kept by this Mac's own clock beside the fleet book. A kept time more
  than a minute past that clock (it stepped back since: set by hand, or a time-server
  correction) reads as no answer, and the next answer stands over it. When no member
  answers now, the away line is followed by `Away from every member since 15:58 (2h ago): the
  last answer one gave this Mac.`, and each member that did not answer gets a line of its own
  after the table, `Last answer to this Mac from 1a2b3c4d: 15:58 (2h ago).` (or `none
  recorded`). Every line that was there, the table's rows included, reads as it did, so a
  script that reads them keeps working.
- **Secret entries live in the signed membership log, with the vault envelope kept as a `0.145` mirror.** Signing Genesis v2 now mints per-audience symmetric epochs (`Epoch`), age-encrypted member wraps (`Wrap`), and ChaCha20-Poly1305 entry records (`Put` / `Delete`) into `<name>.records`. Subscribers and local readers materialize secret entries from the log whenever epochs are present (falling back to envelope lockers before Genesis v2), merging concurrent edits per `(Audience, name)` register by lowest `RecordId` so edits on lower-`seq` split islands survive heals, while any admin mirrors the merged log into parentless envelopes for `0.145` Macs (`F14`).

- **A `.csv` or `.tsv` file opens in the Editor as a spreadsheet grid.** `aterm edit` (or
  amacs in an aterm tab) shows a table's rows and columns with the header pinned at the top,
  row numbers in the gutter, and a panel under the grid that holds the current cell in full.
  The arrows, Tab, Home and End move between cells; typing, Return or a double-click opens the
  cell, Return keeps it and Escape drops it. A value with a comma, a quote or a line break is
  quoted for you, and saving changes only the bytes of the cells you changed: a BOM, CRLF line
  ends, the quoting of every other cell and a row with fewer cells stay as they were. ⌘Z takes
  a cell back, and in an open cell ⌘Z and ⌘⇧Z undo and redo your typing. The first column
  stays at the left as the grid scrolls sideways, so you can see which row you are filling in;
  a sideways swipe or the ◂ ▸ marks show the columns off to the side, and the panel is only as
  tall as the cell. ⌘E (C-c C-t, or the toolbar's Text view) shows the text and back, and
  closing the tab with a cell open keeps the cell first. If the file changes on disk while a
  cell is open, Return asks you to confirm which row it goes in. A cell whose quote never
  closes is left alone (⌘E shows the text to fix it). A file over 4 MiB opens as text and says
  why.
- **The spreadsheet grid copies cells and adds and deletes rows.** ⌘C (or M-w) copies the
  current cell's value, not its quoting, and ⌘X, C-w or C-k cuts it; C-y puts the last copy or
  cut in the current cell, and ⌘V still pastes the clipboard. C-o, or Add Row on the toolbar,
  adds an empty row below the current one (as many empty cells as the header, ending in the
  same line break as the row above) and moves to its first cell; C-S-Backspace, or Delete Row,
  deletes the current row. Each row change is one ⌘Z and touches only that row's bytes, so a
  file with CRLF records, LF inside cells or no final newline saves exactly as it was apart
  from that row. A click in the panel under the grid puts the caret there, opening the cell.
- **An open file follows its file on disk.** Every file open in an Editor tab is watched
  (kqueue on macOS, inotify on Linux, a stat poll elsewhere), so when an AI CLI's edit tool,
  `git checkout` or a formatter changes it, a buffer with no unsaved edits reloads in place
  as one undo frame, its caret, mark and scroll kept on their text, and C-/ takes the reload
  back. Over unsaved edits nothing reloads: the header row says the file changed and offers
  Reload (the disk's text; C-/ brings your edits back) or Keep Mine (`keep-buffer-over-disk`:
  your edits stay as they are, unsaved, and Save writes them over the file, which keeps the
  disk's text until then). A file deleted under its buffer keeps the text and offers Keep
  Mine, after which Save writes it again, and the buffer hears the file if it comes back. A
  save that replaces the file by rename is heard as well, as is a change made while the file
  was opening, and a burst of events settles for 80 ms (at most 600 ms) before the file is
  read. Watching a file on a USB drive or network share does not keep it from ejecting.
  `aterm ctl doc ls` shows `disk=changed` while the choice stands, and `act` presses either
  button.
- **amacs undo reaches reloads from disk.** Every change to an open document, yours or the
  file's own on disk, is one labelled undo frame through the editor's one writer, so C-/ walks
  back through all of them in order and the footer names a frame that was not yours ("Undid
  the reload from disk"). Discard Changes and Reload from Disk is a frame too: C-/ brings your
  edits back. The writer labels an agent's edits the same way (`EditorWorkspace::apply`, ready
  for agent apply), and `C-c u` (`undo-agent-edit`) undoes the newest one out of order, as a
  frame of its own that C-/ takes back, or says which later edit to the same text blocks it.
  Undo can no longer fail with "history diverged": a change that went around the writer
  blocks the frames it may have touched, and each refusal says why. Typed characters undo
  together, up to 20 at a time, as in Emacs; a command, a newline or a paste starts a new
  step. C-/ stops at a draft recovered after a crash rather than put the file's text over the
  only copy of it (`revert-buffer` does that, as a step C-/ takes back). The history keeps the
  newest 4096 frames and 32 MiB of undone text, and says once when it starts dropping the
  oldest. The model is `AmacsUndo` (`aterm-models-native`), its five laws read the text and
  the stack, and it is bound to the code by a conformance test with four mutant controls and
  a seeded fuzz of undo and redo.
- **Signed membership records replicate across vault servers, failover subscribers, and Commons control repair.** Every vault server now keeps a grow-only verified membership-record store (`<name>.records`) beside `<name>.vault`, serving `GET /v1/<name>/records?have=<frontier>` as a long-poll and `POST /v1/<name>/records` for verified record ingestion: a stream with a record that fails verification is refused whole, and a record the store will not keep (from a key no member seated, or past its bounds) is left out while the rest are kept. Peer servers pull missing records from each other (`F6`), member subscribers follow records with candidate failover (`F5`), and Commons control endpoints exchange missing membership records after each completed round while staying compatible with `0.145` peers (`F13`). Until a build compiles ALab's genesis digest, the ALab record store takes only a genesis signed with the ALab vault's key, so a genesis another Mac on the network makes up can never claim it first.

- **Each AI email can name the mailbox its sign-in codes arrive in.** `ai-mailbox.toml`
  takes `[[mailboxes]]` entries, each with its own login, URL, password, second password,
  TOTP secret and `receives = [...]` (an exact address, `*@domain` or `*`; the address beats
  its base address, which beats the domain, which beats `*`, which beats the top-level
  mailbox), so the many Proton addresses read one shared inbox while a Gmail or Outlook
  address reads its own. A file without entries reads as before, and an entry uses the
  password the file already keeps for its login (the top-level one, or a per-email one).
  `aterm harness accounts` names the mailbox each row would use, masked (`mailbox(ab…@…)`).
  An entry with no password is never tried and says `has no password yet`, and a mailbox
  that refuses a login is not tried again on that server for 15 minutes, doubling to 6
  hours, by any row or process, so a wrong password cannot lock the inbox.
  `aterm harness accounts mailboxes import <csv> --into <toml> [--dry-run]` fills the
  entries from the filled-in accounts table (a non-blank correction wins over the guess,
  unless it only says `ok`), keeps every existing secret byte for byte, writes with mode
  600, and prints only counts and masked logins.

- **AI CLIs in aterm know to open files for you in amacs.** When you need to fill in, check
  or change a file (a CSV, a config, a draft), every agent's aterm primer and `aterm help`
  inside a tab now tell it to open the file in an Editor tab beside its own, with the caret
  on the line that needs you, rather than print its path, and say how:
  `amacs --no-wait +LINE FILE` returns at once, `amacs --wait FILE` returns when you close
  the tab, and `aterm ctl @self doc read <file-uri>` reads what you have typed so far.
  Claude Code and Codex also get an `open-in-amacs` skill. `aterm ctl @self status` says
  `editor=amacs` where a tab can open one and `editor=-` where none can (a headless aterm,
  or a session in no window).

- **`--host` takes a Mac's short name.** `aterm ctl --host m102 …`, every verb it takes and
  `survey --host m102`, now finds the peer whose host is `m102-macbook-M4-Pro-24GB-500GB`, as
  every verb that names a peer reads a host's leading `m<N>`. Where no peer answers to the word
  otherwise, `--host` also reads it as the rest of a host's short name: its lead word
  (`MacbookAir`), else a word `m<N>` in it (`m27` of `MacbookAir-m27-M5-32GB-4TB`; a chip's
  `M2` or `M5` never), so `m27` names `m27-mini` before `MacbookAir-m27-…`. A short name two
  Macs answer to is refused, naming each with its address, and a word no peer answers to is
  read as before.

- **The survey shows each Mac's AI accounts.** `aterm ctl survey`, `--fleet` and `--host`
  follow each instance's line with one line of its Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build and Kimi
  accounts, as `aterm harness accounts` lists them: each by its label, with its week and
  five-hour use, how long a wall still stands, or that it is not enrolled or signed out
  (`accounts: claude main 7d 42% 5h 10%, work-2 walled 3h · codex codex-1 not enrolled`),
  and a pool whose records could not be read as `unread`, never as one with no account.
  `--json` carries every row of the survey facts' `account` lines (enrolled, condition,
  both windows, when the week resets, when its wall ends and when a session last used it),
  and each session names the account it runs on (`account=`). No email crosses the fleet:
  a label is sent as it is, and one that holds an `@` as `ab…@…`. An aterm before this one
  says nothing of its accounts, which reads as unknown.

- **`aterm ctl --host any spawn agent=claude -` picks the Mac.** One survey of every fleet
  member picks the Mac a Claude Code or Codex worker goes to: of the members that let this
  Mac drive them and have an enrolled, unwalled account of that program, the one whose
  freshest account has used the least of its week, then of its five hours, then the one
  with the fewest busy sessions. It names its choice on stderr (`--host any: chose
  m16-mini.local (192.168.1.16): claude account main 7d 12% 5h 3%, …`), prints the
  worker's `OK <sid>` as `--host <that Mac>` would, and when no member can take the
  worker it says how many answered and how many let this Mac drive them. The worker's
  `await task`, `@<sid> result` and other `@<sid>` verbs under `--host any` follow it to that
  Mac.

- **Kimi Code is an `aterm ai` connection.** `aterm ai` shows a `kimi` row once Kimi Code is
  installed, `aterm ai login kimi` signs it in (its pool's renewal of a row with an email
  where `accounts-kimi.toml` exists, `kimi login` where it does not), and `aterm ai review`
  asks it. Kimi's one-shot mode always runs without asking anything, so a review asks it at
  the `yolo` level only and skips it at `edits`, `ask` or `plan` with that reason. The login
  and usage-limit words it is read by are Kimi Code 2.3.3's own.

- **LAN sharing of ALab tools has a switch and a status word.** Settings ▸ Packages has a
  "Share ALab tools with the fleet" switch, on by default: turning it off is the same as
  `aterm pkg serve-units --off` (this Mac keeps and serves no toolset archive), and turning
  it back on is `--on`. `aterm ctl @self status` says where sharing stands beside `fleet=`:
  `units=serving`, `idle` (on, with fleet members, nothing listening now), `no-member`,
  `off`, or `-` when the package manager is inert, no store location resolves, or no read of
  it has landed in the last 4 s. A word older than 2 s is read again before the reply. The
  Packages page reads the store again whenever it comes to the front, so a terminal's
  `serve-units --on` shows on the switch, and a failed flip says why under the switch rather
  than in the page's headline.

- `aterm db commons-inventory --table <digest>` reports one shared table's locally
  retained operation counts and fingerprints. Missing storage stays distinct from an
  empty table, and exclusions or conflicting declarations leave uninspected counts unknown.

- **Resource Monitor shows the machine's capacity beside its usage.** Disk and RAM show
  used, available and total amounts in normal window widths. GPU rows name the device and
  core count, with measured allocations and unreported memory capacity kept distinct from
  system RAM. The `sys` summaries show the same disk and memory figures.

- Managed Rust builds record freshly created custom build caches without moving their
  outputs. Automatic disk cleanup can find these caches directly, protect every recorded
  workspace and active Cargo writer, and retire them after all their workspaces are gone.
  Existing unmarked output folders stay unmanaged.

- **What codex-alab does in your name shows on aterm's own surfaces.** When codex-alab
  approves a box or a plan, answers a question, keeps going, resumes past an error or limit, or
  asks its agent to land in a tab, that tab's Autopilot chip lights the act, its hover lists it
  (`codex-alab: ✓ approved 14:05`), and the Settings ▸ Harness row says
  `last: codex-alab: ✓ approved 14:05` and `today: codex-alab did 3 kept going`. Its landing
  shows as the chip's landed face, as before, and is counted. WHAT THE HARNESS DID gives
  codex-alab a row of its own (`codex-alab did`), so aterm's own counts still say only what
  aterm's harness did, and `aterm harness ledger @<tab>` lists each act codex-alab records,
  landings, restarts onto a new build and points left to you included. Before, these surfaces
  counted only tabs aterm's harness drove.

- **A codex-alab tab says when codex-alab stopped typing into it.** codex-alab stops typing
  into its own tab as aterm's harness does, when its agent answers with the same reply twice and
  no work, or six replies in a row with no work, and it now tells aterm so on its claim. While
  that claim stands, `aterm ctl status` prints `held=same-reply` or `held=no-work` for the tab,
  its Settings ▸ Harness row and its menu bar worker row lead with `codex-alab stopped typing:
  <why>`, and its hover and the Overview say `driven by aterm (land: codex-alab stopped
  typing)`. As with aterm's own stop, none of them says it while the tab reads landed or quiet
  (a person's own exchange). The stop goes when codex-alab types again or its claim ends. Before,
  all of these said nothing of it, and `held=` read `-` while codex-alab had stopped. A
  codex-alab that does not tell its stop is shown as before.

- **A codex-alab tab says why its landing still holds.** codex-alab asks its agent to land under
  Land as aterm's harness does, and aterm now shows what a codex-alab tells it of that on its
  claim: when it asked, how many times it nudged since, and what held the last reply it judged.
  While that claim stands the menu bar counts the tab `landing`, `aterm ctl status` prints
  `land_held=`, `land_nudges=` and `land_since=` for it, and its menu bar worker row, its Overview
  line, its hover and its Settings ▸ Harness row say why in codex-alab's name (`codex-alab: not
  landed yet: 2 unpushed commits · 3 nudges`). As with aterm's own hold, none of them says it once
  the tab reads landed or quiet, or another mode. The hold goes when codex-alab lands, leaves Land
  or its claim ends. Before, all of these said nothing of it. A codex-alab that does not tell its
  hold is shown as before. aterm's own hold now shows on the menu bar only while aterm's harness
  holds the tab, as `status` and Settings already required.

- **A codex-alab tab's NEEDS YOU shows every need.** When codex-alab's agent names several things
  only you can give, aterm now shows what a codex-alab tells it of them on its claim, each need
  whole and in the agent's order, as it shows aterm's own harness's: the menu bar's row says the
  first and gives the next two a row of their own one level in (at most 8 such rows in the menu,
  the rest counted as `(+N more)` on the tab's last row), the tab's hover gives every need it was
  told a `Needs you:` line, and its banner and Settings ▸ Harness row say the first need whole.
  codex-alab tells at most 32; any past them are still counted, as its own entry counts them.
  Before, a codex-alab tab showed only its first need, cut short, and how many more stood. The set
  goes when codex-alab takes its need down or its claim ends. A codex-alab that does not tell its
  set is shown as before.

- **A codex-alab tab's session log has turns on a build nobody has measured yet.** Its rollout is
  read as Claude Code's unmeasured builds are, marked `state=partial`, so prompts, tool steps,
  durations and tokens appear, and its working and idle reports open and close each turn
  (`src=engine conf=claim`); a turn they have not opened yet opens from the rollout itself
  (`src=transcript conf=strong`), as on Claude Code. `aterm ctl status` says `rollout=partial`
  there, and `rollout=unknown-meta` where the rollout's `session_meta` names no build the log can
  say or a `history_mode` it does not know.

- **A codex-alab tab's turns stay whole when its rollout is read late or stops being read.** A
  rollout first read after some turns ended (Autopilot switched on mid-session) names the turns
  its working and idle reports logged, one turn each; where the rollout stops being read
  (Autopilot switched off, the file gone) those reports log the turns again; each turn starts
  fresh at the report that opens it; and a turn stopped with Esc, where the rollout says so
  before the idle report, closes `out=interrupted`.
- **The ALab vault's admin Mac forms the default fleet by itself.** On the Mac that holds
  the ALab vault's admin key, the converge pass now forms a fleet with `aterm fleet init`'s
  code where the vault publishes no default fleet, and publishes its join code to every
  member. A Mac that joins the vault then finds the fleet waiting, with nothing typed
  anywhere. Every member can drive the admin Mac that formed it, as every member can drive
  every other, unless you set a level there. Only the ALab vault and only an admin act: a
  member, and a personal vault, never form or publish one, and neither does an admin Mac
  whose vault sync you turned off (`aterm secrets agent off`). Before it forms a fleet it
  reads the vault itself, so a Mac whose copy is behind joins the fleet already published
  instead of forming one. Two admins never make two: the vault keeps the first publish and
  refuses the second, which then finds the other's code, withdraws the fleet it formed for
  its publish (nobody joined it) and joins the vault's. A fleet you made by hand is
  published only by your `aterm fleet publish`. `aterm fleet leave` (its `fleet-off`
  record) turns it off, a level you set with `aterm fleet allow` stands, and a fleet you
  made or joined by hand is never replaced. The step opens only files, with no keychain and
  no dialog. Its publishes from an aterm window wait while macOS has not let aterm use the
  local network, and never ask; the vault subscriber's pass publishes on the network its own
  syncs already use.

- **A codex tab's hover says how much context it has left.** It reads `codex working · ctx 40%
  left`, with the ⚠ a Claude tab's hover shows at 15% or under, from the figure codex's own rollout
  counts. The tab's session log also marks the context at each tenth it crosses and codex-alab's
  goal as it goes on and off, as it does for Claude Code.

- `aterm secrets sync --diagnostic` reports a bounded outcome without secret values,
  filenames or raw errors. Automatic account recovery uses it to distinguish busy local
  state, network or timeout failures and source refusals from an unclassified sync failure.
  Previously recorded `exit 1` failures remain unattributed.

- `aterm ctl @<session> harness recovery` reads the account recovery state shown in that
  session's menu: known and eligible accounts, blockers, sign-in or switch progress and
  observed timing. It distinguishes missing observations from unknown or zero capacity
  and does not trigger a login, probe or retry.

- **The harness claims the free credits Claude Code offers you.** When Claude Code has a
