  write the bus's folder at once, and an `aterm fabric off` typed while the upkeep restarted
  the broker could have that broker come back up after it. The upkeep now leaves the bus for
  its next pass while an `on` or `off` runs, and an `on` or `off` waits (up to 5 minutes) for
  the upkeep's step, then runs whole.

- **The upkeep leaves a broker you run yourself alone.** `aterm fabric on --service none`
  now records that you run the broker, and the upkeep no longer loads a launchd job that an
  earlier `aterm fabric on` left installed once your broker stops. `aterm fabric on` without
  `--service none` hands the broker back to launchd or systemd.

- **A bus job launchd loaded from older settings is reloaded.** Where launchd still ran the
  broker from settings older than the ones on disk, the restart after an update restarted
  those older settings. It now unloads the job and loads the settings on disk.

- **`aterm fabric off` stops a broker launchd would not describe.** Where `launchctl print`
  said nothing, `off` read the job as not loaded and removed its settings while launchd kept
  the broker running. It now unloads the job anyway, and reports a failure unless launchd then
  says it holds no such job.

- **A failed broker restart under systemd is tried again.** Where `systemctl --user restart`
  failed after the unit file was rewritten, the next pass read the new file beside the old
  broker as current. The unit it replaced is now put back, so the next pass writes it again
  and restarts the broker.

- **A test build of aterm no longer becomes the message bus's program.** The upkeep a window
  starts turned the bus on from any aterm build, and where no `aterm` was on its `$PATH` it
  named that build's own file in the broker's launchd job, so deleting the build left a job
  that could not start. It now turns the bus on only from the installed app or where an
  `aterm` is on `$PATH`.

- **The ALab fleet's code stays removed when an admin removes it.** The admin Mac that
  published the default fleet's join code published it again on its next pass after an admin
  removed it from the vault (one that leaked, say). It now leaves it removed and says what to
  do: `aterm fleet publish` puts it back, and `aterm fleet init --rotate` then `aterm fleet
  publish` replaces it. It reads the vault itself before it says so, so a Mac whose copy of
  the vault is behind is brought up to date instead.

- **The upkeep waits for a vault update instead of failing.** On the ALab vault's admin Mac,
  an upkeep pass that ran while the vault was being updated failed its fleet step and exited
  with an error; it now leaves that step for its next pass.

- **`aterm machines` records each step that failed in its change journal.** The agent that
  applies a machine's baseline journaled only the changes it made; a step that failed is a
  line of its own now, with its reason.

- **A failed upkeep step keeps its error in aterm.log, and the change journal records it.**
  The upkeep's one log line cut each step's reason at 160 characters, so a long one lost the
  error it ended on. A failed step's reason now keeps its start and its end (the error), up
  to 480 characters. The change journal (`converge/journal.ndjson` in the state directory)
  now adds a line for each step that failed, naming why, after the line of the change it
  tried.

- **The opt-in limit reset reads Claude Code 2.1.312's words, and still never takes the
  once-a-week reset.** With `[harness] limit_reset` on, a 5-hour or full reset on 2.1.312 was
  backed out at its confirmation (`Refills your 5-hour limit now` did not read), and the check
  that stops every other rule from choosing a reset did not know 2.1.312's once-a-week row
  (`Reset your 5-hour limit now`). Now the confirmation reads on 2.1.312 as on 2.1.311, and only
  where it names exactly the limits its kind refills (any other spelling, a name Claude Code
  never draws there such as `Weekly` or `Fable`, or both builds' words at once, is kept with Esc,
  on 2.1.311 too); and that row, on either build, is never pressed by any rule. No rule had
  chosen it.

- **A Claude Code reply too fast for the screen is a turn in the session log.** On every
  Claude Code build aterm has not measured (all but 2.1.303) a prompt answered within about
  a second left no turn anywhere: the screen looks at the agent at most four times a second
  and never saw it working, and the transcript opened a turn only on a build aterm had
  measured. The transcript's prompt now opens that turn on every build (`src=transcript`,
  `conf=strong` until the build is measured), so it reaches the log, `brief`, the bus and
  `aterm ctl await log close=turn`. On an unmeasured build the transcript still never
  closes or overrules a turn the screen opened. A tool step its turn's close cut off
  (`out=gone`) now takes the transcript's result instead of staying `gone`.

- **A box or question you answered no longer reads as escalated.** When the harness handed a
  box or a question to you and you (or `ctl key`) answered it, the session's need turned to
  `escalated` for a quarter of a second, until the harness took its ask down, so
  `ctl status`, `await log need`, the tab's clause, `brief`, `fabric brief` and
  `aterm link notify --on need` all reported a fresh need right after the answer. The
  harness's ask about a box or question is now that step's need and ends with it. The
  harness's `act word=escalate` is also written when it escalates, on the box, instead of at
  your answer on the tool step beside it. A box that an input stall or a redraw took off the
  screen unanswered keeps its escalation when it comes back.

- **aterm's own log no longer keeps what a supervised agent's screen said.** The harness used to
  write each line of its review into `aterm.log` whole: the reply's last line, a box's command,
  the answer it typed to a question. It now logs each line's words, sequence number and the
  length of its text (`harness @s-…: EVENT idle seq=12 text=48B`). A startup or held deadline's
  task line names its mark and the attention's length, never the attention it raised, and a
  task's exit line keeps the record's words, never its `attention=`. The text stays where the
  harness keeps what it acted on, its 0600 journal and ledger (`aterm drive ledger`).

- **aterm's own log keeps words and numbers, never another program's text or your config
  values.** `aterm.log` used to write whole: the command a supervised agent is told to resume
  with (its system prompt, the directories it was given), a Claude Code footer row it could not
  read, the text of a caught panic (std's messages quote what they cut or compared), an
  `aterm.toml` line that did not parse (in the app's own lines and in a package update's output
  the app copies in), the fabric bridge's command line, a `font_family`,
  `universal_control` or `[packages] prefix` value, a tab's label taken from its program's title,
  a message's title, an exception's reason and `appnotice` text. Each is now logged as its kind
  and length (`run the told command (212B)`, `str-slice panic (48B)`,
  `TOML error at line 2, column 25`, `fabric bridge started: aterm (9 args)`, `title=31B`), and a
  tab by its session id (a Stop Worker message is keyed by it, never by the tab's label). The
  text keeps the place it already had: the tab's mark and the Messages list, Manual, stderr, and
  the crash and harness-fault reports.

- **Sixel images whose final 6-row band is only partly painted no longer fail closed near the
  4 Mi-pixel raster limit.** The Sixel decoder previously rounded its capacity request up to all
  six rows of the current band even when only lower-numbered bits were set, dropping valid rasters
  whose painted `width × height` fit within `SIXEL_MAX_PIXELS` when the band-rounded height did not.

- Corrupt compressed scrollback blocks with zero or out-of-range LZ4 match offsets now fail
  decompression instead of silently copying earlier bytes on the fast decode path.

- **Background opacities just under `1.0` stay translucent on glass, and `DECSCA`-protected
  characters keep their text in row formatting.** `background_opacity` values in `[0.998, 1.0)`
  no longer round background-quad alpha up to solid `255` while the window is still marked
  translucent, and `Row`'s `Display` and `Debug` formatters no longer treat `DECSCA`-protected
  cells as wide-glyph continuations.

- (developer tool) **`verify` no longer ends a check for time it spent waiting for a core.**
  On a Mac busy with other builds, a check's ceiling (`--timeout`, 3 h) counted the time its
  processes were ready to run but given no core as work, so a lint that was still making
  progress was killed at 3 h. The ceiling now leaves that time out, as it already left out
  waits for a lock or for capacity, and the kill line says how long the check waited for a core.
  A check that gets no CPU and does no I/O for 10 s still counts as hung. verify also runs
  compile-only checks at utility QoS only while someone has used the keyboard or mouse in the
  last 10 minutes.
- **`result full` shows a codex-alab worker's whole exchange, and a codex report missed at
  its landing is found later.** `aterm ctl @<worker> result full` on a codex-alab worker always
  answered `ERR result unavailable why=no-transcript`; it now shows the exchange from the task's
  prompt to the end of the worker's rollout, as it does for Claude Code. A codex-alab report not
  yet written when the worker landed, or a rollout aterm could not find then, stayed unavailable
  for good; the next `result` now reads that turn again, and keeps the report once it is there.

- Network State keeps the remembered-machine count visible while observation is
  waiting or unavailable, where the compact row has room.

- **A window no longer starts Grok Build sign-ins that cannot finish.** A window
  renewed a due Grok Build login of your pool (`accounts-grok.toml`) by itself, as it
  does a Codex or Kimi Code one. Each try requested a new xAI device code and then
  stopped at accounts.x.ai's bot-protection page, which aterm's headless browser cannot
  pass and aterm never works around, and it tried again every six hours: up to four
  device codes a day for each Grok Build login that was due or that a session needed. A
  window now starts none. `aterm harness accounts login <label> --cli grok`, which you run
  and approve, signs it in, and the accounts dashboard, the due-login notice, `aterm
  harness accounts --cli grok` and `aterm harness accounts stats --cli grok` name that
  step. Codex and Kimi Code logins still renew by themselves.

- The Network State overview shows its original source observation time, making
  new observations distinguishable from retained ones.

- **One entry that will not go no longer strands a whole build cache.** Every removal the
  build cache's pass makes (a build directory renamed aside, a stage of its stale parts, a
  leftover stage, a tooling entry, verify's old target directories, and `aterm pkg machine
  apply`'s removal of the retired verify gate's leftovers) now removes every entry
  it can instead of stopping at the first it cannot. An entry aterm's own tools left
  unremovable is made removable first, inside the tree being removed only (a stage of the
  build cache, or the retired gate's snapshot and cells lane beside a checkout): on macOS its
  extended ACL is
  cleared (a test scratch's `group:everyone deny delete`, left by a run killed before its
  guard ran, had kept a 260 GB stage at `reclaimed 0 GiB` pass after pass), and a folder gets
  its owner's `rwx` back. The removal walks as `remove_dir_all` walks, by descriptor, so a
  folder swapped for a link or for another folder mid-way leads nowhere outside, no path is
  too long, and no tree is too deep. An entry is changed by its name only once its folder is
  its owner's alone and the name still reads as the entry judged, so a name swapped in the
  meantime is never what gets changed. Nothing is followed through a link, nothing on another
  volume is entered (one mounted at the stage included), a file also named outside the stage
  is never changed, an entry whose attributes cannot be read is left alone, and another
  user's entry is left as it is, a file of theirs in a folder of yours included (one `sudo`
  build can leave one). A stage something still stays in is kept for the next pass and costs
  only itself: each stage now takes a name of its own (`.cargo-build.removing-1` beside a
  `.cargo-build.removing` that keeps an entry, and so on, never over another entry), so the
  next build directory of the same workspace, a live one's stale parts, verify's next old
  target directory and the next copy of the same pinned tool are staged beside it and go in
  the same pass, where one stuck stage used to keep every later one of them for good. A stage
  is reported once a pass: the disk relief line, `aterm pkg machine cache clean` and the
  window's disk ledger say how many entries stayed, name the first few, and count the bytes
  that went. `aterm pkg machine cache` lists a build directory or tool as going only while a
  stage name is free beside it and it can be moved there (on macOS: you may delete it, so no
  `uchg` flag or `deny delete` ACL holds it and its folder takes the change; elsewhere: you may
  write its folder; and it is on the stage's volume), and the pass asks to remove only such an
  entry. verify names an earlier stage of an old target directory that still keeps an entry
  instead of reporting the directory removed, and tries it again on later runs once the
  directory itself is gone.

- **`aterm pkg machine apply` no longer leaves the retired verify gate's snapshot half
  removed for good.** It removed the snapshot (`<checkout>-verify.noindex`) with `git worktree
  remove --force`, which stops at the first entry it cannot delete but drops git's record of
  the worktree anyway: what was left was no longer a worktree, so every later plan kept it, and
  its cells lane with it, as `git does not list it`. Once the plan proves the snapshot clean,
  its `.git` file goes first (one that will not go leaves the snapshot whole, still a
  worktree, for the next apply), then its tree through the build cache's remover above, and
  then git's record of that one worktree alone (`git worktree remove --force` once the tree is
  gone, or its own entry under `.git/worktrees` when something stayed): no other worktree's
  entry, nor the submodule repositories kept in one, goes with it. git is asked again just
  before, and again after, so a lock taken after the plan, or while its record goes, keeps it
  listed and the apply says so. When an entry still stays (a file flagged `uchg`, another
  user's), the apply says how many stayed and names the first few, and puts back the
  snapshot's `.git` file, so the next apply knows the rest again. A snapshot left half removed
  (its `.git` naming a worktree record git no longer has, by this apply or an older aterm) is
  judged on what is left and goes once no file in it has been written for 7 days; the folders
  the removal itself changed do not count. A snapshot `git status` cannot read now says what a person
  must do, repair it or remove it, and when its submodule borrowed objects from a store that is
  gone (an `objects/info/alternates` entry naming a removed worktree's), names the submodule
  and the store, in one line instead of git's raw errors. A snapshot that stays keeps only its
  own cells lane: another checkout's, whose snapshot is gone, goes.

- aCaffeine removes the temporary state files that cut-short saves left in aterm's
  support folder. 0.145.0 started it for every window argument it then refused, so
  an old `aterm caffeine` login job, run every 10 s, left one in most of its runs.
  Each launch of an ordinary window, and `aterm pkg self-uninstall`, now removes
  those over an hour old whose process is gone, along with those that writes cut
  short left of its update bridge's pid file, of its job plists (in its session
  folder and `~/Library/LaunchAgents`), and of all of these under the old
  `caffeine` name.

- aCaffeine's start-up lines in `aterm.log` (what it removed, and why it could
  not start or keep the Mac awake) are no longer lost: its thread logged before
  the window had installed its logger, which drops what comes first. It now
  waits until the window has set up its logging, at most 5 s. If its thread
  cannot be started at all, the window logs that once its logger is up (on
  stderr when no thread can start).

- The Commons runtime's warning in `aterm.log` that its automatic control repair
  refused the local configuration or trust state is no longer lost when it comes
  before the window has installed its logger. A refusal is reported only when
  the status changes, so a lasting one that came that early was never logged at
  all. Its warning that it could not start, which a window always had before
  that logger, is logged once the logger is up, or printed on stderr when no
  thread can start to log it.

- A window started from a shell that still carries an older update's
  descriptor-limit variables says in `aterm.log` that it dropped them. It
  dropped them before too, but its line came before the window had installed
  its logger and was lost.

- Network State no longer labels an observer active when its local network
  sockets are unavailable or no usable interface remains. The explanation now
  follows the same transport evidence as the displayed state.

- The Network State overview keeps the observer's blocking reason ahead of
  service metadata, so a short window explains why observation is waiting or
  unavailable. Explanations wrap or shorten to fit the panel.

- Accounts and Secrets status preserves the age of its original read through
  cached or busy reads. An expired observation stays unknown after a clock rollback,
  including when the window first reads it after the observer has stopped.

- Network State expires each peer's reachability independently of the observer's
  heartbeat and refreshes the peer cells and open details when it expires. Cached
  observations and local relays preserve their original age, so a stalled observer
  cannot look current again after the system clock moves backward.

- A command line that aterm's window answers at once (`aterm --list-fonts`) or
  refuses (a mistyped word) no longer starts aCaffeine, which then kept the Mac
  awake with no window open. Run without a terminal (from a script, a login
  item or an agent's shell), a command line that no verb or other route of the
  front door takes goes to the window, and the window started aCaffeine and the
  Commons runtime before its parser answered or refused. The parser now runs
  first on macOS and Linux, as it already did on Windows.

- **Rewind shows past inline and Kitty images, steps Kitty animation frames, and carries them
  across `aterm ctl rewind check` keyframes.** Inline images (`OSC 1337` and sixel), Kitty
  graphics (stored images, animations, variants, cell placements, relative and floating
  placements, Unicode placeholders, image numbers, chunked transfers, and file/temp/shm loads and
  queries under `allow_kitty_file_transfer`), and autonomous Kitty animation frame advances now
  appear when you open or step Rewind — on the past screen and in its scrollback — keep fast fork
  caching along image-heavy chains under the fork byte cap, and replay across Rewind keyframes in
  `rewind check` without taking a divergence keyframe or recording host paths or clipboard reads in
  exported traces. Distinct image payloads retained by a keyframe count against `rewind_budget_mb`
  and `rewind_total_mb`.

- Private release preparation compiles exported source with the Trust compiler's
  unverified lane, matching the release policy without starting formal proofs.
  Compiler and test failures still refuse staging. Harness version notes now go
  under the actual Unreleased heading when introductory prose mentions its name.

- The Accounts status distinguishes missing local Commons catalog storage from
  missing account proposal storage, and explicitly keeps that separate from the
  harness roster.

- Network history keeps exclusive ownership while compacting a checkpoint. A second
  local aterm can no longer acquire the replacement log mid-checkpoint or write through
  an old file handle, which could leave observation history degraded while repair kept running.

- Automatic upkeep can renew an existing local Claude account linked to Commons
  using a fresh root-approved preparation and an available unattended sign-in
  route. It retains one-use approval consumption and full provider identity checks;
  a refusal never falls back to an ordinary unguarded renewal.

- **Sparkle's paper gold on a light theme is recorded by `aterm ctl aos`.** Each typing-glow
  frame now records whether the glow wears Sparkle's paper gold on a light theme under
  `momentum-glow.state+events` v2, so `aterm ctl aos attach` records and replays that glow
  instead of refusing it, and switching to or from Sparkle on a light theme keeps an active
  recording attached.

- **A seamless update no longer stands down on a passing harness supervisor check.** The
  final Commit now reserves the harness supervisor's state before taking session claim guards
  and marks worker stops only once those claims match, so a background supervisor pass running
  at the same moment cannot make a valid held update reject itself as new activity.

- **A sign-in stopped by Cloudflare's bot check now says so.** When claude.ai or a vendor's
  sign-in page answers aterm's headless browser with Cloudflare's "Just a moment..." check,
  aterm waits for it to clear by itself and presses nothing on it, through the check's own
  reloads. If it has not cleared after 90 seconds, the sign-in ends as a failure, and the
  account's record names the bot check and the host it was on. Before, the record said
  "exceeded maximum steps" or that the page waited for a person. aterm does not ask you to
  step in, and tries again later: Claude Code's sign-in on its usual backoff, from 15 minutes
  up to 6 hours, and a Kimi Code or Codex account's background renewal 6 hours after the bot
  check on its record, a restart of aterm included, rather than every 15 minutes. A renewal
  you run yourself starts at once. It never tries to get past a bot check: no changed user
  agent, no hidden automation, no clicking the check, no solver and no borrowed clearance
  cookie. In Claude Code's record of the routes tried, a headless browser that no route used
  is now listed as "installed; not run" rather than "found".

- **A login item from aCaffeine's old name no longer runs every 10 seconds.** 0.145.0
  renamed `aterm caffeine` to `aterm acaffeine` and said the old launch jobs were gone. But
  an Enable at Startup turned on under the old name stayed in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` when
  its mug was not running at the update, or did not hear the new aterm's answer in time. (A
  running mug that heard it turned the item off as it ended.) At every login the item ran
  `aterm caffeine serve`, which 0.145.0 does not know: it exited 2, so macOS started it
  again about every 10 seconds all session. `aterm caffeine serve` now removes that login
  item and exits 0. It also ends the keep-awake an old mug leaves running across its update
  restart, which otherwise held the Mac awake for up to 21 minutes. Every ordinary aterm
  window also removes old login items whose aterm is gone or is that window's own. While no
  old mug holds its lock, the window also removes the old mug's copies of aterm in
  `~/Library/Application Support/aterm/caffeine-code.noindex`; one macOS may still be checking
  stays, as `aterm.log` notes, for a later launch to remove once the Mac has been awake 10
  minutes since. `aterm pkg self-uninstall`
  removes those and the rest of what the old name left there: `caffeine.state`,
  `caffeine.bridge` and the `caffeine` folder. The lock, `caffeine.lock`, stays, as
  aCaffeine's does. Every other `aterm caffeine` command says to run `aterm acaffeine`.

- **A busy codex tab reads as busy on the Overview, in Settings ▸ Harness and in its tab hover.**
  codex's screen names no state of its own, so these surfaces read it as `unknown`, quiet or `no
  output lately` while the menu bar and `survey` called it working. They now read what codex says
  about itself (its `working`, `blocked` and `done` reports), as `survey` does, for codex tabs in
  another aterm or on another Mac too; `status agent=` still says `unknown`. Settings reads a
  permission box as `waiting on permission`, not `idle at prompt`, and counts it active. The
  Overview, the hover and the footer now agree on who drives a tab: aterm, while it holds the tab's
  claim or a codex-alab carries the tab under its own proven claim, and never a plain codex.

- Commons table repair now resolves simultaneous LAN connections consistently and
  shares one fresh journal admission across each local batch. Source and custody
  changes are rechecked before authorization. Automatic table discovery and exact
  record retention were verified between two physical LAN machines.

- Claude Code's cursor trail now lights the first text queued after Vim's `i` or
  `a` before INSERT redraws, while keeping NORMAL motion dark after Escape.
  Rejected control writes cannot change the editor-mode evidence.

- **A settings page no longer comes up beside another question.** A bare
  `aterm ctl devtools hand-over` request could bring System Settings up beside macOS's
  Local Network question, a page System State had just brought up, or the Command Line Tools
  installer's password prompt. It now waits as System State's own steps do: while the
  installer or a hand-over panel is up, and for 30 seconds after the Local Network question or
  a Settings pane aterm opened with no panel of its own (macOS does not say when either
  closes). A Developer Tools page `aterm doctor` brought up before aterm read your setup
  approval no longer keeps System State from bringing up its own Developer Tools page for that
  approval, and two Macs sharing a home folder, or a dev build beside the release, each bring
  up their Full Disk Access page once for an approval instead of again after the other's. A
  Developer Tools page the helper panel's Show it brings up now counts for your setup approval,
  so System State no longer brings the same page up a second time.

- **A window whose close stopped on a failed save no longer closes by surprise
  later.** If a window could not close because an Editor tab's file had changed
  on disk, the close stayed pending. The next document save anywhere could then
  close the window without asking, even after you had started a job in one of
  its terminals, opened a new tab in it, or closed every other window. The
  close now finishes only while the window is as it was when you asked: no
  terminal added, no command running in the foreground of one of its terminals
  that was not running there then, and not the last window unless it already
  was. A new command is told from the old one by its process group or by the
  shell integration's command marks; like any window close, this one does not
  weigh jobs left running in the background. Otherwise the close is dropped and
  you close the window again, with the usual running-job and last-window
  questions. Two such closes that finish together no longer quit aterm without
  asking, also when they finish while an update is being applied. Discard
  Changes and Reload now finishes a still-wanted close straight away instead
  of at some later, unrelated save.

- **A window close that stopped on a failed save no longer freezes documents.**
  Moving the window's Editor tab to another window (Move Tab to Next Window)
  left that close behind. A later save could then lock the document in its new
  window, refusing every keystroke and holding an update with a false "document
  checkpoint still running". It could also stop every later window close that
  waits on a save until aterm restarted. Closing the window again after the move
  left the document locked the same way. A window's pending close now goes when
  the window closes or when the documents it waits on leave the window, and a
  dropped close leaves every document it held editable. A close that finishes
  while an update is being applied now stops the update and closes the window
  once it has stood down, instead of leaving a window that could no longer
  close; a Quit that arrives meanwhile drops that close, and the window stays
  with its documents editable if you then cancel the Quit. A tab or pane close
  that waits on a save now follows its tab when the tab moves to another window.

- **A text selection you are dragging keeps going when something happens in
  another tab.** An `aterm edit` tab opening behind yours, or another tab
  closing, ended the drag mid-gesture, so the selection stopped following the
  pointer. The drag now ends only when what is in front changes or your pane
  is laid out again (a zoom, a pane beside or below it closing).

- **A close that waited for an update is logged as whoever asked for it.** An
  `aterm ctl close` (or `invoke close`) that arrived while an update was
  handing over waited and then closed, but the session log recorded it as
  closed by you in the window (`ui-close by=human`), and the window it emptied
  as closed by nobody. It now records the ctl close and who sent it, exactly
  as a close that did not wait.

- **`aterm init` installs the whole ALab toolset, every agent CLI included, with no
  window.** A Mac set up only with `aterm init` (over SSH, with no window ever opened) got
  its shell wiring and the Command Line Tools but no toolset: only an aterm window's first
  launch installed it. `aterm init` now has a `base.pkg.toolset` row that runs the same two
  passes that launch runs, `aterm pkg seed` then `aterm pkg update`, once its other base
  rows are done, so Claude Code, Codex, agy, Muse, Grok, Kimi and the verification
  toolchain all arrive. Like the window, it leaves alone what you said: after
  `aterm pkg uninstall --all`, with Automatic updates off (`[packages].enabled = false`),
  with `[packages].auto_install = false`, or for a program you excluded or uninstalled, it
  installs nothing and its row says why. Like the window's, its update waits to switch the
  Trust toolchain while a build runs from it. A program whose signature check did not
  finish in time leaves the row standing aside in atpkg's words, not failed, and the next
  `aterm init` installs it. A second `aterm init` finds the toolset complete and
  reinstalls nothing. `aterm init --only base.pkg.toolset` runs that row alone, and is the
  one `aterm init` that also runs under a scratch `$HOME`, installing into its store.

- **`aterm pkg doctor` counts a missing agent CLI as a missing part of the toolset.** Its
  toolset row weighed only the programs in ALab's signed index. A Mac without Claude Code,
  Codex, agy or Muse still read "N program(s) active", so a fleet Mac's toolset item, which
  installs only when that row is not ok, never ran `aterm pkg install --default-set` for the
  missing CLI. The row now weighs the same default set that `install --default-set` and
  the update pass after a window's first launch install: the index's programs and the
  agent CLIs in atpkg's default set that serve this Mac. It weighs those CLIs even before
  the index has been read, since atpkg installs them straight from their vendors. A missing
  one reads "the toolset is incomplete: … (muse)", with `aterm pkg install --default-set`
  as the fix, and the count it gives is of the default set's programs alone. One you left
  out with `[packages].exclude` is named ("[packages].exclude leaves out muse") and is not
  called a problem.
- Local Network State reads no longer wait for a busy observation publisher. The
  relay refuses that read and leaves existing observation times unchanged.
- Network State no longer waits for a background publisher's lock on the UI thread.
  A busy read keeps the previous observation and its timestamp until the next update.

- **`aterm link notify --on need` runs its command once for each need a session raises.**
  0.145.0 kept one word per session: a notifier started over a standing need ran the command
  for it at the session's next record, a question in a session older than the notifier's
  window never ran it, a failure ran it again once a question that outranked it was
  answered, and a node's reattach ran it again for the needs it restored. Now a need is its
  word and the record that raised it, so each one runs the command once: a need already
  standing when the notifier starts never does, a question or a failure in an old session
  does as soon as the notifier reads the record that raised it, and a node that drops off
  the bus keeps its sessions' needs, so its reattach runs nothing. `--on need:<word>` takes
  only the needs a session's fold raises (`approval:<kind>`, `question`, `wall:<kind>`,
  `unresponsive`, `failure`, `escalated`, `exited`), with `need:approval` and `need:wall`
  taking each of their kinds, and refuses words that never ran it, such as `need:review` or
  `need:ask`; a need a consumer claims with `aterm ctl … mark - need` never runs it, and
  `aterm ctl … await log need` waits on those. A need whose command failed, or that `--rate`
  dropped, runs it again at its session's next record, after a restart or in the next
  `--once` run too. A notifier's state from 0.145.0 carries over without running anything
  again.

- **A session whose Mac dropped off the bus is shown older.** A bridge writes its will as
  `state=away`, and `aterm fabric brief` and the Overview's chip took only the old
  `state=gone` for a node gone, so a crashed node's unfinished sessions stayed fresh and
  counted in the title's "N need you". Either word now marks them `partial` `node-gone`.

- **`aterm fabric tail --json` prints records in offset order under a node's cap.** A
  node's cap does not grant the whole fleet, so `tail` reads each part of the bus the cap
  reads on its own stream, and it printed their records as they arrived: mail could come out
  ahead of an older presence row. A program that stopped after a line and resumed with
  `--from` past that line's `off`, as `tail` says to after a lost link, never saw the records
  printed late. `tail` now prints every record once, offsets strictly increasing, in the
  table and under `--json` alike. It waits on a part only while that part is still replaying
  what came before, and asks the broker where an idle part stands instead of waiting for it,
  so a live record still prints as it lands. Should the broker stop answering for 30 s, the
  error names the `--from` to resume at.

- **A build no longer claims disk for another build root's stale files.** verify, `ship
  trust run` and the lab's VM boots claim what their last runs wrote, or, where their
  directories have been emptied since, what those directories held at a run's peak. A worktree
  whose build directory had grown to 287 GiB of stale builds before the build cache moved kept
  those peaks in its record, so a verify there claimed 263 GiB although no run had written more
  than 0.2 GiB: waiting could never admit it, and `--admit now` held the whole amount against
  every other build on the Mac. A peak is now claimed for no more than what a run writes into
  empty directories (verify's 72 GiB). What a run measured itself writing is still claimed in
  full. A claim that waits, starts short under `--admit now` or is refused now first says why
  it needs what it does (`disk: claims …`): the runs it was read from, the cold budget, or that
  budget capping a peak, and while it does; before, the wait line named the figure alone and
  the reason was said only after the run.

- **A build waiting for more disk than is free no longer stalls every build behind it.**
  verify, `ship trust run` and the lab's VM boots claim the disk they will write before they
  start. A claim needing more than its volume has free above the floor can only start once
  space is freed, because what other builds wrote stays on the volume after they end. Such a
  claim now waits without reserving that disk, so a later build whose need fits starts at once;
  it reserves again once its need fits, and is relieved again then, sized for the builds that
  went first, when one of them reserves disk its last relief was not sized for (a relief that
  already counted every one of them is not asked again, whatever they reserve now). Its wait
  line says that it waits for space to be
  freed and that `--admit now` starts it at once, and the room asked of the window's disk
  watch no longer counts its need.

- **A build no longer rewrites its build directory under a claim sized for a warm one.**
  Before a build waits for disk, its relief frees what nobody uses: the build cache's pass,
  which takes any build directory unwritten for 30 days, and inside aterm the window's disk
  watch, whose own passes empty idle build directories. That could be the build's own, which
  it then wrote again from empty while its claim, sized on what that directory held before,
  reserved only what a warm run adds, so the builds admitted beside it were counted against
  room it was about to fill; and the record kept for its next run said it had grown by
  nothing. The build's own pass now keeps the build's directories, and frees the rest as
  before: a trade of the room a bloated directory of its own would free for a warm build, so
  on a volume where only that directory could go, the build waits for space instead of
  starting cold. After a relief that removed anything, or asked the window's watch, and again
  at the look that admits a build that waited (another build's pass or the watch's own can
  empty its directories meanwhile), they are measured again: a claim that grew says so
  (`disk: its directories hold … now, not the … its claim was sized on, so it claims …`) and
  waits again with that figure, behind the claims that asked meanwhile (or is refused, where
  the volume can never hold it), and what the build writes is measured from there.

- **`aterm pkg capacity` says which waiting builds hold back the ones behind them.** Each
  waiting claim's disk now says how much it reserves against the claims behind it on its own
  volume, and one needing more than that volume has free above the floor is marked
  `unservable`: it waits for space to be freed and reserves nothing, so it holds back no build
  behind it. Each volume a claim's disk is on gets its own disk line, and a claim whose volume
  could not be read says so. `--json` gives every claim `reserved_disk` (bytes, `null` when it
  needs no disk or its volume could not be read) and `unservable` (`true` or `false`, `null`
  where its volume could not be read), by the same reckoning the queue admits by.

- **Network State explains which account data it reports.** The selected account
  service is labelled **Commons account catalog** and identifies its shared
  proposals separately from harness rosters and provider sign-in readiness.

- **Account recovery timing stays visible when no retry time is known.** The menu
  explicitly shows **Next event unknown** and keeps timing near the first blocker,
  ahead of long route-detail lists. Unavailable observation times also say unknown.

- **Account waiting reasons use plain language.** Pending usage checks, reset
  offers, restart holds and refused restart requests now have explanations in
  the recovery details instead of internal reason codes.

- **The account menu names its configuration-folder action accurately.** The item
  now says **Open configuration folder** and opens a terminal in aterm's
  configuration directory. The screen reader uses the same name.

- **The account menu can copy the complete recovery details.** Long route failures
  and sign-in instructions clipped by the menu remain available through **Copy
  recovery details**, along with the observed state, account counts and timestamps.
  Opening the menu does not copy anything or start a sign-in attempt.

- **The account panel stops calling an expired deadline the next event.** A retained
  decision keeps its original observation time and phase, but an elapsed wait no
  longer appears as a future retry. Positive subsecond waits round up rather than
  appearing due in the current second. Retry scheduling is unchanged.

- **Account details show local sign-in activity time.** The account menu keeps the
  blocking reason first and shows the supervisor's recorded activity timestamp on
  its own line, so a recent retry can be distinguished from an older retained failure.
  This is local activity, not proof of successful sign-in or a fresh remote credential.

- **Commons status, account access and revocation no longer trip over aterm's own repair.**
  `aterm db commons-status`, Network State's account access and the Commons repair's
  inventory reads now read the control journal's acknowledged history without its writer
  lock. A long-running aterm verifies each record once and then only what was appended
  since, so a running window no longer makes them busy. Custody observations and journal
  writers (`aterm secrets revoke`, a peer's new record) wait up to a second for another local
  holder instead of refusing at once. Records a peer offers that are already held are
  acknowledged even while the writer is busy. If a holder outlasts the wait, `commons-status`
  reports `control-busy` and Network State shows account access as unknown, without treating
  normal contention as a failed refresh. Corrupt or unreadable state still fails.

- Restoring a terminal preserves pending line wraps under origin mode and horizontal margins,
  including saved cursors and edges changed by rectangle edits, so the next character advances
  instead of overwriting a glyph. Exported histories carry standard cursor-presentation state;
  older readers keep ordinary cursor behavior but approximate those edited-edge and margin cases.

- **Pointer control reaches System Resources and Network State.** Negative rows now cover
  the reserved resource header as well as tab and message rows. Existing message-band
  positions are preserved, and small fonts no longer hit an arbitrary 16-row limit.

- **A Codex worker, review or crash relaunch never runs on your own login while counted as
  another account's.** A Codex account of its own reaches Codex only as `CODEX_AUTH_PATH`, which
  OpenAI's builds (`codex-old`, or `codex` from npm or Homebrew) and codex-alab builds that
  predate it (the store's 0.1.0-dev.13633 among them) ignore: they read and refresh
  `~/.codex/auth.json`, your default login. codex-alab builds from before its cd79a420c read the
  variable but can still share the keyring or a shared Codex daemon across accounts.
  `spawn agent=codex`, `aterm ai review` and the relaunch of a crashed Codex now run under such
  an account only on a codex-alab from cd79a420c on. No such build is served yet; until one
  is, a worker or review starts only on your own login's row (the one with no `dir`): the pool
  picks no other row, and you can still pin one, but a worker or review under that pin is
  refused, naming the pin of your own login's row (`aterm harness accounts use <label> --cli
  codex`; `adopt-default` lists that login first where the roster has no such row). Where your
  own login's row cannot serve, the refusal says why from that row, judged on the usage the
  launch reads: while it is at its limit, the limit and its reset, and that no Codex account
  can run here until then, when that row serves again (no pin is offered, since the next usage
  read would end it); while it is signed out, or `~/.codex/auth.json` is missing, Codex's own
  sign-in in your default home, which `aterm ai login codex` then runs in place of another
  row's and which keeps that row on your own login. While that row is held for another Mac's
  warm set, leased elsewhere, or out of reach because the account broker is unreachable from a
  Mac that is not its home, its fact says so in those words and `aterm ai login codex` signs
  nothing in, saying why at a terminal or none; neither that row nor one whose login still
  works with its renewal due asks you to sign in, in `aterm ai doctor` or in the window.
  On such a build `aterm harness accounts login|renew` refuses that row, by hand or in the
  background, since its staged login would be one of its own that the build never runs; where
  an earlier sign-in already moved the row, the refusal says so instead of naming an
  `adopt-default` that would refuse, and names rotation off (`[harness] accounts = "off"`),
  under which a launch with no pin runs on your own login, and says that this switch also
  turns off the accounts' sync and aterm's own sign-ins and renewals of every AI CLI's
  accounts; a worker refused where the pool picks no account (rotation off with no account
  pinned, or Codex's login kept in the OS keyring, pinned or not) is told instead that one
  whose starter carries no account's `CODEX_AUTH_PATH` runs on your own login, and is told
  rotation is off with no account pinned only where that is why. A worker refused while that
  row is at its limit is held until it resets, and a cold restore moves a Codex session only
  onto that row. Once `aterm pkg update codex` brings such a build, the pool picks
  every row again (`aterm harness accounts use --auto --cli codex` ends a pin). After a
  renewal, the report says whether this Mac's Codex would keep the account's login, and the
  by-hand line says when it will. Signing in, renewing and reading usage never ran on your own
  login while counted as another account's: each runs in a private staging folder or in aterm
  itself.

- **Selected Network State services stay visible in short windows.** Account and secrets
  explanations take priority over general network context. The detail panel uses its full
  width, avoiding the empty second column that unnecessarily wrapped explanations.

- **Network State explains failed service reads.** An account-catalog or vault metadata
  read failure now carries a warning; expected configuration and admission blockers remain
  distinct. Selecting a machine or service wraps long explanations. Cached secrets count
  authorized manifest entries and explicitly distinguish that from file delivery, usable
  provider credentials and current remote state.

- **Macs let in by `aterm secrets password open` now join Commons.** When an admin opened
  a vault at a terminal and said yes to the machines already waiting, those machines got
  into the vault but stayed outside its shared data (Commons), because nothing recorded
  how they were let in. They are now recorded just as the open vault's own approver
  records a machine it lets in, so they share Commons and enroll like every other member.

- **`[harness] accounts = "off"` now turns the accounts' sync off everywhere.** The
  setting turned off only the converge pass's accounts row: the aterm window still synced
  your accounts roster from the vault, the accounts sheet or `[fleet] accounts_source` as
  it kept your accounts, and so did first-run setup, `aterm init` and the sync after
  `aterm secrets join`. With it set, none of them reads a source or writes a roster now,
  for Claude Code's pool or any other CLI's, and `aterm init` shows its AI accounts row as
  not applicable. `aterm harness accounts sync`, which you run yourself, still syncs, and
  automatic sign-ins keep their own switch, `[harness] logins`.

- **`aterm fabric on` no longer fails its proof on a busy Mac.** The proof's note gets a
  minute to come back through the broker, where 5 seconds covered both posting it and the
  wait, so a working fabric on a loaded machine read `proof FAILED`. A wait that runs out
  now says the note did not come back and which grant to check, where it blamed another
  sender's note, and another sender's note delivered first is waited past, not a failure.

- **Network State marks partial retained history.** The observer cell and its
  details disclose when retention limits omitted observations or peers. Repeated
  over-limit peer observations no longer force another history checkpoint.

- **Narrow Claude recovery lines keep the blocker before the retry time.** The
  fitter can omit the timestamp while retaining it in the account disclosure.

- **Stale direct network status becomes unavailable.** Offline, disabled and
  waiting observations now expire like live reachability, preserving history.

- **`aterm link notify` survives a power loss mid-command, and no longer fully flushes per record.**
  A page used to fully flush four files and none of their directory entries, so a power loss
  could undo the page's `firing` line and run the command again as if new. Now the line is on
  the disk before the command runs, and a power loss mid-command runs it again with
  `ATERM_NOTIFY_DUP=1`, as a crash does. A kill just after a page or a `--rate` drop no longer
  charges the page to the budget twice, which dropped a later page, or counts the drop twice in
  `ATERM_NOTIFY_SUPPRESSED`. A record that runs nothing, is not dropped and moves no standing
  value writes nothing: `--on need`, which reads every row a fleet publishes, no longer fully
  flushes its cursor once per row, which made every write to the bus on the same disk wait about
  six times longer on the shipped ordered bus. On macOS a page now takes one full flush, and a
  paged person's ask is released about 1 ms after the bus accepts it, where the pager's full
  flushes held most such releases to about 4.5 ms. On Linux, where every ordered flush is a full
  one, a page now asks for more full flushes than before (7 for an ask or a halt, 9-13 for an
  attention or a need, against 4-6), a cost not yet measured there. The cursor now follows
  within 256 records or a second, and a restart re-reads at most those without running anything
  twice.

- **`aterm link notify` keeps running when its state dir is full.** A follower exited on the
  first write its state dir refused, so the program meant to wake someone for a need stopped
  when the disk filled. Now it warns with the error, keeps what it could not write, and writes
  it again at the next record or tick a second or more later. A page runs its command only once
  its `firing` line is written, so a refused write delays the page and never runs it twice;
  the follower reads nothing past that page, or past a record whose verdict, drop count or
  standing value is unwritten, meanwhile, and writes no cursor past it, so a crash while the
  disk is full neither misses nor repeats a page. `--once` exits 1 and leaves the rest to the
  next run.

- **A blocked Claude recovery shows its current sign-in blocker first.** When no
  alternate is eligible and recovery is waiting or limited, the current login's
  recorded sign-in instruction leads the footer detail. Active recovery actions
  and unknown eligibility keep their existing priority.

- **Claude's account disclosure includes the current login's sign-in blocker.**
  An expired current account no longer loses its recorded sign-in task and failed
  route while alternate accounts' failures remain visible.

- **Account access read failures no longer imply denied membership.** Network State
  marks an unclassified account-session read failure as unknown; definite Commons
  authorization failures retain their specific explanation.

- **Rewind returns memory to macOS and Linux when old history ages out or is forgotten.**
  Heavy output across many recording panes left freed history slices fragmented in the
  allocator, keeping aterm's resident memory up to hundreds of megabytes above its
  `rewind_total_mb` pool after the history was shed. Completed history chains now pack
  small unshared slices into 256 KiB slabs, keyframe grids and evicted history queues
  shrink to fit, and pool sheds and Forget Pane / All History release free allocator pages
  back to the system, keeping twenty flooded panes within the 128 MiB pool across six runs.

- **Other aterm processes can read the local network observer's live view.**
  Network State identifies the supplying aterm and keeps its observation times;
  an unavailable or stale view falls back to retained history.

- **A command's `detail=` names only a program that ran.** `aterm ctl status`, the session
  log, its journal and presence name a running command by its program, read from the line
  you typed. Shell syntax the reader did not model put typed text there instead: an array's
  element (`arr=(one secret two)`), a comment (`make # note; secret`), a continued line, an
  operand inside `[[ ]]` or `(( ))`, a brace list, a pwsh value (`'secret' |
  ConvertTo-SecureString`), a directory zsh's AUTO_CD or fish changed into, or a path you
  typed after handing it to another program (`cat ./secret; ./secret`). The word the reader
  picks is now shown only when it is a shell builtin (`cd`, `export`, `echo`), when it is
  the name the kernel gave a program that started in the command, or when the file your
  shell runs for it (looked up from the command's directory, or on `PATH`, as the shell
  looks it up) is the very file a program started from in the command, compared by device
  and inode, or a `#!` script whose interpreter started. So a link shows the name you typed
  (a native `claude`, `vi`; Homebrew's `python3` only while its first stage is seen, since
  its stub soon re-runs itself as `Python`), and a script its own name (`npm`,
  `./deploy.sh`, a `#!/usr/bin/env python3` tool). When the word you typed is no program
  file that ran (an alias, a function, a path through a variable, a `#!` script whose own
  file was not seen), the first program the command's own job ran stands in for it on macOS
  (`ls` for an alias of `ls`, `sleep` for a function that sleeps, `Python` for Homebrew's
  `python3`), until the word's own name is confirmed; a refused `sudo` shows `sudo`, and a
  program macOS keeps under several names (`git`, `python3` and `make` are one file) stands
  in by the name it was run by. In pwsh, which runs every command in its own process group,
  that group's program stands in too, whatever ran in the tab before; in zsh, bash and fish
  a program of the shell's own group (a command substitution's, a fish handler's) never
  does, from the first command on. A directory zsh's AUTO_CD or fish changed into shows
  nothing, even when a `chpwd` hook runs a program and while aterm is still looking the
  word up on a slow file system, and a missing or pasted path, a file
  that is no program, and a name a process gives itself (a Linux process's `comm`) never
  show their own name. Only programs in the terminal's foreground count, each for one
  command at most, even when you type ahead, and a command whose end was never reported
  stops counting at the next prompt. A prompt hook's program never names a command: aterm
  places each program it sees where the shell's output stood when it started, and the shell
  integration ends a command before zsh's `precmd` function or hooks, bash's
  `PROMPT_COMMAND` (even a hook put ahead of aterm's in it later, as a re-sourced
  `~/.bashrc` does with zoxide's or direnv's, from the next prompt on), a pwsh prompt
  function or a fish `fish_postexec` handler run, and before
  its own prompt code runs a program (the `rm` of a re-key file or a new integration's
  pointer, bash's `stty` terminal repair), and starts it after every preexec hook, so their
  programs land outside it. A hook defined by the very
  line it follows still runs inside that one command, and a fish `fish_postexec` handler
  from your own `conf.d` (which fish reads before aterm's) runs before the command ends. A
  program that exits before aterm reads it, or one a script's own process starts, stands in
  for nothing. A `#!` script in a directory that no `PATH` aterm has seen names shows its
  interpreter, never its own name: macOS hides its own programs' environment, so a `PATH`
  you export in the shell is seen once a program not from Apple runs with it. Each program
  aterm sees costs it a few short, bounded names, never its arguments, and files are looked
  up on a thread of their own, never the one that draws the window: a loop handing a program
  a huge argument no longer grows aterm's memory or slows its window, and a file system that
  stops answering only delays the detail. On Windows nothing reports what ran, so only
  builtins are shown there.

- **A builtin's name after `sudo`, `env` or `nice`, and fish's `begin`, no longer name a command.**
  `sudo -n true` that `sudo` refused showed `true` in `aterm ctl status`, the session log
  and presence, though no `true` ran: a builtin's name now counts only when you type it
  bare, with nothing before it that runs it as a program (`sudo`, `env`, `nice`, `nohup`,
  `exec`, `/usr/bin/time`), so it shows `sudo`; `command true` and `time true` still show
  `true`. fish's `begin; sleep 1; end` showed `end`, and now shows `sleep`.

- **A command's name stays with the command in the session log's ring, across an update and in the journal.**
  Since a command is named only once its program is confirmed, the name is written after
  the command's open record, and under pressure the ring dropped it first: `aterm ctl log`,
  `aterm ctl @<sid> log` and a log carried across a seamless update showed older commands,
  and the running agent's own command, with no name while `status` still had one. The
  record that names a command, an agent's program or model, or the session a restored one
  stands in for, is now kept and dropped together with the open record it names, and a
  journal read that starts in a later file restates it beside that open. Where two records
  name the same thing, the one `status` shows is the one kept.

- **The cursor trail keeps following your typing after you select text or press Escape.**
  In a program that follows the mouse, such as Claude Code in fullscreen, dragging over a
  file path to select it, a click, the scroll wheel, Copy, Select All or a click on a
  tab's own controls left the trail dark for every key you typed next on that line, until
  an arrow key or Return. In the prompt of Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent,
  Escape, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-L and a jump through the scrollback did the same. The trail now
  stays lit. In Claude Code's vim mode, Escape still leaves the trail off for the
  NORMAL-mode keys after it, which move the cursor rather than type, and the trail now
  comes back when you type in INSERT again (after `i`, `a` or another insert command),
  where it used to stay off until an arrow key or Return. In vim mode it also follows the
  keys you type while Claude shows "Press Ctrl-C again to exit", also when you press
  Ctrl-C right after `i`, before Claude shows INSERT. An Escape sent with a guarded
  `aterm ctl key` or `send` (`if=`, `if-gen=`, `if-fp=`, `if-human=`) leaves it off for
  the NORMAL-mode keys after it, as a typed Escape does.

- **An upgrade under `--now` no longer ends a Claude Code reply while its words are still
  being drawn.** Under a status line (aterm's usage tap is one) a reply being written shows no
  busy row, so each look of the live upgrade read it idle, and two looks were enough to take a
  `busy` session status as stale and end Claude Code to restart it. Two idle looks now count in
  a row only when they show the same words above the composer, so a reply that is still
  growing never makes that lag. At a real break this can cost one more look. A status line
  refreshing under the composer does not count as new words. A reply that draws no new words
  between two looks, such as one whose next line Claude Code holds back until it is finished,
  can still be taken for that lag: nothing on its screen tells it from a break.

- **The fabric bridge's log says how a broker subscription ended.** A subscription that read
  nothing from the broker for its 30 s live read deadline was logged as "the broker ended the
  inbox subscription", though the broker had not ended it: nothing had reached the bridge for
  that long. The line now names the end the bridge saw: the broker closing the stream, 30 s with
  nothing read, or the read's own error; and `aterm fabric doctor`'s fix for a `cut-` link
  reason names all three. The link goes down and reconnects as before.

- **The stats deck draws a gridline at every size's start again.** In 0.145.0 a strip
  drew no line where a size began whose boxes are as wide as the size before it: none
  before the 1 minute boxes on a six-hour strip, none before the 10 second, 1 minute and
  1 hour boxes on a four-hour strip, and none before the 10 second boxes on a six-minute
  strip. Each size now starts at a line, whether or not the time scale has room to name
  it.

- **The stats deck draws "aterm crash" only where aterm stopped, from when it stopped.** In
  0.145.0 an update that replaced aterm in place, or a relaunch of the running app, was drawn
  as "aterm crash"; it now draws as "restarted", with the moment between the two drawn as a
  pause. A dev build of aterm running beside the installed app, both keeping the same
  history, took the other's live history for a crash when it started and drew "aterm crash"
  over time that aterm was running, and the two wrote over each other's saved history. Now
  one aterm at a time saves it, and a start beside a running one draws the time since as a
  pause. After a Force Quit or a kill, the crash ran from when the killed aterm was launched,
  so its whole run, its readings and sleeps included, was drawn as one crash; it now starts
  at the killed run's last saved reading. A Force Quit of an aterm that hung while starting,
  before it took a reading, draws its crash from that launch, and the time aterm was off
  before it still draws as paused.

- **Cruise no longer follows every background wake with a second prompt.** When a tab's turn
  ends while the agent's own background work runs, Cruise types its prompt to check on that work
  and keep going, and asks again after 2, 4, 8 … and at most 60 minutes while the agent answers in
  seconds. A background task that finishes (a watcher, an agent, a workflow) starts a turn nobody
  typed, and that turn used to start the wait over, so a session whose watcher woke it every few
  minutes got the prompt after nearly every wake, two turns each time, for hours. A wake now keeps
  the wait growing, and so does a burst of wakes that adds up to little work, or scrolling and
  clicking in the tab. A turn that itself was busy two minutes or more, a message (yours in the
  tab or through Remote Control, or another session's) and a turn that ends with no background
  work left start it over. A reply's text drawn between tool calls no longer counts as the turn's
  end, and the wait still never passes 60 minutes.

- **Cruise's background wait carries across a restart of its harness loop.** Cruise's prompt to
  check on an agent's background work waits 2, 4, 8 … and at most 60 minutes while the agent
  answers in seconds. A restart of the tab's harness loop (a settings change, a seamless update)
  used to start that wait over, so the next turn that ended on background work got the prompt at
  once and the wait went back to 2 minutes. The new loop now takes the wait up where it stood, from the prompts the harness's
  ledger shows it typed and the gaps between them, and the agent's own first wake after the
  restart keeps it growing. A message you sent in the tab after the last prompt, a different
  prompt or a point left to you since, a relaunch of the agent, a switch to Off and back, and a
  last prompt older than its wait by 60 minutes or more still start it over.

## [0.145.0] - 2026-10-27

### Added

- **The paint matrix bounds how tall the rainbow trail stands.** Two new rows type on a
  cleared screen and require the top of the tall body, and of the underline body, to stand
  within set bounds above the typed row, measured from the frames. A build that draws either
  body half or twice as tall now fails them by name; before, every paint row passed it.

- **`git`, `cc`, `make` and friends say the tools are on their way, not "install?".** While a
  new Mac is installing Apple's Command Line Tools, running `git`, `cc`, `clang`, `make`,
  `python3` or another of their names in an aterm shell used to raise macOS's "install the
  command line developer tools?" dialog — once per command. aterm now puts a small shim ahead
  of `/usr/bin` in the shells it opens while setup waits on the tools: the command prints one
  line (`git arrives with Apple's Command Line Tools, installing: about 10 min`) and exits,
  without raising the dialog, and runs the tools' own program the moment they arrive. A tool
  you installed yourself (Homebrew's `git`, say) still wins, and the shim is gone once the
  tools are there or you stop setup. Nothing changes on a Mac that already has them.

- **A Mac that missed the ALab vault at first launch now joins it by itself.** Where the
  first launch finished without a join (the vault was asleep, or this Mac was on another
  network), the aterm window's converge pass looks for the open ALab vault on the network it
  is on and joins it with nothing typed, as System State's Secrets step does. A vault that
  asks a join password or an admin's approval keeps this Mac's request, which its subscriber
  posts again every hour as after any join that waits; no pass joins it again, and System
  State's Secrets row or `aterm init` gives the rest. A Mac an admin removed from its vault
  reads as waiting on a person, never as joined. The pass looks only once macOS has asked
  aterm about the local network, and never from `--check`; after a Don't Allow it never
  looks or asks again. A System State plan without the Secrets vault, or
  `aterm secrets agent off`, keeps the vault out.

- **After an update, the converge pass restarts a message-bus broker still running the
  build the update replaced.** Where `[fabric] command` is set and the broker it names runs
  a program file an update has since replaced, the pass renews it with `aterm fabric on`'s
  own broker step: the job `on` installed is restarted onto the new file at the same path,
  and its plist is left as written. It never turns the fabric on: with no `[fabric] command`
  nothing of the fabric is read. A broker you keep yourself (`--service none`, or one you
  started by hand while `on`'s job is not loaded or runs another process), or one at another
  socket than the command's root, is reported and left as it is.

- **The converge pass now runs by itself after an update, a network move and every half
  hour.** The vault's subscriber starts `aterm init --converge` as it starts (launchd starts
  it again once an update replaced its program), after each version it applies, and once
  this Mac's routes moved or half an hour passed. It never waits for the pass, so a dial of
  the fleet's issuer never holds up its long-poll (or, on an admin Mac, the approver beside
  it), and it runs one pass at a time: one that comes due while another runs, or that found
  another pass holding the lock, runs next. An aterm window starts one at launch and every
  30 minutes beside the subscriber's mend, which reaches a Mac whose subscriber runs a held
  copy of an older aterm; a window whose first-run setup runs starts its lane once the setup
  ends, and the setup's Secrets stage starts one pass as it ends. A pass runs in a session
  of its own, so a subscriber restarting during an update does not end it, and keeps macOS's
  Local Network answer the app's. The pass replaces the subscriber's own `aterm fleet sync`:
  its fleet row syncs from the vault copy already applied.

- **`aterm init --converge` brings a Mac back in line after an update, with no question.**
  It runs one pass. Run by the installed aterm.app, once per build it installs, it re-lays
  the base layer repairs `aterm doctor` makes without asking (command links, shell hooks,
  the shell rc block and shims among them); what doctor asks first (copied commands in
  `~/.local/bin`, a stale rustup trust link) stays doctor's, and one laid is not laid
  again on that build. A pass that could not lay one (the store was busy, it failed) leaves
  it to the next. Then it joins or records the default ALab fleet from the vault copy
  already applied, resyncs the AI accounts roster from its sources (from the subscriber
  only while no aterm window runs), and reports the vault's subscriber, ALab Commons and
  the message bus. Off macOS it leaves the base layer to `aterm doctor`. A choice a person
  made stands: another fleet joined by hand, a subscriber turned off, `[commons] enabled =
  false`, and `[harness] accounts = "off"`, which the pass now reads. `--check` reads the
  same rows and changes nothing. One pass runs at a time (exit 75 while another holds
  `converge/align.lock` in aterm's state folder), and each records itself in
  `converge/aligned.json` beside it and in one aterm.log line.

- **Measure crash recovery from launch to restored tabs.** The explicit
  `verify perf restore-e2e` lane records keeper admission, tab recovery and history import
  for private headless sessions, with the build and machine load beside each reading.
  Missing sessions or a refused experimental arm cannot become a timing entry.

- **The Trust toolchain is usable sooner at first launch, and a LAN Mac can supply it.**
  A toolset archive now decompresses, extracts and hashes *while it downloads* instead of
  after it finishes, so a unit's stage ends about when its download does; the unit that
  carries the Trust toolchain is fetched and lands before the optional units behind it, so
  `targo` works before the rest of the set; and `[packages] peers = ["host[:port]", …]`
  names LAN Macs a download races — a peer's bytes are taken only when they hash to the
  signed digest, so a peer is never trusted, and a corrupted or absent peer just leaves the
  release host's download to finish. `aterm pkg serve-units` (opt-in) serves the archives
  this Mac installs to those peers and keeps each one beside its build until `serve-units
  --off`; no listener opens by default. Every byte still hashes to the signed index before
  it can run; nothing in the integrity gate was weakened.

- **Forget what Rewind kept.** View > Forget Pane History drops the focused pane's kept
  screen history, and View > Forget All History drops every pane's; each pane keeps
  recording from its screen at that moment. The palette and `aterm ctl invoke` offer both,
  `aterm ctl rewind forget` forgets one session, and `rewind forget all` (owner only) every
  session.

- **Rewind keeps to one memory limit.** `rewind_total_mb` (default 128) caps the history
  every pane keeps, and the output still on its way to it, together; past it, the panes
  focused longest ago give up their oldest history first, then all of it.
  `rewind_budget_mb` (default 8) caps one pane. `aterm ctl temporal status` reports
  `pool_used=` and `pool_limit=`.

- **The stats deck's dial steams when the Mac strains.** Above 78 %, where the dial's orange
  glow starts, wisps of steam rise off its face, more of them and denser as the strain grows,
  inside the dial's own space. They move only on the frames the deck's live edge already draws
  after each reading, four in its first second at most, so a hot dial costs no extra frames and
  no timer, and a cool or idle one draws none. There is no steam under Reduce Motion, in
  serious mode, in a window in the background, or while a close-up covers the deck.

- **A program can wait on a session's needs on the bus.** `aterm link notify --on
  need[:<word>]` runs its command once each time a session's need, as `aterm fabric brief`
  folds it from the session's `ev` face, rises to a selected word (none to a word, or one
  word to another). A need that stays standing runs nothing more, across records and
  restarts, however long ago the session raised it: while the notifier holds neither the
  session's start nor a snapshot of all its needs, it runs nothing and clears nothing. One
  that clears and rises again runs it again. A session that exited, or whose node is gone,
  before its close reached the bus clears its need; a session's close raises `exited`,
  which runs the command once, whichever of the two reaches the bus first. The command gets
  `$ATERM_NOTIFY_NEED` (the word) and `$ATERM_NOTIFY_DETAIL` (what the brief shows beside
  it), with the session's `$ATERM_NOTIFY_SID` and `$ATERM_NOTIFY_NODE`. The words are the
  session log's own, and `aterm link notify --help` lists them; any other word is a usage
  error. It reads under the same cap as `fabric brief`.

- **`aterm fabric tail --json` is the bus stream for a program.** It prints one JSON object
  per record, one per line: the offset, subject, the node and session the subject names
  (`null` where it names none), the publisher's clock, kind, length, trust label, sender and
  recipient, the keys `aterm fabric --json`'s traffic already uses. `body` appears only with
  `--bodies`, and holds the same text `--bodies` prints in the table. A gap that retention
  made in what the tail reads is a `{"gap":…}` object in line. `aterm fabric --help` lists
  the keys.

- **aterm names a macOS service that holds the Mac's memory, and restarts fseventsd at a
  press.** The installed app reads what macOS's own services hold once a minute, without root.
  A service past a sixteenth of memory (8 GiB at least) for ten minutes is an entry in
  Messages. fseventsd past a quarter (16 GiB at least) while memory is under pressure is an
  alert with a Restart button. The button opens a tab that asks for your password once and
  restarts that one process; `aterm init --only init.fseventsd` does the same in any terminal.
  A plain `aterm init` never restarts it, because the new fseventsd discards the disk's change
  history and Time Machine and Spotlight scan the disk again. Dismissing the alert holds for
  that fseventsd across aterm's relaunches and updates, and a relaunch picks up where the last
  run left off instead of judging the service anew. `status` carries `service_mem=`, `sys why
  mem` names the service, and it offers the restart to agents only when the alert would rise
  and you have not put it off. `aterm doctor`'s `services:` row says the same.

- **Claude Code explains account recovery at a limit.** Its composer shows the
  observed stop, account eligibility, active sign-in or switching, blockers and
  the next known recheck. Click the limit or account fact for details. Unread
  account quotas stay unknown instead of appearing full.
  A window at rest sets no timer for it: the harness tells the window when the
  account state changes, and the window checks it every second only while a
  switch, its check, a usage check or a sign-in is under way.

- **Network State below System Resources.** Compact machine and service cells show
  current authenticated contacts, retained machine history, and local access to
  shared accounts and secrets. Select a cell for details, or open Network State
  from the View menu. Unverified discovery, cached data and unavailable access
  remain distinct; seeing a machine does not imply account access.

- **aCaffeine is always on and keeps this Mac awake.** `aterm acaffeine` is built into
  every aterm build. Every ordinary aterm window starts it and holds system and display idle
  sleep forever, over a previous off too; headless, diagnostic and private-control launches
  stay inert. The old `caffeine` command is gone. (Corrected after the release: this said it
  held the Mac awake after a reboot and that the old Caffeine launch jobs were gone. Nothing
  started it after a restart until a window opened, and a login item left under the old name
  started aterm every ten seconds; 0.146.0 removes such login items, and a later release
  keeps the Mac awake after a restart.)

- **Check that Rewind's past screens are what was on screen.** `aterm ctl rewind
  check` replays each kept stretch of a pane's history step by step as an Aos task
  under this build, with no effect on the live pane, and says whether every capture
  of the live screen, every reply the terminal sent and every clock matched
  (`verdict=pass`, or the rule that failed and where). `aterm ctl rewind check
  export` writes that stretch as a trace file, which `aterm ctl aos check` replays in
  this aterm or another one of the same build. Replays now run under the session's own
  colours and cursor settings, so a program's soft reset no longer reads as "may
  differ". Tested, not proved.

- **Nag mode has a mascot, and she gets louder.** While anything needs you (a permission,
  a sign-in, a question, a chore), the menu-bar button shows Nag, the scold from every
  kitchen and every review meeting: a bun skewered with a red pencil, cat-eye glasses on a
  bead chain, a reviewer's badge and a clipboard of red X's, beside its count. One need is
  an `ahem` over the top of her glasses. Each further need, and each stuck one, takes her a
  stage further gone: `tsk tsk` and a wagging finger, then `and ANOTHER thing` with the
  pen jabbing and the list unrolling to the floor, then head thrown back, eyes spinning and
  sticky notes flying, screaming `NAGG NAGG!!!!`. She leaves when nothing needs you.

- **A session log cursor can name the log it belongs to.** Two tabs opened in the same
  second get neighbouring epochs, and after an update carries one of them its epoch can
  equal the other's, so a cursor kept from one tab could read on in the other and skip
  records without a gap. `aterm ctl status` now prints `log_base=` beside `log_ep=`, the
  `log` header prints `base=`, and the `subscribe … log` ack prints `log_base=`. `log`,
  `brief` and `await log` take `base=` beside `since=` and `ep=`, and `subscribe` takes
  `log-base=` beside `since-log=` and `log-ep=`. A cursor that names another log is
  answered `gap why=reset`; one that names none is read as before. A session whose update
  carried its ids but not its log now starts from a new epoch above every carried one, so it
  never takes the base of the log opened beside it. The harness passes `base=` on its
  `await log` waits whenever `status` prints `log_base=`, and the drive-aterm,
  supervise-agent and aterm-fabric skills, `aterm help` and the note an update's cut
  `await log` prints show it.

### Changed

- **aterm sets up only once it is installed.** A copy running from a disk image, an App
  Translocation copy or a plain binary no longer offers first-run setup or starts the
  credentials-vault subscriber: such a copy goes away, so it installs itself into Applications
  and relaunches from there first, and the installed copy sets the Mac up. An installed copy is
  unaffected.

- **An update follows a step that cannot be cut in half.** When an item that cannot be repeated
  safely is mid-flight — a sign-out, a clone's publish rename, a launchd bootstrap — an update
  handoff now waits for it, at most ten seconds, then proceeds; the successor resumes the item
  from the setup ledger and finishes it once.

- **Rewind and the shell aterm keeps ready work together.** With Rewind on, a new tab again
  adopts the warm spare shell instead of starting one cold, and its recording starts at the
  screen it had when the tab took it. Every recording pane shares one writer thread instead
  of one each.

- **Every Mac syncs the credentials vault by default, and the ALab workstation profile
