  is only for ALab Macs.** First-launch setup now admits the Secrets vault lane and
  Spotlight on every Mac, not only an ALab one, so vault discovery, the join and the
  Sync rows are on by default everywhere with no action. A Mac counts as ALab's — and so
  signs out of Messages and FaceTime and takes the Dock, Desktop, keyboard and trackpad
  preferences and the GitHub repositories — only once its own login holds an `In`
  membership of the ALab vault (a locker an admin signed for this Mac's own recipient
  key). A probe that merely found the vault's address, a pending join request, a plain
  secrets file, another vault or a fleet key no longer set a Mac up as ALab's; they start
  a join at most. A plan a person shaped, or one already saved, is never narrowed by this.

- **The setup page's progress animation yields to your typing.** While a key was
  typed in the last few seconds in a focused aterm window, the setup page's working
  animation stops waking the window loop, so it never competes with an input frame in
  a split beside it; it resumes on its own once the typing pauses.

- **`aterm fabric post re=` and `aterm fabric tail --from` take a bus offset as `<n>` or
  `@<n>`, digits only.** They now read it with the same parser as `aterm ctl post re=`, so
  a sign is refused: `re=+5` and `--from +5`, which were read as offset 5, are usage errors
  (`… is not a bus offset`), as are `@`, an empty value and `@-1`.

- **A setting you change after setup set it stays yours.** Once aterm has set a Mac setting
  and read it back, a later change of yours is kept: no retry, widened plan, update, other
  Mac's profile or older aterm's records make aterm set it again (before, a new plan's next
  run set the Dock back, with one more Dock write and relaunch; now it makes no Dock call),
  and System State's row reads "Changed by you" until Restore, turning its group off and on,
  or Set up now. An older aterm, run again, may still set it.

- **Every Mac an open vault lets in, and every Mac from before Commons, now joins the
  vault's Commons on its own.** A machine an open vault lets in (as the ALab vault does)
  gets the Commons control entry in the same publish and enrolls over the LAN, as one let in
  by password or code does; before, it stayed outside Commons for good. `aterm secrets
  commons init` also approves every machine already in the vault that has no admission
  record (the ALab fleet's earlier Macs), so they enroll too, where before the founding Mac
  was the only member, and names every machine it approves. Run on a vault an earlier aterm
  founded, once that Commons is ready on this Mac, it adds the approvals that aterm left
  out, never for a machine outside the control entry's audience and never over one recorded;
  on a vault this aterm founded it approves nothing. A machine an admin excludes from that
  audience, or removes, stays out.

- **The setup screen wakes the window loop only while its run animates.** The System State
  page no longer asks the window loop to wake four times a second for the life of an open
  page. Its sub-second tick now drives only the village's walk, so the loop takes it as a
  wake only while a run is going on a shown page; a settled, finished or hidden page owes no
  sub-second wake, and its re-reads, offer answers and retries ride the worker's publications
  and the one-second status poll (which already wake the loop). Idle sub-second wakes on an
  open page drop from ~4/s to 0; the run's walk is unchanged. (The full §5.1–5.5 motion
  engine is MOT-1's; until it lands the page keeps today's static working glyph and
  content-path transitions.)

- **The stats deck's meters say plain facts.** Only the strain dial glows: the live box at
  the start of each strip and the hot CPU core squares are plain boxes in their colours, with
  no halo, fresh or stale.

- **`aterm doctor` and `aterm init` finish in one run while aterm installs its tools.** At a
  terminal, both now wait for the install pass that holds the package store when something
  needs repairing, on one line that shows what it is installing and the time left, and then
  repair; with nothing to repair, the report comes at once. Before, doctor said "nothing
  was repaired" and exited 1, and init exited 75, so you ran them again (a first install holds
  the store for about a minute). Run from a script or an agent, they leave the pass its own
  items (each reads "the running install pass lays these") instead of failing for them. Either
  way, copied commands in `~/.local/bin` are moved aside at once, and doctor also sets stale
  copies of aterm aside. `aterm init --no-wait` keeps the old exit 75.

- **aterm.app sets stale copies of itself aside on its own.** Each launch of the installed app
  moves stale copies of aterm, which reset its privacy grants, to the Trash, moves copied
  commands in `~/.local/bin` aside, and re-points a stale rustup `trust` link. Each change is
  logged, and what moved is one entry in the exceptions digest, never a dialog. Nobody has to
  run `aterm doctor` for them any more.

- **Switching a tab to Land reaches its agent at once.** Choosing Land used to wait for the
  harness's next look: after a short turn that was Cruise's back-off, two minutes or more. Now the
  harness's waits carry the tab's Autopilot word, so a switch wakes them. Once the switch has stood
  for a second (a click that passes through Land on its way to Off types nothing), Land's
  instruction is typed at the agent's next stop, with no back-off. A busy agent gets it when its
  turn ends, never mid-turn. A switch away from Land while the agent works is seen the same way, so
  the instruction is never typed into a tab switched to Off or Cruise. `aterm ctl await
  gone|agent|seq|idle|log` take `autopilot=<cruise|land|off|->` and answer `OK autopilot <word>`
  when the tab's stored word differs.

- **A resume past a usage limit is one line.** When a usage limit resets, a lost login comes back
  or a model's limit is passed on usage credits, the harness used to type Cruise's continuation or
  Land's whole prompt into an agent whose turn the limit ended, not the agent. Now it types one
  line: `[aterm harness] The usage limit has cleared; continue where you stopped.` (`may have
  cleared` when it tries a limit that named no reset, and the same line for an expired login or
  for usage credits). Cruise and Land speak at the agent's own next turn end. Under Land, a resume
  before Land's instruction was given is the instruction itself, so the agent gets one prompt, not
  two, except in a person's own exchange, which Land leaves to them: there the resume is the line. After a `/compact`, the mode's own continuation is still typed, because the compaction took
  the agent's context. A person at the keyboard now holds the resume, a sign-in at the limit
  included, until their two minutes of grace lapse.

- **An API outage is a quiet wait.** When the API was overloaded, answered with a server error or
  could not be reached, the harness typed "Claude Code reported an API error … Carry on from where
  you stopped" into the agent at 1, 5 and 15 minutes, then held the session as answering with the
  same reply, so nothing resumed it once the API was back. Now it types nothing while the outage
  stands. Where aterm measures the route (Claude Code on its default route), a connection error
  waits until the route is back and then types one line, `[aterm harness] The connection error has
  cleared; continue where you stopped.` What aterm cannot measure, an overload or a server error,
  is tried with one line (`The API overload may have cleared; …`) 2 minutes after the wall and,
  while the wall stands again, 4, 8, 16 and so on minutes after each try, never more than an
  hour. Settings ▸ Harness leads the tab's row with `waiting: API overload · next try 14:05`, and
  `aterm ctl status` says `waiting=overload`. A refused request, an over-long reply and a one-off
  cut reply still get their own lines as before.

- (developer tool) **`verify`'s lint builds the other operating systems' code a branch changed.** A dev run (`targo --unverified verify`, or one naming `lint`) now also checks one cross cell per other platform (Windows, Linux, the web build), on this Mac's architecture where it has one, wherever that cell's graph holds a crate the branch changed, so a Windows-, Linux- or web-only `cfg` arm that this Mac's lint and tests never compile breaks the branch's run instead of main's; `verify cells` still checks every cell. The cells lane builds without incremental state, which it never reuses.

- **A new vault is open: its admin's subscriber lets in every machine that asks to join.**
  `aterm secrets create` used to make a vault with a generated join password, so a Mac that
  joined without typing it waited for an admin to approve its code. A new vault now starts
  with `open = yes` in `[join]`, on any network the request comes from, so a new Mac joins
  with no password and no code. `aterm secrets password new` or `set` gives it a join
  password instead, and `password off` leaves each machine to approval by code. A vault made
  earlier keeps how it admits until an admin changes it.

- **The stats deck reads from now, at the left.** Each row's strip starts with its live box
  at the left end, right of the % and the now marker, and its intervals lengthen to
  the right in blocks of 1 second, 10 seconds, 1 minute, 10 minutes and 1 hour, at least
  three of each size a strip draws and five of each in the full deck. Each size starts where
  its age is its own block's, and the time scale marks it there ("–10s", "–1m", "–10m",
  "–1h" in the full deck; folded, the names that fit, and a gridline at every size's start),
  out to how far back the strip reaches, which the label over its right end says
  ("6h ago" in full, "4h ago" folded; narrower decks drop the largest sizes and reach 6 or 1
  minutes). The newest seconds slide right as each reading lands, by the time it covers: a
  whole 1-second box for a reading a second, spread evenly over the next second in Full, and
  still running while a close-up reads twice a second. The longer intervals, the gridlines
  and the time scale stand still, and the box that slides in at the end of the 1-second
  boxes shows their own oldest reading.
  The word "now" stands clear of the live dot's beat, and the now line clear of the row's
  mark on the narrowest decks. How to read, the lens's Cells legend and VoiceOver ("Stats
  deck, newest first") say so.

- **The stats deck draws its original colours again.** Every cell of its strips, the live
  box at their start, the CPU cores' squares, the window sill's core tiles and the CPU
  close-up's per-core history take the deck's one heat ramp, cold to hot, the same colour
  for the same load: the live box no longer turns green on a theme with a green accent such
  as Default, and no cell, the live box included, runs peach, amber, orange and red from
  55 %: the live box is the colour of the strip's own cell for the same load. Orange stays
  where it always stood, on a mark above a cell that ran over its maximum and on the load
  dial, whose bezel and arc still glow orange to red as the load climbs. The scope bars keep
  their colours. Increase Contrast keeps its own ramp.

- **The stats deck's time series take the row, and the columns of figures after them are
  gone.** Each row's strip is now the widest thing on it and reaches back six hours where it
  has the room. In a window about 1,040 points wide it is about 430 points long in the full
  deck, where it was 300 and reached back an hour, and about 285 in each folded block (245 at
  940 points), where it was 80. The scope bar beside it, this Mac in grey with aterm and this
  tab overlapping it in green and bright green, is longer too (about 135 points full, 65
  folded, where it was 95 and 28), and "■ this Mac ■ aterm ■ Tab 1" names its colours once
  above the bars. In the full deck from about 690 points each row then says one reading at
  the bar's end, this Mac's with the row's maximum ("12.6 of 18 cores", "42.1 of 128 GiB",
  "1.11 of 2.00 TB"), and Network its download and upload rates; where that has no room, the
  folded deck included, the legend says the machine's maxima instead ("this Mac · 18 cores ·
  128 GiB · 2 TB"). aterm's and this tab's amounts are in each row's close-up, and the full
  deck's Details say aterm's disk writes. A state such as memory pressure stands after the
  reading where it fits, else in the header beside "now". As the deck narrows the reading goes
  first, then the bar, and the strip, which keeps its share of the row, last.

  A strip's pressure-spike mark now draws the deck's warning colour, as a restart's does,
  where it drew the over-max orange: orange on a strip marks only a load over its maximum.

- **Every % in the stats deck has its scope bar, at every width.** Where a row has no
  room for the bar beside its strip (a folded deck under about 600 points wide, and the
  narrowest full deck), the bar runs as a thin line under the row's %: this Mac, aterm and this
  tab in the same colours, overlapping from the line's left end, each one in use showing at
  least a sliver of its own colour, in both themes and with Increase Contrast, and a click on
  it opens the same close-up. It costs the deck no height. The scope key above it stands where
  the header has room for it; where it does not, How to read names the colours and says the
  line under each % is the bar.

- **System State asks the network for the ALab vault only when something changed, and never
  holds your repositories for a vault this network lacks.** A Mac aterm is still watching for
  the ALab vault no longer asks the network at every window focus: a focus looks only in the ten
  minutes after aterm hears macOS's Local Network question asked (when you come back from
  answering it), while macOS refuses aterm the local network (that look asks nothing of the
  network), and never once a look reached the local network. It also looks when the Mac's IPv4
  network moves (another Wi-Fi with other addresses, a cable, a VPN), when System State comes to
  the front, on Check again and on its slow timer. Another vault's signed
  answer at the vault's address, kept for a day on that network, now spares System State's look
  as it spares `aterm init`'s, and System State keeps its own definite answers for `aterm init`.
  With the vault absent or unanswered on this network, GitHub repositories are set up in the same
  pass from this Mac's own token instead of waiting for the vault; a Mac with no token of its own
  keeps waiting for the vault's instead of being asked to sign in. A join by approval code no
  longer holds the setup run for 20 s: its row names `aterm secrets approve <code>` at once and
  setup goes on the moment an admin approves (a join with the password still waits up to 20 s,
  ending as soon as the Mac is in). The Secrets row says "Local Network is off for aterm" when
  macOS refuses aterm the local network, instead of "The ALab vault did not answer on this
  network".

- **The cursor kitty sometimes crosses your words in front of them.** It used to slip behind
  the letters on every walk, run and leap across a line. Now one leg in three, from its
  gather to its landing, goes over the words whole and undimmed, and the rest still pass
  behind them. While you type, an agent types for you or a command is still printing,
  every leg stays behind, so the kitty only crosses in front of words already on the page,
  and it settles behind the letters when it sits down on them.

- **The stats deck's load dial sweeps like a needle.** It used to jump to each new reading;
  now its needle swings there, most of the way in a quarter of a second and settled within
  about half a second, without overshooting, and the bezel's glow warms and cools with it. A
  reading that lands mid-swing carries the needle on from where it is, so it never jumps or
  steps back, and the warm glow behind the scale grows with the needle without flickering and
  fades in as the load climbs. It moves only in a focused window with motion on (not under
  Reduce Motion), redraws only the dial, and only once the needle's tip has moved at least a
  whole pixel, and goes still once it arrives, when readings stop, or when a reading would
  move it less than a pixel. The % beside it still prints each reading at once.

- **The system performance deck and close-up lenses read across longer spans, name the
  machine's totals, and show live network state.** Each resource strip now pairs a
  live `now` cell with multi-scale time windows (up to `4 h` when folded, `6 h` in
  full) over an X-axis, gliding smoothly between readings. Six hours of strip history (the
  last hour in 10-second steps, the hours before it in 10-minute ones) are saved across
  quits and crashes so sleeping, paused, and crashed intervals appear as
  shaded gaps with vertical wake, restart, crash, and pressure lines across both the deck
  and close-up traces. Each row names its maximum (the cores, total memory, and disk
  capacity), and the folded deck's Cores row names the processor; CPU, Memory, Disk,
  Network, and Processes draw overlapping `this Mac / aterm / this tab` scope bars; the
  strain dial glows orange to red within the active theme; and Network gains live connectivity (`online`, `captive`, `local`,
  `offline`), separate download and upload rates, passive median TCP RTT, and its own
  close-up lens.

- **The rule above an agent's prompt names its harness and build at its right end, beside a
  quiet on/off switch, and offers a newer build of the agent with a ⬆️.** Claude Code,
  Antigravity, Muse Code, and `codex-alab` sessions show `alab claude harness v0.4 (v2.1.305)`
  (the agent's own word, the harness version and the running agent's build, where aterm knows
  it: Claude Code's, a store install's, `codex-alab`'s own) at the far right of the rule above
  the prompt, after a small `● on` or `○ off` in the label's own soft grey, with no box or fill
  behind it: `◐` while it turns, a shade nearer the text's own colour under the pointer, and a
  click anywhere on it turns the harness off or on. Claude Code's own label (the top-effort
  key, a session name) stays whole just left of it. As the pane narrows the label gives up the
  agent's word, `harness`, the build and then itself (with a ⬆️ on the rule, the lockup's name
  goes to its icon before the label gives up the build), and the switch stays to the last;
  hovering the label shows a build it shortens (Muse Code's `-R` revision) or leaves out
  whole. A session name of wide characters or an emoji (`/rename 修复`, `🐛 fix`) no longer
  pushes the label off the far right. When a newer
  build is ready for the tab (a later Claude Code, Antigravity or Muse Code, or a Muse Code
  revision the update lane moves to, not one you skipped), a small ⬆️ centred on the line ends
  the rule: its hover says in the label's place when the update would land (`update to
  v2.1.310 · after 1 shell`, in Claude Code's own words for its running jobs, shortened to
  `v2.1.310 · after 1 shell` to keep to the label's own cells where a whole form fits them, and
  otherwise taking room to its left only as far as a whole form needs, never cutting a word),
  and a click asks for the tab menu's Upgrade Now, which updates at the next safe point with
  every safety check kept and says why if it cannot; the ⬆️ turns to `◐` and nothing else
  moves, and its hover then says `updating to v2.1.310 · after 1 shell`, or `→ v2.1.310 ·
  after 1 shell` where that does not fit. With the harness, or the tab's Autopilot, off, the
  arrow stays as a quiet `↑` in the label's grey, never the colour ⬆️ a click acts on: its
  hover says the update waits (`once the harness is on`) and a click says why it cannot
  update, on the rule and on the messages row with what to do, instead of asking. A
  Claude Code suspended behind another program in its tab puts no ⬆️ on that program's rule. A
  right-, middle- or control-click on the label, the switch or the ⬆️ asks nothing and reaches
  no program. All six harnesses are now version 0.4.

- **Claude Code's mode row shows only what is running.** With the harness on, the row below
  Claude Code's prompt reads just its background work, flush left (`1 shell`, `2 shells · 1
  monitor`, `/rc active`); the permission mode, `shift+tab to cycle`, the key hints, the
  effort hint and the auto-compact reading leave it, and so does a finished jobs' count with
  its key hint (`← 1 done`). The effort hint's level (`◐ medium`, its `· /effort` gone)
  stays, after the jobs, while aterm knows no effort for the session; right after a launch, an
  update or a resume, the rule's `◆` takes the effort from that hint and keeps it once Claude
  Code drops the hint, even where aterm learns of the session only after the hint has gone
  and in a tab, window or Space nobody looked at while it showed (a first launch included),
  where it used to show none until the next turn. An update's or a restart's relaunch of the
  same conversation keeps the effort the rule showed before it, on the same model, even in a
  tab, window or Space nobody looked at while Claude Code showed its hint, and an update of a
  session that had no turn yet, which starts a new conversation, shows the effort its new
  Claude Code names, unwatched too. The permission mode
  lives in the lights on the rule above for every mode, where `YOLO on` and `YOLO off` used to
  stand over Claude's pill: a quiet lowercase `yolo` for bypass permissions (the default, full
  auto), `auto`, `⏸ nag mode` for manual mode (it asks before each tool, so any yolo turned
  off is nag mode; its titles say `stopped in nag mode`), `⏸ plan` and `⏵⏵ accept edits`, and
  a click on a stopped mode there cycles Claude Code back to yolo. A click on a job still
  reaches Claude Code; a click on the cleared cells does nothing. With the harness off, or
  wherever aterm cannot read the row exactly, Claude Code's own row stands. A last item a
  narrow pane cuts that can only be a key hint (`← for ag…` at 80 columns for a few seconds
  after a launch) leaves with the key hints, where it used to keep Claude Code's whole row
  standing, `yolo` gone from the rule and the effort shown twice.

- **The rule below the prompt drops words that say nothing.** A value aterm does not know is
  no longer shown: no `weekly ? · until relaunch` (or its other reasons), `weekly
  unavailable` or `account unavailable`; the account's hover title and the Accounts menu say
  why. A live upgrade's `⇣ Claude Code 2.1.286 is ready · waits while you use this tab` moved
  to the ⬆️'s hover (`update to v2.1.286 · once you stop typing`). The account shows the
  email's name without its domain (`⎆ pat.owner93`), the plan (`Max 20x`) moved to the
  account's hover title, and `Σ 4h53m ↑528M ↓3.8M` reads `Σ 4h53m`, its token counts in the
  usage's hover title; an unread count it could not read is no longer `+?`. The `○ off` and
  `⊘ off` chips, a hidden fact's `off` stub and the top-effort key's `off` ghost now read at
  4.5:1 on every theme, and a short rule sets the Autopilot's worded chip apart from the
  mode's (`○ off ─ yolo`, `⤓ land ─ yolo`), so they no longer read as one phrase.
  On a light theme, the jobs on Claude Code's mode row and its top-effort tag moved beside
  the switch read in a darker shade of Claude Code's own colours.

- **`aterm init` clones your repositories without init.toml or `gh`.** The
  repositories step is now init's default: once the ALab vault's sync has put your
  GitHub token in `~/.secrets/gh_access_token`, init clones every repository you
  own into `~`, leaving out forks and archived ones, up to four at a time, checking
  free space before each. init.toml's `[github]` table now only names another
  `account` or `owner`, another `token_file`, or turns the step off with
  `enabled = false`. A repository init cannot place no longer stops the step: two
  repositories whose names differ only in case (alice/foo and team/foo), a folder
  that already holds another origin, and a name that is a standard home folder
  (Documents, Library, Downloads and the others) are each one "left untouched"
  note, and the step is done once every other repository is present. Before
  changing git's GitHub settings init records the old ones and the line that puts
  them back; a credential helper or account you already set up for github.com
  (gh's, say) is left alone and the row says so. A pass over 50 repositories
  already present and 10 to clone now runs git 286 times instead of 836 and reads
  your GitHub account once instead of three times.

- **`aterm init` runs on Linux.** It no longer refuses: it sets up the base layer,
  joins the ALab vault (asking its join password at a terminal) and installs its
  subscriber, and clones your repositories with the distribution's `/usr/bin/git`,
  keeping the GitHub credential in git's own `store` file. The Mac-only rows
  (preferences, Spotlight, sign-outs, permissions) read "macOS only" instead of
  failing, and a converged machine exits 0.

- **A quick reply between sessions costs the broker one flush, not two.** When a session
  answers a message within 5 ms of its delivery, the bridge now sends the delivery's commit
  and the reply in one write, which the broker flushes once, where it flushed each alone.
  In the measured runs a message and its reply took two flushes where they took four; on
  a strict broker the round trip took half as long (8.5 ms against 16-17 ms at the
  median), and on the default ordered broker its tail shortened (1.6 ms against 2.4-2.9 ms
  at the 95th percentile). A reply that comes later, such as an agent's turn, is
  unchanged, and a delivery nothing answers is committed about 5 ms later than before.

- **Working on aterm brings its own rustup.** `targo --unverified verify provision` now
  places rustup 1.29.2, held to its hash, in aterm's tooling cache, and the checks that build
  on stable (the foreign cells, the wasm checks and lane, the release's x86_64 slice and site)
  use that copy ahead of any rustup on your PATH. aterm no longer looks in Homebrew's rustup
  keg; a Homebrew rustup on your PATH is used only until the copy is placed. The copy is
  placed, not installed: nothing is added to `~/.cargo`, even when a toolchain is installed,
  and your shell profile is untouched. Your toolchains stay in rustup's own home
  (`~/.rustup`), and only what is missing is added there. A check that finds no rustup says
  so and names `verify provision`.

- **A bridge that starts with many quiet sessions delivers their mail sooner.** After a
  seamless update or a bridge restart, the bridge offers each session the mail it had not
  handled yet again, reading from where that session last marked its mail seen. It read
  each session's mail on its own, and the broker scans every record after that point to
  find it, so 32 sessions that had seen nothing for 500,000 records made the broker scan
  the log 32 times over. Their first mail after the restart arrived about 140-170 ms later
  than it would have with nothing to catch up on. Now the bridge reads the sessions' mail in
  one pass from the earliest such point and hands each record to its session. Where that
  pass would mostly carry mail no session is owed (one session far behind on a node whose
  other sessions read a lot of mail), the bridge goes back to reading each session's mail
  on its own after a page or two, so a restart costs at most about a millisecond more than
  it did before. In the measured runs those 32 sessions' mail was visible 272-296 ms after
  the kill (the supervisor's 200 ms restart included), against 393-427 ms before, the same
  as with nothing to catch up on. What each session is offered, and what it is told the
  broker's retention gave up, is unchanged.

### Fixed

- **Claude Code sessions report their usage.** `aterm ctl survey` showed a Claude Code
  session's context left only while Claude Code drew its own `N% until auto-compact` warning,
  so most of a session read `ctx_left_pct=-`. The usage tap now keeps
  `context_window.remaining_percentage` from Claude Code's status line, and a survey row takes
  it when the screen shows none. Rows also carry the plan's windows: `usage_5h_pct=` and
  `usage_7d_pct=` (read in the text form as `5h=7% 7d=1%`), from the tap for Claude Code and
  from the rollout's rate limits for codex-alab.
- **The disk report says when each large build was last built.** Every line under `the
  largest it cannot reclaim` (and the brief a disk-free worker gets) now reads `…, last built
  10h ago (…)`, the newest write into any of its profiles, so a build a finished session left
  reads apart from one writing now; `--json` gives it as `built_s_ago`.
- **Wide characters never leave half a character behind.** Writing over half of a wide
  character (CJK, kana, Hangul, fullwidth forms) blanks its other half in the background
  in use, as xterm and Ghostty do; it was left in the default colour. A styled wide
  character, or one typed in insert mode, with one column left before the right margin
  set by a program wraps instead of straddling the margin. Scrolling, inserting or
  deleting lines inside left and right margins no longer joins half of one wide character
  to half of another, and deleting characters beside a wide character that straddles the
  right margin blanks it whole. On a terminal one column wide a wide character prints as
  a space, where it moved the cursor to the next line and printed nothing.

- **A Claude Code the harness relaunches wears the harness's rules from its first frame.**
  For a fraction of a second after an update's or a restart's relaunch, Claude Code's first
  frames showed a grey top rule, a green `alab`, `∞` without `yolo`, and Claude Code's own
  mode row with its effort hint beside the rule's: the harness took its hold on the tab only
  once the new Claude Code had drawn. It now takes it just before typing the relaunch, and
  gives it back at once where the relaunch does not land. The lockup's hover title (`Claude
  Code`) no longer stays a frame on a rule a relaunch moved from under the pointer; the
  first frame after the move reads `claude`.
- **Rewind, `aterm ctl rewind check`, and exported pane traces replay host actions and live engine state across slices.**
  Rewind and step-by-step pane verification (`aterm.pane.screen`) now record host-initiated
  actions on the temporal spine — Clear Scrollback, Reset Terminal, forced alternate-screen
  leaves, foreground drawer boundaries and retirements, foreground-job folder restoration,
  and shell-integration re-keying — so stepping through Rewind shows those cuts and no longer
  diverges across them, and carry open synchronized-output (mode 2026) frame timers, policy
  and fallback response rate-limit buckets, alternate-screen leave notes, Kitty image
  counters, resize-handback edges, split `DECRQSS` and `XTGETTCAP` terminal queries, the
  security policy, authorized hyperlink schemes, and cell-pixel size changes across slices
  and keyframes, stamping in-flight keyframes with the theme and config the pane held when
  they were projected.

- **Crash recovery no longer waits for the keeper link's next idle tick to serve commands.**
  The link wakes when the keeper answers, and retries an interrupted wake write. A headless
  instance also places every recovered session at its first park, so recovering several tabs
  can finish without waiting for a frame it never presents.

- **On Windows, a program can no longer make aterm pile up helper processes.** Under
  Windows Terminal's console host, a shell prompt on a full-screen app's dead screen
  starts a short helper that makes the host leave that screen. A program that kept
  opening the full screen with a prompt mark on it, leaving it in between, started one
  helper per read, however many were still running; a session now runs one at a time and
  starts the next only once the last has exited. A helper that fails to start, or a
  `mainscreen` whose leave never comes, no longer leaves the dead screen up for good: the
  next prompt tries again.

- **Containment's help says what launchd still does for a contained program.** The 0.103.0
  note said a Containment shell can ask no macOS service to act for it but the user and
  group lookups. launchd itself is the exception: every process reaches it without a
  lookup, and while it refuses a contained program a new job or a change to the session's
  environment, it still restarts, unloads, disables or enables your own jobs (aterm's
  vault agent included) when asked. `aterm help containment`, the manual and the README
  now say so; closing it is open work.

- **A command's `detail=` never names the word after a first word it cannot read as a
  program.** `aterm ctl status`, the session log and presence name a running command by
  its program. When a line's first word had no letter or digit (`: note`, `-- x`, `'' x`,
  `$ x`), the next word, an argument, was shown as the program. The program is now the
  line's first word after any `NAME=value` and the shell's `!`, `{`, `(` or pwsh's `&`.
  A first word with no name shows as itself for `:`, `.` and `[`, and otherwise nothing is
  shown. A history designator (`!!`, `!$`, `^old^new`) and an arithmetic command
  (`((n+1))`) also show nothing. A quoted word that looks like `NAME=value` (`'FOO=1' x`)
  is the program to the shell, not a setting, so the word after it is no longer shown; a
  program word holding such an `=` shows nothing, and `/usr/bin/time FOO=1 x` shows
  `time`.

- **Incoming fabric mail shares a bounded turn without starving terminal events.**
  The bridge considers the waiting item's age as well as the event count, and keeps one
  cumulative budget across short inbox turns when the reader continues to refill them.

- **Resizing a window no longer lets the next character overwrite one already printed.**
  When a line ended exactly at the right edge, or the cursor sat just after a line that a
  resize made fill a row, the first character printed after the resize replaced the
  line's last character: a prompt that filled the narrower row lost its trailing space
  to the first key typed. On the main screen the cursor now keeps its place in its line
  through a resize, as in Ghostty: the next character goes right after the line's text,
  on the same row when there is room and on a new row of that line when there is not,
  which moves any line below down instead of writing over it. A cursor a program moved
  past its text (with a tab, say) keeps its place too, and a position saved with `ESC 7`
  or by a full-screen app's `?1049h` no longer comes back onto the line's last
  character. On the alternate screen, which full-screen apps redraw after a resize, a
  cursor the narrower window cuts off moves onto the last column, as in xterm. Unlike
  xterm and Ghostty, a widening after a line that filled the old width puts the cursor
  in the next column, so a backspace from there lands on the line's last character
  rather than the one before it.
- **The cursor trail keeps following your typing after you select text or press Escape.**
  In a program that follows the mouse, such as Claude Code in fullscreen, dragging over a
  file path to select it, a click, the scroll wheel, Copy, Select All or a click on a
  tab's own controls left the trail dark for every key you typed next on that line, until
  an arrow key or Return. In the prompt of Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent,
  Escape, Ctrl-C, Ctrl-L and a jump through the scrollback did the same. The trail now
  stays lit. In Claude Code's vim mode, Escape still leaves the trail off for the
  NORMAL-mode keys after it, which move the cursor rather than type, and the trail now
  comes back as soon as you type in INSERT again (after `i`, `a` or another insert
  command), where it used to stay off until an arrow key or Return.

- **Shared State names the vault check that blocks secret access.** Changed sources,
  incomplete local files, untrusted pins, admission and unavailable observations
  no longer collapse into one generic not-ready message.

- **Build-cache cleanup keeps a tree when its locks cannot be checked.** Unreadable
  directory entries and a directory at a Cargo lock path no longer let cleanup
  remove the cache.

- **Shared State distinguishes account proposals from deleted or unresolved records.**
  Account details report deletions, conflicts or missing values, stopped records,
  and retained or withheld operations without presenting them as usable logins.

- **Network history no longer labels this process with a saved observer identity.**
  Other local processes and restarted observers keep historical peers visible,
  but show a local identity only after current custody verifies it.

- **The default ALab fleet keeps the level you set and the fleet you joined.** `aterm fleet
  sync`, which the vault subscriber runs, joins the fleet the ALab vault publishes and lets
  every member drive this Mac. It wrote that grant on every run, undoing an `aterm fleet
  allow content`, and moved a Mac off any other fleet, one you joined by hand included. The
  grant now goes only with a first join, or in place of the default grant itself, and the
  next sync writes it when a pass stopped short of it. Sync follows the vault's newer code
  only from the default fleet this Mac is in, and keeps a facts or content level you set;
  drive grants to named Macs go with the old secret, as on any join of a new one. Another
  fleet you joined by hand, one this Mac issues, and a key it cannot read stay, and sync
  names the way out: `aterm fleet leave`, then the new `aterm fleet sync --on`, which turns
  sync back on after a leave. A vault apply that has not finished is now named as what
  keeps the code back, not read as no code published.

- **An update removes the fleet code an older aterm wrote as a file.** aterm 0.144 and
  older did not know `aterm-fleet-code` is consumed in place, so a Mac in the ALab vault
  could hold it as a plaintext file in `~/.secrets`, and a newer aterm forgot that file
  without removing it. The first vault pass after the update now removes it while it still
  holds what the vault wrote, without a new vault version; a file you changed stays. The
  same holds for a Commons control record. A copy that cannot be removed (an immutable
  flag, say) is tried again at the next pass and keeps neither the fleet code nor the
  Commons control from being read.

- **A policy that silences replies silences the size report a program asks for.** When a
  program turns on in-band size reports (mode 2048), the report its request provokes now
  passes the same response policy and rate limit as every other reply, so a policy that
  drops replies drops it and a flood of on/off requests is metered. Reports aterm sends when
  the window resizes are unchanged. A warm spare tab also no longer reads image files a
  program names for Kitty graphics when Settings leaves Kitty file transfer off or the tab
  runs under containment, as a fresh tab never did.

- **A "no vault here" result no longer blocks the vault on a different network.** aterm
  remembers that another store answered at the ALab vault's address so it need not ask
  again on that network, but it keyed that memory by subnet alone, and `192.168.1.0/24`
  is on most networks. It now keys the memory by the network's gateway (its hardware
  address, read with no packet) as well as the subnet, so a result kept at one place never
  stands at another; it is dropped the moment the gateway changes or Local Network is
  granted; and a result is kept only when a store actually answered, never for a timeout or
  a lookup macOS held. A memory keyed the old way is dropped, so the first launch after the
  update looks afresh.

- **Opening Accounts no longer waits on account files on the window thread.**
  The menu reads choices in the background, keeps usable rows while refreshing,
  and ignores late results after the session or menu changes.

- **A failed disk flush is no longer passed over in silence, and a step that must wait for
  it now does.** On a Mac volume that refuses a full flush with `ENOTSUP` (a network or
  external volume), where every write of the updater's records and its boot sentinel failed
  before, those writes now go on, as they always did on Linux. A package reinstall whose
  flush of its old completeness mark fails now stops before swapping, so a power cut cannot
  leave the old mark over a half-written tree, and an uninstall or a discard keeps its
  trees until that mark's removal is on disk. Failed store scans and marker removals
  also retain the package tree. The updater's records, its bundle swap and its
  launch counts log a failed folder flush instead of dropping it, and the updater no longer
  swaps in an update whose crash-loop trial is not on disk ahead of the swap: it takes the
  trial back and tries the update again later.

- **Fleet and fabric report config edits that took effect.** If flushing the folder
  fails after the config rename, the command reports the edit in effect with a
  warning that power loss may undo it, then continues. An error before the edit
  takes effect still fails the step and leaves the config unchanged.

- **Crash and session journal flush failures are recorded.** Cleanup flush failures
  now reach the app log, and the session journal counts failed segment and folder
  flushes while continuing its best effort writes. Required crash-image publication
  flushes retain their existing failure behavior.

- **Known-machine history survives a network observer startup failure.** Saved
  machines remain visible with unconfirmed reachability while independent local
  service observations continue updating.

- (developer tool) **`verify` says when the checkout moved under it.** A run whose checkout's HEAD moved to another commit while it ran (another session fast-forwarding a shared checkout) ends `COULD NOT RUN` (exit 3) and names both commits, with the verdict its checks reached. Its stages read both trees, so a cross cell could report items missing that the newer tree has.

- **Rewind keyframes keep open frames, rate limits and alternate-screen notes faithful.**
  Replay keyframes, live resyncs and background rekeys now carry the live terminal's open
  synchronized-output frame timer, response rate-limit buckets, alternate-screen leave
  notes, Kitty image counters, host alternate-scroll and cell-pixel settings, resize
  hand-back seams and pending restore lineage alongside each checkpoint, so those sessions
  replay faithfully instead of diverging and dropping older history.

- **Layered colour emoji, kerning, and combining marks stack and align across OpenType, AAT, and unhinted-anchor fonts.**
  aterm's font shaper now reads and applies OpenType `GPOS` positioning (single and pair
  adjustments, cursive attachment, mark-to-base, mark-to-ligature and mark-to-mark anchors,
  contextual and chained contextual rules, extension subtables, and variation devices),
  OpenType and legacy AAT `kern` kerning, Apple Advanced Typography `kerx` and `ankr`
  extended kerning and anchor-point attachment, and geometric fallback mark placement for
  faces without `GPOS` mark tables (or without a `hebr` script for Hebrew niqqud). On
  Windows, multi-part colour emoji in Segoe UI Emoji such as holding hands, skin-tone
  couples, and families stack and align inside their cell instead of drawing their layers
  side by side, and combining marks and kerned pairs take their shaped positions across
  every platform.

- **The vault's accounts sheet reaches every Mac again.** A `~/.secrets/fleet-accounts.toml`
  that aterm wrote, in any format any version wrote, now yields to `ai-accounts.csv`
  wherever the sheet gives the Mac rows, and the sync that reads the sheet removes it, so
  each edit published to the vault reaches the roster. A fleet file the vault delivered
  keeps its precedence, a Mac the sheet does not name keeps the accounts found on it, and
  aterm copies only a list it found on the Mac into `~/.secrets`. A sync that keeps failing
  on the same files waits 15 minutes instead of retrying and logging every minute, and
  `accounts` no longer calls aterm's own copy the vault's.

- **Shared-service status survives a network observer startup failure.** Local
  Accounts and Secrets observations can still update while Network State reports
  that its own observer is unavailable.

- **Setup that aterm stopped in no longer loops on one step.** A step aterm was stopped in
  (a crash, a kill, a power loss) resumes once at the next launch with no press, its row
  reading "Resuming after aterm stopped"; stopped there twice, it waits for Check again while
  the other steps go on. Before, a step that ended aterm every time ran again at every launch
  and no later step ever ran (4 launches: the step ran 4 times and the rest 0; now 2, and
  every other step once). A step still running after an hour waits for Check again the same
  way at the next launch, where before it read "running" with no end and ran again first. A
  quit or an update's handoff is no stop. A clone a killed aterm left half done is swept at
  the next GitHub repositories step; one still cloning, or a published clone, is never
  touched.

- (developer tool) **The Windows and libc oracles heal a pruned Cargo registry.** aterm's disk
  pass counts `~/.cargo/registry` as downloadable again, and no aterm build downloads the
  registry `windows-sys` or `libc` the oracles compare against, so after a prune `verify cells`'
  two win32 rows and the release `verify libc` row said COULD NOT RUN ("no matching package
  named `windows-sys`", "the locked dependencies are not on this machine") until someone fetched
  by hand. The win32 `oracle` fetched only when no unpacked source was found, which a prune
  that takes the index and keeps `registry/src` never triggers, and `oracle-052` never fetched.
  Each oracle now resolves its reference workspace offline first and runs `targo fetch
  --locked` once when cargo says it is not downloaded (the win32 driver on any refusal): a full
  cache stays offline, a stale lock is still the libc oracle's finding, and any other failed
  fetch stops the run with cargo's own reason on the line `verify` reports.

- **Stalled shared-service observations become unknown.** Accounts and Secrets
  retain their last recorded evidence, but stop claiming usable access after a
  minute without a fresh check. An open Network State view keeps polling even
  with resource bars hidden, and its cells and details refresh together.

- **Network history keeps honest timestamps.** Last-contact and service-check
  details show their recorded UTC time, even when the network observer stops.
- **Rapid harness off/on toggles retain the Off transition.** Re-enabling an
  agent before its worker is registered no longer loses its resume-from-Off
  state; other running agents are left alone.

- **On a Mac, `aterm init` waits for the local-network answer only when macOS is asking.**
  Its look for the ALab vault said "macOS is asking whether aterm may use the local
  network" and looked again every second for up to a minute whenever a connect found no
  route, to an address off the LAN too, where macOS asks nothing. It now waits only when
  the vault's name resolved to a private or link-local address, the one macOS holds for
  its question; no route anywhere else is "no secrets vault on this network" after one look.

- **A spare shell's check now counts a daemon your startup files start late.** aterm keeps a
  shell ready for your next tab only while your startup files leave nothing running behind.
  On a busy Mac a daemon those files started could be born just after the check's 100 ms
  window closed but before the check looked, and that spare passed. The check on a spare
  now counts everything it lists from the shell's start on. The check on a tab you opened
  still stops at the window, since you may already be typing there.

- **Codex build 13764 session activity is recognized.** Approvals, questions,
  usage and continued conversations now have measured log-format coverage.

- **aterm's disk worker can free space when no other Claude Code session ran a command.**
  aterm proves each of the worker's commands against the shell snapshot Claude Code writes
  once its Bash tool has run one, so a worker started where no running session had run one
  had every command declined, its dry run and `aterm harness disk free` too, with a reason
  that told it to use the very verb it had just been refused; it freed nothing. Its task now
  asks it to run `pwd` first, which Claude Code runs without asking, and a read or aterm
  verb aterm cannot prove is declined with the real reason (for the missing snapshot, with
  that remedy, and to report it if `pwd` did not help). So is an `aterm harness disk free` too long for one row of its box: aterm
  cannot tell a row Claude Code wrapped from a second command, and the worker is told to
  run it again on one row, one path at a time with its home written as `~`.

- **aterm finishes a decline whose reason reads like a lasting grant.** aterm finds the `No`
  it types a decline's reason into by that option's words, so a reason saying "without
  asking" or "always" (a quoted path holding the word included) made the option look like a
  "don't ask again" choice: aterm stopped with "the box has no refusal at option N" and left
  the box open, its reason typed but not sent. The `No` that holds exactly the reason aterm
  typed is now its decline's, whatever those words are.

- **`aterm harness disk why` credits aterm's disk worker with what it freed.** A worker
  that freed space within its first minute, as a quick one does, was said to have freed
  almost nothing ("free space rose 580.0 KiB while it ran" after it freed 2 GiB), in
  `why` and in the ledger's `worker-over` row: its rise was read from the first look
  that saw it running, after its cleanup. It is now read from the free space aterm read
  when it decided to start the worker.

- **`aterm fabric status` warns of an ask to a person whose deadline passed, even after
  the broker let newer mail go.** An ask to a person is kept until it ages out, since
  nothing marks it read, and the broker can let go of mail newer than it that a session
  already read. Status read the mail lanes only from the oldest offset where the broker
  still kept all of it, which was then past the ask, so the unanswered ask dropped out of
  its deadline warnings (and `--json`'s `overdue`) and of TRAFFIC, and a session's
  unhandled ask kept there got no age. Status now reads every record the broker still keeps
  there. It warns of such an ask only while the broker still keeps the replies its asker
  could have had since: an ask whose answer the broker let go, as it lets the asker's read
  mail go, is not listed, since status cannot tell it was answered, and where the broker let
  go of the asker's own "expired" notices, the warning says that instead of claiming none
  was recorded (`--json`'s `expired` is `null`). A broker an older aterm started cannot hand
  those records out, so status reads it as before until it is restarted.

- **Rust builds and test runs no longer feed macOS's file-change service.** On a build Mac
  fseventsd, which macOS budgets 30 MB, grew to 152 GB over 35 days and pushed the Mac into
  swap. In a 20-minute sample, 99% of the file events it delivered came from aterm's own
  work: test scratch folders (89%), the shared Rust build cache and verify's lint builds.
  These now live in `.ubd` folders, whose file events fseventsd drops before it hands them
  to any app or keeps them: `~/Library/Caches/aterm/.ubd/cargo-build.noindex`,
  `<target>/verify/.ubd/`, a release clone's build folders, and test scratch in
  `$TMPDIR/.ubd/` and `/tmp/.ubd/`. A test run then cost fseventsd about a ninth of the CPU
  and left nothing in its history. This is how fseventsd behaves on macOS 27.0, which Apple
  does not document; if a later macOS changes it, only the saving is lost. The daily cache
  pass removes the old cache folder once nothing has built in it for an hour, so each
  checkout builds once from scratch. Until the update that lays the new `targo` shim is
  installed, plain `targo` still builds in the old folder, and `verify` builds there with it
  rather than keeping a second copy. `aterm doctor`'s `services:` row and `aterm init`'s
  Spotlight item say what is kept out. The quiet `TMPDIR` applies to every project's
  `targo --unverified test` under your home folder: a test that waits for FSEvents (the
  `notify` crate on macOS) on a temporary directory hears nothing there, so such a test must
  place its scratch itself.

- **A Claude Code that a quiet upgrade stops is started again right away, even if you typed
  in its tab a minute or two before.** From the keys-only step (an hour behind) on, the
  upgrade may stop an idle Claude Code once nobody has typed in its tab for 20 seconds, but
  relaunching it then waited for two minutes with no typing at all. A keystroke from shortly
  before the stop could therefore leave the tab at a bare shell prompt until the person started
  Claude Code again by hand. Now the relaunch line waits on the same quiet the stop waited on:
  keys typed before the stop never hold it, and keys typed at the prompt after it hold it as
  long as they would have held the stop. Unread input at the prompt or another driver's hold on
  the tab still holds it. If you moved the shell to another directory at the prompt, the line
  carries a `cd` back to the conversation's directory, so Claude Code resumes where it ran.
  When keys hold it, it is tried again one second after they may let it go, not at the next
  back-off step. A Claude Code that ended on its own, including a new build that quit before it
  picked the conversation up, keeps the whole two minutes before a relaunch. A restart in place
  (memory, model or account) no longer stops Claude Code when it cannot write down the restart
  first, which left nothing to start it again. The agy and Muse Code upgrades hold their
  relaunch the same way.

- **When someone else brings back a conversation that an upgrade stopped, the upgrade's record
  says so.** If the person (or another tool) resumed the conversation in its tab before the
  upgrade's own relaunch line was typed, the upgrade took that process for its own. It waited up
  to two minutes for it to settle and wrote "resumed while idle, nothing typed". Now the round
  closes at once as `done:resumed-by-another`, which names that process and says aterm's
  relaunch line was never typed. Nothing is typed into that session. If it runs an older build
  than the target, the round stops (`failed:resumed-by-another`, which its status row explains)
  and the upgrade tries again later.

- **An admin Mac no longer shows a Mac the vault let go as asking to join.** The vault
  server keeps a join request for a week, so the request that let a Mac in stays queued
  after the vault lets that Mac go. An admin Mac's approver stayed quiet about such a
  request only if it read it while the Mac was in the vault, so one that did not (a new
  admin Mac, one asleep while another admin let the Mac in and go, or m22 once updated to a
  build with that record, as on 2026-10-26) showed an "asks to join" notice for each Mac let
  go, whose Approve let it back in. Every version that lets a machine go now names its key
  on a `code-only` line, closed vaults included (where it changes no admission: a password
  or a code still lets the key in, `aterm secrets requests` marks it let go, not code only,
  and opening the vault never offers it), and the approver's record keeps the keys such
  lines named when it last read the vault: a key named anew has its queued request taken as
  answered, unless the approver showed that Mac as asking at the version just before, so a
  Mac held as the vault opened stays shown. A Mac let go that asks again is shown once the
  server moves its request's time, within the hour. A Mac an admin Mac lets in by its code
  is recorded there as it is let in, so a ghost no longer shows on that Mac when its
  subscriber was off or stuck while the Mac came and went. An admin Mac that was away while
  another admin Mac let a Mac in again (by its code, or its approver by the join password)
  and let it go again no longer shows it either: each version notes, in comment lines in
  `[join]`, the version that named a `code-only` key anew, and the approver keeps the
  version it last read, so a key let in and let go since counts as named anew. A Mac held on a
  `code-only` line may wait up to an hour or two to be shown again after an admin Mac's
  first pass on this build, and after versions an admin Mac on an earlier build published.
  Update every admin Mac: one on an earlier build still shows that ghost. The record's new
  lines live in their own files, `answered-queue` and `answered-approved`, so a build before
  them reads its requests whole however many Macs a vault lets go, and the vault server drops
  a join queue left under a vault name it holds no vault for when that name's first version
  arrives.

- **A post the bridge refuses is logged with the reason its client was told.** When the
  bridge retired a post undelivered (an address no node or session answers to, an ambiguous
  session id, a broker refusal, this node's subject budget), the client was told `ERR
  unroutable id=<n>` or the like, but the session log said only `mark - mail-landed
  inbox=<n> by=bridge`, a name that reads as delivered, and the timeline `post-landed <n>
  off=-`. The mark now says `mail-landed inbox=<n> why=unroutable by=bridge` and the timeline
  `post-landed <n> off=- reason=unroutable`, with the same word the client was told. A landing
  carries `off=<n>` and no `why=`, so a program reading `log` or `subscribe log` tells the
  two apart. aterm's own two retirements (`not-carried`, `log-replaced`) still read `by=aterm`,
  and `aterm ctl help post` names `log-replaced`, which a waiting client can also be told.

- **`aterm init` and `aterm doctor` keep another account's Rust docs where that account keeps them.** Run for a user other than the one running it (root setting up a user's account, for one), the Rust docs step read the running process's `CARGO_HOME`, `RUSTUP_HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` as that user's; it now reads them only for the running user's own account and takes the other's default folders.

- **`aterm fleet init`, `join` and `peers` on Linux name a stopped aterm as stopped.** Where this machine's aterm takes a connection but answers nothing because it is stopped (a `SIGSTOP`, a debugger), Linux read it as frozen or too busy; it now reads the process's state as macOS does and says the aterm here (its pid) is stopped and how to resume it.

- **Settings' Text size steps past the automatic size.** Stepping Text size onto the size aterm picks by itself (12 px on macOS, 15 px on Linux, 17 px on Windows) removes the written size; while that removal saved, the slider still read the old size, so the next step wrote the automatic size again instead of moving past it. The field now reads the automatic size as soon as the step leaves it unset, and the next step moves on.

- **The editor's command prompt leaves the document where you scrolled it.** Opening the prompt (M-x) in aterm's built-in editor scrolled the document back to its cursor wherever the prompt's line wrapped onto another row (on Linux's wider type, for one): the row it took counted as a resize. While a prompt holds the keyboard a changed height now only keeps the view inside the document; closing the prompt shows the cursor again.

- **A switch too narrow for its On or Off word draws its track alone.** In a narrow Settings column at large text (Linux's Noto Sans at 1.5×, for one) a switch ran its word into its track; it now draws the track alone, its state still in the track and read out to a screen reader.

- **Messages' filter chips break their words inside the chip.** A chip whose words wrapped ("Prob-" / "lems · 38") could cut its count with "…"; the words now wrap again in the room the chip leaves them.

- **Settings ▸ Home's colours card keeps no blank band under its rows.** Where the cursor trail and playful effects cards beside it stood taller than the whole colour sample (Linux's wider type sets the playful card on more lines), the colours card stretched with an empty band under its rows; the trail's sample now gives back whole rows of its height to even the two columns.

- **A Settings window that takes the toolbar into its list draws its warning where the next frame does.** In a short window at large text, the first frame after the text size changed could dock aterm.toml's reload warning in the toolbar and the next stand it under the page, the page jumping with nothing pressed (Linux's Noto Sans at 919×158 with 2× text, for one): whether a status docks was weighed from the toolbar the last frame drew. A frame that takes the toolbar into its list or gives it back now draws once more with what it chose.

- **Cursor Styles' rows fit a short window at large text.** In a narrow window at large text the check beside the saved style could narrow its name onto one more line than the list had room for, and the default style's "(default)" made its name a row taller than the window ("Rainbow kitty (default)" on four lines, 176 pt in a 152 pt window, on Linux at 2× text). Where a name is too tall for the list, the row now drops the check's room (still drawn selected), and the default style says "Default ·" in its description instead of its name; the button keeps its full name for a screen reader.

- **Font size's row keeps no blank line once a size is written.** In a narrow Settings window at large text, where "Automatic" broke across two lines under the name ("Auto-" / "matic", on Linux at 2× text in a 164 pt window), writing a size left "Changed" over an empty line; there the row now says "Default" at rest, which takes one line as "Changed" does.

- **Messages' scroll to the end shows the last entry.** A scroll to the end of the list just after the tag pop-up closed was clamped by the page's chrome as the pop-up left it, one entry short of the end (Linux at 864 pt wide); the frame that draws the page's own chrome now keeps the list at its end.

- **A native page drawn while fonts load keeps its picture once every character has its face.** On Linux, where a page's fallback faces load as it first draws, each frame found the font coverage changed by its own drawing and painted the whole page again; a page that drew every character now keeps the faces it drew with, and redraws only when a face it lacked arrives.

- **Typing with a cursor trail is quicker again.** The trail's letter guard, which keeps the
  letters beside the trail readable, now redoes only the letters whose light changed, skips
  frames where no light moved, and weighs each letter for less. While typing under the
  default rainbow kitty trail, a frame takes 1.8 ms to prepare instead of 3.2 ms, and a key
  reaches the screen in 3.4 ms at the median instead of 5.0 ms (6.3 ms instead of 9.4 ms for
  the slowest 5%). The trail looks exactly as before. 0.110.0 prepared a frame in 0.6 ms, so
  part of that slowdown remains.

- **A rewound moment whose live capture landed on the same instant as a new keyframe
  stayed `unchecked`.** It is now checked against that capture.

- **The session journal holds its pause under the free-space floor, and a failed write no
  longer marks its records as journaled.** With a journal file open, a volume under 1 GiB free
  paused the journal for 30 seconds, then its next pass wrote anyway from the minute's earlier
  reading and cleared the pause, so the journal wrote under the floor about half the time and
  its notice came and went each minute. The first pass after such a pause now reads the volume
  again: the pause holds and doubles until a reading finds room. And a pass whose write failed
  (a full disk, an I/O error) told the session's log that its records were journaled, so under
  pressure during the pause the log dropped those unwritten records before older ones already
  on disk, and the journal later said them lost (`gap why=evicted`). A write that does not land
  now gives its records back at once, even while the session's log is busy, and one that lands
  keeps them first to go, so a burst of output between two passes, or during a write, loses
  nothing the journal could still write.

- **Release provisioning stops waiting when a signing check cannot finish.** A blocked
  keychain signing check now times out and releases its child process instead of leaving
  unattended provisioning stuck.

- **Restarting Codex resumes its conversation after a clean shutdown.** Codex removes its
  conversation lock when it exits. aterm now recognizes that released lock instead of
  waiting indefinitely for it; a held or unreadable lock still prevents a second writer.

- **A vault the server would not take no longer locks this Mac out of every vault.** `aterm
  secrets create <url>` run from a Mac other than the server's (whose server takes a vault's
  first version only from its own Mac), against a full server, or at a path whose folder is
  missing, kept its unfinished creation for good: every later create and join was refused
  ("an unfinished vault creation reserves this slot"), and the subscriber retried the
  refused upload every pass, until someone deleted files under `~/.config/aterm/secrets` by
  hand. A refusal that stored nothing now ends the attempt: create says so, the Mac keeps
  its identity, and it can create or join a vault at once. A conflict or an unanswered
  upload still keeps the attempt for the subscriber to finish, since that upload may have
  landed, and so does a refusal that follows an unanswered upload (another server answering
  the same name, or a volume not mounted). An attempt left by an earlier build carries no
  such mark, so one refused now counts as never sent: none of them can be told apart, and
  keeping them all would keep every Mac those builds locked out. A mistyped folder, or a
  symlink or file named as one, is caught before anything is prepared.

- **On Linux, a vault server that is down is no longer blamed on a macOS setting.** A Linux
  machine whose LAN vault server was off got "macOS lets aterm reach the local network only once
  allowed (Privacy & Security > Local Network)", and its subscriber, taking that for macOS's
  permission question, retried every few seconds for as long as the server stayed down instead
  of backing off to once a minute as its log line said. Only macOS gates the local network: on
  Linux the same failure names the address and backs off like any other.

- **A session is told when an update or a recovery cost it mail the broker no longer
  keeps.** After a seamless update or a recovered aterm, the bridge offers each session the
  mail it had not handled yet again, from the bus, and mail the broker's retention had let go
  of meanwhile was skipped with only a line in the bridge's own log. Now that session alone is
  told: `aterm ctl inbox`'s header ends `lane_given_up=@<a>..@<b>` (the broker offsets it
  lost) and its log marks it once (`mail-gap`), unless its inbox still holds that mail. The
  same goes for an ask whose deadline the bridge judged after the offsets its answer would be
  at were let go of, and for a broadcast topic replayed from an offset the broker no longer
  keeps, whose range `aterm ctl topic ls` names on the topic's row. `given_up=` still names
  only the node's unread mail given up before the bridge read it, and the two are told,
  marked and carried apart, so neither is marked twice or takes the other's place. The refill
  tells a session that never ran `inbox seen` nothing, by choice: with no watermark the bridge
  cannot tell the mail it handled from the mail it did not. An aterm older than its bridge is
  told nothing new.

- **A Mac waiting to join a vault kept at a path is told the approval that works.** A vault
  at a path has no join queue, so an admin approves a new Mac by its key and name
  (`aterm secrets approve age1… --name <host>`), but `aterm secrets join`, `status`, `aterm
  init` and System State's Secrets row all said `aterm secrets approve <code>`, which no admin
  Mac can run for such a vault ("no machine waiting to join has code …"). Every one of them now
  names the key and name for a vault at a path, and the code for one at a URL.

- **A vault join from `aterm init` that fails part-way no longer leaves the Mac half-joined.**
  When the join request itself failed after the Mac had already been set to the vault (the
  server's queue full, an error, or a lost reply), `aterm init` and System State reported the
  failure but installed no subscriber, so nothing asked again or finished the join once an admin
  approved it. The subscriber now goes in, as `aterm secrets join`'s does, and the row says the
  Mac is set to that vault and will ask again shortly.

- **Typing sound no longer carries a low-frequency hum.** The ambient keystroke bed
  now defaults off (`trail_sound_bed = false`); when turned on, its voice plays an
  octave higher (a warm C4 sky pad) through a 220 Hz high-pass filter, and the audio
  engine finishes with a master DC blocker so typing stays crisp and free of sub-200 Hz
  rumble or clicks.

- **The rainbow cursor trail stays unbroken across wrapped composer lines and bordered
  boxes.** Typing across word wraps inside indented prompt lines or four-sided composer
  frames no longer triggers a 10-second blackout or leaves unlit border cells between
  the end of one line and the start of the next.

- **A Mac serving its own vault no longer takes the ALab name or the ALab vault.** `aterm
  secrets serve` and `server on` with no flags now advertise `alab-secrets.local`, and take
  the ALab vault from another Mac, only on ALab's server: one whose store holds the ALab
  vault, or one started with `--advertise alab-secrets`. Before, every server on macOS did
  both. A personal server on a network with ALab Macs, even briefly (a café, or the ALab
  office while its server sleeps), took their copies of the ALab vault and then served them
  as ALab's on its owner's own network, where every new Mac read as an ALab Mac and got the
  ALab profile, including the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs. A server that had already taken
  such a copy stops too, since a copy counts only on a Mac that follows the ALab vault. A new
  ALab server with an empty store starts with `aterm secrets server on --advertise
  alab-secrets`.

- **The cursor kitty no longer runs in place beside a busy Claude Code.** Resting in the
  footer under the composer while Claude Code worked, a bored kitty could set off to hide
  behind the end of a footer row's words. When those words are aterm's own (the mode row
  aterm rewrites, whose whole original width it keeps clear), every step was put back beside
  them, so the kitty ran on the spot, legs turning and going nowhere, until you typed. The
  kitty now hides only where it may walk, and gives up a hide or a chase the moment a step
  toward it is put back. On its way back to the cursor past a chip of aterm's on its row, it
  hops the chip instead of running against it.

- **The cursor kitty rests by the words in Claude Code's footer, not out in empty glass.**
  Where aterm rewrites Claude Code's mode row to its jobs (`1 shell`), it blanks the rest of
  the row out to where Claude Code's own words ended. The kitty reads Claude Code's text, so
  it took the hidden words for ink and the blank for aterm's chrome, and rested past them:
  some 60 columns right of the cursor, in glass that looked empty. It now reads that blank as
  the empty glass it is and rests beside the words aterm shows, or by the cursor, never on
  them.

- **Grok Build reads the accounts sheet's `x` column.** The ALab vault's
  `ai-accounts.csv` heads its xAI column `x`, which Grok Build's pool now reads as it
  reads `xai` or `grok`, so a Mac that keeps a Grok Build roster takes its rows from the
  sheet instead of reporting that the sheet has no Grok column. A sheet that heads `x`
  beside `xai` or `grok` is refused as ambiguous. A note's `x` still names no vendor, so
  `x banned` drops the row from every pool, as an unscoped `banned` does; `grok banned`
  or `xai banned` drops it from Grok Build's pool and leaves Codex's and Kimi Code's.

- **A newer package index cannot move a program back to an old source.** Each Mac now
  holds a newer signed package index to the publisher's rules against the last index it
  trusted: no pinned build goes down, and a program moves to another repository only with a
  new build. An index that breaks either rule is refused whole, so a stale publisher with
  a valid key can no longer send the ALab codex back to OpenAI's build. The Mac stays on
  the index it trusted, and `aterm pkg doctor` names the rule the refused index broke.
  (developer tool) `atpkg-publish status` names which publisher wrote the channel's head
  and flags one from the retired shell publisher, and `atpkg-publish index` refuses a
  repository move under the same build for every program and target.

- **A cask that ships as a disk image installs on a busy Mac.** `brew install --cask`
  copies the app out of the image it mounts, then detaches the image. When another process
  still held the volume for a moment, such as a system scanner reading the app just copied
  and more often on a loaded Mac, the detach was refused as busy and the install failed with
  `abrew: dmg detach failed`, though the app was wholly copied. The forced detach that follows
  now takes the image down and the install goes on; one that still leaves the image attached
  fails as before, keeping the image for you to look at.

- **A coding agent's sign-in reads its page and code whatever order its output arrives in.**
  When a sign-in prints a line such as Grok Build's `To sign in, open this URL in your
  browser:` and the address on the next line, a line the CLI wrote to its other stream in
  between could take that place, so the address or the code was missed and the sign-in
  ended without a login. Each stream's next line is now read as its own.

## [0.144.0] - 2026-10-26

### Changed

- **Secrets lets a new Mac in within moments and asks the server far less often.** An admin
  Mac's subscriber now waits on the server's queue of joining Macs instead of asking every
  2 s, and stretches the join password once rather than on every look: a Mac that types the
  join password is in after a median 0.3 s instead of 1.5 s (the slowest of 16: 0.45 s instead
  of 2.4 s), and an idle admin Mac asks 144 times an hour instead of 1,800. A subscriber that
  could not reach the server asks again as soon as its network changes (another Wi-Fi, a VPN,
  a wake) instead of waiting out its retry, and a held request lasts 25 s instead of 50-55 s,
  so a Mac that slept hears the next version sooner. Writing a version of 20 entries takes 3
  full disk flushes plus 20 ordered ones instead of 42 full flushes.

- **`aterm secrets create` prints the line to paste on each new Mac.** For a vault at a URL it
  prints `aterm secrets join http://<this Mac>:7484/v1/<name>#<key>` and, at a terminal, the
  join password. `create --serve` sets up this Mac's server first. `aterm secrets server on`
  now returns once the server answers (it waits up to 60 s), so a `create` right after it
  works. The server's log says once when another device on the network takes its `.local`
  name.

- **The secrets subscriber and server can be set up over SSH.** With nobody logged in at the
  Mac's screen, the job goes in your background launchd domain and runs until the Mac
  restarts; setting it up again once you are logged in at the screen moves it there. Login
  Items lists it under aterm. On Linux, setting one up over SSH or on a machine with no
  display runs `loginctl enable-linger`, so it keeps running after you log out, and says so
  in one line. `aterm help secrets` now starts with join, approve and status.

- **Codex accounts, goals and agent state run without external helper tools.** Codex
  accounts now pass their login file directly through `CODEX_AUTH_PATH` instead of
  layering links over a shared `.codex` folder, and `aterm harness accounts` signs in
  with PKCE and reads Codex rate limits in-process without starting `codex app-server`.
  `codex-alab` publishes its active goal in its session record so `aterm ctl survey` and
  the session header read it directly, and Muse Code goals and Antigravity session state
  read their SQLite files in-process without running `sqlite3`.

- **Messages between sessions on one Mac cost the fabric's state folder less.** The
  bridge kept each message's sequence reservation and its record in flight as files of
  their own, two written and two removed a message; it now appends them to one journal
  in its state folder. In the measured runs a local message's round trip took half as
  long on a broker that flushes nothing, and a burst went out 2.3-3.3 times as fast; on
  the default ordered broker a burst went out 1.0-2.5 times as fast and the round trip's
  tail is the broker's flushes, as before. A bridge of an earlier aterm sharing the folder
  still finds every reservation: a stop hands the journal back as the files it reads, and
  after an earlier aterm's bridge ran past it the journal's records in flight are set
  aside rather than sent again.

- **Mac setup waits quietly for what it needs, and says what is left.** While setup
  waits only on you (a grant in System Settings, an admin's step), it no longer looks
  again every minute: it wakes when a grant lands, when you come back to an aterm
  window, when the vault's folder, the network or Apple's Command Line Tools change,
  or when a retry falls due. On a standard account the Debugger and Developer Tools
  rows say they need an administrator and name the one command an admin runs
  (`sudo dseditgroup -o edit -a <you> -t user _developer`); the rest of setup
  finishes without them. A change macOS puts off to a later moment no longer counts
  as needing attention. `aterm.log` gets one short line per pass naming only the
  rows not in place, at info level for a not-yet and a warning only for a real
  failure. `aterm doctor --check` prints its verdict and the rows not in place;
  `--check --verbose` lists every row. A setting you change after setup set it is
  left as you set it, and the exceptions digest says so once. `aterm ctl @self
  status` gains `setup=` (`done`, `pending`, or `pending:fda,devtools,…`), read from
  what System State already knows.

- **`aterm init` waits less, and signs out of Messages and FaceTime in one run.** After
  it changes the Dock, Finder or widgets, init now watches the relaunched process itself
  every 20 ms instead of starting a `sleep` per second, skips the session check when you
  are at the Mac, and reads each preference domain once per look: a whole Dock, desktop
  and widgets pass runs 120 commands instead of 187, and a pass with nothing to change
  28 instead of 59. It reads your account, the Mac's chip and its macOS version without
  running a command. The Dock pins the aterm you are running when it lives where it
  stays (such as Applications or ~/Applications), and never a copy on a disk image or
  one macOS moved aside (App Translocation): that row now says to move aterm.app to
