  Applications. At a terminal, signing out of Messages and FaceTime asks macOS for
  Accessibility once and goes on the moment you switch it on, instead of ending and
  asking you to run init again; if you leave it off, the app opens for you to click Sign
  Out yourself and init goes on once you have. Init asks macOS's Automation question for
  System Events before it opens either app, never types a key, and stops clicking if the
  app leaves the front. In Low Data Mode, the Command Line Tools' half-gigabyte download
  waits and says how to go on; where Apple's catalog lists no tools, Apple's own
  installer opens instead and init waits for it. A Mac with Xcode but not the Command
  Line Tools sets up with Xcode's git instead of waiting for the tools. Every `aterm
  init --only …` that `aterm doctor` and aterm's tools print is one `aterm init`
  accepts; where your System State plan keeps rust-docs in Spotlight, the Spotlight
  row's rust-docs fact names `aterm init --only init.spotlight`.

- **`aterm doctor` says in one line whether anything needs you, and takes about a third
  less time.** Bare `aterm doctor` now prints a verdict line, such as `aterm doctor:
  healthy` or `aterm doctor: 1 needs you, 1 not measured — 44 checks ok`, and then only
  the rows that need you, went unmeasured or changed, each on one line of at most 160
  characters with a single fix. `--verbose` prints every row as before, and `--json` is
  unchanged. Readiness follows `aterm pkg doctor`: a package warning that `aterm pkg
  doctor` passes, such as a managed agent shadowed by another copy outside an aterm
  shell, no longer makes doctor fail. The `devtools:` row names one action, the
  `exceptions:` row shows the top three open exceptions, and bare doctor keeps an
  indexed rust-docs folder out of Spotlight itself, unless your System State plan left
  Rust in Spotlight unchecked or cannot be read. Doctor also spawns fewer programs: it
  remembers the C toolchain verdict until Xcode's selection or compiler, the Command
  Line Tools receipt or the SDK changes, a clean Spotlight verdict for the day, and a
  signature report and the solver's and compiler's versions until their files change. It
  reads both Universal Control switches with one `defaults` run, reads tccd's log over
  the last 2 minutes, and skips that log when aterm's Developer Tools switch has been on
  since before the run started. In a macOS guest up 12 minutes, bare doctor went from 23
  lines in about 1.25 s to 3 lines in about 0.81 s, `aterm doctor --read-only --json`
  from about 1.24 s to 0.84 s, `aterm pkg doctor` from about 1.40 s to 0.84 s, and the
  programs doctor starts from 14 to 8 per run.

- **`aterm help doctor` fits on one screen, and setup has its own page.** `aterm doctor
  --help` prints the grammar and five common forms; `aterm help doctor` is 18 lines with
  the exit codes; the first-launch setup prose moved to `aterm help setup`. `aterm help
  privacy` is another name for `aterm help permissions`, and that page now opens with a
  short table of each permission's current state and its fix, the details below it.

- **The Overview's "On the fabric" group and Summarize's fabric read list other nodes'
  sessions only, and say so.** The fabric is one machine's bus: each home folder has one
  fabric root and one broker socket, and no aterm command puts a second node on it. So on
  one Mac the group stays empty, and every session `aterm fabric brief` names is one of this
  Mac's own. The 0.113.0 and 0.138.0 notes said the group and Summarize covered "your
  fabric's other machines"; they do not. Summarize now runs `aterm fabric brief --json` and
  tells its worker that a session with `"this":true` is one of this Mac's own, already in the
  survey, and that any other names its node, so the worker no longer reports this Mac's
  sessions as another machine's. A bus between machines is not built.

### Fixed

- **A Mac serving its own vault no longer takes the ALab name or the ALab vault.** `aterm
  secrets serve` and `server on` with no flags now advertise `alab-secrets.local`, and take
  the ALab vault from another Mac, only on ALab's server: one whose store holds the ALab
  vault, or one started with `--advertise alab-secrets`. Before, every server on macOS did
  both. A personal server on a network with ALab Macs, even briefly (a café, or the ALab
  office while its server sleeps), took their copies of the ALab vault and then served them
  as ALab's on its owner's own network, where every new Mac read as an ALab Mac and got the
  ALab profile, including the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs. A new ALab server with an
  empty store starts with `aterm secrets server on --advertise alab-secrets`.

- **The fabric's state folder no longer keeps the files of sessions a restart of your Mac
  ended.** The bridge keeps a few small files per session (a keyed post's reservation, a
  receipt's, its refill floors on the topics it follows, its place in each topic and in its
  mail) and never removed those of sessions that ended with an earlier boot, so the quit
  after an update flushed every reservation and floor of them to disk again, and a leftover
  receipt reservation kept its session's names counted against the node's budget on the
  bus. The first start after a restart now removes them once it has listed aterm's
  sessions (a start that cannot list them leaves them to the next restart). It leaves them
  where an aterm attached to the bus since the restart, an older build that keeps no record
  of its run and whose sessions may still use them, and in a state folder off the startup
  disk, which records no boot for an attach. A reservation or floor that does not read
  whole stays where it is, for a repair; a place in a topic or in the mail goes whatever it
  holds, as no session reads it again. A bridge also forgets, for the rest of its run, a
  receipt's file and a closed session's once it removed them, where its stop used to look
  for each again.

- **The request to free disk space names the asked tab's own build when another tab's
  is larger.** When the first tab asked freed nothing and the request moved on to the
  next, that tab's line named only the largest builds left, often just the first tab's,
  and could say nothing of the asked tab's own, pointing its agent at another session's
  build. The line now names the largest build and the asked tab's own, marked "this
  tab's", and when it has room for only one, the asked tab's own.

- `aterm secrets join` of a vault at a path that this Mac pins to a signer, or one typed with `#<signer>`, refuses when the file now holds plain text. It used to read the file as a plain secrets file without a word and drop the pin, so whoever could write the file decided what went into HOME from then on.

- A vault at a path no longer puts back, every minute, a file a program keeps rewriting, moving the program's copy aside each time. Like a URL vault, it puts a changed file back once per version and set of changed files.

- First-launch setup no longer treats a Mac as ALab's because it joined a vault of its own, reads a plain secrets file, or holds an `aterm fleet` key. Each of these used to count, so such a Mac got the whole ALab profile, including the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs that nothing undoes. Only membership of the ALab vault counts now, judged by its signing key rather than its address, or a request to join it, or the ALab vault answering on this network.

- `aterm secrets agent on --program` and `server on --program` refuse a program that does not start as aterm, instead of installing a job that never starts, and so do the commands and repairs that put a subscriber back on the program it already runs. A copy of the app's executable outside aterm.app is one: macOS kills it at launch, and the refusal says to sign the copy ad hoc (`codesign --force --sign - <path>`); an app's own executable killed so is named a damaged install, to install again.

- `aterm secrets sync`'s first line now counts the files it could not write or remove (`, 1 failed`), as the subscriber's log line does. An automatic sign-in that refreshed the vault this way and still found no route, or whose route failed, logs `vault(applied seq N, some files failed)` instead of reading the sync as a clean apply.

- **One unreadable row no longer hides the recovery history from `aterm doctor`.** A
  row the doctor could not parse, such as one a newer aterm wrote, made it treat the
  whole recovery ledger as unreadable. The doctor now skips such rows, reads the rest,
  and adds a note giving the number it skipped.

- **Text fields show where they are.** The command palette's search field had a
  faint 1.5:1 outline, the find bar's query field was only a shade off the bar
  around it (1.2:1 in GitHub Light), and on macOS the field that renames a tab
  had no edge at all. A field whose fill does not stand out from what is around
  it now draws an edge at least 3:1 against it, as every Settings control does:
  the palette's field a rim, the find and rename fields a line along their foot.
  While you compose text with an input method in the find field, the composition
  is underlined twice, so it stays apart from that line. On Windows a find bar
  too small to draw its accent line under the field (a small font, a pane's own
  bar, a one-row pane) showed no edge at all; the field now underlines it there,
  and a one-row bar's bottom rule no longer paints over the field's edge.

- **The config editor shows several rows of the file at a large text size.** An
  80x24 window at 2x text showed aterm.toml one row at a time under two rows of
  buttons and the help line. Where the file would get fewer than six rows, the
  toolbar's extra rows give way first (each of their buttons is also a key and a
  command by name), and the help line gives way only where the file would
  otherwise show fewer than four rows; both come back when the window has room.
  An 80x24 window now shows four rows at 2x and five at 1.5x. Opening the list
  of suggestions (Ctrl-Space, or M-x for commands) left the one row being edited;
  now, where the list would leave fewer than four rows, its rows close up and the
  buttons step aside until it closes (in a file opened for another program, its
  Done and Abort row too; C-c C-c and C-c C-k still work), so the file keeps three rows at 2x, four at
  1.5x and five at 1.25x. The editor also no longer draws a sliver of the row its
  footer covers: it shows whole rows only. While you type a new key, the error
  that aterm.toml cannot be read until its `=` wrapped to three rows and left
  the file two rows at 2x, one with the list open; the error now says only what
  is wrong ("expected `=` after a key", without repeating the line and column),
  and where it would cost the file its four rows it shows a shorter form on one
  row. The file also no longer scrolls sideways while its line fits: with the
  caret at the end of `agents_auto_prime = false` at 2x, every row lost its
  first four characters.

- **`aterm fabric brief --json`'s mail counts follow a session's mail.** Mail crosses the
  bus only as a session's counts, and those crossed only in a snapshot of the session taken
  every 64 records the bus carries, so `mail_in` and `mail_out` lagged by up to 64 records, or
  for good once the session went quiet. A snapshot is now also taken once a
  session's mail counts move, at most one a second. A count held back by that rate tells the
  bridge when it is due, and the bridge takes it then, so the counts follow within about a
  second. A session that closes takes its last counts with it.

- **The Overview's "On the fabric" chip keeps a limit's reset, and no longer counts a
  session that exited without its close.** A chip for a usage limit read a bare `limit`,
  because the reset the fabric's log gives (`in 1m`, `9am tomorrow`) holds a space and was
  dropped. It now reads as the session's own tab does, `limit · in 1m`. A need of a session
  whose own presence says it exited, but whose close never reached the bus (`aterm fabric
  brief` marks it `partial` with `no-close`), was shown fresh and counted in the title's "N
  need you", although nobody there can answer it. It is now shown as older and not counted,
  as a session whose node is gone already was.

## [0.143.0] - 2026-10-26

### Added

- **One walk through macOS's permissions at first launch.** Full Disk Access,
  Developer Tools, Accessibility (only for the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs)
  and debugger access used to come one at a time, each waiting for its own quiet
  moment and ten minutes behind the last; on the owner's own Mac the Full Disk
  Access page came up almost 23 hours after it was queued. Now aterm's helper
  panel walks you through every grant it still lacks in one go, beside System
  Settings, showing "Step 1 of 3": as soon as a switch reads on (aterm checks four
  times a second) the same panel turns to the next page about a second later,
  a grant you already gave is skipped, and Not now moves on. macOS's password
  dialog for debugger access comes after the last page, once you are back at System
  State, rather than at a quiet moment hours later. It starts by itself
  once on a new Mac when you are at System State and not typing; the Permissions
  rows, `aterm doctor` and `aterm init` (for a person at this Mac) and
  `aterm ctl permissions walk now [fda|devtools|accessibility|debugger]` start
  it too (`devtools hand-over now` is now the same walk). The Full Disk Access
  page tells you to choose Later on macOS's Quit & Reopen sheet, since a window
  you started already sees the change; the debugger alert is two lines instead
  of eleven; and if you decline Full Disk Access, the Documents, Desktop and
  Downloads questions come back to back instead of one after the other.

- **About aterm has its own tab.** The About menu, version badge and About
  shortcut open a dedicated screen with the running version, author and project
  site. Details shows build information and font credits. Returning to About
  keeps its view, and opening it leaves Settings and unfinished settings edits
  in place. About tabs also survive session restoration and live updates.

- **The harness frees disk space before the disk fills.** System State's Disk
  view could say the home volume would be full in half an hour while aterm did
  nothing: it acted only once free space was already below its floor, and kept
  removed worktrees' build caches for their one-day quiet window. Now a fill that
  the Disk view's slope says crosses the floor within two hours counts as
  pressure. aterm's cleanup runs its pressure tiers and removes a removed
  worktree's cache whole, then asks one agent session to free space, with the
  fill rate and the time left in its line. If no session can act, or the one
  asked has not freed enough in time, aterm starts a Claude Code worker of its
  own under Autopilot Land, in a folder of its own: at most one per volume per
  episode and none within six hours of the last. It removes only caches that
  rebuild, through `aterm harness disk free`, never your folders or another
  session's work, and reports what it freed and what only you can free. You are
  alerted on screen only when no agent can act in time; otherwise the filling
  disk is an entry for later. `aterm harness disk why` says each step and why.

- (developer tool) **`lab autopilot-captures` shoots Land stopped by the same reply.** On
  Claude Code, agy and Muse Code a sixth scene holds a Land tab whose agent gave the same
  reply twice: the tab at rest and with the chip's title hovered, both with the Messages band,
  the Overview, and Settings ▸ Harness turned to the held session's state line, with the tab's
  hover and `ctl messages` beside them as text.

- (developer tool) **A development build's `aterm ctl chrome` prints the harness's screen-reader
  nodes.** After the `autopilot` lines come `a11y` lines: each Autopilot chip's and each Messages
  band row's node (its role, label and description) as the window's accessibility tree is built
  for a screen reader. `lab forever` wants a stopped tab's chip node, and the loud stop's band
  row node, to say the stop, and `--window` now also reads same-land's stop off a real window.

- **`aterm harness accounts browser` brings its own browser.** On a Mac or a Linux
  desktop with no Google Chrome for Testing or Chromium installed, it refused and told
  you to install one. Now it downloads the Google Chrome for Testing build aterm pins
  (about 190 MB) into aterm's browser cache first, checked against its pinned size and
  SHA-256, and opens the sign-in window in it; Control-C stops the download, and a
  download that does not match installs nothing. Grok Build's sign-in request names
  `accounts browser` only where it can open a window on that machine (a Linux session
  needs a display; then a browser installed, or downloadable with no download failed
  in the last hour), and otherwise leads with the mailbox step.

- **The help every agent reads says how to read the session log on the bus.** `aterm help
  fabric` has a section on it: `[fabric] log`, the `mirror=` that `aterm ctl fabric status`
  prints, `aterm fabric brief [--json]` and answering by mail. The agent brief (`aterm help
  agent`) names `@<sid> brief`, `@<sid> log`, `await log need,close=turn` and `aterm fabric
  brief --json`, and so does the aterm-fabric skill, the one codex-alab, Muse Code and
  opencode get. The supervise-agent skill no longer says a reply crosses to another Mac: the
  fabric is one machine's bus.

### Changed

- **`aterm init` waits less, and signs out of Messages and FaceTime in one run.** After
  it changes the Dock, Finder or widgets, init now watches the relaunched process itself
  every 20 ms instead of starting a `sleep` per second, skips the session check when you
  are at the Mac, and reads each preference domain once per look: a whole Dock, desktop
  and widgets pass runs 120 commands instead of 187, and a pass with nothing to change
  28 instead of 59. It reads your account, the Mac's chip and its macOS version without
  running a command. The Dock pins the aterm you are running when it lives where it
  stays (such as Applications or ~/Applications), and never a copy on a disk image or
  one macOS moved aside (App Translocation): that row now says to move aterm.app to
  Applications. At a terminal, signing out of Messages and FaceTime asks macOS for
  Accessibility once and goes on the moment you switch it on, instead of ending and
  asking you to run init again; if you leave it off, the app opens for you to click Sign
  Out yourself and init goes on once you have. Init asks macOS's Automation question for
  System Events before it opens either app, never types a key, and stops clicking if the
  app leaves the front. In Low Data Mode, the Command Line Tools' half-gigabyte download
  waits and says how to go on; where Apple's catalog lists no tools, Apple's own
  installer opens instead and init waits for it. A Mac with Xcode but not the Command
  Line Tools sets up with Xcode's git instead of waiting for the tools. Every `aterm
  init --only …` that `aterm doctor` and aterm's tools print is one `aterm init`
  accepts; the Spotlight row's rust-docs fact now names `aterm init --only
  init.spotlight`.

- **Work that has stopped comes first in the menu bar's Needs you.** An approval box no
  harness presses, a question, a frozen or stalled agent, or another owner's request now
  lists before a `NEEDS YOU:` report its agent carries on past, however old the report:
  a two-minute-old box in one tab reads above a three-hour-old credential report in
  another, where the older report used to lead. Stuck still comes before decide, and
  within each kind the oldest comes first. The window's pressing session (the session its
  border is lit for, `presence pressing=` in `aterm ctl chrome`), the next need the pill's
  `+N` opens and Agents ▸ Next That Needs You (⇧⌘J) start from the stopped work too. A
  report's row says on hover that its program carries on meanwhile (`Claude Code carries
  on meanwhile`), or, where that need alone holds its Land session, `Claude Code's
  landing waits on this alone`. No row, mark or glyph is added, and the bar's `❯N` is
  unchanged. Another aterm's and a fleet Mac's reports list after every request too, and
  after this aterm's own: `aterm ctl survey`'s facts row now says `needs_by=harness` for a
  harness's report (an older aterm's rows still say `-`). (developer tool) The forever
  lab's N4 writes a stand-in direct ask beside `cruise-n`'s report and wants it listed and
  pressed first; `verify appkit`'s toolbar drive reads the order and the report's tip off
  a real status item's menu.

- **Cruise asks for a new kind of work at each done claim.** When a reply says the
  work is done, Cruise no longer types one fixed check: each claim gets the next of
  six asks in turn (run the widest check on the merged tree; review the landed diff
  as a hostile reviewer would; do what the reports called out of scope; measure
  against the main the work started from; take the next open issue or TODO; land
  every worktree, branch and stash the session made, leaving the ones it did not
  make exactly as they are), then the first again. Each still says to put what only
  a person can give on a `NEEDS YOU:` line and to defend `Nothing left:` with what
  it ran. Where git finds work in the repository that no remote main has, the check
  now asks the agent to land what of it the session made and to leave the rest
  (another session's stash or worktree) exactly as it is, instead of telling it to
  commit, merge and push all of it; Land still asks for all of it. The count carries
  across a harness restart and starts again at someone's turn or a switch out of
  Cruise. Cruise also no longer accepts Claude Code's grey suggestion bare: it types
  its own continuation over it. `aterm harness policy` names the six asks
  (`done_check_angles=`) and their shared ending (`done_check_tail=`).

- **A tab aterm stopped typing into says so.** When an agent answers Autopilot's acts with
  the same reply twice and no work, or six replies in a row with no work, aterm stops typing
  into its tab. Every place you read that tab now says it. The chip's title and spoken
  description, the menu bar's worker row and the Settings ▸ Harness state line say
  `stopped typing: …` first; all but the worker row add that it types again at your turn or
  once the agent works (the lapsed `pausing until …` is gone while it is stopped, and under
  Cruise the stop replaces the mode's `keeps going for ever` promise); the tab's hover and
  the Overview say `stopped typing` after the mode (`driven by aterm (land: stopped typing;
  …)`). `aterm ctl status` prints `held=same-reply`, `held=no-work` or `held=-`, and the
  session's journal names the same. Under Land, when the repository still holds work no
  remote main has and no manager waits on the session, one Messages band, `aterm stopped
  typing in window W, tab N`, says so and is withdrawn when typing resumes; it names aterm on
  agy and Muse Code, where a resume ask used to say `Claude needs you`. Every other stop
  raises no band, an API error retried until its tries are spent among them.

- **First-launch Mac setup starts at once, with no countdown and nothing to confirm.**
  System State no longer shows `Apply (30)` and Cancel: the first moment you are at the
  Mac (a key, click or trackpad within the last minute, the screen unlocked), it sets up
  what it shows, whether or not an aterm window is in front. A first launch whose window
  was not focused used to be refused and offered again up to a minute later; it now
  shows the offer at once. Clicking, scrolling or typing in the page no longer holds
  setup back. Pressing a group before setup starts starts it with your choice, and only
  Join sends a vault address and password you typed. Rust's offline documentation now
  leaves Spotlight's reach in under a millisecond, where rustup's removal held setup for
  3 to 4 seconds (52,000 files): its folder is set aside as `html.noindex` at once,
  and rustup removes it in the background instead of holding up the steps after it.

### Fixed
- An admin Mac's approver no longer reports itself stuck when another admin Mac let the same Mac into the vault a moment before: a publish the vault turned away before storing it is read again two seconds later, and reported only if approving keeps failing. The notice's Approve now refuses a joining Mac whose key waits under two names, as `aterm secrets approve` by code already did, and the notice then says why and gives the command that approves the Mac under the name it asked for.

- A Mac in your ALab fleet joins the vault within seconds of answering Allow to macOS's Local Network question on its first launch, instead of waiting for System State's next retry a minute or more later. Answering Don't Allow ends aterm's wait for the vault at once, instead of after three minutes.

- **Allowing Full Disk Access brings the Developer Tools step in the same run.** On
  a new Mac aterm cannot read the Developer Tools list until it has Full Disk Access,
  so the list read nothing at launch and the Developer Tools page waited for the next
  launch or update. Now the moment Full Disk Access reads on, aterm reads the list at
  once and, if aterm is not on it, queues that page in the same run. The `spctl` step
  that puts Terminal on an empty list runs as soon as the page is queued, so the page
  opens at its moment without waiting for macOS's check.

- **An update no longer misreads Full Disk Access as switched off.** In its first
  second an updated aterm could read a grant you had made as off, before macOS knew
  the new process was aterm. aterm now waits until the process has run for 90 seconds,
  reads again, and logs `reads held now` or `still off`. Only a grant still off then is
  treated as switched off: the System State menu line names it as before, now with "The
  update needs Full Disk Access re-allowed." under it when an earlier build had it. It is
  read once more when you next switch to aterm.

- **Opening System Settings no longer stalls aterm's windows.** aterm opened the
  privacy pages with a call that waited while System Settings launched. Every window
  could freeze for about 200 ms when a permission page came up. The page now opens
  without aterm waiting for it.

- **Turning on Notify Me When I'm Needed is the only notifications question.** aterm
  now asks macOS at first launch to deliver its notices quietly. This shows no dialog,
  and aterm posts nothing until Notify Me is on. Turning Notify Me on asks for banners,
  as before.

- **Move Tab to Next Window brings a minimized destination back.** Shift-Cmd-M could
  move a tab into a window minimized to the Dock and leave it there, while aterm treated
  that hidden window as the one in front: Cmd-V pasted into the moved tab, Cmd-W closed
  it, and Cmd-C, Cmd-F, Cmd-T and `aterm ctl` commands that name no session acted there
  too, though you were still typing in the window you could see. The destination now
  comes out of the Dock, and those shortcuts stay with the window that has the keyboard
  until the destination takes it. On Wayland, where aterm cannot move the keyboard to
  another window, they stay with the window you are typing in.

- **Find stays open when a tab closes behind it.** With the find bar open, a background
  tab whose shell exited, a tab closed with `aterm ctl close`, Settings closed with
  `aterm ctl settings close`, or a split pane beside yours exiting closed the find bar
  mid-query, so the rest of what you typed, and Enter, went to the shell, and an
  input-method composition in the field was cancelled. Find now closes only when what
  is in front changes: a tab switch, a move to another pane, or a close of the tab it
  searches.

- **A Mac you revoke no longer shows up as asking to join again.** After a revoke, an
  admin Mac could show a standing `… asks to join the vault` notice for the Mac it had just
  removed, for up to a week, built from the old request that let it in; Approve would have
  let it straight back in. That old request is now left alone, and the Mac shows up again
  only when it asks again.

- **A second admin of a vault made by `aterm secrets create` can revoke a lost Mac.**
  `aterm secrets admins add` now brings the new admin into the vault's Commons control, so
  once enrolled there it can revoke. Before, an admin that had come in through an open vault
  stayed outside that control, every revoke it made failed with "needs locally applied
  control custody", and a stolen Mac kept getting new versions whenever the first admin was
  away. A revoke it cannot make yet names the admin that can and, for an admin added by an
  earlier aterm, the command to run there. The ALab vault has no Commons control, so this
  never reached it.

- **Moving aterm.app no longer stops the vault server for good.** On the Mac
  that serves the vault, moving or deleting aterm.app made the server stop
  within seconds, and nothing started it again, so new Macs found no vault and
  members got no new versions. The server and the background subscriber now
  keep running when their program's file is gone, and quit only when an update
  puts a new one in its place. The next time aterm opens from its new place, it
  points both background jobs at itself, the server with the same settings.
  That repair now also runs while System State's setup is still waiting on
  you. An admin Mac whose subscriber stopped no longer keeps showing
  `… asks to join the vault` notices whose Approve no longer works.

- **A pane close that had to wait no longer flips tabs.** Some pane closes wait
  before they run: an `aterm ctl … close` sent while an update is being handed over,
  and, on Linux and Windows, a busy pane's close question. When such a close finally
  ran for a pane in a tab behind yours, aterm brought that tab to the front for a
  moment to close the pane. That cleared the red mark of a failed command in a tab you
  never looked at, and sent focus-lost and focus-gained reports to the program in your
  own tab. When the pane was its tab's last, the tab next to it could come forward and
  lose its mark too. The pane now closes behind your tab, and the tab and pane you were
  on keep the focus.

- **An `aterm edit` that opens behind you no longer flickers your tab's focus.** When
  a program in another tab opened a file with `aterm edit` (for example `git commit`
  with aterm as the editor), the edit tab was brought to the front for a moment before
  aterm put your tab back. The program in your tab was told it lost focus and got it
  back, so an editor set to save on focus loss saved every buffer. The edit tab now
  opens behind your tab, marked, without touching its focus.

- **A secrets file you delete is written again without waiting for a new
  version.** A vault value this Mac already held when the vault arrived (the
  same token in `~/.secrets`, a `gh` `hosts.yml` of its own) stayed this Mac's
  file. Deleted, it was not refilled until an admin published a new version, and
  `aterm secrets sync` said `up to date`. Now the next sync, or the background
  subscriber within a minute, writes the vault's value into the gap. A vault
  server that went back to an older version also gets this Mac's newer copy back
  from a pass that was repairing files, not only from one waiting for news. A
  file whose write failed partway is no longer taken for this Mac's own file
  afterwards. And waiting for an admin Mac to approve this Mac in System State or
  `aterm init` ends on time, and stops within a second at Ctrl-C, instead of
  running up to 15 seconds over.

- **Text fields show where they are.** The command palette's search field had a
  faint 1.5:1 outline, the find bar's query field was only a shade off the bar
  around it (1.2:1 in GitHub Light), and on macOS the field that renames a tab
  had no edge at all. A field whose fill does not stand out from what is around
  it now draws an edge at least 3:1 against it, as every Settings control does:
  the palette's field a rim, the find and rename fields a line along their foot.
  While you compose text with an input method in the find field, the composition
  is underlined twice, so it stays apart from that line.

- **The config editor shows several rows of the file at a large text size.** An
  80x24 window at 2x text showed aterm.toml one row at a time under two rows of
  buttons and the help line. Where the file would get fewer than six rows, the
  toolbar's extra rows give way first (each of their buttons is also a key and a
  command by name), and the help line gives way only where the file would
  otherwise show fewer than four rows; both come back when the window has room.
  An 80x24 window now shows four rows at 2x and five at 1.5x.

- **Automatic bold draws the font's own Bold.** With SF Mono, the Bold font row
  said "Automatic (SF Mono Bold)" while bold text was drawn at weight 700, which
  is not SF Mono's Bold (its Bold is weight 683). Bold text now draws a variable
  font's own Bold, and bold italic its Bold Italic. Where your Variable font
  weight is too close to that Bold (584 and up for SF Mono), bold text is drawn
  heavier than your weight and the row names the weight it draws: "Automatic (SF
  Mono at weight 700)".

- **Trail diagnostics identify their actual owners.** Historical cursor-trail
  verdicts retain the view and session that produced them after a tab or pane
  switch. Unbound sources are marked unknown, and trail readers report the
  actual front window and view they inspect, including for mirrored sessions.

- **Typing after a composer submission keeps its trail.** After text was sent
  through control commands, submitting it to a busy foreground program could
  leave new typing classified as program output. Enter now clears that stale
  caret state while keeping the established input row and background-output guards.

- **Working-directory metadata notices a host change.** Two reports could name
  the same path with different hosts without notifying the GUI. The stored host
  now participates in its change epoch, including while an explicit terminal
  title is set.

- **Session commands in a tab menu keep the pane they described.** A delayed
  Hand Back could release a sibling pane's hold after focus changed or the source
  pane closed. Hand Back, Take Over, Rename, Set Role, Harness Log and the copy
  commands now retain the original pane and session, and cancel if it has left.
  Close Tab continues to close the whole tab. Enabling the in-grid strip also
  refreshes Rename and Set Role availability without waiting for a session event.

- **`aterm ctl help status` and `help log` say what aterm writes.** `help status` gave
  `rollout=<ok|missing|stalled|->`, words aterm never prints; it now names the words
  `rollout=` takes: `bound`, `unbound`, `unmeasured`, `no-rollout`, `no-meta`, `other-thread`,
  `no-thread`, `stale`, `stopped` and `-`. `help log` says again that a run keeps at most 64
  program marks, the oldest taken first and counted in `lost=`, and that past 20 at once they
  are written one a second, a flap at its newest state. It names the `shown` mark, what the
  person is shown, which stays on this Mac and is never mirrored. It says a closed session is
  journaled only while `journal` and `restore_session` are on and the instance is not headless,
  on macOS and Linux, where it named `journal = false` alone. And it says `detail=` keeps a
  command's program name and, for a listed tool, one known subcommand word, where it said no
  argument was kept.

- **Earlier notes on the session log, Settings and the man page say what aterm does.** A tab's
  `now:` line gives a usage limit's reset as the notice prints it, so a 14:05 reset reads
  `now: limit · 14:05`, not `now: limit · resets 14:05` as the 0.108.0 notes said. Since
  0.118.0, `aterm ctl timeline` reads its `program-state` rows from the session log, so they
  follow the log's rule: at most 64 a run, and a program that changes state many times a second
  shown at its newest state; the 0.109.0 notes, which brought those marks to the log, did not
  say so. The session journal keeps a command's program name (a wrapper's own name when aterm
  does not know the wrapper's flags) and, for a listed tool, one known subcommand word, such as
  `git push`; it never keeps the command's other arguments, where the 0.106.0 to 0.108.0
  notes said it kept a command's first word as typed and no argument. A closed session is read
  with `aterm ctl @<sid> log` and `aterm ctl @<sid> brief`; the 0.106.0 notes gave
  `aterm ctl log @<sid>` and `brief @<sid>`, which aterm refuses.

- **`aterm ctl post re=` takes a bus offset as aterm prints it.** `re=@<off>`, the form
  `inbox`, `cause=` and `aterm fabric brief`'s `head=` print, is taken as `aterm fabric post`
  takes it; `aterm ctl post` and `await inbox re=` refused it with a usage error. `aterm ctl
  help fabric` names `mirror=unserved`, which `fabric status` prints while no bridge serves
  the closed sessions' logs this instance keeps.

- **The config editor's help line shows its whole text.** The line above the
  file that says what the setting under the caret does was one row, so at 50
  columns it was cut ("Prime coding agents automatically · agents_a…"). It now
  wraps onto the rows it needs, up to three. What the setting does shows whole,
  even at a large text size (unless the file would then show fewer than four
  rows); the facts after it take only rows the file can spare, and where those
  run out it leaves out its last facts (the default, then the type) rather than
  cut a word.

- **`sys why` counts a build's work in the tab that runs it.** A build does most of
  its work in compilers and scripts that start and finish between two of aterm's
  readings, and `aterm ctl @self sys why cpu` counted a tab's CPU only in processes
  alive at both ends of its 5-second window. So during a build it said `this tab's
  share is not read now`: under four lanes of short jobs in a tab it read
  `tab_mc=≥39` beside `unattributed_mc=3480`, with the headline `no cause aterm can
  name: aterm`. On macOS a tab's figure now also holds the work of the processes
  its own processes started and waited for, which the kernel adds to each parent
  as a child finishes. Under the same jobs it reads `role=main cpu_mc=3933`, the
  headline says the tab's work is the main cause, and Why now in the CPU close-up
  names the tab's work. A process counts in the tab that shows it, keeps its tab
  after the process that started it quits, and is told apart from a later one
  given the same pid, also one another user's process takes. A
  tab keeps its count while it is open, also when you close its first pane, move
  it to another window, or show one of its panes in a second window too (Open
  Active Session in New Window; that pane's work then counts in one of the two
  tabs, and the rest of the tab's stays with it). A build you stop with Control-C, whose
  compilers macOS then cleans up, hides at most the work the tab finishes in the
  next reading or two, never later work. Where aterm knows the tab's figure may be
  short, it reads as at least (`tab_mc=≥` with `cpu_at_least_mc=`), even where
  `unattributed_mc=0`, since macOS's own count of aterm's work falls short by
  about a millisecond for each process that exits and can hide the gap: after such
  a stopped build; when a process ends that outlived the one that started it, or
  ends under a `sudo` that is still running; when a program aterm saw ignoring
  its children's exits (`SIGCHLD`) runs jobs, which macOS then counts twice, so
  aterm leaves the doubled count out; when a job another app runs for the tab
  starts or ends a process; and when a program was still starting as aterm read
  while a later one had already started, its work until the next reading left
  out. Two gaps stay unmarked. A process that outlives the one that started it,
  and starts and ends between two of aterm's readings, is in no reading and no
  parent's count, so its work can be missing from a figure that reads exact, and
  may show as `unaccounted` instead. And a program that ignores
  its children's exits where aterm cannot see it, one that starts and ends between
  two readings or ignores them only around its jobs' ends, has those jobs counted
  twice, so the tab can read up to twice their work as exact, and `unaccounted` may
  read below zero. Linux and Windows are unchanged.

- **An account you add with `aterm harness accounts add` closes aterm's sign-in sooner.**
  An account added by `aterm harness accounts add` or `accounts adopt-default` while a
  Claude Code tab stood on a sign-in aterm opened was noticed only at aterm's next look at
  `accounts.toml`, up to a minute later, and the tab sat on the method list meanwhile.
  Both commands now tell a running aterm as soon as they write the account, as `accounts
  sync` does, so aterm closes its own sign-in with Esc at the tab's next look, within about
  20 seconds. An account you write into `accounts.toml` by hand is still noticed within a
  minute. When aterm closes its sign-in that way, the tab's record now says that aterm
  backed out of the `/login` it typed, instead of crediting `Login successful` on the
  screen or the agent working.

- **A cursor pet waking from a nap no longer keeps its window busy drawing nothing
  new.** When a key woke the sleeping pet, its window redrew about sixty times a
  second through the whole stretch, though the stretch holds still after its first
  reach, and through the life of the z it pops even while text hid that z. The window
  now sleeps through both and wakes only as they change: a key that wakes the pet costs
  its window about 20 fewer wakeups (65 to 68 instead of 86 or 87 in a lab window), and
  13 or 14 of those left draw nothing new, not 34.

## [0.142.0] - 2026-10-26

### Added

- **An admin Mac shows each Mac that asks to join the vault and is not let in by
  the join password.** A Mac that asked with no password, a wrong one, or a
  `code-only` key gets its own notice, `m31 asks to join the vault: code …`,
  with the code that Mac shows, and its Approve lets exactly that Mac in.
  Approve is never the default button: compare the code first. The notice ends
  once that Mac no longer asks.

### Changed

- **install.sh opens aterm itself, so the ALab tools start installing at once.**
  It ended by asking you to type `open …/aterm.app`, and the ALab tools waited
  for that. Run from a terminal at this Mac's screen, it now opens the app it
  installed and ends with `install.sh: aterm is opening; it installs the ALab
  tools now`. Over SSH, under CI, without a terminal, as root, while aterm is
  already running, or with the new `--no-open`, it prints the launch line as
  before.

- **`aterm init` prints what changed as it happens, and runs its three parts at
  once.** It printed nothing until the whole run ended, then about forty lines,
  most of them saying a setting was already right. Now each change, failure or step
  that needs you prints the moment it finishes, and the run ends with one line such
  as `aterm init: 27 ok · 3 changed · 1 needs you: Full Disk Access`; `--verbose`
  prints every row. aterm's own repairs, the secrets vault and GitHub, and your Mac's
  preferences now run side by side, so a run takes about as long as its slowest
  part. Init asks nothing about what to set up: at the console it applies the
  workstation profile, the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs and your GitHub clones, as
  the first launch's setup does; `--profile`, `--sign-out` and `--clone` run only the
  ones named, and are refused where nobody at the Mac's console made them (over SSH,
  from a coding agent, or with no terminal). While aterm.app runs a setup pass, only
  init's preference changes wait for it, saying so; a whole profile init applied is
  recorded, so the next launch does not apply it again. A row never lands inside a
  password prompt: it waits until the prompt is answered.
  An `init.toml` that cannot be read, or a keyboard list macOS answers oddly, now
  leaves only the rows that need it unread instead of stopping the run;
  `--only init.spotlight` (or any setting's id or family) runs just that; and a row
  for each macOS permission still off says how to switch it on, naming the app it
  goes to (Terminal, when init runs in Terminal); one init cannot read fails nothing.
  `aterm help init` and `aterm init --help` are now one 25-line page naming each
  setting as System State does, and say that aterm.app's first launch does all of
  this by itself: init is for SSH and Macs used only from a terminal.

- **`aterm doctor` prints its report first and reads only what you ask.** The report
  comes at once and always goes to stdout, so `aterm doctor | less` and a captured
  stdout read it on a failing run too. Where aterm is missing from Developer Tools,
  doctor opens System Settings only after the report, and only for a person at the
  Mac's console: with an aterm window open it says one line and exits, since the window
  confirms the switch; otherwise it waits for the switch, reading it four times a
  second, and Enter ends the wait. `--json`, piped output, SSH and coding agents never
  open or queue a pane. Doctor's checks now run side by side, and `--only` reads only
  the checks it names: `aterm doctor --read-only --only base.shell.starts` checks the
  shell alone.

- **`aterm doctor` and `aterm init` say where their time goes.** With `--json`, each
  row carries `elapsed_ms`, the milliseconds the run spent on it, and the report gains
  `phases`: doctor's gather, lock, census, repairs, packages and develop, and init's
  context, questions, base and workstation. Each run also writes one line to
  `aterm.log` with those phase totals. The text output is unchanged, and a report
  written before this change still reads.

- **A seamless update hands the fabric to the new aterm at once.** During an update the
  new aterm's fabric bridge waited for the old one by trying its lock once a second, so
  mail and presence paused for up to a second after the old aterm quit (about half a
  second on average). It now takes over the moment the old bridge lets go, however that
  one ended, a crash included: in a debug build the pause from the quit to the new bridge
  carrying every session went from about 580 ms to about 35 ms (from about 620 ms to
  about 110 ms on a busier Mac).

### Fixed
- **What lands while you work in another app waits for you.** A landing in aterm's front
  tab while another app was active counted as seen, because aterm's last window still
  counted as looked at while any of it showed. It now leaves `❯•` on the menu bar and its
  row under ❯ ▸ Done for you until you come back to that window: by focusing it, switching
  tabs in it, or pressing the row's Go. While aterm is the active app, a landing in its
  front tab is seen as it lands, as before, and the front tab still never wears `•`. A
  worker's done in the front tab waits the same way. A Codex turn end there stays unseen
  until you return, so its tab wears `•` if it goes behind first.
  (developer) `App::window_looked_at` now needs the window's real key-window focus
  (`WindowState::os_key`, written only by the window's own focus events and its attach-time
  `has_focus()`), so `aterm ctl … focus in|out` never moves the look, and the focus-gained
  look runs after the key window is stored; the debug build's `person look` still stands in
  for a headless window. `targo --unverified lab look-away` drives it on a real window.

- **Closing an `aterm edit` tab you moved to another window leaves the old
  window alone.** Closing it there switched the window it came from to the tab
  that ran `aterm edit`: the tab strip named that tab while the window still
  showed yours, and the next redraw brought the other terminal forward. Now only
  the window the edit tab closes in returns to the tab that ran it.

- **`aterm secrets revoke` works again on a vault created before Commons custody.** Builds
  from 0.138 counted such a vault's admin locker as a bound Commons authority and then refused
  every revoke, and every edit that dropped a machine, because the vault had no Commons control
  to retire the machine through. A vault without Commons control now removes the machine from
  the vault alone, as builds before 0.138 did; where Commons control exists, revoke still
  retires the machine's Commons membership first.

- **`aterm init` no longer skips the ALab vault for a day after one failed look.** A look
  that timed out, was refused (the vault's Mac asleep or its server restarting), reached a
  server holding no vault yet or got an error page back was kept as "no vault on this
  network" for 24 hours. Only another vault's signed answer is kept as that now, so the next
  `aterm init` looks again; a record an older aterm kept is not read.

- **The secrets server and subscriber stay up through a full disk and a crash.** A log line
  they cannot write is dropped instead of ending the job; the server starts its keep-awake
  again if it ends; a publish lock left from before a reboot no longer refuses every publish
  until a person removes it; a join verdict that lands while a request is stored is kept; a
  second vault file that changes after the subscriber put back the first is put back too,
  instead of leaving the vault "still syncing" until the next version; and an admin publish no
  longer refuses an approver that can read the new admin locker format.

- **First launch keeps a finished repository clone when another Mac joins the vault.** Every
  open-vault join publishes a new vault version, and a clone that finished while one landed
  was thrown away and started over, so a burst of new Macs could keep each other's setup from
  ever finishing. A clone is now kept unless a file the vault wrote on that Mac changed.

- **One stale link no longer stops aterm from clearing idle builds when the disk runs
  short.** When free space falls below its floor, aterm empties the builds of checkouts
  nobody has touched for a week, except a build that a link in `~/.local/bin`,
  `~/.cargo/bin`, atpkg's bin folder or `~/.rustup/toolchains` points into. A single link
  there whose target was gone, such as a tool from a deleted checkout, made aterm keep
  every such build on the Mac. Now that link keeps only the build it points into.

- A verified whole-profile `aterm init` or `aterm doctor --apply` now keeps its
  completion if saving the final summary is interrupted, so the next launch
  does not repeat its settings or sign out an account you signed into afterward.

- **A repair no longer moves the secrets subscriber onto a different aterm.** `aterm init`
  reinstalled a running subscriber whenever a vault file was out of date, and System State,
  the window's mend and an admin command that needs an approver reinstalled a stopped one,
  each with the aterm doing the repair, replacing a program the person chose (`agent on
  --program`, a held snapshot on a vault's admin Mac). On an admin Mac that could rewrite the
  vault's admin locker for good. `aterm init` now leaves a running subscriber alone, a repair
  keeps the program the job names while it can run and lasts, and only `agent on` or a join
  moves it.

- **`aterm init` preserves pending Restore work.** A full setup now checks that
  every original still owed by Restore is available before replacing its setup
  records. Missing or incomplete backups leave that work intact.

- **Tab context-menu commands leave other windows' rename drafts alone.** A
  delayed Close Tab, Copy Session ID or other tab command could commit a rename
  in a different window. Commands now validate the original tab first and settle
  only their own window's edit. A tab that moved to another window or disappeared
  drops its queued command.

- An admin command typed with a newer aterm no longer silently stops an older approver on the
  same Mac. A publish (or `revoke`) that rewrites the admin locker into a newer format now first
  checks the program this Mac's subscriber runs and the one its job starts next (a `--program`
  snapshot): if either is older, its release or the job's state cannot be read, or neither can
  be named, it is refused and says why, naming an older program as the one to publish with
  instead, or, for a subscriber about to restart into a newer one, to publish again once it has. Another admin Mac's approver cannot be checked: update every admin Mac's
  subscriber first. The approver now says once in its log when it stays stuck (`not approving:
  …`, then `approving again`), and `aterm secrets status` shows it, and also shows a subscriber
  too old for the locker's format. A build that meets a newer admin locker names the format it
  found instead of "unsupported custody version".

- **A timeline's Rewind row keeps its original terminal pane.** If focus moves to
  another pane before a queued menu action arrives, Rewind opens the recording the
  row described. If the original pane has closed or moved away, the action cancels
  instead of opening a sibling's history or another view of the same session.
  Native and in-grid menu rows retain the same original target.

- **A running command's name is only its program's name.** aterm reads one name from a
  running command, the program it runs, and keeps it in the session's journal, on the bus and
  in `status`, `survey` and the fleet's survey. One list of wrapper flags served every wrapper,
  so a word that was a flag's value or an argument could be kept as that name:
  `sudo -n ./deploy.sh --token X` kept `X`, and so did `sudo -D /tmp/X make`, `sudo -p X ls`,
  `env -C /tmp/X make` and `time -o X make`. Each wrapper's flags (`sudo`, `env`, `time`,
  `nice`, `command`, `nohup`, `exec`) are now read by that wrapper's own rules, so those lines
  keep `deploy.sh`, `make`, `ls`, `make` and `make`. A flag its rules do not know, or one that
  runs no program (`sudo -l`, `sudo -e`, `command -v`), keeps only the wrapper's own name, such
  as `sudo`. A redirection's file could be kept the same way, with a wrapper or without one
  (`sudo >/tmp/X make` and `2>/tmp/X make` kept `X`, `sudo -S <<<X apt` kept `<<<X`), and so
  could a here-document's last line, a word inside a quoted `env -S` string
  (`env -S "-C '/tmp/X dir' make"` kept `dir`) and a word of a `$(..)` or backtick
  substitution. Redirections and here-documents are now left out as the shell leaves them out;
  a substitution, whose output names what runs, keeps no name past the wrapper's, and an
  `env -S` string that holds quotes, a backslash, `$` or `#` keeps only `env`.

- **System State respects “Not now” when saving fails.** Full Disk Access and
  Developer Tools stay declined for the current approval. A person's press or a
  new approval can open them again, and failed saves still retry.

- **Vault workers can retry a failed start.** A later setup request retries only
  the background workers that could not start, without duplicating one already
  running.

- **A font named with its weight draws that weight.** `font_family_italic = "SF
  Mono Light Italic"` (a name the font list used to offer) drew SF Mono's Regular
  Italic while Settings still said Light Italic, and `font_family = "SF Mono Light"`
  drew Regular. A name for one of a variable font's named instances now draws
  that instance, as a static font's Light face does, and keeps it under Variable
  font weight; a font named by its family or style (`SF Mono`, `SF Mono Italic`,
  `SF Mono Bold`) still follows the weight you set. The Bold, Italic and Bold
  italic lists offer a variable font's other instances (`SF Mono Light Italic`,
  `SF Mono Heavy`) beside its styles, no two names in a list draw the same, and a
  variable family named in the Bold row is no longer marked as another style. A
  style row that names a face of another style says what that face is
  ("“SF Mono Bold Italic” is a bold italic face"), where it said "is not an italic
  face" of a bold italic one.

- **The Text & Fonts preview names the display face it draws.** With a display
  face on (`display_font = "pixel"`), the preview drew Pixel's letters but its
  caption said only the font ("Font: Automatic (SF Mono)"), so once the Display
  faces card scrolled until only Bubble's row showed, nothing in view said which
  face was drawn. The caption now reads "Font: Pixel over Automatic (SF Mono)".

- **Japanese text shows on a page's first open.** A Settings, Manual or editor
  page opened while aterm was still loading its Japanese font drew no Japanese
  text at all, and stayed blank until something else redrew the page. The page
  now draws again as soon as the font has loaded.

- **The Manual reader reads 100% at the end of a document.** Its share read
  counted from the top of the page, so at a document's last page it could say
  "78% read" with Next already off. It now counts what the page has shown, and
  Next turns off once the end is in view, so a document that fits one page is
  no longer paged onto a page of its last line alone.

- **The config editor's help line shows its whole text.** The line above the
  file that says what the setting under the caret does was one row, so at 50
  columns it was cut ("Prime coding agents automatically · agents_a…"). It now
  wraps onto the rows it needs, up to three. What the setting does always shows
  whole, even at a large text size; the facts after it take only rows the file
  can spare, and where those run out it leaves out its last facts (the default,
  then the type) rather than cut a word.

- **The config editor keeps the file's name whole.** In a narrow editor at a
  large text size the header shortened `aterm.toml` to `ate…oml` to keep the
  caret's `Ln, Col` beside it. The caret's place now gives way first; the name is
  shortened only where it does not fit even alone.

- **Native tab clicks and drags retain the tab they acted on.** On macOS,
  queued select and close callbacks could act on a replacement tab after a
  reorder, and dragging could reorder another window. Callbacks now retain
  stable tab and window identities. A drag retains its pressed adjacent pair
  through a row update and cancels if that pair no longer remains adjacent.
  Stale callbacks leave replacement tabs and rename drafts alone.

- **Closing a background tab leaves you on the tab you were using.** Closing
  Settings from behind (`aterm ctl settings close`) moved you to the tab beside
  Settings, so the next command ran in another shell. A refused close of a
  background document, such as one with unsaved changes closed from its close
  button, middle-click, tab menu or `aterm ctl tab close`, brought the document
  to the front while it saved, and typing went into it. You now stay where you
  were; the document stays open, saved. Nor does closing Settings or an Editor
  buffer from behind (C-x k from another tab included) count a failed command in
  a neighbouring tab as seen, file a config problem in the message band away as
  if Settings had shown it, or bring forward the terminal that ran `aterm edit`.
  Closing Settings or an Editor buffer that shares a split leaves the focus on
  the pane you had focused.

- **Cmd-W closes the pane you see focused after an update replays a close.**
  When aterm replayed a pane close it had held back during an update in a
  background split, that tab showed one pane focused while its layout kept
  another, so a later Cmd-W closed the other pane without asking about its
  running job.

- **Full Screen and new-window shortcuts retain their source window.** Configured
  Full Screen could toggle another window. Cmd-Shift-N and Cmd-Shift-O could move
  or share another window's tab or session after waiting on the event loop. They
  now retain the window that received the key; queued new-window commands cancel
  if that source tab or focused content has changed. If a new window cannot be
  attached, the original tab and previously front window are restored.

- **A closed session's fabric subjects go back to its node.** A node may hold 4,096
  distinct bus subjects, and every session it ever hosted kept its presence row and each
  mail lane the node wrote to it for good: past seven eighths of that, mail to a new
  session was refused, and the only remedy was a new node id. Now, five minutes after a
  session leaves and once nothing the node owes names them, its bridge gives the session's
  presence row and those lanes back to the node, lanes to another node's departed session
  included (the bridge keeps looking while it holds one), and each attach gives back what
  earlier runs left. A session that comes back in the meantime (an update's handoff,
  recovery after a crash) keeps its row, its pin and its mail: the bridge gives back only
  the exact record it read. A post to a session that has left, from its own node or
  another, is refused at the sender as unroutable, whether its row still reads `exited` or
  has gone back; an `@<sid>@<node>` address now routes only while that node advertises the
  session live. Each topic a session broadcast on still keeps one subject for good.
  `aterm fabric status` warns past three quarters as before and says what goes back and
  what stays, and `aterm fabric doctor` says to close sessions before reaching for a new
  node id.

- **UI and tab-move shortcuts stay in the window that received them.** Configured
  Control Panel, About, command palette and theme palette shortcuts could open or
  close the other window's page or palette. Move Tab to Next Window could move
  that other window's tab, even closing its window, and the harness log shortcut
  could export the other session. They now use the receiving window and preserve
  unrelated drafts and palette previews. Palette accessibility updates use that
  same window.

- **Cmd-W closes the tab you are looking at after a document save lands.**
  When a document leaf in a split finished saving while a later tab was in
  front, the split's terminal took that tab's place in the window's terminal
  list, so the next Cmd-W, split or pane shortcut acted on the hidden tab
  instead.

- **Reopening a closed split tab no longer marks another tab's failure as
  seen.** While the reopened Settings or app leaf was rebuilt, the window
  briefly fronted its last tab, which cleared that tab's unseen-failure badge
  and tripped a debug check.

- **Reopening a closed aterm.toml tab keeps the one already open.** With
  aterm.toml open again in the window, Reopen Closed Tab took over that tab:
  it left the tab strip and its editor moved into the reopened tab. The
  reopened tab now gets its own view of the file.

- **A drive to a Mac whose aterm is restarting says to try again.** When the other
  aterm's fleet listener closed just as `aterm ctl --host` connected, macOS can reset
  the connection instead of refusing it, and the drive ended with `Connection reset by
  peer (os error 54)` as if trying again could not help. A reset now reads like a
  refusal: the drive says the listener is closing or restarting and to try again.

- **Recovered installer tabs stay linked to System State.** With the terminal
  keeper enabled, a Command Line Tools tab recovered after a crash holds off
  other setup prompts and another install while it runs. Recovery keeps the
  existing tab and never retypes its command.

- **`sys why` counts a build's work in the tab that runs it.** A build does most of
  its work in compilers and scripts that start and finish between two of aterm's
  readings, and `aterm ctl @self sys why cpu` counted a tab's CPU only in processes
  alive at both ends of its 5-second window. So during a build it said `this tab's
  share is not read now`: under four lanes of short jobs in a tab it read
  `tab_mc=≥39` beside `unattributed_mc=3480`, with the headline `no cause aterm can
  name: aterm`. On macOS a tab's figure now also holds the work of the processes
  its own processes started and waited for, which the kernel adds to each parent
  as a child finishes. Under the same jobs it reads `role=main cpu_mc=3933`, the
  headline says the tab's work is the main cause, and Why now in the CPU close-up
  names the tab's work. Each process counts at most once, in the tab that shows
  it, keeps its tab after the process that started it quits, and is told apart
  from a later one given the same pid, also one another user's process takes. A
  tab keeps its count while it is open, also when you close its first pane, move
  it to another window, or show one of its panes in a second window too (Open
  Active Session in New Window; that pane's work then counts in one of the two
  tabs, and the rest of the tab's stays with it). A build you stop with Control-C, whose
  compilers macOS then cleans up, hides at most the work the tab finishes in the
  next reading or two, never later work. Where aterm knows the tab's figure may be
  short, it reads as at least (`tab_mc=≥` with `cpu_at_least_mc=`), even where
  `unattributed_mc=0`, since macOS's own count of aterm's work falls short by
  about a millisecond for each process that exits and can hide the gap: after such
  a stopped build; when a process ends that outlived the one that started it, or
  ends under a `sudo` that is still running; when a program that ignores its
  children's exits (`SIGCHLD`) runs jobs, which macOS then counts twice, so aterm
  counts them only as far as it read them; and when a job another app runs for the
  tab starts or ends a process. One gap stays unmarked: a process that outlives
  the one that started it, and starts and ends between two of aterm's readings, is
  in no reading and no parent's count, so its work can be missing from a figure
  that reads exact, and may show as `unaccounted` instead. Linux and Windows are
  unchanged.

- **Pane shortcuts stay with the window that received the key.** With two
  windows open, a queued focus, zoom or split shortcut could act on the other
  window. A focus shortcut could also reach the shell when its own window had
  a neighboring pane. Configured and built-in shortcuts now use their receiving
  window for both availability and execution, including native application panes.

- **aterm reads Claude Code's sign-in in its fullscreen view.** When Claude Code draws
  its screen in its fullscreen view (`/tui fullscreen`, `CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1`, or a
  view Claude Code picks by itself), its `/login` sign-in sits in a panel at the bottom of
  the screen. aterm did not recognise that panel: after it typed `/login` into a lost
  login it flagged the tab as waiting on "a dialog of no kind aterm reads", and it never
  closed a sign-in it had opened for an account it signs in by itself. Now aterm reads
  the panel as it reads the sign-in in Claude Code's ordinary view, also while Claude
  Code's effort hint is drawn into the panel's top line: it asks you to pick a sign-in
  method where that is yours to do, closes its own sign-in with Esc where an account in
  your `accounts.toml` covers the login, and still never closes a `/login` you typed. In
  the fullscreen view aterm leaves the sign-in method to you even where it picks your
  subscription's in the ordinary view, because what Claude Code shows once a method is
  picked there has not been checked yet.

- **An account you add while aterm's sign-in is open is noticed.** An account added to
  `accounts.toml` by hand or by `aterm harness accounts add` while a sign-in aterm opened
  stood on its method list went unnoticed until something else changed, so
  aterm kept asking you to pick a sign-in method for a login it signs in by itself. aterm
  now notices a changed `accounts.toml` within a minute and closes that sign-in with Esc.
  An account named in the instant aterm answered the method list can no longer have the
  subscription method picked for it, which would have opened a browser sign-in.

- **Only a person at the Mac changes it.** `aterm init` run by a coding agent or
  without a terminal now runs the base layer and a vault or GitHub profile you
  recorded, over SSH the base layer alone, and leaves Caps Lock, scrolling, the
  Desktop, widgets, the Dock, the Messages and FaceTime sign-outs and Rust's
  Spotlight settings to one deferred row, `needs a person at this Mac's console
  … run aterm init there`; that run exits 0. `aterm doctor --apply` and
  `--restore` refuse with the same line there. A terminal session over SSH no
  longer turns Universal Control off, and a window started there or outside the
  console's own session never starts first-run setup. System State's
  `Apply (30)` counts down only while the screen is unlocked and someone used
  the keyboard, mouse or trackpad in the last minute. After an update relaunches
  aterm, setup nobody reviewed is never offered: a note, `Mac setup is
  unfinished`, opens System State, and a setup you already applied carries on.

- **A Linux machine that cannot resolve `alab-secrets.local` is told why.** glibc
  resolves `.local` names only through Avahi's nss-mdns (or systemd-resolved with
  MulticastDNS on), and without one a vault join failed with a bare `Name or service
  not known`. The error now names what is missing, and that a URL with the server's
  address needs neither.

- **A window with Settings open no longer redraws for every tab hover update.**
  With the in-window tab strip on and a Settings tab, or a terminal beside
  Settings, active or ahead of the active tab, each change to an agent's tab
  hover or to a background tab's title redrew the window though the strip had not
  changed. It now redraws only when the strip does.

- **Screen readers name each tab's own theme in the tab strip.** With a Settings
  tab, or a terminal beside Settings, ahead of a terminal tab that has its own
  theme, the strip described a tab with the next terminal tab's theme and left the
  themed tab with none. Each tab now announces the theme of its own terminal.

- **Left and right margins behave as in xterm.** With DECLRMM (`CSI ? 69 h`)
  on and margins set by DECSLRM (`CSI Pl ; Pr s`), text that wraps on the right
  margin goes on at the left one, and a line feed, reverse index or wrap at the
  edge of the scrolling region scrolls only the rectangle between the margins.
  Carriage return, cursor left and right and tab stop at the margins unless the
  cursor already stands beyond them, CHA under origin mode counts from the left
  margin, and NEL or a newline-mode line feed from past the right margin scrolls
  nothing. Outside the margins, inserting or deleting characters or lines
  changes nothing, not even a pending wrap, and a cursor restore puts a saved
  pending wrap back wherever the cursor lands, as xterm does, even after the
  margins moved (the next character starts the next line instead of overwriting
  the last one). Full-screen programs that split the screen into side-by-side
  panes with these margins now draw as they do in xterm.

- **After a resize, text resumes right after the line the cursor was saved on.**
  When output ended exactly at the right edge and a program saved the cursor
  there (a pager or editor does as it starts), then the window was resized, the
  first character after the restore (the shell's prompt, once you quit the
  pager) overwrote the line's last character. It now lands in the next cell, as
  in Ghostty, and the line reflows intact when the window changes size again.

- **The cursor pet no longer twitches late.** Once it settled beside the caret, the
  pet could slip a last pixel, hold a pose or puff a z up to most of a second late,
  whenever its window next woke for something else, and about one settle in four left
  it a pixel short of its place. It now lands exactly in place as its glide ends,
  changes pose and puffs each z when they are due, shows or hides a z behind text as
  the z moves, and keeps step with a typing rhythm instead of catching up in jumps. It
  also sets off on time when a landing or a pause ends with its place moved or the
  typing it waits ahead of stops, starts a flinch, a fade-in or a glance at the
  pointer from the beginning rather than partway through when its window had been
  asleep, stays seated after it wakes and stretches instead of showing a seat for a
  moment and standing, and comes to rest in its place rather than wherever it passed
  its front seat on the way back. A pet asleep or curled up with its head at the edge
  of a line of text no longer fades out and back in with each breath, waking its
  window each time. Its window wakes once more as a held pose ends, and draws frames
  while a typing rhythm carries the pet ahead.

- **The request to free disk space passes over tabs that are waiting.** A tab stopped at
  a usage limit, or at a question aterm has passed on to you, is no longer chosen while it
  waits there, however much of the disk its checkout holds: it cannot take the line until
  it is past. A chosen tab that stops at one goes back to the request at no cost, and can
  be chosen again once it is past; if it stops at one again after that, it is released, so
  the other tabs get their turn. Before, such a tab was chosen anyway, waited out half an
  hour and used up one of the request's choices, and a request whose only tab it was gave
  up for six hours. When every tab that could be asked is waiting like that, the request
  waits for the first one to be past instead of giving up for six hours, and the low-disk
  alert says so. A tab at a usage limit counts as waiting until the reset aterm itself
  waits for, including a later one that a weekly limit names after a session limit.
  `aterm harness disk why` and the next request's low-disk alert no longer name tabs that
  waited at an earlier request's limits as waiting. A tab you have put on hold or taken
  over, and a tab with text left typed in its prompt for a minute or more, are passed
  over the same way while that lasts; before, such a tab was chosen first, its line was
  refused at every turn break, and it used up one of the request's choices with nothing
  typed. Text left in the prompt now also holds back a tab whose turn is over with only
  its own background command or monitor still running (a manager waiting on its
  workers), and keeps holding it back while the agent works on by itself in between (a
  worker's report waking it) with the same text still there: the tab goes back to the
  request at no cost, and can be chosen again once the text is sent or cleared. Before,
  it stayed chosen for half an hour, used up a choice, was not asked again in that
  request once the text was sent, and a request whose only tab it was gave up for six
  hours. Text typed while the agent is still mid-turn does not hold the tab back until
  that turn ends. When the request waits like that after a line already went and freed
  too little, the low-disk alert now says it is waiting, not that another session is
  being asked. The alert and `aterm harness disk why` now say what the tabs are waiting at (a usage
  limit, a question for you, your hold or take-over, or text left in the prompt) and
  what ends the wait (the limit passing, the hold lifted, the text sent or cleared);
  before, they always said a usage limit or a question, also for a tab on hold or with
  text left in its prompt. A tab at a usage limit is now recognised as one: aterm looked
  for a word the agent never shows, so such a tab was still chosen. A tab that aterm keeps from going on
  rather than spend usage credits (the default), a tab signed out of Claude, and a tab
  stopped at another error aterm waits out are passed over the same way, also while its own
  background command still runs, and the alert says what ends the wait (the usage limit
  resetting, signing in again, the error passing); before, such a tab was chosen, nothing
  could be typed into it, and a request whose only tab it was gave up for six hours.

- **The request to free disk space no longer tells a worktree's tab that the main
  checkout's builds are its own.** A tab working in a git worktree inside another
  checkout (such as `~/aterm/.claude/worktrees/<name>` inside `~/aterm`) was credited
  with the enclosing checkout's builds whenever aterm's list of the largest builds held
  none of the worktree's own. Such a tab could be chosen ahead of the tabs working in
  that checkout, and its line called the checkout's shared builds "this tab's", which
  invited its agent to clean builds other sessions use. Each tab is now credited only
  with its own checkout's builds, and a tab whose folder has been removed (a worktree
  its session landed and deleted) with none. When the line has no room to name even
  the largest build as usual, it now names it with its folder shortened in the middle,
  still marked "this tab's" when it is; before, it said aterm had found no build it
  could size. When other tabs work in the same checkout as the asked tab (several agents
  in `~/aterm`, say), the line now calls that checkout's builds "this tab's checkout,
  shared" rather than "this tab's", so the agent is not told that builds other sessions
  use are its own to clean.

- **The request to free disk space credits the session that freed it, and keeps naming
  that tab's build.** When the asked session's cleanup brought the volume back past its
  limit at once, the request ended without crediting anyone: `disk.jsonl` and `aterm
  harness disk why` said the space came back but not who freed it. That session is now
  credited, and the request ends at the next check. On a volume mounted at a long path,
  the line ran past its length limit, or dropped the asked tab's own build and its
  "this tab's" mark for a pointer to `aterm harness disk`. The volume's name is now
  shortened first (in its middle, or to "its volume"), so the line stays within its
  limit and still names the tab's own build.

- **A deferred Restore keeps its pending work if its backup is missing or damaged.**
  System State reports the unreadable backup instead of silently forgetting what
  it still owes. A later Apply cannot replace that missing original with the current
  value; repairing the backup allows Restore to finish on its next retry.

- **Joining a secrets vault is faster, and a mistyped join password is asked
  for again at once.** A join fetches the vault once (it fetched it twice, plus
  the look for a vault before it), a look for a vault gives up after 1.5 s, and
  the join password is stretched while that fetch is out. A join that reaches no
  vault leaves no machine key behind. An admin Mac that refuses a join password
  now says so to the joining Mac, which asks for the password again within
  milliseconds of that admin's check instead of waiting out its ten minutes,
  `aterm init` asks for it again at that check instead of at its 6 s window's
  end, and System State's Secrets row reads `Wrong password` with its password
  field open.
  A Mac that asks again within 10 s of its last request has its request taken
  after the wait the vault names instead of refused. No route to a vault on this
  network is said as the macOS Local Network permission it is. The Secrets row
  names the command an admin runs, `aterm secrets approve <code>`.

- **On a Mac, `aterm secrets agent on` no longer restarts a subscriber that
  already runs as it would set it up**, so a second `agent on` (or setup's) cuts
  no long-poll, and a fresh install starts the job without killing anything
  first. `aterm secrets agent on --force` restarts it.
