  build's partial copy of its binary. A `kill` the instant `--no-toolchain` copies
  `aterm.toml` no longer leaves the copy either. 0.135.0's note said more than holds in
  two places: a `kill` stops the installer cleanly while it puts the app in place, but
  one during a check can still leave that check's file; and with bash 5 a Ctrl-\ while
  `curl … | bash` still downloads the script ends it as a cut download does, having run
  nothing, where a Ctrl-C there ends it by the signal.

- **A download of `install.sh` cut short runs nothing.** A `curl … | bash` cut just
  after `main` on the script's last line (a dropped connection, or a Ctrl-\ under bash
  5) ran the whole install with none of the options you gave it, so
  `bash -s -- --dry-run` cut there installed for real; and one cut inside a name that
  starts a line ran that name's first letters as a command, so a cut just after `bundle`
  ran `bundle install` in the folder you ran it from. The whole script is now one block
  bash runs only once all of it has arrived, so a cut anywhere runs nothing: in the
  script's opening comments it ends the run quietly, and past them it is a syntax error.

- **`--no-toolchain` keeps a whole copy of `aterm.toml` when it cannot finish rewriting
  it, and never says it saved an opt-out it did not.** When its rewrite of the file
  could not finish (a full disk, a quota), the file could be left empty or cut short and
  its only whole copy was deleted; the copy now stays, next to the file (in the
  temporary folder when the file's folder takes no new file), and the note says where it
  is and gives the command that puts it back. A config the installer cannot read was
  reported as written while it still said `auto_install = true`: the run now says to set
  the key by hand, and a `--dry-run` says it cannot read the file instead of stopping
  partway through its plan. A `--dry-run` also says when the run cannot write the file
  (its mode, an ACL, a link into a read-only store, a folder it cannot make the file in),
  where it said it would add the key or create the file.

## [0.136.0] - 2026-10-24

### Changed

- **`aterm ctl ls`, `task` and `await task` say what a codex-alab tab is doing.** Their
  rows carry codex-alab's own report as `program_state=` (working, blocked on an
  approval, a question or a sign-in, idle, done or error), `ls` says whether a
  session's claim is proven (`supervisor_proven=`), and `status` says how long the
  report has stood (`program_state_ms=`). `agent=` stays aterm's own reading, so a
  codex tab still says `unknown` there. To wait on a codex, read `log_seq=` and
  `log_ep=` from `status`, then `await log kind=program`; the help and the skills now
  say so. The menu bar counts a codex tab at rest as resting, not working.

- **codex-old no longer downloads OpenAI's Codex a second time.** Where `codex` is
  OpenAI's own build too (Intel Macs, Linux, or an Apple silicon Mac where you chose the
  vendor build), `codex-old` now copies `codex`'s verified build of the same release
  instead of fetching and unpacking the same ~110 MB again. On a Mac the copy takes no
  extra disk. It is checked the way a download is, and anything that does not match
  exactly is downloaded as before. A first install of both may still fetch it twice.

- **The stats deck stays in its compact form.** On a tall window the deck under the
  titlebar grew into its Full table, a header line, a row per resource and, on a wide
  window, a column of details. It now keeps its compact Folded form, two blocks of four
  rows, however tall the window is, and the terminal keeps the rows the Full table took.
  View ▸ Deck Size: Full still brings the Full table back.

- **The harness switch is the whole harness.** `alab harness ● on` on a coding
  agent's composer stays lit while the session's Autopilot is off, drawn in
  Autopilot Off's white, and a click on it turns the harness off for every
  session (Settings ▸ Harness's Supervise coding agents). The Autopilot chip
  alone turns a session's Autopilot off and on, and an Antigravity CLI session
  under Autopilot Off now wears the same white glass as Claude Code and Muse
  Code.

- **The harness footer shows the account, its plan and its weekly budget as one unit.**
  `⎆ you@example.com · Max 20x · weekly 61% left` is one fact: one mark, its parts joined
  by `·`, the next fact the usual gap away. On a narrow pane it narrows as one, giving up
  the email's domain first, then the plan, then shortening the email and the weekly words,
  and never shows the plan or the week without the account. Pointing at any part of it
  lights all of it. The same for Claude Code, agy and Muse Code.

### Fixed

- **Stop holds a confirmed setup revision after a failed admission save.**
  A staged run cannot start again after its Stop was saved.

- **Closing System State withdraws permission for on-screen setup steps.**
  Off-screen account checks cannot sign out an account found by a later read.

- **Accessibility stays actionable when account sign-outs need it**, even
  with Permissions set to Leave as is.

- **Check again and Stop wake setup retries immediately**, without waiting
  for another focus change or the next minute.

- **Command palettes stay with their window.** Filtering, navigation and
  activation use the palette that received the input, including when focus
  changes while a key waits. Save and Find keep their original target. A queued
  general command is cancelled if its window or active tab or pane changes,
  and closing a palette preserves another window's theme preview.

- **Your first window keeps its size when aterm reopens.** When aterm brought your windows
  back after a quit or a restart, the first one came back sized to whole rows and columns,
  a little off from how you left it, while the others kept their size. It now keeps its
  size too, unless it was maximized, full screen or tiled, or you named its lines or columns
  on the command line.

- **The harness card names the harness's own version, and its banner reads as a link.** The
  line under Claude Code's launch card said aterm's build number as the harness's version; it
  now says the harness's own (`enhanced by aterm harness v0.1`), and Settings ▸ Harness ▸
  Harness updates reads `v0.1 (built-in)` and the aterm build it ships in. The banner over Claude
  Code's update notice now reads `https://alab.systems`, underlined, shows the pointing hand,
  opens on a plain click (once for a double click), and is a link a screen reader can press.

- **Setup waits for the account's home folder before reading its saved plan.**
  A temporarily unavailable folder no longer prevents a pending run from resuming.

- **Restore and Check stay busy when System State is reopened.** Closing the tab
  no longer enables conflicting actions while either operation is still running.

- **Stop covers an ALab setup upgrade before its worker starts.** Quitting waits
  for the upgraded plan's Stop to be saved, including after a failed upgrade save.

- **Debugger access's Turn On… works the first time.** Pressed soon after aterm started (as
  it is right after Full Disk Access's Quit & Reopen), System State's Turn On… for Debugger
  access did nothing: aterm had not yet read whether it is a hardened build, and took the
  press for one on a build that does not need it. The window now reads that as soon as the
  page offers Turn On…, so the first press asks macOS for your password.

- **Claude Code's own Settings panel is no longer called a dialog aterm cannot read.** A
  tab left on the panel `/status`, `/config` or `/usage` opens, with Claude Code idle, was
  read as a dialog aterm could not read: after 30 minutes `aterm.log` got an error saying
  Claude's title had said idle "over a screen this build does not recognise", and after an
  hour To look at would have said "Claude is stuck on a dialog aterm cannot read". aterm
  reads that panel, so neither is said over it any more: the harness's journal names the
  panel, `aterm.log` gets no error, and after an hour To look at says the Settings panel
  stays open in that tab and Esc closes it. A screen nothing reads is still noted as
  before, and the harness types and presses nothing new.

- **Typing a vault password protects the form from startup setup.** An input
  method's uncommitted text now counts as a draft, so a delayed offer cannot
  replace it. Closing the composing view also clears its draft from linked views.

- **System State comes up as soon as you answer macOS's Local Network question.** On a
  fresh Mac, aterm's first request to the network raises macOS's Local Network alert,
  which takes the focus from aterm's window just as System State is about to open. aterm
  then waited a minute before it offered the page again, and another if the alert was
  still up: on a fresh macOS 26 Mac the page came up more than two minutes after launch.
  It now comes up within seconds of aterm's window getting the focus back.

- **Cruise goes on after a message the harness typed.** When Claude Code had just
  answered your message and aterm then upgraded and restarted it, the reply to aterm's
  "restore what you rely on" note was still read as part of your own exchange, so
  Cruise typed nothing more and the session sat idle. A turn that answers a message
  the harness typed (an upgrade's restore note, a carry-on) now gets Cruise's
  continuation; a reply to your own message is still left to you.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` when job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose own
  command runs in front is judged by that command; a build whose step stopped at the
  terminal (a `ninja` step at an ssh passphrase prompt, a `ninja &`'s too, also under
  `aterm -e ninja` or after `exec ninja`) still reads `quiet`, a Ctrl-Z'd `cargo nextest
  run` reads `parked`, and so does a `git pull &` stopped at its password prompt in a tab
  without shell integration. After `exec ninja` its build is one row that runs while its
  steps compile, after `exec python3` a REPL hung on a lock no longer reads as the shell's
  `read`, and after `exec zsh` the block ends at the new shell's prompt, also beside the
  `tee` a `.bashrc` logs the session through or from a `case` arm, after a comment or a
  here-document holding a quote, or past `ZDOTDIR=${…}/zsh`, and on macOS whatever the
  line says (a bash line kept out of history, which bash reports only in part), also when
  the first key at the new prompt opens a full-screen history widget (atuin's or hstr's
  Ctrl-R, `$(lf)`), so a background job's lines are its own again; `exec vim` back from a
  `:sh` keeps its row, its `:!make` included, also past vim's hit-enter prompt and when
  picked in atuin's full-screen search. A download pwsh runs in itself (`Invoke-WebRequest`)
  keeps its row, also after `exec pwsh`, beside a zsh it ran or between a loop's `docker
  exec`s, also one whose line a backtick continues, as does a `vared` prompt, and a build
  run by `exec cmake --build` or `out=$(ninja)` is one row as well, also when aterm saw its
  first process a moment before the command started, while one a pwsh `Start-Job` left
  running, by its steps (also those its `make` forks later in pwsh's group) or its lines,
  no longer keeps a later hung `git fetch` reading running, nor does a server
  `Start-Process -NoNewWindow` left printing there keep a deadlocked `dotnet test` running,
  nor one aterm may not read (`sudo log stream`) a hung `sudo mount`, also by the last line
  of one that exits or the lines of one that ran such a program in its place; a `dotnet
  build` in a pwsh run in pwsh, its profile writing the prompt's marks, reads running, as
  does a cmdlet it runs itself or a build printing through its `Tee-Object`, also after a
  command typed ahead with that `pwsh`, and a `ninja` there is one row, while the builds of
  a pwsh `Start-Process` started (a `watch.ps1`, also each `pwsh -File build.ps1` it runs)
  no longer keep a hung `git fetch` running.
  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z
  in the middle of a bash command list (`make; fg %1`) no longer split the resumed job in
  two, drop the earlier command's row, give one command's exit status to the other, or
  leave the resumed job behind the stopped one. A pipeline stage that runs in a group of its
  own (`seq 1 40 | timeout 3600 xargs ./step.sh`) is judged by the lines the tab prints
  once the stage in front exits, when it is the tab's one background job that can run,
  instead of reading `quiet`, then `stuck`; a parked editor no longer takes those lines or
  keeps them from it. A command run with `sudo` (which runs it on a terminal of its own),
  under `script`, or as an agent's tool call on a terminal of its own (Codex, Gemini CLI)
  is one row beside its opener's, judged by what it does: printing, it reads running, and
  hung on a server that stopped answering it reads `stuck` while sudo waits at the terminal
  and the agent's screen keeps moving, also when the agent runs in `nvim`'s terminal or in
  a tab whose shell gave way to it (`exec codex`) or that runs it in place of a shell
  (`aterm -e codex`). A Ctrl-Z'd `sudo vim` reads `parked`; a command hung in front of
  `script`'s shell beside a job that shell stopped reads `stuck`, and a program there
  waiting for your keys (`vim`, a password prompt, the shell itself) reads by that
  terminal's own mode: fine. That mode is your wait only once your keys were seen reaching
  that terminal twice within a minute, and stays so while you type in another `nvim` window
  or Emacs holds your keys until Enter, so a hung call on a terminal Codex or Emacs opened
  (Emacs keeps each in a line mode with no echo) no longer reads fine, while a shell in
  Emacs's buffer at its prompt does, and so does a `node` REPL or a `bash` at `read -t 30`
  there; a REPL there hung on its socket (an asyncio one too), a shell there stuck on a dead
  network share, or one at its prompt beside a hung background job (a Go `./sync &` hung on
  its peer) reads `stuck`, as does `script -q rec.log npm
  install` once the registry stops answering and only its spinner moves, and a loop hung in
  `nvim`'s terminal while you type in another window, while `pytest` printing its results in
  `nvim`'s terminal reads running, and so does `mvn verify` there, whose JVM keeps waking. A `ping host &` of a `bash` run in the
  tab reads running while that bash waits at its prompt. A `tail -F app.log | xargs …`
  whose xargs reaps its finished children late reads waiting, fine, not zombie, while one
  whose ingest deadlocked with its children unreaped reads zombie, as does a deadlocked
  `python3 crawl.py | less` or a script deadlocked under its own pager, while one that
  waits for you to page on reads fine, and a `python3` at its `>>>` holding a child it has
  not reaped reads fine, also beside a server it started, what is left of one it killed or
  multiprocessing's resource tracker, under `make shell` or in a pwsh tab, while a script
  deadlocked beside its server in `nvim`'s terminal reads zombie; an `irb` at its prompt in
  Emacs reads fine, also beside a server it spawned or run by a shell there, while one
  beside that server waiting on a hung child's output reads zombie; a script blocked
  writing to an `ssh` asking for a password (`python3 export.py | ssh nas …`, also `| sudo
  tee` on Linux) reads waiting on you, as does `ssh nas pg_dump app | python3 load.py`
  asking for one and a `git push` asking for one under `python3 deploy.py | tee /dev/tty |
  gzip`, and one deadlocked with a `gzip` it both feeds and reads under `less` reads
  zombie, also on Linux, as does a deadlocked `crawl.py | more` (util-linux `more` reads
  its keys from its standard error), while on Linux a build writing its warnings into
  `less` on page one reads fine; an `ssh` asking for a password under `python3 sync.py |
  tee sync.log` reads waiting on you, also through a `grep`, and a script whose `make`
  waits for you to page on in `less`, also through a `grep`, reads fine. A
  command no longer reads running on lines
  another program printed (a hung `git push` beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung
  background job beside a prompt that redraws its clock, a hung `sudo` command beside a
  printing background job, also a `sudo` one or one that ended, a hung `git fetch` as
  zsh prints that a background job is done, a waiting loop such as `until pg_isready; do
  sleep 1; done` beside a logging `rails server &`, a deadlocked `java` whose timer threads
  keep waking it beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung client whose own timer wakes it beside
  a `tail -f &` when aterm reads it twice in quick succession, a hung `curl` beside a logging
  JVM in the background whose line aterm reads a moment after its last look), and a loop such as `while sleep 2; do date;
  done` reads running beside an idle `python3 -m http.server &` or a Ctrl-Z'd `ninja`
  whose finished steps wait unreaped, as does `./gradlew test` beside a `tail -f &` when
  aterm reads it twice in quick succession, while `ssh host make` over a shared
  connection and `tmux
  attach`, whose output a server outside the tab writes, still read running; a log stream
  printing thousands of lines a second, in a cooked or raw terminal, no longer reads
  `quiet` now and then. A `ninja`, `cmake --build`, `meson
  compile` or `cargo nextest` run, whose program starts each step in a group of its own, is
  one row judged by its steps' work, where it read `quiet` and then `stuck` while it
  compiled and showed each step as a row. An async prompt's worker (pure, spaceship)
  belongs to no command's row, also in a zsh run in the tab's or one started before the
  shell's first prompt, and a `curl … &` that a
  `bash` run in the tab put in the background is a row of its own. A row no
  longer outlives its command because a process substitution (`vim <(tail -f log)`) or a
  server its script left behind lives on.

- **A Ctrl-\ stops `install.sh` cleanly, and so does a `kill` while it puts the app in
  place.** A Ctrl-\ now ends the run after its cleanup, even when a held key sends it
  twice: with bash 5 (Homebrew's on a Mac, or Linux's) the run went on, and the Mac's own
  bash stopped without cleaning up. A `kill` of the installer's own process (a TERM or a
  hang-up) while it unpacks the download or puts the app in place waits for that step,
  then cleans up: it used to leave the unpacked download or a partial copy in the
  Applications folder behind, or, in the instant between the swap's two renames, no
  aterm.app. A Ctrl-C or a `kill` while `--no-toolchain` rewrites `aterm.toml` no longer
  leaves the file empty, or its copy behind. A Ctrl-C during any of the installer's checks
  no longer leaves its temporary files behind, even in the instant the check makes one,
  and the notes the cleanup then prints reach the terminal, where they were lost; one
  while a Linux install cleans up no longer leaves the downloaded files. The commands
  `install.sh`'s notes print, and its `export PATH=` and `launch:` lines, paste back right
  whatever a folder's name holds; a note's command starts with `sudo` when acting in its
  folder needs it, and always to remove a previous copy this account just failed to
  remove. Two exceptions stand: a Ctrl-C during the cleanup of a run that had already
  refused leaves that run's error status, and with bash 5 a Ctrl-\ while `curl … | bash`
  still downloads the script ends it as a Ctrl-C there would, with a syntax error or
  status 0, having run nothing.

## [0.135.0] - 2026-10-24

### Changed

- **codex-alab 0.165.0-dev.13594 is now one of the builds aterm reads the turns of.** Its
  own record of each turn, tool and token count reaches `aterm ctl log` (`src=transcript`),
  and `aterm ctl status` says `rollout=bound` for it, as for 0.164.0-dev.13172 before it.

- **The stats deck stays in its compact form.** On a tall window the deck under the
  titlebar grew into its Full table, a header line and seven rows of detail. It now keeps
  its compact Folded form, two blocks of four rows, however tall the window is, and the
  terminal keeps the rows the Full table took. View ▸ Deck Size: Full still brings the Full
  table back.

- (developer tool) **`lab forever` watches a held chain a minute past aterm's stop, and fails
  a stop nothing on screen says.** aterm stops typing into a tab whose program answers its acts
  with the same reply and no work (`EXCEPTION … kind=stalled`), but the forever lab stopped
  watching land-b to land-i 3 s after the nudge's `WAITING`, and `cruise` and `wrote-c` at their
  second done check, so Land failed with "no WAITING decided" and Cruise passed while it had
  stopped for good. Those chains are now watched 60 s past their last act's point (its
  `WAITING`, or the stop). A chain whose stub answers alike (land-b to land-i, `cruise`,
  `wrote-c`, and the new `same-land` and `same-cruise`, scenarios HL and HC) is brought in front
  twice in that minute and fails "HELD, NOT SAID" unless its chip's description and title, or
  with no chip its tab's hover, say `stopped typing`. It also fails "HELD, THEN LIFTED WITH NO
  NEW REPLY" when aterm takes the stop back before its next act while the stub read nothing new
  from the agent (Gemini CLI's land-d does, when its tab comes in front). Any other chain of the
  measured pass or `--mode cover` fails at the hold. `status held=`, the state line's stop words
  and the `Stopped typing` row in `ctl messages` are named UNOBSERVED skips until aterm says the
  stop itself, so until then the lab is red on those chains on every harness. A held chain runs
  about a minute longer.

### Fixed

- **Autopilot goes on past Claude Code's grey suggestion.** Claude Code 2.1.310 draws
  the next prompt it suggests in grey after a reply, with its first letter under its
  own cursor. The harness read that letter as words you had typed and pressed Enter,
  which sends nothing, so a Cruise or Land session stopped at the suggestion. It now
  reads the letter after the cursor, takes the suggestion for what it is, and goes on.
  Four recorded runs of a real Claude Code under Land and Cruise now pin what the
  harness types: a landing, a hold over an untracked file, a hold on the same reply,
  and a done check typed over the suggestion.

- **Setup keeps a newer pending vault choice.** Changing another group or
  pressing Set up now in an older tab no longer replaces that vault address.

- **ALab setup recovers after an older run's delayed Stop.** A failed upgrade
  save can retry without another launch when that Stop cannot affect it.

- **The AI page's Install and Sign in work on Windows.** Each opens a tab that runs
  `aterm pkg install …` or `aterm ai login …`, but it named the program the window itself ran
  as. On Windows that is `aterm-gui.exe`, the name the Start Menu and jump list launch (on a Mac,
  a window started as `aterm-gui`), which answers only window words, so the tab printed
  "unknown command" and nothing was installed or signed in. The tab now runs `aterm`.

- **The Claude Code harness wakes a turn the Mac slept through.** A Claude Code
  turn whose request went out while the Mac slept could sit in Claude Code's own
  network retry after the Mac woke, the screen busy and your queued words unsent,
  until you pressed Esc. Once the Mac is fully awake and aterm has measured the
  API reachable since the wake for ten seconds, the harness now presses that Esc
  itself, once, on the retry row alone, and never over a draft you are typing.
  Claude Code then sends what you queued; a turn it stopped with nothing queued is
  continued as any other turn's end.

- **Permission buttons keep their target.** A queued Full Disk Access press
  can no longer open a different grant after the page updates.

- **ALab detection survives a watch that could not start.** Setup retries
  the missing watch, and starts it again after Stop followed by Set up now.

- **A group pressed while Restore runs no longer undoes the Restore.** While "Restoring
  previous settings…" ran, System State's groups still took a press, and the plan the
  press sent turned Keyboard & Trackpad and Desktop & Dock back to Set up, so the next
  run set again what you had just restored. The groups now take no press while a
  Restore runs. And a choice now carries only the groups you pressed: aterm applies
  those onto the plan in force, so a page left open during `aterm doctor --restore` or a
  change in another window never sets again a group someone else left as is, and never
  drops your own press.

- **Restore previous settings keeps aterm's permissions going.** A Restore ended the
  run in a way that also stopped Full Disk Access, Developer Tools, the debugger and
  Local Network from being set up by themselves, until a later choice. A Restore puts
  back Mac preferences only: aterm's permission steps now go on after it, as they are
  approved by default. Only your own Stop holds them.

- **`aterm doctor --apply` after a Restore finishes.** It left its run unfinished, so a
  Widgets change it owed never followed and the next launch ran setup again. It now
  finishes the run, the Widgets change follows once aterm has Full Disk Access, and
  the next launch reruns nothing. Its plan keeps aterm's permissions after a Restore.

- **A Widgets change made at the end of a setup run is no longer misread.** The
  Notification Center widgets change setup makes once it has Full Disk Access ran at
  the end of a run without the guard its other steps have, so a reading taken while it
  ran could show its row's old value. Its row is now busy while it runs, and readings
  taken meanwhile are dropped.

- **A Restore that waited for Full Disk Access finishes by itself.** Without Full Disk
  Access a Restore could not put Notification Center's widgets back, and nothing put
  them back once aterm got the grant: you had to run Restore again. It now puts them
  back by itself as soon as aterm records the grant, or at the next launch, with no
  press, unless you turned Desktop & Dock back to Set up since.

- **A session is told when the bus broker gives up mail nobody read.** `aterm link broker`
  keeps unread mail for up to 7 days within 64 MiB, and a session's inbox skipped mail given
  up past that with nothing said. Now the node's bridge is told, and since which session the
  mail was for went with it, every session on that node names it: `aterm ctl inbox`'s header
  ends `given_up=@<a>..@<b>` (the broker offsets the mail was at) and `given_up_count=<n>`
  where the broker counted it, and the session's log marks it once (`mail-gap`). A person's
  `aterm fabric inbox` prints the range as a line of its own. An aterm older than its bridge
  is told nothing new.

- **Init keeps recovering an interrupted automatic upgrade.** A failed save or
  temporary state-read error no longer ends the vault watch before setup runs.

- **Automatic secrets repair respects Sync off.** A delayed repair or an old
  failed install no longer turns the subscriber back on.

- **Set up now checks current state before running.** A click queued before
  the page settles or starts waiting no longer repeats setup.

- **The harness sees Claude Code's context running low again.** Claude Code draws its
  `N% until auto-compact` indicator at the end of the row under its prompt, and the
  harness's context watch looked for it above the prompt, where older builds drew it. So
  the watch never noted the context running low or a compaction (`aterm drive ledger`'s
  `context` row stayed at `0 context · 0 compacted`), and `aterm drive phase` never
  printed `context <n>%`. The watch, `aterm drive phase` and the footer now share one
  reading, and a compaction is noted only when the indicator's place is left empty: the
  `/` and `@` menus, the shortcuts or one of Claude Code's own notices standing there for
  a while is not one. The watch also reads the screen while Claude Code sits at rest, so a
  `/compact` typed there is noted once Claude Code's notice leaves the slot. The reading also
  holds in a narrow pane, where Claude Code puts the indicator after a single space or on a row
  of its own, and in shell mode (`!`), so there the tab's hover (`ctx 7% left`) and
  `aterm ctl survey`'s context now show it too.

- **Developer Tools' recheck works in a window started as `aterm-gui`.** Once you switch
  aterm on in the Developer Tools list, aterm asks macOS to check it again. In a window started
  by its `aterm-gui` name that request failed, so each new program kept waiting for macOS's
  first-run check until aterm restarted.

- **System Settings' Quit & Reopen brings aterm back.** Once you turned Full Disk Access
  (or another access) on or off for aterm, System Settings asked aterm to quit and reopen;
  aterm asked whether to quit, and by the time you answered, System Settings had stopped
  waiting, so aterm quit and stayed closed. Its Dock icon could then do nothing. aterm now
  opens itself again once it has quit, and brings back the agents it ran, as after a
  restart.

- **Init recovers from an interrupted automatic offer.** A withdrawn answer
  or rejected receipt no longer leaves permission guidance blocked after a
  fresh status confirms the saved policy.

- **System State keeps a vault address being composed.** Status updates and
  startup offers no longer discard marked text in the URL field.

- **Setup recovers a new choice after an older Stop arrives late.** Retrying
  its final save keeps the choice and join password; a Stop for that new run
  still takes effect.

- **Setup preserves restore history when a state read fails.** A partial
  preferences pass no longer marks untouched restored groups as applied.

- **The Overview and the command palette are as wide on a Retina display as on any other.**
  Each card's widest (760 points for the Overview, 820 for the palette) was counted in the
  display's pixels, so on a Retina display it came out half as wide on the screen: the
  Overview cut its lines short and its key hints lost `esc close`. Both cards are now the
  same width on the screen at every display scale, and each draws in less time than before,
  so the full-width card on a Retina display draws no slower than the narrow one did.

- **Restore keeps your previous preferences after an interrupted save.**
  An unrelated System State choice no longer reapplies them when Restore
  could not finish saving its plan.

- **System State retries saving debugger answers.** Failed writes or worker
  starts retain the answer, including Cancel, without another permission action.

- **System State recovers failed permission saves.** aterm retries saving Local
  Network results and Full Disk Access or Developer Tools answers. Unreadable
  history is preserved.

- **System State protects a newer vault join when a settings read fails.**
  Setup involving Secrets requires a readable vault configuration before
  approval and can retry after a read error.

- **System State's Developer Tools step follows Full Disk Access at once.** On a new
  Mac, once Full Disk Access was on, the step that brings up System Settings for
  Developer Tools could find aterm's own Full Disk Access reading not yet back, take it
  for off, and wait until aterm's window lost and regained focus, a minute or more later.
  It now reads again two seconds later and goes on.

- **System State keeps your latest permission answer.** A second Not now after
  a grant replaces the earlier answer. Simultaneous permission updates preserve
  both rows.

- **Restore previous settings says what it did in System State's own words, and leaves
  what it put back as is.** After a Restore the page listed each preference key it put
  back (`com.apple.dock show-recents`, …) and a line for each setting that loads at the
  next login, even one the Restore could not write. It now says it in one line, in the
  page's row names: "The Desktop, Widgets and the Dock are as they were. Caps Lock key,
  Natural scrolling and Trackpad scrolling come back at your next login." It names only
  what it put back and that stayed back; a setting whose app did not relaunch comes back
  at your next login too, never as the app's name. A value macOS hid ("Widgets stayed as
  they are: macOS hid their earlier value.") and one waiting for Full Disk Access are
  part of that line, not failures. Only a setting Restore could not put back is a
  failure, named as Restore's: "Restore previous settings failed: Widgets", with the
  reason under it and `System State: Restore failed for Widgets` in the menu. Keyboard &
  Trackpad and Desktop & Dock turn to Leave as is, so the settings you just restored no
  longer count as changes to make; one press of Set up on either group sets that group
  alone, and no run starts by itself. Until your next login the Caps Lock key and a
  scroll direction, left as is, read the value they have now, marked: `Control · until
  login`; turned to Set up, they show the value the Mac has after that login, `Caps Lock
  → Control`. This replaces 0.133.0's note that a group no pass has set since a Restore
  "still reads restored": its rows read their values, left as is. `aterm doctor
  --restore` still lists each key and relaunch.

- **System State says a login-time change and an unfinished step in its own words.** A
  setting a run set for your next login (Trackpad scrolling) reads its value with a
  check and the note "Fully in effect after your next login", not `All on · at login`;
  the Caps Lock key reads in place at once, since its live mapping takes effect
  immediately. A change that did not take reaches the page under its row's name ("Dock
  failed. The change did not take."), never as the preference key or keyboard ID
  behind it, and what the run put back is one calm line ("aterm put back what it could
  not finish. The Dock is as it was."); `aterm doctor` still lists each. Putting a
  change back also restores the live value of a setting whose saved value was already
  back. A reading that did not finish no longer leaves "Checking this Mac…" up for good:
  the headline names the row, which says to Check again. A page opened before aterm
  knew your plan reads your Mac as soon as it does, not a second later, and a plan
  changed outside the page (`aterm doctor --restore` in a terminal) has its rows read
  again.

- **System State keeps deferred Widgets changes within the approved setup.**
  An interrupted Restore cannot revive an old change after an unrelated choice
  or Join. Deferred work waits for the current plan's approval to finish saving.

- **System State keeps vault choices and readings current.** A password retry
  preserves the machine name and refuses a configuration changed by another
  process. Refused read starts retry while the page is visible; reopening reads afresh.
  Failed reader starts and interrupted readings no longer strand queued checks.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` when job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose own
  command runs in front is judged by that command; a build whose step stopped at the
  terminal (a `ninja` step at an ssh passphrase prompt, a `ninja &`'s too, also under
  `aterm -e ninja` or after `exec ninja`) still reads `quiet`, a Ctrl-Z'd `cargo nextest
  run` reads `parked`, and so does a `git pull &` stopped at its password prompt in a tab
  without shell integration. After `exec ninja` its build is one row that runs while its
  steps compile, after `exec python3` a REPL hung on a lock no longer reads as the shell's
  `read`, and after `exec zsh` the block ends at the new shell's prompt, also beside the
  `tee` a `.bashrc` logs the session through or from a `case` arm, after a comment or a
  here-document holding a quote, or past `ZDOTDIR=${…}/zsh`, and on macOS whatever the
  line says (a bash line kept out of history, which bash reports only in part), so a
  background job's lines are its own again; `exec vim` back from a `:sh` keeps its row,
  its `:!make` included, also past vim's hit-enter prompt. A download pwsh runs in itself (`Invoke-WebRequest`)
  keeps its row, also after `exec pwsh`, beside a zsh it ran or between a loop's `docker
  exec`s, also one whose line a backtick continues, as does a `vared` prompt, and a build
  run by `exec cmake --build` or `out=$(ninja)` is one row as well, also when aterm saw its
  first process a moment before the command started, while one a pwsh `Start-Job` left
  running, by its steps (also those its `make` forks later in pwsh's group) or its lines,
  no longer keeps a later hung `git fetch` reading running, nor does a server
  `Start-Process -NoNewWindow` left printing there keep a deadlocked `dotnet test` running,
  nor one aterm may not read (`sudo log stream`) a hung `sudo mount`, also by the last line
  of one that exits or the lines of one that ran such a program in its place; a `dotnet
  build` in a pwsh run in pwsh, its profile writing the prompt's marks, reads running, as
  does a cmdlet it runs itself or a build printing through its `Tee-Object`, and a `ninja`
  there is one row, while the builds of a pwsh `Start-Process` started (a `watch.ps1`) no
  longer keep a hung `git fetch` running.
  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z
  in the middle of a bash command list (`make; fg %1`) no longer split the resumed job in
  two, drop the earlier command's row, give one command's exit status to the other, or
  leave the resumed job behind the stopped one. A pipeline stage that runs in a group of its
  own (`seq 1 40 | timeout 3600 xargs ./step.sh`) is judged by the lines the tab prints
  once the stage in front exits, when it is the tab's one background job that can run,
  instead of reading `quiet`, then `stuck`; a parked editor no longer takes those lines or
  keeps them from it. A command run with `sudo` (which runs it on a terminal of its own),
  under `script`, or as an agent's tool call on a terminal of its own (Codex, Gemini CLI)
  is one row beside its opener's, judged by what it does: printing, it reads running, and
  hung on a server that stopped answering it reads `stuck` while sudo waits at the terminal
  and the agent's screen keeps moving, also when the agent runs in `nvim`'s terminal or in
  a tab whose shell gave way to it (`exec codex`) or that runs it in place of a shell
  (`aterm -e codex`). A Ctrl-Z'd `sudo vim` reads `parked`; a command hung in front of
  `script`'s shell beside a job that shell stopped reads `stuck`, and a program there
  waiting for your keys (`vim`, a password prompt, the shell itself) reads by that
  terminal's own mode: fine. That mode is your wait only once your keys were seen reaching
  that terminal twice within a minute, and stays so while you type in another `nvim` window
  or Emacs holds your keys until Enter, so a hung call on a terminal Codex or Emacs opened
  (Emacs keeps each in a line mode with no echo) no longer reads fine, while a shell in
  Emacs's buffer at its prompt does, and so does a `node` REPL or a `bash` at `read -t 30`
  there; a REPL there hung on its socket (an asyncio one too), a shell there stuck on a dead
  network share, or one at its prompt beside a hung background job (a Go `./sync &` hung on
  its peer) reads `stuck`, as does `script -q rec.log npm
  install` once the registry stops answering and only its spinner moves, and a loop hung in
  `nvim`'s terminal while you type in another window, while `pytest` printing its results in
  `nvim`'s terminal reads running, and so does `mvn verify` there, whose JVM keeps waking. A `ping host &` of a `bash` run in the
  tab reads running while that bash waits at its prompt. A `tail -F app.log | xargs …`
  whose xargs reaps its finished children late reads waiting, fine, not zombie, while one
  whose ingest deadlocked with its children unreaped reads zombie, as does a deadlocked
  `python3 crawl.py | less` or a script deadlocked under its own pager, while one that
  waits for you to page on reads fine, and a `python3` at its `>>>` holding a child it has
  not reaped reads fine, also beside a server it started, what is left of one it killed or
  multiprocessing's resource tracker, while a crawler it started that deadlocked with its
  workers unreaped reads zombie, as does a script deadlocked beside its server in `nvim`'s
  terminal or a crawler a `python3` there started; an `irb` at its prompt in Emacs reads fine, also beside a server it spawned or run by a shell
  there, while one beside that server waiting on a hung child's output reads zombie; a
  script blocked writing to an `ssh` asking for a password (`python3 export.py | ssh nas
  …`, also `| sudo tee` on Linux) reads waiting on you, and one deadlocked with a `gzip` it
  both feeds and reads under `less` reads zombie; an
  `ssh` asking for a password under `python3 sync.py | tee sync.log` reads waiting on you,
  also through a `grep`, and a script whose `make` waits for you to page on in `less`, also
  through a `grep`, reads fine. A
  command no longer reads running on lines
  another program printed (a hung `git push` beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung
  background job beside a prompt that redraws its clock, a hung `sudo` command beside a
  printing background job, also a `sudo` one or one that ended, a hung `git fetch` as
  zsh prints that a background job is done, a waiting loop such as `until pg_isready; do
  sleep 1; done` beside a logging `rails server &`, a deadlocked `java` whose timer threads
  keep waking it beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung client whose own timer wakes it beside
  a `tail -f &` when aterm reads it twice in quick succession, a hung `curl` beside a logging
  JVM in the background whose line aterm reads a moment after its last look), and a loop such as `while sleep 2; do date;
  done` reads running beside an idle `python3 -m http.server &` or a Ctrl-Z'd `ninja`
  whose finished steps wait unreaped, as does `./gradlew test` beside a `tail -f &` when
  aterm reads it twice in quick succession, while `ssh host make` over a shared
  connection and `tmux
  attach`, whose output a server outside the tab writes, still read running; a log stream
  printing thousands of lines a second, in a cooked or raw terminal, no longer reads
  `quiet` now and then. A `ninja`, `cmake --build`, `meson
  compile` or `cargo nextest` run, whose program starts each step in a group of its own, is
  one row judged by its steps' work, where it read `quiet` and then `stuck` while it
  compiled and showed each step as a row. An async prompt's worker (pure, spaceship)
  belongs to no command's row, also in a zsh run in the tab's or one started before the
  shell's first prompt, and a `curl … &` that a
  `bash` run in the tab put in the background is a row of its own. A row no
  longer outlives its command because a process substitution (`vim <(tail -f log)`) or a
  server its script left behind lives on.

- **A Ctrl-\ or a `kill` stops `install.sh` cleanly.** A Ctrl-\ now ends the run after its
  cleanup, even when a held key sends it twice: with bash 5 (Homebrew's on a Mac, or
  Linux's) the run went on, and the Mac's own bash stopped without cleaning up. A `kill`
  of the installer's own process (a TERM or a hang-up) while it unpacks the download or
  puts the app in place waits for that step, then cleans up: it used to leave the unpacked
  download or a partial copy in the Applications folder behind, or, in the instant between
  the swap's two renames, no aterm.app. A Ctrl-C or a `kill` while `--no-toolchain`
  rewrites `aterm.toml` no longer leaves the file empty. A Ctrl-C during any of the
  installer's checks no longer leaves its temporary files behind, even in the instant the
  check makes one, and the notes the cleanup then prints reach the terminal, where they
  were lost; one while a Linux install cleans up no longer leaves the downloaded files.
  The commands `install.sh`'s notes print, and its `export PATH=` and `launch:` lines,
  paste back right whatever a folder's name holds; a note's command starts with `sudo`
  when acting in its folder needs it, and always to remove a previous copy this account
  just failed to remove. Two exceptions stand: a Ctrl-C during the cleanup of a run that
  had already refused leaves that run's error status, and with bash 5 a Ctrl-\ while
  `curl … | bash` still downloads the script ends it with status 0, having run nothing.

- **`aterm ctl sys jobs` right after an agent's turn says it waits for you.** The first
  `sys jobs` a minute or so after Claude Code finished a turn could show the idle agent as
  `polling`, from a reading of its terminal taken before the turn's last redraw, and aterm
  then woke once more 2 seconds later to read it again. aterm now reads every terminal
  afresh for such a read, so it says `waiting` (`tty-raw`) at once and aterm stays at rest.

- **On Linux, a program with keys it has not read is no longer called waiting for you.**
  `aterm ctl sys jobs` calls a full-screen program at rest waiting for you (`tty-raw`)
  only while nothing typed into its terminal is still unread. On Linux
  aterm could not count those keys and took that as none, so a program with your keys
  piling up unread (one hung, or busy past your typing) read as waiting for you, and aterm
  stopped checking on it. aterm now counts them on Linux too; where they cannot be counted
  it no longer calls the program waiting for you, and keeps checking on it.

- **On Linux, aterm counts the keys a program has not read yet.** `aterm ctl status` said
  `input=-` there; it now reports `input=`, `input_bytes=` and `input_wait_ms=` as on macOS.
  Input verbs warn when keys have sat unread for a second and refuse to queue more behind
  a stopped program's, `signal … quiet=` refuses while keys are unread, and a typed answer
  presses its next digit only once the program has read the one before. Only macOS
  watches for a program that stopped reading (`stalled`) and drops the keys it left unread.

## [0.134.0] - 2026-10-24

### Changed

- **Grok Build installs on Linux, from npm's registry-signed package.** `aterm pkg install
  grok` now works on Linux (x64 and arm64, glibc or musl) as well as on macOS. aterm takes
  the version xAI's own pointer names, checks npm's registry signature on xAI's
  `@xai-official/grok-<platform>` package for that version against the registry key aterm
  ships before any of the build is downloaded, unpacks the binary from that package, and
  installs it only when it is byte for byte the build xAI's own bucket serves (and, on
  macOS, signed with xAI's Developer ID). A build the two disagree on is refused and not
  fetched again. An install downloads npm's package and the bucket's compressed copy: on a
  Mac about 103 MB (Apple silicon) or 114 MB (Intel), where it downloaded the 179 MB or
  194 MB binary before, and 105 to 113 MB on Linux.

### Fixed

- **System State keeps delayed actions current.** A failed Restore preserves
  settings still waiting for login. Finishing Widgets after Full Disk Access
  refreshes its row. A queued permission page opens only while its row still
  needs it. Composed text stays with its original field, including passwords.

- **System State clears interrupted workers.** A setup panic releases its
  running stage and refreshes the readings. Delayed vault actions respect
  controls disabled by a run already in progress.

- **System State shows failed steps and Restore’s logout instructions.** A failed
  step stays in the headline with Show even when fresh readings look complete.
  Restore keeps logout instructions as notes. Interrupted setup discards readings
  taken before cleanup, so they cannot report a false recovery.

- **System State keeps Restore history through startup recovery and retries Mac settings when due.**
  An interrupted group change preserves settings still restored, whatever the next
  launch's setup offer is answered with: it sets only the groups you turned on. A
  failed Mac setting gets its allowed second attempt after ten minutes, even if setup
  has already parked. Join waits for the saved plan to load and keeps typed credentials.

- **aterm no longer breaks a program's network or socket connections when it starts
  another program.** To tell which job is stuck and on what, aterm looks at the
  connections of the programs in each tab. A look at a program that was just being started,
  or at the program starting it while it let go of the new program's end of a connection,
  could break the connections the two shared: macOS then failed every read that had to wait
  on one of them, with "Bad file descriptor", for good. aterm now looks at a program's
  connections only once it has been running a while and has started no program in the last
  2 seconds (a server's worker that runs no program of its own, nginx's or gunicorn's,
  counts once it has run 2 seconds), and `aterm fabric`, which looked at every program's connections to find the bus broker, now
  finds it in macOS's own list of local sockets and looks at no program's. aterm's own
  sockets (its control socket, the keeper's, the fleet's and the bus broker's) no longer
  reach the programs it starts, so no such look, `lsof`'s included, can break them.

- **Stop and withdrawn Permissions end automatic folder prompts.** A delayed setup
  acknowledgment cannot restart them; a new choice, Join or Set up now starts a fresh
  pass.

- **A Ctrl-C always stops `install.sh`.** A few programs `install.sh` runs catch a Ctrl-C
  and exit instead of stopping: Python while it starts up, and `hdiutil` while it opens a
  disk image. After Python the run went on: a Linux install said it needed Python 3.11
  and OpenSSL, skipped the app and went on to the toolset. After `hdiutil` the run ended
  with an error status rather than by the Ctrl-C, so a script running `install.sh`
  carried on. The run now ends at the Ctrl-C whatever the program does with it, and a
  Ctrl-C while `install.sh` cleans up no longer cuts the cleanup short, leaving a staging
  copy or the old app set aside. A disk image the cleanup could not detach stays mounted,
  and `install.sh` prints the command that detaches it.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,

  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z

## [0.133.0] - 2026-10-24

### Changed

- **System State is redesigned, and Mac access is approved with it.** The page groups Mac
  setup into Permissions, Keyboard & Trackpad, Desktop & Dock, Messages & FaceTime and
  Workspace, each set to Set up or Leave as is, in place of its list of switches and
  Apply, and every row shows what this Mac has now beside what aterm wants. One
  aterm · ALab rainbow kitty is the page's mark, and the Rainbow Kitty Village beside it
  has a station for each setting, built as that setting gets to where aterm wants it, with
  its kitties walking while a setup run goes on a page you can see (standing still between
  runs, through Check again and Restore and with Reduce Motion, and left out in serious
  mode, at high contrast and where the pane is too narrow). A run starts once the
  page is shown, with no countdown; Stop ends it between steps, the Messages and FaceTime
  sign-outs run last, and Restore previous settings puts back the Mac preferences aterm
  changed. In a narrow pane or at a large text size the rows, group headings and buttons
  take more lines and keep their words whole (down to 128 points at 1x text, 160 at 1.5x
  and 200 at 2x). In a short window the brand and then the title give way, and the list
  shrinks to as little as one row's height (it scrolls), before Stop, the headline's
  button, Check again or Restore previous settings leaves the window: 320 points wide,
  with a headline that names one row, they stay in view down to 200 points tall at 1x
  text, 320 at 1.5x and 440 at 2x. The brand and the title stay put while a run starts,
  needs you or fails one step; a headline naming several failed steps that stands taller
  counts its own height. The list also takes the 8 points the page left under the
  footer. Rust in Spotlight is one row for rustup's offline docs and aterm's own build
  folders (Docs indexed or Builds indexed, then Kept out). aterm keeps its own Rust
  toolchain out of Spotlight by itself: while the toolchain it is using still sits where
  Spotlight indexes it, a quiet note says aterm moves it out at its next update, never a
  step for you. Your projects' build folders Spotlight indexes (each folder cargo tagged
  as its build folder, whatever its name, counted once; cargo's own download caches in its
  home are not, which aterm knows by the files cargo keeps there even when only your shell
  names that home) are yours, which the row counts in a quiet note and never moves; the
  search for them asks Spotlight for build folders alone, so it answers in a large home
  too, and Check again searches anew without waiting on a search under way. Only
  an ALab Mac (a vault or fleet member, or one that reaches the ALab vault) sets up more
  than Permissions by itself, and the secrets vault is joined from its own row, which says
  that a blank password joins an open vault or waits for an admin Mac's approval; joining
  there turns sync on and runs only the vault steps again, never the Dock or the
  sign-outs, a group turned to Set up later sets only its own preferences, and one turned
  to Leave as is changes nothing, also after a choice before it was cut short (it is
  measured from the run that choice left) and after Restore previous settings (Set up now
  sets them all again; a group no pass has set since still reads restored, and once each
  group you set up has been set again the settings read applied; a choice cut short before
  it was recorded is kept, and one never admitted before the Restore is dropped). Full
  Disk Access, Developer Tools, Local Network and debugger access are approved by default
  with Permissions: each comes up once per approval, only while System State is in front
  and on screen (never behind a lock screen, display sleep or a screen saver), one macOS
  dialog at a time. aterm's own alert "Allow debugger access on this Mac?" is gone:
  macOS's password dialog is the one step left, and Cancel there settles it for the Mac.
  The setup sheet and setup's entries in Messages are gone too, Developer Tools' and the
  vault's among them; a row that needs you marks the tab and puts one line in aterm's
  menu-bar menu, which opens System State (a new window when none is open), and a vault
  line an earlier version left in Messages opens System State too. A step aterm retries by
  itself (up to ten times, a minute apart) shows its failure on the page only, and reaches
  the menu and the tab once the retries stop. A vault member whose sync process is not
  running reads Not syncing (Not set up when none is installed), and Set up now starts it;
  one that does not come up is a failed step naming its log. Turning the sync off (`aterm
  secrets agent off`, or `--no-agent` on `join` and `create`) is remembered as your
  choice: the row reads Sync off with nothing to change and a quiet Turn On Sync, and
  setup, System State's and `aterm init`'s alike, leaves it off. `[privacy] enabled`,
  `check` and `notice` still hold every step back: turned off, a step waits with no answer
  recorded, and goes on once they are on again, including the Full Disk Access check, the
  Developer Tools check and the folder questions when a switch was already off as aterm
  started.

- **Publishing a package no longer needs the zstd tool.** aterm's package publisher now
  compresses every package itself, with aterm's own Zstandard encoder, so a publish host
  needs no `zstd` installed. Packages come out smaller than `zstd -19` made them (the
  Trust toolchain's by about 8%), because the encoder matches repeats across a 128 MiB
  window. aterm installs them as before, holding up to that window in memory while it
  unpacks a large one (about 140 MB at the peak for the Trust toolchain, up from 13 MB).
  Another Zstandard decoder reads them only with a window limit of 128 MiB, which `zstd -d`
  has by default; one held to the 8 MB the format recommends refuses any package over
  128 KiB unpacked.

### Fixed

- **System State keeps setup errors visible.** An unreadable saved plan shows
  that setup needs attention, even after earlier readings looked complete.
  A successful read clears the error.

- **System State keeps Restore history through startup recovery and retries Mac settings when due.**
  An interrupted group change preserves settings still restored. A failed Mac
  setting gets its allowed second attempt after ten minutes, even if setup has
  already parked. Join waits for the saved plan to load and keeps typed credentials.

- **aterm no longer breaks a program's network or socket connections when it starts
  another program.** To tell which job is stuck and on what, aterm looks at the
  connections of the programs in each tab. A look at a program that was just being started
  could break the connections it shared with the program that started it: macOS then
  failed every read that had to wait on one of them, with "Bad file descriptor", for good.
  aterm now looks at a program's connections only once it has been running a while, and
  `aterm fabric`, which looked at every program's connections to find the bus broker, now
  finds it in macOS's own list of local sockets and looks at no program's. aterm's own
  sockets (its control socket, the keeper's, the fleet's and the bus broker's) no longer
  reach the programs it starts, so no such look, `lsof`'s included, can break them.

- **System State checks the saved plan and verifies settings after shared app relaunches.**
  Check again waits until the saved plan loads. A setup run rechecks settings that
  were already correct when another setting relaunches their app. Account setup also
  resumes when a dialog it waited for closes.

- **Restore verifies preferences after apps relaunch.** It catches apps rewriting an
  original value after an interrupted Restore, and System State shows originals it
  could not restore. A setting that comes back only at the next login, such as the
  Caps Lock key, is a note to log out, not a failure.

- **Stop and withdrawn Permissions end automatic folder prompts.** A delayed setup
  acknowledgment cannot restart them; Set up now starts a fresh pass.

- **A Ctrl-C during a download leaves nothing running.** With bash 5 (Homebrew's on a
  Mac, or Linux's), a Ctrl-C while `install.sh` downloaded aterm left its progress meter
  running after the run ended: it printed "No such file or directory" over your prompt
  every 2 seconds and outlived the terminal, until you killed it. With macOS's own bash
  the run said the download had failed. The meter now ends with the run, and the run
  ends at the Ctrl-C.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` when job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose own
  command runs in front is judged by that command; a build whose step stopped at the
  terminal (a `ninja` step at an ssh passphrase prompt, a `ninja &`'s too, also under
  `aterm -e ninja` or after `exec ninja`) still reads `quiet`, a Ctrl-Z'd `cargo nextest
  run` reads `parked`, and so does a `git pull &` stopped at its password prompt in a tab
  without shell integration. After `exec ninja` its build is one row that runs while its
  steps compile, after `exec python3` a REPL hung on a lock no longer reads as the shell's
  `read`, and after `exec zsh` the block ends at the new shell's prompt, so a background
  job's lines are its own again. A download pwsh runs in itself (`Invoke-WebRequest`)
  keeps its row, also after `exec pwsh`, and a build run by `exec cmake --build` or `out=$(ninja)`
  is one row as well.
  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z
  in the middle of a bash command list (`make; fg %1`) no longer split the resumed job in
  two, drop the earlier command's row, give one command's exit status to the other, or
  leave the resumed job behind the stopped one. A pipeline stage that runs in a group of its
  own (`seq 1 40 | timeout 3600 xargs ./step.sh`) is judged by the lines the tab prints
  once the stage in front exits, when it is the tab's one background job that can run,
  instead of reading `quiet`, then `stuck`; a parked editor no longer takes those lines or
  keeps them from it. A command run with `sudo` (which runs it on a terminal of its own),
  under `script`, or as an agent's tool call on a terminal of its own (Codex, Gemini CLI)
  is one row beside its opener's, judged by what it does: printing, it reads running, and
  hung on a server that stopped answering it reads `stuck` while sudo waits at the terminal
  and the agent's screen keeps moving, also when the agent runs in `nvim`'s terminal or in
  a tab whose shell gave way to it (`exec codex`) or that runs it in place of a shell
  (`aterm -e codex`). A Ctrl-Z'd `sudo vim` reads `parked`; a command hung in front of
  `script`'s shell beside a job that shell stopped reads `stuck`, and a program there
  waiting for your keys (`vim`, a password prompt, the shell itself) reads by that
  terminal's own mode: fine. That mode is your wait only once your keys were seen reaching
  that terminal twice within a minute, and stays so while you type in another `nvim` window
  or Emacs holds your keys until Enter, so a hung call on a terminal Codex or Emacs opened
  (Emacs keeps each in a line mode with no echo) no longer reads fine, while a shell in
  Emacs's buffer at its prompt does, and so does a `node` REPL or a `bash` at `read -t 30`
  there; a REPL there hung on its socket (an asyncio one too), a shell there stuck on a dead
  network share, or one at its prompt beside a hung background job (a Go `./sync &` hung on
  its peer) reads `stuck`, as does `script -q rec.log npm
  install` once the registry stops answering and only its spinner moves, and a loop hung in
  `nvim`'s terminal while you type in another window, while `pytest` printing its results in
  `nvim`'s terminal reads running. A `ping host &` of a `bash` run in the
  tab reads running while that bash waits at its prompt. A `tail -F app.log | xargs …`
  whose xargs reaps its finished children late reads waiting, fine, not zombie, while one
  whose ingest deadlocked with its children unreaped reads zombie. A
  command no longer reads running on lines
  another program printed (a hung `git push` beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung
  background job beside a prompt that redraws its clock, a hung `sudo` command beside a
  printing background job, also a `sudo` one or one that ended, a hung `git fetch` as
  zsh prints that a background job is done, a waiting loop such as `until pg_isready; do
  sleep 1; done` beside a logging `rails server &`, a deadlocked `java` whose timer threads
  keep waking it beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung client whose own timer wakes it beside
  a `tail -f &` when aterm reads it twice in quick succession), and a loop such as `while sleep 2; do date;
  done` reads running beside an idle `python3 -m http.server &` or a Ctrl-Z'd `ninja`
  whose finished steps wait unreaped, as does `./gradlew test` beside a `tail -f &` when
  aterm reads it twice in quick succession, while `ssh host make` over a shared
  connection and `tmux
  attach`, whose output a server outside the tab writes, still read running; a log stream
  printing thousands of lines a second, in a cooked or raw terminal, no longer reads
  `quiet` now and then. A `ninja`, `cmake --build`, `meson
  compile` or `cargo nextest` run, whose program starts each step in a group of its own, is
  one row judged by its steps' work, where it read `quiet` and then `stuck` while it
  compiled and showed each step as a row. An async prompt's worker (pure, spaceship)
  belongs to no command's row, also in a zsh run in the tab's or one started before the
  shell's first prompt, and a `curl … &` that a
  `bash` run in the tab put in the background is a row of its own. A row no
  longer outlives its command because a process substitution (`vim <(tail -f log)`) or a
  server its script left behind lives on.

  answer recorded, and goes on once they are on again, including the Full Disk Access

- **Deploying the site no longer needs node or firebase-tools.** `targo --unverified ship
  site` deploys straight to Firebase Hosting over its REST API, using the site's deployer
  service-account key (`FIREBASE_SA_KEY`, else `publish/site.toml`'s `firebase_sa_key`).
  It reads the site's `firebase.json` for headers, redirects, rewrites and URL rules, and
  refuses one it cannot express, or a link or a service-account key under `public/`,
  before writing anything. It uploads only the files Hosting does not already hold, each
  compressed as small as `gzip -9`, and the live site changes only at the last step. A
  failed deploy names its rerun, `ship site --latest --redeploy`. `--dry-run` lists every
  file it would deploy. `ship provision` checks for the key where it checked for node and
  firebase-tools. The site is `firebase.json`'s `hosting.site`, else `FIREBASE_SITE` or
  `firebase_site` (which replace `FIREBASE_ACCOUNT`); when two name different sites,
  nothing is written.

### Fixed

- **A program can no longer book reminders as a tab it is not in.** If a tab's shell exited
  while the tab stayed open and macOS gave its process number to another program, that
  program's children passed as the tab's for `aterm ctl @self wake`, `waits` and `park`.
  aterm now knows a tab's shell by its start time as well, and refuses the stranger.

- **`aterm lab linux vz-host` no longer fails with "Invalid argument" as the VM stops.** A
  `down`, `status`, `up` or `exec` that connected just as the VM helper finished on its own
  failed with that error; it now reads as the helper having ended.

- **Option-Delete deletes a word in a Settings or System State field.** These fields now
  take the editing keys the find bar, the tab-rename field and the command palette take:
  Option-Delete and Option-Forward-Delete delete a word, Command-Delete deletes to the
  field's start, Command-Left and Command-Right go to its start and end (with Shift they
  select), and Ctrl-H deletes a character. Each of those Option and Command keys deleted
  or moved one character, and Ctrl-H did nothing. Off macOS, Alt-Backspace, Alt-Delete and
  Ctrl-Delete delete a word.

- **A root install no longer hangs at its folder check while a share elsewhere is not
  answering.** On macOS, `install.sh` run as root (`sudo -H`, a root shell or an MDM
  job) read the mount table with no time limit to learn whether its folder's volume
  ignores owners, so a network share whose server stopped answering hung it before the
  download. It now reads the table within a minute, as its walks do, and that read ends
  at the minute even while `mount` is still waiting on the share. A share that holds the
  install folder itself still has to answer.

- **Ctrl-C stops `install.sh` while it waits on a check.** A Ctrl-C while `install.sh`
  waited on `codesign`, Gatekeeper or a program it asked what it is was taken as that
  check's answer, and the run went on: run again over a current install, it said the app
  had FAILED signature verification, then downloaded and reinstalled it. It now ends the
  run there, as a Ctrl-C anywhere else in it does.

## [0.131.0] - 2026-10-24

### Added

- **`aterm ctl @self status` counts your tab's programs macOS is still checking.** On
  macOS, `status` adds `program_check=<n>:<oldest_ms>` after `job_quiet_ms=`: how many of the
  programs this tab's jobs started (and those they left running) wait at macOS's program
  check now, and how long the oldest has waited. It reads `program_check=0` when none
  waits, and `-` on Linux and Windows or before aterm has a recent reading.

  back: turned off, a step waits with no answer recorded, and goes on once they are on
  again, including the Full Disk Access check, the Developer Tools check and the folder
  questions when a switch was already off as aterm started.

### Fixed

- **The cursor trail no longer hitches once after an update.** On macOS aterm built a
  cursor effect's GPU pipeline the first time a frame drew it, so after an update that
  changed aterm's shaders the first trail frame stalled for about 70 ms. aterm now builds
  every effect it can draw on a background thread as a window opens.

- **System State's list scrolls in steps it shows, and VoiceOver reads its headline.** In
  0.130.0 a wheel notch or an arrow key moved the list 40 points and a page key eight of
  those, so in a short window, where the list can be one row tall, a step carried it past
  notes and rows it never showed whole. A step now moves the list no further than it shows
  (a page key its height less a line) and stops where a note, a row or a control would
  otherwise never show whole, and a focused field stays in view as the window shrinks.
  VoiceOver reads the page's headline and brand, which it read as empty, and its headings
  as headings, not as plain text. The vault's address and password fields take the keys a
  Settings field takes: Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E and the other readline keys, Option-Left and
  Option-Right by word, and Home and End, where Ctrl-A selected the whole field and an
  Option-arrow moved one character.

- **System State respects Stop and newer Sync off choices during handoffs.** Stop
  remains owed if you quit just after accepting setup. Permission pages reserve
  the dialog slot before opening, and a vault approval notice stays until its
  current Secrets row can replace it.

- **"Mac setup needs attention" no longer comes back as a new message after every
  update, and a setup or vault message is no longer marked fixed when nothing fixed
  it.** At each launch, including the one after every automatic update, aterm's Full
  Disk Access check ended every privacy message as fixed, not only its own: Mac setup,
  Developer Tools and the secrets vault's join messages among them. Setup then posted
  its message again a moment later under a new number, so the same unresolved message
  was retired and re-posted at every update. That check now ends only its own Full
  Disk Access messages; the others stand under their own number until what they report
  ends. The messages an older aterm left that System State now carries end as withdrawn,
  not as fixed, and so do those an older aterm raised while the update was taking over.
  When a `[privacy]` switch or `[ai]` is turned off, or you chose *Not now* for Full
  Disk Access, the messages that silences are withdrawn instead of marked fixed, and one
  you had already dismissed stays dismissed.

- **System State keeps setup handoffs in order.** Queued checks respect newer choices,
  Local Network owns the dialog slot before raising its prompt, and an explicit Join
  retains its intent through startup. Repaired or updated local credentials can wake
  a held setup attempt.

- **System State refreshes its readings after Restore.** Earlier checkmarks are cleared
  while preferences are restored, and a reading taken before Restore cannot put them
  back. An interrupted `aterm doctor --apply` also resumes the full preference profile
  instead of retaining the scope of an earlier group change. Partial runs highlight
  only the settings they change.

- **System State recovers interrupted upgrades and keeps vault readings current.**
  Stop survives an interrupted upgrade; old approval codes disappear when the vault URL
  changes. Repository setup uses a complete secrets snapshot and waits when it changes.
  Missing credentials and developer tools keep their specific guidance, and unread rows
  no longer imply setup is complete.

- **Muse Code's launch card is decorated again.** Muse Code makes room for its banner by
  scrolling down from the top of the screen, right where it starts, then erases those
  rows and draws in them. aterm counted those rows as someone else's and left the card
  bare. Rows a running agent opens at its own starting row are now its own, and so are
  blank rows it erases just above it (the next entry); either change alone brings Muse
  Code's card back. A card left by an earlier run, or by another program, still stays
  bare.

- **Claude Code's card stays decorated when you resize the window.** After a width
  change, inline Claude Code erases the whole screen line by line and draws its card
  again from the top, over the command line that started it. aterm counted those top
  rows as the shell's, so the card lost its decoration until the next launch. Blank rows
  that a running agent erased itself, directly above where it started, are now its own.
  Rows that still show another program's text stay out, so an older card above stays
  bare.
- **A Claude Code stopped with Ctrl-Z keeps its card however many stopped agents end
  after it.** A tab keeps the place of at most eight stopped Claude Code, agy and Muse
  Code cards, and made room by forgetting the oldest. A stopped agent that had since
  exited kept its place, so after enough of them a Claude Code still stopped in the tab
  came back from `fg` with its card bare. On macOS a stopped agent's place now goes when
  it exits.

- **A `sudo` install's mount check matches each folder by identity and holds it, and
  a container whose `/` is FUSE installs again.** In 0.130.0 the check matched the mount
  table's text. On macOS a way spelled through `/System/Volumes/Data/…` or in another
  letter case passed an image an account attached there, a tree or `PATH` folder spelled
  so or with a leading `//` (on Linux too) passed a mount inside it, a mount named
  `X (old)` made a plain `X` refuse, and an account could make root refuse a system
  folder by naming its own mount after it; on Linux a container whose `/` is FUSE,
  virtio-fs or 9P refused every root walk at `/`. The check now looks only at what a
  walk crosses, and on macOS reads the mount table within a minute or refuses, so a
  share elsewhere whose server stopped answering no longer hangs a walk. On macOS each
  volume on the way passes only when its device is the kernel's `/dev` or a disk that a
  local mount no account made names, and no other mount names; on Linux each folder's
  own filesystem is read, but for the one `/` is on, and a tree's mounts are placed by
  their text. It also refuses a way of more than 40 links through such a volume, and
  opens each folder on the way before root judges it, refusing when its name no longer
  leads to that folder at the end (a volume taken off it, or put on it and left there).

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` when job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose own
  command runs in front is judged by that command; a build whose step stopped at the
  terminal (a `ninja` step at an ssh passphrase prompt, a `ninja &`'s too) still reads
  `quiet`.
  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z
  in the middle of a bash command list (`make; fg %1`) no longer split the resumed job in
  two, drop the earlier command's row, give one command's exit status to the other, or
  leave the resumed job behind the stopped one. A pipeline stage that runs in a group of its
  own (`seq 1 40 | timeout 3600 xargs ./step.sh`) is judged by the lines the tab prints
  once the stage in front exits, when it is the tab's one background job that can run,
  instead of reading `quiet`, then `stuck`; a parked editor no longer takes those lines or
  keeps them from it. A command run with `sudo` (which runs it on a terminal of its own),
  under `script`, or as an agent's tool call on a terminal of its own (Codex, Gemini CLI)
  is one row beside its opener's, judged by what it does: printing, it reads running, and
  hung on a server that stopped answering it reads `stuck` while sudo waits at the terminal
  and the agent's screen keeps moving, also when the agent runs in `nvim`'s terminal or in
  a tab whose shell gave way to it (`exec codex`) or that runs it in place of a shell
  (`aterm -e codex`). A Ctrl-Z'd `sudo vim` reads `parked`; a command hung in front of
  `script`'s shell beside a job that shell stopped reads `stuck`, and a program there
  waiting for your keys (`vim`, a password prompt, the shell itself) reads by that
  terminal's own mode: fine. That mode is your wait only once your keys were seen reaching
  that terminal, so a hung call on a terminal Codex or Emacs opened (Emacs keeps each in a
  line mode with no echo) no longer reads fine. A command no longer reads running on lines
  another program printed (a hung `git push` beside a printing `tail -f &`, a hung
  background job beside a prompt that redraws its clock, a hung `sudo` command beside a
  printing background job), while `ssh host make` over a shared connection and `tmux
  attach`, whose output a server outside the tab writes, still read running; a log stream
  printing thousands of lines a second, in a cooked or raw terminal, no longer reads
  `quiet` now and then. A `ninja`, `cmake --build`, `meson
  compile` or `cargo nextest` run, whose program starts each step in a group of its own, is
  one row judged by its steps' work, where it read `quiet` and then `stuck` while it
  compiled and showed each step as a row. An async prompt's worker (pure, spaceship)
  belongs to no command's row, also in a zsh run in the tab's, and a `curl … &` that a
  `bash` run in the tab put in the background is a row of its own. A row no
  longer outlives its command because a process substitution (`vim <(tail -f log)`) or a
  server its script left behind lives on.

- **`install.sh` leaves an aterm macOS may still be checking where it is.** On macOS
  27.0.1, replacing a program macOS has not finished checking can stall every program
  start on the Mac until a restart. `install.sh` replaced an installed aterm.app, and the
  toolchain store's `aterm`, without knowing whether it had ever got past that check. It
