  now asks each program it would replace `--version` first (as `nobody` when root may not
  run it), before it downloads or builds the replacement and again right before the
  swap, and replaces it only once that run printed a line or ended on its own, or the Mac
  refused to start it at all (an Intel-only one on a Mac without Rosetta). Otherwise it
  leaves it, says why, and asks you to run it again in 10 minutes or after a restart. When
  root could not ask it as `nobody`, it asks you to run `install.sh` without `sudo`, and
  when it could not start a program for another reason (a denied file, a missing
  interpreter), to remove it yourself after a restart.

- **A program macOS is still checking is no longer taken for one that stopped reading.** A
  program in the foreground that macOS's program check holds before its first instruction
  reads no keys because it has not started yet. Up to 0.129.0 its waiting input could read
  `input=stalled` after five minutes (longer on a busy Mac), and then `aterm ctl send` and
  `turn` refused to type into the tab (`ERR busy input-unread`). Now its input reads
  `input=pending` for as long as macOS holds it, also once it is resumed from a stop or
  when it replaces a program whose input read `stalled`, and a key sent meanwhile is typed
  with the usual `warn=input-unread`.

- **`aterm fabric on` repairs a bad node file and a cap left from another fleet.** When the
  fabric's `link-state/node` held something that is not a node id, `on` said it provisioned
  one but left the file as it was, so the bridge still refused to start. After `aterm fabric
  off`, `on --fleet <other>` kept the old fleet's `node.cap`, so the broker refused all the
  bridge's traffic. `on` now moves such a node file to `node.aside` (or `.aside.N`) and
  writes the new id, and mints the cap again for the fleet it turns on. A ring under the
  root's mint secret that `on` could not mint again (one for another node id, or one with
  grants off this fleet that is not the ring `on` mints for another fleet, such as one
  minted by hand) is kept as `node.cap.aside` (or `.aside.N`).

- **`aterm pkg install <program>` puts back the commands an installed build lost.** When
  `aterm pkg unlink` could not restore a build's commands, or one of them was deleted from
  aterm's `bin` folder, `install` answered "already current" and left them off your PATH,
  and `aterm pkg repair` laid back only the commands still there (for a program such as
  `trust`, which has no command of its own name, it laid a `trust` that runs nothing). Each
  build now keeps a list of the commands it puts on PATH: `install` lays back every one that
  is missing, and `repair` lays back what the list names once a build has one. A build
  installed before this release has no list yet, so `install` reads it from the build's
  signed manifest, which needs the network: offline, `install` leaves the commands as they
  are, and fails saying why when none of them is left under its own name.

- **`aterm theme import` converts Terminal.app profiles and WezTerm colour schemes.** A
  `.terminal` profile exported from Terminal.app was read as an iTerm2 theme and a WezTerm
  scheme as an Alacritty one, so the import failed with "sets no foreground colour", though
  aterm's error for such a file in the themes folder told you to run that very import. Each
  is now recognised as what it is and converted: a Terminal.app profile's text, background,
  cursor, selection and 16 ANSI colours and its name; a WezTerm scheme's `[colors]` (with its
  `ansi` and `brights` lists, split line and active tab) and its `[metadata]` name and
  author. A Terminal.app colour is read from the components it was saved with, and a named
  colour (`textColor`) from the fallback saved inside it, with a note that Terminal.app
  shows the system's own colour for that name. Each gets a note when its colour space is not
  sRGB, or when it lies far enough outside sRGB that clipping it to fit changed it. A profile
  that sets no colours of its own, like Terminal.app's Basic, still has none to convert.

- **`aterm fabric on` no longer says no broker answers when one does.** When the broker
  answered but refused the root's ring (one minted by hand whose grants had lapsed, say),
  `on --service none` reported "no broker answers" and told you to start one, and under
  launchd or systemd `on` said the job "did not bring" the socket up. The broker step now
  says the broker answers and why its bus cannot be read, with the renewal for a lapsed
  ring. `aterm fabric`'s CONFIG row says "no node id" for a node file that holds none,
  where it said there was no node file.

## [0.130.0] - 2026-10-24

### Added

- **aterm counts your programs macOS is still checking where you already look.** `aterm
  ctl privacy`'s `devtools` line ends `program_check=<n> program_check_oldest_ms=<ms>`
  (`--json` too): how many of your programs wait at macOS's program check now, and the
  longest wait. `aterm doctor`'s `devtools:` row says the same while any wait ("now 2
  programs of this user wait for macOS's program check, the oldest started 9 h 59 m ago"),
  and where aterm is already on the Developer Tools list the row turns to a note asking you
  to look at aterm's row there (not right after doctor switched aterm on: the programs
  waiting then started before it). The message log records when a backup of the check
  began (saying so when aterm started none of its programs, so its grant would not help)
  and when it drained, and aterm waits for the backup to clear before it asks macOS about
  itself again after you switch it on.
- **`aterm ctl sys jobs` names programs that never started for another reason.** An Intel
  program Rosetta is still translating reads `finding kind=translating`, and one whose
  program sits on a volume aterm cannot prove local reads `finding kind=not-started`; the
  message log notes each once ("translating (Rosetta), which aterm's Developer Tools grant
  does not reach"). Neither counts as waiting at macOS's program check. While the check is
  backed up, a program that started but sits with its CPU still and a freshly built dylib
  open reads `finding kind=probably-program-check … heuristic=fresh-dylib`: probably
  waiting in the same line, a guess and marked as one.
- **`aterm ctl sys net` and `sys` report TCP connection states and per-link packet, error
  and drop rates.** `aterm ctl sys net` (`--json` too) and `sys` / `sys global` now report
  machine-wide TCP connection counts by state (`established`, `listen`, `syn_sent`,
  `syn_recv`, `time_wait`, `close_wait` and `total`, read from macOS
  `net.inet.tcp.pcblist64` and Linux `/proc/net/tcp` and `/proc/net/tcp6`) alongside each
  active network link's byte, packet, error and drop rates. The Network close-up lens in the
  stats deck shows the live TCP connection summary and link error/drop rates when non-zero.
- **Subagent rows and open background panels in `agy` wear the rainbow and live status
  dots.** `agy`'s transcript subagent rows (`● Spawning …`, `└ Agent(…)`,
  `● Agent(…) needs approval …`), open background panel (`● Agent(…)  <activity> · <elapsed>`)
  and footer subagent badge now unwrap `Agent(self: Role)` to the role's name, render
  subagent names in contrast-floored full-spectrum rainbow ink, and drive the agents panel's
  animated status dots across running, in-flight tool (`Reading file`, `Running command`,
  `Searching web`, …), idle and approval states.

### Changed

- **The harness waits on the session log while an agent works.** Once the screen shows a
  turn running, from the first turn on, the harness waits with `aterm ctl await log
  close=turn,need,kind=agent` from the point its last `status` printed: for the turn's end,
  a box or a question, or the agent's state to move. Before, it waited for the busy row to
  leave the screen. It still reads the screen before it presses or types anything. A turn
  the log closes while the screen still shows the agent working is read as still running.
  When that `status` already shows a box, or a screen reader that has lost track of the
  agent, the harness waits on the screen for that turn. An older aterm that keeps no log,
  or answers that wait `ERR usage`, is watched on the screen for the rest of the session,
  as before.

- **System State is redesigned, and Mac access is approved with it.** The page groups Mac
  setup into Permissions, Keyboard & Trackpad, Desktop & Dock, Messages & FaceTime and
  Workspace, each set to Set up or Leave as is, in place of its list of switches and
  Apply, and every row shows what this Mac has now beside what aterm wants. One
  aterm · ALab rainbow kitty is the page's mark, and the Rainbow Kitty Village beside it
  has a station for each setting, built as that setting gets to where aterm wants it, with
  its kitties walking while a run goes (standing still with Reduce Motion, and left out in
  serious mode, at high contrast and where the pane is too narrow). A run starts once the
  page is shown, with no countdown; Stop ends it between steps, the Messages and FaceTime
  sign-outs run last, and Restore previous settings puts back the Mac preferences aterm
  changed. In a narrow pane or at a large text size the rows, group headings and buttons
  take more lines and keep their words whole (down to 128 points at 1x text, 160 at 1.5x
  and 200 at 2x). In a short window the brand and then the title give way, and the list
  shrinks to as little as one row's height (it scrolls), before Stop, the headline's
  button, Check again or Restore previous settings leaves the window: 320 points wide,
  with a headline that names one row, they stay in view down to 200 points tall at 1x
  text, 320 at 1.5x and 440 at 2x. The brand and the title stay put while a run starts,
  needs you or fails one step; a headline naming several failed steps that stands taller
  counts its own height. The list also takes the 8 points the page left under the
  footer.
  Rust in Spotlight is one row for rustup's offline docs and the build
  folders Spotlight indexes (Docs indexed or Builds indexed, then Kept out). Only an ALab
  Mac (a vault or fleet member, or one that reaches the ALab vault) sets up more than
  Permissions by itself, and the secrets vault is joined from its own row, which says that
  a blank password joins an open vault or waits for another Mac's approval; joining there
  runs only the vault steps again, never the Dock or the sign-outs. Full Disk Access,
  Developer Tools, Local Network and debugger access are approved by default with
  Permissions: each comes up once per approval, only while System State is in front, one
  macOS dialog at a time. aterm's own alert "Allow debugger access on this Mac?" is gone:
  macOS's password dialog is the one step left, and Cancel there settles it for the Mac.
  The setup sheet and setup's entries in Messages are gone too, Developer Tools' and the
  vault's among them; a row that needs you marks the tab and puts one line in aterm's
  menu-bar menu, which opens System State (a new window when none is open), and a vault
  line an earlier version left in Messages opens System State too. A step aterm retries by
  itself (up to ten times, a minute apart) shows its failure on the page only, and reaches
  the menu and the tab once the retries stop. A vault member whose sync process is not
  running reads Not syncing (Not set up when none is installed), and Set up now starts it;
  one that does not come up is a failed step naming its log. Turning the sync off
  (`aterm secrets agent off`, or `--no-agent` on `join` and `create`) is remembered as
  your choice: the row reads Sync off with nothing to change and a quiet Turn On Sync, and
  setup leaves it off. `[privacy] enabled`, `check` and `notice` still hold every step
  back: turned off, a step waits with no answer recorded, and goes on once they are on
  again, including the Full Disk Access check, the Developer Tools check and the folder
  questions when a switch was already off as aterm started.

- **`verify provision` also builds bash 5.3 on a Mac.** Beside macOS's bash 3.2, the
  bash integration's tests now run GNU bash 5.3.20, which `targo --unverified verify
  provision` (and so `aterm init --develop`) builds from GNU's source and its twenty
  official patches, each held to its sha256, with the Mac's own compiler and nothing from
  Homebrew, into `~/Library/Caches/aterm/tooling.noindex`. Every bash test of the
  integration runs on both bashes, so the 5.3-only paths (the fileless read of a typed line
  through `${ ...; }`, its writable-folder check, the PS0 hook a running shell takes from a
  newer body) are checked on every Mac run. Without the 5.3, each such test runs its 3.2
  lane and then reports COULD NOT RUN naming that command, instead of passing on a bash
  that never runs the code it checks.

### Fixed

- **The harness holds on `agy`, Muse Code and Gemini CLI network outages instead of typing
  into a failed turn.** When `agy` prints `⚠ There was a network issue connecting to the
  server, please try again.`, or Muse Code or Gemini CLI reports a statusless unreachable
  network error (`ENOTFOUND`, `ECONNREFUSED`, `ENETUNREACH`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `fetch failed`),
  the phase readers now classify the screen as an unreachable API wall rather than an
  ordinary idle turn end, and the supervisor keeps watching API reachability while a
  standing network retry wall is active even after the notice scrolls off screen.

- **The rainbow cursor trail follows 1- and 2-row composer shifts and rapid chained word
  kills without a gap.** When typing or deleting in a multi-line composer (`agy`, Claude
  Code, Gemini CLI, Codex) shifts the composer box vertically by 1 or 2 rows, or when
  chained word kills (`Alt+Backspace`, `Ctrl+W`) retract across a space boundary, the typing
  ribbon and caret lift now carry the live trail across the shift and preserve right-to-left
  retraction order instead of dropping a gap.

- **Unenrolling a Mac from `aterm machines` keeps aterm.app's first-start record.** On macOS
  27.0.1, replacing a program macOS has not finished checking can stall every program start
  on the Mac until a restart. The agent's uninstall removed the record that keeps a newly
  placed `/Applications/aterm.app` from being replaced before it has run, so enrolling the
  Mac again right away could replace an aterm.app macOS was still checking. The uninstall
  now leaves that record, as it leaves the folders of its own programs that have not shown
  they ran, to the one-time cleanup that removes them after 10 minutes of awake time or a
  restart, and refusing to enroll an enrolled Mac says how long to wait before removing the
  agent by hand.

- **The session log no longer records a 0 ms turn when Claude Code's turn end is read
  late.** If Claude Code went idle and you typed again before aterm had read the end of the
  last turn from its transcript, that late end closed the new turn at once, as a turn of
  0 ms, while the agent was still working on it. The late end now counts toward the turn
  it belongs to, and the new turn stays open until it ends itself.

- **`sudo sh install.sh` checks a checkout as `sudo bash install.sh` does.** Up to
  0.129.0, `sh` (on macOS, bash 3.2 in POSIX mode) ran install.sh with a command
  substitution that keeps `set -e`, so a root source build's check of the checkout stopped
  early on a tree with thousands of files another account owns, before naming one, and the
  build went ahead as root. install.sh now leaves POSIX mode before it runs anything, and
  a check of what a root build reads that stops without an answer refuses the build.

- **A `sudo` source build on macOS finds `cc` and `git`.** In 0.128.0 and 0.129.0 a root
  source build on macOS kept only `/bin` and `/sbin` of `PATH`: `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin`
  hold programs a system account owns (`_uucp`'s `cu`) on the read-only system volume,
  which install.sh's check of where root may take programs from refused, so the build
  found no `cc` to link with. The OS's own program folders, which root's own tools already
  come from, now count as root's. Their `cc`, `ld` and `git` run the developer folder's
  (Xcode's or the Command Line Tools'), so the build now runs only when that folder, its
  SDK and the way to each are root's alone, and pins both: an Xcode in `/Applications`,
  which the admin group can write, is refused, naming the `DEVELOPER_DIR` (for the run) or
  `xcode-select` (for every account) that picks the Command Line Tools, or the
  `DEVELOPER_DIR` or `SDKROOT` to unset when that is where the folder came from, and the
  compiler no longer searches `/usr/local/include` and `/usr/local/lib`.

- **A `sudo` source build judges a link by the whole way it leads.** In 0.128.0 and
  0.129.0 a root source build judged a link in the checkout or cargo's home only by where
  it ended, and a link in a `PATH` folder only when it led to a file: a link that came
  back into the checkout through a link or folder another account can change, or a `PATH`
  link that led to nothing yet, or to a folder, where another account can write, let that
  account change what root read, or put a program root then ran by name. Each path is now
  walked name by name as the kernel walks it, every link on it followed wherever it sits,
  and each folder on the way must be root's alone, and on macOS each link on it too, since
  its owner could remove it; a link whose target holds a newline, or that leads below a
  folder that does not exist yet (such as one a disk image would get in `/Volumes`), is
  refused, and so is a cargo home or install folder still to be made below one.

- **A `sudo` install trusts no owners it reads on a network, FUSE or account-mounted
  volume.** There the owners and modes root reads do not say who can change what the
  volume holds: an NFS or SMB server, or the FUSE daemon of the account that mounted it,
  decides that, and on macOS a disk image an account attached shows root the owners the
  image carries, and that account can detach it and attach another in its place. Up to
  0.129.0 a root run judged a folder on one by those owners alone. A root run now refuses
  a program, a toolchain, a checkout, a developer folder or the app's install folder whose
  way from `/` passes through such a volume (on macOS one `mount` lists as not `local`, or
  as `mounted by` an account; on Linux one whose filesystem type is a network or FUSE
  one's), or a tree it reads or a `PATH` folder it takes `cc` from with one mounted inside
  (on Linux, one can be mounted on a file), and refuses as well when it cannot read the
  mount table.

- **A `sudo` install says why it links no CLI to an app in `/Applications`.** Root runs no
  program another account can change, and the admin group can write `/Applications` and
  the app's folders in it, so a root run never links the app's `aterm`. It said instead
  that the installed app shipped no toolset and to update or reinstall it, which could not
  help, and `--dry-run` promised the link, the toolset and the `PATH` block. Both now name
  the folder and the remedy (install the CLI as your account, or `ATERM_INSTALL_DIR` at a
  folder only root can write); `--dry-run` says the toolset and `PATH` halves are SKIPPED
  when no `aterm` root may run is left, and a root run that builds the CLI from source
  instead says why.

- **A `sudo` install skips a folder on a volume that ignores ownership before it
  downloads.** On an exFAT or FAT volume, or one with "Ignore ownership on this volume"
  on, root cannot make the app's staging folder its own: 0.128.0 and 0.129.0 downloaded
  and verified the app there, then stopped with "could not stage aterm.app", which also
  ended the CLI, toolset and `PATH` halves, and `--dry-run` planned the install. The app
  half is now SKIPPED up front, in `--dry-run` too, naming the volume's `noowners`.

- **A `sudo` install keeps its downloads in `/tmp`.** A root run made its temporary folder
  wherever `TMPDIR` said; under `sudo -E`, doas's `keepenv` or a musl `sudo` that was the
  account's own folder, where that account could put a folder of its own in place of
  root's between root checking a download and running it. Root's temporary folders now go
  in `/tmp`, whose sticky bit lets no account rename them.

- **`sudo … --dry-run` plans an install folder still to be made as the run makes it.** In
  0.129.0 a root dry run with an `ATERM_INSTALL_DIR` that did not exist yet said the app
  half was SKIPPED because the folder carries an ACL, while the real run made the folder
  and installed. It now judges such a folder by the ACL entries the folder above it passes
  on to the folders made in it.

- **On Linux, a `sudo` install without `getfacl` says why it refuses.** Root then takes
  each file and folder it checks for one an ACL lets another account change, as 0.129.0
  did without saying why; it now says so once, up front, naming the `acl` package that
  brings it.

- **On Linux, the folders install.sh makes are writable by you alone under a default
  ACL too.** Below a folder with a default ACL, Linux ignores the umask, so install.sh made
  `~/.local/bin`, the store and the folders above them with the modes that ACL passes on
  (`0777` under one that lets every account write), and the store's check then skipped the
  binary after `--dry-run` had planned it. install.sh now takes group and other write back
  from each folder it makes, and with them the ACL's mask.

- **`--dry-run` plans no folder at or below a link that leads nowhere.** A dry run passed
  over such a link to the folder above it, so it planned an install folder `mkdir -p`
  cannot make, and the real run then skipped that half.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` when job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose own
  command runs in front is judged by that command; a build whose step stopped at the
  terminal (a `ninja` step at an ssh passphrase prompt) still reads `quiet`.
  A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z
  in the middle of a bash command list (`make; fg %1`) no longer split the resumed job in
  two, drop the earlier command's row, give one command's exit status to the other, or
  leave the resumed job behind the stopped one. A pipeline stage that runs in a group of its
  own (`seq 1 40 | timeout 3600 xargs ./step.sh`) is judged by the lines the tab prints
  once the stage in front exits, when it is the tab's one background job that can run,
  instead of reading `quiet`, then `stuck`; a parked editor no longer takes those lines or
  keeps them from it. A command run with `sudo` (which runs it on a terminal of its own) or
  under `script` is one row judged by what it prints, not extra rows that read `quiet`.
  A row no longer outlives its command because a process substitution (`vim <(tail -f log)`)
  or a server its script left behind lives on.

- **`aterm pkg self-uninstall` keeps an aterm.app macOS may still be checking.** On macOS
  27.0.1, removing a program macOS has not finished checking can stall every program start
  on the Mac until a restart. Up to 0.129.0 `install.sh --uninstall` gave each installed
  aterm a minute to say what it is, and the uninstall it then ran removed every aterm.app
  seconds later, one that had not answered included. The uninstall now asks each program in
  an aterm.app (`aterm`, and any other, such as an older toolset's `aterm-cli` and `atpkg`)
  `--version` first, and removes the app only once each run has ended, or the Mac refused
  to start the program at all (an Intel-only one on a Mac without Rosetta); an `atpkg`
  whose `uninstall --all` already showed it ran is not asked again. One that does not
  answer within a minute is kept, as is one a root uninstall could not ask through sudo,
  and its SKIPPED line says to uninstall again in 10 minutes or after a restart.

- **System State's debugger-access step no longer touches your home folder while
  aterm's windows wait.** Before it turns debugger access on, aterm records the Mac
  beside `aterm.toml`; that record, and the one it writes when debugger access is
  settled already, are now written on a thread of their own, so a home folder on a
  network volume that stopped answering can no longer freeze aterm's windows at that
  moment. The record's folder is now flushed with it, so a power cut just after it was
  written cannot bring the step back. And when another aterm on the same config folder
  is changing debugger access, aterm now reads that change at once and settles the step,
  instead of looking again every few seconds until it gave up.

- **Debugger access and its help now say what "once per Mac" means.** The record of the
  Macs where System State's debugger step ran lives in your account's config folder, so
  a second account on the same Mac gets the step once too. `aterm help permissions` and
  `aterm ctl help privacy` say once per Mac and account, and that the step belongs to
  the setup System State runs with its Permissions group. A Mac where debugger access
  was turned off in a way aterm did not see (`DevToolsSecurity -disable` in a terminal,
  or from aterm in another account) gets the step once: macOS's `DevToolsSecurity
  -status` cannot tell that from never turned on. `aterm help permissions` also says that
  lldb attaches over ssh, with no dialog, to a program you signed with the
  `get-task-allow` entitlement (measured on macOS 26.6 and 27.0).

- **System State's debugger-access step is no longer lost, or taken, once aterm has
  recorded the Mac.** In the moment between recording the Mac and starting the change:
  an answer you gave the debugger-access alert in Settings now ends the step instead of
  bringing up macOS's dialog a second time; a No you had just given another of aterm's
  Security alerts now makes the step wait, instead of skipping it for good; debugger
  access you turned on yourself meanwhile starts nothing, and neither does debugger
  access you turned off; a `[privacy]` switch you turned off meanwhile pauses the step
  until it is on again; first-launch setup holding the permission pages back no
  longer keeps it from ever coming; and when macOS's check of whether debugger access is
  on fails or times out just then, the step checks again, for five minutes and at least
  three tries. Setting Permissions up again while macOS's dialog
  is up waits for your answer there instead of recording the new approval declined.

- **`aterm ctl ready` answers `OK ready prompt` at your shell's prompt.** Under aterm's own
  shell integration (bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell), a shell waiting at its prompt read as
  `OK ready idle`, and only once the screen had been quiet for a moment, so a script could
  not tell it from a quiet running command. It now answers `OK ready prompt` at once there,
  with or without a line typed at the prompt.

- **A tab theme you have not installed is refused, not silently ignored.** `aterm ctl theme
  session set` and `spawn theme=` took a community pack theme missing from your themes
  folder, answered OK, and the tab went on drawing the window's theme. They now refuse it
  and change nothing; `aterm theme install <id>` adds it, and `aterm ctl theme preview`
  still shows one without installing it.

- **`aterm ctl await block` answers when a command finishes under PowerShell.** It looked
  only at whether the newest command block read as finished at the end of each burst of
  output, so when the shell sent its next prompt in the same write as the command's end
  mark, as PowerShell always does, the wait ran to its timeout. It now answers once any
  command finishes after the wait is armed, and output at a prompt (a keystroke's echo)
  never answers it. The supervise-agent skill now waits for a command it ran with `wait`,
  which also answers a command that finished before the wait was asked.

- **A keyed `turn` or `key` that typed nothing can be retried with the same `id=`.** A
  `key id=…` with a misspelt key name, or a `turn` that stopped before typing anything (its
  `if-gen=` or `if-rows=` fence saw the screen move, a `typed=1` turn ran out of time
  before its first key, a hold or a `yield=` wait stopped it, the session had exited, or
  the program's input queue was full), used up its id, so the retry answered `ERR
  in-doubt` or `OK 0 dup=1` and typed nothing. Now the id is given back. A `turn` whose
  first paste or key is refused by a full input queue or by its `if-supervisor=` fence now
  answers `ERR busy …`, as `send` does, instead of `ERR paste delivery failed` or `ERR key
  delivery failed`. A `turn` whose `submit=` names no key, or into a session that
  has exited, no longer pastes its text before it refuses, and a guarded `turn` whose Enter
  the program never took now answers `ERR key delivery failed sink=busy` instead of `ERR
  busy sink`, so a retry cannot type the text twice. When only a guarded `turn`'s retried
  Enter is refused by a busy program, after an earlier one went, the `turn` now answers with its verdict (`submitted=0
  pressed=<n>`), so the supervisor no longer takes text that may have been sent as left
  unsent.

## [0.129.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- **`aterm pkg install grok` and `aterm pkg install kimi` install xAI's Grok Build and
  Moonshot AI's Kimi Code from their vendors.** Neither joins the default set: each lands
  only when you install it by name, and is kept current once installed. Kimi Code (macOS,
  Linux and Windows; no musl build) is checked against two release manifests, one on
  cdn.kimi.com and one on its GitHub release, which must name the same SHA-256. Grok
  Build (macOS only) comes from xAI's own bucket, which carries no digest (xAI's npm
  packages carry a registry-signed one for the same bytes, which aterm does not read yet),
  so aterm measures the download, checks its Developer ID signature is xAI's before
  anything runs, and then remembers that digest: a different file under the same version
  is refused as a re-cut. Both run with their own updaters off and with yolo by default,
  like the other agents (`--always-approve` for grok, `--auto` for kimi). For kimi,
  aterm's `--yolo` means `--auto` (Never Ask) and takes over Kimi's own `-y`/`--yolo`
  (Ask When Needed); on Linux and Windows nothing signs Kimi's binary, so the two
  manifests' agreement is its only check.

- **aterm counts your programs macOS is still checking where you already look.** `aterm
  ctl privacy`'s `devtools` line ends `program_check=<n> program_check_oldest_ms=<ms>`
  (`--json` too): how many of your programs wait at macOS's program check now, and the
  longest wait. `aterm doctor`'s `devtools:` row says the same while any wait ("now 2
  programs of this user wait for macOS's program check, the oldest started 9 h 59 m ago"),
  and where aterm is already on the Developer Tools list the row turns to a note asking you
  to look at aterm's row there (not right after doctor switched aterm on: the programs
  waiting then started before it). While the check is backed up with programs aterm started
  and aterm is not on the list, the Developer Tools line in the digest leads with that
  count in place of why the list matters, following it as programs join and leave, and the
  message log records when the backup began (saying so when aterm started none of them, so
  its grant would not help) and when it drained. aterm waits for the backup to clear before
  it asks macOS about itself again after you switch it on.

### Changed

- **A tab says when the harness is the one acting.** For 30 seconds after the harness
  restarts or upgrades an agent, or types its carry-on after a full disk or a usage limit,
  the tab's tooltip and menu read `now: restarting · by the harness` (or `upgrading to
  2.1.0`, `resuming after disk`, `resuming after limit`). The words are fixed, never the
  agent's. Anything that needs you still comes first: a restart that left a failure
  standing still says `now: failed`, and a limit that is still on screen says `now: limit`.

- **The session log names the harness when it types.** A restart's carry-on, an upgrade's
  announcement and a resume after a full disk now show as `by=harness` in `aterm ctl log` and
  `brief`, where they read `ctl` before. `aterm ctl history` already named them
  `by=harness`, and `aterm drive ledger` already left them out of the manager's turns.

- **Word cats, the pet, the dog, the kitty cursor, the nuke cloud and the matrix rain are
  drawn by the same sprite path as the harness card.** On the GPU they now land the CPU
  renderer's pixels exactly wherever the art is opaque, at every scale. Four visible
  differences follow. A companion half under a card or a band keeps the half beside it
  (before, it vanished or was cropped). A companion scaled by a non-whole factor, such as
  the pet at 1.5×, can show a column or row one texel over from before. A rain glyph at
  the edge of a split pane is drawn only when the whole glyph fits in the pane. A
  companion at a pane's edge can now spill into the window padding, as the other effects
  do. The scrollbar is drawn the same way, pixel for pixel as before, except where a menu
  card's edge crosses it: the part beside the card now stays and is cut at the card's
  edge (before, the bar's rows level with the card vanished).

### Removed

- **`aterm drive ledger --source anchor` is gone.** The ledger has read the session log by
  default since 0.127.0; the old way, which guessed each time from when aterm's control
  socket was made, now answers that it was removed and to leave the flag out. `--source log`
  is still accepted and changes nothing.

### Fixed

- **The cursor kitty no longer hitches about once a second.** While a System State tab was
  open, its status clock woke aterm dozens of times in a row every second, and aterm's guard
  against such wakes then pushed the kitty's next frame back behind them. The tab now asks
  for its status when it is due, and a wake that is late no longer delays a frame that is
  due sooner.

- **A `sudo` install reads ACLs, not only owners and modes.** Earlier releases let an
  account that an ACL entry on the app's install folder allowed to add entries make a
  folder of its own named `aterm.app` in the moment the swap leaves that name free, and the
  new app then landed inside that folder. A root run now SKIPS the app when its install
  folder (for a link, the folder it leads to) carries an ACL, and names the `chmod -N` that
  removes it. Root also runs no program that carries an ACL or lies below a folder with one,
  and a root source build is SKIPPED when the checkout, anything in it, a folder above it,
  a `.cargo/` config above it or cargo's home carries one; it takes `cc`, `ar` and `ld`
  only from `PATH` folders where nothing does. On Linux these read the ACL with `getfacl`,
  and without `getfacl` root refuses as if each entry had one. With `ATERM_INSTALL_DIR` a
  link, the app's folders take the group and group write of the folder it leads to, not of
  the link, which a umask of 002 made look group-writable. The app keeps no ACL on a link
  inside it, and the staging folder loses its ACL without the strip following a link.

- **A command stopped with Ctrl-Z stays `parked` while the next one runs.** `sys jobs` read
  a stopped job as parked only while the shell held the terminal, so a `vim` stopped with
  Ctrl-Z read `stop=held`, then `quiet` and in time `stuck`, once the next command ran,
  and so did `gdb` waiting at its prompt while the program it debugs sat at a breakpoint.
  Now a stop is `parked` whenever job control took the terminal from it, and a job whose
  own command runs in front is judged by that command. A `fg` typed ahead of the end of a
  command, a `fg %1` right after a Ctrl-Z, and a Ctrl-Z in the middle of a bash command
  list no longer split the resumed job in two or drop the earlier command's row.

## [0.128.0] - 2026-10-23

### Fixed

- **System State fits a narrow pane and a large text size.** Up to 0.126.0 a pane up to
  about 200 points wide (290 at twice the text size) painted setting names as word
  fragments or not at all, and one under about 165 points (250 at twice the text size) cut
  its buttons' names short. At a large text size the page's lines could overlap, a
  switch's Off could run into its knob, and the title and an offer's guidance could be
  cut, the guidance before saying how to stop the offer. Now a setting's switch stands
  under its name wherever the column beside it cannot hold every word of the names, or
  where that shows more of the checklist. The buttons stand one to a row where two side by
  side would cut their names, unless that would leave the checklist no whole row. Lines
  stand further apart as the text size grows, a switch and the brand's name widen with the
  text, and the title wraps where it does not fit on one line, read by VoiceOver as one
  title. An offer's guidance always says how to stop it. Where Apply's face cannot show
  the countdown, the guidance leads with it, figure first, in the fullest words the page
  holds ("30 s to Apply. Click, type or scroll to stop.", down to "30 s. Click to stop."),
  ahead of any result, and Apply's face shows the plain word, so the countdown shows once.
  On a tall, narrow page the help and an offer's warning take the lines their words need.
  A row too tall for a short page ends in an ellipsis, and the scroll caption shows only
  where it fits whole, shortening to fit ("3–5/21", then "5/21"). An ellipsis follows a
  whole word where the line has room for one (each Chinese or Japanese character counts as
  a word). A row's state after its name shows whole, or only its current state, or not at
  all. Only the results on the page are wrapped to fit, so hundreds of them cost the page
  less.

- **A `sudo` install copies the app where no other account can reach it, and builds only
  what no other account can change.** Up to 0.127.0 a root run copied the app into its
  folder before making it root's, so for the length of the copy the app's folders were the
  release builder's uid 501's, and on a Mac where that uid is another person, that account
  could add to the app root then installed. The copy is now made inside a folder only root
  can open, which also drops an ACL an entry on the app's folder would pass down
  (`/Applications` takes none), and the app keeps no ACL. A root run of the version already
  installed also reinstalls an app that every account can write in, or that carries an ACL.
  A source build under root is now SKIPPED, naming the path, when another account could
  change a rustc wrapper the environment names, the checkout, anything in it (`target/`
  included) or a folder above it, a `.cargo/` config above it, cargo's home, or the git
  folder the checkout's `.git` file names. It takes `cc`, `ar` and `ld` only from folders of
  root's on `PATH`, and the git it runs reads, from git 2.32 on, no `~/.gitconfig` or system
  git config, only the checkout's. When the only way to the Trust toolchain is an `aterm`
  root will not run, the SKIPPED line says to run install.sh as that `aterm`'s account, not
  `aterm pkg install trust`. Run as you, a source build no longer stops for a crate, index
  or lock file root's in `~/.cargo`: it asks only the folders the build writes in.

- **aterm Caffeine keeps an `aterm caffeine on` made as a span ends.** When a timed span
  ended, the mug saved off over the state file, so an `aterm caffeine on` (or a new span)
  saved a moment before was replaced with off and the Mac could sleep. The mug now reads the
  file again as a span ends and keeps what another command saved there; with nothing saved,
  it saves off as before. A span another command saved a moment before the mug read the
  file is also left as written, where the mug could save it back a second or two shorter.

- **`sys jobs` sees what a tab prints and which command it runs.** The stuck-process
  engine never saw a tab's output, so a command printing a line every few seconds, such as
  `ping -i 5`, read `quiet` while it printed (φ 3.05 after 7 minutes in one run). Nor did it
  see the shell's command blocks, so a loop typed at the prompt, such as
  `while :; do sleep 1; done`, was a new job at each `sleep` and could never read stuck.
  Now a tab's new lines count as its command's progress (for a full-screen program, any
  change on the screen does; a write that changes nothing on the screen, or the echo of a
  typed Enter, never counts), and with shell integration a command is one job from start
  to end, named `b<n>` after its block in `aterm ctl blocks` (or `j<pgid>` when it was
  seen a moment before its block), that keeps its exit status even when the next command
  starts at once, and stays one job through Ctrl-Z, `bg` and `fg`.

## [0.127.0] - 2026-10-23

### Changed

- **`aterm drive ledger` reads the session log by default.** Each turn is placed by the
  session log's own record of it, and each message by the log's record of the mail, so a
  ledger no longer guesses the time from when aterm's control socket was made, and the
  window's ⇧⌘L page reads the same way. `--source anchor` keeps the old way until the
  release after this one, and is removed then.

### Fixed

- **`aterm fabric` names the broker by the socket it listens on.** The broker's pid, and
  with it the durability, log and health snapshot the report reads from that process, is
  now the one process of yours holding the listening socket at the broker's path, as the
  kernel records it, not the first command line that names the path. A broker whose socket
  path has a space in it is found, and a command that only names the socket is never taken
  for it. `aterm doctor`'s fabric row and `aterm fabric on`'s wait for a starting broker no
  longer read any other process's command line, so on Linux the doctor row runs no `ps`.

- **`aterm doctor`'s `instances:` row names a broker left by a removed worktree.** On
  Linux an aterm program from a build directory whose binary file was deleted is now named
  ("from a build directory; running a deleted binary"); before, the row said this only of a
  program launchd adopted, which Linux cannot tell. An installed aterm still running the
  binary an update replaced is counted, not named. A window started with its input
  redirected (`aterm </dev/null` on a terminal) is counted as a window, because the row now
  reads each instance's input as the front door does, not its terminal. And these are no
  longer counted as unreached windows: `aterm --version`, `--help` and `--completions` run
  without a terminal; `atpkg`, `abrew`, `agh`, `amacs` and `aterm-askpass`, which are names
  of the aterm program and are now listed by those names (`atpkg`, not `aterm update`); and
  development tools such as `aterm-verify`.

- **A shared session's needs pill uses the tab already in view.** If the same
  session appears in two tabs, its active tab no longer gets a background-tab
  label and age, and Restart or Resume remains available there. Clicking the
  pill keeps that view instead of switching to its background copy.

- **System State fits a narrow pane and a large text size.** Up to 0.125.0 a pane under
  about 150 points wide painted setting names as fragments or not at all and cut its
  buttons' names short, and at a large text size the page's lines could overlap, a switch's
  On could run into its knob, and the title and an offer's guidance could be cut, the
  guidance before it said how to stop the offer. Now a pane too narrow for a setting's name
  beside its switch puts the switch under the name, the buttons stand one to a row where two
  side by side would cut their names, lines stand further apart as the text size grows, a
  switch widens with the text, and the title wraps where it does not fit on one line.
  Where Apply's face cannot show an offer's countdown, the guidance leads with it, figure
  first, in the fullest words the page holds ("30 s to Apply. Click, type or scroll to
  stop.", down to "30 s. Click to stop."), ahead of any result, and Apply's face shows the
  plain word, so the countdown shows once. A row too tall for a short page ends in an
  ellipsis wherever the checklist has room for a one-line row and its scroll caption, and
  the caption shortens to fit ("3–5 of 21", then "3–5/21"). An ellipsis follows a whole
  word where the line has room for one (each Chinese or Japanese character counts as a
  word), and a row's state after its name shows whole or not at all. VoiceOver reads the
  vault and restore hints on the password field and on Restore when a short page leaves
  them out. Only the results on the page are wrapped to fit, so hundreds of them cost the
  page less.

- **A `sudo` install leaves aterm.app root's, and as root runs no `aterm` another
  account could change.** A root run (`sudo install.sh`, an MDM script, `sudo -i`) kept
  the owner the release archive recorded, the release builder's uid 501, so on a Mac
  where uid 501 is another person, or no one, that account could change the app every
  account and root then run. A root run now makes the app root's: its folders writable by
  the group that can write the folder it goes in (`admin` for `/Applications`), so an
  admin can still replace it on update, and its files by root alone. A root run of the
  version already installed reinstalls an app another account owns files in, or whose
  files a group can change, instead of keeping it. Under root, install.sh no longer runs
  an `aterm` that another account could change, or that sits in a folder or behind a link
  another account could change, to ask its version, to find the Trust toolchain or to
  install the ALab toolset: it says SKIPPED and names what to run instead. A source build
  under root likewise runs no cargo, rustup, rustc or trustc whose program file another
  account could change, and is SKIPPED, saying which. A root run over a `HOME` that does
  not exist yet is judged by the folder it would be made in, so one inside another
  account's home is refused as that home is. Run as you, a source build in a checkout
  whose `target/` or `~/.cargo` an earlier `sudo` install left root's files in, where the
  build writes, is SKIPPED from the start, as `--dry-run`'s plan says too, naming the
  `sudo chown -R` that gives them back (the folder a link leads to, when `target/` or
  `~/.cargo` is one). The NOTE naming root's leftovers also names aterm's desktop entry
  and icons on Linux, and spells its `sudo chown -R` so bash, zsh and fish each read
  every path as one word.

- **Installing an aterm from before Caffeine turns Caffeine's Enable at Startup off.**
  With Enable at Startup on, `install.sh --version` with a release before 0.107.0, which
  has no Caffeine, left the login item in place, and macOS started that aterm at every
  login and again every 10 seconds after it failed, all session. install.sh now asks the
  aterm it installed whether it has Caffeine and, when it answers that it does not, turns
  Enable at Startup off and says so; an aterm that gives no answer, or a Ctrl-C while it
  asks, leaves it on. An aterm with the Caffeine menu turns it back on.

- **aterm Caffeine's timed spans last what you picked when the Mac's clock changes.** A
  span (Activate for 1, 8 or 24 Hours, or `aterm caffeine on <span>`) ended at a time on the
  clock, so setting the date or time back, or the Mac correcting a clock that ran fast, kept
  the Mac awake that much longer: set back a day, Activate for 1 Hour kept it awake for 25
  hours, its menu row read "24 h 59 min left", and the tooltip and `aterm caffeine status`
  agreed. Setting the clock forward ended a span early. A span now counts the time that
  passes, time asleep included as before, whatever the clock is set to, and `status`'s
  `until=` is its end as the clock reads now. A span that was on when this update arrived
  keeps the time it had left, and never more than it was set for. While this version's
  Caffeine is running, an earlier aterm on the same Mac (a second install, or one rolled back
  to) reads the same end, within a minute of the clock changing.

- **aterm Caffeine removes its copy of aterm when a logout, restart or shutdown ends it.**
  The mug runs from its own copy of aterm.app, which it removed when you quit it but not
  when the Mac logged out, restarted or shut down, so the copy stayed in
  `~/Library/Application Support/aterm/caffeine-code.noindex` until Caffeine next started
  or quit. Once an update replaced aterm.app, that copy took as much disk space as the app.

## [0.126.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- **The harness tells an agent about its own hung background call.** If one of the
  agent's background calls in a tab has made no progress, the next continue, done check
  or land prompt the harness types ends with one note naming it, for example `(aterm: a
  background call (pid 27098) has made no progress for 31 min)`. The note goes once each
  time a call stops making progress, never in an answer or in your own draft, and is left
  off if the prompt would be too long. `[harness] facts = false` turns the notes off. A
  separate `[harness] stuck_break_note = true` lets the harness type the note as its own
  line when the agent sits idle on the call and no prompt is coming (under Cruise or Land,
  at most one such note each 20 min). It is off by default.

### Changed

- **Effects draw faster on Macs with Apple silicon.** The Claude Code card's animations, the
  cursor glows, fire, rain and sparkle words now blend inside the frame's single GPU pass,
  where they used to open up to four more. The card's animations and the Rainbow Kitty glow
  take about 13 % less time to draw (present p95), and output scrolling under a card takes
  about 5 % less. A frame with nothing animating draws as before, and every pixel is
  unchanged. Before using the faster path, aterm checks once that the GPU returns every colour
  exactly, off the path of the first window; until that check is done, and on a GPU that does
  not pass it or a Mac with an Intel or AMD GPU, effects draw the earlier way. On a light theme,
  the card's background now draws in the frame's first pass on every GPU, which takes about 5 to
  8 % off its animations on the earlier way. `aterm ctl metrics` reports the check's result as
  `gpu_fetch_probe`.

### Fixed

- **A `sudo` install leaves aterm.app root's, and as root runs no `aterm` another
  account could change.** A root run (`sudo install.sh`, an MDM script, `sudo -i`) kept
  the owner the release archive recorded, the release builder's uid 501, so on a Mac
  where uid 501 is another person, or no one, that account could change the app every
  account and root then run. A root run now makes the app root's, writable by the group
  that can write its folder (`admin` for `/Applications`), so an admin can still replace
  it on update; a root run of the version already installed reinstalls an app another
  account owns files in instead of keeping it. Under root, install.sh no longer runs an
  `aterm` that another account could change, or that sits in a folder or behind a link
  another account could change, to ask its version or to install the ALab toolset: it
  says SKIPPED and names what to run instead. A root run over a `HOME` that does not
  exist yet is judged by the folder it would be made in, so one inside another account's
  home is refused as that home is. Run as you, a source build in a checkout whose
  `target/` or `~/.cargo` an earlier `sudo` install left root's files in now says so
  before it starts and names the `sudo chown -R` that gives them back. The NOTE naming
  root's leftovers also names aterm's desktop entry and icons on Linux, and spells its
  `sudo chown -R` so bash, zsh and fish each read every path as one word.

- **aterm Caffeine's timed spans last what you picked when the Mac's clock changes.** A
  span (Activate for 1, 8 or 24 Hours, or `aterm caffeine on <span>`) ended at a time on the
  clock, so setting the date or time back, or the Mac correcting a clock that ran fast, kept
  the Mac awake that much longer: set back a day, Activate for 1 Hour kept it awake for 25
  hours, its menu row read "24 h 59 min left", and the tooltip and `aterm caffeine status`
  agreed. Setting the clock forward ended a span early. A span now counts the time that
  passes, time asleep included as before, whatever the clock is set to, and `status`'s
  `until=` is its end as the clock reads now. A span that was on when this update arrived
  keeps the time it had left, and never more than it was set for.

- **`sys jobs` judges an agent's background call by its own pace.** Every call Claude Code
  makes runs under its `zsh` wrapper, so aterm put them all in one class and judged each
  call by the pace the earlier ones had kept: after a few quick builds, a silent `sleep 600`
  read `quiet` after about a minute and `no_progress` after about 3. A call whose command
  aterm cannot name is now judged by its own pace, else the default (quiet after about 7
  minutes of silence, no progress after about 18), and teaches no class.

- **The harness names a hung background call as soon as it reads one.** If the harness had
  just recorded a stall without naming a call, a call that then read no progress waited out
  the 30-minute pace before the `STALLED` record named it, and its exception came later
  still. It is now named at once.

## [0.125.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- **The harness tells an agent about its own hung background call.** If one of the
  agent's background calls in a tab has made no progress, the next continue, done check
  or land prompt the harness types ends with one note naming it, for example `(aterm: a
  background call (pid 27098) has made no progress for 31 min)`. The note goes once each
  time a call stops making progress, never in an answer or in your own draft, and is left
  off if the prompt would be too long. `[harness] facts = false` turns the notes off. A
  separate `[harness] stuck_break_note = true` lets the harness type the note as its own
  line when the agent sits idle on the call and no prompt is coming (under Cruise or Land,
  at most one line of aterm's own each 20 min). It is off by default.

- **The Deck's CPU row says when Spotlight is why the CPU is busy.** Once Spotlight's work
  has used at least one core, and at least 40% of the busy CPU outside aterm, for about
  15 seconds, the row's details read `load 5.6 on 18 cores · ∵ Spotlight, after start-up ·
  busiest siriactionsd, 0.7 cores` (`since wake` after a wake, or plain `∵ Spotlight`),
  and the clause goes 30 seconds after Spotlight stops. `∵` is a new mark, "the cause aterm
  names"; How to read lists it, and a screen reader hears "Why: Spotlight, after
  start-up." In a narrower window the clause shortens to `∵ Spotlight` and outlasts the
  busiest process. It comes from the same reading as `sys why`, and has been on the Deck
  since 0.122.0. It is macOS only: it reads the groups of processes macOS keeps, so on
  Linux and Windows the row never shows it.

- **The CPU lens has a Why now section.** While a cause is open (from the second reading
  in a row that finds it until 30 seconds after it stops), the CPU lens adds four rows:
  the cause and the cores it uses (`∵ Spotlight, after start-up 1.42 cores`), the split of
  the busy cores into macOS services, your other processes, aterm and this tab, adding up
  to the busy figure (`macOS services 2.17 · others 0.73 · aterm 0.40, Tab 1 0.20 3.30
  cores`), whether this tab is the cause, and either "nothing needed" or "no step offered
  yet", with how aterm knows (`measured per coalition, Spotlight by its code signature`).
  In a short lens it folds to one line, `Why now ∵ Spotlight, after start-up; this tab is
  not the cause`, and it never pushes out the lens's other sections. It says what `sys
  why` says, from the same reading, and has been in the CPU lens since 0.123.0. Like the
  Deck's clause, it is macOS only: on Linux and Windows the CPU lens never shows it.

- **Coding agents learn to ask `sys why`.** The agent primer (v36) names `aterm ctl @self
  sys why` beside `sys`, and the system-state skill (v6) gains a Why section: what each
  line of the reply means, that `role=` on the `you` line says whether this tab is the
  cause, that `src=` says where a fact came from, and that `cannot` lines and
  `unavailable(…)` mark what was not measured, never zero.

- **`aterm ctl @self sys jobs` names a program macOS is still checking.** A job whose
  program macOS's program check holds before its first instruction now reads
  `wait=program-check verdict=fine`, where it read as an unnamed wait that went quiet. A
  `finding kind=program-check pid=… exe=… for_ms=…` line says how long each of your
  programs has waited (one in no tab shows at `scope=global`; `--json` has it too). While
  one waits, aterm reads again every 30 s with no window open, and stops about a minute
  after the last one starts.

### Changed

- **codex-alab 0.164.0-dev.13172 is now one of the builds aterm reads the turns of.** Its
  own record of each turn, tool and token count reaches `aterm ctl log` (`src=transcript`),
  and `aterm ctl status` says `rollout=bound` for it, as for 0.164.0-dev.12672 before it.
  13172 is the first of these builds that tells aterm when it leaves a turn to you
  (`left-to-person@v1`).

## [0.124.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- **`aterm doctor` checks the aterm checkouts of a Mac set up to work on aterm.** Where
  `aterm init --develop` recorded a checkout, doctor (bare or `--read-only`) now also says
  whether it is behind origin as it was last fetched, whether its `vendor/astream` is
  checked out, and whether the tools its tests run against are in place (its own `verify
  provision --check`, which may first build in the checkout's `target/`, and which doctor
  stops after two minutes). Doctor goes online for none of this and changes none of it; a
  row with something to do names `aterm init --develop`, or the one git command that
  records origin's default branch in a checkout that has lost it. A checkout on another
  branch is reported as it is, and its tools are read as `aterm init` reads them; one with
  uncommitted work, a detached HEAD or another origin is reported as it is, and none of its
  code runs. A Mac without a `[develop]` table shows no such row, and doctor runs nothing
  for it; an `init.toml` doctor cannot read is one row saying why, with every other check
  read as before.

### Changed

- **The usage tap ships on.** `[harness] usage_tap` now defaults to `true`: a Claude Code
  that aterm relaunches (a restart in place, a relaunch on exit, a live upgrade) carries
  aterm's status-line tap, so its composer gains a `5h N% · 7d N%` row (the share used). It
  rides only in the machine's own Claude home, on its default login, its lone listed login,
  or, where `accounts.toml` lists two or more accounts, any login it lists or one a renewal
  moved one of its rows away from (a single listed account's tap follows only its current
  login); never over your own statusLine, `apiKeyHelper` or credential settings,
  `--settings` or `--bare`, and nothing is written to a settings file. Its figures now also
  time the continuation after a usage limit, which can wait for the later of the reset they
  read and the one the notice names, and on a machine with listed accounts they feed early
  rotation. The account-stats recorder rides on the same switch, so it is on too.
  `usage_tap = false` stops tapping new relaunches; a session tapped before keeps its row
  and its readings until it is relaunched.

### Fixed

- **`sys why` no longer says nothing needs doing while a core of work belongs to no one.**
  CPU that no group of processes held over the window (one that ended inside it, or one
  the kernel's list left out), at least a core and a tenth of the busy figure, is now its
  own cause, `no cause aterm can name: unaccounted` (`cause id=unexplained
  part=unaccounted`), so the reply prints `cannot what=remedy` instead of `do class=none`
  and a bare `sys why` no longer answers calm beside it. The `who` rows and `more` now add
  up to the split on a busy Mac too, where hundreds of near-idle groups each rounded down
  had left them a few millicores short; an idle tab's role no longer flips to
  `unavailable(not_sampled)` on a millicore that was only rounding; and the Deck's cause
  reading costs less, since a group's signer is read again only after its lead runs a new
  program.

- **A Claude Code tab's footer shows its weekly budget, and says why when it cannot.** The
  footer reads the weekly figure that tab's own tap last wrote (`weekly 62% left`), beside the
  one Claude Code keeps from `/usage`; the newer wins. Whichever source read it, a figure 15 to
  60 minutes old shows its age (`weekly 62% left · 40m ago`) and an older one is not shown.
  With no figure the footer names the reason: `weekly ? · /usage` (the tap is off, this
  Claude Code has a home, login, option, `--settings` or statusLine the tap never rides on,
  or an `apiKeyHelper` or credential in its settings, or aterm does not restart this tab, as
  with its Autopilot off), `weekly ? · restart tab`
  (it was started without the tap, which a restart in place adds; the restart resumes the
  conversation with a note to carry on, which takes a turn), `weekly ? · no reply yet` or
  `weekly ? · no reply 1h`; the account menu says it in full, and a narrow pane keeps
  `weekly ?` beside the account. A Claude Code under a `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `HOME` of its
  own never shows the machine's own account's week. The account menu's rows show how old a
  figure is past fifteen minutes.

- **`sudo` install.sh refuses over another account's home however `HOME` spells it, and
  names more of what an earlier `sudo` install left root's.** 0.123.0 compared `HOME`
  with the account's home as text, and looked up one account by the name `ls` prints, so
  a root run over another account's home spelled `//Users//them`, `/users/them` or
  `/System/Volumes/Data/Users//them`, or over the home of a second account sharing that
  uid, ran as root there. It now refuses over any spelling of every home of that uid, as
  it does over the plain one. A CI container's `HOME`, outside every such home, still
  installs as root; there, as before, the store inside that `HOME` is skipped as a path
  its owner could replace, so point `ATERM_STORE_DIR` and `ATERM_BIN_DIR` at folders
  root owns (`/usr/local/lib/aterm/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`). The NOTE naming root's
  leftovers now also names each entry another uid owns inside aterm's own folders
  (atpkg's store and lock, the shell hooks, state and logs) and the man page (`aterm.1`,
  which is rewritten in place), not only the folders on the way to them, and its
  `sudo chown -R` quotes an account name with a space. On Linux it looks in aterm's data
  and state folders (`~/.local/share/aterm` and `~/.local/state/aterm`, or under
  `XDG_DATA_HOME` and `XDG_STATE_HOME`) instead of macOS's `Library` ones. A `HOME` you
  can write but do not own is no longer looked in.

- **System State holds still in a short window.** In 0.123.0 a short page's vault fields
  and buttons could still move when an offer's first click landed, a Check ran or a row
  was switched off, and a page shorter than 80×24 pushed them past its bottom edge. What a
  page shows, and where its fields and buttons sit, now follows its size alone. A page
  shorter still gives up its title, then its guidance's later lines, keeping the first,
  where an offer's warning and a result show: two rows of buttons stay whole from 216
  points tall, one row from 172. Apply keeps one face for the whole countdown, and where
  that face or the page has no room for the countdown, the guidance leads with it
  ("Applying in 30 s."). Every page keeps the narrow margin, so a window made taller no
  longer loses its banner, its restore hint or a checklist row. A setting's name is never
  cut short for its state, and a word or line too long for the page, such as a path in a
  result, wraps instead of being cut off.

## [0.123.0] - 2026-10-23

### Changed

- **The Linux installer no longer needs Python or OpenSSL once a release pins its
  verifier.** Each release built on the Linux workers now also publishes a small static
  verifier per architecture (`aterm-bootstrap-verify-<version>-linux-<arch>`), built from
  the same source as aterm. When install.sh pins one by its SHA-256, a Linux install
  downloads it and refuses it unless the digest matches. It then checks the release with
  it: the same signature chain, update floors, install-directory and executable checks as
  before, with the same messages. That leaves curl, and `sha256sum` or `shasum` to read
  the digest, as the installer's only requirements. Until a release pins the verifier,
  and on an architecture with no digest pinned, install.sh keeps its embedded verifier,
  which still needs Python 3.11+ and OpenSSL. The downloaded verifier is removed when the
  run ends, and `--dry-run` names the one a real install would fetch, with its size,
  without downloading it.

- **aterm run outside aterm.app no longer posts its notifications through
  terminal-notifier.** They go through macOS's own `osascript` (shown as Script Editor's)
  whether or not terminal-notifier is installed, and the Notify Me hover says so. Run from
  aterm.app they are aterm's own, as before.

- **aterm runs macOS's own `git`, `curl`, `open`, `osascript` and its other system tools
  by their fixed paths** (`/usr/bin/git`, `/usr/bin/curl`, …), never whichever copy comes
  first on your PATH, such as Homebrew's; `ssh` alone is still your PATH's. `git` is the
  Command Line Tools' (`aterm init --only base.clt` installs them).

### Fixed

- **`sudo` install.sh over a CI container's `HOME` installs as root again, and names
  what an earlier `sudo` install left root's.** 0.122.0 refused a root run over any
  `HOME` another uid owns, which stopped CI containers, whose `HOME` the host runner's
  uid owns. Now a root run refuses only over another account's own home or a folder in
  it; over a home whose owner is no account here, or one outside its owner's own home
  (a CI container's `HOME`, even when an account of the image shares that uid), it
  installs as root, as before 0.122.0. Folders an earlier install under `sudo` left
  root's, which no run as you can change, are named once at the start with the
  `sudo chown -R` that gives them back, and a skip into one points there instead of at
  `ATERM_BIN_DIR`; a folder you can write, one reached through a symlink, and any folder
  of a `HOME` that is not yours are never named.

## [0.122.0] - 2026-10-23

### Changed

- **`aterm machines`' starter baseline installs no Homebrew, Emacs or Caffeine.** A new
  controller's `baselines/default.toml` no longer installs Homebrew and its ten formulae
  or any app. A starter you never edited follows on its own, and one you edited keeps
  what you wrote. A `[homebrew]` table or an `[[app]]` row of your own still installs what
  it names. To keep a Mac awake or edit a file, use `aterm caffeine` and `aterm edit`.

- **Turning widgets off also clears Notification Center's widgets.** `[consumer] widgets =
  false` now also empties Notification Center's widget list. It does this only on a Mac
  where remote users have Full Disk Access, the baseline's `[person]` step; until then,
  that row says it waits for the grant. `widgets = true` leaves the list for you to fill.
  In `aterm init` and System State, the widgets setting is now three rows: desktop,
  Stage Manager and Notification Center. Each finishes on its own, so a slow Dock no
  longer fails Notification Center's row.

- **Settings that one app reads relaunch it once.** When several catalog or `[[defaults]]`
  rows change what one app reads, that app is relaunched once, after the last of them.
  Before, it was relaunched once per row. The run checks the rows only once the app is
  up again. `aterm doctor`'s Restore and rollback also wait for the relaunched app. If the
  app did not keep a restored setting, the row says so instead of "restored".

### Fixed

- **`sudo` install.sh over your own home installs as you.** macOS's `sudo` keeps your
  `$HOME`, so a root run made `~/.local`, the `aterm` link, the store and `aterm.toml`
  root's, which your own aterm could then not change, and lanes such as `--no-app` seeded
  the toolset as root. Now a root run over the home of the account that typed `sudo`,
  `--uninstall` included, runs the installer again as that account, over the same home,
  with the same arguments, `PATH` and the settings it reads (`ATERM_*`, `XDG_*`,
  `CARGO_HOME`, `RUSTUP_HOME`, and curl's proxy and CA variables), and says so. It
  installs nothing, and says what to run instead, when it is piped (`curl … | sudo sh`),
  over any other account's home, from a copy that account cannot read, or told to install
  into a folder that account cannot write. `sudo -H` still installs as root, over root's
  own home: the way to fill folders only root can write.

- **System State shows its checklist in a first window.** A window as short as aterm's
  default 80×24, at any width, left the checklist no room, so the setup offer counted
  down to Apply with none of its rows on screen. A page that short now keeps a narrow
  margin and drops the banner, then the restore hint (a narrow page also puts Check and
  Restore beside Apply and Cancel where all four labels fit), then the vault hint, until
  two rows and the scroll caption fit wherever the list is scrolled and whatever a result
  says; a larger window brings them back.

## [0.121.0] - 2026-10-23

### Changed

- **Working on aterm no longer needs node.** The wasm checks (`verify wasm-smoke`,
  `verify wasm-glue`), the `wasm` performance lane and the glue tests run in the
  chrome-headless-shell that `targo --unverified verify provision` pins, the browser
  engine the web terminal runs in, and `verify list` names it where it named node. `verify
  glue` writes only the ES module glue a page loads; `--flavor nodejs` is refused. The
  `wasm` lane's baselines were recorded again in that browser. Only publishing the site
  still runs node, for firebase-tools.

### Fixed

- **System State shows its checklist in a first window.** A window as short as aterm's
  default 80×24, at any width, left the checklist no room, so the setup offer counted
  down to Apply with none of its rows on screen. A page that short now keeps a narrow
  margin and drops the banner, then the restore hint (and, in a narrow page, the Check
  and Restore row), then the vault hint, until two rows and the scroll caption fit; a
  larger window brings them back.

## [0.120.0] - 2026-10-23

### Added

- **`aterm ctl @self sys why` says who is using the CPU or memory, and why.** `sys why
  cpu` and `sys why mem` ask about one; a bare `sys why` picks what stands out most, and
  on a calm Mac answers in two lines. The reply opens with one sentence, such as `global
  cpu: 3.3 of 18 cores busy, easing; mostly macOS services (2.17c); Spotlight, after
  start-up; this tab is not the cause`. The CPU reply then splits the busy cores into
  your tab, the rest of aterm, your other processes, system services and what is
  unaccounted; says whether your tab is the main cause, part of it, not the cause or
  uses none; lists the busiest groups of processes macOS keeps (an app with its
  helpers), other users' among them, by their lead's pid, executable name and who
  signed it; names the causes (Spotlight's work, a tab's work, aterm itself, an app
  running as you, or none aterm can name) with when each began and its evidence, and
  whether it came after start-up or a wake, under memory pressure or while throttled;
  and says what it cannot measure here. The memory reply ranks the groups by footprint
  and adds memory by kind. A caller without owner rights sees only the groups wholly
  inside its own tab, never aterm's, with the rest summed on `withheld`, and another
  tab's work reads as "another tab's work". A text reply keeps to 2 KB, moving its last
  rows into `more`, unless `top=` is given; `--json` (cut by `top=` alone), `fresh=` and
  `since=` work as on the other views. On Linux and Windows the split is by subtraction
  and no group rows print, and where memory pressure, swap or the thermal state cannot
  be read a bare `sys why` never answers calm. `aterm help sys` has a new WHY section.

### Changed

- **`aterm doctor`'s `instances:` row counts the other aterm programs.** It reads the
  kernel's process table instead of running `ps` twice, knows an aterm process by its
  executable, never by its name, and looks at nothing on disk. A window is told from a
  session as the front door routes it (a window opened by `aterm new-window`, or one
  Finder started with flags, is a window; a bare `aterm` typed on a terminal is not). An
  unreached instance's line shows its launch flags with control characters escaped, and
  no longer the session's command after `-e`. Besides the instances no control socket
  reaches, it counts the other aterm programs running as you (`aterm link broker`,
  `aterm ctl`, …), and names each one whose launcher exited and that launchd adopted,
  saying "from a build directory" or "running a deleted binary" where that holds; only an
  unreached instance makes the row a note. The arguments of a program macOS's program
  check holds are never read. `aterm ctl instances` tells a private instance launchd
  started from one launchd adopted after its launcher exited, and offers a `kill` only for
  the adopted one: where the lineage cannot be read (and on Linux) it keeps its words and
  offers none.

### Fixed

- **The needs pill's `+N` no longer opens Overview on the report you are already
  looking at.** When the front tab held only a worker's report and two or more other
  sessions needed you, `+N` could open Overview at that same front report every time
  instead of at another need. It now starts from the front tab and opens Overview at
  the need after it, skipping the session the pill already names; with only the pill's
  session and the front report waiting, it still opens Overview at the report.

- **Autopilot reads Claude Code 2.1.309's new rm warning as its rm circuit breaker.**
  Claude Code 2.1.309 can draw `Dangerous rm operation not ruled out — the shell may read
  this command differently than it was parsed` on a Bash permission box, even over a
  command with no `rm` in it, and Autopilot took it for an ordinary note. It now reads
  it, and any other `not ruled out — …` reason, as Claude Code's rm circuit breaker.
  Under `approve = "safe"` such a box that fits on the screen is never pressed for you:
  it waits for you, named as the breaker in Claude Code's own words. In a session with
  permissions bypassed, under `approve = "safe"` or `"all"`, such a box taller than the
  screen is now declined instead of waiting for you, and Claude is asked to split the
  command into shorter, plainer commands run one at a time, any removal among them on
  its own, with its paths written as absolute paths.

- **aterm sees Claude Code 2.1.309's disk-full notice on a failed command.** When a
  command fails on a full disk, Claude Code 2.1.309 prints `Disk full: …`, `Nearly out of
  inodes: …` or `Disk quota used up: …`, naming its temporary directory, on the row
  under the command's `Error: Exit code …` line. aterm knew neither those words nor that
  row, so it missed the notice. It now reads it there, and 2.1.308's `Command output was
  lost: …` there too, in any Claude Code session whose Autopilot is not Off. aterm's disk
  watch sees it within a minute and, on a volume already low on space, runs its cleanup
  then instead of at its next scheduled pass.

- **Setup signs out of Messages and FaceTime on macOS 27.** On macOS 27 the sign-out
  found none of the account controls in either app's Settings window, so the Messages
  and FaceTime rows of `aterm init` and System State failed with "… account Settings
  controls were unavailable; sign-out remains unverified" and the account stayed signed
  in. aterm now looks through every control in each window, matching it by its name or
  its accessibility description, and opens Settings by clicking the ⌘, item in the
  app's own menu, typing ⌘, only when that menu has none.

- **Settings keeps the control you are on, and the place you scrolled to, when the
  window or text size changes.** Resizing the window, changing the text size, or a
  status or the Reload warning bar coming or going no longer takes the control the
  keyboard is on out of view where the list has room for it: shown whole before, it
  stays whole, and shown in part, no less of it shows, even after a size in between
  showed less of it. In Settings ▸ Themes the Filter themes field, the Community
  disclosure, the Dark | Light choice and the Customize sheet's Done could end up past
  the list's top or bottom edge, most often after a taller window had held the filter
  or Done in place outside the list. Where you turned the wheel or swiped a trackpad,
  the list keeps that place through such changes and moves only as far as keeping the
  keyboard's control in view needs, so going back to the size or text size you
  scrolled at shows the screen you left, not a row further on, the list's top or its
  end (unless a size in between showed the keyboard's control whole, which then stays
  in view). Themes still opens on the theme in use and keeps its row in view through
  these changes until you click, press a key or scroll; where the row and the
  keyboard's control do not fit together, the control wins, and closing the Customize
  sheet with Done now shows Customize, where the keyboard goes back to, not the
  theme's row. Updates Settings gets on its own (the Messages list's update each
  minute, a refresh, a save finishing) no longer count as something you did, so they
  no longer make Themes let go of the theme in use or the list let go of your place.

- **A status in Settings leaves room for the control you are on in more places.** A
  status at the bottom of a Settings page (such as "Color theme set to Dracula")
  shortens, down to one line whose words scroll, where its full height would leave the
  list too little room for the control the keyboard is on. On the Themes list and the
  Customize sheet it left room for the control alone, not for what the list shows
  above it on the same screen, so at 2× text in a narrow window it could still push
  Done or the theme in use's row under the list's bottom edge; it now leaves room for
  the control where the list puts it. While Themes is still showing the theme in use,
  the bar now shortens for the keyboard's control too, not only for that row. And
  under the Reload warning the bar shortens as well, where it kept its full height and
  could leave Done or the Filter themes field on no screen of the list.

- **Two admins publishing to a secrets vault in a shared folder at once no longer lose a
  change.** For a vault kept at a path rather than served at a URL, a publish (`aterm
  secrets edit`, `set`, `approve`, `revoke` and the other admin commands) checked that
  its version was newer than the folder's and then wrote it, with nothing held in
