  drawn only where the harness would supervise the agent, as in a window with a socket, and the
  input box's rules carry no harness border at all without a socket.

- **Claude Code's permission mode is read under vim's INSERT mode.** With Claude Code's vim
  editor mode on (`editorMode: "vim"`), its mode row opens with `-- INSERT --` before the mode
  pill, and aterm read no mode there: the permission-mode light and the `YOLO on` label lost
  the pill. They now read the pill after it, as on any mode row. The composer rule's facts
  still type nothing into a vim composer.

- **The harness card's box no longer covers the launch card's last letters in a narrow pane.**
  Where Claude Code's launch card fills the pane to its last column (33 and 31 columns), the
  box's right side was drawn in that column, over the version's last digit and the model's
  `…`. The box now stays open at the pane's edge there; wider panes keep it closed.

- **The input box's rainbow border runs the whole rainbow.** The coloured top border of Claude
  Code's input box, under Cruise, stopped at green: it read only the first half of the rainbow's
  colours. It now spans the whole rainbow, red to violet, as the harness card's border does:
  from violet beside the agent's icon back to red at the harness switch, whose letters carry it
  on to violet again.

## [0.110.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- **One place for a tool's non-urgent reminders: `aterm ctl notice later`.** A tool that
  needs you, but not now (an account's security setup, a renewal due next month), files
  `notice later <key> [tag=<tag>] [url=<https-url>] <title> -- <reason> -- <step>[ --
  <detail>]` as one entry of the list under the menu-bar item and in Settings ▸ Messages,
  never a row over your tabs. One entry per key however many tabs or launches say it
  (`OK later=<id> how=<new|restated|duplicate|quiet>`); once you dismiss it, the same key
  stays quiet for a week, then four weeks, then three months, across restarts. With
  `url=`, a plain `https` page with no user or port, the entry's one button is **Open in
  browser** and its details name the page's host; pressing it files the entry.
  `notice done <key>` ends it, and at most four such entries are open at once, never
  displacing aterm's own. An older aterm answers `ERR usage: notice <post|…`.

- **System State setup tab.** Review Mac preferences, Spotlight, permissions,
  vault sync and GitHub setup in one checklist. Apply starts after 30 active
  seconds; interaction stops the timer and Cancel skips the offer. Rerun setup
  or restore backed-up preferences from the tab. Check follows the current
  checklist. Reviewed inputs stay available if Apply cannot start or another
  System State tab closes. Results and approval guidance stay visible above
  the checklist, and Cancel retries if its saved decision cannot be written.

- **File → Save for amacs documents.** Save writes the active edited file through
  the editor's existing conflict checks and file access. It is disabled when the
  file has no changes or the active tab is a terminal or another application.

- **Gemini CLI, agy and Muse Code workers.** `aterm ctl @self spawn agent=gemini -`,
  `agent=agy` and `agent=muse` start a worker on that agent, as `agent=claude` starts a
  Claude Code one: the task is its first prompt, given on its own command line from the
  task file and never typed (`gemini --prompt-interactive=…`, `agy --prompt-interactive=…`,
  `muse -- …`), and the agent stays interactive after it. `model=` becomes each one's
  `--model`. The worker runs the same program its starter runs when the starter is that
  agent (with agy's data folders and Muse Code's provider settings), and the window harness
  carries it under Autopilot Land like any worker: the folder its spawn named is trusted for
  that worker alone (agy's trust box answered there; Muse Code's `--trust-workspace` for that
  run when the shell starts there; Gemini CLI by a trusted-folders file of the worker's own
  that names that folder alone, never `--skip-trust`, and its own folder-trust dialog is
  never pressed, since its restart would send the task twice), its startup read by its own
  screen reader even after a seamless update, `await task` waking on its landing, and
  `aterm ctl @<sid> result` returning the words its screen showed where the harness asked it
  to land (its report), then those of that landing. agy's task file holds no blank line
  (the fact line goes on the line under the task), since agy draws a blank line in a
  message exactly as the gap under it and the rest would read as its reply.
  `agent=codex` is still not a worker.

### Removed

- **Named session identities.** The New Window/Tab With Identity and Show Identity
  commands, identity picker, `aterm ctl identities`, `spawn identity=` and
  `identity_themes` configuration are removed. Sessions use the usual agent
  configuration; saved identity labels are ignored. Existing running shells keep
  their environment. The former identity directories are neither migrated nor deleted.

### Changed

- **The Autopilot chip's title says what each mode does in plain words, why a landing holds and
  what a harness needs.** Point at the chip (or select it with ctrl+shift+tab) and, where the
  rule has room, Cruise reads `autopilot: cruise — keeps going for ever, finding more to do`,
  Land `autopilot: land — wrapping up: landing everything on the remote main branch, then
  stopping`, and a timed Cruise `… keeps going until then, finding more to do`; the record a
  change of mode leaves, the mode buttons and the Default autopilot note in Settings ▸ Harness
  use the same sentences, and so does `aterm help harness`. Under Land, once the harness has
  typed Land's instruction the title adds `· landing since 14:02`, and after a reply that did
  not land it says why instead: `autopilot: land — not landed yet: needs you: rotate the deploy
  key; 2 unpushed commits · landing since 14:02, 3 nudges`. Where a harness needs you, every
  chip it runs adds the need in the worker's own words after what the mode does: `· needs you:
  grant Screen Recording to aterm (+1 more); carrying on`, the worker's own ` · ` and ` — `
  written `, ` so a narrow rule still cuts the title in the right places. A screen reader hears
  the same as sentences in the chip's description (`Not landed yet. Needs you: rotate the deploy
  key. 2 unpushed commits. Landing since 14:02, 3 nudges.`); the chip's label stays `Autopilot:
  land.`. `aterm ctl chrome` prints that description on each `autopilot` line
  (`description="…"`, `description=-` where there is none). The chip at rest draws exactly the
  cells it drew before, and a need or a landing that moves while nobody points at the chip costs
  no frame.

- **Search commands are grouped under Edit → Find.** Find…, Find Next and Find
  Previous retain their shortcuts and command-palette access. The standard
  macOS AutoFill, Dictation and Emoji & Symbols entries remain available.
  The palette presents one Find command for the active tab, without duplicate
  editor or Settings search entries.

### Fixed

- **agy waiting at its prompt no longer wakes aterm every 2 seconds.** Antigravity CLI keeps
  its own log on its standard output and adds a line to it while it waits for you (every 5
  seconds when its telemetry cannot get through). aterm counted those lines as work, so it
  checked on agy every 2 seconds with no window showing. A program waiting for your keys at
  its prompt now costs no wake, whatever it writes off the screen.

- **A burning row's contrast halo keeps its top edge when only the row above repaints.** With
  the fire effect on, the dark ring drawn around each glyph a flame engulfs reaches a pixel or
  two above its cell. When aterm repainted just the row above (a cursor or glow changing
  there), the GPU skipped the ring's part inside that row for every glyph whose own ink stays
  in its cell, leaving those pixels unringed until the next full repaint: two pixel rows across
  the burning cells, in nine of the ten text sizes tested on Linux. The ring is now drawn there
  too, matching a full repaint pixel for pixel.

- **Cancelling search or Go to Line follows edits from another view.** If the
  same document changes elsewhere, the return position moves with those edits
  instead of jumping to an outdated byte offset.

- **Find Next and Find Previous follow the active editor.** In amacs, both
  directions use that view's query, including after accepting the search, and
  wrap through its matches. They no longer consult an earlier terminal search.
  Configured navigation shortcuts work in editor tabs too. The menu and command
  palette disable search actions when the active tab cannot use them.

- **Editing after a save clears the stale “Saved” footer.** The editor shows its
  current modified state while retaining errors and other command feedback.

- **Markdown page keys now match the Previous and Next buttons.** Page Up and
  Page Down use the reader's visible body size in Preview, Source and Split
  views, so the toolbar and outline no longer make the keys skip too far.

- **The fabric bridge keeps each message exactly once on a full or failing disk.** The bridge
  records what it sends and delivers in its state folder, and a write there can fail: the disk
  is full, or a flush returns an I/O error. Some of those failures broke what the fabric
  promises. A message the bridge had sent could be judged forged once its log had moved
  (`cap-compromised`, whose remedy is a new mint secret for the whole fabric); a message could
  reach its recipient twice after the broker lost it and moved on; and after a power cut, a
  recovery step the full disk stopped was never tried again in that boot, so the bridge would
  not attach until a reboot, and the session-log mirror stopped or counted fewer bytes than it
  had sent; quitting aterm then could leave the next start trusting a damaged file. The bridge
  now waits for the disk instead. A message whose record cannot be written is neither sent
  nor delivered until it can be. A recovery a full disk or an I/O error stopped is finished
  before the bridge attaches, and until then its link reads down for an error; each try
  moves a damaged file aside once, however many tries it takes. A recovery a damaged file
  stops, which no amount of waiting fixes, is reported and the bridge goes on as before: the
  session-log mirror stops, and its message names the file to repair. The mirror's floor and
  a pin naming which machine a session is on are written again when their flush failed,
  rather than trusted. The fabric simulation, whose state-folder disk now fails writes
  (`EIO`, `ENOSPC`, a flush that fails after its rename, a full disk), found each case.
  With these fixes, 4,000 seeds of its usual worlds, and 4,000 of each of the two harshest
  (the disk failing throughout, aterm quitting now and then), break none of its laws.

- **A session an earlier bridge left in the same boot no longer stays `live` on the bus.** When a
  session closed while the fabric bridge was down, or aterm went with the machine's power,
  its presence row kept saying `live`, and mail to it went nowhere. The bridge retired such a
  row only if it had written it itself or had seen its writer's last word on the bus; if that
  bridge stopped again within five minutes, no later bridge would touch the row, and only
  `aterm fabric doctor --retire-ghosts` cleared it. Each session's presence row now names the
  state folder and kernel boot whose bridge wrote it (`statedir=`, a hash of the boot, node,
  device and inode), and a later bridge of the same folder in that boot retires what an earlier one left, after the same five
  minutes with nothing hosting it. A copy of the folder has a name of its own, so a second
  aterm run from a copy never has its live sessions retired by this one's bridge. Nothing more
  is written to disk. Device and inode can repeat on a cloned machine, so missing or older
  boot identities grant no retirement by mark; unwitnessed older ghosts still need the doctor.
  Live node rows and wills also name the writer, so a copied bridge that takes the same
  current incarnation and then loses a publish collision cannot have its will mistaken
  for the surviving writer's death. Unmarked legacy rows require the doctor's retirement.

- **A seamless update no longer holds the fabric for about 160 ms of disk flushes.** Since
  0.109.0 the fabric bridge, as it stopped, wrote every file a power cut could tear to disk,
  one full flush after another, so that a later power cut could not damage them. On a
  seamless update that stop sat between the old bridge's last word and the new one's first:
  with eight sessions in use (sixteen such files) it took 38 full flushes, 149.7-153.8 ms, and
  the new bridge then wrote its start record to disk again, 8.4-9.4 ms more. A handoff is not
  the end of the bridge's run: the new bridge carries it on in the same boot. So the old
  bridge now flushes nothing, the new one writes nothing, and the files are written to disk
  when the run really ends. The price is the short gap between the old bridge's exit and the
  new one's start, or the rest of that boot if no new bridge starts (its `[fabric] command`
  removed, say): a power cut there now counts as an unclean stop, so the next start sets
  aside the files it tore and moves posts still in flight to the quarantine, where before it
  sent them. The run's real end, at a quit, no longer takes two full flushes a file either:
  each file is flushed where it is behind the disk's ordering barrier, and the stop ends with
  one full flush, so a power cut after it still finds every file whole and the next start
  still treats damage as a bug. For the same sixteen files the quit's stop went from 38 full
  flushes in 146.8-148.1 ms to 21 barriers and one full flush in 15.7-17.2 ms (a development
  build on an Apple SSD; the bridge logs each stop's count and time).

- **Torn fabric files leave the list once you empty their quarantine.** After a power cut the
  fabric bridge moves the files it found torn into a `quarantine` folder in its state folder,
  and aterm lists "Torn fabric files set aside" among the things to look at later. Nothing
  ended that line but a dismissal, and a dismissal also kept the next power cut's from being
  listed for a month. The bridge now tells aterm how many torn files the quarantine still
  holds when it starts, and again within about two seconds of that count changing while any
  are left (within five while the fabric cannot reach its bus). Once it holds none (you
  removed them, or the whole folder), the line ends, and a dismissal of it is forgotten, so a
  later power cut's is listed again. Its step now says to empty the folder, in the state
  folder `aterm fabric` shows, once you have looked through it. A bridge from an older aterm
  (the bridge is whatever `[fabric] command` names) says nothing of it: its line stays until
  dismissed, as before, and now says so.

## [0.109.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- **`aterm harness accounts stats` shows each window of the account, with its age.** Beside
  the plan and credits it now prints a `5h` and a `week` row (percent used and left, when
  the window resets and how long until then), a `Fable` row as last seen, a `≈$` row of
  list-price dollars, and a `used` row with the Claude Code sessions running on the home now
  and, for a renewable roster row, the login's state. Every figure says how old it is, where
  it came from (the usage tap, the `/usage` panel Claude Code caches, a wall, a warning) and
  which machine read it. A window whose reset has passed reads `window reset 18:05, no
  reading since`, never 0%. Every empty figure says why, for example `usage_tap off
  ([harness] usage_tap = true turns it on)`, `no /usage seen on this home`, or, for a login
  no row of the roster names (or under a roster that is refused), that the tap records no
  reading of it. The usage tap now keeps the vendor's tenth of a
  percent (42.5%) and the session's model, and `--json` (schema 1) carries `used_pct_x10`,
  `resets_at`, `state` (`current` or `void`), `as_of`, `source`, `by` and `missing.reason`
  for each window. `aterm harness accounts` shows the same figures through the same view,
  the `/usage` probe's figures among them, and its `--json` gains each account's `key` and
  `windows`. The dollars come from folding the home's transcripts in memory at each run;
  nothing writes the spend file yet. This machine and Claude Code only for now.

- **`aterm ctl sys`: what the machine, aterm and your tab use, for agents and scripts.**
  `aterm ctl @self sys` answers one sentence each for the machine, every aterm process
  and this tab (CPU in cores' worth, memory, swap and pressure, the GPU, free disk), each
  with its age; `sys cores`, `gpu`, `mem`, `disk`, `procs`, `global`, `aterm` and `tab`
  go deeper, `sys jobs` says which of this tab's commands (and an agent's own tool calls)
  are still making progress and which are stuck, waiting on whom, `--json` gives one object
  per reply, and `since=<cursor>` answers only what changed. No Deck has to be on screen: a request reads the machine when its reading is
  too old. `aterm ctl await sys quiet for=20s` (or `'cpu<30%'`, `mem=normal`, `'swap<1MB/s'`,
  `'tab<0.5c'`, `job=<id> done,stuck`, `jobs.stuck=0`, …) waits for a state instead of
  polling; a job that already exited still meets `done`, and one that cannot meet the wait
  answers `ERR gone job=<id>` at once. `sys disk` and `sys tab` size each folder your tab
  works in from the folder walker. An agent hears about its tab's jobs without asking: `status` says `job=` (the
  worst live job's verdict) and `job_quiet_ms=`, `brief` adds a `jobs …` line while one
  runs, and `subscribe … events` pushes `EVENT <n> job <verdict> job=<id> …` when a job
  turns stuck, done or quiet. Another process's arguments are
  never printed, and paths only for your own tab. On Linux and Windows `sys mem` adds the
  commit charge (enforced or advisory) and Linux's thermal throttling reads as an estimate.
  `aterm help sys` lists what this machine can and cannot measure, asked at that moment;
  the aterm primer and a new `system-state` skill for Claude Code teach it.

- **A warning for a folder with too many entries in it.** A folder holding 100,000 entries
  or more now raises a digest entry, because a program launched from it makes macOS read the
  whole folder (a build's `target/debug/deps` is the usual one, and then its entry says
  `targo clean` removes old build outputs); it clears once the folder is back under 75,000.
  aterm checks the build profiles of every checkout in your home folder for this every ten
  minutes, one entry count each, on a background thread at throttled disk priority. It never
  asks macOS for anything inside a privacy-protected place (Desktop, Documents, Downloads,
  Mail, Messages, Photos, other apps' containers, iCloud Drive, other users' homes,
  `~/Library` outside aterm's own folders), however the path is spelled or capitalised,
  never follows a link, and never touches a network, removable or auto-mounted volume, nor a
  folder reached through one.

- **Edit files natively with amacs.** When a program in an aterm tab asks for an editor
  (`git commit` with `core.editor=amacs`, or Claude Code's Ctrl-G with `EDITOR=amacs`),
  amacs opens the file in an aterm editor tab next to the tab that asked, and the program
  waits for you. A row across the top of that tab says who is waiting and how to answer.
  C-c C-c (or C-x #, or clicking "done") saves the file, closes the tab and tells the
  program you are done. C-c C-k (or clicking "abort") throws your changes away, closes the
  tab and tells the program the edit was abandoned, so `git commit` stops without
  committing. Abort never throws away changes you made outside the edit: if you had
  unsaved changes to the same file in another tab, that tab keeps them. Closing the tab
  any other way leaves the file as you last saved it, and the program carries on, as with
  emacsclient. If the program stops waiting (you pressed Ctrl-C in it), the row says so
  after five seconds and your typing stays. C-c C-c still saves, and abort refuses,
  because no program would hear it. `amacs --no-wait` opens the tab without making
  anything wait. `amacs notes.txt` for a file that does not exist yet opens an empty
  buffer, and your first save creates the file.

- **`aterm ctl person`, a development build's stand-in for the person at the window.** A
  debug build launched with `ATERM_DEBUG_PERSON_INVOKE=1` takes `person look <window>|off`
  (a look at a headless window: while it is the frontmost window, its front tab's end is seen
  by the same rule a real look follows, and nothing else counts the window as on screen) and
  `person menubar press <at>` (a click on the menu-bar row at the path `chrome`'s `statusmenu`
  lines now end with, `at=`), and its `status` says `end= end_seen= end_cheered=`, whether an
  end was looked at and whether its cheer is spent (a pet cheered it, or a seamless update
  carried it) kept apart. A release build prints none of this and refuses `person`.

- **Every need an agent names, whole.** When a supervised agent writes `NEEDS YOU:` lines,
  its harness now hands the window all of them, each whole up to 160 characters (in any
  script) rather than cut to the entry's 64, before the needs entry goes up, and the window
  keeps them beside the session for as long as that entry stands, including while a change to
  it is on its way, so the words it holds never show cut while the change lands. The window
  keeps them in memory only: after a seamless update, until the agent's next report, a tab
  shows its entry's own short form, as before. The menu bar's Needs you section now lists each
  further need on a row of its own, one level in under its tab's row and with no mark, and a
  click on any of them goes to that tab; hovering one names whose need it is (`Claude Code in
  proj-api needs this too`), which VoiceOver reads too. At most 2 such rows a tab and 8 in the
  menu; the rest are counted on the tab's last row as `(+N more)`. The tab's row, its
  Settings ▸ Harness state line and the banner (where you turned banners on) say the first
  need whole where there is room, and the tab's hover gives every need a `Needs you:` line of
  its own before `Claude Code carries on meanwhile`, refreshed as soon as the agent's needs
  move. `aterm ctl chrome` prints such a row with `indent=1`. A debug build's `aterm ctl
  status` says how many needs it reads, `needs_told=2` (`stale` where they were told for an
  entry that is not up, `-` for none); a release build prints none of it.

- **Claude Code's composer has an on button for the harness.** Wherever the harness is off
  for a session — its Autopilot off, Claude Code's own switch off, or the harness switched off
  in Settings — the top rule of the input box now reads `claude harness ○ off ▐ on ▌`, and one
  click on `on` turns the harness back on from whichever switch held it off (a switch in
  Settings is turned on in aterm.toml); nothing opens. With the harness on it reads `claude
  harness ● on` as before, and a click there still turns it off for the session. The `⊘ off`
  chip on the bottom rule now turns the harness on the same way instead of opening Settings, and
  a double click on the switch counts as one click. agy's and Muse Code's composers have the same
  switch. An aterm with no control socket runs no harness, so it draws no switch and no harness
  branding on these rules.

- **`aterm ctl chrome` reads each Autopilot chip as it was drawn.** For every pane the
  harness supervises, in every window, `chrome` prints an `autopilot` line naming the window:
  the chip's face now, its cells exactly as the last frame drew them and what a screen reader
  says of them, printed only for a pane that frame drew, so a tab behind, or a chip the link
  caption covers, says `drawn=- why=not-drawn` instead of an old face. Gemini CLI and
  codex-alab, which have no composer footer, say `why=no-footer`. A script or an agent can
  check what each chip shows without a screenshot; nothing on screen changes, and a frame does
  no more work for it.

- **Programs that report their state with OSC 7501 now appear in `aterm ctl log`**
  (`kind=program`, on the run in front), and `await log kind=program` and `subscribe … log`
  see each change, at most 64 per run. A program that changes state many times a second is
  recorded at its latest state (`coalesced=` says how many changes it stands for); its newest
  state is never lost. It is still a claim: nothing aterm decides reads it.

- **`aterm ctl status` says whether a codex-alab tab's own record of its turns reaches the
  session log.** `rollout=bound` means the turns, tools and tokens codex-alab writes reach
  `aterm ctl log` (`src=transcript`); otherwise it says why not, for example `unmeasured`
  for a codex-alab build aterm has not been checked against, or `stopped` once codex-alab is
  no longer in front and aterm has stopped reading its record. `rollout_asks=` counts how often
  aterm has read that record, so a script can wait until aterm has read it twice more and
  then read `log`, knowing nothing more from it is still on its way. codex-alab
  0.164.0-dev.12672 (the build with FOREVER CRUISE and FOREVER LAND) is now one of the checked
  builds.

- **A landing that has not landed says why.** Under Autopilot Land, once the harness has typed
  Land's instruction, a session's row in Settings ▸ Harness says why its work is not on the
  remote main yet, in the order you can act on it, then the pause it waits out: `not landed yet:
  needs you: rotate the deploy key; 2 unpushed commits; open work in its report: follow-up ·
  landing since 14:02 · 3 nudges · pausing until 14:40 (3 short turns in a row)`. The open work
  is named as the nudge names it in the agent's pane, never in quotation marks, since Land may
  name a kind of line (`unchecked box`, `a part`) the report never spells. Before its first
  reply is read it says `landing since 14:02`. The tab's hover says it without a clock (`driven
  by aterm (land: not landed yet, needs you; 2 unpushed commits; open work in its report:
  follow-up)`) and follows it as it moves; the Overview says it on a line of its own under the
  session's, so the session's own line keeps `typed by`, and a line too long for the Overview
  ends in `…`. In the menu bar a worker reads `● bench — landing 12m` once Land's instruction
  has been typed to it (`working` before), its tip what holds it, and its manager counts it
  `landing`. `aterm ctl status` prints `land_held=needs,repo,open land_nudges=3
  land_since=<unix s>` after `pause=`, each `-` outside a landing or where this aterm's harness
  holds no claim on the session. Gemini CLI, which has no chip, gets all of it. The chip itself
  is unchanged.

### Removed

- **`◐ ctx auto` is gone from the coding agents' composer rule.** Where aterm had not read how
  much context a Claude Code, agy or Muse Code session has left, the rule under the input box
  said `◐ ctx auto`, which told you nothing. It now shows no context fact without a reading:
  while Claude Code shows its own `84% until auto-compact` indicator the rule reads
  `◐ ctx 84% left`, also through a dialog or the `/` menu that hides the indicator for a while,
  and the fact goes when Claude Code's indicator goes, as after `/compact`. The ten or so cells
  the placeholder took go back to the bare rule and to the Autopilot chip's title while you
  point at it.

### Changed

- **A limit reset used inside a window no longer leaves the window shown as still used.**
  The usage tap kept a window's largest figure until its reset, so after a limit reset
  refilled it (the reset keeps the window's end) the old 100% stood until the week was
  over. When the same Claude Code session, served since, reads a figure lower by a whole
  point under the same reset, aterm now records the refill (a `reset` row in `aterm
  harness ledger accounts`) and no figure from before it counts again. Every session on
  the account sees the one refill, and it is recorded once. A limit reset aterm used itself
  (`[harness] limit_reset`) does the same for the window it claimed; a limit that reset on
  its own refills nothing.
  A reading's time is when its figure was served: the tap's re-reports every ten seconds
  keep the first report's time, so a figure from before a limit reset that aterm reads late
  is still cut by it. A reading under another account signed in to the home starts the
  figures again (an `epoch` row), and the figures, walls, warnings, credits word and reset
  offer recorded for the account before it are dropped. The figures start from the first
  reading served a minute after that one: a running Claude Code can still be served on the
  old login for about 30 seconds, and its figures would otherwise be kept as the new
  account's. Until then neither `aterm harness accounts stats` nor `aterm harness accounts`
  shows the old account's figures under the account the home now names: its windows read
  `no reading yet` (or `usage_tap off`), as for an account nothing was read of. The home's
  list-price dollars since another account was seen there (that change, or a cached
  `/usage` body naming another account) are marked `unattributed`, and no capacity or
  `left` is claimed from them until the window that saw it closes. Under a roster of several
  accounts, whose logins all share the default home's one profile, no reading is keyed by
  that profile, so one login's profile refresh no longer drops another account's figures,
  walls and warnings; the home's dollars are `unattributed` there, and no capacity is
  claimed while a Claude Code on the home runs on an API key, Bedrock or Vertex.
- **This machine's id in the accounts state is minted once and kept.** It lives in its own
  small file beside the state, written by the first change to the state or by `aterm harness
  accounts stats`, so every instance and every read names the same machine. Before, a
  machine with no saved state minted a new id at each read.
- **The fabric bridge no longer waits on the broker for its own bookkeeping.** The bridge
  that carries an aterm instance's sessions onto the fabric used to stop after each
  delivery until the broker had written down that the message was delivered, and to stop
  again for every publish's acknowledgement whenever it ran out of work, so a reply posted
  the moment a message arrived sat in the outbox meanwhile. It now sends that record and
  goes on, and reads an acknowledgement once it has arrived. It still waits for one where
  it must: before reading the outbox again while a post is in flight, before a sender's
  next post, and before judging a message on its own lane. With nothing else to do, it
  also waits for a post's acknowledgement, so on an idle bridge `post --wait` returns as
  soon as the broker has the post. Any other acknowledgement is read within 5 ms of the
  bridge going idle. If a failed disk write makes the broker refuse that delivery record,
  the bridge sends it once more instead of reconnecting. What is delivered, and exactly
  once, is unchanged. Measured on one Mac (docs/measured/fabric, 2026-10-21, dev build): in a
  request-and-reply exchange the bridge spent 4.6% of its time waiting on an ordered
  broker instead of 8.3-8.7%, and 26-27% instead of 52% on a strict one. The waiting
  that remains is for the posts' acknowledgements a sender needs. Over two runs each,
  burst throughput and a bridge restart could not be told from before. The round trip
  itself did not change in that set, because aterm now hands the bridge a session's
  events at most every 16 ms. And the bridge never lets more than 64 of its sessions'
  events in a row go ahead of mail waiting to be delivered, so a node with many busy
  sessions cannot hold a delivery back.

- **What an agent needs from you reads in its own words.** When a supervised agent writes a
  `NEEDS YOU:` line, the window now says that need without aterm's `claude needs you: … —
  carrying on` around it. The menu bar's Needs you row shows the need clipped to the room the
  tab's name leaves and always keeps its age (`· 3m`), which a long tab name used to push off;
  a fleet Mac's row reads the same way. The window's pill reads `needs you: <the need> (1 more
  need)` and the Overview's line `needs you: <the need> (+1 more)`, keeping the count of further
  needs, which a long need used to cut away. The tab's hover says `Needs you: <the need>`, then
  `Claude Code carries on meanwhile`. A banner, where you turned them on, carries the need
  without aterm's frame and says how many more stand. Settings ▸ Harness counts the sessions
  that need you on STATUS (`4 of 4 supervised · 2 need you`) and starts a session's state line
  with its need (`needs you: … (+1 more); carrying on`), following it while the page is open,
  and `aterm ctl status` adds `needs_n=`, how many needs stand. A long need in a script whose
  letters take three bytes each (Hindi, Thai, Bengali) is cut shorter, so the attention entry
  still ends with its count and `carrying on`; otherwise the entry, which scripts, the survey
  and the fleet read, is unchanged.

- **A landing says `landed` everywhere, seen or not.** In the menu bar a worker whose Autopilot
  landed its work reads `✓ lint — landed 4m`, its manager counts `2 landed`, and This Mac counts
  landed tabs apart from exited ones (`3 working · 1 landed · 1 exited`), a landed tab that is no
  worker included; a Done for you row stays `landed` after you look at it. Rows that share a name
  say where each one is (`✓ Claude Code in tab 2 — landed 1m`). A tab's hover and its Overview
  line say who drives in the Autopilot chip's own words — `driven by aterm (land, landed)`,
  `(land, quiet)`, `(cruise, lands at 18:00)` — and the hover follows the chip as soon as it
  changes, instead of when something else next redraws the tab. A task an older aterm finished
  by its retired rule, or one marked done by hand (`aterm ctl task mark done`), still reads
  `done`.

- **Settings ▸ Harness counts landings.** The Every session row tells sessions still landing from
  ones that landed and ones you took over (`4 sessions: 1 cruising, 1 landing, 1 landed, 1
  quiet`), and its Cruise button says the same of what it moves (`Cruise 3 sessions: 1 landing,
  1 landed, 1 quiet`) instead of calling them all `landing`. WHAT THE HARNESS DID gains a
  `Landed` row over `Land prompts` (`2 today · 9 in 7 days`: each landing counted once, however
  often its session restarted), and under `Kept going` an `of them` row says how many of those
  turns claimed to be done and were sent back to defend that and look further (`a done claim
  checked 4 today · 12 in 7 days`). STATUS's numbers for today and each session's day line
  start with the day's landings (`2 landed today · 31 approved · 4 kept going`). With the page
  open, a landing marks these counts `Newer` and reads them again a few seconds later, as an act
  of the harness does, so they never stay a landing behind.

### Fixed

- **Music effects' short status line is whole in a narrow Settings window.** Under Music
  effects on Home and Sound, the one-line reason the sounds are quiet was cut off in a
  narrow window with larger text: "Audio unavailable", which every Linux and Windows window
  shows (aterm plays its sounds on macOS only), needed 181 points of the 126 a phone-width
  window gives it at 2x text, and "Some sounds paused" was cut on a Mac too. The line now reads "No audio", "Volume 0",
  "Notes off" or "Some off", each whole at 1x, 1.5x and 2x text in that width; the full
  sentence is still what VoiceOver reads.

- **A message the bus lost no longer comes back out of order after a power cut.** When the
  bus log sits on another disk, it can lose a message that had already been delivered while
  the rest of the machine keeps running. If the same session's later messages then arrived
  and the whole machine lost power afterwards, the bridge could find its record of the lost
  message still waiting to be sent, because the power cut undid the step that had cleared
  it. It sent it again, and readers saw it after the messages that followed it. A message's
  sender and recipient both end with the reboot, so the first bridge after an unclean
  shutdown now moves every such waiting message, with its exact bytes, into the `quarantine`
  folder in its state folder (named `retired.inflight.<n>`) instead of sending it again.
  Nothing is deleted, nothing changes while the machine stays up, and no extra disk write is
  made per message. If the bridge cannot record the new boot in its state folder after such a
  shutdown (a full disk, say), it waits to connect until it can, so a later bridge in the same
  boot never takes a running session's waiting message for an old one. A state folder on a
  separate disk that loses power on its own while the machine stays up is not covered.

- **Fabric messages arrive in about a millisecond again, not on a 16 ms beat.** Since aterm
  began pacing what an event subscriber reads, so a flood of a program's output could not
  keep it busy, everything a session recorded waited up to 16 ms before a subscriber heard
  of it, the fabric bridge included. On the default ordered broker a post took about 18 ms
  to reach its recipient and a request and its reply about 35 ms; on a strict broker, which
  stores each message on disk before it answers, about 12 ms and 34 ms. aterm now reads a
  session's own records (fabric posts and deliveries, turns, status and other timeline
  rows) at once and keeps the pace for the program's output alone, so a flood is still
  read at most once every 16 ms, and the bridge answers the posts that queued while it was
  busy with one outbox drain. Measured at the median (dev build, six runs each,
  `docs/measured/fabric`): on the ordered broker a post reaches its recipient in 1.00 ms
  against 17.88 and a request and its reply take 1.76 ms against 35.61; on a strict broker
  4.35 and 16.92 ms against 12.42 and 33.94. Not everything got faster on the ordered
  broker on a busy machine, as those runs were. In them up to one request and
  reply in fifty took about 60 ms (the slowest 1% at 60.30 ms against 39.49): about every
  100 ms that broker has the disk write out all it holds, which then takes 30-60 ms, and a
  message in flight waits for it. In the same runs a burst of 500 posts arrived at 1233.9
  messages a second against 1260.2, each message 36.09 ms after it was posted against
  30.84, and a message was on disk 81.00 ms after it was posted against 71.70. On a quiet
  machine no request and reply took over 7 ms, a burst arrived at 1941-2007 messages a
  second, and a message was on disk after about 53 ms.

- **A power cut no longer stops the fabric bridge for good.** A power loss can leave a file
  the bridge had written but the disk had not yet stored empty or cut short. A few such
  files (a message in flight, a post's reserved number, a broadcast's refill floor) were
  refused as damaged at every start after the reboot — and a message in flight cut at the
  wrong byte could still read as a reply with no record of which log it belonged to, which
  was refused the same way — so the bridge never connected again until someone repaired its
  state folder by hand. Each of those files serves only sessions, which the reboot ended,
  so when the last bridge did not stop cleanly before a reboot, the first bridge after it
  now moves each such file that is not provably whole, with its exact bytes, into a
  `quarantine` folder inside the bridge's state folder and carries on. Nothing is deleted,
  and aterm lists it once among the things to look at later. Damage found within one boot,
  on any disk, or after the bridge stopped cleanly (a clean stop now writes those files to
  disk first) is still refused, because then it is a bug and not a power cut. The
  session-log mirror's own file follows its own rule (the next entry).

- **A power cut no longer stops the session-log mirror for good.** With `[fabric] log =
  "turns"`, the bridge keeps the batch it is publishing, the node's alias key and its running
  count of mirrored bytes in one file in its state folder, `logpin`, which is not written to
  disk at once. A power cut could leave that file cut short, and the mirror then stopped at
  every start until someone repaired the folder, because the key and the count were kept
  nowhere else. The key now has a file of its own, `logkey`, written to disk before the first
  message that uses it, and the count has a floor, `logfloor`, written to disk ahead of what
  is sent (once per MiB of messages). After a reboot that followed an unclean stop, a
  cut-short `logpin` is moved into the `quarantine` folder with its exact bytes, a whole one is
  written from the two copies in its place, and the mirror carries on under the same key,
  counting from the floor: each edge keeps its one alias on the bus, and the count is never
  lower than what was sent. A power cut that brought back an older `logpin` no longer lowers
  the count either, and a clean stop now writes `logpin` to disk. The price is paid at every
  reboot after an unclean stop, which cannot tell the newest `logpin` from an older one: the
  count is raised to the floor, up to 1 MiB (and one batch) more than was sent, so each such
  reboot brings the node's 256 MiB cap up to 1 MiB nearer. The new `logpin` is of a version
  an older aterm refuses: an older aterm's bridge running on the same folder afterwards (the
  bridge is whatever `[fabric] command` names) stops its mirror and keeps the file rather
  than mirror past a floor it does not keep or under a key it minted itself. Where the
  copies cannot cover the damage (within one boot, after a clean stop, in a folder only an
  older aterm mirrored in, with `logkey` missing, or a cut-short older aterm's `logpin`), the
  mirror still stops and keeps the file, and the bridge's log now says which file to move
  aside and what resuming then costs.

- **The fabric's mint secret is checked and read as one file.** `aterm fabric on`,
  `aterm fabric mint-for`, `aterm link mint` and `aterm link broker --secret-file` checked
  that the secret file was readable by you alone and then opened it again to read it, so
  a file swapped in between could be read without the check. They now check the open
  file and read its bytes through the same open, by the rule astream's own broker uses,
  and a refusal says `<path> is mode 0644: a secret file must be readable by its owner
  alone (0600 or tighter); run chmod 600 <path> …` (or that it holds fewer than 32
  bytes). What is accepted is unchanged: an owner-only file of at least 32 bytes, used
  byte for byte.

- **The context reading works on Claude Code 2.1.305.** That version draws its `N% until
  auto-compact` indicator at the right end of the row under its input box, where aterm did not
  look, so the rule above it said `◐ ctx auto` beside Claude Code's own `0% until auto-compact`,
  and the tab's hover and `aterm ctl survey` (`ctx_left_pct=`) gave no figure. aterm now reads
  it there too: the rule says `◐ ctx 0% left`, and the hover and the survey give the same
  figure.

- **The cursor kitty no longer flashes its standing pose between two runs.** When it all but
  stopped between two late keys and set off again, it stood for a frame or a few, a blink
  several times a minute; a walk could stand for a single frame. A stop now lasts at least
  one stride before the kitty runs on.

- **amacs in a terminal says why a save failed in plain words.** A refused save read the
  system's account of it ("Could not save notes.md: could not open save lock …: Permission
  denied (os error 13)"); it now says what is wrong and what to do ("~/notes isn't writable ·
  check its permissions", "another program is saving notes.md · try again in a moment"), the
  same words aterm's own saves of aterm.toml and Manual's documents give. Opening a link to a
  file that is gone says so, rather than asking you to try again.

- **After a Themes Revert, the status says it reverted.** Once a Revert of a kept theme saved,
  the status read "Color theme set to Dracula" or "Changed 3 settings"; it now reads "Reverted to
  Dracula", and a Revert that could not be saved says "Couldn't revert to Dracula". Keep colors
  only likewise says "Kept Studio's colors and your type settings", not "Changed 3 settings".

- **Text without spaces wraps at a narrow window.** A Chinese, Japanese or Korean title on the
  message band was left out of its row at a narrow window, Settings and Messages broke such text
  with hyphens ("設定ファイ-"), and a line could start with "。". Manual's Markdown reader drew such
  a paragraph past the edge of its column. Such text now breaks between its characters, keeping
  closing punctuation and small kana with the character before them and opening punctuation with
  the one after, everywhere aterm wraps text. On macOS, Settings and Manual also drew such text as
  blank space; they now draw it.

- **The flying kitty shows in a split pane under a program that hides its cursor, and
  `aterm ctl image` draws it where the window does.** In a split pane, under Claude Code or any
  program that hides the cursor and draws its own, the flying kitty never appeared, because only
  a painted cursor counted there. An image capture had the same rule, so a capture showed no
  flying kitty (and could fade the pet) where the window showed one. Both now follow the caret
  the window's single pane follows.

- **The cursor kitty keeps up with your typing in Claude Code, with aterm's footer chips on
  or off.** With the chips on the composer's lower rule, the kitty dropped off the line as your
  typing reached the chips and waited there, up to fifty columns behind, then leapt; at a wrap it
  took two bounds, or glided across the window with no rise. In a window, where Claude Code
  finishes each frame before showing it, the kitty saw the caret two frames late, and at a wrap
  it hopped to the wrong end of the new line first. It now walks the composer's line beside the
  caret over the chips and makes one bound at each wrap. Where aterm's harness switch sits at the
  end of the composer's top line, the kitty waits on the line short of it instead of hopping off
  the line and back, and at the right edge it no longer lands on the harness's line and vanishes
  until the wrap. It no longer gallops in slow motion as
  it slows into a stop or sets out from one, or stands still in a running pose at the end of a
  line. When the window is resized while you type, the kitty moves with your line instead of
  dropping below it and hopping back, and keeps its place beside the caret.

- **With the harness on, the cursor kitty walks the first line of Claude Code's composer.** The
  harness repaints the line over the composer in its colours, and the kitty treated the whole
  line as off limits: it waited off the composer, up to fifty columns behind your typing, and
  bounded back at every line. Only the harness's name and its switch on that line keep the kitty
  off now, so it walks beside your typing and makes one bound at each wrap. While it walks under
  a line of text it no longer fades to a faint outline and back at every stop, it no longer
  jumps sideways as it gathers for a bound beside the switch, its hop over the caret at the right
  edge lands behind the caret instead of where it started, and a resize while it waits off your
  line carries it with the text instead of leaving it rows above.

- **The editor keeps a file's Windows line ends and byte order mark straight.** Text with
  Windows line ends, pasted or typed into a file that uses them, no longer saves with doubled
  carriage returns. Undoing back to the saved text of such a file, or of one that starts with
  a byte order mark, shows the file as unchanged again. An unsaved draft of such a file now
  rides an aterm update like any other, and discarding changes to it keeps its line ends.

- **The harness reads a usage limit's edges on short panes and under its dialog.** A model
  bucket's notice scrolled off a short pane leaves Claude Code's generic countdown row,
  which no longer ends the bucket's wait as a usage window's continuation. A bucket's
  cancel drawn under the `/rate-limit-options` dialog is read as that bucket. A `/model`
  chosen after the notice left the screen, read from the session's transcript, moves the
  session off the bucket at once. At a limit's reset, a conversation `/resume`d in its place
  that draws no limit notice gets the continue policy's act, not the limit's own resume.

- **The cursor pet brakes to a stop instead of stopping dead.** When you stopped typing, and when
  it reached the right edge of the window, the pet ran on at your typing's pace to where it would
  stand and stopped there in a single frame (from 15 cells a second to none when typing fast into
  the edge), then crept the last fraction of a cell in its standing pose. It now slows down over the
  last stretch at any typing speed and stands where it stops. At the right edge it no longer
  stops dead and hops back over the cursor several columns before the cursor gets there: it waits
  at the edge and hops over the cursor when the cursor reaches it. Walking in to hide behind a word,
  it slows into its crouch; coming out it walks home instead of lurching a step sideways first; a
  walking pet no longer slides along in its braced pose when your typing runs into it; a pet in
  the air no longer turns round mid-leap when the cursor jumps back behind it; a pet that lands
  short and scrambles for footing no longer freezes in its running pose; and a pet hiding behind a
  word no longer redraws the window every frame while it waits.

## [0.108.0] - 2026-10-20

### Added

- **`aterm pkg doctor --json` prints its checks as rows a script can read.** Each check is
  one row of the report `aterm init --json` prints: its id, what it found and what it
  wants, its fix, and whether it decides the exit. `complete` is the exit status, so a
  script reads why doctor exited 1 without parsing its text. `aterm machines` now reads
  a user's toolset this way: a broken shim is reported as that row's change rather than
  as no answer, a toolset removed on that Mac is reinstalled as the baseline says rather
  than counted done, and a Mac whose aterm predates `--json` says so. Each row's `class`
  says what would fix it: `relay` only for what `aterm pkg repair` lays again, `person`
  for what is yours (a file where a stub goes, PATH, an exported variable). The text
  report is drawn from the same rows: an index no host has answered for days is now a
  note (one refused stays a warning), the few lines that said no ok, note or warn now say
  one, a toolset missing programs nothing recorded a reason for names `aterm pkg install
  --default-set`, and a long row keeps the command that fixes it.

- **On Windows, aterm frees build space it can prove nobody uses, as it does on macOS and Linux.**
  `aterm ctl @self status` now says `disk=` and `disk_free_mb=` for the drive a tab works on
  (Windows used to answer `free=unknown`), `aterm ctl @self await sys free>=room` waits while the
  disk watch frees room there, and `aterm harness disk` reports and frees what it found. It finds
  Rust build folders (`target` and other `CACHEDIR.TAG` trees in your checkouts and under your
  home) and Claude Code versions no running Claude Code uses. Before anything goes, the Windows
  proofs hold: no process works in it, runs a program or loads a module from it, or has a file
  open in it, whether its path is spelled long or with 8.3 short names (`LONGFO~1`); no cargo
  build holds its locks; and no tab works there, with the tabs read again at the moment of the
  removal and a tab busy at that moment counted as unknown. A PowerShell tab is placed by the
  folder it reports to aterm, because `Set-Location` does not move the process's own working
  directory. It works on fixed local drives only, each fenced by its volume GUID and serial, so
  a drive letter that moves never points it at another disk. A junction is removed as the link,
  never what it points to. Nothing in OneDrive or another cloud sync folder is searched,
  downloaded or removed: a search notes each sync folder it passes over, and a build folder you
  name inside one is refused with that reason. No look raises Windows' "There is no disk in the
  drive" box. The limits: a PowerShell window outside aterm does not say where it works, so it
  does not keep a checkout's build folder; a build folder outside every checkout that nothing
  owns (a standalone `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`) is never removed whole, on any OS; a `rustc` bootstrap
  tree (`x.py`'s `build/`) only gets a note; and with no `~/.claude/sessions` folder to read,
  no Claude Code session is taken as ended, so its scratch builds stay. A report over a whole
  home takes about half a minute when its folders are cached and a minute or more when they are
  not or the machine is busy building.

- **`aterm ctl pointer wheel` turns the mouse wheel for a script.** `pointer wheel dy=3`
  scrolls three lines down where the pointer is, `dx=` sideways, `unit=pt` a trackpad's
  points instead of a wheel's lines, and `key=<control>` or `xy=<x>,<y>` aims at a Settings
  control or point first. It takes the same path a real wheel does, so over Settings an open
  picker scrolls, a list moves one row a line, and the sidebar scrolls only under the pointer.

- **The stats bars can live in the window's bottom margin, and open into a close-up.** View ▸
  Stats Bars now offers Deck (the band under the titlebar, still the default), Sill and Off, and
  saves your choice. Sill draws the same picture in the padding under the last terminal row, so
  it takes no row from your terminal: one small square per core, three thin lanes for Global,
  aterm and the current tab (the tab lane lights once a window has two tabs), the GPU, memory
  and the disk; as the window narrows the disk folds to a mark that shows only when it is nearly
  full, memory to its pressure, then the cores to one square per cluster. On a translucent or
  wallpapered window each instrument sits on a small plate of the terminal's background, so it
  stays readable while the rest of the margin stays clear. Both forms now carry the stuck-job
  marks: ⊘ for a stuck job, ☠ for unreaped children a tab's process holds, ◔ for a job gone
  quiet (its arc fills as it nears stuck), ◇ for a job waiting for you and a pause for a parked
  one; a calm machine shows none. Rest the pointer on either form for a quarter of a second,
  click it, or press ⌘I (View ▸ Stats Lens), and a lens opens over the terminal: the last minute
  of every core as a heat strip, the busiest processes and whose they are (aterm's, a tab's or
  another app's), the GPU, a gibibyte-per-square picture of memory and swap, the disk, and the
  jobs that are stuck, quiet, waiting or parked, each with its tab, its program and why. With ⌘I
  the arrow keys move between instruments and bars, Return keeps it open, ⌘C copies the selected
  bar's sentence and Esc closes it; any other key closes it and types as usual. A click outside
  it or leaving the window closes it too, and in a window too small to hold it, it does not
  open. The lens is yours: `aterm ctl invoke ToggleStatsLens` is refused, so an agent cannot put
  it over your terminal. The band's words now meet WCAG AA contrast on light themes too, a share
  always says what it is a share of ("39% of busy"), and labels and figures no longer collide
  or get cut mid-word in narrow windows. VoiceOver reads each bar as a group of level indicators
  with the value, its direction and its scope, the cores as a grid, and the open lens as a group
  you can move into; with Differentiate Without Color on, a falling load also gets a shape, not
  only a colour. In a window with two or more tabs, each tab's chip now carries a thin line
  along its foot once the tab uses a tenth of a core, its length that tab's share of all cores,
  so a busy background tab shows without switching to it; it goes away when the stats bars are
  off.

- **`aterm ctl metrics percentiles` reports the GPU's own time per frame.** Until now
  every frame figure was CPU time. `gpu_time_p50/p95/p99_ms` (with `n_gpu_time` and
  `gpu_time_source`) is how long the device itself worked on each present: on macOS from
  Metal's command-buffer clocks, read after the frame without waiting on it; on Windows
  and BSD from timestamp queries where the graphics adapter grants them; never on the GL
  fallback, which says so rather than reporting zero. Beside it, `gpu_encode_p50/p95/p99_ms`
  is the CPU's half of the present, and `passes_last`, `instances_by_stream`,
  `instance_bytes_last`, `gpu_build_last_ms` and `gpu_stage_last_ms` describe the last
  frame's shape. The summary's `fx_streams_last=` counts every effect stream in the frame
  (cursor glow, card light, rain, sprites, recoloured glyphs, fx layers). The development
  harness records the GPU clock's CPU cost separately, on Metal and through the same wgpu
  code on a Mac.

- **The fabric's broker can ack once a post is in order on the disk, and keeps what a person
  would miss.** `aterm fabric on --durability ordered` (or `aterm link broker --durability
  ordered`) now serves the ordered tier instead of serving it strict: the broker
  acknowledges a post once the disk has been told to keep it in order behind everything
  before it (on macOS `F_BARRIERFSYNC`, a fraction of a full flush's cost) and flushes it in
  full a tenth of a second after the first post no full flush covers, once the batch in
  hand is written. A halt (on and off), a person's own posts, mail onto a person's lane and
  a person's inbox read mark are flushed in full before anyone sees them or is told they
  were sent, whichever aterm build wrote them; a relaxed broker now keeps them the same way.
  A kernel panic or forced power-off can lose the rest (agent posts, presence, receipts)
  acked in the last tenth of a second, plus a batch and a full flush: up to 145 ms of them
  in the measurements below, on a loaded Mac. The log keeps a prefix of whole batches; its
  next open moves the log's generation and every bridge and notifier resumes where it
  continues. A kill -9 or a clean stop costs nothing. `aterm link notify` pages an ordered
  broker's record only once the broker says it is on the disk (a halt or an ask to a person
  at once, an attention row once the next full flush covers it), so nobody is woken for a
  record a power loss could take; if its bounded holding buffer fills, it warns and pages
  what it holds before the broker says so, and those records can still be lost in a power
  loss. Off macOS, and on a Mac for a log off the boot volume, the broker serves ordered as
  strict, and `aterm fabric` says so and why. `aterm fabric`, doctor and the broker's own
  start line print each tier's promise as the broker reports it, horizon and the count of
  rules it flushes in full included, and say when a broker checks no capabilities, so that
  rules naming a person by principal match nobody. `verify perf fabric --durability strict,ordered,relaxed
  --horizon-ms 1000,100 --passes 2` measures the tiers side by side, each with the
  ping-pong arm. 0.106.0 and 0.107.0 take `--durability ordered` and serve it strict; a
  build older than 0.106.0 refuses it, so run `aterm fabric off` before going back to one
  of those.

- **Typing prediction now shows ←, → and Backspace too.** With `predictive_echo` on, over a
  slow link (ssh) a bare ← or → (the keypad's too) moves the cursor at once, and a Backspace at
  the end of the line takes the last character at once, on a line that has shown it echoes what
  you type. In `adaptive`, the default, an arrow shows only after the shell has echoed an arrow
  on that line exactly, so a program that echoes `^[[D` instead (`cat`, a cooked prompt) never
  shows one; `always` shows arrows at once, unproven, as it shows typing. A frame shows a whole
  edit or none of it. Typing that was already showing stays on screen when you press an arrow,
  where it used to vanish until the echo. `predictive_echo_editing = false` (Settings › Keyboard
  & Input › Predictive editing) turns it off.

- **Typing prediction learns Home, End, Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E and Delete.** In a shell aterm started
  with its shell integration, on a line where prediction is showing (a slow shell, or
  `predictive_echo = always`), Home and Ctrl-A move the cursor to the start of what you typed, End
  and Ctrl-E to its end, and Delete takes the character under the cursor, at once. Nothing is
  assumed about what your shell binds them to: each key shows only after the shell has echoed its
  usual effect twice, so `zsh -f` (Home unbound, a `~` typed for Delete) or vi insert mode (Ctrl-A
  typed as a character) never shows a wrong move, and a key the shell answers otherwise is
  forgotten. They need the prompt's signed start-of-input mark, which only aterm's own
  integration sends, so over ssh they work as before. They apply to a line whose first key is the
  first one typed at a fresh prompt; a line pulled back from zsh's buffer stack (push-line,
  `print -z`), or one started after another key at the same prompt, is left to the shell. End at
  the end of the line is left to the shell (an autosuggestion is accepted there), and so are
  Ctrl-A and Ctrl-E while a program uses the Kitty keyboard protocol or xterm's modifyOtherKeys.

- **`aterm init` sets the preferred scrolling direction and recovers interrupted setup.**
  Natural scrolling is turned off using macOS's own setter and saved across logins.
  Desktop changes remain pending until their consumers have stopped, so a failed
  relaunch cannot be hidden by already-written preferences. Dock checks also verify
  the real application paths, and empty widget lists clear leftover placements.

- **`aterm init` configures this Mac's login.** Caps Lock acts as Control now and
  across logins; widgets are removed, and the Dock pins aterm, System Settings and
  Safari. Messages and FaceTime are signed out, with durable account state checked.
  `--plan` previews changes, `--check` verifies without writing, and `--json` reports
  each setting. Missing permissions and unreadable settings are reported explicitly.

- **Managed agents run yolo by default, and `--yolo` spells it on every name.** A managed
  `claude`, `codex`, `agy` or `muse` launch now runs with every approval and sandbox off —
  AIs here have full access to do the work — each in its vendor's own spelling:
  `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for claude and agy (both refuse the literal `--yolo`),
  `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` for codex, and muse's four switches
  (`--disable-approval --disable-sandbox --trust-workspace --disable-request-user-input`).
  Typing `--yolo` (or `aterm claude --yolo`) asks
  for the same and always works. The exact command as run is printed once on stderr
  (`aterm: yolo (default): running 'claude' '--dangerously-skip-permissions' …`). A launch
  that types its own posture (`--permission-mode plan`, `-sread-only`, a posture-carrying
  `-c` override, …) runs exactly as typed, so a resumed session keeps its mode. Only the
  managed copies are rewritten; your own copy on PATH never is (`aterm help pkg`).
- **`brief` notes the task mail a turn probably answered.** When a turn that named no
  cause starts within a minute of exactly one delivered `kind=task` mail, its line in
  `brief`, `brief all` and `survey --brief` ends its fields with `mail=@<offset>~`, while
  it is an open turn or the newest closed one. The `~` says it is a guess, and it is never
  printed without it. A turn you started yourself never gets one, and a turn that named its
  cause still says `cause=@<offset>` instead. `log`, the fabric's log mirror and `aterm
  fabric brief` never print the guess.

- **A tab whose agent landed while you were away wears a mark.** When a Claude Code session
  under Land lands — all of its work on the remote main branch (`landed`), after at least 30
  seconds of the agent's own work since the task began — in a tab nobody is looking at, that tab
  wears the dot a finished worker already wears (`Finished; not yet looked at`), under every
  mark that needs you; `aterm ctl chrome` lists `"done"` in its states (a headless instance,
  which has no toolbar, now prints the `toolbar-tabs` line its strip would show). Cruise never
  ends, so it never marks a tab. The mark goes when you look — the front tab of the front window
  while it is on screen, or Go from the menu bar — and a landing in the tab you are looking at is
  seen as it lands. A new landing marks again, and someone else's turn takes the mark down. A
  restart that says the landing again marks nothing, and nor does work no loop watched (the
  session set Off, worked, then Land again): work done while the session is Off is yours, and
  never counts toward the 30 seconds. After aterm itself restarts, a reply of 30 seconds or more
  can mark a tab whose work had landed before. In Settings ▸ Harness's Ends row a second landing
  in one Land stretch is timed from its own task's start.

- **See who set a session's Autopilot.** Seeing `○ off` on a tab, you can now read whose hand
  it was. Every change of a session's Autopilot leaves its record in the message log
  (`messages tag=harness`), a change made over `aterm ctl` too, which used to leave none, and
  the record's last line names the hand: `set from the chip`, `set from the composer border`,
  `set from the Autopilot menu`, `set from Settings ▸ Harness`, `set from Settings ▸ Harness,
  every session`, `set over aterm ctl` (your shell, a script or an agent: aterm cannot tell
  them apart, so it names no tab), `set over the fabric`, or `set at the 18:00 timer`. The
  Autopilot menu says it under its name, at its clock time (`set 14:05 over aterm ctl`),
  where the session runs under its own word; in a pane too short for the whole menu, that
  note is the first row to go. Each row of Settings ▸ Harness ▸ SESSIONS says on a line
  under it whose word it runs under, `its own setting, set 14:05 over aterm ctl` or
  `follows the default`, so a press changes that line's words and moves no row. `meta` prints
  `autopilot_by=` (`human:chip`, `ctl`, `aterm`, … `restored` for a word carried from an
  older layout) and `autopilot_since=<unix s>` after `land_at=`, and who set it survives a
  restore and an update with the word.

- **The menu bar lists the agent work that landed while you were away.** On macOS, a Claude
  Code session under Land whose task landed in a tab you were not looking at — the same
  landing that puts the mark on its tab — is a row under ❯ ▸ Done for you
  (`✓ proj-api refactor — landed 3m`), newest first, and `❯•` shows while nothing needs you.
  Cruise never ends, so it adds no row. The row names the tab, says how long ago as the menu
  opens, and a click goes to that tab, which counts as looking: the row and the tab's mark go
  together, as they do when you look at the tab yourself, and both go when a new turn opens the
  task in that tab. The row carries no live words, so it never shows a stale state. A worker
  already listed there for its finished task keeps that one row, worded `landed` while its
  landing stands unseen, and reading its result counts as looking; a worker its manager here
  waits on is listed under its manager, as before. `aterm ctl chrome`'s `statusitem` line now
  counts the Done for you rows (`done=1`).

- **The kitty cheers when an agent's work lands, the first time you see it.** The landing that
  wears the tab's mark (a Claude Code session under Land reaching `✓ landed` after 30 seconds
  or more of its agent's work) is now cheered once by the pet in that pane, as a long green
  build is: on open ground beside the agent's last words, where its notes can be read, the cat
  stretches awake if it dozed, perks, frolics and throws three ♪/♥. A cat on screen hops there;
  one hidden at its home under the agent's input box, as it is when you switch to the tab or
  come back to the window, appears there. Then it goes home, or, where that home is under the
  input box, fades away, so nothing keeps moving once the cheer is over. While you are away (the
  window unfocused, another tab in front) it waits, and plays on the first look; switching to
  the tab is the look, and with two windows the first to show the pane takes it. A key typed
  before it plays spends it; it never plays later. A person's own exchange (`⤓ quiet`) cheers
  nothing, nor does Cruise, which never ends, nor a pane without the pet (another trail style,
  serious mode); under reduced motion the pet's contentment moves and nothing plays. On a light
  theme the pet's ♪/♥ take the ink the paper marks use, so they stay legible on white and cream.

- **With the PTY keeper on, a crash keeps each tab's turn history.** The turns an agent or a
  script drove into a tab (`aterm ctl … turn`, the window harness's own) now survive a crash,
  a Force Quit or the system ending aterm, as they survive an update: after the next launch
  restores the tab, `aterm ctl history` still lists them, marked `carried=1`. Each tab's
  record of them is kept beside its screen in the shared memory the keeper holds (never on
  disk): its newest turns that fit 64 KiB, a few hundred long prompts, rewritten at most
  every two seconds while turns land. So a turn that finished in the last two seconds before
  the crash can be missing, and so can a tab's whole history if the crash lands in the
  moment its record is being rewritten. `history` says so with `unheld_below=`, and a
  resumed `subscribe … since-turn=` is told it may have missed turns, never left to think
  none landed. New turns continue with ids above every id the crashed aterm used (the
  shared memory also keeps the id count, as each id is handed out); only a crash that leaves
  no tab with a crash journal (`status journal=off`) starts them over. `aterm ctl status`
  says `journal_ledger_lag=`: the tab's turns its crash record does not hold, not written
  yet or too old to fit (0 once it holds them all).

- **`aterm fabric`, `aterm fabric doctor` and `aterm doctor` say what the broker says of its
  log.** A broker whose log is poisoned still answers every read, so the report's own probe
  succeeded over it, and the report showed the poison only once a bridge's write had been
  refused (`fabric=stalled reason=poisoned`), and not while no bridge had written. Now the
  BROKER section has a `health` row, the broker's own word in its answer to every
  connection: whether its log is POISONED (refusing every write until it is reopened) and
  why, and how many flushes it has made since it opened, failed ones included. A poisoned
  log is a WARNING with its fix, and so is a failed flush, which says only that the disk
  failed one: astream counts a failure before it publishes the poison that may follow. A
  `holds` row reads the snapshot the broker now keeps beside its log, `<log>.health` (0600,
  rewritten every 30 seconds, at once on a poison, and once more when the broker stops
  cleanly, which a strict broker stopped by a signal does not): records and their bytes,
  subjects, pending wills, group commits, connections and parked tails. It is called
  current only while the broker that wrote it still serves the socket; otherwise the row
  says whose last word it is. `aterm fabric --json` carries both under `broker.health`.
  `aterm fabric doctor` prints them as facts, and `aterm doctor` has a `fabric:` row for
  the broker the configuration names: whether it answers (or answers in another astream
  protocol), the tier it says it serves, and whether its log is poisoned, a counted
  warning when mail cannot move, never a failure. The facts are the bus's own (astream's
  health entry and snapshot format): aterm reads them and writes none of its own.

- **The stats bars read Linux and Windows machines.** On Linux the cores are grouped the way
  the machine is built: an Intel laptop's P and E cores, an ARM board's big and little cores
  (a core taken offline keeps its place among its kind). Memory is counted in the kernel's own
  classes, with shared memory as in use and the kernel's reclaimable caches as cache, as `free`
  counts them; memory pressure comes from PSI. An AMD GPU's busy share is read only where
  reading it cannot keep the card awake, and a GPU the kernel put to sleep is never woken to
  ask. On Windows aterm reads every core across processor groups, P and E cores from their
  efficiency classes, memory with its commit charge, the process table (aterm's and each
  tab's share) and the drive's free space. When the commit charge is at or past 90 % of its
  limit, the Global bar says `commit 93% of limit` in the warning colour: past that limit
  Windows refuses new memory even with RAM free. The lens's memory view shows the commit
  charge on both systems (an estimate on Linux, where the limit is advisory). Whatever an OS
  does not report, such as Windows' compressed memory or a GPU nobody may read, is left out or
  marked unavailable, never shown as 0.

### Changed

- **`aterm doctor` now restores what aterm lays, and reports your packages too.** Bare
  `aterm doctor` puts back a deleted command shim, a missing `~/.local/bin/aterm` or
  `atpkg` link (and re-points one into an `aterm.app` you moved), the shell hooks and
  the private `~/.aterm` and `~/.aterm/shell.d` folders they live in, atpkg's block in
  an rc it never wired, the reroute stubs, the rustup link and the exec roots, reads
  each one back, and lists what it restored on its new `repair:` row. A shell rc you
  removed atpkg's block from stays as you left it (`aterm pkg repair` lays it again).
  When an install pass holds the package store, doctor repairs nothing and says so in a
  note; it never waits for the lock and never fails for it. A store lock that cannot be
  taken at all is a warning naming what was left. Run under `sudo`, with another
  `$HOME`, or for an isolated aterm instance, doctor and `aterm pkg repair` read
  everything and change nothing, saying what is not as laid and why it was left. A new
  `packages:` row is `aterm pkg doctor`'s verdict and its problems. `--read-only` still
  changes nothing, `--json` prints every row in the report `aterm pkg doctor --json` and
  `aterm init --json` print, and `--only <id,...>` narrows the run to those items,
  families or layers; a word that names nothing is refused before anything is read, so
  it never opens the Developer Tools page first. The exit is unchanged: 1 only when your
  shell cannot start, so `aterm doctor && aterm` still works. The macOS workstation
  settings profile is `aterm doctor --check`, `--apply` and `--restore` alone (and the
  first interactive launch); bare doctor and `--read-only` check no setting, which
  `aterm init` applies at the console.

- **`aterm pkg repair` runs as a list of items and takes `--json`.** Each of its steps
  (copied commands, the `~/.local/bin` links, the shell hooks and rc block, the reroute
  stubs, the rustup link, a held update, the shims, the exec roots, the installed
  builds) reads what it would change first and reads it back after, and `--json` prints
  those rows and nothing else on stdout. A program whose development link cannot be read
  no longer holds back every other program's commands, a step whose state cannot be read
  is attempted and exits 1 if it still cannot be read, and an rc it left alone (one you
  opted out of, one behind a macOS privacy fence, one that is not a plain text file) is
  named with why. Its usage now names everything it restores. An unknown or repeated
  argument is refused before the store lock is taken.

- **`aterm init` works over SSH and with someone else at the console.** It first
  restores what bare `aterm doctor` restores, which needs only your account, then
  applies the keyboard, scrolling, widgets, Dock, account and GitHub settings, which
  need this Mac's console: elsewhere each is reported blocked, and nothing of the
  console session is read. Root is still refused. It holds the package store's lock only
  while it restores, never while a console setting waits on you. `aterm init` exits 75
  when the only thing left is what an install pass's store lock held back, 77 when it is
  what waits for a permission you grant, and 69 when it is what waits for the network; a
  store lock that cannot be taken at all is a failure (1), since no retry takes it.

- **A new bash tab reaches its prompt sooner, and bash and fish tabs no longer pay for shell
  integration work they never use.** Before its first prompt every bash moves aterm's command
  folders back to the front of PATH, and macOS's bash 3.2 matched that pattern in wide
  characters, converting PATH again at every place it tried: 1.06 ms with a 13-entry PATH and
  1.65 ms with 23 entries. It now matches bytes, 0.22 and 0.33 ms. The once-per-shell cleanup
  of an old `~/.aterm/bin` entry, which only a shell an older aterm started can need, moved out
  of the script every new zsh, bash and fish reads into a file only such a shell opens, and fish
  no longer reports its folder at startup as well as at its first prompt, where zsh and bash
  report it. In a terminal replay of each build's own new-tab environment, a new bash's work to
  its prompt fell from 77.7 M instructions on main (76.0 M before the integration scripts grew)
  to 69.2 M, and fish's from 164.2 M to 163.0 M.

- **A first launch starts installing the ALab tools, and says so, about 0.2 s sooner.** The
  tools' signed manifests now arrive in one batch instead of a batch of ten and then one more,
  and they are fetched while aterm waits for the agents' vendors to answer instead of after; the
  writes that stood between the last manifest and the announcement are out of its way. Measured
  on an empty store against the published index (30 rounds each, interleaved, on a busy Mac):
  the announcement came at 763 ms instead of 969 ms (median), sooner in 28 of 30 rounds. With a
  vendor that never answers it came 0.55 s sooner (8 of 8), and the first download with it.

- **On Linux a new window's shell starts before aterm connects to the display, once the display
  answers.** The first tab's shell used to wait for aterm's connection to X11 or Wayland, which
  took 9.3-9.9 ms on X11 and 1.6-1.8 ms on Wayland in a test VM. It now runs its startup files
  while that connection is made, as it already did on macOS. With startup files that outlast the
  window's appearance (oh-my-zsh, nvm, conda), the prompt shows that much sooner: about 9 ms on X11
  and about 2 ms on Wayland (medians of 12, interleaved). aterm asks first whether a display server
  answers where the window will connect. Where none does, the connection still comes first, so a
  launch that cannot open its display leaves your saved windows for the next one and starts no
  shell. That covers a stale `DISPLAY`, a display over `ssh -X`, and the BSDs, which have no such
  check. A shell never inherits a compositor connection handed to aterm by number
  (`WAYLAND_SOCKET`): only aterm can use it, and Wayland programs run from the shell would have
  tried it instead of `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`.

- **aterm starts faster when its code is not in memory, and uses far less memory as it
  starts.** That is a start after a restart, an update, or a busy Mac pushing aterm's files
