  out of memory. Every start used to read the whole aterm program, about 120 MB, to work out
  the build signature that About and `aterm ctl version` show. The signature now comes from
  the code-signing hash macOS already holds, so a start no longer holds a 120 MB copy of the
  program: a windowless start's memory peaked at 142 MB and now peaks at 22 MB. A window now
  also asks for all of aterm's code in one read, where it used to load one small piece at a
  time as each was first needed. Measured with aterm's code out of memory, a start reached
  ready in 47 ms instead of 77-81 ms; a start with it in memory is unchanged. The Signature
  in About is now the first 16 digits of the code-signing hash (`codesign -dvvv` shows it as
  CDHash), so it differs between the Apple silicon and Intel halves of the app.

- **Rust builds and toolchains no longer keep Spotlight busy.** On macOS, a build through
  `targo` whose target folder you chose (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, `--target-dir`), and a `targo
  trust` run, now keep their intermediates in `<target>/build.noindex`, which Spotlight
  skips, as plain builds already did in aterm's cache; only the finished binaries land in
  your target folder. The first such build after the update builds once from scratch.
  `aterm init` now sets rustup to its minimal profile and removes the offline Rust docs
  (`rust-docs`, some 85,000 pages Spotlight indexes) from the toolchains rustup installed,
  and `aterm doctor`'s new `spotlight:` row shows what Spotlight still indexes of Rust build
  output and those docs, and where.

- **The harness card's kitty is the original cat again, and its rainbow sparkles.** The chibi
  kitten on Claude Code's launch card is gone: the kitty is the cat it replaced, a blocky head in
  the spirit of Claude's mascot with pointed ears lined pink, a pink nose, a pale belly, four legs
  and its tail up. It blinks and flicks its tail straight back over the rainbow, and its eyes keep
  the darker pupil so they still read on a grey coat. The rainbow still runs right up to it. One
  to three small four-point sparkles now sit on the rainbow's stripes, as Claude Code's own `✦`
  sparkles at its mascot's wand: while the card moves, each flares bigger (and on a dark
  background brighter; on a light one it is already the paper's white) as the rainbow's sheen
  passes over it, then settles back; at rest they stay small and still, so a card
  at rest still asks for no frames. The current layer path keeps its bounded item count and
  shared art cache; the settled frame asks for no animation wakes.

- **The harness card is drawn once and kept, and its trail holds still a little sooner.**
  The card's border, trail, kitty and stars are now two layers the renderer keeps from frame
  to frame. A card at rest is no longer drawn again on every frame, and when Claude Code's
  inline output scrolls the card up the screen the built frame is retained and moved.
  Translated GPU instances may still be staged again. The cap of 680 rectangles that could leave a large card's
  last stars out is gone. One thing looks different: while the trail ripples at the start of
  an episode, its end now holds still from the width of the kitty's rim before the kitty
  (it held still from the kitty's own edge), so the bright rim round the kitty never lies on
  the rainbow.

- **A new tab costs the main thread far less when many tabs are open, and a launch does less
  before its first frame.** Each pass of the tab-status sweep asked every tab for the process
  group in front of its terminal three times, and a new tab's first second runs that pass
  over every open tab several times; on macOS that one question costs about 51,000
  instructions. It is now asked once per tab per pass. At launch, finding where each coding
  agent's update marker lives (atpkg's settings read once per agent, a folder made, each path
  resolved) moved off the main thread onto the thread that watches those markers. And the
  warm spare's check of your startup files reads each file's details once instead of twice.
  Measured on headless instances of profiling builds (the main thread's own instruction
  counter, 10 new tabs per arm, two runs): at 40 tabs a new tab now costs the main thread
  24.9-27.7 M instructions, down from 45.5-47.7 M, and the longest main-loop turn after it fell
  from 1.05-1.36 ms to 0.56-0.77 ms; at 1 tab the whole app's work per new tab is 25.8-27.4 M
  instead of 28.3-29.5 M. At launch the step that joins the configuration work does 5.6 M fewer
  main-thread instructions (0.68 ms to 0.07 ms in the probe), and launch-to-app-built about 12%
  fewer.

- **The debugger-access alert is short lines and a list, not a wall of text.** Settings ▸
  Security's **Allow Debugger Access…** and the once-per-Mac launch ask now say in one line
  what the change allows; then, as bullets, that it is for the whole Mac, what it
  exposes (Homebrew tools, node, gpg-agent, cargo builds), what
  stays protected, and that Apple advises administrators not to change the rule; then that
  macOS asks next for an admin password (your own on an admin account) in a dialog named
  "SamplingTools", which aterm never sees; and last how to undo it. The launch ask opens
  with "aterm asks this once per Mac." and its undo points to aterm's Settings ▸
  Security ▸ **Turn Off Debugger Access…**. A development build adds a bullet saying it is not
  protected. The Turn Off alert is two short paragraphs. The facts and the buttons are
  unchanged.

- **On macOS a tab's reader observes program changes through a process watch.** Each tab's
  reader now watches its shell through the kernel's process events (a kqueue). Observed forks,
  `exec`s and exits can trigger an identity read before the next output batch; a captured
  change cuts the previous holder at `at` and starts the new drawer at `lay = max(at, filled)`.
  Bytes in `[at, lay)` belong to neither holder. This is bounded observation, not a guarantee
  for every program's first byte: the watch follows at most 16 children, its initial child
  listing may be incomplete, events may coalesce or fail, and identity reads are sampled
  kernel snapshots. The author's historical headless report for build `054d5cdcdd` records
  about 35–40 µs of CPU per fork and a 1000-command loop within the off arm's spread; those
  measurements were not repeated for this composition. On
  Linux, and on a Mac whose aterm has run out of file descriptors for the watch, tabs keep the
  output-driven detection they had. `aterm ctl metrics` reports the watch:
  `proc_events`, `proc_drain_ms`, `exec_edges`, `procwatch_fallbacks` (readers that wanted a
  watch and got none) and `procwatch_overflow` (a shell's children past the 16 it watches),
  and beside them what each command costs: `holder_cuts`, `fg_handbacks`, `parse_holds`,
  `parse_lock_waits`/`parse_lock_wait_ms` and `status_sweeps`/`status_sweep_ms`.

- **`aterm help keeper` says what a crash brings back.** With the PTY keeper on, a crashed
  window's tabs come back with their screens as they were, their scrollback and their turn
  ledgers; the page now says so, what `restore=exact`, `restore=screen` and `restore=meta`
  mean in `aterm ctl status`, and that memory pressure gives up the recorded scrollback
  first. The recovery ledger (`aterm doctor`'s `recovery:` row reads it) also records each
  launch's keeper setting and whether a keeper answered it (`keeper=off`, `on`, `absent`
  when the setting is on and no keeper was running yet, or `armed` for the copy an update
  started), and, after a crash, how many kept tabs could not be taken back
  (`restore_refused=`), so how the crash restore does on real crashes can be counted.

- **Autopilot is Forever Cruise or Forever Land, in every harness, and asks for no
  `ATERM-TASK-DONE`.** The window's harness carries Claude Code, agy, Muse Code and Gemini CLI
  sessions the same way, and codex-alab carries itself alike:
  - **Cruise never ends.** Every turn end is continued toward more complete and more correct
    work (the new default `continue_text`: "Autopilot is Cruise: keep going. Finish everything in
    hand, verify it and land it, then keep hunting for what would make the work more complete and
    more correct. …"). A report that says it is done, in words, with an idle line, with the old
    `ATERM-TASK-DONE` or with a `Nothing left:` defense, no longer ends the job: it gets a prompt
    to land every open item, review the work adversarially, widen the checks and find more,
    naming the open work the report still lists and what `git` finds in the session's repository
    that no remote main has. The pause after short turns (2 minutes, doubling to an hour) still
    paces it.
  - **Land lands everything onto the remote main branch.** It asks the agent to finish, verify,
    commit, merge and push all of the work, remove its worktrees and merged branches, and leave
    nothing unlanded, parked on a branch or for later, then nudges it at every turn end with no
    limit (it used to stop after two nudges). It ends only when a reply defends in a few lines
    starting `Nothing left:` that nothing is left, names no open work (one blamed on a blocker
    included) and no need, while `git` finds nothing in the repository that the remote's default
    branch lacks; then nothing more is typed until someone else's turn. The whole reply is read,
    even one taller than the window, and a need said earlier in the same turn counts; `git`
    honours your global excludes, and a stash another branch made is not this one's. A question
    gets the option that lands the work on the remote main soonest (pushing and merging are fine;
    never a force-push or a deletion), and every other prompt the harness types under Land — the
    resume after a usage limit or a sign-in among them — is Land's own, never Cruise's.
  - **NEEDS YOU is loud and never blocks.** An agent puts what only a person can give on a line
    of its report starting `NEEDS YOU:`. aterm shows it at once ("claude needs you: … —
    carrying on" on the window's border and pill, the tab's ◇, the menu bar's ❯N, `status
    needs=ask`, the survey and the fleet) and keeps the agent working on everything else,
    telling it once that its need reached you. `NEEDS YOU: nothing`, your own next turn there, or
    Off takes it down. Every prompt and answer the harness types says how.
  - **Workers land.** `aterm ctl spawn agent=claude` starts a worker under Land unless it says
    `autopilot=cruise`; its `done` is its landing (`task … why=landed`), its `result` the report
    before the land instruction and the defense after it, and a Cruise worker is never done. A
    worker's `NEEDS YOU:` line wakes a manager's `await task`. A worker an older aterm started
    keeps Land across a relaunch, and Summarize's worker starts in aterm's own folder, not in
    the focused pane's checkout, so it has nothing to land.
  - **Three faces.** The Autopilot chip, the harness card, Settings ▸ Harness and `status`/`ls`
    `task=` read `open`, `landed` or `theirs`: `✓ done`, the `⤓ quiet` of a landing that ran out
    of nudges and Cruise's `∞ ✓ done` are gone, and so are `task=done` and `task=spent`.
    In Settings ▸ Harness's EFFECT OF EACH AUTOPILOT the Ends row counts landings alone (no
    quiet ends), and the agent's time at its prompt splits into the harness's pause after short
    turns and, under Land, the time after the work landed (no Cruise time after a done); a timed
    Cruise's record at its time says the harness lands all of the work, never that the task was
    already done.
  - **The token is retired.** Nothing aterm writes or types asks for `ATERM-TASK-DONE`: the agent
    primer (v31) states the Autopilot and NEEDS YOU facts instead, and the supervise-agent skill
    (v7), `aterm help` and `aterm ctl help` describe them. A line that is only the token, from an
    agent an older primer taught, is still dropped from results and the survey and read as a
    claim of done, which ends nothing; so is the done note an older build's journal or task
    record carries.
- **The repository check also counts commits the remote's default branch lacks, and gates
  Land's landing.** Besides uncommitted changes, untracked files git does not ignore, stash
  entries and commits no remote holds, aterm's look at the session's repository now counts
  commits on the current branch that the remote's default branch (`origin/HEAD`, else
  `origin/main` or `origin/master`) does not have yet, so a commit pushed only to a feature
  branch has not landed. What it finds no longer opens a challenge of its own: under Cruise it is
  named in the prompt that answers a done claim (which repository, how many of each and the
  first few paths, to commit, merge and push to the remote main); under Land the work has not
  landed while the repository holds any of it, a landing kept over a turn nobody asked included,
  and the next nudge names it. A check that cannot run still finds nothing.
- **The open work a report still names goes back to the agent, and Land reads it strictly.**
  Under Cruise the prompt that answers a done claim names the open work the report lists; under
  Land any item counts, whatever blocks it, and so does work not on the remote main branch (`not
  pushed`, `not merged`, `parked`, `WIP`, `left on a branch`, `for later`, `follow-up`): a
  defense that names any of it lands nothing, and the next nudge names it.

- **Settings lists every cursor style on one Cursor Styles page, each described and previewed.**
  Off comes first, then the companions (Rainbow kitty, the default, Rainbow underline, Rainbow
  dog, Flying kitty and Flat rainbow), then the trails (Phaser, Fire, Water, Lightning, Comet,
  Sparkle, Lumen, Beam and Classic). Laser is listed as Lightning, and every name on the list,
  typed into `aterm.toml`, selects its row. `aterm ctl settings set cursor_trail_style` and a
  Settings re-save accept every spelling `aterm.toml` loads (`nyan rainbow` among them) and
  write the row it names, keeping the old `classic mono` spelling as written; a misspelling is
  still refused. A spelling like `nyan rainbow` saved in `aterm.toml` selects its own row in the
  Cursor & Motion picker instead of adding a second one. The looping cursor preview is its own
  Pause/Play control: activating it holds one frame with the trail lit, and activating it again
  plays on. A style you point at starts its loop from the first key, and the Fire shimmer row
  says the preview cannot show the heat shimmer, which the terminal draws.

- **The harness card is decorated on its first frame, and only on Claude Code's own card.**
  aterm now learns which Claude Code build is running from the system as the program
  starts, and which rows it drew from the terminal itself, so a Claude Code from aterm's
  package store or the vendor's installer has its launch card decorated on the first frame
  the card is drawn, on either renderer. On the inline renderer the card used to stand bare
  for 88-170 ms while aterm waited for Claude Code's own record of the session. A card that
  is not the running Claude Code's own stays bare: one left from an earlier run, one
  printed by `cat`, another build's, and one the shell wrote over while Claude Code was
  stopped with Ctrl-Z. agy's and Muse Code's cards are judged by where they were drawn. A
  Claude Code binary installed some other way (Homebrew, a development link) is still held
  to the build its session record names, and aterm now reads that record the moment it is
  written (on macOS and Linux) instead of checking every tenth of a second: five file reads
  per launch where the old check made up to fifty, and the card bare for about a frame; such a
  Claude Code stays decorated when it is stopped with Ctrl-Z and resumed with `fg`. A
  Claude Code run by `node` (an npm install) is not decorated: the program the system
  started is `node`, which names no build. Its footer no longer takes the model and effort
  from its launch card either, and names them from its first answer on. The footer takes a
  model only from the card the running program drew, never from an earlier run's card or
  one printed under it, and agy's and Muse Code's footers follow the model their status line
  names after the card has scrolled away. A card that goes bare and comes back, as when
  Claude Code is stopped and resumed, shows again at most three times a second. When the
  build Claude Code reports differs from the build aterm launched (from its package store
  or the vendor's installer folder), aterm lists it in `aterm exceptions` as "Claude Code
  reports another build". That listing never changes whether the card is decorated.

- **On macOS, `aterm fabric on`'s broker now acks in order by default.** A bare `aterm fabric
  on`, and a broker job that names no tier (an earlier `on`'s included, once its broker next
  starts), runs `--durability ordered` at a tenth-of-a-second horizon: the broker
  acknowledges a post once it is in order on the disk and flushes it in full a tenth of a
  second after the first post no full flush covers, once the batch in hand is written, and
  flushes a halt, a person's own posts, mail to a person and a person's read mark in full
  before anyone sees them. Measured on one Mac, a shared machine, in a
  same-day set against strict (docs/measured/fabric, 2026-10-20, dev build): a message from
  post to visible in 1.50, 2.32 and 1.71 ms at p50 against strict's 4.37, 5.29 and 10.25
  ms; a burst of 1137.7, 884.8 and 950.6 messages a second against 248.6, 239.1 and 138.8; a
  bridge's restart with 8 sessions back on the bus in 6.6, 5.0 and 6.1 ms against 20.9,
  20.6 and 37.5; a request and its reply between two sessions in 4.0-5.5 ms instead of
  17.2. What it costs: a kernel panic or forced power-off of the broker's Mac can lose the
  machine records (agent posts, presence, receipts) acked in the last tenth of a second,
  plus a batch and a full flush (up to 145 ms of them in that set), and readers resume where
  the log continues; under continuous traffic the broker flushes in full up to ten times a
  second, plus once for every batch that carries a halt, a person's post, mail to a person
  or a read mark. A broker that names no mint secret stays strict. Off macOS, and on a Mac
  for a log off the boot volume, the broker serves the ordered default strict, and `aterm
  fabric` says so and why.
  A tier you name, strict included, is kept: `aterm fabric on --durability strict` returns
  to acks on the disk. A build from before this one runs a bare job strict, so going back
  needs nothing.

- **aterm now keeps a journal of what your sessions did, on by default on macOS and Linux,** so
  `aterm ctl log` and `brief` can still answer about a session after a restart or a crash. It
  keeps a command's first word as typed (so a secret typed at a prompt and run as a command is
  kept too), folders, the values of meta fields, and who mailed whom; it never keeps screen
  text, a command's arguments or an agent's transcript. Only you can read it. aterm deletes its
  oldest files to keep it near 64 MiB, though files a running aterm is still writing can hold it
  above that for a while. It follows Restore session at launch, so a headless instance keeps
  none. Turn it off with `[session_log] journal = false`, or in Settings; off, aterm creates no
  file or folder for it and deletes nothing.

- **A terminal tab's tooltip and context menu say what the tab is doing, by default.** A `now:`
  line names it (`now: running shell`, `now: approval · bash`, `now: limit · resets 14:05`), and
  while the tab needs you (a box, a question, a limit) that comes first. A label another program
  set with `aterm ctl mark` never shows there. The tab's name is unchanged. Turn the line off
  with `[session_log] clause = false`, or in Settings; off, the tooltip and menu are exactly as
  they were.

- **Settings › Themes shows four community themes under their family's name.** TokyoNight Day,
  Moon and Storm read Tokyo Night Day, Moon and Storm, beside the built-in Tokyo Night, and
  Everforest Dark Med reads Everforest Dark Medium. Nothing you wrote changes: `theme =` and
  `aterm theme install` still take the old names, and a copy you installed before counts as
  installed and is not offered again. `aterm theme install` takes the new spelling too.

### Removed

- **GitHub Light Default is no longer in the community theme pack.** The built-in GitHub Light
  is the same palette, with a selection you can see. A copy you installed keeps working;
  `aterm theme install "GitHub Light Default"` now says to use `theme = "GitHub Light"`.
- **The harness settings button (`⚙`) is gone from Claude Code's composer.** The rule under
  the input box now carries the Autopilot chip alone (`∞`, `⤓ land`, `○ off`, `⊘ off`), with
  no gear beside it to hover, click, tab to or hear from a screen reader. Settings ▸ Harness
  is still one step away: right-click the Autopilot chip (ctrl-click on macOS) and choose
  Harness settings…, or use View ▸ Coding Agent Harness… or the palette; with the harness
  switched off in Settings, a click on `⊘ off` still opens the page at its switch.

### Fixed

- **The cursor pet's ♪ and ♥ no longer bunch into one blot.** A green build's cheer, a
  landing's cheer, a treat, a song and pets sent their notes and hearts up from almost one spot,
  so the big cheer's ♪ hid behind a ♥ and the two ♥ shared most of their ink. Each now rises in
  its own lane, clear of every other ♪ and ♥ in the air and of the pane's edge, so each reads
  whole at 1x and 2x. A cheer plays the same notes at the same beats, for as long. A landing's
  cheer finds room for its lanes on one side of the pet and faces that way, so it still shows
  its notes in a pane as narrow as 41 columns; where no room for the lanes is within reach, it
  throws them close together as before.

- **The cursor pet no longer stretches over words.** Woken where a line of text runs over its
  body (a landing's cheer in front, a key or a command beside a shell's last line of output, a
  command that succeeded with its output across the pet, a line typed beside it that wraps under
  it), it drew its stretch behind the letters, its tail or ears through the foot of a word. It
  now stretches only where its body lies on blank ground, and elsewhere wakes without the
  stretch. The pet itself still rests behind a line of text where it rested before, sitting or
  asleep; there a command that succeeds gets no stretch and no other sign.

- **After a seamless update, a session's own Autopilot word is obeyed again.** The new aterm
  starts watching its agents a moment before its control socket answers, so its first read of
  each session's Autopilot word could fail. The watcher then ran the session under the
  `[harness] autopilot` default instead of its own word, and never read it again until a
  permission box or a question happened to: a session you had set to Land and that had landed
  came back under Cruise and had its done check typed into the finished work. A word that has
  not been read yet is now read before the watcher decides anything, and a landing carried
  across the update is neither shown nor decided until it is read: a session under Cruise no
  longer shows as landed in the meantime, and one set to Off keeps its landing.

- **Closing a Settings tab behind the one you are using no longer moves you to another tab.**
  The tab's ✕, the tab menu's Close and `aterm ctl tab close` on a Settings (or any other
  app) tab in the background selected the tab beside it, and if that tab's work had landed
  unseen, its `•` went as though you had looked. The tab in front now stays in front, and
  `tab close` reports it as the active tab. Closing the Settings tab you are on still moves you
  to its neighbour, as before.

- **Settings ▸ Harness: the Every session row's open Timer shows its last choice at large
  text.** At 2× text on a narrow page, opening the row's Timer left `at 18:00` under the bottom
  edge of the list, and neither the wheel, a trackpad nor Tab could bring it into view: the
  list only scrolled by whole rows, and this row is taller than the space under its card's
  heading. Opening a Timer now scrolls the list just enough to show all of its choices, and
  moving the keyboard to a control the list cuts scrolls it into view the same way, keeping the
  card's heading at the top where there is room for both. Closing the Timer puts the list back
  where it was. The wheel and a trackpad still move the list a whole row at a time, so from the
  row they go past it: press Timer, or Tab to its choices.

- **Settings ▸ Harness: a session row's Timer choices line up when they wrap.** `1 hour`, `2
  hours`, `4 hours`, `at 18:00` and `Cancel` each took the width of their own words, so a second
  line stood off the first line's columns. Where they take more than one line they now share the
  widest one's width, as the Every session row's choices already did; on one line each keeps
  its own.

- **aterm's tests no longer touch your shell configuration, and a missing tool no longer
  fails or passes them.** One test ran your own fish with your real home directory and
  created `~/.config/fish/config.fish`, and another saved the commands it typed into your
  `~/.bash_history`. The tests that run a real shell for atpkg's hooks and setup, for the
  shell integration and for a tab's processes now give it a scratch home and scratch
  config, data, state and cache directories, and no `BASH_ENV` of yours. A test whose
  outside program is missing (fish, PowerShell, vim, zstd, a recent Python and OpenSSL)
  now ends COULD NOT RUN and says what provides it, or that nothing does yet, where some
  failed outright and others passed having run nothing. `targo --unverified verify list`
  prints every outside program the checks run, why, and what provides it, and no message
  from aterm or its checks tells you to `brew install` anything any more.
- **The cursor kitty no longer jumps and jitters while you type in Claude Code.** As you typed,
  the pet stepped aside from each letter aterm drew ahead of the echo and was pulled back a
  moment later, on every key. Its legs swapped between the walk, the amble and the run several
  times a second, and after a pause or a landing it galloped at walking pace. When the prompt
  wrapped with aterm's footer chips on the composer's rule, it was knocked sideways as the rule
  came down onto it. At every wrap it landed well behind the caret and leapt a second time.
  Now it treats your typed letters as text it can stand beside and keeps one gait while you
  type. When the composer grows a line, it moves down with the text around it. It lands one bound
  ahead of the caret, and a held backspace startles it once instead of freezing it until the
  caret is fifty cells away. The flying kitty stays at the caret through a program's repaints,
  even one that never marks its frames finished, its hover no longer flips at each key, and it
  no longer dips behind and back at the end of a line.

- **The pet can find a clear seat across the pane.** When nearby ground is protected,
  its final search now uses a finite reach covering the pane, so distant clear ground
  remains available without relaxing the checks around protected content.

- **A Linux window no longer waits about 400 ms for a desktop portal that cannot start.** At
  launch aterm reads the desktop's light/dark setting and its reduced-motion setting from the
  desktop portal (xdg-desktop-portal), each read limited to 200 ms. Where the portal is installed
  but cannot start (no backend for your desktop, a container, a bare window manager), each read
  started it and waited its full 200 ms before the first tab's shell and window. aterm now asks
  only a portal that is already running at launch; one that starts later is still followed, as
  before. In a test VM whose portal cannot start, with empty startup files, a window's first frame
  came 76-93 ms after aterm started instead of 507-573 ms (warm launches), and the prompt 17-25 ms
  instead of 237-273 ms. With a running portal, the launch reads it in-process (0.6 ms) instead of
  starting a `gdbus` helper (2.8-3.3 ms). With the change to the launch order above, the first
  prompt comes 6.9-7.2 ms sooner there, and a warm launch's first frame 6.8 ms sooner (medians of
  12, interleaved).

- **A fabric node no longer stops reaching the bus for good after its broker goes away in the
  middle of a delivery round.** When the broker stopped while the bridge was answering a
  session's decision, the bridge could note the receipt as in flight without naming the bus log
  it was meant for. Every later bridge then refused to attach until someone deleted the file by
  hand. Its sessions stopped getting mail, and their posts and receipts stayed queued. Nothing
  is noted for a receipt or a post that could not be sent.

- **A post the fabric refused is no longer sent after a power cut anyway.** When the broker
  turned a post down and the sender was told it was not delivered, a power cut could bring
  back the bridge's note of it. The next bridge then published the post after the sender's
  later ones, sometimes to a session that had already gone. The note of a refused post or
  receipt is now removed durably. A receipt the bridge noted on an older bus log is also no
  longer published on a later one where it names a different record.

- **A closed tab's fabric presence no longer stays `live` when the broker turns its last row
  down.** When a tab closed and the broker refused its `exited` row (a rolled-back batch, which
  passes), nothing ever wrote the row again, so `aterm fabric status` showed the session live
  and mail to it was routed to nobody until the bridge restarted. The bridge now writes the
  row again on its next presence sweep, within a minute.

- **Fabric mail is no longer shown to a session twice after the bus log moves twice around a
  bridge restart.** When a power loss took the newest records of the bus log (a Relaxed or
  Ordered broker) and the bridge was stopped right after telling aterm of the move, a second
  move before the next bridge started made aterm forget every message its sessions already
  held, and the next bridge delivered them again. A session that already follows a later
  generation of the same log now keeps what lies below the point the logs part, as one that
  follows the earlier generation always did.

- **The rainbow trail stays on Claude Code's composer while Claude Code works.** With a tool
  running, each result scrolls the screen and Claude Code redraws its input box in place, so
  a link you pasted, and the words you typed after it, lost their rainbow: the band jumped off
  the box onto the spinner and tip rows above it and melted there, or flashed there for a
  frame, while the text stayed dark. The band now stays on the box through every tool step: a
  paste whose echo lands in the same frame as a tool result is lit, a key pressed as a step
  lands keeps its light, a line of one letter keeps its light, and a line that wraps keeps its
  light on both rows, in a single pane and in split or zoomed panes alike. A link copied with
  its line ending, which puts the link on its line and starts a new one under it, is lit too;
  before, only the words you typed on the new line were.

- **Text a program writes at the cursor stays dark again when you type past it.** A
  completion or other output inserted at the caret with no key behind it was lit as soon as
  you typed the next letter, because the rainbow bridged any gap of up to four cells between
  your typed runs. It no longer bridges a gap. A key whose echo comes back late while Claude
  Code or agy repaints its footer two or three rows under the box keeps its light, and the
  footer stays dark. A key pressed as the cursor jumps two or more rows without printing
  there (vim's `}`, `3k` or `G`) moves the trail at once instead of waiting up to ten
  seconds for an echo that never comes.

- **The rainbow trail stays on Claude Code's composer when a tool's output pushes it down.**
  In a new session, before the transcript fills the window, each tool step moves Claude Code's
  input box down several rows without scrolling. A link you pasted there, and the words around
  it, melted off at the first step and stayed dark. The band now moves down with the box,
  including a line that wrapped onto a second row and a line of one letter, and a key pressed
  as a step lands keeps its light.

- **Abrew's dangling-pin recovery preserves foreign pins.** `pin` and `unpin` recover a
  marker only when it names exactly one missing version in that package's real Cellar
  directory. A live unowned keg, a version symlink or a path escaping that directory
  keeps its marker.

- **Your last windows come back after aterm crashes or hangs while it starts.** aterm takes the
  windows your last quit saved before it finishes starting, so it can start their first shell
  sooner. A crash, a force quit or a hang in those first milliseconds lost them for good. Now
  aterm keeps the saved windows on disk until it has restored them and saved its own record of
  them. If it dies before that, the next launch brings them back. If that launch dies before
  that too, they are set aside, so windows that keep crashing aterm cannot loop. A second aterm
  started meanwhile never takes windows a running aterm is still starting with.

- **aterm no longer freezes when a network volume stops answering.** When the folder holding
  your agent identities, your network home, or a share your tabs were in stopped answering,
  several things used to hang:
  - **Every window.** The windows hung until the server came back: when you opened New Tab
    With Identity, when a restored tab carried an identity, and when your network home stopped
    answering while aterm ran.
  - **Tabs after an identity spawn.** A spawn under an identity on such a volume never
    returned, and every tab asked for after it waited behind it.
  - **Restores.** A restore of tabs on one silent share waited a quarter second per folder.
    Reopened after a crash, the window did not appear until all those checks had run.

  Measured in a macOS test VM with its NFS server stopped on purpose:
  - **Windows** stay responsive the whole time. A control request now answers in under 2 ms
    where it used to wait out its 30 s limit.
  - **Identity spawns.** A spawn under an identity on a silent volume is refused in 0.26 s,
    naming the folder that did not answer, and the next tab opens in 7 ms.
  - **New Tab while your network home is silent** says that the home did not answer,
    instead of waiting.
  - **More folders on the same silent share.** A new tab into another folder there opens in
    your home folder in 3 ms instead of 0.3 s.
  - **Restores.** A restore of four tabs there takes 0.36 s instead of 1.1 s, and the window
    of a reopened crash comes up in 0.3 s instead of 1.2 s.

- **`aterm ctl identities forget` no longer removes an identity a new tab is still starting
  under.** The forget checked only the tabs already open, so one confirmed while a tab under that
  identity was still starting removed the folder anyway, and the agent in the new tab made it
  again itself, with ordinary permissions instead of aterm's private ones. The forget now answers
  `ERR identity in use spawning=<k>` and removes nothing while a tab under the identity is still
  starting or still closing, or while a shell carried across an update wears it. A
  `spawn identity=<name>` asked for while a forget runs waits for the forget to finish, then
  starts with the identity made anew, empty. A forget that loses a race with another forget of
  the same name answers `ERR no such identity <name>` instead of an I/O error. A forget no longer
  deletes a folder another forget, or another running aterm, is still emptying; a folder a forget
  could not empty (`tombstone=` in its reply) is removed at aterm's next launch once the aterm
  that left it has exited. An agent folder that is a symlink to nothing is refused as one, not
  as `no such identity`.

- **The cursor pet walks beside your typing instead of running and stopping at every key.**
  The pet stood still between keys and sprinted to each one, so at any typing speed it ran and
  stopped, ran and stopped; as a burst slowed it backed off and turned round mid-run, and after
  you paused it slid back in its sitting pose. It now walks on beside the caret at the pace you
  type, slows to a stop when a key comes late, and waits where it stopped for your writing to
  catch up with it. Typing fast and unevenly no longer freezes it mid-stride, and a pet staring
  at a command's streaming output keeps watching it.

- **A headless aterm no longer plays the system alert sound.** An instance started with
  `--headless` has no window, yet every bell its programs rang played the Mac's alert sound,
  with nothing on screen to say where it came from: on a Mac that runs agents' labs, live
  tests and checks, that was the system bell over and over. A headless bell is still counted
  (`aterm ctl subscribe … events` reports it); only the sound is gone. A bell in a window
  rings as before.

- **The cursor pet no longer sleeps on Claude Code's words.** On a fresh Claude Code screen at
  the top of a tall pane, the resting pet sat on the composer's footer, so `⏵⏵ auto mode on`
  read `auto🐱de`. Once the session had filled the pane, it sat on the footer at the bottom the
  same way. aterm draws its own rules and chips round Claude Code's composer, so the pet cannot
  stand beside Claude's caret there. It now takes the nearest blank ground its whole body fits
  on and can walk to: the rows under the footer, the footer's blank end, or the space beside
  the last words above the rule, never a gap between a line's words such as a command list's
  gutter. It stands behind text only when no blank ground is near. It also keeps off the
  harness card: the card's border, rainbow, kitty and stars, and the blank rows round them. A
  turn that moves the composer past the resting pet no longer leaves it leaping in place on
  `✻ Cooked`, and a selection or the Autopilot menu over it no longer sends it across the pane.
  It moves only when its ground is taken, so a command list that changes at every key moves it
  once. Typing a long prompt into Claude Code's composer, or Claude Code's output streaming in,
  no longer sets it hopping in place at the composer's top rule. After a landing's cheer it
  goes back to that ground and stays in view. Beside a shell's caret the pet stands where it
  did.

- **Tab in a Settings list resumes where the keyboard stood after its control disabled itself.**
  When the focused control left the focus order (it disabled itself under the keyboard, as the
  Activity pager's Older does at its end), Tab in a scrolling Settings list jumped to the list's
  first control, and Shift-Tab to its last, instead of the nearest control after it (or before
  it). It now resumes where the keyboard stood, as it already did outside a list.

- **Top Settings on Linux no longer cuts Window appearance's choices or Undo short.** Its Auto,
  Light and Dark choices now go onto as many lines as they need in a narrow window at large
  text, as every other row's choices already did, instead of painting "Au…", "Lig…" and
  "Da…" in a phone-width window at 2× text; and the status bar's Undo (or Redo) widens to
  hold its word instead of painting "Un…" at 1.5× text. Linux's interface font is wider than
  macOS's, which is where it showed.

- **A theme under the pointer in an open picker keeps its hover shading when the wheel can
  scroll no further.** At the top or the end of the list a wheel turn moved nothing but took
  the shading off the theme the pointer was on, until the pointer moved.

- **`aterm ctl pointer` on Settings answers where the pointer is.** A move onto a control, a
  click or a wheel that changed the page (a hover's shading, a switch turned, the list
  scrolled) answered `ERR no presented native frame under the pointer` although it had
  worked, in a window as in a headless aterm. The reply now reads the page the event left.
  And over the message band above a Settings page, `pointer move -1 <col>` answered the same
  `ERR` instead of the band's row, which it now reads back as over a terminal.

- **`aterm ctl pointer move key=` lands on a Settings control the list's bottom edge cuts.**
  Such a control is drawn on past the edge, where it cannot be pressed, and the pointer went
  to the middle of the drawing, often past the edge: the reply named no control and a
  `pointer click` there pressed nothing. The pointer now goes to the middle of the part a
  click presses.

- **A downloaded update starts installing at once on an idle Mac.** Once a new build was
  downloaded and verified, aterm waited half a second before it looked whether the moment
  was quiet enough to install it, and the start of the switch waited with it. It now looks
  at once and waits only for its last check of the downloaded app to finish: in a test VM
  the whole update, from the check that found the build to the new aterm running, took
  0.77 s instead of 1.19 s. A terminal that is busy at that moment still delays the
  install exactly as before. An Install pressed while that last check runs starts within
  20 ms of its end, not up to 100 ms after it.

- **A reply you queued, and a verdict you gave, survive the fabric's broker moving its log
  while aterm keeps running.** When the broker's log moves to its next generation under a
  running aterm (the reopen after a failed flush poisoned the log, a repair's cut, or a
  broker stopped uncleanly where it cannot rule out a lost write: a relaxed log off the boot
  volume, or a host that names no boot), the broker records where the two generations
  agree, and every bridge and notifier already resumed there. aterm's
  sessions did not: a reply queued while the broker was down was dropped (`log-replaced`),
  the receipt for a verdict on a message shown before the move was never sent, so an asker
  that gave a deadline was told its ask had expired, and every `inbox get @<off>` waiting on
  the bridge failed. The bridge now tells aterm where the log continues, and a session drops
  only what names a record the move took. A power loss stops aterm too, and its sessions'
  queued replies and owed receipts go with it, as before. A bridge tells an aterm older than
  this build only that the log changed, and that aterm drops everything as before.

- **When a window cannot start, its alert comes up in front.** A window launch that fails before
  its window opens (for example because the `shell` in aterm.toml cannot run) shows "aterm could
  not start" with the reason. Started without a terminal and not by the Finder or the Dock (from
  a launcher, a script or another app running `aterm --window`), that alert came up behind your
  other windows with aterm not the active app, so the launch seemed to do nothing. aterm now puts
  the alert on screen and then asks to be the active app, as a launch from the Finder or the Dock
  already was. A new build starting during an update still never takes the front.

- **After the harness restarts a session, the session no longer reads as failed.** The old
  agent's end (exit 143, from the restart's own stop) used to stay in `brief` as
  `need=failure`, and in the tab's tooltip as `now: failed · exit 143`, until the new run
  ended. Once the restarted agent is up, the restart marks that end seen, as you looking at it
  does, and fabric members see it lifted too. Only the agent's own end is lifted: a command
  that failed before the agent started still shows, and a turn the harness only typed into
  the agent lifts nothing. If another run in the session also failed, both stay: the session
  did fail.

- **`brief` still says who started an older turn, and which `turn` started it.** On a busy
  session the log drops the oldest records first, and a turn whose opening record was gone lost
  its `by=` and `ledger=` in `brief`. The turn's closing record now carries both, so `brief`
  keeps them (`t3 done 2m10s by=harness ledger=7`).

- **The opt-in limit-reset step takes Claude Code 2.1.304's resets.** With `[harness] limit_reset`
  on (it ships off), the harness again takes a limit reset at a usage limit: a 5-hour, weekly or
  full reset, when it is the only reset the dialog offers. A dialog that offers two or more gets
  its wait row, unless you name the kinds it may spend, first preferred, in the new `[harness]
  limit_reset_kinds = ["full", "weekly", "5-hour"]`: it then takes the first listed kind on
  offer, and never an unlisted one. A Fable reset is never taken. The confirmation must name the
  kind the harness chose, or the reset is kept. A spent reset is recorded as spent even when
  Claude Code rewords the rest of its line. The step's words come from Claude Code 2.1.304
  itself; none of it has yet been seen at a real usage limit.

- **A seamless update keeps a landed agent's mark, its time and its work.** A tab whose agent
  landed while you were away kept its dot only until aterm updated itself: the new aterm knew
  nothing of the landing. Now the update carries it. The tab still wears the dot until you
  look (a landing in the tab you are looking at is seen at once), and the chip's hover help and
  Settings ▸ Harness's state line say `landed 17:42`, when the work landed, not when the new
  aterm took the session over. On macOS its row under ❯ ▸ Done for you stays as it was, with
  the same age. The kitty never cheers a landing that crossed an update: a cheer still waiting
  for your look when aterm updated is not played after it. A task's work also crosses: 25
  seconds of work before an update and 10 after count as 35 toward the 30 seconds a landing
  needs to mark its tab. A tab restored after aterm quit or crashed still starts afresh.

- **A release no longer waits forever on the keychain.** A `git-credential-<name>` helper that
  `ship release` or `ship check --export` starts and that is still running after a minute is
  waiting for a person (a locked keychain, or an access prompt), so it is ended with whatever
  it started, and the release says which helper and why; git then asks its next helper or
  fails. It never falls back to a prompt on the terminal or to an askpass program it was
  handed (an editor's terminal sets `GIT_ASKPASS` to one that opens an input box and waits). A
  `verify export` that ends at its ceiling now stops the release's own git children too, where
  it used to leave one running.

- **`aterm fabric`'s help and the manual say what the bus really does, and `aterm fabric
  doctor --retire-ghosts` does what they say.** A NODES row marked `remote` was described
  as a node "only the bus knows", as if on another computer. aterm's bus is this machine's,
  so `remote` is a node no aterm instance here answers as: one that quit or crashed under
  another state dir, a scratch instance, or one that did not answer. Only that node can
  retire its rows: `aterm fabric doctor --retire-ghosts` run under a `[fabric] command`
  naming its state dir and its cap, and NODES now says so under the table. That command
  sent every row to whichever local bridge was up, which retires only its own node's, so
  with this machine's aterm running a ghost node's rows stayed live and the command waited
  five seconds and exited 2; each node's rows now go to a bridge of that node, or the
  command publishes them itself. A node whose state dir is gone has nothing left that can
  speak as it, and its rows stay. The subject budget was said to be never reclaimed; a
  closed session's own `ev` face is given back when `[fabric] log = "turns"` is on, and
  nothing else is. And the remedy for a leaked capability is now written down: minting the
  cap again does not cut it off. A cap minted with `aterm fabric mint-for --expires` ends
  at its deadline; to cut off every cap, move `<root>/mint.secret` aside and run `aterm
  fabric on`, which restarts the broker it runs on the new secret, then mint each person's
  cap again.

- **aterm's reads of another program's database no longer risk that program's own writes.**
  The Developer Tools check (the panel, `aterm doctor`, `aterm pkg doctor`) reads the switch
  from macOS's system privacy database, `aterm machines` reads it on a managed Mac, and aterm's
  quiet upgrade of agy reads agy's conversation summaries. Each read took a lock on the live
  file. macOS's privacy daemon does not wait for a lock, so a change it was saving at that
  moment (a switch you had just flipped) could fail and be lost; agy waits up to 5 seconds and
  then drops its summary update. aterm now reads these files without a lock: the file as it
  stands, or a private copy of it. On this Mac an answer counts only when the file did not
  change while it was read; otherwise aterm reads it again.

- **A session's log keeps only a command's first word again.** In 0.107.0 a command the log
  first saw already finished, as a quick `echo` or `export` usually is, was logged with its
  whole line, arguments included: in `aterm ctl log` and `brief`, and on disk with the journal
  turned on. The log now keeps its program alone, as it does for a command it sees running.
  Journal files written before keep what they hold until they are deleted as the oldest; to
  remove them now, delete the `session-log` folder in aterm's logs folder while aterm is not
  running.

- **The paste and close questions appear at once on Linux and Windows.** The in-window
  question before a multi-line paste (Linux) and the one before closing a busy tab or window
  (Linux and Windows) waited to appear, and once answered to go away, until something else on
  the screen changed, such as program output or the cursor's next blink. Each now reaches the
  screen on the frame it is asked or answered.

- **A task the harness saw land stays landed when the harness is stopped right at its
  landing.** When the agent landed its work under Autopilot Land and its harness was stopped at
  that same moment, the landing never reached the session's journal. That happens when aterm's
  quiet upgrade or a relaunch takes over at the landing, Autopilot is turned Off, a SUPERVISION
  setting is saved, aterm updates itself or quits, the host cuts the harness's connection, or
  an `aterm supervise watch` loses the reader of its output. The next harness on the session
  then started the task as open and stamped the landing with its own time, and after Off it
  could type the land instruction into the landed work. The landing is now journaled right
  after the point it was read at, before anything can stop the harness, and the next harness
  under Land restates it with its first time and types nothing (under Cruise the session goes
  on, as Cruise always does). Also, the first harness after an update from 0.106.0 or earlier no longer
  continues sooner than the old one would have: it now keeps the old harness's short-turn
  back-off across a usage limit, and its pending retry of an overloaded API request.

- **A tab that ran `/login` for a shared Claude login carries on when you sign in elsewhere.**
  When tabs share one Claude login and it expires, one tab runs `/login` for all of them. If
  you left that tab's sign-in, or pressed Esc on your own `/login`, and then signed in from
  another tab, it stayed stopped under a "sign-in cancelled" notice although the login was
  back. It now sends its interrupted turn again, as the other tabs do, and the notice goes;
  if you renewed that account meanwhile, it moves onto the renewed login instead. A tab whose
  supervision restarts while `/login` is open on its screen no longer runs `/login` again.

- **Claude sign-in notices start with what to do.** Each one opens with its step and a Show
  tab button. On an account from your roster it names the account to sign in with, since
  signing in another one there merges two roster rows. Console's own sign-in menu is no
  longer reported as a stopped sign-in, a draft in the prompt that keeps aterm from running
  `/login` has its own notice, and the manual lists every `aterm harness accounts` command.

- **Crash restore under memory pressure brings back the tab's own screen, and erases the
  scrollback you clear from the record it replaced.** When memory pressure took a tab's
  recorded scrollback away while the keeper was slow to read, the keeper could be left
  holding the record from the moment of the shed, so every later crash brought back that old
  screen instead of the tab's own; the new record is now handed over again until the keeper
  takes it. Scrollback cleared (`clear`, ⌘K) while a tab waited for its smaller record, or
  while the keeper's queue was too full to take it, is erased from the old record at once,
  a tab paused inside an escape sequence no longer retries the shed five times a second, a
  pressure spike that ended before aterm looked is read as ended (the scrollback comes back
  a minute later, not at the next spike), and `aterm ctl pressure` reports the level macOS
  gave even before any tab was recorded. `aterm ctl status` says `journal_ring=shedding`
  while a tab's old record is still in memory, until the keeper has been handed the new one.
- **After an update, the agents in your restored tabs read the new aterm primer.** The
  window wrote the coding-agent primer (the aterm block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`,
  `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` and the other detected agents' files) only when it opened a new
  session. A seamless update hands every running tab over to the new window without opening
  one, so their primer files kept the previous version's block until a new tab was opened
  or `aterm agents install` was run. The window now refreshes those files in the background
  when it starts too, once its first frame is on screen, so opening the window never waits
  on them; the first start of each new version also refreshes each existing agent
  identity's own copy (`spawn identity=`).
  This pass does not delay an agent restart: an agent that reads its context before the pass
  finishes can still load the previous complete block. A window an update starts writes
  it only once the old window has handed the tabs over for good, so an update called off
  midway leaves the old version's block in place. It still runs at most once a minute, in
  the background, and never in a `--headless` instance, an app not named `aterm.app`, or
  with `agents_auto_prime = false`.

- **A fabric broker whose log stops taking writes now restarts itself.** When a full flush
  of the broker's log fails with acknowledged records it was to cover, or a failed write
  cannot be rolled back, the log is POISONED: it refuses every write until it is reopened.
  Nothing reopened it. Every post, halt acknowledgement and presence row on the host was
  refused and retried for as long as the broker ran, while `fabric=` still said
  `connected`. The broker now checks every 2 seconds. On a poisoned log it writes one line
  to `broker.err` saying so and why, then exits with status 75, and its launchd or systemd
  job starts it again on the reopened log. A broker that no `aterm fabric on` job runs
  (`--service none`) exits too, and its line names the command that starts it again. Every
  bridge resumes where the log continues, and the refused message lands once. A bridge
  refused by a poisoned broker that keeps serving (one from an earlier release) reads
  `fabric=stalled reason=poisoned` instead of `connected`, and `aterm fabric doctor` names
  the remedy for that and for a broker that exited. A disk that keeps failing flushes makes
  the broker exit again after each restart, which launchd paces to one start every 10
  seconds and systemd to about one every 3. Each restart moves the log's generation, and a
  reader away for more than eight of them forgets where it was, as after a log repair.

- **A warm spare comes back about 60 ms sooner after a new tab takes it.** Before a spare
  shell is offered to the next tab, aterm waits out a 100 ms window after its start and then
  checks that its startup left no process behind. That wait ran on a low-priority thread, whose
  timer macOS coalesces: it woke 61-75 ms late. It now wakes on time, so a spare is ready again
  283-289 ms after the tab that took it opened, instead of 343-345 ms (median of 20, zsh and
  bash with empty startup files).

- **A new tab opened right after another takes the warm spare instead of starting cold.**
  While aterm checked a new spare's startup for leftover processes (the 100 ms after its
  startup files finished), a new tab started its own shell cold, though a tab asked for a
  moment earlier, while those files were still running, took the spare. It now takes the
  spare during the check too. And the check no longer waits for 2 seconds to pass since the
  previous one: with tabs opened in quick succession, the next spare was held back for up to
  2 seconds, and so was starting the one after it. A second tab asked for 200-250 ms after
  the first now gets its prompt from the spare 35 times in 40 (0.7 ms for bash, 2.9 ms for
  zsh, with empty startup files) where it almost always started cold (12 ms and 18 ms), and
  tabs asked for every quarter second all came from the spare (40 of 40, against 23-28 of
  40).

- **Tabs flooding output in the background cost aterm's UI thread less on a busy Mac.** Once a
  program's output has streamed for a frame (16 ms), aterm takes it in at most once every 4 ms
  instead of once per read. A writer that paused for 4 ms or more before its output had streamed
  for a frame started that count over, and on a busy Mac that happened thousands of times a
  second across ten flooding tabs: each restart cost one UI-thread pass per read for up to a
  frame again. Output now also counts as streaming after 16 passes, so a restart costs at most
  16. Ten tabs each printing half a million lines behind a window's idle front tab, beside eight
  busy processes: 24,700 output passes instead of 131,000, 63 ms of UI-thread work per second
  instead of 104, and the output done in 12.9 s instead of 13.5 (medians of 4); with no window,
  16,200 passes instead of 93,200 and 12.2 ms/s instead of 31.4 (medians of 3). A typed echo
  (about seven reads) is still never held.

- **A prompt shows as soon as the shell draws it, even after a flood of output.** A program's
  start or end now ends its output's burst, so the shell's prompt after a command is never held
  behind the 4 ms batching that output got. In a window, aterm took in the prompt after a 40 ms
  flood 1.05 ms after its last line instead of 2.63 (3.71 with the change above alone), and after
  40 quick lines with a 6 ms pause before the prompt, 8.53 ms instead of 8.74 (12.55 with the
  change above alone; medians of 20). A loop of short programs pays one UI-thread pass per
  program for it.

- **Live bus connections keep timeout failures visible.** A macOS timeout-setting error
  is treated as a closed connection only when both socket directions are observed closed.
  Live and half-closed connections keep their error; buffered mail can still be read
  before a full close.

- **`aterm fabric tail` reads a broker that marked the tail and hung up.** When the broker told a
  caught-up tail it was idle and closed the connection before the tail re-armed its liveness
  bound, macOS refused that socket setting and the tail failed with a bare "Invalid argument (os
  error 22)", without what the broker had sent after the mark. It now prints those records, then
  says the broker closed the stream.

- **On dark themes the comet, lumen, phaser, sparkle, laser and beam trails lie under the
  letters you type, in their own colours, and the newest letters stay readable.** Their streaks
  were light laid over the text, which washed the fresh letters behind the caret out (to about
  1:1). Each now lays a band in its own colour beneath the letters it crosses, as bright as the
  text allows while it still reads 4.5:1, and the band fades as the light did, so the comet
  still tapers, lightning's freshest cell is still its brightest and the beam still powers down.
  Over blank cells and into the cursor the streak is light at full strength. The cursor's glow,
  the sparks and stars, the landing ring and the typing glow share one budget over the letters,
  so together they keep the newest letter at 3:1 or better and the lines above and below at
  4.5:1 (fire and water too), and that budget dims them only over the letters: the glow around
  the cursor stays whole over the blank cells beside it. The comet's band is a tail that tapers
  away three cells behind the cursor, and the comet no longer tints whole cells grey behind it.
  The phaser's band keeps to blue, violet and magenta under the letters, where an orange or a
  yellow would turn brown. Sparkle is a gold comet: a gold head, glow and tapering line under a
  quiet dusk behind the letters, shedding brighter stars, crescent moons and gold glitter. Each
  shows its full colours on a thin bright line in the gap under the row (where the line below is
  blank); with a trail colour set, Classic's one-colour face draws a bright tracer in it and one
  soft round bloom at the cursor instead of a stepped square box. The landing ring after a jump
  is a soft round glow instead of a thin square outline. A jump across rows left blank is drawn
  as the trail's full light. Classic's shifting colours keep their look. Inside a typed run every
  cell holds its own light, so the trail no longer dims and re-brightens with each key you type.
  On light themes those trails draw as ink beneath the letters, inside their own line: the comet
  as a wedge that widens toward a dense head just behind the cursor (no longer poking past its
  edge), the beam as one even tube as tall as the letters' x-height, lightning as a thin line,
  the phaser as its band of spectrum, sparkle as a band in its rolling colour, and lumen as a
  quiet tracer that glows behind the cursor; the beam's stardust is not drawn there. Over
  Chinese, Japanese, Korean or emoji characters those bands give way to thin lines along the top
  and bottom of the line, so a wide character's box is not filled, and a band that crosses lines
  (Enter, a jump) draws only on the line the cursor lands on. Lightning flashes once per bolt and
  no more than three times a second, and on a light theme it, the water wake and the particles
  of every trail are drawn as ink beneath or beside the letters instead of white light;
  particles no longer fly over the text or stick out from under the cursor. Fire rests as an
  ember you can see on its page; on dark themes its flames rise above the line as tapering
  tongues, bright over a blank line and faint over text, instead of a dim column over the newest
  letter, and the dark outline that separates letters from the blaze no longer smears dark
  letters on a bright prompt; on light themes it draws soft orange-to-yellow flame tongues rising
  from the letters you type, each letter keeping its contrast, with small sparks instead of round
  blots; and its steam no longer settles on the line above.

- **The comet, beam and sparkle cursor trails wear their own colours again.** Since July they
  took your theme's cursor colour (green on the default theme), so the terminal never showed the
  glacial comet, the ice-blue beam or the gold sparkle. They now keep those colours unless you
  set `cursor_trail_color`, set a `cursor_color`, or a program sets the cursor colour (OSC 12),
  which they then wear. The laser stays violet unless you set `cursor_trail_color`. A comet's
  trail now heats toward the same ice white as its head, not a warm amber. With no trail colour
  set, Settings names the colour a style draws in ("Pale blue (default)" for the comet, "Violet
  (default)" for lightning). A cursor colour you pin is the cursor's colour at rest on every
  style.

- **Trail intensity now dims every part of the cursor trail.** The comet's head and the cells it
  leaves behind, the rainbow, water and phaser cursors, the light rod and the typing glow stayed
  at full strength at any setting above zero, and at zero the comet still drew its cells.

- **`aterm ctl trail status` says `resolved=off` for `off` instead of `lumen`, and says when a
  style was not used as written.** The row now ends with `issue=` (`unknown` beside the default
  trail drawn instead, else `none`), `comet_cells=` and `comet_alpha_max=` (the comet's cells on
  screen), and prints `ribbon_look=none` for styles without a ribbon.

- **The cursor stays easy to see with every trail style, on light and dark themes.** On a light
  theme the laser, lumen, beam, sparkle, water and comet cursors used to fade toward white while
  you typed, as low as 1.2:1 against the page. They now deepen into their colour instead, and
  their glow no longer lightens the cursor or the letters beside it. Every effect cursor, and the
  letter under it, keeps at least 4.5:1 against the cell it sits on (the page, or the colour a
  program gave that cell, as in a reverse-video status line; the rainbow cursor, a coloured
  block, 3:1), so the fire cursor on a dark theme rests as a red you can see instead of a maroon
  the page swallowed. The typing glow on a plain cursor never drops below the contrast of your
  theme's own cursor, so it does not jump as it starts and stops. On a light theme the sparkle
  trail's stars now show as ink instead of white light, and the cursor-trail bloom fades out.
  The comet's round head no longer piles up its glow on the letters beside the cursor, and the
  sparkle cursor's shimmer and the rainbow cursor's twinkle stay under three flashes a second.

- **The typing glow no longer washes out the letters you just typed, and it goes out when it
  cools.** On a dark theme the glow around the cursor while you type fast stacked about four
  times the light the other cursor effects allow over the letters beside it, so typing quickly
  left the newest letter as low as 2:1 against its background. It is now one soft glow that
  fades smoothly from the cursor instead of a stepped grey bullseye: as large as before, dimmer,
  and on its own never enough to drop a letter under it below the legibility bar the other
  effects keep. On a light theme it is one round glow of ink beneath the letters of the line you
  are typing on, in the trail's own colour (the cursor's colour with no trail). With a steady
  cursor (`cursor_blink = false`, or a program that asks for one) the glow used to stop partway
  through cooling and stay on screen until something else redrew; it now cools all the way out.
  In a web page the glow, and the rainbow cursor's colour, also finish cooling instead of
  freezing.

- **The Classic trail shows on light themes, and stops when you leave it.** On a light theme it
  drew nothing you could see and briefly washed out the letters under the caret; it now draws in
  ink beneath the letters: a typed run as a thin underline in the trail's colours inside its own
  line, under a soft round tint on the cursor's line that deepens as you type faster and fades
  when you stop (the glow a dark theme shows around the cursor, sized by Glow size), and a jump
  (Ctrl-L included) as one unbroken stroke along the move, with the landing ring as a tinted
  glow. Switching to another style or turning trails off while Classic was still lit
  left aterm treating the trail as live until the window was resized (on the web build the page
  kept animating), and coming back to Classic drew a stray streak from where the caret used to
  be. Switching to Classic while another trail was still lit kept aterm redrawing every frame for
  as long as Classic stayed on, and leaving Classic could draw the next trail from where the
  caret stood before you picked it. Pressing Enter at the bottom of a full screen no longer draws
  a streak along the new prompt line; typing a wide character (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, emoji)
  reads as typing rather than a jump with a ring; the streak ends on a bar cursor instead of half
  a cell past it; the landing ring keeps its weight on Retina screens; a jump's streak animates
  to the end on its own instead of waiting for the next redraw; and `aterm ctl trail status`
  counts Classic's sparks and its spawns.

- **`aterm fabric tail --filter` refuses a malformed filter before dialling the broker.** The
  filter is checked against the bus's own grammar at the parse, so `/f/lab/>/x` (a `>` that is
  not the last segment) is a usage error naming the filter. Before, the tail connected and failed
  with the broker's misleading "unauthorized: capability does not grant this subject/filter". A
  well-formed filter your node's capabilities do not grant is still the broker's to refuse.

- **Emoji and other characters past the BMP survive a width change at the screen's top.** When
  a resize brought back the start of a wrapped line from scrollback, an emoji, a ZWJ sequence or
  a character like `𝔄` on that line came back as `�`, and its true-colour background or
  foreground as the default. They now keep both.

- **Settings ▸ Harness lands on all of a session's row at large text.** Opened for a session
  (`⚙`, Harness settings…) at 2× text in a narrow window, the page drew the row under the
  SESSIONS caption it keeps at its top, and the row's last line and the selection's bottom edge
  fell under the window's edge. The caption now scrolls away so all of the row is on screen
  wherever the window holds it; only a row taller than the window still lands at its top.

- **A session row's buttons on Settings ▸ Harness wait for a look when the page moved them.** A
  row's state line coming or going (`done 14:05` as a task finishes, `lands at 18:00` as a
  timer is set or fires), an open Timer's choices or a session closing moves the rows under
  them, so a click could press a button the page had just moved under a still pointer, another
  row's Cruise or Land. That click now only lights the button and the next one presses it, as
  on the Every session row. Keyboard, VoiceOver and `aterm ctl act` presses are unchanged.

- **The Every session row's Timer choices line up where they wrap.** Beside the row's words they
  take the row's own button slots, two to a line, so `1 hour` and `4 hours` stand under Timer
  and `2 hours` and `at 18:00` under Follow the default; where a choice is too wide for a slot
  (`at Sat 18:00`), and where the row's buttons stack, each takes the widest choice's width, so
  they still stand in columns.

- **Settings' fact cards keep their labels whole at large text, and wrap a long value instead
  of cutting it.** On Settings ▸ Harness (STATUS, EFFECT OF EACH AUTOPILOT, WHAT THE HARNESS
  DID), Tab Control (FLEET & TAB SUMMARY) and AI CLIs (WHO REVIEWS, WHAT IS HELD), each card's
  label column is sized from its own labels at the text size, as far as it leaves each value
  its longest word, so `Supervision`, `Waited at limits` and `System Vitals` are no longer cut to
  `Supervi…`, `Waited at li…` and `System …` at 2× text. On every fact card, About's included,
  a value too long for its line now wraps between its words, each fact it lists starting a line,
  where it was cut: at 2× text in a narrow window `Cruise said done 6 ti…` now reads `Cruise said
  done 6 times (30 s of work or more)` over three lines. A value runs to eight lines (it was
  three) before it ends in `…`. About's cards keep their label column.

- **Settings ▸ Harness reads its counts when a restored window opens on it.** A window brought
  back on Settings ▸ Harness, by a restart or by an update, showed only the new run's counts
  (`Ends: none yet` where the run before had ended a task) until you pressed Refresh; it now
  reads the ledgers once as it opens, and after an update once the new version has taken over.

- **Settings ▸ Harness reads its counts without sweeping the fleet.** Each reading also asked
  every Mac in the fleet and every other aterm for their tabs, and slept 30 ms for a CPU sample
  of this Mac and ran `sysctl` twice and its other system probes, all before the counts came
  (about 80 ms of a 600 ms reading with 20 sessions' ledgers). Only Tab Control asks the fleet
  now, while it is shown, using the window's own measure of this Mac wherever the window has
  one; Tab Control opened while the counts are being read gets the fleet in that same reading.

- **Ctrl-R and Ctrl-S belong to your shell again.** At a bash or zsh prompt, in fish, a REPL,
  vim or any other program, a bare Ctrl-R and Ctrl-S reach the program, so bash's
  `(reverse-i-search)` opens and steps back with each further Ctrl-R, as in every terminal.
  aterm's find bar opened on them instead. An editor an agent opens (Claude Code's Ctrl-G
  `$EDITOR`) gets them too, on macOS and Linux. Ctrl-S reaches the terminal first, which
  pauses output until Ctrl-Q (or, on macOS, any key) unless you have run `stty -ixon`.
  Inside an agent's composer (Claude Code, Codex) they still open aterm's find, and ⌘S / ⌘R
  (Ctrl+Shift+F off macOS) open it everywhere; once the bar is open, Ctrl-R and Ctrl-S step
  through its matches.

- **The menu-bar ❯N drops another Mac's need when its read turns five minutes old.** A need
  on another Mac counts on ❯N only from a read no older than five minutes. If those five
  minutes ran out just as aterm finished telling the menu bar about a read (a Mac that missed
  that read keeps its last rows, which can be a moment from turning five minutes old, or this
  Mac slept just then), aterm missed the moment to drop the need. ❯N then kept counting it
  until the next read or until something else redrew the menu bar. It now drops at the
  five-minute mark, even when the clock passed that mark while the menu bar was being told.

## [0.107.0] - 2026-10-20

### Added

- **Managed agents run yolo by default, and `--yolo` spells it on every name.** A managed
  `claude`, `codex`, `agy` or `muse` launch now runs with every approval and sandbox off —
  AIs here have full access to do the work — each in its vendor's own spelling:
  `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for claude and agy (both refuse the literal `--yolo`),
  `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` for codex, and muse's four switches
  (`--disable-approval --disable-sandbox --trust-workspace --disable-request-user-input`).
  Typing `--yolo` (or `aterm claude --yolo`) asks for the same and always works. The exact
  command as run is printed once on stderr (`aterm: yolo (default): running 'claude'
  '--dangerously-skip-permissions' …`). A launch that types its own posture
  (`--permission-mode plan`, `--sandbox workspace-write`, …) runs exactly as typed, so a
  resumed session keeps its mode. Only the managed copies are rewritten; your own copy on
  PATH never is (`aterm help pkg`).

- **The real-Claude lab (`crates/aterm-lab`) is now in the public source.** It runs the real
  Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, agy and Muse Code inside a private headless aterm, in a macOS
  sandbox, against a local stub of each one's API, with no login, no tokens and no network
  (`targo --unverified lab help`; `lab instance` is the isolated aterm to check a change on). The
  public source also carries the workspace's `.cargo/config.toml`, so `targo --unverified lab`,
  `verify` and `ship` work in a public clone, and the lab's sandbox now keeps `~/.aterm` and
  `~/.secrets` out of reach too.
- **The step-in: one Mac of a fleet drives another, where that Mac's person lets it.** The
  fleet stays read-only by default. On a Mac, `aterm fleet allow drive --from <host|node>`
  lets the Mac that word names in its book drive its sessions; that grant holds the key the
  book bound the node to, so a node id bound afresh to another key drives nothing until it
  is granted again, `aterm fleet peers rm` takes a node's grant away (on a member too,
  where the node stays in its copy of the issuer's book), so does a read of the issuer's
  book that binds the node no more or binds it to another key, and joining another fleet
  takes every grant. A node a hand-named `[[fleet.peers]]` entry shares a place with is
  still granted by its host, node or place, or by the entry's own `host:port`, under the
  key the issuer's book binds. On a member, a Mac that only its copy of the issuer's book
  binds drives against a copy under a minute old; past that the member reads the issuer's
  book again before it admits the drive, and while the issuer cannot be reached refuses
  it, saying so. Nothing else turns it on: no join, no peer, no `settings set`.
  The named Mac then runs a worker's verbs there with a host named: `aterm ctl --host <h>
  spawn agent=claude cwd=<absolute path> - < task`, `await task @<w> since=0` (and `@<w>:<rev>`
  for every later wait), `@<w> result|status|text|screen|turn|key|send`, `hold <w> on|off`,
  and `@<w> close` of a worker it spawned since that aterm started; anything else is `ERR
  denied`. It dials only a Mac its book records, and each drive proves its node's own key, so
  the fleet secret alone drives nothing. A drive has its own share of the listener's
  connections beside the reads', and a wait's leg the peer was too busy to serve is asked
  again. A turn names a `timeout=` of at most 22 s, the drive's connection lasting 30. The
  driven Mac types each line as `<that Mac> (node <8 hex>) over the fleet` (`status
  typed_by=`): the host is that Mac's own word, the node the key it proved, and no tab of
  its own is named so. It keeps each act in its Messages. Its person wins: Take Over refuses
  every write from the other Mac, a turn already typing stopped at its next key with no
  Enter, and takes its hold away, and Hand Back lifts it. In the menu bar, a need on
  a Mac that lets this one drive it offers Take Over and Hand Back on that Mac, and every
  session this Mac holds there is listed under ❯ Held from here, with its Hand Back,
  whatever its need. Driving a Mac is typing into its shells: grant it as you would an ssh
  login. `aterm help workers` (ON ANOTHER MAC) and `aterm help fleet` (DRIVE) have the rest.

- **`aterm ctl chrome` reads the ❯ menu without a click.** On macOS, after its `statusitem`
  line, it prints a `statusmenu` line per row of the menu-bar item's menu, as the menu's own
  builder composes it now: each row's label, whether it is enabled, whether it is checked
  and its hover, `---` for a separator, and a submenu's rows indented under it (the Fleet
  row's from the fleet glance's last read). So an agent can see Take Over on <Mac>, Held
  from here, or Notify Me's state as a person clicking ❯ would, and nothing of the menu
  changes.

- **A tab says who last typed into it.** When a control client types into a tab (`aterm ctl
  send`, `key`, `paste`, `turn` and the rest), aterm credits it once per connection: by the
  tab whose shell started it — its role, else the tab name you set, else its session id;
  never a title its program set, nor a word aterm credits by — else by its process
  (`python3 (pid 4242)`); `aterm` for aterm's own harness, `the message bus` for the
  bridge, and another Mac's drive as `<that Mac> (node <8 hex>) over the fleet`. The tab's
  hover says `last typed into by lab-sweep at 14:02`, the Overview's line `typed by
  lab-sweep 4m ago`, and `aterm ctl status` and the survey's rows `typed_by=<pct|->
  typed_ms=<ms|->`. Your own keys never count.

- **Each Mac of a fleet proves which machine it is with a key of its own.** The fleet's
  secret says a machine is of the fleet, never which one, so `aterm fleet init` and `join`
