  mint `<state>/fleet-node-key` (0600; `leave` keeps it) and every fleet connection proves
  it; an older aterm proves none, and old and new still read each other. The issuer binds a
  member's node id to the key it first registers with and refuses another key for it after
  (`aterm fleet peers rm <node>` on the issuer lets a machine that lost its key join
  afresh); a member binds its issuer's key at join. An issuer from before node keys mints
  its key only at `aterm fleet init` (an update mints none), so a member that joined it
  earlier joins again after that; `aterm fleet join` says so when its issuer proves no key.
  `aterm fleet peers` lists the key each entry binds (`unbound` for one an older aterm
  recorded), and a read names a peer that claims a bound node without its key, never
  showing what it sends under that name, nor what a Mac sends whose survey names another
  node than the one it proved. No Mac of the fleet passes for yours, so none drops out of
  the menu bar's Fleet row or `aterm ctl survey --fleet` that way: one whose survey names
  another node than it proved is listed among the Macs that did not answer, and one at a
  place named by hand (`aterm fleet peers add`) that names your Mac's node without its key
  is listed unproven. Only your Mac's own key leaves it out of its own read, so a Mac that
  holds no node key (it joined before keys came) lists its own place named by hand,
  unproven, until it joins again.

- **A done report no longer ends a job while anything of it is left.** When a supervised agent
  reports its job done (in its own words after the done check, or with the legacy
  `ATERM-TASK-DONE`), aterm now looks at the repository the session works in
  (with `git`, in the background, for at most ten seconds, and never inside a folder macOS
  protects): if any change is uncommitted, any file untracked, anything stashed or any commit not
  pushed, the job goes on, and the agent is told which repository, how many of each and the first
  few paths, and to commit and push them without deleting, overwriting or force-pushing anything.
  The same goes for a report that still names any follow-up, open item or next step, one that is
  blocked on a person or a decision included: the agent is told what its report names. The
  challenge comes back at every such report, not once a job, at the same growing pause the done
  check uses (2, 4, 8 … up to 60 minutes; a worker another session waits on gets it at once for its
  first three short turns), so an agent can never talk its way out of unfinished work, and is
  never pushed in a tight loop either. This holds in cruise and in land (where it asks for the
  step in hand to be finished and what is left to be written down and committed), and after a
  relaunch or an update. The agent primer (v29) teaches agents the rule, and the supervise-agent
  skill tells a lead what a worker's `done` now means. A report that says
  `Nothing left` or `Left: none` over a clean, pushed repository still ends the job at once.
- **aterm Caffeine: a mug in the menu bar that keeps your Mac awake.** `aterm caffeine` puts
  a coffee mug with an "a" on it in the menu bar. A click fills it and keeps the Mac, and its
  display, from sleeping while idle until the next click empties it. A right click (or a
  Control-click) opens its menu: a line about it, Activate for 1 Hour, 8 Hours, 24 Hours or
  Forever (the one in effect is checked, and a timed one shows its time left), Enable at
  Startup, which puts the mug back in the menu bar at every login, and Quit Caffeine, which
  turns it off and takes the mug out of the menu bar. From a terminal,
  `aterm caffeine on [1h|8h|24h|forever|<n>h|<n>m]`, `off`, `status`, `startup on|off` and
  `quit` do the same. Only idle sleep is held off: closing a laptop's lid or choosing Sleep
  still sleeps the Mac. A timed span runs on the clock, so time asleep counts, and a restart
  of the Mac starts the mug off. The mug runs as its own background job from its
  own copy of aterm (removed when it quits), so quitting aterm leaves it running and opening aterm from the Finder or
  the Dock still opens a window. Uninstalling the last aterm asks it to quit and removes its
  login item; shared files stay while another install uses them or if shutdown or an idle
  lock cannot be confirmed. The small lock file itself remains. Status reports the saved
  request and mug process, while the icon and tooltip follow whether the mug holds an
  activity. macOS only;
  `aterm help caffeine` has the rest.
- **Every window shows what the machine, aterm and the current tab are doing.** A band under the
  titlebar, on by default, draws each CPU core as a square that fills with its use, glows while
  load is rising, keeps a faint mark of its recent peak and frays when the load is jumpy, grouped
  by performance and efficiency cores. Beside them sit the GPU, and three rows (Global, aterm and
  Tab), each with its share of all cores, a one-minute trace and its memory, with memory pressure
  and swap on the Global row. Under them are the free space on the disk the tab is in, the
  busiest process and the tab's program. It updates once a second while a window is focused,
  every five seconds when none is, and not at all while every window is hidden. To turn it off,
  set `stats_bars = "off"` under `[sys]` in `aterm.toml`; the change applies at once.
- **A supervised Muse Code moves onto a newer build by itself, when it is idle.** When aterm's
  package manager installs a newer Muse Code, a Muse Code that aterm supervises is restarted onto
  it at a genuinely idle point: its turn over, nothing of its own still running (a shell it sent
  to the background, the turn it takes when that shell ends, a subagent's work), no process under
  it at all, nothing in its prompt and nobody typing in its tab, and the new build checked to
  start. Muse Code is then ended and started again through your managed `muse` on the very same
  session, in its project folder, with the options it was launched with, and nothing is typed into
  it before or after: its next turn simply runs on the newer build with every earlier turn. A Muse
  Code that its supervisor keeps going turn after turn is moved at the end of a turn too: the
  supervisor holds its continuation for the moment the restart needs. aterm never asks Muse Code
  to stop first (`[harness] upgrade_ask` is Claude Code's alone), and never moves one that is
  busy, mid-turn or waiting on its own work. A newer Muse Code wakes only your Muse Code tabs: a
  Claude Code tab's own upgrade is not disturbed by it. `[harness] upgrade = false` or
  `[harness.muse] enabled = false` turns it off.

- **A Gemini CLI tab is brought back after a crash, and when aterm restores its windows.**
  When Gemini CLI crashes in a supervised tab (its node process or the child it runs killed),
  aterm types `gemini --resume <id>` for the very session it was in, in its project folder,
  through the `gemini` on your PATH, with the `--model`, approval mode and other options it was
  launched with — but never its first prompt again — and once it is back on that session and
  idle tells it to carry on. Gemini CLI writes no record of which session a running process
  has, so aterm reads it from the one session file of that project begun right after the
  process started; where that cannot tell (a `/clear`, an in-app `/resume`, or another Gemini
  CLI started in the same project at the same moment) aterm types nothing and tells you so.
  Gemini CLI's own resume loads an empty copy of a session after two resumes in a row with no
  turn between; aterm reads the session's files first and, where that would happen, tells you
  instead of typing it, and never suggests resuming it. Its own exits (`/quit`, Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D twice) and a start it refused are left alone, a
  session that took no turn is not resumed (you are told), and a resume it refuses is typed
  once, never again. After aterm crashes or quits, the reopened tab brings its Gemini CLI back
  on its session the same way. Gemini CLI is not moved onto a newer build while it runs (it is
  a Homebrew or npm install), and `aterm ctl restart` does not end it (it ignores SIGTERM).

- **An agy tab is brought back after a crash, and when aterm restores its windows.** When agy
  (the Antigravity CLI) crashes in a supervised tab, aterm types `agy --conversation=<id>` for
  the very conversation it was in, in the folder it was launched from, through your managed
  `agy` (so the newest installed build, with its own updater off), with the `--effort`,
  `--model` and `--mode` it was launched with, which a conversation does not keep — but not
  `--agent`, `--add-dir` or a project, which it does — and once it is back and idle tells it
  to carry on. A crash is told apart by the crash report agy leaves behind only when it is
  killed: every way out of its own, and a SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGINT, are left alone, and
  Ctrl-Z, which only stops it, is never taken for a crash. Nothing is typed while another agy
  has that conversation open, however it was opened there (`--conversation`, `-c` or
  `/resume`). If agy refuses the relaunch, aterm types it once, never again;
  if agy comes back on a fresh conversation instead of its own, aterm tells you and types
  nothing into it. After aterm crashes or quits, the reopened tab brings its agy back on its
  conversation the same way, and `aterm ctl restart` (and `[harness] stall_term`) can restart
  a frozen agy on its conversation, but only where aterm can start it again: through your
  managed `agy` for one aterm installed, or on its own program for any other. An agy run as
  its tab's own program (`aterm -e agy`, or after `exec agy`) has no shell to come back in, so
  it is neither relaunched nor restarted there, as a Claude Code or Muse Code run that way is
  not. agy is not yet moved onto a newer build while it runs.

- **Windows: the app folder carries its own console host.** `apps/aterm-win/build.ps1` lays
  Microsoft's signed OpenConsole.exe 1.25.2609.30003 beside aterm.exe, pinned by version and
  SHA-256 (from nuget.org's Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY), `install.ps1` installs it with
  its licence and notices (and removes it when installing a folder built with
  `-NoOpenConsole`), the MSIX carries it and `uninstall.ps1` removes it, so `conpty = "auto"`
  no longer needs Windows Terminal or copies anything into `%LOCALAPPDATA%`. A copy taken from
  Windows Terminal now replaces the older ones instead of piling up, and `aterm --window
  --show-config` gains a `console_host:` row naming the host a new tab gets, with its version
  and path.

- **Windows: the taskbar jump list offers your recent directories.** Right-clicking aterm's
  taskbar button (or its pinned tile) now lists, above New Window, a Recent group of the last
  six folders you ran a command in, each opening a new aterm window there. Only local drive
  folders that still exist are offered (never network shares, `\\wsl$` or a WSL or SSH
  tab's Linux path); "Remove from this list" removes one until you work there again; and
  while Windows' "Show recently opened items in Start, Jump Lists and File Explorer" is off,
  aterm keeps no list at all. The list lives in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\aterm\jumplist-recent.txt`.

- **Windows: a bell in a window you are not looking at badges its taskbar button.** Besides
  the brief flash, an orange dot now stays on aterm's taskbar button until that window comes
  forward (screen readers read it as "A tab rang the bell"). Windows' "Show badges on taskbar
  apps" setting hides it.

- **Windows: an overlay scrollbar.** Each pane shows where it is in its scrollback in its right
  gutter, as Windows Terminal and every Fluent scroll view do: nothing at the live bottom, a
  thin thumb while the view scrolls that fades a second later, and a quieter thumb that stays
  while the view is parked in history, so a view that is not live always says so. Under the
  pointer the thumb widens over a faint track: drag it to move through history, or click the
  track to page. At rest it is WinUI's two-pixel indicator (four at 200%), the same width and
  shade at the window's edge and on the divider between two split panes, where it covers the
  divider's line and leans away from the focus line beside it; the thumb on the divider used
  to be a one-pixel lit line and the one at the window's edge a three-pixel grey pill, two
  scrollbars in one split. It draws in the window's padding (for an inner pane, on the
  divider, clear of the text) and never takes a column, so
  showing it resizes no program; Reduce Motion hides it
  without the fade. `scrollbar = false` in `aterm.toml` turns it off; macOS and Linux keep
  the brief scroll pill unless `scrollbar = true`. A Settings page that scrolls shows the same
  thumb at the window's edge, in the page's margin outside the cards, at the same two pixels
  and shade as the terminal's (on every platform, in its own chrome's width), where it was a
  third style, a blurred three-pixel grey bar inside the cards that ran across the gaps
  between them.

- **Set every session's Autopilot at once.** Wherever two or more coding-agent sessions are
  open, Settings ▸ Harness's SESSIONS ends with an **Every session** row that says how they
  stand (`5 sessions: 3 cruising, 1 landing, 1 off`) and offers **Cruise**, **Land**, a
  **Timer** (1 hour, 2 hours, 4 hours, or until `[harness] land_at`) and **Follow the default** for all
  of them. Before you leave, Land or 2 h; when you are back, Cruise. A press never turns the
  harness on for a session that is off, by its own setting or the default's: Land lands every
  cruising session, Cruise gives Cruise back to every landing or timed one (so it undoes a
  bulk Land or Timer, though not the timers a Land cancelled), a Timer lands every cruising
  session at the same moment, and Follow the default clears each session's own setting but an
  Off. Each button says how many sessions it moves, the timers it cancels and what stays
  (`Land 3 sessions and cancel 2 timers; the 1 off stays off`), and a press that moves nothing
  writes nothing. There is no bulk Off: Supervise coding agents is that switch, and turning it
  back on gives every session back as it was; only under a default of Off does Follow the
  default turn sessions off, and it says so (`…, which is Off: the harness lets go of them`).
  The row sits after the sessions' own rows, so its coming or going moves none of their
  buttons; it moves with them, so a click that a session opening or closing (or a press) moved
  onto it under a still pointer, or onto a session's button from it, does nothing but light
  what is there now, and the next click is the one you meant. `aterm ctl act` presses it by its keys, `harness/session/all/…`, which are
  Owner-only like a session's.

- **Settings ▸ Harness lists the choices the harness made for you today.** A new card,
  DECIDED FOR YOU, under SESSIONS shows the question dialogs it answered and why it took that
  option (`no option was marked Recommended, so it took the first`), the questions asked in
  prose it answered and with what, the boxes full power answered that no safe rule proved
  (`pressed Yes`, or `chose "Not now"` where it took another option; a run of presses of one
  command under one switch is one row, `×3`, naming Approve permission boxes: All), the boxes
  it declined with the reason it gave, and the limit resets it kept unspent, with why in
  words. Each row has its clock time, names its session by its tab, and has **Show tab**
  while the session is open; the newest three are shown and **Show all** lists the rest of
  the day's. STATUS counts them (`3 choices made for you`). The card is drawn only on a day
  with a choice, is read from the ledgers in the page's one reading, and is no alert.

- **Settings ▸ Harness ▸ Tab Control lists the tabs of every aterm on this Mac.** A new page
  (`/tabs`) lists this Mac and the Macs `aterm machines` manages, the aterms running on each,
  and every open tab with its program and what its AI CLI is doing (working, waiting on a
  permission box, idle at its prompt), with **Show tab** for a tab of this aterm. Another
  aterm's tabs are read over its control socket with that aterm's own token, the way `aterm
  ctl` reads them; nothing is sent to an aterm whose token cannot be read.

- **`aterm machines`: configure and keep configured a lab of Macs from this one, over SSH on
  the LAN, with no MDM and no Apple account.** One Mac, the controller, keeps an inventory
  (`machines.toml`, edited without losing your comments), the baselines each Mac should hold,
  a fleet SSH key and two signing keys. After one visit to each Mac (Remote Login with full
  disk access for remote users, Screen Sharing), `enroll` installs a root agent under one
  digest-pinned sudoers rule; the fleet key runs only the agent's dispatcher, and everything
  done as root needs an envelope the controller signed, which the Mac checks with Apple's own
  `ssh-keygen`. `plan` and `apply` bring Macs to their baseline, each setting probed, changed
  and read back: Caps Lock as Control for every keyboard, Siri, analytics, ads, AirDrop and
  widgets off, no Setup Assistant panes, names, firewall, power, time and update settings,
  the Command Line Tools, Homebrew and its formulae, pinned apps (Emacs, Caffeine, gh) checked
  by hash and Team ID, aterm itself with its CLI and toolset, and a per-Mac GitHub key for each
  user, registered with a GitHub machine user by the key itself (`github revoke` keeps a
  revoked key from ever being registered again). The plain commands take the defaults and
  ask nothing: `init` makes the signing keys with no passphrase unless you pass `--passphrase`
  (a key with one is asked for once per command, and not at all once ssh-agent holds it),
  `enroll <address>` logs in as your login name and trusts the Mac's host key on first use
  unless `--fingerprint` checks it, and `plan` with no host plans them all. `status` and
  `outstanding` read the newest reports, with any refusal (a changed host key, a busy host)
  beside them as a failure, never as "unreachable"; after `enroll` and an `apply`,
  `person <host> --here` at the Mac walks the Full Disk Access and Developer Tools switches
  only a person can flip; `screen <host>` walks them over Screen Sharing and locks the Mac
  again if you logged in there, also when you stop it with Ctrl-C, and the Mac locks itself a
  minute after aterm is killed or cut off from it; and `scan` lists the Macs on the LAN. aterm
  now declares Local Network use (`_ssh._tcp`, `_sftp-ssh._tcp`, `_rfb._tcp`), so macOS asks
  once before aterm reaches the LAN. Every Mac is named for what it is by default: `apply` renames it from what
  it reads of itself, `m10 MacBook Pro M4 Max 36GB 1TB` (`m10-MacBook-Pro-M4-Max-36GB-1TB.local`;
  the disk is its internal one at the size Apple sells it, whatever disk it started from),
  keeping the tag its old name started with, which is also the name `enroll` gives it, and
  finds it at its new `.local` name even when the apply's report was lost, as it finds a Mac
  held by an IP address that DHCP moved, once ssh answers there under its pinned host key.
  `enroll --found` enrolls every Mac `scan` sees (or `enroll` several addresses) with the
  admin's password typed once, kept in memory only and fed to each Mac's ssh and sudo through
  pipes, and `apply --all --only names` renames the whole fleet without the rest of the
  baseline. macOS only. `aterm help machines` has the rest.

- **The menu-bar ❯ reads the fleet.** On a Mac in a fleet, its Fleet row says how many
  Macs answered, how many agents they run and when it read them, and opens onto the Macs
  that need you or are working (needs first), the quiet ones, the ones that did not
  answer, the ones whose key is not proven (each row marked `key not proven`: what that
  Mac says is its word alone, so none of its needs counts or posts a notice, nothing
  offers Take Over or Hand Back on it, and neither the node nor the host it names for
  itself is taken; its row says to update aterm there and join it again, and `aterm
  fleet peers` shows its KEY, or, where this Mac binds no key to its issuer because it
  joined before node keys came, that no Mac's key is proven here until this Mac joins
  again, once its issuer has a key: `aterm fleet init` there mints one) and the ones on
  an older aterm (listed, never counted: update them), with Read the Fleet Now. This
  Mac, named by hand among its own peers, proves its own node key there, so the read
  takes it for this Mac and the menu leaves it out.
  A need on another Mac counts on ❯N, from a read no older than five
  minutes, and its row offers Read This Session (the survey in a tab), Screen Sharing to
  that Mac and Copy "ssh <it>", and Take Over and Hand Back on that Mac where its person
  lets this Mac drive it (see the step-in above); any other Mac's row says it is
  read-only from here. The read is one
  `aterm ctl survey --fleet` child at a time, every minute on the issuer or with
  `[fleet] watch = true`, else when the menu opens; a read that fails never moves the
  count, and a Mac that misses one read keeps its last rows (for up to five minutes). When every Mac refuses with no route, the row says to allow aterm under Local
  Network in Privacy & Security (a click opens it), and one line under To look at says
  so too. Once you turn on ❯ ▸ Notify Me When I'm Needed, a need on another Mac posts one
  desktop notice, as a local one does, and only one while it stands, however old the last read or however often that Mac misses one,
  and across a seamless update of aterm (a need that arose during the update is told);
  a restart of aterm tells the needs standing then once more.

- **A fleet: the aterms of your LAN read each other's sessions, and drive one only where
  its person lets them.** Run
  `aterm fleet init` on one machine. It becomes the fleet's issuer, mints a 160-bit secret
  and writes the join code to a file (0600) whose path it prints; the code carries the
  secret, so it is never printed. The code names the issuer by its LAN name (on a Mac the
  HostName an administrator set, else its Bonjour `<LocalHostName>.local`, which DHCP does
  not change; `--host` names another), and a member joins under its own the same way. Copy
  that file to each other machine (AirDrop or scp, not a chat) and run `aterm fleet join
  --code-file <file>` there (or pipe the code in, or type it at the terminal, unshown); a
  code is never taken as an argument, and a failed join (a typo, an issuer that is down)
  writes nothing of the fleet (no key, book or `[fleet]`; at most this machine's node id).
  Both write `[fleet] listen` and `allow` into aterm.toml, and the running aterm starts
  listening (port 7100 unless `--port` names another) without a relaunch. `aterm ctl survey
  --fleet` then reads every session on every machine of the fleet, run on any one of them,
  each machine within one deadline (3 s, `--timeout` up to 10; past the first 32 at once, a
  machine waits for a free place and has the deadline of its own), with one line and its
  reason for each machine that did not answer. The issuer keeps the fleet's roster, its book
  of members; a member asks the issuer for that book first, under the same deadline, and
  keeps a copy for the times the issuer is asleep. An issuer running an older aterm shares
  no book: the read then ends with a line saying it reached only the machines this one
  knows. `--host <name|node|address>` reads one machine in full. `--allow facts` (the
  default) lets a peer read programs, agent states, roles (a label word, redacted; a role
  written as text is content), task records and models, and no other text anyone wrote;
  `--allow content` adds tab titles, cwds, prompts, an agent's newest words and a shell's
  last lines, each redacted. The read names the peers that allow facts alone in one closing
  line, so a reader knows why it has no words of theirs, and a peer running more than one
  aterm says `1 of N instances read` on its header: the instance holding its fleet port is
  the one read. `aterm fleet peers` lists and checks the machines this one knows (3 s,
  `--timeout` up to 10; `peers add` and `rm`, and `[[fleet.peers]] host = "…"` in
  aterm.toml, name them by hand), `aterm fleet init --rotate` gives the issuer a new secret
  after a machine is lost (the book keeps every member and the report lists them: each joins
  again, and the lost one is yours to `peers rm`), and `aterm fleet leave` removes this
  machine's secret, code, book and `[fleet]` keys (on the issuer, the fleet goes with it).
  The listener speaks TLS 1.3, and every connection proves the secret both ways before a
  byte of the survey moves; it admits loopback, private and link-local addresses only, holds
  at most 16 connections (8 for an app the Dock launched), and answers a peer `survey`, at
  the level this machine allows, and `version`, and on the issuer a member's `join` and its
  read of the book of members (node ids, host names, addresses, ports and versions, never a
  session's words), nothing else. No peer types into a session unless this Mac's person
  lets that one machine drive it (the step-in above). On macOS 15 and later the first connection into the LAN asks to let aterm find
  devices on the local network, and aterm's request says why: allow it. When no peer could
  be reached because every connection had no route to its host, which is how that privacy
  setting turns an app away, the survey says where in System Settings to allow it; when
  every one had no route to its network, that this machine is offline or a VPN holds the
  route; when a sandbox around the reader (Claude Code's) refused every connection, to read
  from outside it. Each peer's own line leads with its cause and remedy, which a long
  machine name gives way to.

- **Workers: a Claude Code session hands a task to another Claude Code in a new tab, waits
  for it, and reads its report.** `aterm ctl @self spawn agent=claude -`, with the task on
  stdin (up to 64 KiB, any number of lines), opens a background tab of your window in this
  folder (`cwd=` names another, `model=` its model, `identity=` a login of its own) and
  starts Claude Code there with the task as its first prompt: the task goes to a 0600 file
  the new shell names, and none of it is typed or pasted. It runs the Claude Code its starter
  runs, under the same Claude home and login: a relative `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as the directory
  it named for the starter, and the starter's own `HOME` where that is not yours and its
  Claude Code keeps its records there. The window's harness carries the
  worker until it is done, which is when it ends its report with `ATERM-TASK-DONE` or says
  twice that it is done. `aterm ctl @<sid> task` is its record: `working`, `done`,
  `exited`, or `stalled` (its shell drew no prompt within 20 s, or no Claude Code composer
  showed within 120 s, and its attention names what holds the screen; or, started, it sat
  120 s at a screen no harness rule knows with nothing moving, `why=held`, and its attention
  names what the screen shows). `aterm ctl await task @a,@b since=0`, run as a background
  command, exits once one of them has news, and every later wait names the rev each worker's
  last row printed (`@b:<rev>`), so nothing that finished in between is missed. `aterm ctl
  @<sid> result` prints the report the worker ended its task with, read from its transcript,
  never its screen (`result full`: the whole exchange); where the harness's done check
  ended the task, that is the report before the check followed by the reply's own words,
  when the worker verified or fixed more in answer to it. A one-line follow-up is `aterm ctl
  @<sid> turn typed=1 settle=submitted '<line>'`, which answers as soon as the line has left
  Claude Code's input box (see Changed), not when the screen goes quiet, which Claude Code's
  animated screen never does; `await task @<sid>:<task_rev>` then waits for that follow-up's
  own done. `spawn agent=` answers `ERR unsupervised: <switch>` and spawns nothing when the
  harness would not carry the worker (`[harness] enabled = false`, `[harness] headless =
  false` in a headless instance, `[harness.claude] enabled = false`, or `[harness] autopilot
  = "off"`). A worker that cannot start is closed again and its task file removed, a
  worker's task file and its result files go when its session closes or aterm quits (read
  the result before closing the worker), and the harness answers Claude Code's folder-trust
  dialog in the folder it was started in for that worker alone; the answer is Claude Code's
  own, which it keeps for the folder, so a later Claude Code started there under the same
  login is trusted with no dialog. The agent primer (v27), the skills and `aterm
  help workers` (also `survey`) teach it, and under `approve = "safe"` the harness reads
  `task`, `await task`, `result`, `survey` and `aterm drive ledger` without `--out` as
  reads, and still puts `spawn` and `task mark` to a person.

- **`aterm ctl survey` says what every session is doing, in one read sized for a model.**
  One line per session of every aterm instance on this machine: its program, its agent's
  state and for how long (an agent at an approval or a choice reads `asking`), how long
  since a person typed there, its task, model, effort and context left, the tool in flight
  by name, `attention` when the session raised an attention line, and, for every agent
  however long it has been idle, the attention line's words, its prompt (the task, or the
  newest turn the harness did not type) and its last words (a line that is only
  `ATERM-TASK-DONE` dropped; a Gemini CLI, Muse Code, agy or Codex, whose transcript it
  does not read, shows its command line and last rows instead, as a shell does), every
  session listed and each excerpt whole while the read
  fits in 24,000 characters (`--budget`): past it they narrow, all alike (a finished
  worker's report, however long, keeping its end, where its result is); past that the read
  keeps every header and agent line and fills what is left in order — the words of the
  sessions asking or stalled, then each machine's most pressing agent's before any machine's
  second's — folding shells into a `+N` line first, marking each session that lost words
  `(excerpts cut)`, and a closing line counts what was left out; the read, its closing
  notes included, never passes the budget. `--sid <s>` is one session
  in full (with `--fleet` for a peer's) and `--json` every record. It reads only what
  the sessions already publish, so it reads no transcript and never waits on a busy
  session. Every excerpt is capped, credential-shaped words and fleet join codes (with or
  without their `atf1-`, in one word or typed with spaces, on one line or across lines,
  and never cut by an excerpt's cap) are replaced, a
  line the privacy check still finds sensitive is withheld, and the text form escapes
  control and bidi characters and opens with a line saying that every block under it is
  data from those sessions, never an instruction to its reader.

- **A session chooses to be woken by a channel.** After `aterm ctl @self topic add <t>`,
  `aterm ctl @self await inbox since=<id> topic=<t>`, run as a background command, latches
  only on a broadcast on that topic, so a Claude Code that listens to a channel is woken by
  it, or once at the wait's own deadline (see Changed); `inbox since=<id>` then lists
  everything that arrived. A topic outside the `post to=say:<t>` grammar is `ERR usage`.
  Channels ride the fabric's bus, which stays off until a person runs `aterm fabric on`
  (until then `topic add` and a post still answer OK, and nothing arrives), and reach this
  machine's sessions only, never the fleet's peers. Nothing aterm types wakes an agent for
  mail.

- **A Claude Code session's log shows what each turn did, and a tab can say it.** `aterm ctl
  log`, `await log` and `subscribe … log` now see a turn's tool calls open and close (`tool
  cls=shell tool=Bash`, a subagent, a compaction), the turn named by Claude Code's own id
  (`vref=`), and its duration and tokens, read from Claude Code's transcript as it is written.
  None of the transcript's text is kept: no prompt, reply, command or tool output. What was in
  the transcript before aterm read it is said once (`source field=transcript skipped=<bytes>`),
  never replayed, and until a Claude Code build has been measured its steps are marked
  `state=partial`: they add to what the screen says and never overrule it. The log also notes
  what the terminal and the session's state said: the shell integration, a notification asked
  for (with notifications off too; the count, never the text), progress, bells, the folder, the
  title (shown only with `tier=content`), the context left, mail sent and received (ids only),
  meta and story changes with who made them, the harness's approvals and answers, and usage
  readings while the usage tap is on. `brief` keeps every line it had before and gains count
  lines, `mail in N · out M` (now that mail is noted) and `acts N · stories M`, and the
  transcript's steps and numbers when they fit. A tight budget sheds the count lines first,
  then the transcript's steps and numbers, before any line it had before. With the journal on, the folder, meta values (the supervisor's attention text only
  as a fingerprint) and mail's senders and recipients reach it too; never a command's arguments,
  an OSC title or the transcript's text. With `[session_log] clause =
  true` in `aterm.toml` (off by default), a terminal tab's tooltip and context menu add a `now:`
  line (`now: running shell`, `now: approval · bash`, or a label the harness or you set; never
  one another program set with `aterm ctl mark`). Off, the tooltip and menu are exactly as they
  were.

- **A session's log says who dismissed an approval box or question, and what a worker's task
  did.** `aterm ctl key` and `send` take a leading `act=approve`, `act=deny` or `act=answer`
  saying what the input means for the box or question it dismisses (given twice or misspelt, it
  is refused and nothing is typed), and the window's harness now sends it with each press that
  dismisses a box or question. In `aterm ctl log` the box then closes `out=approved`, `declined`
  or `answered` when the harness dismissed it, and `out=passed by=<who>` for anyone else (`by=-`
  when no input closed it); an input whose box had already closed when it was typed is marked
  `re=<that box>` and dismisses nothing. Acted inputs are marked one by one while their
  author's mark allowance lasts, and the next one says how many went unmarked (`dropped=`). A
  worker's task moving (working, done, exited, stalled) is a `task` mark, and a self-supervising
  codex-alab's acts are `act` marks. A person's first input to reach the program after mail
  arrives is marked `human`, and a burst whose input reached no program (a view scroll, a
  selection) is marked `human reached=0`, which answers no mail. `aterm ctl help log` and the
  drive-aterm and supervise-agent skills now say how to read `log` and `brief`. An aterm older
  than this types `act=` as text, so send it only where `aterm ctl help send` names it. Nothing
  new is turned on by default, and no new kind of record reaches the fabric.

- **aterm keeps a short log of what it did itself, and one read briefs every aterm on this
  machine.** `aterm ctl log n` (yours only, like `brief all`) reads the instance's own log, kept
  in memory and never written to disk or the fabric: when it started and how the run before it
  ended (`start prev_end=`), each move of its fabric link (`link state=`), and each setting that
  changed on a reload (`config key=`, the name only, never the value). `aterm ctl survey --brief` prints, for
  every aterm running here, newest first, the latest 32 records of that log and its sessions'
  briefs, all within one budget (`--budget`, 24,000 characters by default), and counts what it
  left out. `aterm ctl await log` takes a comma list of up to four waits (`need,close=turn`),
  answered by whichever comes first. When the window's harness relaunches a session or moves it
  onto a new build, the session's log says so (`act word=relaunch`), counted in `brief`'s `acts`
  line. A turn's close now repeats the turn's `ledger=`, and `aterm drive ledger --source log`
  times the manager's turns and mail by the session log's own records, joined by id and never by
  time (the default, `--source anchor`, is unchanged); a turn the log no longer holds is
  counted, not guessed. Claude Code 2.1.303 has been measured, so its transcript's steps are no
  longer `state=partial`: its transcript can close a turn and confirm a usage wall. Every other
  build stays partial. `aterm ctl metrics percentiles` says how long reading a Claude Code
  transcript held the session (`n_tx_chunk`, `tx_chunk_p50/p95/p99_ms`, `max_tx_hold_ms`).
  Nothing new is turned on by default, and nothing new reaches the fabric.

- **On each Mac, aterm asks once whether to allow debugger access.** When lldb or Xcode takes
  control of a program, macOS can stop it with a "Developer Tools Access" password dialog that
  waits, for hours if nobody is at the Mac, until someone answers it; macOS's developer mode
  stops that dialog for administrator accounts (measured with lldb on macOS 26.6 and 27.0) and
  for standard accounts in the `_developer` group (measured on 27.0). So the first time aterm runs
  on a Mac, after the Full Disk Access and Developer Tools pages and before it asks for your
  folders, it waits for a pause in your typing and asks once, in its own alert: the same alert
  as Settings ▸ Security's **Allow Debugger Access…**, saying what the switch changes for the
  whole Mac and what it exposes. **Allow…** turns it on as that button does: macOS then asks
  for an administrator password in its own dialog, which names Apple's tool SamplingTools
  rather than aterm, and which aterm never sees or answers. **Cancel**, the default, leaves it
  off. Either way aterm does not ask on that Mac again, unless its record of the Macs it asked
  on (beside `aterm.toml`) is deleted, or a config folder shared by more than eight Macs drops
  the oldest; you can change your answer at any time in
  Settings ▸ Security, or turn it off in a terminal with `/usr/sbin/DevToolsSecurity -disable`.
  Turned off either way, macOS then asks for the password at every new debugger, not once
  every 10 hours as before debugger access was ever on; the Turn Off alert and Settings say so.
  A Mac you already use aterm on is asked once too, when this version first runs there. aterm
  does not ask where debugger access is already on or was on before, where it would not help
  your account, or from a development build, and `[privacy] notice = false` keeps the question
  from coming up.

- **The debugger words in `aterm help permissions` are measured now.** `sample`, `leaks`,
  `vmmap`, `heap` and `atos` do not raise the "Developer Tools Access" dialog, where the help
  said they should not: measured with developer mode off on macOS 26.6 and 27.0. The help no
  longer says a parked debugger finishes whenever the dialog is answered: lldb waits about 30
  seconds, and answered later its attach fails and the program it was attaching to is killed,
  so the help says to tell your operator before attaching to a program you cannot restart.
  Cancel does not end lldb's attach either: it asks again, ten times in all. The help also
  names the route that needs no dialog: a program you built, signed ad hoc with
  `com.apple.security.get-task-allow`, takes lldb's attach without asking. Over ssh, where no
  dialog can appear, the help says lldb fails at once and only developer mode changes that.

- (developer tool) **`lab reduce` turns a Claude Code transcript or a Codex rollout into its
  keys alone** (`lab reduce <file> --program claude|codex [--out FILE]`): the rows' own keys, row
  order, numbers and the closed words the readers read are kept; a key inside a tool's input or
  output (the second copy of each call's input Claude Code keys by the call's id among them), in
  a tool's schema wherever it sits (all three places Claude Code writes its tool list among
  them), in what Claude Code sends or attaches for the model, or naming a file it tracks, is
  renamed; dates (Codex's millisecond times with them) are moved to a fixed day; ids are
  remapped one to one, where a key names one too; a notice becomes its wall's canonical phrase;
  and every other string is emptied, so a lab-read build's rows can be committed without
  anything anyone said. A relative `<file>` or `--out` is read from the directory you ran it in.

- (developer tool) **`lab crash` crashes a lab's aterm and starts it again on the same state**
  (`lab crash <tag> [--gap SECS] [--keep-tree]`): the lab's own instance, by the pid its
  `env.sh` records and only while that pid is still the lab's, is SIGKILLed, and after the gap
  (a day at most) it is relaunched as `lab restore` does. Without `--keep-tree` what of its
  tree outlives it 15 s is ended by pid; with it, under a PTY keeper, the agent lives through
  the crash and the next instance's loop follows the first loop's records. `LAB_INSTANCE_ENV`
  at `up` names variables (`TMPDIR` and the `ATERM_DEBUG_*` dev seams only) every launch of the
  lab's instance gets; any other name is refused.

- (developer tool) **`lab sleep` puts a lab's aterm through a sleep of the Mac, and the Mac
  never sleeps** (`lab sleep <tag> --for SECS [--hold SECS] [--at-act [--rule RULE] [--within
  SECS]]`, on a lab brought up with `LAB_CLOCK=1`). `LAB_CLOCK=1 lab up` builds the lab's clock
  (`crates/aterm-lab-clock`), a library that moves the wall clocks, and the clocks that count a
  sleep, of the lab's instance and its Claude Code by an offset the lab keeps. The system clock
  is never touched. Claude Code's hardened runtime refuses the library, so the lab runs an ad
  hoc signed copy of it. `lab sleep` stops the lab's own instance, by the pid its `env.sh`
  records and only while that pid is still the lab's. It moves the offset by `--for` seconds,
  keeps the instance stopped `--hold` seconds more, and continues it however the verb ends. With
  `--at-act` it first waits for the harness to type its next continuation (of `--rule` alone if
  given) and stops the instance the moment it is journaled, so the sleep falls inside that
  turn. An instance that ends while it is stopped is reported gone, with the offset it left.
  `LAB_INSTANCE_ENV` and `claude -e` still refuse the clock's variables.

### Changed

- **The session journal stays opt-in.** `[session_log] journal = true` in `aterm.toml` still
  turns it on, and it stays off by default, now as a settled choice rather than a pending one:
  the journal keeps each command's first word as typed, so a secret typed at a prompt and run
  as a command would be kept on disk, and that should happen only on a Mac whose person asked
  for it. Off, aterm creates no file or folder for it and deletes nothing, as before.

- **Settings ▸ Harness leads with the verdict, and counts what Land delivers.** EFFECT OF
  EACH AUTOPILOT now comes right after the page's buttons, ahead of SUPERVISION and WHAT THE
  HARNESS DID. Where Cruise and Off each have 10 minutes of working time, it opens with
  `Working time held at a box or a question` and each side's share in large type, each with
  its own working time (`<1% of 6h 10m on Cruise   14% of 25m off`), so 14% of 3 minutes off
  no longer reads like 14% of 3 hours; the Held row, which said the same, gives way to it.
  With Cruise time and no Off time it says `Set a session Off to measure plain Claude Code
  beside Cruise`. A new Ends row counts Land's landings and quiet ends, each once however
  often a restart restates it (a landing that went quiet and then landed after all is one),
  and the median time from setting Land to landed (`Land landed 5, quiet 1 · Land to landed:
  about 6m (5)`; a landing begun before a relaunch or an update counts with no time), kept
  in the same 7-day book as the card's other numbers: a seamless update keeps only what the
  page had read before it, so the count can be lower than the landing records in Settings ▸
  Messages. The Ends and Unsupervised rows now stand before they count anything (`none yet`,
  `none`), so a landing in the background changes their words without moving the switches
  under them. Measured says the moment the numbers stop at (`7 days, since Mon 09:12, to
  14:05`). The book's files stay readable by older aterm builds, which skip the new counts.

- **Agent image changes wake tab naming.** aterm samples the foreground image at observed
  handoffs and after accepted shell command markers, and rechecks unresolved shells and its own
  launchers as output arrives. A relevant image publication wakes naming without waiting for the
  next periodic status pass. These sampled observations do not guarantee detection of every exec
  or a fixed time to naming.

- **The harness no longer carries a Claude Code session onto usage credits unless you turn that
  on.** Continuing on usage credits is now an opt-in, `[harness] usage_credits = true` in
  aterm.toml (only the `[harness]` table's own line turns it on; Settings ▸ Manual lists it as
  "Continue on usage credits"). By default the harness keeps every session on your subscription:
  - a Claude Code box that asks to go on with usage credits (`Continue with …` under
    `<model> now uses usage credits`, or the Usage credits dialog's `Continue with usage
    credits`) is no longer taken for you: it is cancelled with Esc, which saves nothing
    (`credits-decline@v1`), and goes to the menu bar only where it shows no `Esc to cancel`.
    Taken, a model's `Continue with <model>` is kept by Claude Code for good for that model and
    account; the Usage credits dialog's saves nothing and carries the session onto the credits
    already on in your account. With the key on, its yes is logged as `credits-consent@v1`;
  - a model's limit that asks for that consent gets what `continue = false` gives it: a move to
    another account where your accounts advise one, else your `model_fallback`, else the limit's
    reset waited out. A limit only usage credits lift, naming no reset (`You're out of usage
    credits`, `<model> requires usage credits`), is relaunched on your `model_fallback` where it
    can be, else told to you once;
  - while Claude Code says usage credits carry a session (`Now using usage credits` with credits
    switched on in your account, or `<model> is drawing from usage credits` for a model billed
    per request), the harness types none of its own turns into it (no continuation, retry,
    `/compact` or limit's continuation either), and holds its own steps there too; your own
    turns are yours. It moves the session to another account where your accounts advise one; a
    model's credits relaunch it on your `model_fallback`, and back at the reset their notice
    named; else it waits for that reset. The hold stands once the notice has left the screen,
    while its reset is still ahead. With no reset named it tells you once and types one turn
    after five hours (a model's credits: nothing until the session runs another model). The
    turn typed past a reset, or after those five hours, is a probe: where another window still
    binds, that one turn is billed to credits, and the hold begins again. The hold reads Claude
    Code's screen, so credits it never names there are not held;
  - no upgrade, fallback or return moves a session onto a model your account bills to usage
    credits: Fable where your Claude Code profile says it runs on credits only, once its included
    limits have ended, or where the profile cannot say (none read, two logins listed, a plan it
    cannot place); and any model Claude Code keeps your consent to bill to credits, or marks
    credits-only.

  With `usage_credits = true` the harness does what it did before. Purchases stay refused either
  way: no rule buys credits, raises a spend limit, turns credits you switched off back on, or takes
  a paid upgrade. Claude Code 2.1.304's spend-limit nudge (`Adjust monthly spend limit: $N`) gets
  its `Wait for limit to reset` row (`no-spend@v1`). With the key off, the Messages line for a
  week nearly used says the session stops until the week resets, and that turning credits on
  takes `[harness] usage_credits = true` as well.

- **On Linux a new tab's prompt is ready in about 6 ms instead of 41.** aterm keeps a zsh, bash
  or fish shell started ahead, as it already did on macOS, and a plain new tab takes it instead of
  starting one. Your startup files run in it unseen only once three tabs in a row have run them
  cleanly in view: nothing read your keyboard, nothing took over the terminal, nothing rang the
  bell, asked the clipboard or aterm itself, and nothing was left running after the tab (aterm
  reads `/proc` to see what a tab's startup left behind, such as an `ssh-agent` or a tmux server).
  Until then, where the shell reads a system file before aterm can pause it (Ubuntu's
  `/etc/zsh/zshenv` and `/etc/bash.bashrc`), no shell is started ahead, and with
  `spare_shell = "parked"` none ever is: that mode promises nothing runs before you ask. Where no
  such file exists, a shell started ahead waits before any startup file, as on macOS. On macOS too,
  a shell is no longer started ahead in the instant before aterm had checked for `/etc/zshenv`, nor
  once such a file has appeared while aterm runs (installing zsh and making it your shell, say).
  Measured on Ubuntu 24.04 (zsh 5.9, headless, medians of 30, interleaved): a new tab's first prompt
  in 6.4 ms from a shell started ahead, against 41.4 ms before and 41.5 ms with
  `spare_shell = "off"`; a shell paused before its startup files, 36.3 ms. Windows tabs still start
  cold.

- **A new window's shell starts before aterm connects to the window system.** On macOS the first
  tab's shell used to start only after aterm had set up its connection to the window system, which
  took 28.6 and 60.2 ms in the two launches aterm's own log timed (on Windows, after its event loop
  was built). It now starts first and runs its startup files while that connection is made;
  everything it prints meanwhile is kept and shown. With startup files that take longer than the
  window takes to appear (oh-my-zsh, nvm, conda), the first prompt comes sooner by up to that
  much. A headless macOS instance makes no such connection. On Linux and the BSDs a window still
  connects first: there the connection can fail, and a launch that cannot open its display leaves
  your saved windows for the next one. The first launch of a build also starts its shell 0.3 ms
  sooner: the folder its shell integration is installed in is named in 0.03 ms instead of 0.6 ms.
  Measured headless on an otherwise idle Mac (medians of 12, interleaved): a first launch reaches
  its prompt in 25.3 ms, against 25.9 before and 27.5 for 0.106.0; a later launch is unchanged
  headless (25.2 ms against 25.1), as there is no window-system connection to overlap.

- **On Linux, a command you typed while its tool was still installing starts the moment the tool
  lands.** A command such as `targo` that aterm is still installing waits for it, and on Linux it
  looked for it only every quarter second; it now watches the install folder, as it already did on
  macOS, and runs the moment the tool is in place, or says at once that nothing is installing when
  an offline install gives up. Measured in a Linux VM: from the tool landing to the command
  finishing, 132 ms became 3.7 ms (medians of 30), and the offline answer came after 34 ms instead
  of 257 ms. Windows watches the folder the same way.

- **A new tab that starts its own shell answers a little sooner.** A tab that cannot take the
  shell aterm keeps ready (`aterm ctl spawn cwd=`, a connected tab, a tab under an agent
  identity, or any tab before the waiting shell is up) now gets its own setup done while aterm
  finishes the turn that asked for it, and waits for aterm only right before the new shell is
  started, instead of before all of it. Measured headless, `aterm ctl spawn` answered 0.13 ms
  sooner with one tab open and 0.18 ms sooner with 40 (2.4 and 3.1 ms), and 1.0 ms sooner with
  40 tabs when an idle Mac runs its cores slowly.

- **A window's border now says that something in it needs you, whichever tab it is in.**
  The coloured rim used to follow the front tab alone and lit for things that needed nobody:
  approval boxes the harness answers seconds later, a peer's drive lease, unread task mail.
  Now it reads the one need verdict every surface reads (`status needs=`): red while a session
  is stuck (frozen, a stalled worker, a login, a wall nobody answers), amber while it waits
  for your decision (an ask, an approval no harness presses, a question), steady, with no
  pulse and no wash — for the most pressing session in any tab or pane of the window. A
  pill at the right end of the tab strip says what and where ("◆ fmt (tab 4) · never started
  · 2m"); a click goes there, to the pane in a split, and its `+2` opens Overview at the
  window's next need;
  on the front tab's frozen program it offers **Restart** where aterm can carry it, and on a
  job stopped with input queued **Resume** (`signal cont`); where it offers no Restart (an
  agent aterm does not supervise, a program that is no agent, a tab you took over) its words
  say what to do instead: "⌃C or close the tab, then `claude --resume <id>`", or "Hand Back
  to let aterm restart it"; hovering it shows its whole
  sentence, and a screen reader hears it without the ticking age. Each tab
  carries its own mark: ◆ stuck and ◇ decide, only while a need stands, a quiet dot for a
  finished worker you have not looked at (still seen after a seamless update) or for a
  codex in a background tab that finished its turn while you were not watching, and a short
  dash for a command that failed (which used to wear the amber ◇ of a need). The tab's hover says the need and the agent's state. View ▸ Show Needs in Windows (`[presence] rim`) turns the border and the pill off;
  `aterm ctl chrome` prints `presence rim= pressing= pill=`. On Windows and Linux the pill
  and the marks are in the tab strip in the window.

- **Workers and their managers say who drives.** A worker's tab title opens with `↳` and a
  manager's ends with `⇉3`, in both tab strips. In a Claude Code tab, the rule under the input
  box carries a chip beside the harness's: `⇠ lab-sweep` on a worker (a click goes to its
  manager, in the window you clicked), `⇉3` on a manager (a click opens Overview at it, its
  workers listed under it) and `✋ you` on a tab you took over (a click hands it back). The tab's hover adds who drives it: `worker of lab-sweep`,
  `manages 3`, `driven by aterm (cruise)`, and a hold (`aterm ctl hold`, or one over the
  message bus), which used to be the red rim and `·fleet🔒`. A worker that `aterm ctl` started
  (`from=ctl`) wears none.

- **The menu-bar ❯ shows what needs you and what everyone is doing, and takes you there.**
  Its title is `❯N` while N tabs need you, in this aterm or another aterm on this Mac (read
  every 15 seconds while one runs), red
  while one of them is stuck (frozen, stopped, stalled, logged out, out of memory, at a
  wall), `❯•` while something waits for later, and `❯` otherwise; hover it for where. The
  menu lists, each part only when it has something: Needs you, each row naming its tab and
  how long, a click going there (in another aterm too); This Mac, how many tabs are
  working, need you, waiting, resting, done or plain shells (a stuck tab is never counted
  as working); each manager with its workers, a click going to
  one and a finished one's result opening in a tab; Done for you, results nobody here waits
  on, until you look at them; Waiting, one line per cause, never one per tab (a script's
  `kind=wait` in its own words: "⧗ tab 4 — waiting for CI on PR 412 (ci)"); the held tabs;
  To look at; then Overview…, Read This Mac (the survey in a tab) and Notify Me When I'm
  Needed. A seamless update keeps every age and what you have read off Done for you. The
  Operator rows, the window rows and the
  "Sessions · Connections" line are gone, and a `role` is just a label. Its rows and
  notifications used to fire for waits aterm settles itself: a usage limit the harness waits
  out, a memory banner the harness restarts at its next idle point, and an API that cannot
  be reached, which raised one row per tab. Those are no longer rows. An unreachable API is
  one line under "To look at", counting the tabs, which goes about ten minutes after the
  network comes back; a limit nobody waits out becomes a need once its reset has passed
  ("session usage limit reset at 5:11pm — continue it there").
  Under another supervisor's claim (`meta set supervisor`), an overload, an API error or a full
  context is that supervisor's to retry, as its boxes are, and raises no row. While a tab is
  held, no harness can retry or compact for it, so those walls are needs there, as a held
  tab's boxes are. Every row now
  starts with its tab's name. For scripts: `aterm ctl status` and the survey's records add
  `needs=`, what the session needs of you now (`frozen`, `stopped`, `stalled`, `login`,
  `memory`, `wall`, `ask`, `approval`, `question`, or `-`), and `hold_by=`, whose hold stands
  (`person`, `remote`, `local`, `bridge` or `-`; `hold=` still says only whether one does). `meta set
  attention owner=<k> kind=wait <text>` marks an escalation as something its writer is waiting out,
  which is never a need; `kind=ask` is one, and so is no kind, except a `limited:` entry
  while the harness answers the wall. Only the supervisor's own wait (`owner=supervisor`,
  under a live supervisor claim) waits a limit out; another writer's wait never hides a
  limit you must continue. `meta` lists each entry's kind in `attention_kinds=`, and `aterm
  ctl chrome`'s `statusitem` line says `needs=` and `stuck=`. `aterm help needs` explains
  the words, the badge, the border and the pill.

- **aterm's own desktop notices stay off unless you turn them on: ❯ ▸ Notify Me When I'm
  Needed.** It is the opt-in (as is `desktop_alerts = true` in aterm.toml); off, the
  default since 2026-09-28, aterm posts no notice of its own, and you learn of a need from
  the menu bar, the window's border and the tab's mark. Once on, a notice is only for what
  only you can act on: one per need while it stands (none for a wait, and none for the tab
  you are looking at), a macOS permission only you can grant, and an update only you can
  unstick. Run from the aterm app, aterm posts only as itself: turning it on asks macOS to
  let it, as does the first notice while it is on where it was turned on another way (it
  never asks at launch, nor while Notify Me is off); allowed, the notices are aterm's own,
  and a click on one about a tab on this Mac takes you to that tab and pane (any other
  brings aterm forward); until macOS allows it, and once refused, none reach the desktop
  (allow aterm in System Settings ▸ Notifications). Run from one in your Desktop, Documents
  or Downloads folder (macOS guards those, so aterm does not read the app's name there),
  none reach the desktop until you move it to Applications. Started through a link to the
  app from outside it (tools/install.sh's `~/.local/bin/aterm`), aterm does not read its
  identity either, so none reach the desktop: open aterm.app itself. Not run from the app,
  with terminal-notifier installed (on aterm's PATH or from Homebrew) they are
  terminal-notifier's banners; without it macOS shows them as Script Editor's. The Notify
  Me row's hover says which you would get. A seamless update tells no standing need
  again.

- **The Fabric menu is now Agents: what needs you, who drives what, and stepping in.** Next
  That Needs You (⇧⌘J) goes to the tab that needs you most, and pressed again to the next.
  Overview… (⌃⌘O, was Show Connection Map) lists every session with what it needs or is
  doing, its task, who drives it and which manager runs which workers: Enter goes there,
  `t` takes it over or hands it back, `r` reads a finished worker's result and ⌫ stops a
  worker once you press ⌫ again (Enter only ever goes there). Take Over This Tab and Hand
  Back This Tab (were Hold and Lift; the next entry), Harness Log for This Tab
  (⇧⌘L, was Ledger for This Session) and Set Role… (moved from Window) are there too, with
  Read This Mac and Read the Fleet (`aterm ctl survey`, with `--fleet`, in a tab) and
  Summarize the Fleet in a New Tab (Summarize This Mac outside a fleet): one Claude Code
  worker reads the survey once and writes what needs you, what everyone is doing and what
  finished. A command read into a tab never raises an error row: a message bus that is off
  or a Mac that did not answer is what its tab says.

- **Take Over This Tab: you step in, and only you type there until you hand it back.**
  Take it from the Agents menu, the tab's right-click menu or Overview's `t`; hand it back
  the same ways, or from the needs pill or the `✋ you` chip. It sets a hold of yours that
  no script, manager or the tab's own agent can lift: the harness parks, a manager's
  `turn` and every script's write to the tab get `ERR halted … origin=person`, a wire
  `hold` naming `origin=person` is refused, their `hold off` answers `OK hold=1` and lifts
  only their own hold, and `invoke TakeOver` is denied to every socket. Your keyboard
  still works and the agent finishes its turn. The cost, while you hold any tab: agents on
  this aterm also cannot use `invoke`, `tab`, `pane`, `hwkey`, `pointer` or `confirm`, or
  open the palette, a tab menu, the Autopilot menu or Overview, and a `sudo` with no
  terminal cannot ask you for its password in any tab (`aterm ctl help hold` says why); a
  script's keys into an open Overview cannot stop the agent in a tab you hold, or leave a
  stop armed for your next key, and put nothing on your screen when refused. The tab wears
  a thin outline, a hollow-square mark and the pill "You have this tab · Hand Back"; ❯
  lists it under You hold, with how many writes it refused, and Hand Back All. `status`
  and the survey say `hold_by=person`, and a hold left for 30 minutes is one line under To
  look at, gone once you hand the tab back (an update restarts its 30 minutes). A crash
  keeps your hold: a tab aterm recovers after a crash or Force Quit comes back still yours
  until you hand it back or quit and relaunch aterm. Where no hold of yours stands, Hand
  Back lifts a script's or agent's own `hold … on` (which halts the same app verbs for every
  agent here), as its own `hold off` would, and one left 30 minutes is a line under To look
  at too; a hold over the message bus stays the bus's.

- **A tab's right-click menu has an AGENT section in place of CONNECTIONS:** Take Over or
  Hand Back, Harness Log and Set Role…; on a worker, Go to its manager and Stop Worker…
  (after you click Stop on its sheet, its agent gets SIGTERM and its task reads exited;
  Return cancels; a worker with only its shell in front, no agent, is not signalled and
  you are told to close its tab; where there is no sheet, as on Linux and Windows, it opens Overview with
  that worker's stop armed; a script choosing it puts nothing on your screen); on a manager, one row per worker.

- **View ▸ Show Needs in Windows replaces Presence Band and Presence Rim,** saved as
  `[presence] rim`; it turns the needs border and its pill on or off together (the band
  itself is gone). The message bus's Status, Turn On… and Turn Off… are palette rows now
  (Message Bus: …), as are Show Identity and Fleet Machines (`aterm fleet peers`).

- **A new tab from a tab where an agent is running opens as fast as one from a prompt.**
  Cmd-T, a split or a new window from a tab running Claude Code, vim, ssh or any other program
  now takes the shell aterm keeps ready, which waits in that tab's folder, instead of starting
  a new one: on a Mac busy building, its prompt came in 3.5 ms instead of 16.8, and `aterm ctl
  spawn` answered in 0.7 ms instead of 2.4. A tab asked for in another folder (`aterm ctl
  spawn cwd=`, or a tab opened right after a `cd`) takes the waiting shell too while that shell
  has not run your startup files yet: it moves to the folder first, before anything of yours
  runs, and reads exactly as a shell started there (`$PWD`, `$OLDPWD`); such a tab answered in
  0.8 ms instead of 3.4. The waiting shell is never moved onto a network volume, a folder that
  another machine's shell reported through ssh gets a fresh shell, and so do tabs under an
  agent identity and connected tabs.

- **A downloaded update is ready about 0.4 s sooner.** Before it marks an update ready,
  aterm checks the new build's signature and starts it once, and macOS spends about 0.9 s
  inspecting a program the first time it runs. aterm now starts that inspection while the
  signature checks run, instead of after them: the new build is held before its first
  instruction and runs only once every check has passed, and a build that fails one is
  stopped without ever running. Getting an update ready took 0.93 s instead of 1.32 s in our
  measurements.

- **A fresh install starts on the ALab tools sooner.** Each release now carries the package
  index it saw when it was built, so the first launch finds the newest index in one batch of
  requests instead of three (407 ms instead of 725 ms measured), and announces the tools and
  starts their first download about 0.3 s sooner. When the index has moved on since the
  release (by up to about 30 builds), finding it takes two batches. An automatic update woken
  by a newly published index finds it in one batch instead of two. What a release carries is
  only a guess: every index is still checked against its signatures before anything installs.

- **Settings ▸ Themes is one chooser list beside a live demo.** The highlighted row is the
  theme tried: arrow through the list and the demo plays each one. **Keep** or **Revert** on
  the strip ends the trial, and **Keep ▾** offers **Keep colours only** for a theme that
  carries type settings; the demo draws the face Keep would give. Community themes you do not
  have yet are under **Community**: the highlighted one is tried straight from aterm's pack,
  and Keep adds its file and selects it. **Customize**, **Save as theme** and the **Themes
  folder** stay on the page. The gallery, its chips, Try and Get More are gone. The list is one
  Tab stop, a screen reader hears each row as a list option with its selected state, and a row
  scrolled out of view is reported off screen and scrolls back on request. On Windows the demo
  is a Windows 11 aterm window: minimize, maximize and close at the right of its tab row, the
  selected tab opening into the terminal as the real one does and outlined where the real one
  is (on every light theme, where the demo's Default Light tab had none), and PowerShell and
  Command Prompt tabs, and it plays a PowerShell session: `PS C:\src\aterm>` prompts, the commands in
  PSReadLine's colours, git, a cargo test run with Windows paths, where it played a zsh session
  with a starship prompt. Settings' colour and cursor samples use pwsh prompts there too
  (`PS C:\src> git status --short`, `PS C:\> cat notes.md`, where they read `$` and `~/demo $`).
  The demo and the samples are drawn under the contrast floor a tab applies to the theme's own
  colours (4.5:1 on Windows while Minimum contrast is unset), so Default Light's FAIL badge reads
  5.3:1 and its PASS badge 4.7:1, as they do in a tab, where the demo drew them at 1.5:1 and
  2.7:1. macOS and Linux keep the zsh session and the `$` samples.

- **Windows: tabs run in the OpenConsole shipped beside aterm by default.** With no `conpty`
  in aterm.toml, every tab's console host is the pinned OpenConsole.exe the app folder carries
  (the Windows console host when a build has none), so a console program's questions to the
  terminal reach aterm (the background colour for picking light or dark, synchronized output,
  the palette, XTGETTCAP; Git Bash's colour questions never leave the MSYS2 runtime under
  either host), sixel and kitty images draw, `SGR 58` underline colours arrive intact,
  and bulk output is up to 4 times faster for less CPU (an MSYS `cat` of 20.8 MB in 0.25 s
  instead of 1.05 s). Ctrl+C, the time to a prompt and Git Bash after a resize measured the
  same. `conpty = "inbox"` keeps the Windows console host; `"auto"` still also tries a copy of
  Windows Terminal's, which the default never takes. In pwsh, the cursor's offset after an
  emoji typed at the prompt now shows as you type rather than after End (PSReadLine counts its
  width itself), and `aterm doctor` notes a build whose OpenConsole.exe is missing. A tab that
  runs a windowed program (`aterm -e explorer .`, `pythonw`) starts it once, on the Windows
  console host, and a console host slow to answer a new tab costs that tab alone its
  OpenConsole until it has been slow three times running. One thing is worse: cmd.exe's `type`
  of a file with emoji shows more of them as two ◊ (25 replacement characters against 11 in
  12 lines of 50 🌈), because OpenConsole converts each of cmd's 80-unit writes on its own and
  splits a character that straddles two; pwsh and Git Bash print the same file whole.

- **Windows: a compact find bar that answers F3.** The find bar drops its empty top row, its
  query field closes on an accent line as a Windows text box does, and while it is open F3
  and Shift+F3 step to the next and previous match (Ctrl+S and Ctrl+R still work); its hint
  row teaches them and spells Enter and Esc. Its field row is a toolbar, as in Windows
  Terminal and VS Code: the `Aa` (match case) and `.*` (regex) toggles sit right after the
  query as two buttons, on a quiet fill even when off (on a light theme a step darker than
  it was, `#bdbec1` at 1.45:1 on the bar where `#cccdd0` at 1.24:1 barely parted from it; dark
  themes keep theirs), and the count with ↑, ↓ and ✕ buttons
  you can click (previous, next, close, as Shift+F3, F3 and Esc) ends the row at its right
  edge, ✕ last; on a full-width pane that group used to stop at four-fifths of the bar, 160
  px short of its end, and the query field is now at most 40 cells (360 px at 100%). In a
  split pane the toggles stay: at 55 columns, half of a 111-column window, the bar used to
  drop them to keep the count, and now gives the query field the room instead (15 cells at
  least). The field's caret is your accent colour, like the line under it, instead of the
  terminal cursor's green. The bar is drawn like the tab strip and the pane headers: `Find:`,
  the query, the count and the hints are in Segoe UI (the hints a size smaller) instead of the
  terminal's monospace, as Windows Terminal's search box sets them; the query field and the
  two toggles are rounded (4 px corners at 100%) and stand 3 px off the line above the bar
  and off the row's foot, where they sat square on that line; ↑, ↓ and ✕ are drawn in the
  weight of a tab's close mark; and a toggle that is on is filled with your accent colour, its
  `Aa` or `.*` in the colour that reads on it (4.5:1 or better), as in Windows Terminal,
  instead of the bar's text colour turned inside out. A click in the query field lands on the letter under the pointer. Until Segoe UI
  is loaded, and for a query no system font can draw (an emoji), the bar keeps its monospace
  look.

- **Windows: Settings switches and menus look like Windows'.** A switch is the bare track a
  Windows toggle is, outlined when Off with a small thumb (the boxed switch with a filled Off
  track read as disabled), and a drop-down ends in the thin Windows chevron.

- **Windows: the command palette reads like a Windows flyout.** Its words are set in Segoe UI
  instead of the terminal's monospace, the section names line up in one column, a thin
  indicator shows when the list scrolls, and the window behind it is dimmed. It opens on the
  everyday commands, with About, Settings… and Exit last; Window ▸ Zoom is Maximize (Restore
  Down on a maximized window), Quit aterm is Exit, and Check for Updates… is no longer listed
  where aterm has no in-app updater. It is topped by a search box (`Search commands`, or
  `Search themes`) instead of a `Commands` title over a filter field shorter than its own
  words, whose descenders sat on its outline and whose count crossed it: the box is a row and
  a half tall, white on light themes, with your accent along its foot and a caret after what
  you type. The selected command is marked as Settings marks its page, with a quiet fill and
  a short accent pill, instead of an accent outline. The search box's hint, the count, the
  section names and the key hints are in the secondary text colour (4.5:1 or better; they
  were the disabled grey at 3.1 to 3.6:1), so only a command you cannot run looks disabled;
  the session picker's and Overview's key hints too.

- **Windows: aterm's own shortcuts leave PowerShell its selection and editing keys.** As in
  Windows Terminal, Ctrl+Shift+←/→ (select by word), Shift+Home/End (select to the line's
  ends) and Ctrl+Shift+Enter (insert a line below) now reach PSReadLine. Tabs move on
  Ctrl+Tab / Ctrl+Shift+Tab and Ctrl+PageDown / Ctrl+PageUp, the scrollback jumps to its top
  or bottom on Ctrl+Shift+Home / Ctrl+Shift+End and pages on Shift+PageUp / PageDown or
  Ctrl+Shift+PageUp / PageDown, and Ctrl+Shift+Z zooms a pane. macOS and Linux keep their
  chords.

- **Windows: the title bar and the tab band are one surface.** The title bar takes the tab
  band's tone instead of the terminal's, so the top of the window reads as one chrome block
  over the terminal rather than dark, grey, dark; without a tab strip it takes the colour of
  the terminal under it, a tab's own theme or a program's background colour included. The
  band's bottom rule now sits on the band's last pixel row, with 6 px of the terminal's own
  background under it before the first line (the line used to touch the rule, with 12 px of
  padding on the other three sides), and the tabs are centred in the band. Window
  appearance's automatic choice says what it does: "Match terminal".

- **Windows: the tab strip draws Windows 11 tabs.** The selected tab is the terminal's own
  background, its top corners rounded, and opens through the band's rule into the terminal
  below it, as in Windows Terminal; the other tabs are bare titles on the band, parted by a
  hairline, with a wash under the pointer, and the `+` is a bare glyph. The strip used to
  float a grey capsule for every tab, and on a light theme the selected one was the darkest
  (`#c8cacc` on a `#e2e3e5` band) and read as pressed; it is now the lightest surface there.
  Titles are centred on their whole height, so a `g` or a `p` keeps a pixel of the tab under
  it at 100% instead of sitting on its edge. The selected tab is one surface with what lies
  under it: the terminal; a split's pane headers, which now wear the pane's own background
  instead of the band's grey (the tab was a dark island in a grey 48 px slab, and in a window
  the 6 px under the rule a dark stripe between the band and the headers); Settings' page
  (`#1e1e20` dark, `#eaebeb` light, where the tab was the terminal's `#111318` stepping down
  onto a lighter page); on a light theme the selected tab wears the band's rule as a
  one-pixel outline, as WinUI's selected tab carries its stroke, whatever it selects, so a
  terminal tab and Settings are one shape in every light theme (the outline came only where the
  page was a hair off the band, 1.08:1, so in Default Light the Settings tab had it and a
  terminal tab, 1.20:1, did not); dark themes keep the outline only for a tab that would
  otherwise fade into the band. Over the find bar or the
  message band it stands on the rule, so the find field no longer fuses with it into one dark
  L. On a light theme the wash under the
  pointer darkens the band (`#d3d4d7` on `#e2e3e5`, Windows 11's subtle hover) where it rose
  toward the selected tab and read as a second one, and the selected title reads at one weight
  on light and dark themes (mean ink 0.55 and 0.53 of full at 100%, where it was 0.45 and
  0.65). A title with a colour emoji (`🚀 deploy`) is a tab like the others, the emoji in
  colour from the terminal's emoji font beside its Segoe UI letters, where it was a square
  block in the terminal font, set low in the band, with a plain `X`. A title in Chinese,
  Japanese, Korean or another script Segoe UI lacks (`日本語 notes`, `한국어`) is a tab like
  the others from the first frame it shows, at the other titles' size and weight and parted
  from its neighbours by the hairline; until the band had drawn it once it was set in the
  terminal's font, larger and bolder, with no hairline on either side. Its Chinese, Japanese
  and Korean text is set in the fonts Windows itself puts beside Segoe UI, Yu Gothic UI and
  Malgun Gothic, and on the selected tab in their Semibold and Bold. It was the terminal's
  Microsoft YaHei Bold and Malgun Gothic Bold on every tab, so a quiet tab's `日本語` and
  `한국어` read bolder than the `notes` beside them (mean ink 0.63 and 0.60 against 0.51 at
  100%; now 0.45 and 0.49, about the same ink per pixel of width as the Latin, and at 200%
  0.65 and 0.66 against 0.68). aterm reads these fonts in the background as it starts
  (about 180 ms of one core and 3 MB, after the first frame); Linux's tab band reads its own
  Chinese, Japanese and Korean font the same way.

- **Windows: tabs are as wide as their titles need, up to one width for every count.** A lone
  tab was 28 columns wide, narrower than each of two tabs, so Claude Code and Git Bash titles
  were cut with half the strip empty; every tab now grows to Windows Terminal's 240 px tab
  (where 48 columns left a short title alone at the far end of a 432 px pill), counted in
  pixels at every scale (27 columns of the rounded-down cell cut at 150% and 200% a title that
  fit at 100%), and while the strip has room a tab whose title is longer grows to seat it, up
  to 432 px: `less -R +1200 CHANGELOG.md` and a Claude Code task title read whole in a lone tab
  instead of cut at 27 columns with 700 px of empty strip beside them, and a spinner's frames
  never move the close button. A command line longer than that keeps its file, cut in the
  middle: `vim -n -R -i NONE -c … crates/aterm-gui/src/platform_win.rs` in a lone tab and
  `…platform_win.rs` among five, where the cut took the end and with it vim's file
  (`…crates/aterm-gui/src…`); a folder keeps its last name as before. The shell integrations
  (pwsh, bash, zsh, fish) title a running command with the whole line up to 256 characters,
  where they cut it at 64, and end a longer one with `…`; such a title is cut at its end, so
  a cut-off path is never shown as the file (`vim … crates/aterm-gui/src/plat` for a 70-character
  vim line in Git Bash, `Get-Content … C:\Users\you\aterm\crates\a` in pwsh). Titles are cut in the
  tab font rather than in terminal cells (no more `Settin…` in a roomy tab) and start at the
  tab's leading edge, as in Windows Terminal. Each tab's title is cut to its own tab, in the
  selected weight, so it reads the same selected or not and whatever its neighbours say: one
  long title cut every other tab shorter, so at 150% and 200% a Claude Code task read
