  `Claude Code: rev…` beside a `C:\Users\you\aterm` tab and `Claude Code: revi…` beside
  another folder, and at 100% a selected `vim` or `less` command cost it a letter. Git
  Bash tabs drop their `MINGW64:` prefix and read their home as `~` (`~/aterm`, as the prompt
  says, where they read `/c/Users//you/aterm`), cmd.exe tabs read your profile folder as `~`
  (`~\aterm`, as a pwsh tab's title says, where they read `C:\Users\you\aterm`; `ctl title`
  keeps cmd's own), and two tabs in one directory both show the
  directory (`2 · …\work\sub dir`). The busy and status marks beside the close button are
  drawn larger.

- **Windows: the chrome wears your Windows accent colour.** Settings' selection, the command
  palette's selected row, the tab and pane marks follow Personalization ▸ Colours ▸ Accent
  colour (in its light shade on dark chrome and its dark shade on light chrome) wherever the
  theme sets no `accent_color`, and follow it when it changes. Settings marks the page you are
  on as Windows 11 Settings does, with a short accent pill on a quiet fill and its name in the
  ordinary text colour, and heads its groups in sentence case (`Look & feel`) instead of green
  capitals.

- **Windows: the tab band's version label is quiet.** It reads `v0.106.3605` instead of
  `v0.106.3605+g8b6f0a8* · DEV`; a click still opens Settings ▸ About with the full build.

- **Windows: split panes are divided by a hairline, the focused pane is marked in the accent
  on its side of it, and an unfocused pane keeps a hollow cursor.** The divider was a 9-pixel
  slab with a stripe in the text colour beside the focused pane; it is now a one-pixel line
  down the middle of the gap on the terminal background, so text on either side keeps half a
  cell of air, and a one-pixel accent line beside it, on the side of the pane taking
  keystrokes, moves across it with the focus (four pixels at 100%) and turns the corner where
  dividers cross. Under a pane header it starts at the header's accent underline and turns into
  it, one corner, where it ran on up through the header and the underline began three pixels
  to its side. A scrollbar thumb on the divider leans away from the accent line, so a pixel of
  the terminal background (two at 150% and 200%) keeps them apart, where the two touched and
  read as one 4-pixel green-and-grey bar; under the pointer it widens away from the accent line
  too, which stays whole, where the widened thumb and its track lay over it and tinted it, and
  it is one shade over the divider's line, where the line's column showed through lighter
  (`#abacb0` beside `#9b9b9d`). Pane headers sit under the tab strip's one rule instead of a second rule of
  their own, run across the divider as one bar, are set a step smaller than the tab titles
  (11.7 px against 13 px at 100%, where they were 16.6 px), and mark the focused pane with an
  accent dot and underline instead of a `└`/`▸` branch; on a light theme an unfocused pane's
  header keeps a hairline 1.5:1 off its terminal (`#caccce` on `#f6f7f9`, where `#e5e6e8` at
  1.17:1 let the header run into the text). A pane without the keyboard shows
  where its cursor is as an outline in its cursor colour. macOS and Linux keep their dividers.

- **Windows: aterm's icon is the one macOS and Linux show, sharp at every size.** The `>a|`
  prompt mark on its dark tile replaces the green `>_`, with an anti-aliased frame for every
  size Windows draws, 16 to 256 px; the smallest are fitted to the pixel grid by hand, so the
  title bar, taskbar, Alt+Tab, Start and Explorer show clean edges and a readable `a` where
  they showed jagged corners and a resampled neighbour. A faint rim keeps the tile's outline
  on a dark title bar or taskbar.

- **Windows: aterm's windows have a class name of their own, `aterm`.** Window managers,
  FancyZones rules and AutoHotkey (`ahk_class aterm`) can now pick out aterm's windows, which
  had winit's shared "Window Class".

- **Windows: faint text recedes as it does in Windows Terminal.** On a dark theme faint
  (SGR 2) light text kept most of its contrast, so PSReadLine's inline prediction, which pwsh
  draws bright white and faint, read like the command being typed (`#BCBCBC`, 1.5:1 from the
  typed text). Faint light text now recedes as those terminals' alpha blend does, keeping its
  3:1 readable floor: the prediction is `#898989` (5.3:1 on Default, 2.8:1 from typed text) and
  faint default text `#717172` (3.8:1, was 6.5:1). Faint dark text on light themes is
  unchanged, and macOS and Linux keep the faint they had.

- **aterm starts sooner.** A launch is ready for its window about 2.6 ms sooner (11.4-11.8 ms
  after it is started, against 14.1-14.6 ms for 0.106.0 measured the same way in two runs),
  and its first shell shows its prompt 1.5-2.5 ms sooner. The first shell's terminal and its
  identity file are made on a side thread while aterm reads its settings; the word list behind
  the sparkle and cat effects is no longer parsed from text at every launch (it is read when
  aterm is built); the name of the shell-integration folder is worked out with a cheaper hash;
  and on Apple silicon less has to happen before aterm's own code runs.

- **On a busy Mac a new tab's shell starts sooner and answers your keys sooner.** macOS runs
  a terminal's child processes in the band every build competes in, on the efficiency cores
  once the fast ones are taken. Each shell aterm starts now runs in the band of an app's
  interface instead, one step below aterm's own window; the programs you run in it still
  run in the normal band, so a build never gets ahead of aterm. With twelve cores busy beside
  it, a new tab's first prompt came in about 20.5 ms instead of 27, and the shell echoed a
  typed key within about 0.1-1 ms nine times in ten instead of 0.4-2.7 ms. On an idle Mac
  nothing changes: the shell already ran on the fast cores.

- **The first install of the ALab tools starts at once, and a busy Mac no longer starves it.**
  On a fresh install the update that brings the toolset no longer waits for your login shell
  to report its PATH: with a `.zshrc` that takes a second, it started about a second after
  aterm's first check and now starts within a few milliseconds. That first install also runs
  at the system's normal priority instead of the background band, which a Mac with every core
  busy starved: the announcement came after about 1.6 s instead of 11 s, and the Trust
  toolchain was installed in about 25 s instead of about 4.6 minutes. Later updates still run
  in the background and still read your login shell's PATH. The toolchain is also usable
  about 0.7 s sooner, because its check runs while the rest of its bundle unpacks.

- **A new bash tab starts sooner, and a fish tab can open from a warm shell.** bash no
  longer starts a subshell to read the `DEBUG` trap your `.bashrc` set: aterm's share of a
  bash start went from about 4.9 ms to 4.1 ms. fish now gets the waiting warm shell zsh and
  bash have, its startup files already run: a new fish tab shows its prompt in about 1-2 ms
  instead of about 14-26 ms (headless, at the priority a Mac gives aterm). The warm fish is
  checked against every folder fish reads its startup files from, as fish itself names
  them: its system folder wherever its build put it, and each `vendor_conf.d` folder, the
  ones your `XDG_DATA_DIRS` adds included. A file added to or edited in any of them retires
  the warm shell, and the next tab starts cold and runs it.

- **A fish tab that starts cold starts about 0.9 ms sooner, and fish starts each command
  sooner.** The record a new fish sends at its first prompt, which the waiting warm shell
  learns from, cost about 1 ms of every fish start no warm shell serves; it now costs nothing
  measurable, and aterm's share of such a start went from about 3.4 ms to 2.6 ms. fish's
  integration also encodes each command line it reports in a few whole-string steps instead
  of one per character: a typical command line takes about 0.1 ms instead of 0.3 ms before
  the command runs, and a pasted 40-line block about 0.8 ms instead of 24 ms.

- **A window's first frames compile fewer shaders on the spot.** The shader warm-up at launch
  now builds everything a default window's first frames use, the glow, bloom and HDR edge
  included, and builds the window's present pipeline on a lane of its own: a window opened
  as aterm starts waited about 0.1 ms for it instead of about 23 ms, and the first frame with
  the cursor's aurora built its shaders in 0.5 ms instead of 31 ms (measured offscreen).

- **New tabs answer sooner wherever they open, and a new agent identity no longer waits on
  its files.** A tab, split or window that cannot take the waiting warm shell (a connected
  tab, `aterm ctl spawn cwd=`, a split of a pane another program holds, a tab under an agent
  identity, or any tab before a spare is ready) now finds its terminal device, the channel
  that reports its shell started and its nested-aterm token file already made. On an idle
  Mac a cold `aterm ctl spawn` answers in about 2.4 ms instead of 2.9, and with 40 tabs open
  in 3.1 ms instead of 3.7; on a Mac busy building, a connected tab answers in 2.8 ms instead
  of 5.0. `aterm ctl spawn identity=<name>` for a new identity answers in about 2.8 ms
  instead of 13: its agent files are written beside the new shell instead of before it (on
  an idle Mac they are all there about 8 ms after the request, before the shell's first
  prompt), and a spawn refused for its `window=` or `of=` no longer leaves the identity
  behind.
  Closing a tab no longer holds the window while its token file is removed, and a window
  with many tabs no longer reads every tab's connections once per tab when its tab strip
  is rebuilt.

- **A finished agent report that still lists work is caught more often, and a truly finished
  one is sent back less.** When an agent ends with `ATERM-TASK-DONE`, the harness now finds the
  work it leaves open where a sentence says it (`The lexer is still open`, `I did not find the
  cause`, `not measured`, `not compiled`, `didn't fix`) and under headings such as `Still open
  from the review:` or `## Not measured, and why`. An item that names what blocks it in the
  next sentence (`Not compiled. Blocker: no Windows toolchain on this Mac.`), in a sub-item, or
  as a decision (`rejected`, `on purpose`) no longer counts as open, and neither does a check
  with nothing to do (`not run, because no contract was added`) or a phrase in quotation marks.
  On three rounds of aterm's own agents' reports it finds 56 of the 74 excerpts that left work
  open, where it found 19, and sends back 11 of the 150 that left none, where it sent back 65.

- **Settings ▸ Harness's EFFECT OF EACH AUTOPILOT compares boxes and questions, not idle time.**
  The card used to give each Autopilot's share of time "waited for input", which counted an
  agent sitting at its prompt after finishing its work as waiting, so Cruise read `>99%` after
  a quiet minute. It now reads, for the last 7 days: how long a box (a permission box, or a
  question with options to pick) and a question the agent asked in its reply stood under Cruise
  against off (`about 0.7 s on Cruise · about 3m off · median of 41 and 9 boxes seen`, `not
  enough yet (2)` under three), the time at a box or a question as a share of
  working time, how much of each Autopilot's time the agent sat at its prompt and, under
  Cruise, how much of that was after it said it was finished or the harness pausing, Land on
  its own row, and how long it has measured (`7 days, since Mon 09:12`). The `This run` and
  `Finished` rows are gone. The 7 days are kept across a quit and a restart: each aterm
  process keeps its own book under the harness's state directory (`ab/`, the owner's alone),
  written when the page reads its counts and when aterm quits, and the card adds the others'.
  A seamless update keeps only what the page had read before it, since the outgoing aterm
  hands over without quitting; a crash likewise loses what was measured since the last write.

- **The Autopilot chip says when the harness is pausing after short turns.** When the harness
  backs off after a run of short turns (2 minutes, doubling to an hour), the chip's face used to
  read the same as a session at work. Its title now says so after what the mode does (`·
  pausing until 18:41 after 3 short turns`), a clock time, never a countdown; the session's row
  in Settings ▸ Harness reads `pausing until 18:41 (3 short turns in a row)` where no task's end
  or timer has the line, a screen reader hears `Pausing until 18:41.` first, and `aterm ctl
  status` and `ls` print `pause=<unix seconds>` after `task=` (`-` with none). It goes at the
  next decision. The harness decides nothing differently.

- **The harness card's rainbow is vivid on a light theme.** On a light theme (Aterm Day,
  Solarized Light, Linen, Gruvbox Light and the rest) the rainbow trail, the border and the rim
  round the kitty are now solid, full-strength colours, like a rainbow printed on white paper:
  a true red, orange, golden yellow, green, blue and violet, where they were pale salmon, olive,
  periwinkle and lavender with the background showing through. Land's sunset is six distinct
  colours too (red, vermilion, orange, gold, coral and rose). The border keeps its colour all
  the way round, with a lime between the gold and the green and a teal between the green and
  the blue, and its gold is a shade deeper so the thin line stays visible on white. The shimmer
  passes along the rainbow as a white gloss, as on a dark theme, lighter on the top and bottom
  stripes so the band keeps its edges. The stars, the sparkles and the line under the card look
  as before, and so does the card on a dark theme.

- **The harness card's kitty is cuter, and the rainbow reaches it.** The kitty on Claude Code's
  launch card is redrawn as a chibi kitten: a big round head on a small body, big glossy eyes (a
  dark pupil with a white glint over the coloured iris), pink ears, nose and blush, a small `ω`
  mouth over a chin of fur, white socks on its front paws and a two-pixel tail with a curled tip
  (where a long folder path keeps it two rows tall, it lies with its paws tucked under its chin).
  When it blinks its eyes close in happy `^ ^` arcs, and its tail flick sweeps the tail flat into
  the rainbow. The rainbow now runs right up to the kitty, where a strip of background with a
  coloured line in it used to part them, and the end of the rainbow under the kitty holds still
  while the rest of it waves. The same at both heights, on dark and light themes and in every
  coat. A card at rest is drawn in 31 to 56 more pieces than before (the face's detail); the most
  a frame of the card may draw rises from 600 pieces to 680, so no star beside the rainbow is left
  out of a frame as the kitty lands, at any text size.

- **The harness card's border stands clear of the card.** The rainbow border round Claude Code's
  launch card now stands half a row above the card and half a row below it wherever that row is
  blank, as both are when Claude Code starts in a fresh window, so Claude's mascot and the card's
  first line no longer stand on the border and the line under the card no longer runs along it;
  the left side was already about as far from the mascot, so the space is even all round. Where
  the card starts on its pane's first row (the top of the window, or of a lower split) or right
  under the command that started Claude, or one of Claude's notices sits under it, that side
  closes round the card as before. The kitty, its rainbow and the stars stay where they were.

- **The harness card's stars and its line join the rainbow on a light theme.** On a light theme
  the stars round the kitty, the sparkles it sheds as it rides in and the burst of stars as it
  lands are now solid colours from the rainbow itself (its red, orange, gold, green, blue and
  violet, and the sunset's colours under Land), where they were dull, brownish and see-through.
  Where a star lies on the rainbow it is a white glint, so a star of the burst that flies across
  the rainbow's edge is white on the rainbow and coloured off it, whole rather than cut in half.
  The line under the card, `✦ enhanced by aterm harness …`, now runs through the rainbow's own
  colours, each letter as bright as it can be while it still reads clearly on your theme's
  background (at least the 4.5:1 contrast recommended for text, on every light theme, your own
  included), where every letter was a dull, dark shade; its `✦` is solid too. Orange, gold and
  yellow-green cannot be both bright and that readable on a light background, so those letters
  are deeper: burnt orange, bronze and olive green. The `✦ alab kitty` wordmark on the line above
  the prompt reads the same way on a light theme, where its yellow and green letters were nearly
  invisible. On a dark theme the card and the wordmark look as before.

- **`aterm ctl await inbox` and `await agent` wait for news, not for the server's 30 s.**
  The client asks again, with the same words, each time the server's bound ends, until the
  wait's own `timeout=` (or `--timeout`; an hour when neither is given), and only then
  answers `OK timeout` (exit 124). A session that runs the wait as a background command to
  hear its mail or a channel, or to wait out a peer's turn, is no longer woken every 30 s
  with nothing to read. A `timeout=` past the server's 600 s is now the whole wait, not cut
  to 600 s.

- **Waiting out a Claude Code peer's turn no longer answers before it starts.** A `turn`
  into an agent's session now names the verdict rev its Enter found (`agent_rev=<n>`), and
  `await agent idle,prompt,question,wall since=<n>` answers only on a verdict published
  after it. `await agent` is latched, and a `turn typed=1 settle=submitted` answers as the
  line leaves the input box, before the busy verdict is published, so a wait armed right
  after it could answer the idle from before the submit. The brief, `aterm help
  introspection` and the drive-aterm skill teach the `since=` form.

- **A `turn` into Claude Code counts as submitted once the line has left its input box.**
  `aterm ctl @<sid> turn` used to call a submit verified at the first change of the screen
  after its Enter, and Claude Code's animated logo changes the screen by itself, so
  `submitted=1` did not prove the line had landed. Into a session aterm reads as Claude Code
  whose input box shows the typed line, the submit now counts once the line has left the box
  (or a box or a menu took its place), which no animation does; `submitted=0` means the line
  still sits there. Other programs keep the old check. A `turn` into a worker (a session
  started with `spawn agent=claude`) also ends its verdict with `task_rev=<n>`, the task's rev
  as its Enter found it: `aterm ctl await task @<sid>:<n>` answers on that follow-up's own
  done, even one marked before the wait started.

- **The fabric's roster tells the truth.** aterm tells its bridge how it leaves: on a quit
  the bridge withdraws every session it advertised, each of which then reads `exited`, and
  on a seamless update it withdraws none, since the new instance takes the same sessions.
  The sessions of an aterm that was killed, or whose bridge lost its link, read `away`, and
  mail to them queues on the bus until it is back. A post to a session that exited or was
  withdrawn is refused at your own bridge (`ERR unroutable`) instead of being accepted and
  dropped. `aterm fabric`'s BROKER line counts this node's share of the 4096 subjects a node
  may ever mint and warns from three quarters, and says when the roster was longer than it
  read (`rows=4096+ truncated`).

- **`history` and `subscribe … events` say who typed each turn.** Each `history` row
  carries `by=`: `harness` for the window harness's own continuations and checks, `ctl` for
  an owner-token client, `bridge`, an edge's own sid, or `-` when nobody can be named; each
  `EVENT <sid> turn` line ends with the same `by=`, and an update carries it. While the
  harness's records are more than half of a full ledger, its oldest goes instead of the
  oldest record, so a long autonomous run no longer pushes another caller's turns out.

- **The menu bar no longer names an operator.** Not by a tab title starting `operator`,
  nor by `meta set role operator`, and no title starting with `⚠` raises a row: only `meta
  set attention` does. The `operator` and `operator-propose-bin` control verbs, removed in
  0.106.0, answer that they were removed and name what replaced them, and an `[operator]`
  table left in aterm.toml does nothing: Manual says so, and Messages names what replaced
  it until the table is deleted. `aterm pkg doctor`, which already warned about a shell
  that still exports `ATERM_OPERATOR`, now names a manager session (`aterm ctl survey`,
  `spawn agent=claude`) as what replaced it. The menu bar's one worker launch is the
  Agents menu's Summarize (see the Agents entry above).

- **A `[net]` table left from the network drive, removed in 0.106.0, now points at the
  fleet.** It opens no port and dials nothing; Messages says so and names the fleet (`aterm
  fleet init` on one machine, `aterm fleet join` on each of the others, then `aterm ctl
  survey --fleet` on any of them) until the `[net]` table is deleted, Manual marks its keys as
  safe to delete, and `aterm ctl dial` is answered with the same words. A fleet peer
  reads, and drives only a Mac whose person lets it (`aterm fleet allow drive --from`, the
  step-in above). The drive's
  credentials stay where it kept them, and nothing reads them now:
  `aterm-network-drive.token` in the folder of the `[net] key`, that key and the `[net]
  cert`, and each connection's dial token (on macOS a Keychain item, `security
  delete-generic-password -s aterm-net-drive -a <name>`; elsewhere `net/<name>.token` beside
  aterm.toml, which `dial-token` wrote; and any `token_file` it names). Delete them before
  the `[net]` table, which is the only record of where they are; while the table stands,
  Messages names each one. An aterm too old to have lost the drive, still serving `[net]
  listen`, accepts its drive token as the Owner until it is upgraded or that token file is
  deleted. `aterm pkg doctor` still warns about a shell that exports `ATERM_NET_LISTEN`,
  `ATERM_NET_CERT` or `ATERM_NET_KEY`, and now names the fleet (`aterm fleet init`, then
  `aterm fleet join` with its join code) as what replaced them.

### Removed

- **`ATERM-TASK-DONE` from the aterm section of `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `GEMINI.md`.**
  The section aterm writes into each agent's global instructions still says when a job is
  finished, but no longer names the token or says to end a report with it. aterm still asks for
  the token itself, in the done check it types when a worker says it is done. Existing sections
  are rewritten in place the next time aterm primes them.
- **The presence row under the tab bar, and the choice chime.** The row of six slots
  (role, phase, hand, mail, context, link) re-gridded every pane each time it appeared or
  folded; the needs border and its pill say what needs you instead, and nothing presence
  shows ever resizes a pane now. `[presence] band` and `choice_sound` still load and are
  named once as settings that do nothing. `aterm ctl story` takes `chose` alone (the seven
  other words no process sent are usage errors) and records it: `status story=` counts it,
  nothing is drawn or played.
- **The connection rows, File ▸ Driving and the Inbox tab.** Connect to Session…, Configure
  Connection…, Disconnect Session… and the four New Controlled / Controller Session rows are
  gone from every menu and the palette: every in-session client already holds the Owner,
  and workers start with `aterm ctl @self spawn agent=claude`. `aterm ctl invoke` answers
  their names, and `Inbox`'s, with `ERR retired:` and what to use instead (`aterm ctl @<sid>
  inbox` for the inbox). Dragging a tab's status mark onto another tab no longer connects
  them and no confirm card opens; a press on a tab's marks selects that tab, as a press
  anywhere else on it does. `aterm ctl window conn-card` and `controls conn-card`
  are unknown targets now. The `grant` and connection verbs and `aterm conn` still work.
- **`aterm drive` keeps only the window harness's readers: `classify`, `phase`, `answer`
  and `ledger`, and `tape` and `replay`, which read and run again a harness tape a hosted
  loop recorded.** `prompt`, `read`, `shot`, `await`, `await-turn`, `supervise`, `watch`,
  `task` and `report` are gone, and so are the `--timeout`, `--idle` and `--ready`
  options; each removed command says what replaces it. A session is read and driven with
  `aterm ctl` (`text`, `turn`, `image`, `await`, `await agent`), the window's own host
  already supervises every Claude Code, agy, Muse Code and Gemini CLI session, and a Claude
  Code worker is started on a task with `aterm ctl @self spawn agent=claude -` (the task on
  stdin), waited on with `aterm ctl await task` and read with `aterm ctl @<sid> result`.
  The `Inbox: task @<off>` line `drive task` typed is gone with it: nothing aterm types
  wakes an agent for mail. The supervisor's `ESCALATED` and `FROZEN` journal lines no
  longer carry a `mail=` field, since no supervisor mails a manager now, and `aterm drive
  ledger` no longer prints a `reports … complete · … incomplete` row: only `watch --report`
  wrote what it counted.
- **The sealed second-host fabric transport, with `aterm fabric join` and a node's `aterm
  fabric mint-for <node>|new`.** It was compiled out of every shipped aterm (the `sealed`
  cargo feature), which answered these commands by naming the feature; the feature is gone
  as well. `aterm fabric on` no longer takes `--tcp`, `--key-file` or `--allow-remote`,
  `aterm link broker` serves its Unix socket only, `aterm link serve`, `ls` and `notify` no
  longer take `--key-file` or the plaintext `--tcp` (no broker aterm ships served TCP; the
  bridge's TCP-only keepalive went with it), and `aterm fabric` no longer prints a `serves`
  line (`serves_tcp` in `--json`) or the broker's `transport` in `--json`. A person's `aterm fabric mint-for h-<name>|a-<name>`, the cap
  `halt`, `inbox` and `post` take, stays. The fabric is one machine's bus.
- **`aterm fleet` is the fleet's membership: `events` and `exec` are gone.** `events`
  (every instance's events as one NDJSON stream) and `exec` (command lines dispatched across
  instances) each say what replaces them and exit 2, as do the operator's commands that left
  in 0.106.0 (`status`, `inspect`, `manage`, `unmanage`, `next`, `extend`, `ack`,
  `reconcile`, `clear-fault` and `propose`). `aterm ctl survey` reads what every session of
  every instance is doing, `aterm ctl subscribe @a,@b events` streams one instance's events,
  and `aterm ctl @<sid> <verb>` reaches a session of any instance. `aterm fleet` is now
  `init`, `join`, `peers` and `leave`. `docs/OPERATOR.md`, the brief for an agent
  operating this machine's sessions by hand, is removed: the supervise-agent skill and
  Summarize's brief take its place, and `DESIGN-sessions-as-subagents-2026-10-15.md` §7
  records what replaced it.

### Fixed

- **Settings preserve every digit in whole-number edits.** Decimal and exponent input is
  parsed exactly before saving an integer. Rounding no longer turns a fraction into a
  whole number, underflows a small nonzero value to zero, or changes a large integer.
  Exact spellings such as `5000.0` and `5e3` remain accepted.

- **The effects benchmark refuses incomplete CPU samples.** When instruction counting is
  available, every measured phase and reference pass must have a sample before a report
  is emitted. Missing or backwards counter readings cannot become a partial average or
  zero work; hosts without instruction counting keep their existing GPU-only lane.

- **Tap staging preserves existing directories.** Clones use an exclusively owned temporary
  directory and publish without replacing an existing tap. Receiptless package directories
  are left for the existing refusal path instead of being removed as presumed crash debris.

- **`aterm fabric inbox` reads a broker that answered and hung up.** When the broker sent the
  inbox its mail, or refused it, and closed the connection at once, macOS refused the inbox's next
  socket setting and it failed with a bare "Invalid argument (os error 22)", without the mail or
  the reason. It now reads what the broker sent, then says it closed, and still marks nothing read.
  `aterm fabric tail` shows a subscription the broker refused the same way.
- **A hovered Autopilot chip keeps its clicks on a narrower pane.** Where the pane had no room
  to explain the chip's state beside the facts, its title dropped the explanation and both
  `click: …` and `right-click: more` with it, so hovering Cruise's `∞ ✓ done` on a 160-column
  pane read only `autopilot: cruise, done 13:04` (and Land's `✓ done`, `✓ landed` and `⤓ quiet`
  the same on most panes). It now gives up the explanation first and keeps the clicks: beside
  Claude Code's usual model, folder and branch, `autopilot: cruise, done 13:04 · click: land ·
  right-click: more` from about 116 columns and `… · click: land` from about 96.

- **A done task keeps the time it finished when its supervision restarts.** Under Cruise, the
  chip's `∞ ✓ done` clock (its title, the row in Settings ▸ Harness and the timer's record read
  the same) moved to the time of the restart whenever the harness's watch of the session started
  again: the agent's switch in Settings ▸ Harness off and on, Autopilot Off and back, a policy
  change. It now keeps the time the task was done. After a seamless update of aterm both the
  done and the landed clock moved to the update's time; they now keep theirs too. A done turn
  that ended while nothing watched it (Autopilot Off) is stamped when the harness reads it again,
  and a task done before aterm itself was relaunched is stamped at the relaunch.

- **The Autopilot timer's record says what happened in the chip's words.** When a timed Cruise's
  time came, the record was titled `Autopilot began landing` even over a finished task, an agent
  switched off or a tab with no agent, and its line said `the word turned land`. It is now
  `Autopilot switched to land`, its line `at 18:00 Autopilot switched to land` and what that did
  (`nothing to land, the task was done at 17:42`). The done chip's title says `at 04:22 Autopilot
  switches to land` the same way.

- **A timer over a pane with no agent names that pane.** In a tab split between Claude Code and a
  shell, a timer set on the shell's pane was recorded `Tab 1: … no agent runs in the tab`, beside
  a pane where Claude Code runs. It now names the pane (`Tab 1, right pane`) and says `no agent
  runs in this pane`.

- **Copying a build onto `aterm` no longer kills every aterm window.** `~/.local/bin/aterm` is a
  link to the app's own executable, so a `cp` of a build onto it (an agent installing its debug
  build) wrote into the running app: macOS killed aterm with every window, and the copy, cut short
  with them, left an app that would not start until it was reinstalled. The app's executable now
  ships read-only, which its signature and the updater are indifferent to: a `cp` onto the link is
  refused, and `cp -f` replaces the link and leaves the app alone
  (`/Applications/aterm.app/Contents/MacOS/atpkg repair` links the app back). The agent primer
  says so as well. This takes effect from the update that installs this version.

- **`aterm machines enroll` asks for the admin password once, and a typo costs nothing.** When
  the lab's admin account is not called what your login here is, enroll asked for the password
  a second time after you typed the right name; now it asks for the name once and tries the
  password you already typed under it on every Mac that refused. A mistyped password at one
  Mac's prompt no longer skips that Mac when the next password you type is right: each password
  that works is tried on every Mac still refusing. A Mac that refuses under the new name too is
  told by that name, not the old one. A second enroll takes the admin name the Macs were
  enrolled with, a Mac already enrolled is "nothing to do" and exits 0 rather than counting as
  skipped, and with several Macs one whose Remote Login is off is said before the password is
  asked.

- **`aterm machines apply --only names` takes a hand-set HostName off with the rename.** The
  starter baseline left a HostName someone had set by hand at the old name, so `hostname`, shell
  prompts and ssh kept showing it after the rename. The baseline's `[names]` now holds
  `host_name = ""`, which unsets it so the new Local hostname shows; a dotted name sets one. A
  controller set up before this keeps its baseline file, so a starter baseline nobody edited
  (byte for byte one aterm wrote) is brought to the new starter; an edited one is left alone,
  and needs `host_name = ""` added under `[names]` by hand.

- **`aterm machines` says what it did in plain words.** Enroll names each Mac by what it is
  (model, chip, macOS, serial), says a first connection is remembered once the Mac is
  enrolled, says why the admin password is needed this once, and its summary gives each Mac
  not enrolled its own line with what to do. Report rows read by their titles instead of item
  ids, the status line drops the agent's hash, and `unenroll` says ok, not changed, for what
  was never there.

- **The harness reads Claude Code 2.1.304's spend-limit and credit-purchase rows as purchases.**
  Claude Code 2.1.304 can show, in its usage-limit menu's place, a prompt to raise your account's
  monthly spend limit (`Adjust monthly spend limit: $50`), and a screen that sells credits
  (`Pay $10 · Get $12`). The harness's test for an option that buys knew neither label, so its last
  check that no press buys would not have stopped one. No rule is known to have chosen either, and
  neither has been captured on a screen yet (both were read from the 2.1.304 program). Both are
  now purchases at every approval level, whatever `[harness] usage_credits` says; the prompt's
  `Wait for limit to reset` row is still the one that waits.

- **aterm run from its app no longer posts Script Editor banners.** Where aterm's own
  notices were on without macOS ever being asked (`desktop_alerts = true` in aterm.toml,
  or Notify Me turned on before aterm asked), every notice went out through `osascript`,
  as a Script Editor banner whose click opened Script Editor, for good. Now the first
  notice asks macOS to let aterm post as itself, and goes out as aterm's own if macOS
  allows it, unless by then you turned Notify Me off or went to the tab it is about; none
  reach the desktop until macOS allows it. Programs' notifications (OSC 9, 99, 777) follow
  the same rule, and one that arrives while Notify Me is off asks nothing. An aterm app in
  your Desktop, Documents or Downloads folder (macOS guards those, so aterm does not read
  the app's name there), one started through a link to the app from outside it
  (tools/install.sh's `~/.local/bin/aterm`, where aterm does not read its identity either),
  or one macOS gives no notification center, no longer posts the old way, as
  terminal-notifier's banners or Script Editor's: it posts none, and the Notify Me row's
  hover says why and what to do (moved to Applications, or opened as aterm.app itself, it
  posts as itself).

- **The harness no longer takes a program's words for Claude Code's limit or login notice.**
  Where it could not find a session's transcript, aterm typed `/login` into a logged-in Claude
  Code because a custom status line printed `Not logged in · Run /login`, because a Stop hook's
  reason sat under a verbose prompt hook's row, or because a tool's output had scrolled its
  call off the screen; and a hook message wrapped onto a second row, or a Stop hook's reason
  taller than the 40 rows the harness reads, could name a usage limit that was never hit.
  Claude Code's notices are now read only where it draws them: the footer's banner and the
  notices it draws against the pane's right edge or under the mode row, never the status line
  (a field of a multi-field status line is not a notice); a hook's words up to the hook
  summary's own `Stop hook error:` and `Stop hook feedback:` rows; a wrapped message's rows as
  its own; and a row whose owner is above the rows read, together with the rows above it — the
  whole screen, then the scrollback, or on the alternate screen aterm's archive of the rows
  that scrolled off it. A real context wall drawn where a hook's words stand (a hook that
  blocks with a blank reason) is now found from the transcript and compacted. One behaviour
  changes with no transcript: a real wall under a tool's output whose call row scrolled off
  was compacted (or `/login` typed) and is now left to you, as a wall under a call on the
  screen already was, and so is one whose call row is evicted, past a gap in the archive or
  more than 400 rows up. With the session's transcript it is acted on as before.

- **A tab's drive journal past 16 MiB is cut back too.** When a loop starts on a tab, each of
  its files in `<aterm state>/drive` is cut back to its newest rows; a file past 16 MiB was
  left whole, so a 171 MB journal an older build wrote (one wait, twice a second, for four
  days) never shrank. The cut now reads the file a row at a time, whatever its size, holding
  only the older rows a standing state still reads; it keeps a file whole only where those
  rows pass 16 MiB, or where the file changed or could not be read while it was cut.

- **Drive ledgers are preserved when cross-instance liveness is unknown.** Automatic sweeps
  leave the shared state folder's `drive` groups alone. One instance's roster and discovery
  registry can omit another running instance, so neither they nor a week without writes prove
  a tab's records unused. Pruning remains an explicit operation requiring the complete
  protected set; the directory can still grow past its budget.

- **`aterm ctl video … keys` says how many keys it could not log.** A recording's key ledger
  holds 1024 entries. Keys typed into the recorded window after it was full were dropped
  without a trace, so a long take's `inputs=` looked like every key it saw. They are now
  counted: they join `unlogged_inputs=` on the reply, and `index.json` lists them on their own
  as `unlogged_over_cap`, beside the ledger's size, `inputs_cap`.

- **With Claude Code 2.1.304 the harness still never spends a limit reset on its own.** Claude
  Code 2.1.304 offers several kinds of reset (5-hour, weekly, full, Fable) in one dialog, and its
  rows now read `Use a 5-hour reset (1 left, until Oct 25)` and `Yes, use my weekly reset`
  instead of `Use your reset now` and `Yes, use my reset`. The harness's check that no rule but
  the opt-in limit-reset step chooses an option that spends a reset knew only the old words, so
  it let the new rows through; the confirmation that follows them was still refused. Both
  spellings are now spends, at every approval level. The opt-in step itself
  (`[harness] limit_reset`, off by default) does not use a 2.1.304 reset yet: it reads only the
  old dialog and takes no row it does not read exactly.

- **On Linux, the harness footer counts a subagent that starts just after it last looked.** The
  footer re-reads a Claude Code session's usage when one of its files or folders changes. Linux
  stamps a folder from a coarse clock (a few milliseconds; a whole second on some file systems),
  so a subagent whose transcript appeared in the same tick as the footer's last look changed
  nothing the footer checks, and its spend stayed out of the count until the main conversation
  moved, which can be minutes while subagents work. A folder that changed within two seconds of
  the footer's look is now listed again on the next check.

- **Settings' sidebar no longer cuts a page's name at a larger text size.** Settings follows
  your system's text size (on Windows, Settings > Accessibility > Text size; macOS and Linux draw
  it at the standard size). The sidebar beside its pages had a fixed width, set for the faces
  aterm was designed in at the standard size, which in a medium-width window gave each name 120
  points: from 125% the longer names lost their ends ("Keyboard & In…", "Wallpap…"), most often
  the selected one, which is drawn in semibold, and a wider face cut them in a wide window too.
  The sidebar now grows to its longest name in your system's face, measured in that semibold, so
  moving between pages never changes its width. Where every name fits, as at the standard text
  size, it keeps its width.

- **The harness card's decoration comes on with the card.** When the harness supervised a new
  Claude Code under Cruise or Land, the card stood bare for about a second and a half before the
  rainbow border, the kitty and the `✦ enhanced by aterm harness` line came on, and the kitty's
  ride-in and the footer's chips arrived that late too. aterm takes the running build from the
  session file Claude Code writes as it starts, and that file appeared a moment after aterm first
  looked; the next look came two seconds later. aterm now looks again every tenth of a second
  until the file is there, for up to five seconds, so the decoration, the ride-in and the footer
  come with the card: on its first frame where Claude Code writes the file before it draws the
  card, as its fullscreen renderer did in every launch measured, and a tenth of a second or so
  into it on the inline renderer, which draws the card first. A card from an older build left on
  the screen after a relaunch still stays bare.

- **A new tab finds a tool an installer just added to your PATH.** An installer such as Go's
  or MacTeX's puts its folder on your PATH by adding a file to `/etc/paths.d`, which macOS
  reads when a login shell starts. A tab that opened from the warm shell aterm had started
  before the install did not have the folder, so the tool was not found until a tab started
  cold. aterm now retires the warm shell when `/etc/paths` changes or a file in `/etc/paths.d`
  is added, removed or rewritten, as it does when your startup files change, and the next tab
  starts cold and finds the tool. A fish warm shell is also retired when the `default.theme` fish 4.3
  and later read from your `themes` folder changes.

- **A download whose connection dies silently picks up again within seconds.** When the
  network under a download went away without a word — a Wi-Fi switch, a router forgetting
  the connection, a sleeping peer — aterm waited out a two-minute stall, retried on the same
  dead connection twice more, and then started the archive again from its first byte; every
  ALab tool queued behind it waited too. On a first launch whose `trust` download went silent
  at 30 MB, `targo` became usable after about 400 s. Now a transfer that stops moving is given
  up about 10–14 s after its last byte and continued from where it stopped, on a new
  connection, in the same install: `targo` was usable after about 33 s in the same replay. A
  connection reset is continued at once. The same applies to aterm's own update download. A
  slow link is not mistaken for a dead one: at 64 kB/s, any pause shorter than 12 s goes
  unnoticed, and a longer one costs a reconnect, never the bytes already downloaded; a link
  that keeps dropping can continue after each connection that moves at least 1 MiB, within
  the call's time and total-resume bounds; shorter attempts share a sixteen-resume budget.

- **`aterm ctl survey` hears every aterm on this machine.** With two or more aterm instances
  running, all but one were reported `did not answer: timed out after 2s`, a different one each
  time, because the survey asked them all at once through a dialer that takes one call at a
  time. It now asks them in turn.

- **A worker that ends every report with an idle line is let finish.** A Claude Code that
  closed each report with a line such as "no lander is running" went back and forth between
  aterm's done check and `keep going` for good. An idle line that is the whole answer to the
  done check, in a short turn, now ends the task. A long turn, or an idle line beside the next
  step, is still continued.

- **An answer quicker than aterm's next look at the screen counts.** When Claude Code answered a
  line aterm typed (its done check, `keep going`) before aterm saw the turn run, aterm took the
  line as never received: a done report there was not counted, and `keep going` was typed where
  the task should have ended. The line now counts when the screen shows the answer under it, or
  the conversation's record shows its turn, but not when Autopilot was turned Off over it or a
  usage limit or an error answered it.

- **A done check that a prompt hook stopped no longer ends the task.** When a
  `UserPromptSubmit` hook stopped aterm's done check (`"continue": false`), Claude Code's own
  `Operation stopped by hook: …` line was read as the worker's answer, so aterm could end the
  task on a check the worker never received. That line, and Claude Code's `… operation blocked
  by hook` lines, are no longer taken for the worker's words: the check stays unanswered and the
  session is continued after the usual back-off.

- **A done check that a full context cut is asked again after the compaction.** When Claude
  Code's context filled up during aterm's done check (or its open-items question, or Land's
  instruction), aterm typed `keep going` after the `/compact`, and the done reply that followed
  counted only as a first done report, so the check was asked once more. aterm now types the
  check itself again, so the answer that follows is the check's.

- **After an update from 0.105.0, the harness takes up what the older build's loop held.** The
  first loop of the new build could ask a job's open-items question a second time, continue once
  an exchange of yours that the older loop had left to you, and miss that Autopilot Off had stood
  over a landing or a done check. It now reads those from the older loop's journal notes and from
  the conversation's own record.

- **A loop that takes over a session at a usage limit keeps the first loop's retry times.**
  After a relaunch, restore or handover the new loop took a limit's last try for a new one and
  could retry a rung early: 30 minutes after it attached, where the loop that watched would wait
  6 hours from the try on a spend limit. It now dates the try from what it can read (the
  transcript's limit notice, the done row Claude Code drew) and never retries sooner than the
  first loop would, and a turn aterm began before the Mac slept is dated from aterm's own act.

- **A usage-limit retry that spans a sleep of the Mac is no longer taken for work.** Claude
  Code times a turn by the wall clock, so the turn of a retry aterm typed just before the Mac
  slept is drawn as long as the night (`Baked for 30m 3s` for a retry the limit answered at
  once). aterm read that as the retry's own work and started the limit's retries over: on a
  spend limit the next retry came 30 minutes after the Mac woke, 90 minutes before the 2 hours
  a retry the limit answered waits. aterm now takes the sleep it measured since it typed the
  retry out of that turn, so such a retry keeps its wait, and a retry that really worked for
  10 minutes still starts the retries over.

- **A turn that spans a sleep of the Mac is read by its work, not the sleep, whoever began
  it, and also after aterm restarts.** Taking the sleep out of a retry's turn covered only the
  retry aterm typed and watched across the sleep. Your own turn across a sleep still read as a
  job as long as the night. So after the limit's retry, aterm typed `keep going` into what had
  been a quick exchange of yours. And when aterm took over a session after a sleep it never
  watched (it was restarted, or crashed and came back), it read the retry's turn whole and
  started the limit's retries over: on a spend limit the next retry came 30 minutes after that
  turn, where a retry the limit answered waits 2 hours. aterm now reads every turn less the
  sleep inside it: a limit's retry, your own turn, and a turn already running when the Mac
  slept. The sleep is the Mac's own count since it booted, and each retry's record keeps that
  count, so an aterm that takes over counts the sleep since the last retry. A retry keeps its
  wait, a quick exchange of yours stays yours, and a turn that really worked still counts as
  work. On macOS and Linux a clock set forward is no longer counted as a sleep.

- **A draft aterm cannot safely send over an older Claude Code's `@` menu is told to you.** On
  Claude Code 2.1.289 and earlier a one-entry `@` menu shows its selection in colour only, so
  aterm cannot tell whether Enter sends your draft or completes the entry. It still presses
  nothing there, and now tells you once, where before it waited silently for as long as you
  were away. Once you send or clear the draft, the notice comes down and the session goes on:
  before, a draft that held the session this way, or aterm's own words left in the prompt,
  kept its notice up and the session idle after you had cleared it, and a quick reply to the
  draft you sent went unread. A question the turn ended on is still told once: clearing a
  draft under it leaves that notice up.

- **An Edit-shaped permission box keeps every possible tool's owner hold.** Claude Code
  draws a Bash `sed -i` as the same `Edit file` box. A matching Edit row and transcript can
  still describe an older pending Edit while the current Bash call's `Waiting…` row is off
  screen. An Edit-shaped box therefore stays yours under a Bash ask rule or a hook that can
  match Bash, at every level; screen and transcript agreement never removes that hold.

- **An agent the upgrade ended is said down in an Autopilot Off tab too, and the alert comes
  down once you resume it.** A Claude Code that the live upgrade had already ended when its tab
  went Off (or its agent's switch off) stayed down with nobody told; it now raises an alert with
  the line that resumes it, and the alert is lowered once its conversation is live again,
  resumed by you on any build. Such a tab no longer says "did not exit … Press Ctrl-C" over an
  agent long gone, and `aterm harness upgrade --status` says `stuck:exited`, never "has not
  exited", as soon as the agent is gone.
- **On Windows, a dead key followed by Space types the accent.** On a German keyboard `^` then
  Space typed a space instead of `^`, and on US-International `'` or `"` then Space typed a space
  instead of the quote, so a shell command like `git show HEAD^` or `echo 'hi'` lost a character.
  It now types what Windows typed, and holding Space after it repeats spaces, as everywhere else
  on Windows.

- **On Windows, the bell's taskbar badge comes back after a failed icon.** If Windows once
  refused to make the badge's icon (out of GDI handles, for a moment), no bell badged a window
  at that display scale again until aterm restarted; the next bell now asks again.

- **Windows PowerShell tabs set to Emacs mode by an earlier aterm get Windows' keys and the
  readline keys back.** An earlier aterm setup wrote a four-line block headed `# aterm: emacs
  line-editing so Ctrl+A/Ctrl+E/Ctrl+K/Ctrl+U... move the cursor` into the Windows PowerShell
  profile, and its Emacs mode kept every such tab out of the readline keys aterm now lays over
  Windows mode: Alt+U/L/C typed u, l or c, Ctrl+Z typed `^Z`, and Ctrl+←/→, Alt+←/→,
  Ctrl+Backspace/Delete, Escape and Ctrl+Enter did nothing or something else. A tab whose
  profile holds that block exactly, and names EditMode or a key binding nowhere else, now starts
  in Windows mode with the readline keys, as a tab with no profile does. An Emacs or Vi mode you
  chose yourself is left as it is, and so is the block's when you set
  `ATERM_DISABLE_READLINE_KEYS`, add a comment naming EditMode (`# EditMode Emacs: mine`) or
  change any of its lines. No part of aterm writes the block.

- **On Windows, closing a pwsh tab ends the programs it started, as closing a cmd or Windows
  PowerShell tab does.** pwsh from the Microsoft Store is a packaged app, and Windows starts
  its programs outside the tab's job, so a program a pwsh tab started without a console of the
  tab's (a hidden dev server, say, or one with a window of its own) kept running, and holding
  its port, after the tab closed. Closing the tab, its shell exiting and quitting aterm now end
  every program still running below the shell, as they end the rest; nothing older than the tab
  and nothing outside it is touched. A program whose launcher has already exited (`cmd /c start
  /b server`) is still out of reach in a Store pwsh tab, as it is in every tab under Windows
  Terminal, which ends only the programs sharing the tab's console.

- **On Linux, Nerd Font icons draw as icons on a system with no Chinese, Japanese or Korean
  font.** Without Noto CJK or Droid, DejaVu Sans is the last face aterm falls back to, and it
  drew its own unrelated glyphs for 95 icons a prompt or `eza` uses, the git branch among them.
  Those icons now come from the icon font aterm ships.

- **On Linux, bold text in a variable font is the font's real bold.** With a variable font
  configured, bold text was the regular weight thickened by a pixel, which could bleed into the
  next column ("command" reading as "commmand"). It now draws the font's own bold weight, as
  macOS and Windows do.

- **On Linux, a window that opens on a 2x Wayland display no longer resizes your shell twice as
  it starts.** Under a compositor that tells a window its scale only once the window is on
  screen, such as weston, the window's first size at that scale was counted in the cells of the
  scale it started at, so the shell was told it had a 162x50 terminal and then 80x24 again. The
  window now catches up with its scale before it counts, and the shell is told one size.

- **aterm learns to keep a shell ready for your next tab even while other terminals close.**
  Before keeping a shell ready with your startup files already run, aterm watches a few of your
  tabs start and checks that their startup files left nothing running behind. A shell that
  another terminal left behind as it quit, started while your tab's files ran, was taken for
  something your files left running, so aterm did not learn, and new tabs kept starting from
  scratch. Anything started by a program older than your tab's shell is no longer counted.

- **A worker a manager started in its first second now starts.** A Claude Code whose first
  turn ran `aterm ctl @self spawn agent=claude` before aterm had read its screen gave each
  worker a launch line naming plain `claude`, which the worker's shell did not find: no
  worker started, each tab held its shell, and two minutes later every task read
  `stalled why=startup`, with nothing in the log. The line now follows the manager's own
  Claude Code read off its terminal, and `aterm.log` says each line a worker's launcher typed
  (its program, where it was found, what became of the write), and, for a worker that never
  started, whether its line was typed at all.

- **Closing the palette or a card from the keyboard no longer lights a tab.** The close
  re-read the pointer where it was last seen even after it had left the window (or, in a
  headless window, at the corner it never left), so the first tab under that spot took the
  hover wash and its close button with no pointer on it until the mouse came back. The pointer
  is now re-read only while it is in the window. On Windows and Linux, whose strips have a
  hover.
- **aterm reaches its first window up to 1.5 ms sooner.** The disk watch's
  first reading saved its free-space record to disk with a write-through flush on the
  thread that builds the window, in the middle of startup: 2 ms on every launch, about
  5 ms more whenever another program was flushing the disk at the same moment. It now
  runs beside startup. Measured on headless launches: ready for the window 15.1 to 13.6 ms
  on a fresh install and 13.3 to 12.8 ms on an ordinary launch; with another program
  flushing, an ordinary launch went from 25.4 to 20.6 ms.

- **Output that arrives a line at a time no longer keeps aterm busy.** A program that writes
  one line per call (a pwsh pipeline such as `Get-Content`, cmd's `type`, a build log) handed
  aterm one read per line, and every read woke its event loop: 17,800 wakes for 20,000 lines
  of `Get-Content`. Once such output has streamed for a frame, aterm now looks at it at most
  every 4 ms, and the last line still shows within 4 ms; a key's echo and other short bursts
  are handled at once, as before (40 typed keys take no hold). Measured on a debug build with
  and without the change, under the bundled OpenConsole: 20,000 lines cost 148-159 wakes and
  1.2-1.6 s of aterm CPU instead of 3.3-3.9 s, and 200,000 lines (20 MB) 678 wakes and 11.6 s
  instead of 140,273 and 24.7 s; `cat` of the same 20 MB is unchanged. On every platform;
  `aterm ctl metrics` names the new wake `output_cadence`. On Windows the session reader also
  stopped paying for each line: while such output is held, a short read collects what the
  console host queued behind it (until just before the hold ends, 16 KiB, or a key press) and
  parses, records and announces it as one batch, so a held line shows within about 5.5 ms
  instead of 4. Measured on release builds run alternately with the build before: 200,000
  lines of `Get-Content` cost 0.7-1.25 s of aterm CPU instead of 7.1-7.3 s while `aterm ctl
  await` watched the screen, and 0.8-1.0 s instead of 3.8-4.1 s when nothing did (`cat` of
  the same 20 MB: 0.19-0.31 s on both), with about 5,600 parses instead of 197,000; cmd's
  `type` of it 0.56 s instead of 8.8 s; typed echoes as before (p50 0.43-0.46 ms on both).
  On a busy Mac (a build beside it) such a program pauses for 4 ms and more dozens of times a
  second; a pause shorter than 16 ms now keeps its output on the 4 ms pace instead of starting
  the first frame over at one look per line. Ten tabs each printing half a million lines beside
  eight busy processes: aterm's main thread does 20 ms of work per second instead of 45, and
  the output finishes in 13.45 s instead of 14.07 (medians of 4); on a quieter Mac, 10.7 ms per
  second instead of 12.1 (medians of 10). During such a flood aterm answers a command in
  0.38 ms and echoes a key sent to a quiet tab in 0.47 ms (95th and 90th percentiles, timed
  from a client at the interactive priority), as with no 4 ms pace at all (0.47 and 0.54 ms).
  A client at the default priority shares the cores with the ten printing programs and waits
  for one: 4.9 ms, against 1.0 ms with no pace, under which the same output takes 14.4 s
  instead of 9.1.

- **Windows: aterm reads when a process started from Windows itself.** It asked
  `ps -o lstart=`, which Windows does not have (Git's MSYS `ps` refuses `-o`), so every read
  named no start and, with Git on PATH, spawned a `ps` for nothing: nothing that tells one run
  of a program from the next by its start could tell them apart. It now reads the creation
  time Windows keeps (`GetProcessTimes`), as macOS reads its own record. With it
  `aterm ctl instances`, `ls` and `windows` pass over a graph entry whose pid Windows has
  since given to a younger process, as on macOS and Linux, instead of listing and dialing
  that stranger.

- **Windows: the app folder and the install carry every licence text their NOTICE names.**
  NOTICE.txt pointed at licence files the folder did not have (aterm-font's rustybuzz and
  fontations terms, the MIT and Apache texts of the lz4, zstd, serde and win32 code built into
  aterm.exe), and `install.ps1` left LICENSE.txt, README.txt and VERSION.txt behind.
  `build.ps1` now lays every licence text NOTICE cites into `licenses\` (54 files, against 28)
  and points NOTICE.txt's citations at them, and stops on a citation that names no file;
  `install.ps1` installs LICENSE.txt, README.txt and VERSION.txt with the rest. VERSION.txt
  carries the build number and trust anchor `aterm --version` prints, as README.txt promised,
  and README.txt names OpenConsole.exe as Microsoft's console host, not one of aterm's images.

- **Windows: a cmd.exe default tab, and `shell = "gitbash"`, get their shell integration.**
  On a machine with neither pwsh nor Windows PowerShell on PATH the default tab ran
  `%COMSPEC%`'s cmd.exe with pwsh's integration command line, so it had no prompt marks and
  `aterm ctl blocks` found nothing; it now runs plain `cmd.exe` with cmd's prompt marks (after
  `echo hi`: 4 marks and 2 blocks, against 0 and none). The integration now follows the
  program a tab runs rather than the name it was given, so `shell = "gitbash"` (or
  `"git-bash"`) gets Git Bash's integration as `"bash"` did (6 marks and a block with its
  command and exit code, against none).

- **`aterm ctl settings set|unset` names a key written by hand.** `conpty`,
  `windowing_behavior`, the `[fleet]` keys and the other keys aterm.toml takes but Settings
  does not show were answered `unknown key` although `--help` and the starter config teach
  them; the answer now says the key is set in aterm.toml by hand and that Manual completes and
  checks it.

- **Windows: under OpenConsole, a killed `less` or `vim` no longer garbles the tab.** A
  full-screen program ended by `Stop-Process` or Task Manager left the console host on its dead
  screen while aterm left its own, so after the next full-screen program the prompt and what you
  typed landed on the wrong rows. aterm now has the console host leave that screen at the
  shell's next prompt (and on `aterm ctl mainscreen`), and the tab follows the switch the host
  sends, so both stay in step; `aterm ctl cast drift` and `temporal` replay it as the tab ran
  it. In pwsh the prompt drawn on the dead screen comes along to the same row, so the lines
  you type next no longer overwrite the output above them or leave the old command line's tail
  behind (`pasted-after-killt\usr\bin\vim.exe` before; every line whole after, measured
  2026-10-18); the earlier output scrolls into the scrollback when the program left its cursor
  above it. cmd and Git Bash, which draw their prompt on the restored screen, are unchanged.
  The dead program's mouse tracking, cursor-key and keypad modes and scroll region go with its
  screen, so the wheel scrolls and clicks select again, and the leave touches nothing else:
  an ssh or WSL session in the tab keeps its Ctrl+C. `mainscreen` answers `ERR timeout` when
  the console host does not leave. Under the Windows console host nothing changes. The killed
  program's bracketed paste and size reports go at that prompt too: after a killed `vim`, every
  resize typed `[48;30;90;690;810t` into the prompt of pwsh, cmd and Git Bash, a paste arrived
  in `[200~` brackets (cmd then ran it as a command, Git Bash reported a syntax error), and
  pwsh's next line failed with `900t: The term '900t' is not recognized`; now the typed line,
  the paste and the resize stay clean in all three (measured 2026-10-18). The pwsh and cmd
  prompts also turn both modes off themselves, so a program that leaves them on outside a
  full-screen screen no longer breaks every later paste and resize either; bash, zsh and fish
  keep the bracketed paste they set for their own prompt. A command that turns size reports on
  at the prompt itself no longer has the first report typed into the next command line
  (`[48;30;100;0;0techo first-after`, a ParserError in pwsh): under OpenConsole the report the
  switch-on sends waits until a full-screen screen comes up, where vim and neovim turn the
  reports on and still get it at once. A size report vim asked for while it sat idle no
  longer reaches the shell after the kill: when the font size or display scale changed (or
  `aterm ctl image` first drew a headless tab) the report waited for vim's next output, and
  after a kill that was the shell's, so pwsh showed no prompt, typed `[;;;…;690;900t` into
  the next line (a ParserError) and drew it over the rows above, and Git Bash answered
  `syntax error near unexpected token ;`. The report now goes out at once, and the prompt
  that proves the program dead drops any report still waiting for it and turns its mouse,
  cursor-key and keypad modes off there rather than at the console host's switch. pwsh's
  prompt now lands whole wherever vim's cursor was, the typed lines after it whole and the
  earlier output in the scrollback (measured 2026-10-18 with vim's cursor on rows 0, 1, 10
  and 27). Git Bash now echoes what is typed after such a kill too: MSYS2 reports the killed
  program's exit as 0, and the bash integration put back the terminal settings a raw program
  left only after a command that failed, so nothing typed was echoed until `stty sane`. It now
  also checks them after a command that ran a second or more, whatever its status (one `stty
  -a`, about 50 ms in Git Bash, after a command that long; none after a quick one), and the
  typed, pasted and later lines read whole with vim's cursor on rows 0, 1, 10 and 27 and at
  home (measured 2026-10-18).

- **Windows: a console program that turns on xterm's modifyOtherKeys no longer takes your
  chords.** After a native program wrote `ESC[>4;2m` (a `[Console]::Write` of it, or a tool that
  asks for it), PowerShell got nothing for Shift+letters, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+K, Alt+B and the
  other Ctrl and Alt chords, under both console hosts and after the program had exited, because
  aterm then sent those chords in a form no console host reads. Windows tabs now refuse
  modifyOtherKeys as they refuse the kitty keyboard protocol: the request is ignored, a query
  reads level 0, and every chord arrives as before.

- **Windows: Git Bash keeps every key after a resize under OpenConsole, and reads emoji whole.**
  Git Bash and the other MSYS2 programs (Git's `less` and `vim` in a pwsh tab included) lost
  the first key or the paste's opening ESC after about one resize in four under `conpty =
  "auto"` or a path; now a second console client gives their runtime a record to drop instead
  (24 of 24 measured with OpenConsole 1.24 and 1.25), so `auto` runs Git Bash tabs in
  OpenConsole too. Under the Windows console host, an emoji or other character beyond U+FFFF
  typed or pasted into Git Bash arrived as U+FFFD; it now arrives whole. An MSYS2 program left
  running by an earlier tab (an `ssh-agent`) no longer counts as running in a new one. Dragging
  the window's edge no longer types into Git Bash: under OpenConsole a stray `R` or `;1R` and a
  bell landed before the next line after resizes 50 to 300 ms apart (4 of 4 lines), because
  aterm's answer to the console host's own cursor question waited behind that second client
  while the host waited for the answer. The answer now goes at once: 75 of 75 lines whole with
  three resizes 50, 100 or 300 ms apart before each, in a Git Bash tab and nested in cmd and
  pwsh 7, and Git Bash usually redraws after a resize in about 10 ms instead of half a second.

- **Windows: Git's vim redraws at the new size after every resize, under either console host.**
  Under OpenConsole, after about one resize in four, vim showed `900t` or `630t` in its
  bottom-right corner and kept drawing at the old width: the size report vim asks for lost its
  first byte to the same MSYS2 runtime drop the second console client guards against, and vim
  read the rest as typed keys. Under the Windows console host, vim kept the old size after about
  one resize in four until you pressed a key. aterm now sends the reports it sends unasked as the
  input they are, behind the guard, and sends the guard by itself when no key follows a resize.
  Measured with six resizes in a row: vim in a pwsh or Git Bash tab redrew 36 of 36 times under
  each host, against 27 and 26 of 36 before; Git's `less` 36 of 36, as before.

- **On Windows, an aterm run as administrator can no longer be driven by your other programs.**
  An elevated aterm now keeps its control socket and token in a folder of its own
  (`%TEMP%\aterm-elevated`) that only administrators and SYSTEM can open, so a program running
  without elevation, even as you, can neither read the token nor connect, and so cannot type
  into an elevated shell. Its windows read `Administrator: …` in the title bar, taskbar and
  Alt-Tab, as Windows Terminal's do; an elevated launch opens its own elevated window, never a
  tab in an unelevated one (as `windowing_behavior = "attach"`, or `aterm` run elevated from
  inside an aterm tab, could do before); and `aterm ctl` lists and drives only the
  instances of its own elevation, saying where the others are when it finds none. Before, an
  elevated aterm either ran without a control socket or, started first, left one that
  unelevated aterm windows could not use.

- **Windows: a PowerShell command block reports the code of the line that failed.** After a
  native program failed (`cmd /c exit 7`), every later failing cmdlet (`Write-Error`, `throw`,
  `Get-Item` of a missing path) read as exit 7 too, in pwsh 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1,
  until a native command succeeded. A cmdlet's failure is now exit 1, the same native failure
  twice is its code twice, and a line Ctrl+C stopped (`Start-Sleep 60`) reports what `ping -t`
  stopped by Ctrl+C does. `$LASTEXITCODE` is untouched.

- **Windows: a command Ctrl+C stopped reads "interrupted".** The tab's status read `failed
  (exit -1073741510)` after Ctrl+C in pwsh or cmd and `failed (exit 130)` in Git Bash; both
  now read `interrupted` (`exited (interrupted)` for a tab's own program). `aterm ctl status`
  and `blocks` keep the exit code.

- **Windows: `aterm` in a tab is the build that opened it.** A tab put its window's folder on
  PATH only inside a macOS app bundle, and on Windows the registry PATH went ahead of what
  aterm put in front, so a tab of a portable or newly built copy ran the installed `aterm` (or,
  with none installed, found none). The folder holding the window's `aterm.exe` now leads
  every tab's PATH, behind the managed agents directory.

- **Git Bash records the command line as typed and gives a line that opens with a subshell
  its block.** On Git Bash (bash 5.3, which Git for Windows ships) `ls /nope` was recorded as
  its alias's expansion, and `(exit 3)` or `( cd sub && make )` started no block, so its exit
  code was lost; `true && (exit 4)` was recorded as `true`. bash 5.3 and later now record the
  line from history and start its block before its first command, whatever it is.

- **Windows: a Git Bash tab starts as the login shell Windows Terminal starts, half a second
  sooner.** Windows Terminal's Git Bash profile, Git's own `git-bash.exe` and VS Code all
  start Git Bash as a login shell; aterm started a non-login one that read the login files
  itself, and Git's `/etc/bash.bashrc` then loaded its prompt and completion
  (`git-prompt.sh`, `git-completion.bash`) three times, with `~/.bashrc` twice where
  `~/.bash_profile` reads it (as the one Git for Windows writes does). A tab now starts as
  `bash --login` and reads what a login Git Bash reads, once: `/etc/profile`, then the first of
  `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` and `~/.profile`, and `~/.bashrc` only where that file
  reads it, as in Windows Terminal. Its prompt, completion, aliases and history file are a
  login Git Bash's. The first prompt came 1.28 s after launch against 0.74 s for a plain login
  Git Bash (measured by the 2026-10-18 verifier); it now comes at 0.82 s by the tab's own
  clock against 1.27 s for the build before (medians of seven launches each; launch to prompt
  0.92 s against 1.34 s, a debug build against a release one).

- **Windows: Ctrl+J at a PowerShell prompt runs the line**, as readline's C-j does on macOS
  and Linux. The console host read its line-feed byte as Ctrl+Enter and inserted a line above;
  aterm now sends it as the J key, which the PowerShell integration binds to AcceptLine (and
  leaves alone when your profile binds it, or `ATERM_DISABLE_READLINE_KEYS` is set). A
  program that reads the character still gets a line feed: Git Bash runs the line.

- **`aterm ctl screen` reports blinking text.** A cell's `attrs` listed `bold`, `italic`,
  `underline` and `strike` but never `blink`, which `aterm ctl cell` reported for the same
  cell.

- **Windows: "Close all windows" asks each window in turn.** Closing a second window while
  another window's "Close all tabs?" question stood did nothing, so after the first answer
  that window stayed open. Each window's question now waits its turn and is asked once the
  one before it is answered (as a quit once that window is the last). The window asking is
  brought forward, so a question over a background or minimized window is seen.

- **Windows: new and restored windows appear finished.** A second window (Ctrl+Shift+N, a
  tab moved to a new window) appeared at the default spot with a light title bar and then
  moved, resized and darkened on screen; a restored window appeared elsewhere and then
  jumped back, and a maximized one appeared at its normal size before maximizing. Each now
  appears at its size and place, maximized when it was, with its title-bar colour.

- **Windows: a minimized window stops drawing.** A minimized window kept rendering and
  presenting every frame of streaming output; it now pauses until it is restored. A capture
  of it (`aterm ctl image`, `aterm ctl window`) and a recording still get their frames.

- **Windows: clicking a notification brings its tab back.** A notification from a tab now
  carries aterm's icon instead of a generic ⓘ, a click on it raises the window and selects
  the tab that sent it, and a headless instance posts none.

- **Windows: the bell plays your sound scheme's Default Beep** (silent under a silent
  scheme), not the fixed simple beep.

- **Windows: double-clicks follow your double-click speed.** Double-clicking the tab band to
  maximize, a chip to rename it, or text to select it used a fixed 500 ms; it now uses the
  speed set in Windows' mouse settings.

- **Find works in a split.** The find bar now sits on the focused pane and highlights every
  match in it, and the pane beside it keeps its own rows; it used to cover the top rows of
  every pane and highlight only the current match.

- **The current find match stands out.** While the find bar is open the current match is a
  solid block in the accent colour, a clear step from the tint the other matches wear; it
  used to differ from them only in hue. The find bar's bottom rule also runs along the bar's
  edge instead of through the descenders of its key hints. Its text is in the terminal's
  background colour, as a block cursor's is: in the default theme `#111318` on the bright
  green at 13.5:1, where it was a washed-out grey (`#535353`, 5.6:1); on Default Light's dark
  green it stays white.

- **Windows: non-US keyboard layouts type the layout's characters.** Shift typed the US
  layout's symbol over the one the layout gave: German Shift+7 typed `?` for `/`, and on
  French AZERTY Shift+& typed `!`, so digits could not be typed. Caps Lock with Shift now
  types lowercase, as in every other Windows program, and a dead key that does not combine
  with the next letter types both (US-International `'` then `s` is `'s`, not `s`); held,
  that letter repeats alone, as in Windows' own programs.

- **Windows: Alt codes type their character.** Holding Alt and typing 0233 on the keypad
  types `é`; the digits used to reach PowerShell as Alt+digit and the character was lost.

- **Windows: more keys reach console programs as themselves.** Ctrl+Break now reaches them
  (`ping -t` prints its statistics and keeps going), and PowerShell can tell the
  keypad's keys, Shift+Space, Shift+Backspace and Ctrl+Space from the keys they used to arrive
  as; Git Bash and WSL get the same bytes as before, and Ctrl+Alt+Space now reaches them whole.

- **Windows: the keypad's 5 with NumLock off no longer clears the PowerShell line.** Under
  the bundled console host, the default, it reached PowerShell as Escape and `[E`, which
  cleared what you had typed and left `[E`; now it does nothing there, as in Windows Terminal,
  and Git Bash still gets the keypad-5 bytes, now with Shift, Ctrl and Alt in them. Under that
  host F13 to F20 now reach PowerShell (`[Console]::ReadKey` read nothing for them). And a
  program that turns on keypad application mode gets the keypad's digits, operators and Enter
  under both hosts, as in Windows Terminal: a console program got none of them under the
  default host, and in Git Bash vim paged on keypad 3 and 9 and nano typed no keypad key at
  all (measured 2026-10-18 with `ReadKey`, PSReadLine, Git's vim and nano).

- **Windows PowerShell 5.1: Alt+U, Alt+L and Alt+C change a word's case.** They typed a stray
  `u`, `l` or `c`: 5.1's PSReadLine 2.0.0 lacks the functions pwsh 7 binds to them. aterm's
  integration now brings its own, which upper-case, lower-case or capitalize from the cursor to
  the end of the word, as pwsh 7's do.

- **Scrollback shortcuts reach full-screen programs.** Shift+PageUp and the other scrollback
  chords moved nothing on a full-screen program's screen, which has no scrollback, and the
  program never saw them; now less, vim and other full-screen programs get the key.

- **Windows: the window menu matches a dark title bar.** Alt+Space and a right-click on the
  title bar or tab band opened a light menu under aterm's dark title bar on a light desktop;
  the menu now takes the title bar's side.

- **Windows: the title bar no longer shows a frozen spinner.** While Claude Code or Codex
  works, the title bar, taskbar and Alt+Tab showed one stuck frame of its spinner (`◐ …`);
  they now show the title alone, and the tab keeps its activity mark.

- **Windows: `aterm ctl chrome` reports the title bar's colour.** Windows 11 will not read the
  caption colours back, so `caption_color` and `caption_text` said `n/a`; they now report
  the colour aterm set, marked `(set)`, beside the new `caption_surface`.

- **Settings no longer clips the Top Settings colours card on a short window.** At Windows'
  1.1 line height a 568×320 Settings window in Serious Mode cut the card's last point off.

- **Windows: emoji are in colour, whole, and fill their two cells.** `😀 🚀 ✅ ❌ ⭐ ⚡ 👍` drew
  as grey outlines from Segoe UI Symbol, and the emoji that did come from Segoe UI Emoji
  (`⚠️ ❤️ 👍🏽 🧪`) were drawn oversized and cut off at the right and at the bottom of the row.
  Every emoji now comes from Segoe UI Emoji in colour, whole and centred, about 16 px across
  its 18 px slot at the default size. ZWJ sequences, families included, draw as one emoji
  (`👩‍💻`, `👨‍👩‍👧`), and a flag Windows has no picture for as its two letters
  (`🇯🇵` as `JP`, where it drew a lone `J`), as in Windows Terminal; an unknown flag pair draws
  its two letters on macOS and Linux too.

- **Windows: Claude Code's spinner reads as a star again.** Its `✢ ✳ ✶ ✻ ✽` and the `⏵⏵` of
  `bypass permissions on` had become the default font's own small marks, the size of an `*`;
  the `⏵⏵` are drawn with the fuller glyphs aterm drew before, and up to the 175% display
  scale the five spinner frames are drawn from the cell, as crisp stars, spokes and petals:
  from a font at those sizes, `✳` and `✶` came out soft grey (8.5% and 14% of their ink solid
