  at 100%, about half the ink of `✽`), so the spinner dimmed on those frames. Each frame now
  reaches full ink with at least 30% of it solid at the default size, no frame has more than
  1.4 times another's ink, and `✶` is a six-pointed star with open notches, as tall as a
  font's, where it had drawn as a hexagon with stub points. From 200% (32 px text and up) the
  font's own frames are crisp, and aterm keeps them: a thin cross, a slender star and whole
  teardrops, each at least a fifth solid. Their weights are evened, so the spinner no longer
  pulses thin to heavy each cycle: the font's `✽` carried 2.5 times the ink of its `✳` and
  2.2 times its `✢`, and `✳` read pale on a light theme. Each frame's outline moves in or out
  by a fraction of a pixel until no frame has more than 1.4 times another's ink: `✢ ✳ ✶`
  gain about two fifths, `✽` gives up a sixth, and `✻`, the frame Claude Code rests on and
  prints beside every finished turn, is unchanged. Below 32 px of text (the default size
  under 200%), and on macOS and Linux, nothing changes.

- **Windows: Claude Code's spinner no longer jumps up on its `*` frame, and `*` sits on the
  line in code.** Outside Ghostty Claude Code animates `· ✢ * ✶ ✻ ✽`, and that `*` is the
  font's own. Iosevka Term, the default font, raises its asterisk like a superscript, so at
  100% that frame stood 5 px above the others and the spinner hopped twice a cycle. The
  default font now draws Iosevka's own low asterisk, the one its JetBrains Mono style picks,
  centred on the line like its `+` and like Windows Terminal's Cascadia Mono, in all four
  styles and at every size: the spinner stays level, `a * b` reads as multiplication, `/*`
  opens a comment at the slash's middle and `git log --graph` marks each commit on its rail.
  The bundled font carries only Iosevka's default asterisk, so aterm moves that glyph, in whole
  pixels so it stays crisp, to where the low one sits. Another font, an installed Iosevka and
  `font_family = "Iosevka Term"` keep their own asterisk.

- **A kitty image placed with both `c=` and `r=` fills its box.** `a=T,…,c=8,r=2` drew the
  image as a centred square inside the 8x2-cell box, with empty space beside it; it now fills
  the box from the cursor cell, as kitty does. With only one of `c=` or `r=`, the other still
  follows the image's aspect and the image keeps its shape.

- **Windows: Chinese, Japanese and Korean text matches the weight of the text around it.**
  Beside the default Iosevka Term Semibold, Han and kana now come from Microsoft YaHei Bold and
  Hangul from Malgun Gothic Bold, where the Regular cuts drew thin grey strokes; a lighter or
  Regular `font_family` keeps the matching lighter cut.

- **The I Ching line symbols sit at mid-line.** `⚊ ⚋` drew as a low underscore from the
  built-in DejaVu Sans Mono beside the mid-line bars of `☰ ⚌`; they now come from a symbol
  font that draws them at mid-line too.

- **Windows: the title-bar, taskbar and notification icons match your display's scale.** At
  125 %, 150 % and above, the title-bar icon was the 16 px image stretched by the shell, and a
  window kept its icons' size when moved to a display of another scale; the notification area
  got the 32 px image squeezed into its 16 px slot. Each now loads the frame made for its size
  at the window's scale, and a window moved between displays takes the new display's.

- **On Windows, pwsh's directory names and every coloured cell read clearly.** `Get-ChildItem`
  drew directory names in the light text colour on palette blue at 2.2:1, Default Light's
  `White on DarkBlue` was 1.35:1 and black text vanished on the dark theme. Wherever a cell's
  text and background are both the theme's own colours (its 16 ANSI colours and default text
  and background), the text is now held to 4.5:1 on a coloured cell and 3:1 on the theme's
  background (4.5:1 for aterm's own red, green, yellow, blue, magenta and cyan), the way
  Windows Terminal adjusts such pairs; a program's own 24-bit and 256-colour choices, box
  drawing, block elements and powerline separators are left exactly as sent. Text that has to
  turn dark (or light) to be read on its cell takes the theme's own background (or text)
  colour, not the first grey that passes: labels on yellow and green were `#535353` (4.52:1)
  and `#3E3E3E`, and one powerline segment turned dark grey beside white ones; on red, green,
  yellow, magenta and cyan they are now the page colour `#111318`, 5.8 to 10.8:1 where the
  greys were 4.5 to 5.7:1. So are labels on the colours lighter than the text itself (white,
  bright white and the bright green, yellow and cyan), which were still `#535353` and
  `#686868` (5.0 to 6.1:1) beside `#111318` labels in the same row; they are 10.4 to
  18.6:1 now. Coloured text that only needs darkening keeps its colour: green on white is a
  darker green, red on yellow a darker red. A light theme that draws white as dark text for
  its page (Default Light's bright white is the slate `#474D57`) draws a program's white on a
  colour in the page colour wherever that reads better, since white there means light text:
  in Default Light white and bright white on black (`ESC[37;40m`, `ESC[97;40m`) are
  `#F6F7F9` at 12.8:1 where they were the greys `#979CA6` and `#91949A` (4.5:1), and
  bright white on a program's own 24-bit or 256-colour cell, which the floor leaves
  alone, went from 1.2:1 to 6.6:1. A test runner's `FAIL` badge
  (bright white on red) and pwsh's `White on DarkBlue` stay `#F6F7F9` (5.35:1 and 5.86:1),
  where the theme's own slate would be 1.49:1 and 1.35:1; white on the page keeps the slate
  (PSReadLine's numbers, 7.9:1). Setting `minimum_contrast` replaces it with that
  floor on every cell (`1.0` turns both off). macOS and Linux are unchanged.

- **On Windows, Default's blue works as a background, bright blue is brighter than blue, and
  green, yellow and cyan match red and magenta.** Blue (`#2973D0`, was `#3B8EEA`) now carries
  the light text pwsh and `ls` put on it, and as text it draws `#3E81D5`, 4.7:1 (dim blue
  3.0:1, where it had dropped to 3.9:1 and 2.8:1); bright blue (`#6EA8FE`, was a violet
  `#5C5CFF` at 3.9:1) is the lighter shade of the same hue, so bold directory names in Git
  Bash and `Write-Host -ForegroundColor Blue` are 7.7:1 instead of dimmer than plain blue.
  Green, yellow and cyan were xterm's fully saturated `#00CD00`, `#CDCD00` and `#00CDCD`
  beside red `#E06C75`, so a `git diff`'s additions shouted while its deletions were soft;
  they are One Dark's `#98C379`, `#E5C07B` and `#56B6C2` (9.2, 10.8 and 7.8:1), the family red
  and magenta come from: git's hashes and hunk headers, PSReadLine's strings and Git Bash's
  prompt with them. Their bright shades are now the same colours, lighter: bright green
  `#BBEC98`, yellow `#FFEE99`, magenta `#E9A3FF` and cyan `#73DEEC` (9.9 to 15.9:1, each
  about 1.5:1 above its normal, so `Yellow` and `DarkYellow` stay two colours), where
  Dracula's neon green, lemon, pink and pale sky made bold text change colour as well as
  brightness, so PSReadLine's commands were lemon beside amber hashes and git's branch names
  neon. Bright yellow leans 16° from amber toward yellow, because amber's own hue that light
  is a cream that would leave PSReadLine's command names the colour of their arguments; no
  bright sits closer than 0.09 in OkLab to Gray, White or the default text. macOS and Linux
  keep xterm's and Dracula's.

- **On Windows, vim and other programs pick the palette for aterm's theme.** Tabs are started
  with `COLORFGBG` set from the theme they draw (`15;0` dark, `0;15` light), a tab's own theme
  or its identity's included, because the Windows console host does not pass on the
  background-colour query: Git Bash's vim used its light-background colours on the dark theme.
  A shell already running keeps the value it started with when the theme later changes.

- **On Windows, Settings' cards rise above the page on light themes.** On a light theme the
  cards and the sidebar were drawn darker than the page around them (1.14:1 below it); they
  are now lighter, as on dark themes and in Windows' own Settings. Drop-downs, buttons and the
  search box rise above their cards too, near-white as Windows' own controls are (`#fcfcfc`
  on a `#f6f6f6` card in Default Light, where they were a sunken `#ececec`). macOS and Linux
  are unchanged.

- **On Windows, Settings' text buttons look like buttons.** Browse themes…, Reset, Import…,
  Folder and the other buttons that were drawn quiet had no border and a fill one step off
  their card (`#f8f8f8` on `#f6f6f6`, 1.01:1, in Default Light), so they read as plain text
  beside Customize. They are now Windows' standard button, as in Windows' own Settings: a
  near-white fill inside a hairline border (`#fcfcfc` in `#c9cacb`; `#313132` in `#464647` in
  Default). Icon-only buttons stay borderless, and macOS and Linux are unchanged.

- **On Windows, Settings' colour preview draws its title bar the way the window will.** With
  Window appearance on Match terminal (the default) the preview's small title bar followed
  Windows' own light or dark mode, while aterm's real title bar follows the terminal theme: a
  light theme previewed on a dark desktop wore a dark title bar (`#20222a` over Default
  Light), and a dark theme on a light desktop a light one. It now follows the theme, and a
  screen reader hears that it matches the terminal theme. It is also the colour the title bar
  actually wears, the tab band's (`#E2E3E5` in Default Light, `#303135` in Default), not a
  stock grey, and where that sits close to the page it has the band's hairline round it: on
  Default Light it was 1.04:1 off the page and only its glyphs showed.

- **Importing a theme or installing a pack theme over an existing one no longer fails on
  Windows with "Access is denied".** A theme file written a moment earlier is often still held
  by a virus scanner or the search indexer; the replace is now tried again for up to half a
  second, whether the hold answers "Access is denied" or "being used by another process".

- **Clicks and menu commands keep their order with a new tab.** A click right after Cmd-T now
  lands after the new tab, in order with the keys around it, and moving the mouse while the
  tab opens no longer crowds out held keystrokes. Keys typed right after Cmd-T or Cmd-N chosen
  through the menu's shortcut go to the new tab or window, not the old one. A click in the
  old window while Cmd-N's window opens is no longer read as a Cmd-click. Input held for a tab
  that takes longer than 15 s to open is dropped and reported, instead of replayed into it
  after keys typed later went to the old tab, and a held click on the tab strip is dropped
  rather than replayed onto a tab that moved.

- **A home folder on a network volume that stopped answering no longer freezes aterm.** The
  first tab, and any tab started without a folder, checks a home on a volume that is not local
  first: if it does not answer within 250 ms the shell starts in `/` and says why, instead of
  holding the window for up to 10 s. A home behind `/home` (the automounter) is recognised as
  remote. A network home that answers is used as before, and a local one is never checked.

- **An update from 0.105.0 brings the Full Disk Access page instead of three folder
  dialogs.** An update that landed within ten minutes of 0.105.0's Developer Tools page, or
  that checked before the outgoing version had exited, gave up on the Full Disk Access
  hand-over and later read Documents, Desktop and Downloads, so macOS asked about each. The
  page now comes up at the next quiet moment instead.

- **bash keeps the `DEBUG` trap your `.bashrc` set, and aterm's command marks with it.** On
  macOS's bash 3.2 a `.bashrc` that set a `DEBUG` trap (bash-preexec, atuin) replaced aterm's,
  so commands lost their blocks, exit codes and titles; on bash 5 aterm's replaced yours. Both
  now run.

- **Ctrl-C works at a zsh tab's first prompt when your `.zshrc` left the terminal raw.**
  The first prompt repairs the terminal as soon as aterm reads its state, so Ctrl-C clears the
  line there (`$?` 130) instead of inserting `^C` or beeping.

- **On Linux, a folder on a network share that stopped answering no longer stalls a new tab,
  and times follow a time zone change.** aterm reads the kernel's mount table to tell a share
  from a local disk, so a hung share is judged as on macOS, and asking for the same hung folder
  again answers at once instead of waiting another 250 ms. Times aterm shows follow a daylight
  saving switch or a changed `/etc/localtime` without a restart, and a program started right
  after it was written is no longer refused as busy.

- **Chrome setup's consent is never chosen, and its install offer is answered "Not now".** As
  Claude Code 2.1.302 draws the setup, each option's description beside its label, the harness
  read "Continue with browser tools" with its description as a label it did not know, and could
  choose it, which keeps the browser tools on in every later session. It now never chooses it,
  whole or cut short (below 49 columns Claude Code draws it "Continue with browser…"), and
  answers the setup with "Continue without browser tools", which saves nothing; in a pane
  narrower than 54 columns, where Claude Code cuts that name short too, the setup waits for you
  instead. The offer that opens the setup, "Claude wants to use your browser", which the
  harness left to you as Claude Code 2.1.302 draws it, is now answered "Not now" at full power:
  that saves nothing, and Claude Code does not make the offer again in that session. The
  harness never chooses "Install extension", nor "Don't ask again", which turns the offer off
  for good; Esc saves nothing either. Claude Code makes the offer only when it finds a
  Chromium-family browser, and never while the session allows tool calls without asking
  (bypass permissions).
- **The harness no longer stops on a dialog read half drawn.** A screen read while Claude
  Code was still drawing a dialog, only its first option row on the screen, stopped the
  harness with an internal error when it went to wait on the dialog; it now waits for the
  screen to change.
- **The harness reads the MCP server dialog's answers whole in narrow panes.** In a narrow
  pane Claude Code wraps a long option over two rows or more ("Use this and all future MCP
  servers in this project" below 55 columns, over three rows at 30), and the harness still
  read some of those rows as options of their own (a row that opens with a capital, as "MCP
  server" under "Continue without using this" at 31 to 34 columns, or a row the widest row on
  the screen seemed to leave room for): with the "New MCP server found" dialog cut by a short
  pane, or worded differently, it could Escape it or choose "Continue without using this MCP"
  — each saved for good, turning the server off. Its answers are now read whole from the rows
  they are drawn on, wherever Claude Code draws them, also under the `↑`/`↓` it draws when a
  pane too short for the dialog hides some options, and the MCP server dialog waits for you.
  Other wrapped options are read as one only where a rule across the pane shows its width;
  with no rule on the screen they are read a row at a time, but for an answer saved for good,
  read whole when its rows spell it.
- **A codex-alab that crashed in the middle of a task carries the task on again once aterm
  brings it back.** Since 0.106.0, when aterm relaunched a crashed codex-alab on its
  conversation (and likewise after a stall or memory restart, or when it restored the tab after
  aterm's own crash), aterm let go of the tab the moment the new codex-alab appeared, a few
  milliseconds before codex-alab looked for aterm's hold as its proof that aterm had typed the
  line. So codex-alab never continued the interrupted task, and the conversation waited at its
  prompt. aterm now keeps its hold until the relaunched codex-alab has taken its claim, which
  it does only after that look, and shows its first screen: usually about a second, at most a
  minute, and less if it ends first. 0.105.0 also held on until the relaunched Codex was idle,
  for at most 15 seconds. codex-alab then continues the task once by itself. aterm still types
  nothing after the relaunch line, and lets go at once if you start a turn yourself first.
- **On Linux, only a display server that went away ends aterm as a logout.** Since 0.106.0,
  when the X server or Wayland compositor under aterm crashed, was killed or restarted, aterm
  has quit as a logout does: it saves your windows, tabs and the agents in them for the next
  launch, says `the display connection ended (…)` and exits with status 69, where before it
  crashed with the display and lost them. But 0.106.0 also ended that way on any other
  window-system error, among them an X error still pending when you quit aterm yourself, so
  such a quit exited 69 and said the display had gone. Now only a display connection that died
  ends aterm this way, and the line says how it died (`end of file: the X server closed the
  connection`, `Connection reset by peer`, `Broken pipe`), where under X11 it said `its event
  loop failed with no error code`. Any other window-system error is reported as itself (`the
  event loop failed (…)`) and exits with status 70, and quitting aterm yourself exits 0.
- **With the session keeper on, closing a tab ends its shell even when the keeper drops the
  window's connection, and quitting aterm never relaunches it.** When the keeper dropped a
  window's connection before it had read that a tab closed, that tab's shell stayed in the keeper
  until the window ended, and came back as a tab after a crash. A current keeper now confirms each
  tab close, and the window tells it again on its next connection until it does (an older keeper
  that cannot confirm is told once, as before). Separately, if a window's connection to the keeper dropped while it started, and its
  goodbye was lost when the person quit it, the keeper relaunched aterm after that quit whenever
  another window had crashed. The keeper now reads that end as the quit it was.
- **`⚙` lands an open Settings ▸ Harness on the session's row.** With a Settings ▸ Harness tab
  already open, scrolled or at its top with the row below the fold, `⚙`, `⊘ off` and the
  Autopilot menu's Harness settings… raised the tab but left the page where it was, with no row
  selected, whenever one of the page's refreshes finished before the next frame (in a headless
  aterm, every time). The page now lands on the session's row, or on SUPERVISION, every time.
  View ▸ Coding Agent Harness… opens the page at its top, an open one too, where a scrolled page
  stayed where it was; and opened from it, the page no longer jumps, with no row selected, to a
  session whose `⚙` was pressed before the page listed it.
- **The Settings ▸ Harness row `⚙` opens on is drawn whole.** Its accent outline ran through the
  row's first letters and along its buttons, and left the row's `last:` or `lands at` line and
  its day outside, reading as another row; it now goes around the whole row, its open timer too,
  clear of every word and button, and nothing on the page moves when a row is selected. The
  page scrolls until all of that row is on screen wherever the window holds it: it stopped once
  the row's buttons were, which on the shipped window left the row's day and the outline's
  bottom edge below the page.
- **Settings ▸ Harness names each count one way.** WHAT THE HARNESS DID said `Continued` and
  `Escalated` where STATUS, each session's day and the Autopilot chip say `kept going` and
  `needed you`; it now says `Kept going` and `Needed you`. Its Approved row said `unproven`
  twice (`1 today · 1 unproven · 1 in 7 days · 1 unproven`), the ledger's word for what DECIDED
  FOR YOU calls a press no safe rule proved; the row under Approved now says it once, in those
  words, as a part of Approved (`of those  no safe rule proved 1 today · 1 in 7 days`).
- **`nothing yet today` is no longer the loudest line on Settings ▸ Harness.** It, and
  `reading…` before the first reading, were drawn in the page heading's large type meant for
  today's counts; they are now in the page's plain type, in the room the counts take, so nothing
  under STATUS moves when the first reading or the day's first act brings them.
- **The Autopilot menu says the session's whole name and stays in its pane.** In a tab split
  between two Claude Code panes the menu's header cut the session's name once it named the pane
  (`Autopilot · tab 1, right pane “✳ Claude Cod…`), the right pane's menu at a narrow window was
  drawn over the left pane, and the menu of a pane above or below another opened over that one.
  The name now goes on the row under the pane where one row cannot hold both, and the menu is
  drawn inside its own pane: as wide as before wherever the pane holds it; in a narrow pane it
  gives up its side margins before a letter, so in a 64-column window each pane's menu names its
  pane and every choice whole, and where the pane is narrower still the place goes on two rows
  (`Autopilot · tab 1,` then `right pane`); where neither side of its chip holds it, it covers
  the chip's row to stay whole, and only a pane shorter than it shows its first rows, the modes
  always among them. Only a pane too short for its header and modes lends the menu the window's
  rows; across, the menu never leaves its pane, and in the narrowest pane that shows the chip it
  cuts the ends of its longest choices (`Cruise 4 hours, then…`). Where the menu comes up over
  the chip, a click without moving the pointer that opened it only lights the choice under it,
  as where rows move under a still pointer; it no longer armed a timed Cruise or opened
  Settings that the pointer had never been moved to.
- **`kill <pid>` quits a headless aterm.** `SIGTERM` (and `SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`) to an `aterm
  --headless` instance used to end it on the spot: its workers' task files and its crash
  marker stayed behind, and an `aterm ctl subscribe` watcher heard nothing and waited 30 s for
  a successor that never came. It now quits as the Quit verb does, with a control socket or
  without one — every `sessions` watcher
  is told `EVENT * bye quit` (with no fabric bridge attached too), the task files and the
  crash marker are removed, every shell is hung up — and then dies of the signal as before,
  so its parent reads the same status; a second signal ends it at once. A `subscribe` that
  was told `bye quit` ends as soon as the connection does (exit 75). A window's terminate
  path is unchanged.
- **An `@` that names no session is refused, never read as the front tab.** `aterm ctl @
  <verb>` (what `aterm ctl @$W <verb>` becomes when `$W` is empty) used to act on the
  instance's front session, so a script or an agent whose session id came out empty could
  type into, or stop, the tab the person was looking at. `aterm ctl` now answers `ERR
  usage: empty or malformed selector` without sending anything, and so does the server to a
  client that sends one (in a `subscribe` or `await task` list too). `@.` still names the
  active tab outright.
- `aterm ctl spawn cwd="$PWD"` in a folder whose path holds a space opens there instead of
  answering `ERR usage`: the client quotes a `cwd=` it is given as it quotes the folder it
  fills in for a worker, which the server reads whole. A folder holding a space and a `"`
  is refused before anything is sent.
- **A control request line past 64 KiB is answered, not dropped.** The server answers `ERR
  request line too long (max 65536 bytes)` and closes, where a client used to read a bare
  end of file; `aterm ctl` refuses such a line before it sends it, and points `send` and
  `paste` at their `--stdin` forms.
- **The harness no longer takes a Claude Code run as its tab's own program for a shell's
  job.** In a tab opened with `aterm -e claude`, or after `exec claude`, a live
  upgrade no longer announces itself to the agent and ends it with no shell to start it
  again in; a person's restart there answers `not-relaunchable`, and a crash's mark says the
  agent ran as its tab's own program, with no shell to come back in.
- **`ship provision` installs the clippy `verify cells` lints with.** It installed stable
  with the minimal profile, which has no clippy, so on a freshly provisioned machine
  `targo --unverified verify cells` skipped every foreign cell with `has the std but no
  clippy`. Stable is now installed with clippy, and a stable that lacks it gets it added.
- **`verify wasm-glue`'s oracle row runs from every checkout, and `ship provision`
  installs its wasm-bindgen.** The row looked for wasm-bindgen 0.2.108 only on PATH,
  beside rustup and in the checkout's own `target/tooling`, so a CLI installed in one
  checkout left every other checkout and worktree skipping the row. It now also reads the
  machine-wide tooling directory (`~/Library/Caches/aterm/tooling.noindex`, elsewhere
  `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/aterm/tooling` or `~/.cache/aterm/tooling`); a full `ship provision`
  installs the CLI there at exactly the pin (`targo --unverified install wasm-bindgen-cli
  --version 0.2.108 --locked --force`, so a copy there that does not answer the pin is
  replaced, which cargo refuses to do unforced), and the row's skip names that install.

## [0.106.0] - 2026-10-17

### Added

- **A Muse Code tab is brought back after a crash, and when aterm restores its windows.** When
  Muse Code crashes in a supervised tab (killed, or any other abnormal end), aterm types `muse
  resume` for the very session it was in, in that session's own folder, through your managed
  `muse` (so the newest installed build), with the settings that launched it — but not
  `--yolo`, `--model`, a permission mode or an effort, which the session keeps itself — and
  once it is back and idle tells it to carry on. If Muse Code refuses that resume (its session
  is gone, say), aterm types it once, never again, and tells you the session was not brought
  back. Muse Code's own `/exit` is left alone, and so, by its exit status, are a Ctrl-C, a
  SIGTERM and a start Muse refused (an unknown session, bad arguments); nothing is typed while
  another process holds the session. After aterm crashes or quits, the reopened tab brings its
  Muse Code back on its session the same way. A frozen Muse Code is warned about but never
  ended for you: `aterm ctl restart` is not offered for it yet, and `[harness] stall_term`
  warns instead. Muse Code is not yet moved onto a newer build while it runs.
- **`aterm fabric brief`: what every session in the fabric is doing, read from the bus
  alone.** A node whose config says `[fabric] log = "turns"` now copies each session's turns,
  command runs, needs (approval, question, usage limit, stall) and their steps from its session
  log onto the fabric, so a program on any host can follow them with `aterm fabric tail` and
  `aterm fabric brief` folds them per session the way `aterm ctl brief` does, even after that
  aterm has quit. Only counts, fixed words and session ids go out: never a command line, a
  title, a directory, note text or a mail party; a session that drove another appears as an
  opaque `by=e…` name, never its id, while a spawned or restored session's open names the
  session it came from (`parent=`, `prev=`, `lineage=`). Records lost to a full ring or a long outage are said
  (`op=gap why=evicted n=…`), never silently skipped, and the brief counts none twice. The default
  `"off"` sends nothing; a node stops at 256 MiB of records until the broker keeps a
  retention policy, and `aterm ctl fabric status` says so.

- **With the PTY keeper on, a crash brings each screen and its scrollback back exactly.**
  Each session now keeps a running record of its screen and scrollback in shared memory that
  the keeper holds beside the shell (never on disk, never sent anywhere), so after a crash, a
  Force Quit or the system ending aterm the next launch restores every kept tab's screen,
  modes and half-typed escape sequences as they were, with no redraw for a shell at its
  prompt. When something could not be reproduced (output read in the last instant, a resize
  nothing recorded yet, a kitty image drawn or a Kitty unscroll in the moment before the
  crash, output a tab with a theme of its own was still writing) the screen still comes back,
  its program is asked to redraw over it, and `aterm ctl status` says `restore=screen` with
  what was lost; the recovery row says how many were repainted and how many started blank.
  Each tab's whole scrollback comes back too (its newest 1,048,576 lines, as an update
  carries; a tab already at its scrollback limit keeps up to 1,000 of its oldest lines fewer
  until new output refills it, as after an update), below its screen at the same line
  numbers, with the shell prompts of its last 512 lines still there to jump to, and after a
  second crash as well; lines that could not come back (a flood still being recorded when
  aterm stopped, a window rewrapped in the seconds before, the scrollback of a screen left
  blank because the recovery's memory budget was spent) are counted, in `aterm ctl status`
  (`history_lost=`) and the recovery ledger, and said on the recovery row, never dropped
  silently. Scrollback a program cleared (ED3) or a reset erased is gone from the record as
  well. The record's memory is counted (`aterm ctl status` `journal_bytes=` for each tab,
  `aterm ctl metrics` `journal_resident_bytes=` for the window), and when macOS reports memory
  pressure aterm gives up the recorded scrollback first, the largest tabs' until half of it is
  gone, every tab's when the pressure is critical: the screens still come back exactly after
  a crash, the scrollback above their last few hundred lines is counted lost, and each tab's
  scrollback is recorded again, one tab a second, once the pressure has eased for a minute
  (`journal_ring=shed` until then; `aterm ctl pressure` shows where it stands).

- **`aterm machines`: configure and keep configured a lab of Macs from this one, over SSH on
  the LAN, with no MDM and no Apple account.** One Mac, the controller, keeps an inventory
  (`machines.toml`, edited without losing your comments), the baselines each Mac should hold,
  a fleet SSH key and two signing keys. After one visit to each Mac (Remote Login with full
  disk access for remote users, Screen Sharing), `enroll` installs a root agent under one
  digest-pinned sudoers rule; the fleet key runs only the agent's dispatcher, and everything
  done as root needs an envelope the controller signed, which the Mac checks with Apple's own
  `ssh-keygen`. `plan` and `apply` bring Macs to their baseline, each setting probed, changed
  and read back: Caps Lock as Control for every keyboard, Siri, analytics, ads, AirDrop and
  widgets off, no Setup Assistant panes, names, firewall, power, time and update settings,
  the Command Line Tools, Homebrew and its formulae, pinned apps (Emacs, Caffeine, gh) checked
  by hash and Team ID, aterm itself with its CLI and toolset, and a per-Mac GitHub key for each
  user, registered with a GitHub machine user by the key itself (`github revoke` keeps a
  revoked key from ever being registered again). A signing key with a passphrase is asked for
  once per command, and not at all once ssh-agent holds it. `status` and `outstanding` read
  the newest reports, with any refusal (a changed host key, a busy host) beside them as a
  failure, never as "unreachable"; after `enroll` and an `apply`, `person <host> --here` at
  the Mac walks the Full Disk Access and Developer Tools switches only a person can flip;
  `screen <host>` walks them over Screen Sharing and locks the Mac again if you logged in
  there, also when you stop it with Ctrl-C (not when aterm is killed, which it warns of);
  and `scan` lists the Macs on the LAN. aterm now declares Local Network use
  (`_ssh._tcp`, `_rfb._tcp`), so macOS asks once before aterm reaches the LAN. macOS only.
  `aterm help machines` has the rest.
- **A community theme pack: 36 well-known themes, ready to add.** Catppuccin Frappe and
  Macchiato, Kanagawa Wave, Lotus and Dragon, Tokyo Night Storm, Moon and Day, Rose Pine,
  the GitHub themes, Iceberg, Nightfox and its family, Melange, Everforest, Ayu, Doom One,
  Snazzy, Sonokai and more now ship inside aterm. Only themes whose own project carries a
  permissive licence (MIT or Apache-2.0) and that pass `aterm theme check --strict` exactly
  as their authors made them are included. `aterm theme pack` lists them and says which you
  have; `aterm theme install "<name>"` (or `--all`) copies one into your themes folder as an
  ordinary file you can edit, and names its light or dark partner. In Settings ▸ Themes,
  **Get More** shows the ones you don't have yet: a press adds one and tries it, and Keep
  selects it. Nothing is downloaded. `aterm theme pack --licences` prints every palette's
  attribution and licence, and now also credits the projects aterm's built-in ports (Dracula,
  Nord, Tokyo Night, Catppuccin, Gruvbox, Solarized, One Dark, GitHub Light) come from.

- **Themes can carry type settings.** A theme file may now name its fonts and set
  `line_height`, `ligatures`, `font_features`, `font_weight`, `font_size_scale` and the other
  font keys, by family name and value, spelled as in `aterm.toml`. Your own `aterm.toml` key
  (and `--font` or `display_font` for the family) still wins. Trying a theme stays colours
  only, and the trial bar lists what its type settings would change once kept. **Keep colours
  only** keeps the theme's colours and pins your current type settings instead; it is not
  offered for a theme that sets `font_weight`, which no setting can pin. Save as theme gains
  **Include type settings**. `aterm ctl theme` reports `typography=`, `typography_keys=` and
  `typography_shadowed=`.
- **Themes can colour aterm's own chrome.** `accent_color` (the selected tab's rule, the
  message band's meter, Settings' selected rows), `active_tab_color`, `border_color` (split
  dividers and the tab strip's and find bar's seams) and `search_match_color` (find's other
  matches), in a theme file or in `aterm.toml`. Each is optional, derived from the theme when
  left out, and raised to a readable floor where it is drawn; `aterm theme check` warns below
  it.
- **A theme can derive the whole 256-colour palette.** With `palette_generate = true` in a
  theme, slots 16-255 (the colour cube and grey ramp) are blended from its own colours, so
  256-colour programs stay readable on a light theme. aterm's four signature themes set it.
  `palette_generate = "always"` or `"never"` in `aterm.toml` overrides the theme.
- **One tab can have its own theme.** View ▸ **Choose Tab Theme…** previews themes on the
  front tab only (Enter keeps, Esc reverts) and View ▸ **Clear Tab Theme** hands it back to
  the window's theme. A split from a themed pane inherits it, and it survives a restore and an
  update. From a script: `aterm ctl @<sid> theme session set "Hearth"`, `theme session`,
  `theme session clear`, or `spawn theme=<name>` for a new tab. `identity_themes = { worker =
  "Hearth" }` in `aterm.toml` gives every session of an agent identity its own theme.
- **Windows: the macOS line-editing keys work at the PowerShell prompt.** In an aterm tab
  running pwsh 7 or Windows PowerShell 5.1, Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E go to the start and end of the
  line, Ctrl+K and Ctrl+U cut to the end and to the start, Ctrl+W cuts back to the previous
  space (as in zsh and bash, so it takes a whole `C:\Users\foo` path), Ctrl+Y pastes back
  what they cut, Ctrl+B and Ctrl+F move a character, Ctrl+P and Ctrl+N walk the history,
  Ctrl+D deletes forward (and on an empty line exits the shell, as on a Mac), Ctrl+T swaps two
  characters, Ctrl+_ undoes, Alt+B and Alt+F move a word, Alt+Backspace cuts one, and
  Alt+←/→ move a word. Where pwsh 7 shows a grey inline suggestion from your history, Ctrl+E
  at the end of the line also accepts it, as with zsh-autosuggestions on a Mac; from inside
  the line the first Ctrl+E moves to the end and a second accepts, so Ctrl+E then Enter still
  runs what you typed. With a PSReadLine newer than Windows PowerShell's stock 2.0.0 (pwsh 7's
  included), Alt+U, Alt+L and Alt+C change a word's case. Before, PowerShell's Windows edit
  mode left most of these keys unbound, so they typed invisible control characters (`^E`,
  `^K`) into the command line; Ctrl+A selected the line, Ctrl+Y redid, and Alt+B typed a `b`.
  aterm's PowerShell integration binds a key only while it is unbound or still holds its
  Windows default, and never a key that starts one of your profile's two-key chords: a key
  your `$PROFILE` binds to something else keeps your binding, and a profile that picks Emacs
  or Vi mode is left alone. Tab completion, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+←/→, Ctrl+Backspace and
  Escape keep their Windows meaning. To keep the stock Windows keys (Ctrl+A select-all and
  Ctrl+Y redo among them), put `$env:ATERM_DISABLE_READLINE_KEYS = '1'` in `$PROFILE`. A tab
  opened before the update keeps its old keys until it is opened again. Claude Code already
  answered these keys itself and is unchanged.

- **Autopilot can cruise until a time, then land.** Right-click the Autopilot chip in a
  Claude Code footer (ctrl-click on macOS, or press `↓` with the chip
  selected) for its new menu, which the chip's title now offers (`· right-click: more`):
  Cruise, Land now or Off; cruise for 1, 2 or 4 hours, then land; cruise until the time
  you set in Settings ▸ Harness ▸ "Land at" (`[harness] land_at = "18:00"`), which the menu
  and the Timer offer as `Sat 18:00` once today's 18:00 has passed, naming the day it would
  land (a menu or page left open says so from that minute on); or cancel a landing time
  already set. The chip then reads `∞ ⤓18:00`, and at that time the harness
  wraps the work up at its next point, never mid-turn. A timer only ever takes power away: it
  only moves Cruise to Land, and any change you make to the session's Autopilot — the chip, the
  menu, Settings or `meta set` — cancels it and always wins; the menu's Cancel drops only the
  landing it shows, and an open menu redraws when the session changes elsewhere, so it never
  offers a stale choice. From a script: `aterm ctl
  @<sid> meta set autopilot cruise until=18:00` (or `until=+2h`), answered with the exact
  time it lands (`OK land_at=… local=2026-10-17T18:00+01:00`); a clock time a daylight-saving
  change skips is refused with its date. Settings ▸ Harness gives each session a Timer with
  the same choices and a line saying when it lands. The timer survives a restart and an update,
  and one whose time passed while aterm (or a closed tab you reopen) was closed lands as it
  comes back, its record saying which. `status`, `ls`
  and `meta` print the time as `land_at=`, and `aterm ctl controls autopilot-menu` reads the
  menu. Hovering the chip on a pane too narrow for its whole title gives the title's parts up
  in turn: first the list of recent acts, then `· right-click: more`, then everything but the
  mode, so a pane that showed the title before this release still shows it; in a split pane
  whose long working directory is cut to `…/<dir>`, the title stands in the room that leaves.
  On Linux, where aterm publishes an accessibility tree, the chip says it has a menu and a
  screen reader can open it from there, and the open menu is a menu read in words
  (`Cruise for 1 hour, then land`), its mode marked checked, its disabled rows disabled and the
  highlighted row focused; a reader can choose a row, and a choice heard before the menu's rows
  changed is refused rather than taken as whatever row now stands in its place.
- **Autopilot says how a landing ended.** Under Land, the Autopilot chip now shows `✓ landed`
  once the agent says it is done after the land instruction, `✓ done` when it had already
  finished before a landing was asked, and `⤓ quiet` when the harness has stopped typing (no
  done reply after the instruction and both nudges, or the turn was your own exchange). The
  chip's title, the line under Claude Code's launch card and each session's row in Settings ▸
  Harness say the same, and `aterm ctl @<sid> status` and `ls` print it as
  `task=open|landed|done|spent|theirs`, so a script can ask "did it land?" without reading the
  journal. When someone else's turn starts after a landed or done task, the face goes back to
  `⤓ land` at once, not when that turn ends. A landing that lands or goes quiet leaves one record
  in the message log; neither is an alert. A landed session stays landed across a seamless update
  and a restart of its harness loop (a settings change, Off and back): it reads `task=landed`
  from the new loop's start, writes no second record, keeps its landed time within the same
  aterm, and the harness no longer types the land instruction into finished work after every
  update. A tab restored after aterm quit or crashed is a new session: it starts from what its
  screen says (the agent's `ATERM-TASK-DONE` reads `✓ done`).
- **The harness supervises Gemini CLI** (measured on 0.46.0 in the lab against a local stub of the
  Gemini API, no account). It runs as `node`, so the window's harness names it by its screen. At
  full power it presses `Allow once` on its shell, write and edit boxes and `Trust folder` on its
  folder-trust dialog, never `Allow for this session` or `Modify with external editor`; any
  other box goes to the menu bar; its question gets its first answer; a turn's end gets the
  continuation and the done check, and `aterm drive task` nudges it. Its usage-limit dialog
  (`Keep trying` / `Stop`) is never pressed, and an API error it does not retry itself is
  escalated with `/stats model`. Settings ▸ Harness has **Supervise Gemini CLI sessions**
  (`[harness.gemini] enabled`). It is read in panes narrower than 80 columns and under a
  wrapped error notice, and a box you refuse with Esc holds that turn for you (one sandbox box
  aside: below). Gemini CLI is not relaunched when it exits.
- **Gemini CLI with its own sandbox on is read as measured** (0.46.0 under its seatbelt and under
  its per-tool sandbox, against a local fake of its API). The footer's `current process` or `all
  tools` changes nothing the harness reads. A command the sandbox denied ends the turn on Gemini
  CLI's reply, which is continued as any turn. The box it offers to widen the sandbox (`To run
  [Shell], allow access to the following?`), after a denial or before a `curl` runs, always goes
  to you, never allowed or declined. Refused with Esc after its per-tool sandbox denied a command,
  that box does not stop the turn: Gemini CLI hands its request to the model as the command's
  error, and the harness reads the turn that ends on its reply as any turn. In a window your Esc
  counts as a key you pressed: on a task the harness is not carrying, the turn is left to you;
  on one it is carrying, the continuation waits `human_grace_s` from that key, and no longer. With both of its sandboxes on, Gemini CLI 0.46.0 failed the shell
  command measured (`touch`) with `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`.
- (developer tool) **The real-agent lab drives Gemini CLI and agy** (`lab gemini`, `lab agy`, their
  `-captures` and `-selftest` verbs) against a local Gemini-API stub, with every other egress
  trapped and `~/.gemini` untouched.
- **The Autopilot chip says what the harness just did.** When the harness approves a box,
  answers a question, keeps the work going, carries it past a limit or an API error, or
  types Land's instruction, a short label shows for 3 seconds right of the Autopilot chip in
  the chip's colour: `✓ approved`, `✗ declined`, `? answered`, `↻ kept going`, `⧗ resumed`,
  `⤓ landing` or `⤓ nudged` (a question dialog's `? answered` until 3 seconds after its last
  answer, so it is seen once the dialog closes). It shows at most once every 15 seconds, so
  a busy session never flickers, and it has no animation: the chips never move, and it never
  takes the place of the model, path or branch: it is drawn beside them as the pane fits them
  (in a split pane, beside the path cut to `…/<dir>`), or not at all. Hover
  the Autopilot chip (or select it with ctrl+shift+tab) to see the last three things the
  harness did, each with the time it happened. `[claude_footer] acts = false` in aterm.toml
  hides the label, and serious mode hides it too; the chip's title and Settings ▸ Harness
  keep the history either way. While Settings ▸ Harness is open, WHAT THE HARNESS DID marks
  its counts as `Newer` after each act and reads them again 3 seconds later, at most every
  10 seconds. On Linux, where aterm publishes an accessibility tree, the Autopilot and
  settings chips are buttons a screen reader can read and press, named in words, with the
  latest act of the last day as the Autopilot chip's description.

- **Session logs cross self-updates, stay readable after close, and record restore lineage.** A seamless
  update carries each session's log to the new process: a command running across it closes
  with its real duration and exit code, an agent mid-turn stays in that one turn, and record
  numbers go on rather than starting over (`mark - handoff carried= shed=` says what crossed).
  After a session closes, `aterm ctl log @<sid>` and `brief @<sid>` still answer for the last
  512 sessions closed in this instance, the newest 32 with retained detail. An established
  read connection keeps access until its grant is revoked. A restored or reopened tab's new session
  names the one it stands for (`open - restore prev=<sid> lineage=<first sid>`); earlier
  processes' logs are not restored from disk unless the opt-in journal below is on. A periodic
  sweep targets 64 MiB across the
  logs, reducing detail while retaining open nodes and the state needed to read them.

- **An opt-in session journal, off by default.** With `[session_log] journal = true` in
  `aterm.toml`, aterm also writes each session's log to disk, under the logs folder's
  `session-log/` (files 0600 in a 0700 folder, at most 64 MiB and 2048 files of its own, the
  oldest deleted first), so `aterm ctl log @<sid>` and `brief @<sid>` answer for a session from an
  earlier run, even one that crashed or was killed: what it did up to the end, then `gap
  why=crash` and its open commands and turns closed `out=gone`. A clean quit closes every
  session `out=app-quit`. The journal keeps the same facts the in-memory log does: each
  command's first word as typed and the foreground program's name, outcomes and durations,
  agent turns, so a secret typed at a prompt and run as a command is kept on disk too; never a
  command's arguments, its folder or an OSC title. Only you can read it (`ctl` with the
  instance's own token). It follows `restore_session`, is a window's only, and runs on macOS and Linux. Off,
  as it ships, aterm creates no file or folder for it and deletes nothing.

- **Programs and agents can follow a session's log live, wait on it, and add notes of their
  own.**
  - `aterm ctl subscribe @<sid> log` (or `@*`) streams each new record as it happens. A
    consumer that reconnects with `since-log=<seq> log-ep=<e>` picks up where it stopped, and
    one `GAP` line counts anything it missed.
  - `aterm ctl await log need` waits until a session needs someone: an approval box, a
    question, a failed command or the session ending. `await log close=turn` waits until an
    agent's turn ends. The log wakes both, so neither polls.
  - `aterm ctl status` now shows the log's position (`log_seq=`, `log_ep=`), the open run,
    turn and step, and what the session needs and since when.
  - `aterm ctl mark` attaches a note, a verdict, a short label, a need or an intended action
    to a session. It is recorded as a claim under the connection that wrote it: `ctl`, the
    window's harness, or the session an edge was granted from, never a name the writer
    chooses. Each author gets about one mark a second, marks hold at most a quarter of the
    log, and a mark never types, presses or answers anything.
  - `send` and `turn` take `cause=` to say which mail or record they answer. The log notes
    who sent control input, never what was sent.
  - `grant` and `connect` refuse the names the log keeps for its own authors (`human`, `ctl`,
    `harness`, `bridge`, `aterm`, `vendor`).

- **Claude Code autocompacts at 400k tokens.** A window now adds `"autoCompactWindow":
  400000` to `~/.claude/settings.json` where the key is unset. On every model it takes the
  place of the window Claude Code would pick itself (a server-tuned one or a model's own
  default included), clamped to the model's context, so on a 1M-context model such as Opus
  5.5 a conversation is summarized at 400k tokens instead of near 1M. A smaller window can
  reduce the conversation carried by each turn; its effect on plan usage and response time
  depends on the workload and caching. Claude Code's own "Want to autocompact at 400k tokens
  instead?" offer no longer interrupts a session. If you answered that offer "Keep", aterm
  adds nothing.
  `/autocompact` still sets the window for a model, a value of your own stays, and
  `aterm pkg doctor` reports which applies.

- **Messages says which tab made macOS ask you about your music library, Photos or
  Contacts.** macOS names only aterm in those dialogs, whichever program in it asked, and Full
  Disk Access does not cover them. When one appears for a program in a tab, Settings ▸
  Messages now keeps a record, such as `Asked for the music and media library`, naming the
  tab. `aterm ctl privacy` lists Contacts among the settings Full Disk Access does not reach,
  and the agent notes aterm installs tell agents that reading other apps' data can raise these
  dialogs.

- **The fabric's broker can ack without a disk flush.** `aterm fabric on --durability
  relaxed` (or `aterm link broker --durability relaxed`) has the broker acknowledge a post
  once it is in the page cache, without waiting for the disk flush (on macOS
  `F_FULLFSYNC`) a strict ack waits for. A relaxed broker survives its own crash or
  restart, but not a power loss, kernel panic or hard reset, which can lose what it
  acknowledged since it last started or stopped cleanly. Its clean stop — at logout or
  shutdown, `aterm fabric off`, an update, ^C — flushes the log first, and the next boot
  carries on as under strict; so does a kill -9 while the log is on the boot volume. After
  a power loss without that stop (or any unclean stop of a log off the boot volume, or on
  a host whose kernel does not name its boot), the log's next open marks it as a new
  generation of the same log and records where the two agree, so every bridge and
  notifier picks up exactly there: a broadcast or an escalation posted after the restart
  is delivered and paged, nothing before that point is read twice, and only the records
  the power loss took are gone from the log (a joined host's own posts acknowledged in
  that window among them). A session's own aterm still treats the move as a new log: a
  reply it had queued while the broker was down, and a verdict on a message it was shown
  before the loss, are dropped as before, and the asker is told the ask expired. Strict,
  the previous behaviour, stays the default. `--durability ordered` is accepted, for a
  later build that serves it; this build serves it strict and says so, and an older build
  refuses it, so run `aterm fabric off` before going back to one. A setting named on
  `aterm fabric on`, strict included, is written into the broker job, a bare `aterm
  fabric on` keeps the setting the job already has, and `aterm fabric` and `aterm fabric
  doctor` show which is in force, as the broker itself reports it.

### Changed

- **Updates arrive sooner after a wake and after a release, and install faster.** When you
  open the lid, aterm checks for an update about 3 seconds later, where it took 10 seconds on
  average and up to 18 (up to 8 without a window). While a new release's app build is still
  being published, aterm looks again every minute instead of every two, so it sees the release
  about 30 seconds sooner on average. Installing an update checks the new copy of aterm and the
  running one at the same time, about 0.4 seconds less at launch and inside a seamless update's
  pause, and a refused install no longer deletes the previous copy an update's window still
  needs. The download's checksum is computed inside aterm on the processor's SHA-256
  instructions: about 19 ms for a 47 MB update, where it took about 100.
- **Settings ▸ Harness reads each ledger once, and says every count it keeps.** WHAT THE
  HARNESS DID reads each session's ledger and journal once per reading for both today and
  the last 7 days, where it read each file written today twice. `Landed` is now **Land
  prompts**: it counts Land's instruction and its nudges typed, never landings. Boxes the
  harness declined and the time it waited at limits are drawn (**Declined**, **Waited at
  limits**), and **Approved** says how many presses were unproven (full power pressed a box
  the safe rules do not judge) where any were.

- **Settings ▸ Harness shows today first, and each session's day.** STATUS now says what the
  harness did today in large type under its two facts (`37 approved today · 12 kept going ·
  4 answered`, then the rest and the time it waited on you), and each SESSIONS row says its
  own day (`today: needed you once, 1m at 18:29 · 31 approved`) with a **Show** button that
  brings its tab and pane to the front. Refresh, Open aterm.toml and AI CLIs moved below
  SESSIONS, so the sessions still start on an 80 × 24 window's first screen. The `⚙` chip and
  the Autopilot menu's **Harness settings…** open the page at that session's row, drawn
  selected; the `⊘ off` chip opens it at SUPERVISION. Past midnight an open page reads the
  new day, with or without `[harness] land_at`. On a narrow page a row's words go above its
  buttons, so its tab and pane are never cut.
- **Under Cruise, the Autopilot chip says when the work is done.** Once the agent says it is
  finished under Cruise (the done check's `ATERM-TASK-DONE`, a `FINISHED` report), the chip
  reads `∞ ✓ done` in Cruise's colour, and `∞ ✓ landed` where a landing ended the task before
  the word went back to Cruise; it used to read `∞`, "keeps the work moving", while `status
  task=done` said otherwise. A pane too narrow for the whole face keeps the `✓`. The chip's
  title (`autopilot: cruise, done 03:49`), its spoken label, the line under Claude Code's
  launch card (`· autopilot ✓ done`) and the session's row in Settings ▸ Harness (`done 03:49`)
  say the same. A done task wins the chip over a Cruise timer: the timer's time moves to the
  title (`…, lands 04:22`) and the row (`done 03:49 · lands 04:22`), and at that time the word
  turns land with nothing left to land. The first turn someone else starts puts the chip back
  to `∞`. `aterm help harness` calls the section HOW THE WORK ENDED.
- **The Autopilot chip's times name their day, and its short title keeps the time.** A face's
  time from another day says which (`landed Fri 18:11`), in the chip's title, its short form,
  its spoken label (`Landed on Friday at 18:11.`) and the session's row in Settings ▸ Harness
  (`landed Fri 18:11`, `last: ✓ approved Fri 17:58`), and a time a week or more back its date
  (`landed 9 Oct 18:11`), where a weekday would name a later day; a page left open across
  midnight moves its rows at midnight. A pane too narrow for the whole title keeps the time
  (`autopilot: land, landed 18:11`, where it said `autopilot: land, landed`).
- **A chip whose agent's own switch is off says so.** With `[harness.claude] enabled = false`
  and the harness on, a Claude Code session's chip reads `⊘ off` titled `Supervise Claude Code
  sessions is off`, its row in Settings ▸ Harness and its Autopilot menu say the same, and a
  screen reader hears `Supervise Claude Code sessions is off in Settings.`; they said `harness
  off in Settings` while the harness supervised every other agent. Every agent's row names its
  own switch the same way (a codex-alab tab's, `Watch codex-alab sessions is off`).
- **The Autopilot timer's records keep to one short title and say what the time did.** Setting a
  timed Cruise is recorded `Autopilot cruises until 18:00` (was `Autopilot set to cruise until
  18:00, then land`); the time coming is `Autopilot began landing` (was `autopilot: cruise
  until 18:00 ended; land`), and a hand change over an armed timer adds `the 18:00 landing time
  is cancelled`.
- **`aterm ctl pointer click` clicks as a Mac does.** On macOS every press and release arrives
  with a pointer-motion event at the same spot, ahead of the button; the scripted click now sends
  it too, so a lab's click meets everything that reads pointer motion as a person's click does.
- **The harness card's kitty stands three rows tall, and the card's line says an armed
  timer.** Where Claude Code's launch card leaves its third row (the working directory) blank
  beside the kitty, the kitty now stands the card's three rows tall, as tall as Claude's own
  mascot, in the same coat, with the same blink and tail flick, and a one-pixel rim in the
  border's rainbow so a black or grey coat reads on a dark background (drawn as ink on a light
  theme). The rainbow trail now runs at the height of the kitty's body, so the cat leads and
  the rainbow follows. A working directory long enough to reach the rainbow keeps the two-row
  kitty, which wears the rim too; a pane with no room beside the card shows no kitty, as before.
  The rim stops where the tail meets the rainbow, and runs under each paw, not under the gaps
  between them. Under Cruise with a timer armed (Cruise
  until a time, then land), the line under the card now ends with the time:
  `✦ enhanced by aterm harness <version> · autopilot ∞ cruise ⤓18:00` (`⤓Sat 18:00` on another
  day); a narrow pane drops the time before the Autopilot's words. Serious mode and reduced
  motion are unchanged, and a card at rest is drawn in about as many pieces as before (at most
  three more, from the rim's run under each paw).

- **The harness card's kitty flies in.** When the card is first shown, the kitty now flies in
  along the rainbow for its first 1.2 seconds, from the trail's start to its seat, quick at
  first and slowing as it lands, laying the rainbow behind it and shedding a few sparkles; the
  stars beside the trail come out as it passes them, and the star burst opens where it lands.
  Then it blinks and flicks its tail as before, and the card comes to rest exactly as it did.
  Once the card has been on screen at rest, it plays again (when Autopilot changes, when the
  window regains focus) with the kitty in its seat and the rainbow whole, the burst opening at
  once, as before. Serious mode, reduced motion and an unfocused window still show the card at
  rest from the start, and Codex still has no card.

- **Linux screen readers reach aterm through aterm's own AT-SPI publisher.** Orca and other
  AT-SPI clients read the same tree as before, with the same names, roles, text, caret and
  events. What changed is the failure: if the accessibility bus goes away, aterm notes it in
  its log and publishes again when at-spi2-core brings the bus back, where it used to lose
  screen-reader access until restarted. The off-by-default `a11y-accesskit` build feature is
  gone with the AccessKit platform adapters it pulled in.

- **Theme tools that print colours now work out of the box.** base16-shell, tinted-shell,
  pywal (`wal -R`), theme.sh and kitty themes over ssh set the 256 indexed colours with
  OSC 4, which aterm used to ignore unless you set `allow_palette_reconfigure = true`. It is
  now allowed by default. What a program sets lasts for that tab only, is never saved and never changes the window's own colours.
  Edit ▸ Reset Terminal (`aterm ctl @<sid> reset`) now also puts your theme's colours back,
  and `aterm ctl @<sid> colors` lists what a program set (`program_palette=`,
  `program_slots=`). `allow_palette_reconfigure = false` still refuses them, and now also
  takes a program's palette out of every open tab at once; turning it back on ends the
  "Program colours were refused" notice.

- **aterm decides whether a background is light or dark by whether black or white text
  reads better on it.** It used to compare a brightness figure against a fixed line, which
  put white text and dark chrome on mid tones where white reads poorly (3.07:1 on
  `#939393`, 1.37:1 on a bright green). Mid-tone backgrounds — greys `#767676` to
  `#969696` and colours of similar luminance, such as bright greens and cyans — now get
  light chrome with dark text, and the black or white ink the tab strip, toolbar and
  Windows caption choose always reads at 4.5:1 or better. A custom theme with such a
  background and no `appearance` key is now measured light; one that declares `dark`
  gets an `appearance_mismatch` warning from `aterm theme check`. No config change is
  needed.

- **Windows: the default font is Iosevka Term Semibold, at 17 px on a 1.1 line height.** With
  no `font_family`, `font_px` or `line_height` set, Windows draws the terminal in Iosevka Term
  Semibold, built into aterm: Iosevka Term's SemiBold cut, with its ExtraBold for bold and
  real italics. It is heavier than the Iosevka Term already built in and draws no programming
  ligatures, so `=>`, `!=` and `->` stay as typed. Its cell is 9x23 where Cascadia Mono PL's
  was 9x21: a window of the same size holds the same columns and about 9% fewer rows, with a
  clear row between descenders and the accents on the line below. Claude Code's `⏺ ✻ ⏵`, the
  arrows and most symbols now come from the font itself, and long arrows (`⟶ ⟹`) stay in
  their own column; emoji such as `✅ ❌ ⭐ ⚡ ⏳` still come from Windows' symbol font, centred
  across their two columns. The 17 px size and 1.1 line height are Windows' defaults for every
  font: a `font_family` set without its own `font_px` or `line_height` (`"JetBrains Mono"`, or
  the system's `"Cascadia Mono"`) now draws a larger, taller cell too, and `font_px = 16` with
  `line_height = 1.0` keeps the previous size and spacing with any font. Cascadia Mono PL stays
  built in and listed in Settings ▸ Text & Fonts; to keep the previous look entirely, put
  `font_family = "Cascadia Mono PL"`, `font_px = 16` and `line_height = 1.0` in `aterm.toml`.
  `--show-config` now prints the line height and whether it is the default. macOS and Linux
  are unchanged.

- **Alt+←/→ reach the program unless there is a pane to move to.** On Windows and Linux,
  Alt+arrow moves the focus between split panes. On a tab with one pane, on a zoomed pane, or
  at the edge of a split, the key now goes to the program instead of doing nothing, so it
  moves by word there, as Option+←/→ do on a Mac: at the PowerShell prompt, in bash, zsh and
  fish with aterm's shell integration, and in Claude Code and Codex. In a split with a pane
  that way, Alt+arrow still moves the focus. A `focus_pane_*` arrow chord you set in
  `[keybindings]` follows the same rule; one on another key (such as `ctrl+j`) keeps its key,
  so it never sends a control character to the shell. `"alt+left" = "none"` always sends the
  key to the program.

### Removed

- **aterm no longer supervises a vendor Codex CLI.** A `codex` tab is shown (its own state,
  from its OSC 7501 report, on the presence row and in `status program_state=`), and its stall
  and disk rows stand, but aterm no longer answers its boxes, continues it, waits out its
  limits, upgrades it, relaunches it or restores it after a restart, and `aterm drive` no
  longer reads its screen (`drive phase`, `await-turn`, `answer` and `report` read nothing on a
  Codex; `report` has no `reply-head-missing` or `search-incomplete` reason any more), and
  `drive task` types its `Inbox: task @<off>` line into no vendor Codex.
  codex-alab, ALab's build of Codex, supervises itself under `[harness]`; aterm watches beside
  it, relaunches it after a crash on the line its own record names, brings it back after a
  restart or a seamless update, and `drive task` types its mail's line into it at its own idle
  point (its session record at rest, its draft empty). `[harness] rate_nudge` is gone.
  The release that carries this change should also publish the codex-alab pin in atpkg's
  signed index, so other machines get codex-alab as their managed Codex instead of a vendor
  Codex that aterm only shows.
- **Explain heavy load is gone.** The message band no longer shows a "Typing slowed by …" row
  when another program loads the Mac, and Settings ▸ Messages loses its switch. A row's own
  load words, such as a toolchain download's `network busy`, no longer appear when typing slows,
  and critical memory pressure is no longer recorded on Settings ▸ Messages (it stays in
  `aterm.log`). An `explain_heavy_load` line in `aterm.toml` now does nothing, and Settings ▸
  Modified says so. `aterm ctl metrics` no longer prints `strain=`, `strain_probe_us_max=` or
  `strain_scan_us_max=`, and reports the retired deadline slot as `retired-40`;
  `aterm ctl messages` no longer prints `level=` or `load=memory`. A system view designed from
  scratch will replace it.
- `targo --unverified verify trust`, the per-change Trust proof and floor check. No landing
  check and no release runs the Trust lane (owner ruling 2026-10-16);
  `targo --unverified ship trust run -p <crate>` checks a library on demand.
- `cells` from the `release` set, and the foreign cells' std from `ship provision`'s audit
  (owner ruling 2026-10-16): the release builds only the macOS bundle, so nothing it builds is
  for those triples, and a Windows-only type error had stopped a macOS release.
  `targo --unverified verify cells` still checks them by hand.
- Vi copy-mode, the keyboard cursor (h/j/k/l, w/b/e, f/t, v) that only a
  `toggle_vi_mode` entry in `[keybindings]` could turn on. A config that still binds
  `toggle_vi_mode` gets the unknown-action warning.
- Robi, the opt-in helper robot, and its tip bubble. A `robi` line left in
  `aterm.toml` does nothing, and Manual says the feature was removed.
- The experimental embedded fleet operator: the `[operator]` setting, `aterm fleet
  status`, `inspect`, `manage`, `unmanage`, `next`, `extend`, `ack`, `reconcile`,
  `clear-fault` and `propose`, and the `operator` and `operator-propose-bin` control
  verbs. It was off by default. `aterm fleet events` and `aterm fleet exec` are unchanged.
- `aterm pkg noindex verify <dir>`, the on-demand Spotlight measurement. Nothing ran it
  once the Spotlight rename pass and the developer root were gone.
- The network drive: the `[net]` TLS listener (`listen`, `cert`, `key` and
  `[[net.connections]]`), the `dial`, `dial-list` and `dial-token` control verbs, and
  `aterm drive --dial`. A leftover `[net]` table is ignored. To drive a session on another
  host, use ssh and `aterm ctl`.
- Trail Packs, the user-authored cursor trails: the `cursor_trail_packs` key and
  `cursor_trail_style = "pack:<id>"`, which now gets the unknown-style warning and draws
  the default trail. The built-in trail styles are unchanged.
- Stream fade ("ink that dries"): the `stream_fade` and `stream_fade_ms` settings. It was
  off by default.
- Old spellings that still loaded: the `game_font` key (use `display_font`), the
  `… v2` cursor-trail names (`rainbow kitty v2`, `kitty v2`, …), the `v0.28`, `v028`,
  `0.28` and `retro` names for the `classic` trail, and the `[sparkle_words.orca]` table.
  A config that still uses one loads with the unknown-key or unknown-style warning.

### Fixed

- **The harness waits for work agy or Muse Code left running, as it does for Claude Code's.**
  When an agy turn ends with a command, a timer or a subagent still running in the list under
  its input box, or a Muse Code turn ends with a backgrounded shell or a monitor running in its
  panel, the harness no longer types `keep going` into the session while that work runs: each
  agent takes a turn of its own when its work ends. `aterm drive phase` now says `busy` there,
  with `reason its own background work: …`. As with a shell Claude Code leaves running, a
  question the turn ended on is not answered while agy's work or Muse Code's backgrounded shell
  runs; a question asked over a Muse Code monitor alone is still answered. A usage limit or an
  error the turn ended on is still handled as before, and a usage limit the harness is waiting
  out is still waited out when its notice leaves the screen while that work runs (after you
  scroll up, say), as in a Claude Code tab. If that work never ends (a dev server, a daemon),
  the harness says so as it does for Claude Code: a `STUCK` line in the journal after 30
  minutes of nothing changing, a record at the window after 90, and a line asking you to look
  at the tab after 3 hours, each naming that agent and its background work (not Claude). In agy, the input box is read again while that list
  is shown: text you typed there is seen as your draft, and a turn started while a task runs
  reads busy; before, that screen read as having no input box at all.
- **A draft over an older Claude Code's `@` menu is not sent onto an entry you selected.**
  Claude Code 2.1.289 and before mark the selected entry of the `@` menu of files and agents
  in colour only. After you arrowed to an entry, a draft left standing there was sent with an
  Enter that completed that entry into it instead (`read @no` became `read @novel.txt`) and
  sent nothing. The harness now reads the entries' colours: it sends the draft when no entry
  is selected, tells you once when one is, and leaves it alone where the colours cannot say
  (a menu of one entry).
- **An agent moved onto a Claude Code build that will not start goes back to the build it
  ran.** A build can pass the upgrade's start check (`--help`) and still fail at a real start
  (a crash in its interface, a resume it refuses). The one agent moved onto it first then
  stayed down until you resumed it by hand; the build's failure held every other move and you
  were told once (`build-fails`). That agent is now relaunched at once, in the same shell, on
  the build its process ran, resuming the same conversation; the failure is still noted and
  still holds every move onto that build.
- **A conversation you `/resume` during a usage limit is not told to keep going at the reset.**
  When you `/resume`d another conversation while a session waited on a usage limit, the
  harness typed the limit's own `keep going` into it at the reset, even with
  `continue = false`, though the limit had stopped nothing in it; with a background shell
  running there, even into its done report. That conversation now gets what `continue` gives
  any turn end, shell or not: nothing under `continue = false`, the done check for a done
  report. The conversation the limit stopped is still resumed at its reset.
- **Another day's `continuing automatically` no longer ends a usage limit's wait early.** A
  conversation you `/resume`d during a usage limit could show an older limit with the same
  reset clock (`resets 6pm`, from another day) that Claude Code went on from. Where aterm
  could not read that conversation's record (a harness that took the wait over, `aterm drive
  supervise`), that old word ended the wait and the harness typed into the standing limit
  before its reset. Claude Code goes on at the reset itself, so its word read earlier is now
  taken as another day's, and the wait runs to the reset.
- **A model's usage limit that Claude Code continued by itself is not continued again.** A
  model limit (Sonnet's, say) that resets within a day is drawn like the five-hour window's,
  with Claude Code's own `continuing automatically at …` countdown under it. The harness read
  that countdown as a session window's, not the model's: when Claude Code went on at the reset
  the harness still typed `keep going` a few minutes later; Esc on a countdown that answered
  the harness's own try had `keep going` typed again half a minute on; and a `/model` after
  Esc did not free the session. Each is now read as the model's limit, as for the five-hour
  window.
- **A session moved to the fallback model no longer waits out the limit it left.** When the
  harness moved a session off a model's usage limit (Sonnet's, say) onto the fallback model,
  and its first try had to wait (you were typing, or a hold stood), a limit notice the old
  Claude Code wrote meanwhile was read, once the relaunched one redrew it, as the fallback's
  own limit: the session sat until the old model's reset, up to days, though the fallback
  could work. A notice older than the relaunched Claude Code is now read as the one it left.
- **A relaunched Claude Code at a usage limit is not continued before the reset.** When Claude
  Code was relaunched (an update, a crash, your own restart) into a conversation stopped at a
  usage limit that its screen no longer drew, the harness could decide the relaunched agent's
  first turn end from what it knew of the old process, miss the limit, and plan a `keep going`
  into it. It now reads the conversation's record after every turn it saw run, the
  relaunched agent's start-up among them, and waits for the reset.
- **A conversation moved off a limit stays moved off when its upgrade record closes.** When
  aterm moved a session to another account or a fallback model at a limit, and the upgrade
  record that remembered the move was closed before the session's first turn after it (you
  reached that build by hand, or the record was a week old), a later relaunch held its
  carry-on behind the limit the move had left, until that limit reset. The move is now kept
  beside the closed record for as long as any limit from before it could still stand.
- **After a restore, a usage limit the old Claude Code counted down is resumed at its reset.**
  Claude Code's own `continuing automatically at …` countdown dies with its process. When
  aterm was restored from a cold start onto a tab whose relaunched Claude Code redrew such a
  limit, the harness had never read the limit before the new process started, so it waited
  for the countdown nobody held and resumed ten minutes past the reset. It now reads when
  the conversation's record says the notice was written, and a notice older than the running
  Claude Code is resumed a few minutes after the reset, as a relaunch already was.
- **A usage limit's hold ends when the work comes back, however fast.** When the turn after
  a usage limit was answered too quickly for any read to see Claude Code at work (as a local
  stub answers), the limit's `limited:` badge stayed up and the tab's automatic update and a
  relaunch's carry-on waited for an hour past the reset, or for good where the limit named no
  reset. The limit now ends where the harness reads the reply that answered it.
- **An error right after a prompt command is no longer continued once.** When a prompt command
  (a `/review` of your own, `/doctor`) was run just after Claude Code showed an error, and its
  own request met a new error drawn like ordinary text, the harness could read the turn before
  the error reached the conversation's record and type `keep going` into it once. It now reads
  the record again, as it already did after a plain prompt.
- **A full context an image fills says to go back to before the image.** Where Claude Code
  said an image, or the images and attachments, made the request too large and three
  `/compact`s did not help, the harness's exception said "go back a few messages", which need
  not reach them. It now says to go back to before the image, or before the attachments.
- **A login Claude's API refuses with a 403 is signed in again.** A turn that ended on Claude
  Code's `authentication_failed` row with status 403, in words aterm does not name or drawn as a
  bare `API Error: 403 …`, was retried slowly as a refused request and then left to you; it is
  now the lost login it is, answered with `/login` (or your renewable login's renewal) at once.
- **`aterm drive watch` and `aterm drive supervise` read the agent's own record.** On a named
  tab (`@sid`) they now read the transcript of the Claude Code in it, as the window's harness
  does, and only read it. A wall drawn under a tool's output (a full context after a Bash or
  MCP output) was refused there for want of a transcript and left to you; it is now confirmed
  and answered (`/compact`), while a tool's printed words that only look like a wall are still
  refused. The record's finished task, the API errors only the transcript names and a usage
  limit the screen no longer draws are read there too. With no tab named, the screen still
  decides alone. A run recorded with `--tape` replays with no agent behind it.
- **At a usage limit's end a question gets an answer, not `keep going`.** When Claude Code went
  on by itself at a limit's reset and its reply asked a question or a choice, the harness's
  resume typed `keep going` into it, even with `answer_questions = false`, where the same
  question at any other turn end goes to you. It is now answered exactly as at any other turn
  end: the question priority's answer, or the menu bar under `answer_questions = false`.
- **With the session keeper on, closing a tab ends its shell even when the keeper drops the
  window's connection, and quitting aterm never relaunches it.** When the keeper dropped a
  window's connection before it had read that a tab closed, that tab's shell stayed in the keeper
  until the window ended, and came back as a tab after a crash. A current keeper now confirms each
  tab close, and the window tells it again on its next connection until it does (an older keeper
  that cannot confirm is told once, as before). Separately, if a window's connection to the keeper dropped while it started, and its
  goodbye was lost when the person quit it, the keeper relaunched aterm after that quit whenever
  another window had crashed. The keeper now reads that end as the quit it was.
- **Two agents in one tab no longer look the same.** Where a tab is split between two coding
  agents, Settings ▸ Harness's rows, their buttons, the Autopilot menu's header and the
  harness's messages name each one's pane (`tab 1, left pane`, `tab 1, right pane`), where
  both rows and every button read alike and every menu said `Autopilot · tab 1`.
- **Settings ▸ Harness shows a landing time set from a script at once.** After `aterm ctl
  @<sid> meta set autopilot cruise until=+2m`, the session's row read its last act until
  something else redrew the page, while the chip already said `∞ ⤓04:22`; it now reads
  `lands at 04:22` in the same moment.
- **The timer's record no longer promises a landing that cannot happen.** At a timed Cruise's
  time the message log said "the harness wraps the work up at its next point, then stops" over
  every session — one whose task was already done or landed, one with the harness switched off
  in Settings, one whose agent's own switch was off, and a tab with no agent at all. It now
  says the work is wrapped up only where the harness carries it, and otherwise why nothing is
  landed (`nothing to land, the task was done at 17:42`, `no agent runs in the tab, so there is
  nothing to land`).
- **Land's amber and the permission light read on light themes.** The `⤓ land` chip, its
  `✓ done` and `✓ landed`, a timed Cruise's `⤓18:00` and Land's act label were drawn in one
  fixed amber, 1.88:1 on Aterm Day's background, and the permission light beside them in
