  graph queries as soon as it requires checking the whole workspace.

- **`ATERM-TASK-DONE` now means done: a report that still lists work the agent could do is
  sent back once.** The agent primer (v20) defines a finished job exactly: every part the
  agent can still do is done and verified (built, tested, measured where numbers were asked
  for, committed and landed), and what is left needs a person (a credential, a decision,
  physical access) or cannot be done on that machine, each item named with what blocks it.
  A slow check is not blocked, and a deliberate trade-off is a decision stated with its
  numbers. The done check the harness types says the same. When an agent ends a report with
  the token while its own words still name open work without a blocker (`Still open:`,
  `Left:`, `Next steps`, `not run`, `skipped`; never `Nothing left` or `Left: none`), the
  harness types one challenge at once (`continue-open-items@v1`) instead of stopping, and
  the job's next finished or done reply ends it, so it never loops. Autopilot land, which
  asks for what is left beside the token, still takes it at once, and a person's own
  question or message is still left alone. With a long `rules_file`, the standing rules
  riding on the done check or the challenge are cut short at a word, so the text stays one
  Claude Code draws as typed rather than as `[Pasted text]`. The aterm window rewrites its
  primer block in each agent's context file when it opens a session, so v20 reaches a
  machine with the release that carries it, and an older aterm no longer rewrites a newer
  primer block with its own older text: `aterm agents status` shows such a block as `newer`
  and leaves it as is.
- **Under `approve = "safe"` the supervisor trusts no folder until you list it.**
  `[harness] trust_roots` is now empty. It named `~/aterm*`, `~/ay*` and `$HOME/trust*`, which
  were folder names from one person's machine, and `/private/tmp/claude-*`, Claude Code's
  own temp root. Nothing about a session or about Claude Code makes a folder safe to
  trust: that temp root sits in `/tmp`, and a session trusted there also reads the
  `CLAUDE.md` files any local user can leave in `/tmp`. This matters only under `approve =
  "safe"`. There every folder-trust dialog now goes to a person, and a Read is answered
  only under `/usr`, `/etc`, `/opt/homebrew` and the folders you list. That includes a
  Read in the temp root, since on a shared `/tmp` another local user could make your
  `claude-<uid>` first and turn the file a Read was judged by into a link to one of your
  secrets. To have your own folders' trust dialogs and Reads answered, list them:
  `trust_roots = ["~/src/app*"]`. A `claude-*` you list under `/tmp` or `/private/tmp`
  still means only your own `claude-<uid>`. The default `approve = "all"` answers every
  trust dialog, as before.
- **aterm waits for a quiet moment before it brings up the Developer Tools list by itself.** It
  used to open System Settings as soon as it found itself missing from the list — once 1.7
  seconds after an update, with nothing on screen to say why. Now it waits until an aterm window
  is in front and you have been at the Mac within five minutes but have not typed or moved the
  mouse for ten seconds, aterm has been running at least 90 seconds, and no update is switching
  versions. It still does this at most once per version, and now also never within ten minutes
  of the last time, never on an ad hoc or dev build (which no longer brings the list up by
  itself), and never while your **Not now** holds.
- **The checks are one command anyone runs when they want; only a release requires
  them.** `targo --unverified verify` runs the dev checks (formatting, the source guards,
  the L0 censuses, tippy, the tests and the doctests) in place and offline on what a
  branch changed; `-p <crate>` narrows it, `--all` takes the workspace, `verify list`
  names every check, and any check runs by name (`verify lint -p aterm-grid`, `verify
  measure --app <APP>`). A skip names its fix and fails nothing. `verify export` is
  `ship check --export`, the publication engine's dry run: it needs the network and judges
  only a commit already on origin/main. `targo --unverified ship release` runs `verify
  release --app <bundle>` over the release commit and the bundle it signs, and any red or
  skip refuses the publish. `docs/PROCESS.md` §4 has the rest.
- **The harness leaves a person's own questions and messages alone: its continuations are
  for jobs.** When a person opens a turn in the window and the agent answers within ten
  minutes (however long it thinks or looks things up), with no wall or Esc, on a task the
  harness was not already continuing, the harness types nothing after it (no
  `keep going`, no `answer_text`, no done check), whatever the reply says, and the journal
  says why once (`LEFT … rule=left-to-person@v1`). A person's quick check-ins inside a run
  the harness is carrying stay on its ladder. The harness reads the person's stamp from the
  screen read itself, not a stale `status` stamp. The agent primer (v18) says a reply to a
  person's question or message carries no `ATERM-TASK-DONE`; the token still ends a
  finished job's continuations.
- **Publishing atpkg packages is one Rust tool, `atpkg-publish`, which replaces its shell
  scripts.** It packs program builds and sysroot bundles, signs their manifests, publishes
  the signed index as a typed change to the verified channel head (`atpkg-publish status`
  shows the head, `atpkg-publish index --pin <program>=<build>` signs the next one),
  mirrors exactly what an index pins, publishes the rustc group from one seal, and runs the
  unattended Apple and Linux lanes. The client's own verifier checks every manifest and
  index it writes before anything is uploaded. A lane runs only the snapshot
  `atpkg-publish lane install` built from a clean checkout: its launchd or systemd unit
  names the snapshot's sha256, and `lane run` refuses any other binary. `ship provision`
  installs the stock toolchains it audits, replacing `tools/bootstrap-publisher.sh`.
- **The Trust lane's floors for aterm-codec, aterm-digest and aterm-lz4 count what the
  rustup `trust` channel's toolchain, trust-edbb3f30, proves, not the retired seal
  321aaeda7.** The floors are 372 proved obligations for aterm-codec (from 383), 46 for
  aterm-digest (from 47) and 61 for aterm-lz4 (from 36). trust-edbb3f30 carries Trust's
  fixes for the four proofs aterm had lost, so aterm-wasm meets its floor again unchanged.
  The codec and digest drops are Trust counting the same obligations differently, one
  digest obligation Trust declines on soundness grounds (`self.buf[self.buf_len..]` at
  sha256.rs:148), and 8 `trailer[..]` slice checks in aterm-codec's inflate.rs that this
  toolchain leaves to a runtime check; codec's floor goes back up once the channel carries
  Trust's fix for those 8. `crates/aterm-release/trust/floors.tsv` gives each lowered
  floor's reason.
- **The kitty-command listener and flash are formally modelled.** When a typed line may move
  the cat, and the flash's pane scope and revoke, are bounded `ty_model!` models proved in
  `aterm-spec` and checked against the shipping code by conformance tests.

### Removed

- The merge contract, inherited reds, baselines, the snapshot worktree,
  `tools/verify.sh`, `tools/freeze-safety-gate` (its censuses are now `aterm-census
  --all`) and `tools/temporal-extract`.
- **Smart Titles: every tab and window now shows the session's title alone.** The
  generated "what is it doing" half of the tab and window label is gone, with everything
  that produced it: the built-in activity summarizer, the optional Ollama and
  OpenAI-compatible provider worker, the aterm-managed Ollama runtime and its model check,
  and Settings ▸ Window & Tabs' Smart Titles group with its live-status card. A tab's
  label is your `meta set title`, else the program's title, else its directory, the same
  in the tab strip, the native toolbar, the window title, the accessibility tree and
  `aterm ctl inspect app/v1 tabs`. An authored `meta set description` and the session's
  status line still show in the tab's tooltip and menu. The 14 keys (`descriptive_titles`,
  the `title_summary_*` keys, `tab_title_format`, `window_title_format`) do nothing now: an
  `aterm.toml` that still sets them, `title_summary_provider = "ollama"` included, loads
  with every other setting and is told each key was removed, and
  `aterm ctl settings set|unset` on one answers the same rather than calling it unknown.
  aterm no longer starts or contacts an Ollama. `metrics` reports the retired deadline
  slot as `retired-30`. A better account of what each session is doing is planned on the
  session log.

### Fixed

- **The harness's restart and relaunch of an exited Claude Code do what they say.**
  `aterm ctl restart` no longer ends a Claude Code started under another `HOME`, which its
  relaunch would refuse: the act is refused (`ERR restart unavailable: not-relaunchable`) and
  the agent keeps running. A crashed agent is moved onto a newer build only once that build has
  been seen to start, else it comes back on the build it ran, and your own restarts no longer
  make a later crash wait ten minutes. A crashed agent's relaunch that keeps failing now marks
  its tab with the command that starts the agent by hand, where it was only a record, and the
  mark goes once aterm stops trying. One held by its conversation open in another tab says to
  close it there instead. When aterm cannot bring an agent back, its tab's mark names the
  command, with the agent's own `HOME` where it ran under another, and stays until that
  conversation runs in the tab. An agent an upgrade restarted just as a hold landed is
  relaunched once the hold lifts. The "Start Claude Code again" row of an upgrade that started
  its agent afresh ends once a Claude Code runs in the tab again, and `status upgrade=` names
  the tab's newest move.
- **`aterm drive answer` answers a Muse Code question** by moving the cursor to the answer and
  pressing Enter, trying again when the question's ticking clock moved the screen under a key; a
  narrow tab's wrapped question and file box are read too.
- **Codex 0.163.0's screens are read as they are drawn** (re-measured on the build atpkg ships):
  a turn past a usage threshold is no longer read as running forever (the right-aligned
  `⚠ 5h limit` notice and the `⚠ Heads up` warning end it); a question with its notes field
  open is still a question; a `└ Tip:` under an answer no longer hides it; a refused API key
  is a lost login, `unexpected status <n>` an API error, the `experiencing high demand` row an
  HTTP 500, and a stream cut off before it finished a cut-off reply retried at once.
- **The workspace-member `Request increase?` banner is never answered Yes**, and nothing is typed
  while it stands. **An owner's own Codex `prefix_rule(…, decision="prompt")` box is never
  pressed** at any approve level. **The Codex folder-trust gate is judged by the repository
  root it trusts**, which must be under a trust root.
- **`--context-warn` works for Codex**: 0.163.0's default footer draws no `% context left`, so
  the figure is read from Codex's own records.
- **`aterm harness limits` reads Codex 0.163.0's box-less `/status` card** and its 12-hour reset
  times; the newest card wins even when it shows no quota.
- **The `codex resume` command aterm tells you carries `CODEX_HOME`**, and a relative
  `CODEX_HOME` is resolved against the Codex's own folder, as Codex resolves it.
- **`aterm drive report` reads a Codex worker in Codex's grammar**: from the archive on the
  alternate screen and from the scrollback inline, opening at the turn's `›` row (never the
  prompt Codex pins on top), with `--final`/`--messages` keeping Codex's messages and end rows;
  `--max-rows` keeps the turn's end. `aterm drive phase` prints `interrupt esc` under a Codex
  question (Esc ends the turn), and `aterm drive answer` never presses a digit unfenced.
- **Restored-tab records survive stale layout entries and shutdown races.** A missing
  duplicate no longer hides the notice for a surviving held tab. Shutdown follows the
  latest conversation after stopping workers, and a closed restore queue cannot publish
  an older in-flight read or discard the relaunches still owed to the next instance.
- **Copying on Windows now supplies the clipboard owner Win32 requires.** Windows file
  drops answer COM interface queries and release each acquired medium through its owner.
  On macOS,
  accessibility caret offsets now count UTF-16 units, so an emoji before the caret no
  longer shifts its reported position.
- **Linux file drops preserve encoded separators and filename whitespace.** URI-list
  entries are framed before decoding paths, and malformed XSettings counts stop cleanly.
- **Scrolling within horizontal margins keeps real spaces distinct from wide-character
  wrap padding.** Resizing no longer deletes a printed space that inherited an old padding
  mark. Newly reconstructed padding also retains the wide character's background color.
- **Web terminals retain cursor and selection presentation settings when initializing
  their GPU renderer.** Invalid line-height requests keep the previous valid geometry;
  extreme selection coordinates remain off screen. Renderer construction and font-size changes
  also reject non-finite or unrepresentable geometry. Refused variable-font settings retain
  the previous instance and caches; font previews follow the same admission rules.
  Reduced motion now stops output streaks.
- **Control and harness paths reject malformed success replies and surplus image-read
  arguments.** JSON field names and federated event addresses are escaped correctly;
  oversized notification rates and process ages are refused without arithmetic overflow.
  Long Unicode keeper status and recovery metadata remain valid when truncated.
  Codex numbered answers retain their generation fence when a host rejects it.
  Reports preserve search completeness and screen coordinates, and unreadable history
  cannot masquerade as the end of a complete transcript.
- **Keeper release uses the complete process identity throughout cleanup,** preserving
  another process's claim when a PID is reused. Remote control also checks the explicit
  endpoint certificate pin before presenting its authentication capability, and token
  discovery keeps a dangling per-socket entry from selecting a legacy credential.
- **File hashing handles option-like and escaped filenames correctly,** and refuses
  malformed checksum output. Search omits fuzzy hits with no display width, and selection
  scroll/splice rejects the first row beyond the live screen.
- **Codex walls and boxes are handled by Codex's own rules, not Claude Code's.**
  - Under `approve = "safe"`, aterm now answers Codex's folder-trust prompt for a folder you
    list in `trust_roots`, checked the way Claude Code's trust dialog is (the session's own
    folder, under a trust root, one trust choice and one quit choice). Every other Codex box
    still goes to you under "safe"; the help for `approve`, `trust_roots` and `rm_breaker_ask`
    says which agent's boxes each covers.
  - A Codex spend cap, an empty credit balance, a limit still in force after its reset, and a
    lost login no longer tell you to use claude.ai or `/login`: they point to Codex's own
    notice, its `/status`, and `codex login`.
  - A Codex usage limit drawn right above `1 background terminal running` waits for the
    limit's own reset; the line was read as part of the reset time, which no clock can parse.
- **`aterm drive` reads a Codex worker as Codex.** `drive phase` and `drive await-turn` describe
  its box, busy row and context in Codex's terms; `drive answer` answers its question by the
  answer's number or exact label (`recommended`, `human` too), guarded on the question's title
  and leaves `None of the above` to a person; `drive report` finds the turn's `›` row on the
  screen or in the scrollback and reports the whole turn.
- **A Codex started with `CODEX_HOME=<dir>` comes back under that folder when aterm relaunches
  it** (the live upgrade, a relaunch after a crash or restart, and the relaunch after aterm
  ended). The relaunch line sets the variable to the value Codex was started with, and a
  relaunch that cannot carry it is refused.
- **A Codex tab counts its usage-limit wall down to when the harness will continue.** The reset
  is the one the harness placed in that Codex's own time zone (a `TZ` the tab exported), not
  aterm's; with none placed, aterm's zone as before.
- **The installed-agents record counts each agent's sessions against its own build.** A Codex
  tab running an older build than the installed Codex CLI was counted nowhere; each agent now
  has its own count ("1 running Codex session moves onto it on its own").
- **A Claude Code started as `claude-code` gets the footer, Autopilot chips and harness card**,
  as the harness already supervised it. A program with that name that is not Claude Code shows
  nothing.
- **A tab running an agent under `node` (an npm install) is treated as an agent tab.** The
  installed-agents record no longer tells you to type the hook line into it, a tab that lost
  its shell integration is told the harness's next move gives it back, and `status copy=`
  reads `foreign`. `program=` still names `node`.
- **Folder-trust answers yield when a person keys during the answer.** Both the focus
  move and Enter are fenced on the judged screen's person count. Recent gestures
  still retain their ordinary human grace: a later status publication and the
  harness's first sight of a dialog do not prove that the gesture launched it.

- **A fresh Codex session reads as idle again, so `aterm drive task` nudges it.** Since 0.158.0
  Codex draws its session card with no box, and a session nobody had asked anything read as
  idle with no evidence, so nothing that acts on evidence acted there. The card's title row now
  says it (measured on 0.163.0, the build atpkg ships).
- **`aterm drive task` no longer reports `nudged=0` for a nudge the worker took.** On a screen
  that never holds still (Claude Code 2.1.301's), the nudge's Enter is written with no time left
  to see it land. `drive task` now reads the worker's composer: gone from it is `nudged=1`, still
  typed there, or a composer it cannot read, is `nudged=0` and an error that says which.
- **Settings ▸ Packages no longer says it manages only Claude Code and Codex.** Its subtitle is
  "ALab tools and coding agents", since agy and muse are managed too.
- **The harness no longer types into a Claude Code session that is retrying its own usage
  limit.** With `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG` set by hand (aterm never sets it), Claude Code
  shows no limit notice; it keeps the request and shows a ticking `Session limit reached ·
  Retrying in 2m 28s (8:48am) · attempt 1/300` row until the reset. With a statusLine
  configured that row was read as a finished turn, and the harness typed `keep going` into the
  waiting session. The row is now a turn in progress, at any width and on both renderers: nothing
  is typed while it stands, the retry carries on as the turn, and Esc on it ends the turn as Esc
  ends any other.
- **A Claude Code or Codex CLI build installed from the old ALab index moves to the vendor's
  latest even when the signed index no longer lists the program.** aterm reads such a
  build's version from its signed manifest to know whether the vendor's latest is newer, and
  it found that manifest only through the program's entry in the index. The index still lists
  both, but once those entries go, a build from one of its later pins would have been kept,
  with a line saying its version could not be read, until you ran `aterm pkg update claude`
  (or `codex`) by hand. The manifest is now read from the index's own repository whenever the
  index does not list the program, and is still checked against the signed roster. For
  publishers, `atpkg-publish index` now names Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity CLI and Muse
  Code as vendor-direct when it refuses `--pin` or `--target-pin` of one. It now takes a yank
  of any of them, such as `--yank agy@1.4.0` or `--yank muse@1.4.9-R6297.1`, whether or not
  the index pins it, and retiring one of them keeps its yanks. It refuses a yank spelt in a
  form the program's versions never take, such as `--yank muse@1.4.9`, which would have
  matched nothing. Re-run `atpkg-publish lane install` on every armed lane machine before the
  first such yank or a `--retire` of claude or codex: an older lane drops a yank of an
  unpinned program on its next publish.
- **Pressing the Developer Tools line in "To look at" no longer counts as opening Settings for
  Full Disk Access.** It quieted the Full Disk Access card as if you had looked at it. And when you
  come back from System Settings after aterm brought you there, aterm now reads the list at once
  instead of up to a minute later.
- **The kitty-command flash lands on the copy of the word that fired.** A word typed twice in a
  burst (`sit sit `) flashes the first copy, the one the cat answers, not the second.
- **Inside tmux or another scroll region, the shell's own output no longer flashes in place of
  your kitty command.** `bash: sit: command not found` stays its own colour, and your `sit`
  flashes once the next prompt appears. One case remains: output whose word the prompt's width
  lines up exactly with where you typed it can still flash.
- **A pet word typed after Ctrl+Z no longer fires inside text the shell kept.** At a prompt
  Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+\ leave the half-typed line where it is, yet aterm took either for proof the
  line was empty even after Esc, an arrow key or a paste, whose text it never saw: Esc, `sot`,
  Ctrl+Z, `sit ` moved the cat while the shell held `sotsit `. Now only a line aterm knows is
  empty keeps listening through the chord; any other waits for Enter, Ctrl+U or Ctrl+C, the
  prompt an editor returns to after Esc and Ctrl+Z included.
- **Closing a split pane above or below no longer cancels the kitty-command flash in the
  other.** The flash belongs to the pane you typed in and finishes on its own clock. Closing a
  pane beside it still ends the flash: your pane gets wider, and the flash ends whenever the
  width changes, because the text may move when lines rewrap.
- **The harness no longer types `keep going` into a finished Claude Code session after
  Claude Code compacts it.** About an hour after a turn, with nobody at the tab, Claude
  Code compacts the conversation by itself and prints `Compacted while idle, before the
  prompt cache expired`. The harness read that as a new turn end and continued the task
  the agent had already reported done. That compaction is now no turn, and the harness
  reads the agent's last words above it: a finished task stays finished (also for a
  harness that restarts afterwards), a person's own exchange stays theirs, and a question
  held for a person stays held.
- HTTP requests cannot carry a caller-supplied `Transfer-Encoding` beside their generated
  `Content-Length`. Request and response header names share the HTTP token grammar, and
  malformed response fields and control characters are refused.
- Control clients bound the total bytes of a counted reply, including discovery,
  connection metadata and drift results. Relay replies enforce the line limit even when
  the newline arrives in the same read, and an overflowing count is refused before its
  body can be mistaken for another reply.
- PNG decoding bounds encoded input as well as decoded pixels. A temporary directory's
  name prefix cannot escape the requested parent directory.
- Full-line selections copy and highlight the same complete rows whichever side the
  anchor is on. A selection ending before the first representable row is empty instead of
  overflowing its row coordinate. Streaming regex search uses indexed search's
  logical-line budget and reports its results as incomplete when a scan or result cap
  runs out.
- Removing recent scrollback commits its fallible boundary operation before removing
  newer RAM tiers, so a disk I/O failure leaves their contents and accounting intact.
- The development checks' change cone includes consumers of shared source and assets, and
  a change to a vendored package or a submodule bump selects the crates that depend on it,
  read from the resolved dependency graph (an astream bump selects aterm-link and aterm).
  Dependency-graph parsing accepts checkout and package paths containing parentheses.
  Edits hidden by index flags are hashed in bounded argument batches, which cannot
  deadlock the pipe and keep filenames containing newlines or quotes intact.
- Vendored Windows winit files carry modification notices for their windows-sys
  adaptations and typed handle helpers.
- **A Claude Code, Codex, agy or muse download that a pass left unfinished resumes
  instead of starting over.** A pass that cannot reach the vendor, or that installs another
  program, keeps the download of the newest release the vendor named (partial, or complete
  and awaiting its signature check) until that release is installed or the vendor names a
  newer one, so the next pass does not fetch every byte again (368 MB for muse).
  `aterm pkg gc` still removes it.
- **Help and config examples no longer use one person's folder names.** The `status` and
  `sessions` help's example is `cd ~/proj && exec claude`, and the config template's dev-link
  example is `~/src/ay`. The manual's `ay` entry and the Trust toolchain's from-source remedy
  say "that checkout" and "a Trust checkout" where they named a home folder.
- **A session that receives broadcasts no longer loses, or is shown twice, a direct
  message across an update.** Marking a broadcast handled used to move the point the new
  aterm refills direct messages from, so it could skip an unhandled message or bring back
  one already handled. `inbox seen` now reports that point from direct messages alone.
- **An update no longer loses the broadcasts a session has not handled.** The new aterm's
  bridge offers each subscribed topic again from the oldest broadcast the session had not
  marked handled (`inbox seen`), in order and once each, so a broadcast read before the update
  but not handled shows up again instead of vanishing. `dropped=` no longer counts those; it
  still counts the ones no bridge offers again (a bridge from an older aterm, or a topic the
  session dropped). The same holds when a crashed aterm's sessions are recovered.
- **`dropped=` survives an update and counts the broadcasts the update could not carry.**
  It used to restart at 0, hiding earlier drops and the unread broadcasts an update loses
  (broadcasts, unlike direct messages, are not sent again); `aterm.log` names the count.
- **`topic drop` takes effect at once.** A broadcast the bridge was still routing by its
  older copy of the topics is refused (`ERR not-subscribed`) instead of delivered.
- **Receipts and `inbox get @<off>` no longer wait up to 250 ms to start.** `inbox seen`
  and a parked `inbox get @<off>` now wake the bridge as `post` does.
- **`verify perf` runs the lanes you name.** `targo --unverified verify perf [LANE...]
  [--record LANE...]` runs any lane alone or with others, and `verify perf --list` names
  them. A bare `verify perf` runs the headless floor lanes; the real-window arena lanes
  (`start`, `compare`, `cat`, `scroll`, `vte`) run only when named, and replace the
  `tools/perf-arena`, `tools/wasm-bench` and `tools/onglass-bench` scripts. `--record` names
  the lanes whose baselines it rewrites, so a bare `--record` is a usage error (exit 2). The
  baselines and the trend ledger moved from `tools/golden/` to
  `crates/aterm-verify/perf/golden/`.
- **The publication and lab tools are Trust code, and `verify` runs the spec checkers.**
  `targo --unverified ship dev-app` builds and installs `aterm (dev).app` (`ship dev-app
  identity` makes its signing identity) in place of `tools/dev-app.sh` and
  `tools/dev-sign-id.sh`; the publication hooks run `ship hook`, the site sync is `ship
  site`, the real-Claude lab is `targo --unverified lab`, and the libc bindings regenerate
  with `aterm-libc-oracle regen`. `verify` drops the `delivery` check, whose suites are
  ordinary tests now, and gains `spec` (in the `release` set): every registered model under
  `ty`, `ay` and `trust-ir`.

## [0.104.0] - 2026-10-15

### Added

- **Iosevka Term ships with aterm: `font_family = "Iosevka Term"` selects it on macOS, Linux
  and Windows.** Iosevka Term 34.9.0, the narrow, strictly monospaced cut of Iosevka, is built
  in with real Bold, Italic and Bold Italic faces. At the same size its cells are a fifth
  narrower than SF Mono's (12 px against 15 at 24 px), so a window of the same width holds
  about a quarter more columns. It covers Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, box drawing, block elements,
  Braille, arrows, math operators and Powerline, and draws its programming ligatures unless
  `ligatures = false`. The built-in copy leaves out Iosevka's stylistic sets and character
  variants, so `font_features = ["ss08"]` changes nothing on it; an Iosevka Term you install
  yourself is used instead. The default font is unchanged.

- **`aterm doctor` says when macOS is slowing your builds, and where the fix is.** While aterm is
  not on System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Developer Tools, macOS checks each new program
  aterm starts before its first run, one at a time, and under a build or test run those checks
  have held first runs for 25 minutes and more; adding aterm there should end them. The new
  `devtools:` row reads macOS's own answers for aterm from the last ten minutes. It is `ok` when
  aterm is allowed. When aterm is not, it is a `warn` with how many programs macOS checked, the
  System Settings path, the `open` command that shows that pane, and the fact that `sudo killall
  syspolicyd` does not work (System Integrity Protection refuses it). An answer aterm could not
  read says so and never reads as "not listed". A warning never changes doctor's exit code, which
  is still 1 only when the shell cannot start, and the health line counts the warnings.
- **aterm brings you to the Developer Tools switch by itself.** aterm now also reads the switch
  itself (its row in macOS's privacy database, read-only, when aterm has Full Disk Access), so
  the answer no longer waits for a new program to start. When aterm is not on the list, the
  window opens the Developer Tools pane for you once per version and keeps one line in "To
  look at" whose button opens it again; `aterm doctor` opens it too (after `spctl
  developer-mode enable-terminal` on a Mac that shows no such pane yet) and, at a terminal,
  waits up to two minutes for you to switch aterm on. Only you flip the switch: macOS asks
  for your password, and aterm never presses anything in System Settings. It takes effect for
  the next program aterm starts; nothing needs relaunching. `aterm pkg doctor` has the same
  `devtools:` row, and `aterm ctl privacy`'s `devtools` row adds `grant=`, `list=` and
  `list_probe=`. `aterm doctor --read-only` changes nothing.
- **`aterm doctor` moves stale copies of aterm to the Trash.** A copy of aterm signed ad hoc
  (`aterm-prev-<n>.app`, `aterm-local-<n>.app`) beside the installed app resets aterm's privacy
  grants whenever it asks macOS for one. Doctor moves exactly the copies Settings ▸ Security's
  *Move to Trash* offers, never one a process runs from and never a signed release, and says
  which; they stay recoverable in the Trash. `--read-only` only lists them.

### Changed

- **`targo --unverified` and `cargo` builds in an aterm tab keep their intermediate files out
  of Spotlight (macOS).** For projects in your home folder, binaries stay in `target/` and the
  rest goes to `~/Library/Caches/aterm/cargo-build.noindex`, which Spotlight skips. Nothing of
  yours is moved or renamed, and a target or build folder you chose yourself still wins. Each
  project's first build after the update starts from scratch; the old intermediates stay in
  `target/` until `targo clean`. A cache unwritten for a month is removed, most deleted
  projects' after a day, never during a build.

- **What aterm writes into coding agents' context is much shorter (primer v16).** The block
  in their global context files is 15 lines instead of 55 and no longer tells agents to put
  code under `~/Developer`; the four skills it installs for Claude Code are seven tenths to
  nine tenths shorter and point at `aterm ctl help <verb>` instead of copying it. aterm
  rewrites both in place.

- **The facts under Claude Code's input box read as one line.** The model, the folder, the
  branch and the session's totals stood six to nine character widths apart, a gap that grew
  with the text. They are now set like a line of small type: an even gap between every two
  facts, about two and a half characters, whatever their lengths, with the rule running up to
  them, so a narrow pane keeps more of them. At 1x the letters no longer jitter by a pixel
  (`foo ter`, `spac ing`): each small glyph is placed to a fraction of a pixel.

- **The Trust lane's floors for once_cell, smol_str, libc, aterm-sixel and aterm-scrollback
  now count what the current Trust toolchain proves (trust-b58a105d), not what the retired
  seal 321aaeda7 proved.** The new floors are 18, 123, 25, 26 and 284 proved obligations,
  each measured quietly through the gate's own lane. These five libraries had fallen below
  their floors only because Trust now counts the same obligations differently, and no proof
  was lost. It no longer issues a second overflow row for a shift whose `[shift]` row
  already states it, and no longer counts a `Box::new` null check that was a tautology. It
  prints one row where 321aaeda7 printed two identical rows or a proved and a failed twin.
  And a `match`'s exhaustiveness proof no longer counts a second time as the panic-freedom of
  the functions it calls. aterm-hash's floor moved the same way, from 50 to 49: seven of its
  shift rows were counted twice. Each floor's row in `tools/trust-gate-ratchet.tsv` names the
  Trust commits and the evidence. Four libraries are still below their floors on trust-b58a105d
  and keep them, because Trust regressions are under investigation there. aterm-codec lost 2
  proofs (`joint[..held]` at tty.rs:141 and a hardened twin at inflate.rs:911). aterm-digest
  lost 2 (sha256.rs:148, which Trust c888f21ea3/9cc4cdc14b now decline on soundness grounds,
  and the hardened twin at sha256.rs:155). aterm-wasm's `pump_reflow_on_render_tick`
  (lib.rs:1142) no longer lowers (`MalformedTrustIr`). In aterm-lz4 one row is not yet
  explained. A change that touches one of these four fails the merge gate's Trust lane until
  Trust is fixed.

- **The supervisor's trust roots and the publication engine are where they were before
  `~/Developer`.** `[harness] trust_roots` defaults to `~/aterm*`, `~/ay*`, `$HOME/trust*` and
  `/private/tmp/claude-*` again, and the release tools (`ship check --export` among them)
  and the ALab lane read the engine at `$PUBLICATION_ENGINE`, else `~/publication`. `~/Developer`
  is an ordinary folder: name it in `trust_roots` if your checkouts live there. The agent
  primer (v15) no longer says where code lives.

### Removed

- **The developer root: `aterm pkg devroot`, the `devroot:` and `spotlight:` doctor rows,
  and the "Spotlight indexes ~/Developer" entry.** aterm no longer asks you to keep code in
  `~/Developer` or to add a folder to Spotlight's Search Privacy list, and never moves a
  folder of yours. `aterm pkg devroot` (and `move`, `verify`) is gone, both doctors lose
  their `devroot:` and `spotlight:` rows (so neither plants a Spotlight probe any more), the
  window's six-hourly look no longer measures `~/Developer`, Messages ▸ To look at no longer
  raises its line or offers the Search Privacy button, and the disk cleanup walks your home's
  checkouts as it did before, with `~/Developer` one more folder among them.
  `aterm pkg noindex verify <dir>` stays, as an on-demand measurement.

### Fixed

- **A Claude Code that crashes while aterm is busy elsewhere is still brought back.** With
  `[harness] relaunch` on, three kinds of crash could be missed: one during an update of aterm
  that did not complete, one while the harness was recovering from an internal error, and one
  of an agent the harness had just relaunched, before aterm had seen it start. The tab was left
  at its shell with nothing said, or the crash was taken for a deliberate `/exit` because another
  Claude Code had started in the meantime. Each crash is now read the moment the agent ends and
  relaunched on its conversation. While the harness recovers from an internal error, a change to
  `[harness]` (approving less, switching it off) takes effect at once, and supervision comes back
  as soon as an update that did not complete hands the tabs back.
- **A usage limit whose countdown you cancel the moment it appears is still waited out.** When
  the harness's own `keep going` met a usage limit and you pressed Esc on Claude Code's
  `Continuing automatically at … · esc to cancel` before the harness looked at the screen, all
  it ever saw was `Automatic continue cancelled`, and a few minutes later it typed `keep going`
  into the limit again. It now reads the notice above the cancel as the limit that answered it,
  and waits for the reset that notice names. An older limit that a conversation you resume
  ends on is not taken for one.
- **`aterm doctor` typed at a shell measures macOS access again.** Started through
  `~/.local/bin/aterm`, the link the installer lays, doctor took itself for a build outside
  the app and reported its privacy and debugger rows as "not measured (running outside the app
  bundle)". It now recognises the app it is running from however it was started, so those rows,
  and the new `devtools:` row, report what macOS says.
- **A supervised agent's waits count the night the Mac slept, and no turn is typed until the
  network is back.** The harness kept its own back-offs (after an API error, a full context, a
  usage limit's continuation that met the limit again, a run of short turns) and some resets it
  waits for (one whose notice had left the screen, a model switch's return, a Codex hold whose
  reset nobody read) on a clock that stops while the Mac sleeps, so after a night asleep it
  waited out the rest of an hour's back-off, or hours for a reset already past, before trying
  again. They now count the sleep, as the wall clock does. And for 30-90 s after a wake,
  counted from the wake, the harness types no turn into the agent while the network comes back,
  whatever reaches it first: no continuation, no upgrade notice or carry-on, no `/usage` read.
  A reset the sleep carried past had been continued the moment the screen repainted, into an
  API it could not yet reach. A box the agent puts up is still answered: its keys answer a turn
  already running, and start none.
- **The cursor pet keeps its size and height through a screen or pane switch.** When you switched
  split panes or a full-screen program opened, the cat you were looking at fades out where it
  stood, but it was redrawn at its resting size on the ground: a cat caught mid-breath or
  mid-stretch changed size by a pixel or three, and one caught mid-hop dropped to the line below
  it, on the frame the switch landed. It now fades exactly as it was last drawn, and when the
  focus comes straight back the cat there carries on from that size and eases into its own.
- **With the PTY keeper on, a crash keeps the modes of a full-screen program in a wide pane.**
  The keeper is told each shell's terminal modes so that a recovered tab keeps them. That record
  carried one entry per column for tab stops, so on the alternate screen at about 119 columns or
  wider (vim, less, htop, Claude Code) it outgrew its 4 KiB limit and was never sent. It was not
  tried again either, so after a crash such a tab came back with the modes from before the
  program started. Tab stops now travel packed, the record fits at any width, and one that could
  not be sent is retried.
- **Reading a peer's mail in a terminal can no longer retitle your tab, draw over it or set your
  clipboard.** `aterm ctl inbox get` printed a fabric peer's message body exactly as sent, so
  escape sequences in it took effect in your terminal: a new tab title, a forged
  `OK … trust=human` line drawn over the real one, recoloured text, an OSC 52 clipboard write.
  The same held for a status line or refusal a server sent back, a remote machine reached through
  `aterm ctl dial` included. On a terminal `aterm ctl` now shows every control character as
  text (`\x1b`, `\u{009b}`, `\u{202e}`); piped or redirected output is byte for byte what it was.
  `--json` output now also escapes C1 controls, DEL, bidi controls and U+2028/9, and still
  decodes to the same strings.
- **Find reports a hit in the cells it is drawn in.** Find measured each row from its text, so
  on a row where a program had drawn two halves of a flag, a skin tone and its emoji, or a
  joined pair out of order, or where a ✔️ or ⚠️ sat in a wrapped line's last column, the
  Cmd-F highlight and the columns `aterm ctl search` reports landed one or two cells off,
  further with each such glyph. Hits now come from the grid's own cells, on the screen and in
  history.
- **One very long line no longer breaks regex find for the whole tab.** A `cat` of a minified
  file or a one-line JSON reply could exhaust the regex budget on that one line, and every regex
  search of the tab was then refused as a bad pattern. The budget now grows with the line; a
  line it still cannot finish keeps the matches found, the find bar says `line cut short`, and
  `aterm ctl search` says `incomplete long-line`. Every other line is searched. When a list is
  short for more than one reason, `aterm ctl search` now names each of them.
- **Find keeps working in a tab that has printed more than four billion lines**, where it had
  answered "no matches" for everything, and its index of non-ASCII scrollback takes a fifth of
  the memory it did (370 MiB for 100,000 rows of CJK became 79 MiB).
- **Text a program prints lands the same however it arrives.** Depending on where a read from
  the program happened to split its output, the screen could differ: an old accent, skin tone
  or link reappeared on new text written over it in colour; text under left and right margins
  (tmux's `margins`) printed past the right margin; trailing spaces were kept or dropped, so a
  copy across a wrapped line could join two words; and a repeat of a toned emoji repeated the
  wrong part. Each now comes out the same whatever the split.
- **The presence row draws names in CJK and other wide scripts at their width**, where it had
  squeezed each wide character into one cell, and it strips the invisible characters that
  could hide text from a person while an agent reading `aterm ctl chrome` still saw it.
- **A terminal query split by a live update is still answered, and a device-control string
  whose header holds a byte above 0x9F is no longer printed on screen as text.**
- **Scrollback no longer garbles once its history is full and the tab grows taller.** Once a
  tab's history had filled (about 6,100 lines at 80 columns) and the tab then gained rows — a
  taller window, a dragged split divider, a status row folding away — the next lines a program
  printed went into the middle of the history instead of its end. For as many lines as the tab
  had gained, each new line was written over the bottom row and kept the old line's tail, blank
  lines appeared in the history, and colours, links and accents moved up a row without their
  text; under an inline program such as Codex, its input rows were overwritten. New lines now
  land at the end of the history. This had been so since 0.100.0.
- **Scrollback keeps every line, in order, when you resize the window.** Dragging a window to a
  new width could drop the oldest lines the resize pushed off the screen, or leave newer lines
  ahead of older ones in the history for good, and a long line could come back with a stray row
  in the middle of it. With `scrollback_lines` at or below the in-memory part of the history
  (512 to 10,000 lines, by width), a width change could also wipe the history or leave a gap in
  it, and one drag step while a rewrap was running could lose the whole scrollback. History now
  comes back from a resize as it went in.
- **Links and underline colours in scrollback stay on their text.** After a ❤️, ✔️ or ⚠️ that
  had sat in a row's last column, every link and underline colour after it on that history row
  sat a cell to the left of its text, on a blank; and a wide character a one-column pane could
  not hold left its link on the empty cell behind it.
- **A double-click selects and copies the word drawn where you click.** After a ✔️ or ⚠️ at the
  end of a wrapped line, or flag halves a program drew apart, a double-click further along the
  line selected the wrong word or a single cell. In scrollback such a click could select one
  cell and copy nothing, and after a live `ambiguous_width` change it copied the wrong
  characters. In the web builds a link after CJK text could not be opened, and words and links
  after such glyphs were looked up in the wrong cells.
- **A program can no longer slow a window's drawing by printing emoji clusters chosen to
  collide.** aterm remembers how it drew each emoji cluster, keyed by the cluster's text, under
  a hash that was the same on every machine. A program could print a screen of clusters chosen
  so that each lookup compared against all of them: a full repaint of such a 32×128 screen took
  15.7-18.5 ms instead of about 2 ms, and every tab in the window waited on it for as long as
  the clusters stayed on screen. That memory, the one for ligature runs, and the word
  decorations' memories of rows and finished marks now hash under a secret each aterm picks for
  itself. Ordinary drawing is as fast as before.
- **Two files can no longer share one unsaved-draft journal.** The editor's crash-recovery
  journal was named by a public hash of the file's path, so whoever names the files you open
  could pick two names with the same journal. Opening the second could then show the first's
  unsaved draft as its content, and Save wrote it there. A journal is now named by a keyed hash
  under a secret kept in the draft directory (`.journal-key`, created on first use). Drafts an
  older aterm journaled are still recovered. If that file is damaged or has the wrong owner or
  permissions, the editor opens no document and its message names the file; aterm never
  replaces it, so every draft keyed under it stays recoverable once it is repaired.

- **A Containment tab's program can no longer reach the clipboard, your files or desktop
  notifications through aterm.** aterm itself is not sandboxed, and it acted on a contained
  program's escape sequences as it does for any tab. So a `--sandbox` program could set the
  clipboard with OSC 52, read it back when `allow_osc52_query` was on, post desktop
  notifications when `allow_notifications` was on, and, with `allow_kitty_file_transfer` on,
  have aterm read a file its sandbox denies it: aterm drew the file in the tab, and the answer
  told whether the file existed and its size. A Containment tab now gets none of these. A kitty
  image client there falls back to sending the image inline, which still works. What you do
  yourself in the tab (paste, drop a file, click a link) works as before. A plain
  `aterm --sandbox` run inside another terminal is still subject to that terminal's own
  policy.
- **A Containment program can no longer raise its open-file limit.** Containment's 8192 limit
  is now a hard limit; before, one `ulimit -n` lifted it. A contained shell whose startup file
  raises the limit now prints the shell's refusal and keeps 8192. Safety's limits are still
  soft, and the docs now say so.
- **The network drive stays reachable while someone floods its port.** With `[net] listen` on,
  a peer that held 64 idle connections open, reconnecting each one when its 10-second
  handshake ran out, turned every dialer with a valid token away. A newcomer now takes the slot
  of a connection that has not authenticated, from the address holding the most of them, or
  from one that has gone 2 seconds without authenticating. A connection that has
  authenticated is never cut.
- **A smart-title error now names the HTTP status, and an error answer is never used as a
  title.** A bad API key (401), a rate limit (429) or an Ollama out-of-memory (500) showed up as
  "response did not contain message content". A 503 that carried a completion became the tab's
  title. A managed model that failed to load was treated as ready. The status now shows in
  Settings and the log, with the provider's own message unless that message looks like it holds
  a credential. An endpoint written as `localhost`, `*.localhost` or `localhost.` is now dialed
  at 127.0.0.1, then ::1, and never at whatever a DNS server answers for that name.
- **`aterm ctl await gone` and `turn … settle=gone:` no longer report a row gone while it is
  still on screen.** A row too long or complex for the pattern's scan budget counted as "not
  matching", so the wait ended at once. Such a row now counts as undecided, and the wait goes on
  until a later scan can read it. The supervisor's busy check reads rows the same way.

- **Text an input method commits can no longer run a command by itself.** A commit holding a
  line break, Escape or another control character went to the program as typed keys, so it
  skipped what a paste gets: its line break pressed Enter at the prompt, and it never met the
  multi-line paste question or the paste cleanup. Clipboard history in an input method
  (fcitx5's, which a program can fill by writing to the clipboard) and dictation commit text
  this way. Such a commit is now pasted as ⌘V pastes. Escape and the other control
  characters are removed, the text is marked as a paste when the program asks for that, and
  at a prompt that does not ask, a commit holding a line break waits for your OK. A "new
  line" dictated within a phrase therefore inserts a line break instead of running the line.
  A commit that is a single key (Enter, Tab, Backspace or Escape, which an X11 input method
  commits while you are composing) and ordinary commits (Chinese, Japanese and Korean text,
  accents, emoji) are typed exactly as before.

- **The merge gate's test that an update's successor stops when the old aterm dies tests that
  again, and no longer fails by chance.** The test starts a stand-in successor and hands it a
  pipe. Built with a Trust toolchain from seal `62f89f11` on, the stand-in never received the
  pipe: it stopped at once for an unrelated reason, and the test passed on that exit whether or
  not a successor would notice a dead parent. When the exit came early enough the test failed
  instead (about 1 run in 280 with 18 at once, and one merge run on 2026-10-13). The pipe is now
  handed over in a way that works under every toolchain, and the stand-in refuses to go on
  without it. The stand-in's parent now ends only once the stand-in has said that it is still
  watching, so a stand-in that stopped before saying so fails the test. Two can still pass: one
  that stops in the moment between saying so and its parent's exit, and one that the machine
  was too busy to run for a quarter of a second. A second test covers what the first cannot
  see: a successor stops when the old aterm closes the pipe without committing, and with exit
  status 74. aterm itself is unchanged.

- **`aterm` in a terminal ends when its shell does, and applies every resize at once.** A job
  the shell left behind that still held the terminal (a `nohup`ed command run with `&`, a
  daemon started with `setsid`) kept the session open after you typed `exit`, until the job
  let go of it: on Linux any such job, on macOS one that opened the terminal again. The
  session now ends with the shell and returns its exit status, and a job still holding the
  terminal is hung up, as closing a terminal window hangs it up. A resize that arrived at an
  unlucky instant could also wait for the next key or output before the program saw the new
  size; it now reaches the program at once.

- **A second interrupt that reaches an interrupted merge gate ends it at once, and the gate now
  kills a helper a suite left running and a child a stage was just starting.** An interrupted gate
  sends each shell suite `SIGTERM` and waits up to 10 s for its cleanup. A second interrupt during
  that wait (another Ctrl-C, a `kill`, a closed terminal) either went unheard until the wait was
  over or ended the gate on the spot, with a helper the suite had left behind still running. It now
  ends the wait, and whatever the suite left is killed before the gate exits. Closing the terminal
  on a running gate no longer cuts that cleanup short: a terminal hangs its job up twice, and the
  gate took the repeat for a second interrupt. An interrupt that arrived just as a stage was
  starting a child could also miss that child, which then ran on by itself (about one interrupt in
  10,000, by estimate). The gate now waits for such a child, a little over a second at most, and
  kills it with the rest. A second Ctrl-C reaches the gate only while it is the terminal's
  foreground job, which under `targo --unverified verify` ends with the first; send it with `kill`
  there.

- **A merge gate that kills a stage no longer leaves the process that stage was just starting.**
  When a stage outlived its time limit, or the gate was interrupted, the gate killed everything
  the stage had started with one signal to its process group. On macOS that signal reaches the
  processes the group has at that instant and misses one that is being created right then, so a
  stage killed in the middle of starting a helper could leave the helper running, and the gate's
  report said the whole group was gone. In a test whose stage starts helpers back to back, that
  one signal left a helper running after 27 to 80 of every 300 kills. The gate now sends the
  kill again every millisecond until 40 in a row have found nobody, which left none in 500 of
  each kind of kill. Every kill the gate sends therefore takes about 50 ms longer, including the
  usual one whose first signal ended everything: a time-limit kill, an interrupted gate's exit,
  and a suite that exited when asked to. That cost is deliberate. A kill is rare, and stopping
  at the first signal that finds nobody still left a helper running after 19 of 3,000 kills of
  a stage that starts helpers from a second thread, as `targo` and a test harness do. A third of
  a second is the most it can add; if a group still holds a process after that, the timeout
  report says so. Still not reached: a process that left its group on purpose, and a helper that
  takes longer than those 50 ms to appear. The kill is repeated on macOS only. Linux needs no
  second kill (read from its source, not run), and on other Unix systems nothing was measured,
  so a group gets one kill there as before.

- **An interrupted merge gate can no longer kill a process that is not its own.** The gate ends
  a stage by signalling the stage's process group, which the system names by the process id of
  the stage's first process. Once the gate had collected that process's exit status the system
  was free to give the number to something else, and the gate went on using it: the kill it
  sends when a suite's 10 s cleanup wait is over could land on whatever had been given the
  number since. In a test it ended an unrelated program 10.6 s after the Ctrl-C. The gate now
  signals a group only while it still holds the stage's first process. After an interrupt it
  collects no more exit statuses, so every number stays its own until it has exited, and a
  stage that was running reports `the gate was interrupted while this child ran` where it used
  to report the signal that killed its child. A time-limit kill and the gate's git calls to the
  remote now collect the exit status last, after the kill. On Linux an interrupted gate now
  waits out a suite's whole 10 s cleanup time unless it is interrupted again (read from the
  kernel's source, not run). On Unix systems other than macOS and Linux the gate cannot hold
  those numbers, so it no longer forwards an interrupt to its stages there.

## [0.103.0] - 2026-10-10

### Fixed

- **A Containment shell can ask no macOS service to act for it, but the user and group
  lookups.** Those two refusals closed one service each, and any other service that works
  for its caller outside the sandbox stayed reachable. Now a contained program can look up
  no system service except the two read-only directory queries that name you and your
  groups. Shells, git, Python, make, clang, targo and `codesign` work as before. What no
  longer works in a Containment shell: `pbcopy` and `pbpaste`, the keychain (`security`
  lists no certificate; the system roots stay readable at `/etc/ssl/cert.pem`), `mdfind`,
  `diskutil`, `pmset -g`, and a contained program's `os_log` lines, which no longer reach
  `log stream`.

- **Typing prediction no longer shows a password as you type it.** With `predictive_echo`
  on (`adaptive`, the default, or `always`), a key typed at a prompt that hides its input
  could be painted: at a local `sudo`, `read -s` or passphrase prompt, at a remote password
  prompt printed on the same line as an answer you had just typed, at one that output
  scrolled onto that line, and for a password typed ahead after a command sent with
  Shift+Enter, Ctrl+Enter, Ctrl+J or Ctrl+M. A local prompt that turns echo off is never
  predicted now, and the proof that the program echoes ends at every key the predictor does
  not model, whenever output moves the screen's lines, and at any cell but the one the last
  echo left the cursor in.
- **A word you erase on a slow connection no longer lingers as a faded copy.** Typing ahead
  of the echo and then erasing (Backspace, Ctrl+W, Ctrl+U, Ctrl+H, Alt+Backspace or a key
  you remapped to one of them) left a dim copy of the erased text on screen for up to two
  seconds.
- **aterm's log keeps its history under a flood.** A resize while a program streamed
  output, a shell without aterm's integration (`sh`, `dash`, nushell) whose command scrolled
  out of history, or a stream of refused connections to the network drive wrote a log line
  per line, per look or per connection, and could push everything else out of `aterm.log`
  (within seconds for the resize and the connections, within hours for the shell). Each now
  writes a few lines that carry the counts.
- **`aterm --window -e` hands the program its arguments exactly as you typed them.** An
  argument that is not UTF-8 text (`aterm --window -e printf %s $'\xff'`) reached the
  program as U+FFFD, the replacement character; it now arrives as the bytes you gave it. A
  `shell_args` entry holding a NUL character now stops the shell from starting, with an
  error naming the entry, instead of being dropped and moving the entries after it. A
  `shell` setting holding one stops it too, where it used to start `/bin/sh` instead (on
  Windows, the program named by the part before the NUL).
- **`aterm pkg` installs nothing another user can change, whatever your umask.** Under a umask
  of `000` or `002`, an install left the package store, each program's folder in it, the new
  build and folders inside it, and the download folder writable by your group or by everyone,
  and the two small records it keeps beside a build too. Those folders are now `0755`, the
  download folder `0700`, and the records `0644`.

## [0.102.0] - 2026-10-09

### Added

- **Code has one home, `~/Developer`, and aterm measures that Spotlight skips it.** Spotlight
  indexes every text file in your home and, since macOS 27, attaches an embedding to each, so
  source trees there cost `mds_stores` real CPU. Apple documents one way to keep a folder out
  of the index: System Settings ▸ Spotlight ▸ Search Privacy. Add `~/Developer` there once per
  Mac. `aterm doctor` and `aterm pkg doctor` gain two rows: `devroot:` names the git checkouts
  and worktrees under your home that are not in `~/Developer`, and `spotlight:` MEASURES
  whether Spotlight skips `~/Developer` (a probe file and a later control, both removed), never
  assuming it from the name (a `~/Developer` that is a link is never opened, and is not
  measured). `aterm pkg devroot` lists each checkout outside, where it would go and what
  holds it; `aterm pkg devroot move --all` (or named checkouts) moves them, refusing the
  whole run while any has uncommitted work, a process working in it or in another checkout
  of its repository, or an agent session, and never splitting a repository that has
  submodules (their links are relative). It moves one repository at a time and repairs what
  names the old paths — worktree links (`git worktree repair`), the git config and
  alternates of every git directory, submodules' included (a cut clone's
  `aterm-release.receiptsFrom`), Claude Code's `~/.claude/projects/<path-key>` folders (not
  the transcripts in them), `aterm pkg link` dev links and the publication engine's registry
  rows — then checks that every checkout still answers `git status`. A ^C waits for it to
  finish. `aterm pkg devroot verify` measures the root on demand. The window's six-hourly look
  raises one entry in Messages ▸ To look at, only when it measures Spotlight indexing the
  root, and its button opens Search Privacy. The move is a one-time migration: it goes once
  every owner Mac on the release roster reports a clean `devroot:` row; the survey, the rows
  and the measurement stay. The window's disk cleanup looks for idle build output in the
  checkouts in `~/Developer` as it does in your home's.

### Changed

- **The supervisor's trust roots and the publication engine follow `~/Developer`.**
  `[harness] trust_roots` defaults to `~/Developer/aterm*`, `~/Developer/ay*`,
  `~/Developer/trust*` and `/private/tmp/claude-*`, so a checkout left in your home is
  no longer answered for. The release tools and the export content scan read the engine
  at `$PUBLICATION_ENGINE`, else `~/Developer/publication`. The agent primer (v14) says
  where code lives. Run `aterm pkg devroot move --all` right after updating: until the
  checkouts move, the merge gate's `export content` stage is NOT RUN (its reason names
  `~/Developer/publication` and the move), and the supervisor answers for no session in
  the old checkouts.

- **A bare `cargo` or `rustc` in a session now says what it is about to run — Trust or
  stock, by name — and inside a Trust source checkout a stock one does not run.** The line
  used to say "running upstream 'rustc' (no proof claim)" whatever that name ran, so after
  `rustup default trust` it said it over Trust itself. Now aterm asks the copy on PATH what
  it is (through `rustup which` when it is rustup's proxy, `+toolchain` included, then that
  file's `-vV`) and names it: `-> Trust 7d5533b2, via rustup trust (the rustup default)`, or
  `-> STOCK rustc 1.97.1 (…), via rustup 1.97.1-… (pinned by ./rust-toolchain.toml); not
  Trust`, plus one line naming the file. STOCK is said only when nothing in the answer marks
  Trust: a build that prints a Trust mark but no `trust:` version (the cargo of the Trust
  seal e9ca4908) is "not known to be Trust", and so is a copy that does not answer as a Rust
  tool; neither is ever called Trust. Inside a Trust source checkout (an `x.py` beside a
  `src/stage0` saying `compiler_dist_channel=trust`) a `cargo`/`rustc` that is not Trust
  exits 2 without running, naming the Trust spelling and how to run it anyway, a session
  started with `aterm --no-reroute`: there a stock compiler would build part of Trust. A
  `cargo`/`rustc` a tool spawns there by name is judged the same — a cargo subcommand, an
  xtask, a build script running `rustc +nightly`, the compiles a stock cargo started by its
  path spawns — including beneath a Trust cargo the reroute let run (its children are not
  announced again, but no longer inherit the escape), with no package store resolving, and
  with aterm's package manager unreachable (then a stub refuses there outright). A compiler
  run by its own path, or handed to cargo as `RUSTC`, is looked up by no name and is not
  judged. `[reroute] announce = false` does not silence the refusal. The answer is cached in
  the package prefix (`reroute-identity.cache`), but only for rustup's answers and a
  toolchain's own compiled `cargo`/`rustc`; a wrapper or shim in front of them is asked on
  every call, because it can run a different compiler in each directory.

### Removed

- **The Spotlight rename pass and `[machine] spotlight_noindex`.** aterm no longer walks your
  home renaming cargo `target` folders to `target.noindex` behind a symlink: the name trick is
  not an Apple mechanism, and the developer root above replaces it for your checkouts.
  `aterm pkg noindex scan|migrate|apply`, the Spotlight half of `aterm pkg machine apply`,
  its row on Settings ▸ Security and the `spotlight_noindex` key are gone (a file that still
  sets the key gets the ordinary unknown-key note). `aterm pkg noindex verify <dir>` stays,
  as the measurement. Folders an earlier pass renamed are left as they are, and still build.
  The trees aterm's own gate and release tools make beside a checkout keep their `.noindex`
  names for now (`<checkout>-verify.noindex`, `-verify-cells.noindex`,
  `<clone>-release.noindex`, `<checkout>-cut.noindex`, `dist/cut-<build>.noindex`): on a
  Mac whose code is not yet in `~/Developer` they keep Spotlight off build output, and they
  go once every owner Mac has moved.

### Fixed

- **A pane kept open after its command ended has no clickable links in its scrollback after an
  update.** Since 0.101.0 a `--hold` pane's scrollback crosses an update along with its last
  screen. The links on that screen were removed, because nothing runs behind the pane, but the
  links in the scrollback above it could still be clicked. The scrollback now crosses with every
  word and colour and no links, the same as the screen.
- **Resizing the window no longer deletes spaces or misplaces the prompt.** A space just before a wide
  character (CJK, emoji) at the end of a wrapped line was deleted by a width change, words in history
  could run together after a rewrap, and after a full-screen program exited following a resize the
  prompt could land on top of earlier output.
- **Neovim's cursor stays on the right character on lines with CJK or emoji.** Neovim 0.11 and later
  turn on a grapheme mode in which aterm moved the cursor by whole characters instead of by cells.
- **Copy and find give back exactly what is on screen.** Copying a wrapped line no longer drops the
  space at the wrap point; with right-to-left text (Hebrew, Arabic) the selection now copies the words
  it highlights; find and double-click measure wide ambiguous characters as drawn; find gives the same
  results for a line on screen and in history; and dragging over double-width text selects what is
  under the pointer.
- **Wide ambiguous symbols are two cells in wide mode.** With `ambiguous_width = "wide"`, symbols such
  as ★ ♪ ☎ ❶ were drawn one cell wide.

- **A terminal session no longer freezes when you paste into a program that is not reading.** Running
  `aterm` as a session in another terminal, pasting or typing ahead more than about a kilobyte into a
  program that prints but does not read its input (`ping`, `tail -f`, a build) stopped everything for
  good: no output, no keystrokes, no resize. The program's output keeps flowing now, and what it has not
  read yet waits until it does.
- **A resize while `aterm` starts reaches the program.** A terminal resized in the moment a session
  started (a window manager or split laying it out) left the program at its starting size until the next
  resize.
- **Zooming the font over a picture no longer uses gigabytes of memory.** An inline image (`imgcat`,
  sixel, Kitty) was decoded at the size of its cells at the new font size, so zooming a window-wide
  picture to the largest font asked for about 2 GB a step and could reach 13 GB. A picture now decodes
  to at most a full-window raster, however far the font is zoomed.
- **Screens full of pictures or large emoji repaint without starting over.** Showing more images than
  the image cache held at once (two window-wide photos, layered Kitty images, a sheet of thumbnails)
  decoded every one again on every repaint, a tenth of a second to seconds each time; drawn without a
  GPU, a screen of distinct emoji at a large font was rasterized again on every full repaint. What the
  screen shows now stays decoded and rasterized between repaints.

- **Caps Lock and non-US keyboard layouts type what the key shows.** Caps Lock + A typed `a`; on a
  German, French, Russian or other non-US layout, Shift typed the US character for that key (German
  Shift+2 gave `@`, French number-row digits could not be typed, Russian capitals came out lowercase),
  and Ctrl with a Russian letter typed the letter instead of the control key (Ctrl+С now interrupts).
  Typing now sends the character your layout produced, and Ctrl+letter on a non-Latin layout sends the
  same control key as on a US keyboard.
- **Option keeps working on Backspace, Enter, Tab and Escape when Option is not Meta.** With
  `option_as_meta = false`, these keys lost the Option modifier (Option+Backspace erased one character
  instead of a word in shells that bind it).
- **Ctrl+Alt+Backspace deletes a word and Ctrl+Alt+Space reaches the program.** They were sent without
  the Alt. Ctrl+~ now sends the control character other terminals send.
- **The mouse over a split pane talks to that pane.** Hovering, scrolling or right-clicking over a pane
  that does not have focus went to the focused pane's program instead; a button released after switching
  tabs or panes went to the wrong program; releasing one of two held buttons stopped drag reports; and a
  program tracking the mouse got a report for every pixel moved inside a character cell.

- **Output that scrolls a huge count no longer freezes the window.** `CSI 65535 S` (scroll up) archived one
  history line per count, so a few kilobytes of it from any program, a `cat` of a file or an ssh session,
  held the terminal for seconds and froze the window's redraw. A scroll of a screenful or more now
  archives exactly that screenful and leaves the screen blank, as xterm does.
- **Links in scrollback can no longer use gigabytes of memory.** The web addresses of links (OSC 8) that
  had scrolled into the in-memory history were counted by no limit, so output full of long, distinct
  links could hold about 4 GB in one tab, out of reach of the memory-pressure trim. They now count
  toward the tab's history budget: past a quarter of it, the oldest rows' links are dropped (the text
  stays), and the memory-pressure trim frees them.
- **Copy mode's cursor stays on its text.** With output streaming, the vi cursor on a fixed row below a
  scrolling area (Codex's composer, apt's progress bar) was dragged up a row per line of output; it now
  stays put while rows in the scrolling area and in history still carry it with their text. A resize,
  `clear` or a lowered history limit no longer leaves it off the grid or on other text.

- **A control client that stalls or stops reading no longer turns the other clients away.**
  Eight connections could tie up every control thread, and every other client (`aterm ctl`,
  each supervised tab's harness) was then answered `ERR control server busy; retry` until
  they let go. A connection did this by stopping part way through its `AUTH` line (no token
  needed), stopping part way through a request or a `feed-bin`/`paste-bin` body, or not
  reading a long answer (`aterm ctl help --full` into a pager that pauses). A control thread
  now takes a connection only once it holds a whole request, and it does not wait for the
  client to read the answer; a pager that pauses still gets every byte.

- **The control verbs `wait`, `ready` and `await` refuse a timeout that is not a whole
  number of milliseconds.** `wait 2s`, `ready timeout=1.5` and `await idle 500 timeout=5s`
  waited the 30 s default instead, and `wait 2s` answered a command that had already
  finished as if `2s` were fine. They now answer their usage line, as `turn timeout=`
  already did. A number still waits that long, held at 600 s.

- **The cursor pet no longer flashes an old cat you could not see after a screen or pane switch.**
  When the pet changed breed under a text selection, the cat it was replacing was hidden by the
  selection, yet an alternate-screen enter or a split-pane switch brought it back at full
  brightness for a moment (or let the new cat jump straight to full brightness beside it). A cat
  now crosses those switches at the brightness it was last drawn at, and one that was hidden
  does not come back.

- **`aterm --headless` no longer connects to the WindowServer (macOS).** A headless
  instance built the real AppKit event loop, and creating its application object opened
  a WindowServer connection, so WindowServer ran a synchronous privacy check of the
  binary on its own main thread for every headless launch: one per idle instance, 50 in
  one run of the headless integration tests. From a build directory holding a very large
  number of files that check has outlasted WindowServer's watchdog and taken every window
  on the machine down with it. A headless launch now runs a display-free event loop with
  no application object, so neither opens a WindowServer connection and LaunchServices
  holds no record for the process. (A headless render on the GPU of a Mac with several
  GPUs, none of them low-power, still asks Metal for the system default device, which
  does connect.) `aterm ctl chrome` on a headless instance now answers `menu (none)` (it
  answered AppKit's default menu, which only existed because of that object), and a
  headless instance paces its frames at the fixed 8 ms interval, as a display-free Linux
  run always did.

- **Vi mode moves by the text you see when the view is scrolled back.** Scrolled back, a
  motion on a line of the live screen (`w`, `e`, `b`, `^`, `%`, `{`, `}`, `f`, `t`) read the
  history line that many rows above it and landed mid-word; `H`, `M` and `L` jumped to the
  live screen instead of the top, middle and bottom rows on view; and output that scrolled
  the screen left the cursor on its row while its text moved up, so it sat on the wrong line.
  Every motion now reads the line the cursor is drawn on, and the cursor moves with its text.

- **`aterm pkg verify` no longer calls an untouched install drifted.** On a Mac's default
  case-insensitive disk, an archive that laid two directories whose names differ only in case
  or Unicode form (`Dir/` and `dir/`) merged them on disk while aterm recorded both, and a
  home folder on an HFS+ disk stored an accented name under other bytes than the archive's, so
  the install's recorded fingerprint described files that were not there. Such an archive is
  now refused at install, with nothing left behind.

- **A Containment shell can no longer change your preferences or register a login item.**
  Under `--containment containment` (`aterm --sandbox`), a contained program could write any
  app's preferences (`defaults write`), which the macOS preferences daemon saves outside the
  sandbox, and could ask the ServiceManagement daemon to register a login item or launch
  daemon that runs outside the sandbox later. Both are refused now; shells, git, Python,
  compilers and `codesign` work as before.
- **A program's output can no longer change what Escape and Enter send.** Output holding
  the sequence a Windows console host uses to ask for key records (`cat` of a file, an ssh
  session) switched the tab's Escape, Ctrl+[, Alt+[, Alt+Backspace and Shift/Ctrl+Enter to
  Windows key-record sequences for every program after it, until a reset: vim read them as
  stray keys, and an agent's Escape did not stop it. Only a Windows console host turns that
  mode on now; a web host in front of one turns it on with `set_win32_input_enabled`.
- **Dropping a file into PowerShell or Git Bash can no longer run code from its name
  (Windows).** A dropped or pasted file whose name held `$(…)`, a backtick or a curly double
  quote (a download, a file from an archive) ran a command when you pressed Enter. Such a
  name is now inserted in single quotes.
- **Pasting text that holds a NUL character or half an emoji works (macOS).** A clipboard
  holding a NUL character pasted only the text before it, and one holding half of an emoji
  (left by an app that cut text in the middle of one) pasted nothing. Copied text beginning
  with an invisible byte-order mark (U+FEFF) lost it. Text now crosses the clipboard, input
  methods, the tab-rename field and dropped file names exactly, and a lone half of an emoji
  shows as �.

## [0.101.0] - 2026-10-08

### Added

- **Settings ▸ Security and `aterm ctl privacy` show whether aterm is allowed on macOS's
  Privacy & Security ▸ Developer Tools list, and how many new programs started in aterm that
  macOS checked first.** While aterm is not allowed there, a build or test run
  that starts many new programs waits while macOS checks them one at a time. aterm reads
  macOS's own answer from its log (on an administrator account; no dialog, no Full Disk
  Access) and shows it with how many programs were checked in the last 10 minutes. *Open
  Developer Tools…* opens the list; adding aterm there is your decision, because being
  listed should also skip macOS's first-run malware scan for everything run in aterm, agents
  and downloaded tools included. `aterm help permissions` explains the wait (SLOW FIRST
  RUNS).

- **On Windows, the version now sits at the right end of the tab strip.** Windows has no menu
  bar, so the version was nowhere at a glance; the strip now shows what the macOS menu bar
  shows (`v<version>`, or `v<maj.min>.<dev>+g<hash> · DEV` on a build from source, `*` for a
  dirty tree, an arrow while an update is staged), drops the hash and then steps aside when
  tabs crowd it, and opens Settings ▸ About on a click. `aterm ctl chrome` reports it as
  `strip-version`.

- **Low disk space: aterm finds the build folders that fill the disk, clears the ones nobody
  will use again, and names the rest.** Below `[disk] auto_free_gib` (10 GiB), the 6-hourly
  look searches worktrees, projects in your home folder, x.py builds, `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`s and
  Claude Code's temporary folders, removes a finished Claude Code session's scratch build and
  a removed checkout's cells cache once unused for a day (`[disk] target_stale_days`; `[disk]
  dead_build_dirs = false` turns removal off), and takes only the incremental caches of
  projects you work in. If space stays low, "To look at" names the two largest folders it
  cannot clear and what clears each; `aterm harness disk` lists the five largest.

- **The supervisor's journal names the points only a person can answer, with the one thing to
  do.** A lost login (after its one `/login`), a spend, credit or account limit no reset ends,
  a model limit whose fallback has failed for an hour, a `/goal` Claude cleared after an
