- **`aterm drive task --wait` waits through an aterm self-update.** An update that cut its
  wait for the worker's answer ended it with an error; now it finds the answer on the new
  instance within its bound and `--reconnect-s`. A post the update cut says it may have
  landed, rather than "not posted"; one turned away unread (`ERR control server busy;
  retry`) or never sent still says "task not posted". `ERR no such session` from a new
  instance that does not host the session yet is waited through, as is the `--mail`
  catch-up listing.

- **A shell that fails at start keeps its pane on a busy machine, too.** The pane that says
  `[zsh ended at start: exit 1]` instead of quitting aterm was kept only when the shell
  failed within two seconds; on a loaded Mac or behind a slow rc file its only tab closed
  and aterm quit without a word. The window is now a minute.

- **…and for fish and powerlevel10k, whose start asks the terminal questions.** A fish or
  p10k shell whose rc failed still closed its only tab and quit aterm silently, because
  aterm's answers to its startup queries counted as typing. Only a key, a paste or a
  driving program's input counts now.

- **A lock aterm lets go of is free at once, even while a new tab's shell is still
  starting.** A released lock could stay taken until a starting shell finished starting:
  the cleanup of a finished aterm's screenshot and video folders kept its files, and the
  next session-restore save, a debugger-access change and the `[machine]` apply queue
  waited.

- **The rating's own thanks is not what the worker last said.** After a person's `1`, `2`
  or `3`, the supervisor read Claude Code's `Feedback: Bad · Esc to undo` and `Thanks for
  the feedback!` as the worker's last words and reported a turn twice. A rating card held
  over a busy read now says `another driver's hand is on the session` when a drive lease
  holds it, where it said `a person is typing`.

- **A key typed as the harness's `0` lands is no longer journaled as a dismissal.** A key in
  that moment abandons the card and leaves the `0` at the head of what you typed (`0hello`),
  yet the journal said `DISMISSED survey`. It now says `ABANDONED … a 0 of ours may head
  it`, leaves your text alone, and skips the `0` when you key between its read and write.

- **The supervisor sees what a tall pane draws above its 40-row window.** On a pane taller
  than 40 rows (144x53, say) a rating card, a wall's notice, a question or the worker's last
  words drawn above the last 40 rows went unread: the card stayed up, and once `keep going`
  was typed into a session nobody had asked anything. An idle composer is now read whole;
  the rating card is answered about 1.8 s after it appears.

- **Starting the smart-title daemon no longer holds aterm's terminals and locks open on a
  busy machine.** Under load, starting the managed Ollama daemon could hold every tab's
  terminal, the control socket and aterm's locks for seconds. It still runs in the
  background band once started.

- **A control client follows an update it reaches through another aterm, marks what it
  missed, and no longer takes a busy successor or a cut prompt for a final answer.** For a
  session another aterm hosts (`aterm ctl @<sid> subscribe …`, `turn`, `await`), that
  aterm's update ended the stream as if the session were over (exit 0) and failed a `turn`
  with exit 1. Now the forwarding aterm says `ERR gone pid=<n> sock=<path>`, and `aterm ctl`
  follows the host's successor — resuming the stream, asking a read once more, or ending a
  `turn` with exit 75 and a note not to send it again blind. A resumed `subscribe` writes
  `GAP <local> replaced` where the two legs meet and says what was lost. A successor that
  answers `ERR control server busy; retry` is asked again while the wait lasts. `aterm
  drive --socket <S> prompt` exits 75 with the same note, not 1, when its connection breaks
  during the prompt.

- **The PTY keeper keeps working after aterm updates itself.** With `[keeper] enabled` and
  `aterm keeper start`, windows opened after an update could not verify the keeper: nothing
  new was handed to it, and the shells it held when you quit could never be taken back. A
  keeper now runs from its own copy (in `~/Library/Application Support/aterm/keeper-code`),
  removed by `aterm keeper stop` or the next keeper start. A keeper started by an earlier
  version still has the problem: run `aterm keeper stop`, then `aterm keeper start`, once.

- **The PTY keeper stays responsive with many terminals.** With `[keeper] enabled`, after a
  crash with a few hundred terminals open, the next launch could give up waiting for the
  keeper and never get those shells back.

- **Waiting requests and `aterm drive --dial` relays no longer take every control thread.**
  Eight long waits (each `aterm drive --dial` relay counted as one for its whole life) held
  every control thread: new clients were turned away, and every supervised tab's next
  request waited for up to ten minutes. Now a client past the limit gets `ERR control
  server busy; retry` at once, on a connection that stays open, and the other clients are
  still answered.

- **A fault in the control socket's idle-connection keeper strands no connection.** A crash
  there ended every idle connection's next request (each supervised tab's) until new
  clients were turned away too. Now it costs one connection at most, and when it cannot go
  on its clients dial again and the log says so.

- **`aterm ctl ls` says an instance is busy when it is.** It said "the addressed instance
  did not answer (wrong --sock/--pid, not running, or a different user)" of an aterm that
  had answered `ERR control server busy; retry`. It now quotes the busy line and suggests
  retrying in a moment.

- **Update, upgrade, supervisor and `aterm ctl` messages say what is true.** When too many
  tabs are open for an update to install, aterm says so and that closing some lets it try
  again; when a full disk stops one, it names the disk and its free space instead of a
  curl or ditto error code. "Not today" no longer promises a question tomorrow that the
  quiet upgrade never asks, and an upgrade notice says a shared remedy once. The upgrade
  view no longer calls a tab stuck when aterm's own unsent words wait in its prompt: it
  waits on a person to send or clear them. `aterm ctl` offers `kill` for a stray private
  instance even when nothing answers and refuses `--pid 0` up front. A narrowed Trust
  receipt's fix says the larger machine must hold a rostered release key.

- **No descriptor aterm holds reaches the fabric bridge or a shell unless it was handed
  over.** Every program aterm starts now holds only its standard input, output and error,
  except the tools you run through `aterm pkg run`, the reroutes and `aterm ship`, which
  keep your descriptors (a `make` jobserver's, a `3>` redirect). The bridge's launcher runs
  a script with no `#!` line under `/bin/sh` and skips a `PATH` entry it may not execute,
  as a shell does. On macOS, starting a helper no longer costs the window a frame.

- **A weekly limit that resets across a daylight-saving change is waited for at the right
  hour.** A reset naming a date (`Nov 2 at 9am (America/Los_Angeles)`) read before the
  clocks changed was waited for an hour off: before they went back, `keep going` was typed
  into the wall an hour early (and at its ten- and thirty-minute retries); before they went
  forward, an hour late. `aterm harness limits` shows the corrected time too.

- **On Linux, Settings ▸ Software Update shows what the background update check did.** A
  check that installed or held a newer aterm left the page saying "No update staged." or
  "Startup pending." with an old "Checked … ago" until you reopened it.

- **When aterm's folder cannot be written, the update now says so and stops asking again.**
  Where you cannot write to aterm's folder (an administrator-owned /Applications, say), the
  row said "Couldn't install aterm vX — install it from the Version menu", which fails the
  same way, and opening Settings ▸ Software Update retried by itself, piling up failures,
  and could blame the new version after two tries. The row now says "folder not writable"
  and tells you to move aterm somewhere you can write (such as ~/Applications) or have an
  administrator install the update; aterm waits for you, keeps that advice through
  unrelated failures, and goes back to installing by itself once the folder is writable
  and the installed copy is fit to replace; when the folder is writable but the installed
  copy is unfit, every place now gives that copy's advice instead of telling you to move
  aterm.

- **After an update, a warning the old version raised no longer hides the next problem, and
  it goes away once its problem is fixed.** "Couldn't check for updates", "Couldn't
  download updates" or "Update check stopped" carried across an update stayed up forever,
  and a later failure of the same kind showed nothing in the window. The new version now
  clears the carried warning once its own first check succeeds, and reports a new failure
  as usual. The same holds when aterm restarts a stalled update check itself.

- **A failure that spans an update still reaches "To look at", and a healed stall does
  not.** A failing update check or download that crossed an update before its first day
  was up never became a line of "To look at"; now it does, dated from when the failure
  began and with its cause. "Update check stopped" and another aterm holding the update
  check no longer reach "To look at" a day after they healed.

- **An update that installs while no terminal is open now records that installing works
  again.** After "Couldn't install updates", an update installed with only Settings or
  document tabs open (or none) left that warning as Messages' last word on installing.

- **A conversation you begin with `keep going` is no longer restarted without its history
  by a Claude Code upgrade.** A new conversation (after `/clear`, say) whose prompts were
  only the supervisor's usual words — `keep going`, `continue`, your answer text,
  `/compact` — read as nobody's: the upgrade restarted it without `--resume`, and the
  supervisor stopped continuing it. Now a prompt counts as the supervisor's only when it
  typed it; any other is yours, and the conversation is resumed.

- **The quiet upgrade no longer restarts Claude Code over background work aterm could not
  name.** Claude Code 2.1.286's `1 Artifact comment monitor`, `1 MCP task`, `2 background
  tasks` and `◇ 1 cloud session` read as an idle screen, so the default upgrade could
  restart over that work. Anything a finished turn says is still running, and any count of
  shells, monitors, tasks, agents, workflows, sessions or teams in the footer, now holds
  the restart until it ends, and the supervisor waits on it rather than typing `keep going`
  over it.

- **Rainbow Kitty's band on zsh's Ctrl-R match is taken back sooner when a redisplay
  arrives in pieces** (a remote zsh over ssh, or a redisplay longer than one read). The
  match's glyph was lit as if typed and stayed lit for about two seconds; now it flashes
  for at most about a quarter second per torn redisplay, or stays lit through the whole
  search while every redisplay arrives torn (`trail` reports each as `licence=recall`).
  Typed echoes keep their light.

- **An update now says in aterm.log whether it brought aterm to the front.** Since 0.100.0
  an update comes forward only if an aterm window had focus when it began; both versions
  now log which happened and why, so an update that still takes focus can be traced.

- **An update that cannot install no longer relaunches aterm every few seconds.** With only
  documents or Settings open, an update refused for a lasting reason (`/Applications`
  belongs to an administrator, or the installed app is a hand-made copy) closed and
  reopened the window every few seconds with no reason given. aterm now checks the update
  before relaunching, as it does with a terminal open. A refusal only you can fix stops
  automatic updates and shows its reason on the update row; one blaming the update itself
  is retried once soon and once a day later; any other follows the usual schedule (ten
  minutes, half an hour, then hours apart, then every six hours), each retry relaunching
  aterm.

- **An update no longer runs a window's `-e` command again, and a window opened with `aterm
  new-window`, `new-tab` or `split-pane` updates.** A window opened with a windowing verb
  got "unknown command" and never updated, and `aterm new-window` typed while an update
  waited opened no window. A window started with `-e <command>` ran it again as the
  update's first tab, so a script with side effects ran twice. The new version keeps the
  window's settings (`--headless`, `--control-sock`, sizes, fonts, `-d`) and runs its `-e`
  command in every new tab and split, but not again in its first tab. A `-d` folder
  removed since the window opened no longer stops the update (a new launch still refuses
  it).

- **A headless aterm started with `--lifeline-fd` survives its own updates.** An update at
  launch, a crash-loop rollback, or an update applied with no terminal open made it exit,
  so the harness lost its instance.

- **On macOS, a headless aterm no longer vouches for an update's windows.** A `--headless`
  instance of a new version counted as proof it starts, even while its windows crashed
  before their first frame, so the previous version was deleted and no rollback happened.
  Once a window has started the new version, only a window can prove it; `aterm update
  status --verbose` says so, and until when. If no window starts it within two days,
  headless instances settle it again. Where only headless instances run, updates install
  as before, and the previous version stays on disk until the next update.

- **Updates land on a window with many tabs open.** aterm started from the Dock, Finder or
  a login item may keep only 256 files open, so with about 60 tabs or more an update failed
  every time, retried for hours, and never landed until tabs were closed or aterm
  restarted. aterm now raises its own limit for the handover. Shells in new tabs still get
  the limit aterm was started with, and so does an older version you move back to (unless
  its tabs did not fit under it).

- **A tab opened after an update that restarted aterm in place gets the open-file limit
  aterm was started with.** After an update that landed with no terminal open, every new
  shell got the raised limit (4096) instead of the one aterm was started with (256 from
  the Dock).

- **An emoji sequence the emoji font does not join draws every member, not just the
  first.** A sequence no font carries (🚀 ZWJ 🍕) now draws its rocket and its pizza side by
  side in the cluster's two cells. On Windows this should cover 👨‍👩‍👧, which drew one man
  there, but that is not yet measured. A flag the font has no glyph for still draws its
  first letter on macOS; on Windows (Segoe UI Emoji) it is unmeasured.

- **On Windows, an aterm window no longer flashes console windows.** Every program the
  window started put a console window on screen: 42 in ten minutes of an idle window from
  the package manager's `curl` checks, plus one held open for each `atpkg` pass (9 to 18
  seconds), `hostname`, the daily `atpkg machine apply`, the Fabric menu and the ledger key.
  None appears now. Programs started from a terminal, an aterm tab included, still share
  its console. After a Windows Update restart, a crash or a hang, Windows brings back only
  windows of `aterm-gui.exe`, never `--headless`: from `aterm.exe` it came back with a
  console window open, and a headless instance came back as a window nobody asked for.

- **A Git Bash tab on Windows reports its directory as Windows names it.** It sent
  `/c/Windows/Temp`, which the tab showed verbatim, and `aterm ctl tab new` from it opened
  in the launch directory. Under Git Bash, MSYS2 and Cygwin it now reports
  `C:\Windows\Temp`, as pwsh and cmd tabs do. Not yet run on Windows.

- **In an aterm tab on Windows, pwsh reads native programs' piped output as UTF-8.** UTF-8
  from aterm's CLI, git and most tools came back mangled (`aterm help | Select-String`).
  The console keeps UTF-8 for the rest of the tab, so a legacy program writing the old code
  page is the one misread there; consoles outside aterm are untouched. Not yet run on
  Windows.

- **Windows reopened after a quit come back at their own size.** After a quit, a crash, a
  restart or an update that restarts aterm, every window after the first came back with
  the first one's rows and columns. Each now comes back with its own, at its exact size
  when that still fits; maximized and full-screen windows come back as before. This
  applies to windows saved from this version on.

- **An open command palette or connection card repaints when the theme changes.** After a
  colour-only config reload, a theme-catalog reload, or a program's OSC 11, an open
  palette, connection card, connection map or session picker kept the old colours until
  you typed into it.

- **`aterm ctl subscribe` no longer ends silently, exit 0, when an update's new instance
  turns it away.** A busy new instance's refusal now prints with exit 75, like every other
  lost stream, and a live instance's refusal never exits 0. The resume note says whether it
  was an update, a relaunch, or only that aterm was replaced, instead of always "an update".

- **The harness no longer leaves Claude Code's accepted suggestion waiting, unjournaled, in
  the composer.** A suggestion filled while Claude Code redrew its composer waited out the
  draft grace (`human_grace_s`, 120 s by default) and was then sent as a draft left
  standing. Now it is sent, or the journal says `SKIPPED … no composer after the accept
  key`.

- **A client that dials an instance right after an update is no longer refused with `ERR
  auth`.** `aterm link on`, `aterm link`, the fleet menu, `aterm drive --socket` and
  `--dial`, the harness and the live upgrade, and a window forwarding `@<session>` to
  another aterm could send the old instance's token to the new one. A token file that is a
  symlink, or too large to be a token, is now refused instead of read, also on arm64 Linux
  and for `aterm link serve --token-file`.

- **The rainbow trail no longer goes dark under a letter when Claude Code updates a status
  line.** A spinner, timer or token count changing just as you typed could be taken for
  your key's echo, so the band went dark under that letter, mostly after a short pause or
  while output streamed. The letter right after Backspace, an arrow, Home, End, an editing
  key or Shift, the first letter after you submit to Claude Code or Codex, after a paste,
  and while a full-screen Claude Code scrolls its transcript are protected the same way. A
  key driven with `aterm ctl ctrl` counts exactly like `aterm ctl key` or typing.

- **The rainbow trail no longer goes dark under a digit when a Claude Code timer shows the
  same digit.** A timer reaching `…0s` as you typed a `0` put a mark under the timer and
  left your digit dark.

- **Tabs that lost their shell integration in an update now say so, and what gives it
  back.** Their command blocks and exit codes went dark for good, and only `status` and
  `aterm.log` said so. aterm now shows ONE warning, "Tab lost its shell integration" (or "3
  tabs lost their shell integration"), naming each tab by its place (`tab 2`, `window 2,
  tab 1`) and its remedy: a new tab, or — when the harness moves agents (`[harness]
  upgrade` or `relaunch`) — the harness's next move of the agent in it. The warning updates
  as tabs heal, close or change remedy, is logged as fixed ("Shell integration back") when
  the last heals, and is not posted twice across a further update. A tab whose shell
  re-keys itself at its next prompt gets a record, not a warning.

- **A control request whose client has hung up is dropped, not run late.** A request the
  harness had abandoned and re-sent could run hours late: a key pressed twice. A client
  that only half-closed (`nc -N`, `socat`) still reads its reply, and a `turn` whose text is
  already typed still submits it, so text is never left sitting in the input box.

- **The cursor trail no longer jumps to an empty row in Claude Code's question dialog.**
  Moving to "Chat about this" sent the meteor to the blank bottom row, eight rows below.
  ↑/↓ between the other options, and a visible cursor on a blank row (a fresh prompt),
  are followed as before.

- **A trackpad flick that has already reached the end of the scrollback no longer waits on
  a busy terminal.** The flick's leftover momentum waited behind a program printing a flood
  of output, which the window felt. A pager or mouse-using program that comes up meanwhile
  still gets it, as arrow keys or mouse reports.

- **The rainbow caret no longer freezes part-way through fading after you stop typing.** It
  sat at a quarter of its colour until something else redrew the window; now it fades all
  the way to rest.

- **An update no longer closes open document and Settings tabs when no terminal is open.**
  The update came back with a single fresh window: the tabs, and each window's place and
  size, were gone without a word. It now reopens them, as after a quit. If "restore
  session" is off, the update waits, and says so, until the tabs are closed or a terminal
  tab opens; if the windows cannot be saved just then (a full disk, say), it waits and
  retries.

- **Several aterm windows updating at once no longer undo a healthy update.** With three or
  more windows of one version open, the third rolled the new version back, deleted it from
  under the windows already running it, and refused ever to install it again, saying it
  had crashed. A version that really keeps crashing is still rolled back.

- **A window started with `aterm --window` from a terminal stays a window across an
  update.** The update came back as a terminal session in that terminal: the in-place
  update gave up and retried every time, and a window with no open sessions was replaced
  by a session in the terminal.

- **Linux: an update whose kept previous copy had its permissions changed no longer stops
  updating for good.** If the rollback copy lost its execute or read permission, became
  writable by others, or changed owner during the new version's trial, a crashing version
  could never be rolled back, and afterwards every newer release failed to install. Now
  the trial ends and newer releases install as usual.

- **An aterm installed where you cannot write says so instead of freezing on every
  update.** In a folder your account cannot change (an administrator-installed or managed
  `/Applications`), the update froze the terminal and recorded the new version as broken,
  every time, without naming the cause. It now checks first and tells you to move aterm to
  a folder you can write to, such as `~/Applications`, or have an administrator install
  the update. A momentary write failure (a full disk, a quota, a disk error) is just
  retried later.

- **An update to an aterm on an external disk no longer throws away its download when it
  has to roll back.** It had to be fetched and checked again; now the next launch tries it
  again.

- **A stopped aterm can no longer stall the updater for good.** A sibling window paused in
  a debugger or stopped with Ctrl-Z mid-update stalled every later update check, install
  and apply, with nothing said. The wait now gives up after 10 seconds, logs why, and tries
  again later.

- **A quit that is cut short no longer opens every window twice.** After a Force Quit of a
  slow quit, a logout or shutdown, or a power cut, the next launch opened every window
  twice, and the same Claude conversation could start in two tabs. Your windows now come
  back once, also when the older version you updated from made the quit.

- **The message about windows restored after a crash names the right window.** It said an
  agent restarts "in tab 2" without naming its window, and not that the quit windows came
  back too. It now names the window as on screen and says the quit windows came back
  first.

- **After an update, a tab recovered from the PTY keeper opens in its own pane.** With
  `[keeper] enabled` and a crash just after an update, a kept shell could land in another
  shell's pane (with its title and role), or every kept shell in its own tab beside an
  empty pane, and a Claude conversation could start a second time there.

- **An older crashed layout is no longer lost during an update.** The update could take an
  older crashed aterm's layout as its own and overwrite it.

- **More kept shells can come back at launch.** With `[keeper] enabled`, a large number of
  recovered tabs no longer runs out of open files.

- **A very large desk comes back after a quit or a crash.** With more than 64 windows, or a
  window with more than 256 tabs, the next launch opened one fresh window and said nothing.
  Now the first 64 windows come back, a window that cannot be rebuilt is left out on its
  own, and `aterm.log` says how many were not restored.

- **A crash's windows are no longer replaced by another aterm window's older layout.** With
  two aterm windows open, quitting one and then a crash of the other reopened only the
  quit window, and the crashed window's tabs and folders were deleted without a word. Both
  now come back, the quit window's first, also when the older version you updated from
  saved the layout.

- **A crash's windows come back even when another aterm window noticed the crash first.**
  If a second aterm updated itself before you started aterm again, the crash could be taken
  for a normal quit and your windows, tabs and folders did not come back. Windows saved
  long ago no longer reopen beside a real crash's.

- **If aterm crashes just after an update, your windows, conversations and kept shells
  come back.** A crash before the new version had saved its own layout reopened one fresh
  window with every tab and folder gone, or the desk with no conversation restarted; with
  `[keeper] enabled` it orphaned the kept shells and started each agent a second time
  beside its still-running original. The old version's copy is no longer left on disk
  after every update.

- **Another aterm's crash report no longer reopens a desk you left long ago.** A headless
  aterm crashing under a reused process number could make the next launch reopen a
  weeks-old layout as a crash and start its old conversations again.

- **A pane kept open with `--hold` keeps its session id across an update, and comes back in
  every window that showed it.** `aterm ctl @<sid>` requests to it answered that no such
  session exists after every update, and a held pane shown in two windows came back in only
  one.

- **An update that does not land leaves your shells as they were.** A failed update could
  leave a tab's command marks off (`status integration=degraded`) until the next update;
  they now come back at the shell's next prompt. When the failing window was a second view
  of tabs shown elsewhere, the update is tried again rather than held against the new
  version.

- **Control clients keep each session's turns across an update on a large desk, and are
  told what was lost.** With more than about fifty supervised sessions with full turn
  ledgers, the last ones lost their whole ledger at every update: `aterm ctl history` came
  back empty and `aterm drive report` could not find its turn. Every session now keeps its
  newest turns and `aterm.log` says how many older ones were left behind. A turn preempted
  by `lease release force` that finished across the update now gets a `GAP` in a resumed
  `subscribe … since-turn=`, and a session whose screen could not be read keeps its
  scrolled-off rows for `offscreen` and `drive report`.

- **Pasting at the prompt right after an update keeps the view at the bottom.** In a tab
  you had scrolled up in, a paste (⌘V, Edit ▸ Paste, a drop, or `aterm ctl paste`) in the
  moment after the update could jump the view back up under the command you had just
  pasted. A paste now counts the same as a keypress.

- **A tab that was open across an update reports its exit code again.** A shell or `-e`
  command started before an update and ended after it showed `exit_code=-` in `exits`, and
  a `--hold` pane could not say whether it failed. On a busy machine it could also report
  an unrelated program's exit code; that no longer happens.

- **A `[harness]` limit holds when aterm.toml is refused on reload, and always follows the
  newest save.** A settings file with a stray non-UTF-8 byte, or over the 512 KiB reload
  limit, is refused whole and the running settings stay; the harness kept its old policy
  too, so `enabled = false` saved beside the stray byte did nothing until a relaunch. The
  harness now follows the newest file's `[harness]` lines, readable or refused, as launch
  does — lifting a limit as well as setting one — and a live update no longer loses a
  `[harness]` change made during the handover.

- **A window that cannot supervise its agents says so.** A window launched with
  `--no-control-sock`, with no per-user runtime folder, or with a `--control-sock` path too
  long to bind answered no Claude Code or Codex permission box, and only aterm.log said
  why. It now shows "Couldn't supervise agent sessions" with the reason; with `[harness]
  enabled = false` it shows nothing.

- **A tab no longer slips a row when the message band and the tab's agent row move at
  nearly the same moment.** The terminal shrank by a row and grew back within
  milliseconds, and a program on the alternate screen drawing then (a busy Claude Code
  with its spinner) kept drawing one row off. A row above the terminal still appears at
  once; growing a too-small window back, hiding the agent row from the View menu and
  turning the tab strip off are still immediate.

- **`aterm ctl resizes` names a message-band or tab-strip resize as the window's chrome,
  not as the window being resized.** They were booked `site=window`, so a band flap read as
  someone resizing the window. They are now `site=chrome`, and `at=` names the band or
  strip that asked.

- **A handoff refused for the old version's mistakes no longer counts as a failed start of
  the new version.** It could make the old version stop updating after two tries and roll
  the new version back at the next launch. Updating from 0.100.0 and earlier still
  retries as before.

- **A followed `subscribe … events` stream follows a relaunch only on the socket it
  named.** It moves to the new aterm's tab only when aterm quit or crashed and a new one
  started on the stream's `--sock` (with `[keeper]` on, possibly a recovered tab). It stops
  with exit code 75 and says why, without moving, when the new aterm answers on the shared
  `aterm.sock` (no `--sock`), started before or as the old one went away, or started at a
  time aterm cannot read (every system other than macOS and Linux). Setting the clock in
  between no longer misjudges a relaunch (except for the Intel build under Rosetta, which
  still times relaunches by the date clock), and on Linux a relaunch is now followed as on
  macOS.

- **A broadcast that arrives as an update lands is not lost.** It waits for the new aterm
  (`aterm.log` says so every 10 seconds). A broadcast delivered earlier and not yet read is
  not carried over: unlike direct messages, broadcasts are not sent again.

- **An agent that crashes after aterm saved the tabs for an update no longer stops the
  update.** It stopped as "window/tab/pane topology changed"; now the update waits for its
  next try, says an agent's relaunch became due, and the old aterm relaunches the agent. A
  crash in the last instant before the switch can still be missed.

- **A new build that refuses the whole handover stops before it starts anything**
  (0.100.0 exited after starting).

- **The supervisor no longer takes an API error in a tall window for an ordinary idle turn
  end.** In a short conversation the error sat above the last 40 rows, so the tab got no
  wait, no retry and no next-try time, just a `keep going` on the ordinary back-off. A
  plan-approval dialog clipped at the top is read as the plan approval it is, and `aterm
  ctl help status` says a run of 4 or more blank rows counts as one in the 40 rows it
  reads.

- **A Claude Code started again in the same tab is read as itself.** After `/exit` and a
  new `claude` with no `clear`, the old session's last frame read as live: `status` said
  `busy` or `question`, and the supervisor waited on the dead footer 20 s at a time.

- **The chime for a question the supervisor answered plays when it answers,** not when the
  worker's next turn ends (hours later in a workflow, or never after a restart or a short
  reply). A dialog you took part in is never told as the supervisor's choice.

- **The supervisor answers a question dialog about 1.5 s sooner:** a half-drawn dialog
  gets a half-second settle, not a two-second wait.

- **A permission box Claude Code redraws no longer counts as a new one and alerts again.**
  A box rewrapped after a resize, with its highlight moved, its auto-deny countdown
  ticking, or the conversation above it shifting, took the tab's attention mark down,
  raised it again and asked a second time about the same request. It now asks once, and
  not again while someone is answering. A request that comes back after its command ran (a
  retried `git push`, a long `cargo test`) is still new, and two edit boxes for one file
  with different changes are still asked about one each.

- **`aterm drive answer @w recommended` answers a whole multi-select tab,** checking every
  recommended option, not only the first.

- **Remote connections say what is true.** Network drive messages name the right token
  file, the listener's certificate fingerprint and the connecting peer; a certificate
  mismatch shows both digests, and a refused drive token gives the exact `aterm ctl
  dial-token` command. A `dial` whose remote drops exits 75 with a line saying so instead
  of exiting 0 silently; a dialled `turn`, `post`, `await block`, `await consent` or bare
  `await seq` cut that way is told to check the remote before sending it again, as one cut
  by an update is.

- **The keeper, aterm's desktop notifications and the Linux update guide say what is
  true.** `aterm keeper start` and `status` report a keeper as running only when it
  answers; one from another build shows as `keeper=refused`, with `aterm keeper stop`, then
  `aterm keeper start` where that replaces it, and one that never came up points at the log
  with the reason. The recovery row after a crash names the crash log and no longer claims
  each screen was redrawn. A stopped job's notification reads "program stopped" rather
  than frozen, an agent low on memory is no longer called stopped, update banners carry
  aterm's name, and "Update check stopped" is no longer posted while updates still run.
  The Linux update guide says checks and installs wait until the new build is confirmed by
  a healthy start or rolls back.

- **Rainbow Kitty's colours hold still when you edit a line or pause.** Typing in the
  middle of a lit line — after ← or Home, in Claude Code's composer or a shell, `sudo `
  typed in front of a command — no longer steps the rainbow backward: every column keeps
  its colour and the band grows at its end. A line you pause on for a couple of seconds
  comes back in its own colours instead of shifted along the spectrum (including a single
  letter and the first letter of a wrapped line's second row, which could stay dark after
  `cat` or a plain `read`). After a yank or a jump along the line (Ctrl-A, ⌥B) the row
  keeps one rainbow, and the sparkle where a jump lands wears the colour under it.

- **Harness disk and update messages say what is true.** `aterm harness disk` states the
  10-minute keep as aterm's own rule, its pressure legend is one line, and a cache whose
  clock cannot be read says so instead of "written into 0d ago". Update messages say why an
  install waited or failed in plain words (the terminal was busy; the open tabs were too
  much for one handover) and name the one step a stuck download failed at. With desktop
  alerts off, Settings and the `desktop_alerts` help point to `aterm fleet status` (not
  `aterm fleet next`) for the operator's notices, and `aterm keeper start` no longer prints
  `pid=-` for a job that is loaded but not running.

- **`aterm pkg lane`, `which` and doctor say what is true.** `aterm pkg lane` no longer
  calls a Trust toolchain's own cargo (`cargo +trust`) stock Rust, names
  `$RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` as itself rather than as the directory's pin, and exits 1 rather than
  2 on a usage error. `aterm pkg which` says when no upstream copy is on PATH, `aterm pkg
  doctor` lists only the Claude defaults it names, and package-log warm lines show the
  version (2.1.280) rather than a 19-digit build id. `aterm help update` names the Windows
  rebuild the checkout can run.

- **Update, harness and upgrade messages say what happens.** A paused update whose next
  start would roll it back no longer tells you to install it from the Version menu or
  offers Install now; it says a newer release replaces it. The lost-shell-integration,
  no-control-socket and too-many-tabs messages name the real cause and the one fix. A
  frozen agent's warning shows the command that ends it. Claude and Codex upgrade rows no
  longer say an agent waits to go idle, list tab ids you can paste into `aterm harness
  upgrade`, offer `--now` only when a tab will take it, and pressing Upgrade now on several
  tabs says which move and which are only asked again. The harness, keeper and reroute
  help pages match what each does.

- **An update on hold says so, and the help pages match.** When starting a staged update
  again would roll it back, the Version menu and palette say it is on hold and open the
  update details instead of offering to install it, and the Settings button and `aterm ctl
  update apply` start nothing and say it is on hold. The warning for a window that cannot
  supervise agent sessions shows its fix in full on its own line, with the right variable
  on Windows. Help pages describe the quiet upgrade's done row, where a Codex limit's reset
  comes from and when a keeper brings a window back, and the resumed stream's note says
  which events from the gap were not delivered.

- **A usage limit that has ended but whose notice still stands is one line in the log.** A
  tab left at its limit notice after the reset is logged ("Its usage limit's reset passed 4
  h ago, and the last look still read the limit") an hour after the reset, or a week after
  the wait began where no reset was read — never a row, a tab mark or a line of "To look
  at". `aterm harness upgrade --status` shows it as `cause=limit-passed told=limit-passed`;
  `told=` now names what you are told (`-` for a wait, however long), and `--json` keeps
  the class as a sentence in `cause_words`.

- **The "Agent is not back" and "Agent is gone" lines in "To look at" end with their tab.**
  Closing the tab, or an update that restarted aterm, left the line pointing at nothing;
  now it ends when no tab shows the session. A restart whose relaunch came back "left" no
  longer ends the line saying the agent cannot be brought back, and the words no longer say
  "upgrade" for a restart made for another reason.

- **A line of "To look at" that names a cause now ends when the cause ends, across a
  restart.** The lines for a supervisor that keeps stopping, the survey card, a volume aterm
  could not help, an upgrade that could not run and a tab that may be one row off now end
  when their cause does, even after the window that raised them is gone; a supervisor or
  survey line unheard of for half an hour ends by itself. A repaint that gave up on a blank
  agent tab is a log line, not a line of "To look at", and one never tried no longer says
  "no answer". Answering the Full Disk Access line and then granting it no longer keeps the
  next regression quiet.

- **A usage limit that a tab hit while a background shell or workflow was running is now
  seen, waited out and continued.** It went unseen, so nothing was typed past its reset. A
  limit, an API error, a lost login or a full context the turn ended on now outranks
  background work (a shell, a monitor, a workflow, a background agent). A spinner, `esc to
  interrupt`, `Still working`, `ctrl+b to run in background` or the vendor's retry row
  still wins, and Claude Code's critical-memory banner still reads busy. Such a tab reads
  `agent=wall:usage-weekly` (a note on the tab's row, not a stop), and the supervisor
  continues it two and a half minutes past the reset.

- **A limit that Claude Code echoes as `Goal paused` is read as the limit it is.** With a
  `/goal` active, the echo `Goal paused · usage limit reached · send a message after it
  resets to continue` hid the real limit: the supervisor waited a blind 30 minutes, read a
  weekly limit as a session one, and never tried the fallback model for a model limit.
  aterm now reads the limit above the echo, and a countdown toast (`continuing
  automatically at 3pm`) still names the time. An echo saying Claude `continues
  automatically when it resets` is left alone until ten minutes past the reset, and then
  only if the limit still stands.

- **A weekly, model or spend limit whose reset is a bare clock time is placed after the
  moment it was drawn.** `resets 9am` on a weekly limit hit at 8 pm was taken as 11 hours
  in the past, so the supervisor would continue at once and every 30 minutes for thirteen
  hours (in a simulation, not an incident). It is now the first 9 am after the limit was
  drawn, and a stale session limit found after a night is continued at once. The first
  continuation goes 150 seconds past the reset, not 60. `aterm harness limits` shows the
  reset the supervisor will wait for, and a watcher's `EXTEND` budget stretches to it. One
  residual risk: if the server's lift lags the printed clock by more than about two hours,
  the tab is next tried at tomorrow's clock, 21 to 22 hours later.

- **A model limit is answered by the fallback model as soon as the tab's own jobs allow,
  and nothing is typed blind meanwhile.** Claude Code's `You've reached your Fable limit`
  names no reset (Fable `requires usage credits`). The supervisor relaunches the agent on
  the fallback model for this session; while a background job in the tab would be ended by
  that, it asked again for ever, and a tab whose jobs hid the limit was not answered at
  all. It now retries on the restart back-off until the relaunch is made, and returns to
  the limited model only at a reset the notice named. A limit no reset ends and no
  relaunch can answer (a credit balance) is retried every 30 minutes, then 2 hours, then
  every 6 hours.

- **The supervisor reads the composer where it is drawn.** After a window resized twice in
  a millisecond, Claude's own dim suggestion could be taken for a person's draft, and the
  supervisor pressed Enter on it instead of typing `keep going`.

- **A supervisor that restarts at a limit it just continued past no longer types again at
  once.** After a new window, a seamless update or a supervisor fault it continued a second
  time as it attached, and a worker restarting every minute typed every minute. It now
  keeps the ten-minute wait after its last continuation.

- **A limit the supervisor is waiting on is still waited on when its rows leave the
  screen.** Running `/model` or `/usage`, or scrolling up the transcript, at a limit made a
  tab with a background shell read as busy with no limit, and the wait stood forever. The
  supervisor now keeps the limit it waits on (a usage window, a spend limit, a model limit)
  while only background work shows, also across a seamless update. A spinner, `esc to
  interrupt` or a message just submitted still ends it.

- **A full context behind a background shell is compacted on a ladder, never in a loop,
  and no limit's act is typed more than twelve times an hour.** A `/compact` that hit the
  same full context again would have been typed every few seconds. The waits are now 1, 5,
  15, 30, then every 60 minutes after the previous `/compact`, at most twelve acts an hour,
  with the reason in the journal.

- **A failed `/compact` is no longer answered with `/compact` and `keep going` every half
  minute.** After Claude Code 2.1.286's `Compaction failed · conversation could not be
  reduced below the context limit` (or `Error during compaction: …`), the supervisor typed
  `keep going` and `/compact` six times each in under three minutes. The failure now reads
  as a full context, so the ladder above holds, and a compaction that finally works is
  continued as before. A failure naming a lost login or no credit is still that wall, and
  a compaction a hook blocks or a person cancels is still no wall.

- **A limit banner drawn while a turn is still winding down is not the end of the turn.**
  `Usage limit reached · limit resets 9:50pm · clau.de/wrap-up` under the composer while a
  turn waited on its own workflow read as a limit for 41 minutes before the turn ended.

- **Notices that are no limit are no longer waited on, and limits aterm did not know are
  recognised.** `Your usage limit has reset · press enter to continue` and `Usage limit
  reset · continuing automatically` read as a limit still standing, and the supervisor
  waited 30 minutes; now the limit is continued at once, except that when Claude Code
  resumes by itself (`Usage limit reset · continuing automatically`, `Usage limit available
  again · continuing now`) the supervisor waits ten minutes past the reset instead of
  typing behind it. `Authentication error · This may be a temporary network issue` and
  `Could not refresh your login because another Claude Code process is refreshing it` are
  network trouble, retried, not a lost login. `Your seat type doesn't include usage
  credits`, `Your usage allocation has been disabled by your admin`, `Your group's usage
  limit is set to $0`, `This service is disabled for your org` and `Your organization has
  disabled Claude subscription access` are now read as the spend limit. `Goal cleared after
  an unrecoverable error (…)` names its cause, and Claude Code 2.1.284's `Continuing
  automatically at 3pm · esc to cancel` stays with the limit it counts down for.

- **The wait for a reset survives a Mac that slept.** A reset that passed during sleep was
  continued only after the same time awake again. Now it is continued shortly after wake,
  each session adding up to a minute so one account's sessions do not all type at once.

- **Sessions that share an account no longer all continue in the same second.** Each
  session now adds up to a minute to the two and a half minutes it waits after a reset.

- **aterm now asks for Full Disk Access once, when macOS has just shown the "access data
  from other apps" dialog for one of your programs, and then leaves you alone.** It raised
  "Allow Full Disk Access?" at every start — eight times in four days, six within a second
  of an update — and again every day. Now it asks only after macOS shows that dialog for a
  program in one of your tabs (or refuses aterm a read), at most once a week, as one line
  of "To look at" with `Open Settings` (no band row). Details say what the switch grants:
  every program you run in aterm, agents included, can then read protected data such as
  Mail and Messages. Dismissing it files it in the log for a month (`Open Settings` files
  it as answered), and it does not ask again about a window started before you opened
  Settings; once granted, the message log says `Full Disk Access granted` and the line
  ends. macOS keeps asking about a program an update replaced until aterm holds the grant;
  aterm cannot press *Allow* for you, and no program can.

- **A dev build that writes the release's setup no longer stands as a row on the band.** It
  was a warning with no button that stayed until read; it is now one line of "To look at"
  saying what it wrote and the one command that puts it back.

- **Updates that keep failing are one line of "To look at" after a day, and the desktop
  banner is for one cause only.** "Couldn't install updates" still shows for 45 seconds
  and then rests in the log. A failure that has gone on for a day (a restart does not reset
  the count) is now also one line of "To look at" — *Updates are not installing*, *not
  downloading*, *Update checks keep failing*, *The update check stopped*, *Another aterm
  blocks updates* — saying where to go, and it ends when updates heal. The desktop banner
  (with `desktop_alerts` on) is now posted only when the copy in Applications is not the
  signed release, which only you can change.

- **A supervisor that keeps failing no longer marks the tab.** Past five restarts an hour,
  "supervisor keeps failing; restarting in N min" marked the tab though there was nothing
  to press. It is now a log record, and after an hour of failures one line of "To look at"
  (*Supervisor keeps stopping in tab 2*, with the last error), ending once it runs steadily
  for half an hour.

- **"The upgrade cannot run" is one line of "To look at".** When an upgrade's state folder
  cannot hold its lock, only `aterm.log` said so. Now "To look at" says "Fix the folder's
  permissions" for as long as any tab cannot run it.

- **A rating survey the harness cannot close no longer marks the tab.** A card the harness
  will not press is now a log record and, after an hour, one line of "To look at" (*Rating
  card open in tab 2*, "Press 0 in that tab to dismiss it"); a survey that stays open
  through the harness's own `0` presses is a record only. Either ends when the card does.

- **With `[harness] upgrade_ask = true`, the upgrade's notice and the Claude and Codex
  lines that follow it no longer show the tab as being driven by someone else**, and a tab
  another driver holds is waited on, never typed into.

- **A Claude Code the harness relaunches has its rating surveys switched off.** The
  relaunch line now sets `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY=1`, even for a Claude Code
  started with `--setting-sources` that leaves your settings out. A launch line too long to
  take the switch is relaunched without it.

- **The upgrade no longer reads Claude's own suggestion as your draft when the screen is a
  row off.** After a resize left the screen a row off, the upgrade took Claude's dim
  suggestion for your draft and waited. A typed draft is still a draft, and an unreadable
  cell still reads as one.

- **A Claude upgrade no longer inherits the age of a process that is gone.** After you
  restarted Claude by hand, or its own updater moved it on, the next build carried an old
  age onto the new process: "Couldn't upgrade Claude in tab 1 yet · behind for 2 days" and
  a warn row eleven seconds after the build appeared. The age now follows one process. A
  `Not today` follows the session to the next build and to a process you restarted by
  hand, a `Skip` names its build, and a standing `Upgrade now` follows only the process it
  hurried.

- **With `[harness] upgrade_ask = true`, an agent that declines every notice is asked a
  bounded number of times.** An agent that kept starting short jobs was asked after each
  one, up to 144 times a day, each a full model turn in your conversation. It is now asked
  no sooner than ten minutes after the last notice and at most six times in 24 hours, and a
  round declined four times rests 2 h, then 4 h, 8 h and a day.

- **A Claude or Codex upgrade that waits no longer raises a warn row or an orange tab
  mark.** "Couldn't upgrade Claude in tab 1 yet · behind for 2 days" stood on the band for
  seven hours and marked the tab, for a wait nobody could act on. Only an agent the upgrade
  ended and did not bring back, one it restarted that reached no prompt in half an hour, a
  shutdown hung for 15 minutes, or a Codex goal it paused (under an older aterm or
  `upgrade_ask = true`) and could not resume now marks the tab and takes a band row, with
  the exact command ("Resume it in that tab with this command: `claude
  --dangerously-skip-permissions --resume …`"). Other waits go to Settings ▸ Messages and
  `messages.log`, titled "waits", never "Couldn't". A wait only you can end that has lasted
  a day is one line of "To look at" saying why and what to do, with `Show tab` for one tab
  ("Claude in 3 tabs is behind" for several): the agent's own work (naming its `/goal`), a
  draft nobody sent, an agent suspended for an hour, an agent in a tmux pane, a launch a
  resume cannot repeat, a repeating stop, or Codex held by a thread, another window or a
  shell without integration. Dismissing one files it in the log and it is not raised again
  for a week (a month when the cause is how you launched or where you run it). A mark an
  earlier build left is lowered at the first look. `aterm harness upgrade --status --json`
  prints `attention`, `attention_kind` and `cause` for every tab.

- **aterm's footer and network-wall checks no longer open files inside iCloud Drive or
  another sync provider's folder.** A system dialog for those could stall every session. A
  repository there shows no branch in the footer instead.

- **A failed replacement of aterm's own process no longer leaves it able to die on a closed
  socket.** After a refused replacement (an update's rolled-back restart, or the window's
  in-place one), the next write to a client that had gone would have killed aterm and every
  tab.

- **`aterm ctl cast drift` no longer second-guesses a recording that says which resize law
  made it.** Recordings now carry `aterm_resize_undo` in their header (players ignore it),
  so a failed undo reads `unfaithful` instead of being matched away under `undo=off`. A
  recording without the key (an older aterm, a saved file) is matched as before.

- **A resize no longer strips 24-bit colour from what is on screen.** A height-only resize
  (a message-band or presence row appearing, a font zoom that kept the width), and every
  resize of a full-screen program on the alternate screen, turned every truecolor colour on
  screen to the theme default until the program redrew it, in every tab of the window.
  16- and 256-colour text was not affected.

- **The two marks at the right end of a busy tab that needs a look no longer touch.** The
  busy ring and the attention diamond touched on the tab strip and the native toolbar; they
  now have about two pixels between them at 2x. Three and four marks at once still overlap
  slightly.

- **A tab's hover says why its attention mark stands.** It read only "Needs attention".
  When a reason is recorded (`meta set attention`, as the harness and agents write), it now
  reads `Needs attention: <reason>`. Nothing new raises a mark.

- **A band row's words no longer stand on its closing line.** The band's closing line ran
  through the `p`, `g` and `y` of every message, so the band looked sunk and cut off. The
  line is now on the row's last pixel row with the words two pixels higher, also between
  stacked rows and on the web band. The tallest letters of a 16 px face now reach the row's
  top. A band with a progress meter, an outlined button or a strain gauge, and a cell under
  18 pixels tall, keep the old placement.

- **A driver's own `turn` or `lease` no longer re-grids the tab it types into.** The live
  Claude upgrade's attempts to type its notice resized every program in the window about
  once a minute: on one tab 47 attempts typed nothing, and two left Claude Code drawing
  every later frame one row off. The presence row now appears only once the turn settles;
  the window's rim and the tab's chip still change at once.

- **The harness's `0` for a Claude Code rating survey no longer deletes itself, is judged
  only once Claude Code could have taken it, and every kind of card is read.** Every
  dismissal cost a stray `0`, a backspace and about seven seconds, and where Claude Code ran
  a little late the harness deleted its own dismissal on every try. It now sends one `0`
  0.8 s after the card appears and removes only a `0` still standing two seconds later; a
  refused backspace is retried, so no `0` or `1` is left for your next message. The
  long-context, plugin and memory cards are now dismissed too. A card of an unknown shape is
  journaled `EVENT survey … not pressed (…)`, `aterm drive phase` prints `survey withheld
  (…)`, and in a hosted session after an hour it is one line of "To look at" (*Rating card
  open in tab N*, "Press 0 in that tab to dismiss it"). These cards, the transcript-share
  question, the web-setup offer and the "Bug report drafted" card no longer make a busy
  worker read idle; none of the last three is pressed (a window now hides the
  drafted-feedback card with `"feedbackDrafts": "quiet"`). The `0` is still held for a
  person who typed within `human_grace_s`, a typed draft, an approval box and another
  supervisor.
  Journal lines for kinds other than the session survey add `kind=<name>`. The Settings
  entry for `dismiss_surveys` reads "Auto-dismiss Claude Code's rating surveys" and answers
  to "auto dismiss".

- **A rating survey no longer waits for an idle worker.** A card over a worker that reads
  busy (a workflow it waits on for an hour) was left standing; it is now pressed when it is
  seen.

- **A Mac that sleeps over a limit's reset is noticed wherever the sleeping wait ended.**
  Some waits still missed the sleep, so the continuation went out late by the whole sleep.

- **A rating card's `0` is never pressed in front of a draft whose caret was moved home.** A
  draft you had walked back to its start (←, Home, ctrl-a) was taken for Claude's grey
  suggestion. Now grey is the suggestion, plain text is yours, and nothing is pressed in
  front of it.

- **A wall the turn ended on is answered even with a monitor running behind it.** An API
  error, an expired login or a full context behind a monitor (`· 1 shell, 1 monitor ·`) read
  as a worker still at work, so the retry, the login escalation and the `/compact` never ran
  and the tab stood on its error until someone looked.

- **Codex's Esc is recognised again.** Codex 0.159 reworded the row after it (`■ Conversation
  interrupted - use /feedback if something went wrong`), so a turn a person had stopped read
  as an ordinary end that the continuation could type over once the grace ran out. Both
  0.159 and 0.156.1 are recognised now.

- **An agent an earlier aterm told to wind down for an upgrade is released again.** A
  session an older aterm (or `[harness] upgrade_ask`) had asked to reach a stopping point,
  whose own background work never ended, waited for good: an agent that answered READY sat
  stopped, and one that said "not yet" kept avoiding new work. Half an hour past the
  request the upgrade now types the line telling the agent the upgrade is off and to carry
  on, and moves it later at an idle moment; a Codex conversation once asked to stop is told
  to continue after its move. The line no longer promises to ask before a later restart.
  While that work runs, a Claude Code tab's upgrade row names what holds it and offers no
  Upgrade now; once it ends (or for Codex, resting at least two hours) Upgrade now moves the
  session at its next pause.

- **A session whose Claude Code status never returns to idle is no longer said to move on
  its own.** The record said "nothing to do: it starts on its own" and, once overdue,
  offered no Upgrade now. It now says the session moves once Claude Code reports idle, and
  Upgrade now moves it at its next pause while its screen shows no turn running.

- **A pending upgrade no longer holds a supervised agent's continuation while a background
  shell runs.** Each pause kept the supervisor from continuing the agent for about six
  minutes; the move still comes at the first idle moment after the work ends.

- **The upgrade's request and its release line are no longer typed into a turn that just
  started.** With `[harness] upgrade_ask` on, and for the release line in either mode, a
  turn that began just before aterm typed (you pressed Enter, or a background task woke the
  agent) could have the line pasted into it. aterm now waits for the turn to end.

- **An "upgrade stalled" mark no longer outlives its stall across an aterm update.** It
  stayed after the upgrade finished, through every later update, until you closed the tab.
  The new aterm marks only a tab that is still stalled.

- **Skip version and Not today survive a crash or a restart of the agent.** A crashed agent
  was relaunched onto the build you had refused, and a restart in place (after the memory
  warning, or to switch model at a usage limit) moved it there at its next idle moment and
  reset how long it had been behind. Claude Code and Codex now stay on the build they ran
  while your choice stands, keeping your choice and the session's age, also when the
  restart fails part way.

- **Output that arrives while an update takes over a tab looks as it would have without
  the update.** Output still on its way at the takeover lost what the program had just set
  up: an ncurses "repeat the last character" drew nothing, a coloured underline (neovim's
  spelling squiggles) came out plain, the rest of a link's text came out unlinked, a VT52
  cursor move printed as text, a joined emoji (👨‍💻) came out as two and shifted the line,
  a saved style or setting (such as line wrapping) was not put back, and a country flag
  (🇺🇸) printed just before could swallow half of the next. All of it now carries over, and
  an update no longer waits for a link or a VT52 cursor move to finish (an update to an
  older version still waits).

## [0.100.0] - 2026-09-30

### Added

- **A tab at an API error now says when the harness will try again.** While a supervised
  Claude Code sits on `API Error: Can't reach the API server`, the harness waits between
  tries (1, 2, 5, then every 5 minutes for a network error; 1, 5, 15, 30, then every 60 for
  the server's own failure or an overload), and the tab named the cause but not the wait.
  It now reads `can't reach the API → 08:58 · 3m00s` — the local time of the next try and
  the time left — and a screen reader hears "next try 08:58". It shows only while that wait
  is real: once the try is made, or nothing is waiting, the tab goes back to naming the
  cause alone. A usage limit still says when it resets. The time is not part of the
  notification's text, so a retry never posts a second notification.
- **`desktop_alerts`: aterm's own desktop notifications are off unless you turn them
  on.** aterm used to post its own alerts to the desktop — an agent that needs you
  ("aterm · needs you", "agent stopped", "program frozen"), the embedded operator
  ("aterm operator"), a consent prompt, and update health — and on a Mac without
  `terminal-notifier` they arrived as Script Editor notifications nobody could place.
  They now stay where they already were — the message band, the menu bar, the tab's
  attention mark and `messages.log`; the operator's only in `aterm fleet status` and
  `aterm fleet next` — and reach the desktop only with
  `desktop_alerts = true` (Settings ▸ Security ▸ Notifications ▸ Desktop notifications from aterm;
  applied live). The escalation's `aterm.log` line says `suppressed by desktop_alerts
  = false` when the setting held its banner back. Programs' own notifications (OSC
  9/99/777) are unchanged and still need `allow_notifications`.
  Disabling desktop alerts also cancels pending notification retries; enabling
  them again waits for a new event instead of replaying the current alert.

- **The Claude Code footer shows the session's tokens, and a limit it hit.** After
  model, path and branch the footer (in the rule under the input box, below) now ends
  with `Σ opus 48M in 310k out ·
  haiku 1.1M in 20k out`: this session's tokens per model — input (fresh, cache writes
  and cache reads together) and output — folded live from its own transcript and the
  subagent transcripts Claude Code keeps beside it. They are the whole conversation's,
  so a resumed session counts its earlier turns too. A re-read reads only what the files
  appended, and a file that has not changed is not opened; a long session's first read
  catches up over a few refreshes and shows no tokens until it has. At most three
  models are named (`+2` for the rest), and a subagent transcript that could not be
  counted is said, `+1 unread`, never left silently out. When the session hits a usage
  limit, Claude Code writes the notice into its transcript, and the footer then OPENS
  with it: `⧗ 5h limit · resets 3pm`. The reset is placed from the time that row was
  written, correctly across a daylight-saving change, and the notice's zone is kept
  when it is not yours (`resets 10pm (UTC)`). The wall goes once its reset passes (the
  window re-reads a walled tab every minute while its Claude Code runs) or once Claude
  answers again after it (`/limit-reset`, extra usage). In a narrow pane the tokens go
  first and the wall after every fact but the model. Nothing is read off the screen, and
  nothing is installed into
  Claude Code. A closed tab's fold is released when the tab closes, and so is the fold
  of a Claude Code that leaves the foreground (suspended with ctrl-z, or another program
  run in front of it): when it comes back the fold is read again from its transcript,
  and a long session shows no tokens and no wall until that read has caught up.
  The tokens and the wall always come from the same conversation as the model beside
  them: each refresh reads Claude Code's `sessions/<pid>.json` once and takes all three
  from it. Before, the tokens took a second read of that file, which Claude Code
  rewrites on every status change. For up to about 15 seconds after `/clear` or
  `/resume`, that second read could land mid-write and show the previous
  conversation's tokens and limit wall. On Linux, where aterm cannot read a process's
  start time, it hid the tokens and the wall for one refresh.

- **A new Claude Code or Codex build has your account's latest models at its first
  launch.** When aterm installs a new build of `claude` or `codex` — the window's update,
  `claude update`, `aterm pkg update` or `install` — it now runs that build once in the
  background, silently, so the vendor CLI fetches what your account is served (its model
  list and feature flags) ahead of your first launch. Claude Code runs in print mode on
  an input it never sends: no prompt, no model turn, no transcript, no hooks, no MCP
  servers. Codex runs `codex debug models`. The warm uses the program's own sign-in; the
  AI and session variables aterm strips from its shells (a parent Claude session's,
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) are not passed on, but your own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME`,
  `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and Bedrock/Vertex choice are (an identity session's too). It does
  not run claude when you set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC`, a program that
  has never run on your account (a default-set install you never launched), or anything
  as root. It is stopped after 30 s, is never retried,
  fails nothing, and leaves one `warm` line in packages.log. It has no setting of its own
  and follows the landing: `[packages] enabled = false` stops the automatic updates (a
  build you install by hand is still warmed), `exclude` keeps a program aterm has not
  installed from arriving, a pin holds one where it is, and a removed or dev-linked
  program is never warmed. macOS and Linux; not Windows yet. Owner, 2026-09-23: "latest
  models ready immediately".

- **Kitty graphics: placement ids, image numbers, source crops, every delete selector,
  virtual and relative placements, and animation frames.** A put that names an image and
  placement (`i=`, `p=`) it already placed moves that placement; `I=` transmits get an id
  from the terminal, and later commands can name the image by that number;
  `x=`/`y=`/`w=`/`h=` show part of an image; `c=`/`r=`/`z=` on a put lay out that placement
  alone. A `U=1` put makes a virtual placement with its own id and size, and a Unicode
  placeholder picks one by its underline colour. A put with `P=`/`Q=` sits `H=`/`V=` cells
  from another placement, moves when that placement moves and is deleted with it. `a=f`
  frames can carry only part of the image, drawn over an earlier frame or a background
  colour, or edit an existing frame; `a=c` copies a rectangle from one frame to another.
  Every `a=d` selector works, including `d=f`/`F`, which deletes one animation frame (`F`
  deletes an image that has only one frame). Each selector touches only the placements it
  names, and a lowercase selector keeps the image data. iTerm2's `preserveAspectRatio=0`
  stretches the image to its box. Animation playback is not built yet: frames change when
  a program selects one.

- **A Codex that crashes is relaunched on its thread**, as a Claude Code already was. The
  shell's exit status for the command that ran it decides: `0` (its own `/exit`) and
  someone's SIGHUP, SIGINT or SIGTERM are left alone; a SIGKILL, a SIGSEGV or SIGABRT, or
  any failure is a crash. The relaunch resumes the thread the TUI held (its writer lock,
  or the `resume <id>` it was launched with) or, for a client of Codex's shared daemon,
  the one thread its daemon began for it — never a guess between two, nor with another
  client of the daemon in the same folder — and tells it why at its first idle point.
  A tab with no shell integration gives no exit status, and its Codex is left.

- **A worker frozen for ten minutes with nobody at the machine is ended and relaunched.**
  When aterm's server says an agent has stopped reading its input (`status
  input=stalled`) and the stall has stood `[harness] stall_term_after_s` (new, 600 by
  default; `0` never), with no person's keystroke within `human_grace_s` and no lease or
  named turn on the session, the supervisor sends it `signal term` — once an episode,
  said as `SIGNALLED` in the session's journal — and the relaunch resumes its
  conversation. A program that lives through the term keeps the server's "frozen" row,
  whose `signal kill` stays a person's. A stopped job is never signalled.

- **A worker that says it is done is asked once, then left.** A turn whose last words say
  the task is done used to be continued on the back-off for good, and on a small model
  the nudges ended in invented work. It now gets, past its back-off, "If the task is
  finished and verified, reply DONE and stop; otherwise continue"; when that answer says
  done again, nothing more is typed into the session until a person or an orchestrator
  starts a turn there. A turn of theirs that ends on an API error, a usage limit or a
  full context gets that wall's retry, wait or `/compact` as before.

- **`key` and `send` take a person fence: `if-human=<n>`.** The server counts a session's
  person gestures (`status human_seq=`, and `"human_seq"` in `text --json`, read before
  the screen). A write fenced with the count its sender read is skipped (`OK skipped
  reason=person`, nothing written) when a person has keyed the session since, checked
  under the same lock as the screen fences. The supervisor's question and decline keys
  carry it, so a person who answers a box first is never overwritten.

- **A Codex tab comes back after aterm crashes, is killed or the Mac restarts**, as a
  Claude Code tab does since 0.95.0: its tab's record also carries the Codex's thread, its
  home and whether it held the thread itself, and the next launch resumes that thread in
  the reopened tab with a line saying aterm ended while it ran.

- **`subscribe … events` pushes the session's status transitions.** Each time a
  session's classified status moves phase or outcome, its timeline records one
  `status-change` and the events digest pushes `EVENT <local> status phase=<p>
  outcome=<o> exit_code=<n|-> signal=<n|-> confidence=<c>` — one per transition that
  survived the status dwell, so a spinner cannot flood it.

- **`aterm ctl resizes` and `aterm ctl cast drift` show when a resize has left a program's
  screen a row off.** On 2026-09-28 a Claude Code tab was re-gridded 64 → 63 → 64 rows
  within a millisecond. On the alternate screen that pair moves every row up one, and
  Claude Code, which repaints only when it reads a changed size, read the same size and
  kept drawing onto the moved screen. Nothing aterm showed could tell. The terminal now
  undoes such a flap when the program wrote nothing between its halves: the shrink keeps
  the rows it took off and the grow hands them back, so that flap moves nothing. Output
  between the halves (even a mode set) still leaves the shift. `resizes` lists the
  resizes a tab took: what each did to the rows (moved them up, appended or trimmed a
  blank row, pushed rows off the bottom, handed kept rows back as `restored=`), who asked
  for it (`site=`: the input dispatch a ctl `resize` arrives by, the OS window, the
  window's chrome rows, a cross-session `resize`, or `-` for one no path recorded) and
  the runs they form; a run that ends at the size it started from, two or more resizes
  long, is a flap. Rows a grow hands back count for the run that shrank, even when more
  than 250 ms split the two, so an undone flap reads `none`. On the alternate screen
  each run gets a verdict: `silent` while the program has not drawn since, `desync-risk`
  for a flap it then drew over without clearing, `unverified` for a run that left the
  size changed and was drawn over with no clear (aterm cannot tell that draw from a
  repaint), and `healed` once a full clear or a screen switch follows. `status` gains
  `render=<ok|displaced|desync-risk|unverified|-> resizes=<n> flaps=<n>`, and `subscribe`
  carries `EVENT <local> resize` and `EVENT <local> render desync-risk|healed`.
  `cast drift` replays the tab's recording through fresh terminals against the live
  screen, names the resize run the program never repainted after (`verdict=clean`,
  `desync`, `unfaithful`, `unknown` or `empty`; rows the terminal handed back are never
  blamed) and lists every wrong row. It weighs a flap however far apart its halves
  landed: from a shrink that lost rows to the resize that brought the size back is one
  candidate, so a flap more than 250 ms split (a program too busy to read its size in
  between) is named too. Against an aterm that predates it, the `aterm` binary computes
  the report itself from that aterm's `status`, `text`, `cursor`, `modes` and `cast`,
  directly or through `dial <name>` (the header then ends `computed=client`); it refuses
  by name only when the relay cannot carry those reads. Such an aterm also predates the
  undo, so its replay drops it (`undo=off`), and a flap with nothing between its halves,
  which shifted that aterm's screen, is named rather than read as a recording that
  cannot reproduce the screen. It also works offline on a saved recording: `aterm ctl
  cast drift --file <cast> [--screen <text>]`, which drops the undo only when that
  alone reproduces the screen.

- **`aterm pkg doctor` checks that the C compiler can build a program, and Settings ▸
  Packages says when it cannot.** Rust builds stop at the first build script that
  compiles C, and a compiler that answers `--version` can still fail there (a gcc with
  no C library headers, an SDK gone from the developer folder, an unaccepted Xcode
  license). `aterm pkg doctor` and `aterm pkg install --default-set` now have it build
  a small program in a private temporary folder, never run it, and report `C
  toolchain: <compiler> builds a C program` only when that worked. A compiler that
  refuses fails the check with its first error line; a temporary folder the check
  cannot use is a warning, not a failure. On macOS the check builds only once a
  compiler is installed behind `cc`, so it never raises Apple's install dialog.
  Settings ▸ Packages shows the same problem on the Settings badge and in the headline
  once a program is installed: a missing toolchain as `no C toolchain — run
  xcode-select --install` (type it in any aterm tab), a compiler that is there and
  refuses as `the C compiler cannot build a program`, with its error in the detail. On
  macOS `xcode-select --install` would only answer that the tools are installed, so
  neither doctor nor the page tells that compiler to install itself.

### Changed

- **Claude Code's own footer row stays whole; aterm's facts go into the rule above it.**
  aterm no longer paints over Claude Code's mode row: its pill (`⏵⏵ bypass permissions
  on`), `(shift+tab to cycle)`, `← for agents`, `esc to interrupt` and every other word
  Claude draws there stay exactly where and how Claude drew them. `◆ Opus 5.5 xhigh   ⌂
  ~/aterm   ⎇ main` is written into the rule under the input box instead, right-aligned
  the way Claude writes its effort tag into the rule above it, over plain rule glyphs
  only. The rule is the pane's whole width, so the facts fit whole at 80 columns: a
  light's title while you point at, select or switch a light is the first thing to give
  way, shortened or dropped, and a light's reason — where a mode return stopped, a
  refusal — takes the session's tokens', the branch's and the path's room once the path
  is cut, never the model's, the effort's or a limit's. A narrower pane then drops the
  tokens, cuts the path to `…/<dir>` and drops the branch, the path, the effort and the
  model — a limit the session hit (`⧗ 5h limit · resets 3pm`) stands alone last, and a
  pane too narrow even for it shows the model instead — then the chips, the model last.
  The facts now show in default mode too, and nothing is written while a dialog or a
  picker replaces the input box. The lights (`⏸ plan`, `○ fast`) sit at the left of the
  same rule and never replace Claude's pill.

- **An in-session update with more than 62 sessions now hands them all to the new
  build as its own app.** On macOS the outgoing build hands its PTYs to the new one over a
  socket, all in one message, and one message carries at most 64 descriptors, two of which
  are the handoff's own pipes. With 63 or more sessions the update forked the new build
  instead, so it came up as a child of the old process rather than as an app of its own
  (the shape that cannot take the next update), and a pool that grew past 62 while the
  update waited for a quiet moment stood down and retried. Now the grant can span several
  messages, up to the handoff's 256 sessions. It is used only with a new build that
  declares it can read it: its signed `Info.plist` carries `ATermHandoffGrantChunks`,
  which the outgoing build reads only after verifying the bundle, and it then offers the
  new build the capability at launch, which answers with a new claim. Up to 62 sessions
  the grant is byte for byte what every build has sent. A build before this one never
  declares it, so the first update that uses it is from this release to the next. A grant
  cut short is refused whole: the new build closes every descriptor it received, and the
  update stands down as before.

- **The window's disk reclaim takes only an idle cargo profile's `incremental/`, under
  cargo's locks.** It removed whole stale build directories before.
  Below `[disk] auto_free_gib` (10 GiB)
  free on the home volume, the harness host looks in its agents' build directories on
