  that volume (`target`, `target-*`, `target.*`) and reclaims one cache: the
  `incremental/` of each cargo profile (`debug`, `release`, `<triple>/<profile>`, a custom
  one, at any depth) that no compile has written into for `target_stale_days` (1 day, as
  the next entry says). It is the largest share of a debug build and costs only speed:
  the next build of each crate is a full compile of it. Idle profiles go first; more
  recent ones follow only while the volume is still short (see the least-recently-used
  entry below). It is deleted
  while aterm holds every one of cargo's build locks for that profile, so a profile a
  build is using is skipped and a build that starts meanwhile waits. Nothing else is touched: not the build directory (a
  `target -> target.noindex` link keeps resolving), `deps/`, `build/`, `.fingerprint/`,
  the binaries `aterm pkg link` serves, `examples/`, `doc/` or benchmark and coverage
  data, and nothing through a symlink or on another volume. Each removal is written to
  the disk ledger before it starts and again after, with the bytes it actually released
  and any error (the bytes are counted: an APFS clone's shared blocks count); a removal
  that cannot be written there first (a full disk) does not start. `aterm harness disk <dir> --apply cargo-targets` (with `disk.apply =
  true`) reclaims the same cache. Reclaiming the deeper caches is not done yet: cargo
  runs tests without its locks, and they read those. It looks every 6 hours while it
  supervises agents; `auto_free_gib = 0` (or any negative value) turns it off, and
  Manual knows every `[disk]` key.

- **`[disk] target_stale_days` defaults to 1 day (it was 14).** A cargo profile
  counts as idle, and gives up its `incremental/` to the disk reclaim, once no compile
  has written into it for a whole day; one built within the last 24 hours keeps its
  cache. The 14-day window was sized for the old removal of whole build directories.
  The reclaim now takes only `incremental/`, which the next build recreates (binaries,
  `deps/` and `.fingerprint/` stay), and the window's automatic pass runs only below
  `[disk] auto_free_gib`. At 14 days that pass freed nothing: the build directories it
  looks in belong to agents that build in them daily (measured 2026-09-27: every agent
  worktree's newest profile was 0-1 days old). One day alone did not change that for a
  checkout built in at least once a day (measured 2026-09-28: all 12 profiles in the
  agents' build directories here had been written into within about 24 hours, and the
  one just past it had an empty `incremental/`), which is why the pass now goes on past
  the window while the volume is short (next entry). A value you set is read as written,
  and the key keeps its name. `aterm help harness`, `aterm harness disk --help` and
  Settings show the new default.

- **Below the floor, the disk reclaim takes build caches least recently used first until
  the volume has room again.** On a machine running out of disk the window's automatic
  reclaim freed next to nothing (measured 2026-09-27 at a 14-day window and 2026-09-28 at
  one day): it took only profiles no compile had touched for `target_stale_days`, and
  every agent builds in its checkout daily. Now, below `[disk] auto_free_gib` (10 GiB),
  it first takes every idle profile's `incremental/`, as before. It then goes on through
  the more recent profiles one at a time, the one built longest ago first, measures free
  space again before each, and stops once the volume is back at the floor plus 1 GiB. If
  the free figure does not rise (a Time Machine local snapshot can hold the deleted
  blocks for a while), it also stops once the bytes it deleted cover what the volume was
  short, rather than going on through every checkout. A
  profile a build holds is never touched: aterm takes every one of cargo's locks for the
  delete, so a build that starts meanwhile waits. Neither is one built in the last 10
  minutes (an agent usually builds again within minutes, and the cache would come
  straight back), nor anything on another volume. The unit is still only `incremental/`,
  and each removal is journalled before and after, with a `stopped` row saying where the
  pass ended, on what free figure, and which stop ended it. In `aterm harness disk`,
  `reclaimable=` is still what would go whole, and the new `under_pressure_up_to=` is
  what every listed recent profile would free, at most. **`[disk] target_stale_days` means less below the
  floor.** It still decides what is idle: what `aterm harness disk --apply
  cargo-targets` takes at any free figure, and what the tick takes whole before anything
  recent. But a value you set no longer keeps a recently built checkout's cache once free
  space is under the floor. And `target_stale_days = 0` no longer lets any reclaim take a
  profile built in the last 10 minutes; before, it made every profile idle at once. Below the floor, `aterm harness disk` lists each profile it
  would take, in the order it would take them, and `--apply cargo-targets` takes them
  under the same stop.

- **`aterm harness usage` folds this session's transcripts, subagents included.** Run
  from a Claude Code session's own tools, it folds the session Claude Code names
  (`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, else `CLAUDE_PID`'s sessions file) — not the directory's
  newest file, which may be another session's — and a named session with no transcript
  yet folds nothing. Anywhere else it folds the newest and says so, as before. It looks
  under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when that is set, adds the subagent transcripts, reads up to
  4 GiB (was 256 MiB) and says PREFIX only if that cap stops it. `--json` stays schema 1
  and only gains keys: `transcript_pick` can be `session-id`, `claude-pid` or `none`,
  and `complete`, `subagent_transcripts` and `subagent_transcripts_unread` are new.

- **Near its usage limit, Codex saves its work on the cheaper model, then waits on its
  own.** When Codex offers to switch to a cheaper model and its own usage records show the
  window at 90% or more, the supervisor switches, stops Codex's goal, and asks the cheaper
  model for one thing: commit the work in progress on the current branch and push it
  plainly, never force, rebase, reset, stash or switch branches, say what failed rather
  than work around it, then stop. That turn is bounded: if the cheaper model is still
  working 15 minutes into it, the supervisor stops it with one Esc, checks whether the
  work was confirmed saved (if not, you are told), and goes on. It then puts the thread
  back on its own model and effort for this conversation only, through Codex's `/model`
  picker, and types nothing until the window resets. One record in Messages says so in
  plain words, naming the model it waits on and when its limit resets. It looks again
  every 30 minutes, and goes on early if the usage drops below 90% — which it sees only
  when another Codex session on the account records a reading, since it types nothing to
  ask. Then it resumes the goal, or tells the agent to carry on; with `resume_limits` or
  `continue_policy` off it types nothing and tells you instead. Codex's goal is stopped
  with an Esc on any turn it runs while the switch is open, up to three times; if it keeps
  coming back, you are told, and that note stays up — its badge and a record in Messages —
  while the goal runs. A turn you started is not stopped once the supervisor has seen your
  keystroke in it, however long it runs; the goal's own turn that Codex starts after it,
  under the offer's box, is stopped all the same. Three cases are not covered: a message
  you sent before the switch that Codex queued and starts under the offer's box is stopped
  like Codex's own; a turn that had already run unseen for more than 30 minutes when a
  restarted supervisor finds it is not taken for yours; and a turn whose first busy moment
  came more than 30 seconds after your last keystroke is stopped once your 2-minute grace
  has run out. Nothing of it is typed into a thread that fell into a sandbox. When a turn
  ends with a Codex background terminal still running, which Codex shows as busy for as
  long as the terminal runs, the switch still takes its next step there, however the turn
  ended — idle, on a question or on a limit — and nothing else happens at that point; if
  it cannot move for ten minutes, you are told once what holds it — your typing, a draft,
  the terminal, or the supervisor's own wait (a footer that has not shown the cheaper
  model, a sandbox, or a `/model` that did not take) — and nothing is typed again for
  saying it. If the footer still shows the thread's own model while Codex's records say it
  ran the cheaper one since the switch was pressed, the save waits and you are told after
  five minutes. The switch opens only once the box is seen leaving, and its intent is
  recorded before the key, so a supervisor restarted at any step — the save's own turn, or
  between its Esc and the stop it made — carries it on without repeating a note it gave,
  and one restarted before the key went, or before the switch was seen landing, decides
  the box again and stops or types nothing of the switch until the footer shows the
  cheaper model. Any other offer is answered "Keep current model", never "Keep current
  model (never show again)". If the save does not confirm, or the model cannot be put
  back, you are told once, with the steps. Your own message, `/model` (during the wait
  too, even to the cheaper model) or `/goal resume` ends it. The new `[harness]
  rate_nudge` (default on) turns it off, and the box is then yours.

- **Claude Code and Codex upgrades apply themselves, and the longer one waits, the less it
  asks of the moment.** A running agent is still moved onto a newer build at a quiet moment
  in its tab, but that moment no longer has to be a perfect one. Behind 20 minutes, a pause
  that only looks quiet counts, even while the screen redraws a clock or a goal's counter.
  Behind an hour, someone at the tab holds it only by having typed in the last 20 seconds.
  Behind two hours, it moves at the first such pause. It still never types over a draft, a
  dialog or running work, and `Upgrade now` (`aterm harness upgrade <tab> --now`) jumps to
  that last step with the same limits; until now it moved even a second after you typed.

- **A Codex working through a goal is upgraded by pausing the goal for a moment.** A goal
  starts its next turn within milliseconds of the last one's end, so it never gave the
  upgrade a quiet moment: the owner's tab waited ten hours. Now, once the upgrade has been
  behind two hours (or at once on `Upgrade now`), where the goal's own turn is all that
  holds it, aterm types `/goal pause`. Codex takes it while a turn runs, and it stops the
  goal's next turn, not the running one, so nothing that turn is doing is cut off. When that
  last turn ends, Codex is moved onto the new build as usual, and the goal is resumed once:
  the relaunched Codex opens asking whether to resume its paused goal, and aterm answers
  yes, or types `/goal resume`. The goal carries on where it was, and an embedded session
  gets no extra "carry on" over it. If the pause does not show, aterm presses Esc only at
  the very start of a goal turn, before it has done anything. What aterm owes is written
  down before every key, so a restart in between resumes the goal once and never twice. If
  you resume or change the goal yourself, or pause it yourself before aterm has seen its own
  pause show, it is yours and aterm leaves it alone. If the move does not come within an
  hour, aterm resumes the goal and tries again later, except in a Codex thread that fell
  into a sandbox its launch bypassed: there the goal stays paused, and a row says to quit
  Codex and resume the thread with its launch flags. While aterm holds the goal paused,
  nothing types a carry-on into that session, however the move waits (its Codex daemon
  catching up included). While the save-then-wait model switch holds the session, nothing
  is paused, and a switch that opens over aterm's pause resumes the goal at its own reset.
  The relaunched Codex's resume box is answered only on the Codex aterm relaunched, never a
  box your own `codex resume` draws, and aterm waits past the relaunch's first frame for it.
  A narrow pane, whose footer Codex cuts, still reads the goal, and a goal its last turn
  ends (achieved, or out of its token budget) is read as ended: nothing is resumed. The
  waiting note says aterm will pause the goal for a moment and resume it, with nothing for
  you to do; only a goal aterm paused and has not been able to resume for an hour and a
  half is a row ("Codex goal still paused"), telling you to type `/goal resume` in the tab,
  and never while a switch holds the session or the goal's last turn still runs.

- **A waiting upgrade is one note in Settings ▸ Messages that says what it is waiting for.**
  `Codex 0.158.0 installs itself in tab 1` says there is nothing to do and that it starts on
  its own at a quiet moment — from what time as soon as the agent is idle and nobody has
  typed for 20 seconds — or, when something else holds it, what: a draft, a dialog, a goal
  running in that tab, a turn in another Codex session. It puts no mark on the tab and no
  row on the band, and it is not written again each time what holds it flips between looks.
  A row appears only when something really stops it: a wait no pause will
  end (the tab's shell integration not working and no other way to tell which conversation
  to resume, a screen aterm cannot read) for 30 minutes, or six hours behind, and then its
  title says it could not be done yet, never that it "waits". `aterm harness upgrade
  --status` also says which step of the wait it is on (`rung=`, the line's last field).

- **The cursor after a Kitty image, kitty's replies, and image sizes.** After a Kitty image
  the cursor now sits just past the image on its last row, as in kitty (it used to move to a
  new line), and `C=1` leaves it where it was. A transmit, put, frame or composition that
  names an image (`i=` or `I=`) is answered `OK` or with an error, as kitty answers, unless
  `q=` quiets it. A transmit sent from a file, temp file or shared memory when file transfer
  is off gets the same `ENOTSUPPORTED` the `a=q` probe gives. An image given only a width
  (`c=`) or only a height (`r=`) now keeps its shape, and `c=0` or `r=0` means "not given".

- **`aterm harness usage` names the session's model.** The HUD line and the JSON take the
  model from the transcript's newest main-chain row that names a model id, so a `/model`
  switch shows from its first answer; Claude Code's `<synthetic>` rows (an API error, the
  usage-limit notice) name none and never replace it. The windows' figures were never
  filled by anything live and stay unknown (`?%`, `"windows":{}`): `aterm harness limits`
  prints the ones the `/usage` panel painted. `--utc-offset`, which placed only those
  windows' resets, is gone.

- **A failed command's tab mark goes quiet once you have looked.** The red mark a failure
  puts on its tab is for the pane you are NOT watching: switching to that pane (or to its
  window), or the failure happening while the pane is already in front, now clears the
  mark. The failure itself stays on the record — the tooltip and `aterm ctl status
  outcome=` — until the next command, and a new failure marks the tab again.

- **The web terminal's engine draws the cursor the way the app does.** The engine behind
  the website's `/terminal` now runs the app's own cursor and rain code instead of a
  thinner copy: the block-cursor bodies (the rainbow block, the droplet, the comet, the
  phaser, the light rod, the laser bolt), the steady caret while it glows, the
  typing-momentum glow, the `beam` style as the app's plain tube (the page's bloom crown
  and ring are gone), a glow intensity or radius that is not a number read as off, the
  soft fade when the view is replaced, and rain that reacts to a command starting and
  finishing and, when the page asks for it, pauses while a full-screen program has the
  screen. Like the app, it draws none of the cursor's light when the page asks for
  reduced motion. The page changes when the site next takes a new engine.

### Removed

- **The suspended orca sparkle word.** The orca class's water splash had been switched
  off behind a constant since v3 and nobody was building its replacement, so the class,
  its lexicon entry, the splash, its droplet sprite and its hidden Settings row are gone.
  A leftover `[sparkle_words.orca]` table still loads and is reported as having no
  effect — its `ignore_words`, which used to leak into every class's deny list, no longer
  do — and an external lexicon's `class = "orca"` entries are skipped. A word listed
  there no longer masks a lower class either: while suspended, an orca entry (the table's
  `extra_words`, or a lexicon's orca entry) still outranked the animal and emphasis
  classes and drew nothing, so the same word listed under one of those now decorates.

### Fixed

- **`history` says when an update lost part of a tab's turn list.** A tab whose turn
  list an update could not bring across answered `history` exactly as a tab nobody had
  driven, and `aterm drive ledger` then suggested the turns had been typed by hand. The
  reply's header now carries `unheld_below=<id>` (shown by `aterm ctl` on stderr) when
  turns before that id may be gone, and `aterm drive ledger` says the update lost them.
  The note stops once the tab has run enough newer turns that the lost ones would have
  aged out of the list anyway, so a busy tab does not carry it for the rest of its life.
- **`aterm.log` says when an update could not bring a tab's turn list across.** When
  the copy of a tab's turn list and scrolled-off text was too big to send, could not be
  written, or arrived damaged or in a form the new version does not read, the tab came
  up with an empty `history` and nothing said why. Both versions now log a warning
  naming the tab and the reason.
- **A tab whose screen an update had to redraw keeps its turn list and scrolled-off
  text.** When an update could not carry a tab's screen exactly (a screen over the size
  limits, say) and had the program redraw it, it also threw away that tab's turn list
  and the scrolled-off text of its full-screen app, although neither is about the
  screen: `history` came back empty and `aterm drive report` could not find the turn
  just driven. Both now come across; only the bookkeeping tied to the old screen starts
  afresh.
- **Every tab in a large desk keeps its turn list across an update.** The update
  copies each tab's turn list and the tail of its full-screen app's scrolled-off text
  within one shared size limit, and it used to fill that limit tab by tab: with dozens of
  busy agent tabs, the first ones carried their scrolled-off text and the last ones lost
  their whole turn list — the same tabs on every update, so `history` came back empty
  and `aterm drive report` could not find the turn just driven. The turn lists now come
  first for every tab, and the scrolled-off text shares what is left.
- **A turn driven during an update never shares its id with a turn after it.** While
  an update was switching over, the old version still answered `turn`, and the id it
  replied with was handed out again by the new version's first turn — so a `report`,
  `history since=` or `subscribe … since-turn=` naming that id read a different
  exchange, or skipped the new one. The new version now counts on from well above
  anything the old one can still hand out; an old version that somehow hands out
  thousands of turns in those seconds stands the update down and tries again later.
- **A driven turn is no longer lost from a session's turn list across an update, or
  after `lease release force`.** A `turn` still waiting when an update froze the
  terminal finished in the old version after its list had been copied, so the new
  version's `history` never had it, and a `subscribe … since-turn=` resuming from before
  it was not told. The copy now marks such a turn as missing, and the resumed stream
  says so (`GAP … events-resync=`). A turn that a `lease release force` cut short and
  that finished after the turn that replaced it was never streamed to `subscribe …
  events`, and an update then dropped it from the list; it is now recorded under a
  new, higher id — the one its reply prints — and streamed like any other.
- **The message history is complete and in order after a seamless update.** The new
  version read `messages.log` when it started, but the old one kept recording until the
  switch — for up to a few minutes on an automatic update. Settings ▸ Messages and
  `aterm ctl messages` then left out what the old version recorded in that time, showed a
  row it had finished as "stale", and, when nothing was on the band at the switch, gave
  the new version's first messages numbers the old one had already used, so a script
  reading `messages since=<id>` skipped them. The old version now writes its last lines
  before it hands over (waiting at most a quarter of a second), the new version reads the
  file again the moment it takes over, before it records anything, and its numbers always
  continue past every one the old version gave out, including during the switch.

- **"Update waits for you" and "Couldn't install aterm vX" go away when the update
  lands.** A row saying the update had not installed yet stayed on the band of the new
  version for another 45 seconds, next to "Updated to aterm vX", and its Install now
  opened Settings. The new version now takes it down when it lands; Settings ▸ Messages
  keeps it.

- **`aterm ctl notice` during an update's switch is told to retry instead of being
  lost.** While aterm handed itself to a new version, a `notice post` was answered
  `OK message=<id>` but never shown by the new version, and the new version could give
  that id to another message; a `notice dismiss`, `progress` or `act` was undone. Every
  `notice` in that moment is now answered `ERR busy notice: aterm is switching to its new
  version retry_ms=1000`, and the retry reaches the new version.

- **"Screen reader access lost · restart aterm to retry" does not survive an update.**
  The update starts a new process with its own screen reader connection, which is what
  the row asked for, but the row was carried over and stayed up. It is now left behind.

- **An update that lands no longer says checks work again while they still fail.** When
  "Couldn't check for updates" or "Couldn't download updates" was up and a build downloaded
  earlier was installed, the new version took the warning down and recorded "aterm
  updates work again", while Settings ▸ Software Update still said checks were failing
  and the warning came back at the next failed check. An installed update now answers
  only "Couldn't install updates"; the other warnings stay up until a check or download
  actually works, and the new version does not raise them a second time.

- **A shell the keeper was holding for a window is offered again if that window's
  connection drops, and quitting the window no longer relaunches aterm.** When a
  recovering window's connection to the PTY keeper dropped before it took a shell it
  had been offered, the shell stayed promised to that dead connection for as long as
  the window ran, so nothing could pick it up. When the person later quit that
  window, the keeper read the old connection's end as a crash and opened aterm again.
  The offer now goes back to the keeper when the connection drops, and quitting a
  window counts for all of its connections.

- **An automatic update reads the new version's handoff instructions before it freezes
  the terminal.** When the new version's check had not finished yet, an automatic update
  could freeze the tabs and copy them in full before learning that the new version had
  asked for less. It now waits for that answer while the check is still running — a
  check slowed down by a busy machine included — for up to 20 seconds, and never starts
  a second check beside the first. The check itself now always finishes inside that
  time: on a slow machine each of its steps could take 30 seconds, so the update gave
  up waiting and froze the tabs anyway, then sat frozen for up to 10 more seconds
  behind the unfinished check before giving up and trying again later.
- **New tabs keep the system's open-file limit after a second update in a row.** An
  update that raised aterm's own open-file limit to take over many tabs handed new tabs
  the system's usual limit back, but only until the next update: if that one went the
  other way, every new tab afterwards got aterm's raised limit instead. The usual limit
  now carries over every update.
- **A window that fails to open during an update no longer kills the program running in
  it.** If the new version could not open one of the windows it was taking over, it
  closed that window before the switch was final, and in doing so ended the shell or
  program in its first pane — the one the old version was about to take back and keep
  running. The new version now lets go of that window without touching its program,
  and the old version carries on with it intact.
- **A link left open in a busy tab no longer holds an update back.** If a program was
  stopped halfway through printing a link (Ctrl-C during `ls --hyperlink`, say), the tab's
  link stayed open, and while that tab kept printing every update attempt gave up and
  tried again later. The update now waits a moment for the link to close, and then goes
  ahead; the rest of that output simply is not a link in the new version.
- **A pane kept open by `--hold` with a very dense final screen is said, not silently
  lost, across an update.** A held pane whose last screen was packed with long links
  was written out by the old version, read by the new one and then thrown away without
  a word. The old version now leaves out only a screen the new one cannot show, and the
  new one logs when it has to show a placeholder.
- **A new version is no longer written off for its predecessor's mistakes in a handoff.**
  When the running version handed over a tab list that did not match its descriptors, a
  tab without its screen, or a screen file that was missing or misnamed, the new version
  refused the handoff in a way the old one read as the new version being broken, and
  after two tries it stopped updating on its own. These now count as a passing problem
  and are retried.
- **An update the desk is too large to hand over no longer freezes the terminal over and
  over.** When the tabs' records alone would not fit in what the new version reads, the
  old version refused the switch after freezing every tab, and treated it as a passing
  hiccup: it tried again ten minutes later and froze the terminal for the same answer
  until its retries ran out. It is now told as the desk holding the update back, and
  tried again once the tabs change.
- **A tab you were scrolled back in stays at the live bottom when an update carries no
  scrollback.** When the new version asked an update to carry only the visible screen,
  the update still remembered how far back you were scrolled, and after the switch it
  scrolled the tab up into whatever the program had printed since, and stopped the tab
  following new output. It now only scrolls back into lines that actually came across;
  with none, the tab stays at the bottom.
- **"Idle" no longer means "an update paused reading the tab".** While an update took
  over, aterm stopped reading tabs for up to a few seconds; a program still printing
  looked quiet, so `aterm ctl ready`, `await idle` and the end of an `aterm ctl turn`
  could report "idle" while a build was still running. Those waits now pause their
  clock while the tab is not being read. An `aterm ctl turn` in that window also no
  longer presses Enter again because it could not see the first one — a second Enter
  could have answered a confirmation prompt on its own.

- **Commands sent from inside a tab while an update is landing are no longer lost.**
  For a fraction of a second before an update took over, the new aterm already
  advertised itself as the owner of every tab, so an `aterm ctl key`, `send` or `turn`
  from inside a tab could reach it — and it dropped the keystroke with a confusing error,
  or accepted a change that was then lost when the update was called off. The new aterm
  now waits until the update is final before it answers for any tab, and an update
  called off no longer leaves the tabs pointing at it.

- **A message-bus connection started by hand survives an update.** A bridge started
  with `aterm ctl fabric attach` (rather than from the configuration) was not started
  again by the updated aterm: messages stopped, and a fleet-wide halt carried across the
  update could no longer be lifted. The updated aterm now starts the same bridge again.

- **`aterm ctl update check` no longer hides a downloaded update while a dialog is open.**
  With a dialog on screen, or aterm's main thread busy, the check answered OK with "no
  update staged" even when one was downloaded and ready. It now says why it could not
  check (answer the dialog, or retry), and when the settings cannot be read it still
  reports the downloaded update.

- **A command that finished during an update is no longer reported as still running.**
  `aterm ctl await block` (and a bare `await seq`, and `await consent`) cut by an update
  was asked again on the new aterm, after the command had already finished there, and
  timed out. It now stops with exit code 75 and says to look at the session first. An
  `aterm ctl turn` cut by an update now also exits 75 and says its text may already have
  been typed, instead of failing with exit 1 — the code that invited a retry that typed
  the prompt twice. An `aterm ctl post` cut by an update exits 75 the same way and says
  the message may already be on its way — re-post it only with the same `key=`, or it
  is sent twice. A followed `subscribe … events` stream now resumes after the last
  finished command and turn it showed, so one that finished during the update is still
  reported; a stream that named no tab (or `@.`) stays on the tab it was watching, and
  never replays another tab's old commands as new. When aterm was not updated but
  replaced by a fresh instance (it quit or crashed, and a new one took its socket),
  such a stream follows the new instance's own tab instead of stopping with exit code
  75, even after riding an earlier update.

- **An automatic update no longer loses a message waiting to be sent, or a reply
  still owed.** When the message bus was down, a message an agent posted waited inside
  aterm until the bus came back, and so did the "handled" reply it owed a sender. An
  update in that window lost both, silently: the new aterm started with an empty outbox,
  and the agent had been told the message was queued. The new aterm now takes both over
  and sends them. A very large backlog is never a reason to refuse the update: past a
  fixed allowance what does not fit is reported as not carried rather than blocking every
  update attempt. Message, post and timeline numbers now keep counting up across an
  update — including a message that arrives while the update is landing, and timeline
  events recorded in that moment; such a message is taken as usual, never refused, and
  never makes the update give up and try again — and so do the numbers of the closed-sessions list, so a
  script waiting for "anything after number N" no longer waits forever on the new aterm,
  and `inbox seen N` never marks a different message. Updating to an older aterm
  releases its messages exactly as before. A wait for a
  screen change that names a number from before the update now answers at once instead
  of reporting "nothing changed".
- **A Codex 0.159.0 tab is continued and upgraded again.** Codex 0.159.0 ends every turn on a
  row like `Worked for <1s • 2:58 AM`, with `•` where earlier builds drew `·` (and ended a
  short turn on a bare clock). aterm did not read that row as the end of the turn, so it read
  every Codex 0.159.0 tab as still working, and nothing that acts at a quiet moment ran
  there: not the supervisor, not the upgrade, and not the last step of a restart, which
  types the continuation a relaunched Codex is owed. Every Codex that aterm moved onto
  0.159.0, or relaunched after a crash, came back on its conversation and was left there,
  its move never finished. Both marks now end a turn.

- **Revoking a release machine's key no longer stops updates on the Macs that saw
  its releases.** Each update floor (the lowest build an update may be, and the
  highest one staged) was raised by whatever a rostered machine's signed release
  asked for and never lowered, so a stolen key that published a release numbered
  9 999 999 999 held every later genuine release "below the operator floor" on
  every Mac that had looked at it — for good, and as a healthy check. The floors
  now record which machine raised them, and the check that sees a roster revoking
  that machine takes those raises back (never below what the machines still trusted
  asked for). The revoked machine is remembered, so its word never counts again:
  a stage it signed is withdrawn by that check, refused by a check that was still
  downloading it when the revocation landed, and refused by the swap at the next
  launch. A staged build the owner yanks is no longer offered as "verified and
  ready to apply" either — by the check, its backoff line or `update status` —
  and the check that sees the yank discards it. On Linux the minimum-build floor
  is withdrawn the same way.

- **An older aterm staging an update slowly is no longer reported as stuck days
  later.** Another aterm holding the update's staging lock with no sign of life is
  reported as stopped only when two checks in a row find it so. The first finding
  was remembered for as long as aterm ran, so the next slow staging by an older
  aterm — even for a later release, days on — was reported at once as "no aterm on
  this Mac can stage an update until it is continued or quits". A check in between
  that did not need the lock now starts the count again.

- **An update whose staging keeps running out of time is no longer said to "not
  verify".** When every attempt to open a downloaded update's disk image ran past
  its limit, the joined error was cut to 400 characters before it was stored, which
  cut off the words marking it as a passing condition — so after a few checks the
  notice said "updates download but will not verify or install" about a build
  nothing was known against. A long error now keeps its beginning and that marker,
  and the notice describes a standing staging streak by its own error even when a
  network blip was the last thing recorded.

- **A moment when aterm could not open the update's handoff policy no longer
  counts as "the update asks for nothing".** A release can carry a small policy
  asking the running aterm to carry sessions over more conservatively (for
  example, as blank screens that redraw). When opening that file failed for a
  passing reason — no file descriptor free on a large desk, an I/O error — the
  failure was taken as "no policy" and remembered for ten minutes, and every
  update attempt in that time carried sessions exactly the way the release had
  asked it not to. That failure is now a passing refusal: nothing is parked, it
  is not remembered, and the next attempt reads the file again.

- **Linux: a downloaded update held for `aterm update apply` still applies after the
  release roster changes.** A check of a newer release that had no Linux build yet
  — or one the check refused, such as a release signed by a revoked machine, or one
  whose tag did not match its signed version — still recorded that release's
  roster, and the apply then judged the held update's older roster against it and
  refused it as a replay ("machine roster admission refused: Rollback") while the
  update still showed as downloaded. The check now proves the held update again
  under the roster it read, whether or not the newer release itself was accepted,
  and the apply goes through — unless that roster revoked the machine that signed it.

- **A combining accent typed with nothing to its left is no longer thrown away.**
  Measured by the owner: `printf 'abc\r'` followed by U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE
  rendered `abc` with the accent simply GONE. At column 0 the write path asked
  for "the cell before the cursor", got nothing, and DISCARDED the mark. It now
  lands on the cell under the cursor instead — so that sequence accents the `a`,
  exactly as xterm does (xterm resolves the attach column as `cur_col` whenever
  the cursor has moved since the last glyph, which a carriage return always
  counts as). Nothing sanctioned the old behaviour: Unicode 16.0 §3 D57 calls a
  combining sequence with no base *defective* and says in the same paragraph
  that such sequences "are not ill-formed", and that a process "may present a
  combining character without graphical combination; that is, it may present it
  as if it were a base character". iTerm2 keeps the mark too. Where there IS a
  cell to the left, nothing changes — the mark still attaches there, which is
  what iTerm2, Ghostty and kitty all do and is where aterm and xterm have always
  differed by design.

- **EL (`ESC[K`), DECSEL (`ESC[?K`) and ECH (`ESC[X`) are no longer cut short by
  DECSLRM left/right margins.** EL 0/1/2, DECSEL 0/1/2 and ECH were
  clamped to the horizontal margins, so a full-screen program that sets margins
  and then clears a line left stripes of stale text outside the margin span.
  VT510 draws the line the other way round, one sentence per page: EL, ECH and
  ED each "work inside or outside the scrolling margins", while ICH and DCH
  each "have no effect outside the scrolling margins" — erases in place are
  unbounded, operations that SHIFT data sideways are bounded. xterm, Ghostty,
  iTerm2 and WezTerm all implement exactly that split, each of them clamping
  ICH/DCH and leaving the erases at full width in the same source file. aterm's
  in-code justification cited "VT420/VT510 spec" for the opposite of what the
  VT510 ECH page says. ED/DECSED were already correct and are unchanged, and
  aterm's ICH, DCH, DECIC, DECDC and autowrap keep their margins.

- **A back tab (`ESC[Z`) no longer stops at the left margin unless origin mode
  is on.** CBT was clamped whenever DECSLRM margins were armed, justified as
  "matching CUB behavior". VT510 gives CBT's floor as column one and names no
  margin; it is DECOM that makes the cursor unable to leave the margins, so the
  margin binds a back tab only under DECOM — the composition xterm implements
  (`TabToPrevStop` clamps only inside `if (xw->flags & ORIGIN)`) and Ghostty
  states in a comment. Both of them clamp CUB on the margin unconditionally and
  still decline to inherit that for CBT. A cursor already left of the left
  margin now stays put rather than being sent to column 0: a backward tab moves
  backward or not at all. (xterm drags it rightwards onto the margin there,
  which makes a back tab move the cursor forward; Ghostty does not, and neither
  do we.)

- **The footer names the model you selected the moment you select it.** A `/model`
  choice showed no model at all until Claude's next answer — fourteen minutes on the
  session this was reported from — and an `/effort` or `/fast` switch left the old effort
  or model on show. The footer now reads the result Claude writes for its own `/model`,
  `/effort` and `/fast` commands (the top-effort key shows as `xhigh`, the level it runs at;
  the `/fast` result is read with its coloured icon, as Claude reads it). A switch whose
  result names no effort keeps the effort on show only when it was read for the model
  switched to, since each model runs its own: after Opus 5.5 at `xhigh`, a switch to
  Haiku 4.5 shows no effort until an answer or `/effort` names one. Before a session has
  said anything it shows the process's own `--model`, or the model on Claude's launch card
  while Claude's own input box and footer row are up — in every permission mode — and
  never the model of the process before it unless Claude restored that model onto this
  one. The model belongs to the Claude process, so
  after `/clear` the footer still names the model you chose, not the one it was launched
  with; after an in-app `/resume` it names the resumed conversation's own model, as Claude
  restores it, unless the process pinned its model (`--model`, a `/model` or `/fast`
  choice, or an earlier restore). A restore pins the model, as it does in Claude: once a
  `/resume` — or a launch with `--resume` or `--continue` — has restored one, every later
  `/resume` keeps it, and so does the footer, whether the conversation resumed is older
  than that Claude Code or one another tab began since. aterm tells a `/resume` from a
  `/clear` by when it last read the tab — every few seconds while Claude Code's screen
  changes — so two `/resume`s between two reads count as the last one alone, and what
  another tab wrote in those moments, a conversation it began included, counts as this
  Claude's own. aterm keeps what it has read of a Claude Code for as long as that Claude
  runs (of 64 at most); after aterm itself is updated under a running Claude, a pin — a
  restore, or a `/model` or `/fast` choice — made before the update and since left
  behind by a `/clear` is not known, and a `/resume` can name the resumed conversation's
  model where Claude keeps the pinned one, until Claude answers. A launch that resumes a conversation with no `--model` runs
  the model Claude restores from it, and the footer names it at once. A resumed
  conversation whose newest answer is one row too long to read shows no model until the
  next answer, never an older answer's. One huge row — a pasted image, a large tool
  result — no longer blanks a model named above it.
- **The fast light reads Claude's `↯ Fast mode ON` answer under the command.** Claude
  opens that answer with its fast-mode icon, and the light read only an answer that opened
  with the words. At idle it missed the answer and settled on the rule's `↯` alone, so a
  `/fast on` that moved the model never said that Claude had switched the model.

- **The mode lights read Claude Code's mode in a narrow pane.** Claude Code does not
  shorten its `(shift+tab to cycle)` hint in a narrow pane. It cuts the hint between
  words, so at 39–48 columns in bypass mode (30–39 in auto mode) the row ends in
  `(shift+tab` or `(shift+tab to`, with no `)`. aterm read such a row as no mode row at
  all: the mode lights showed no mode there, the mode light could not cycle from plan or
  manual mode, and the footer did not read Claude's launch card for the model. It now
  reads a cut hint as the hint. Claude's row itself stays exactly as Claude drew it —
  aterm writes its facts and lights into the rule above it — so every item on it, a
  `← 1 agent` or `esc to interrupt` cut short with `…` included, stays in Claude's own
  cells. These row shapes were worked out from Claude Code 2.1.284's own rendering code,
  not captured from a running session.
- **A pane kept open after its command ended (`--hold`) comes through an update as it
  was.** Since such panes keep their final screen across an update, the new version
  showed one in the default colours instead of your theme, reported it as an idle or
  stalled session instead of exited (its exit status lost), and dropped the name, icon,
  role and description you gave it with `aterm ctl meta set` and the identity it was
  started under, so the next update lost them too. It now arrives in your theme, exited
  with the status its command ended with, and with its name and identity. A desk with
  many such panes no longer makes the update pause the terminal twice: capturing them
  stops well inside the pause's time budget and at the 64 panes an update carries.
- **An update that had to retry its pause keeps a busy tab's scrollback.** When an
  update's first attempt to pause the terminal missed its time budget and retried half a
  second later, a tab that printed a few hundred lines in between arrived in the new
  version with only its last 256 lines of history. The scrollback copy made beside the
  update is now paused, not ended, while the terminal pauses, and picks up again when the
  pause is retried.
- **An image, clipboard copy or sixel arriving during an update is no longer dropped.**
  When an update paused a tab in the middle of a kitty-graphics image, a large OSC 52
  clipboard copy or OSC 1337 image, or the start of a sixel, with the rest still on its
  way, the new version quietly threw the rest away: the image never appeared and the copy
  never happened. The update now waits for the end of such a sequence, as it already did
  for a sixel whose data had started, and goes ahead a moment later.
- **A tab updated in the middle of a synchronized screen update no longer stays in it.**
  A program that had opened a synchronized update (mode 2026) when an update paused its
  tab, and then exited without closing it, left the tab in that mode for good in the new
  version: the one-second timeout that normally ends it never started. The timeout now
  starts again when the tab arrives.
- **A link or a VT52 cursor move arriving during an update is no longer broken.** When
  an update paused a tab in the middle of a clickable link (`ls --hyperlink`, a compiler
  or an agent printing one) with the rest of its text still on its way, the new version
  printed that rest as plain text, and it stayed unlinked in the scrollback. A VT52
  program paused between a cursor-move command and its position printed the position as
  two stray characters. The update now waits for the link or the move to finish, and
  goes ahead a moment later.
- **A `video` recording is no longer cut off by an update that did not happen.** An
  update stopped any running `aterm ctl video` take, answering "aterm is updating", as
  soon as it paused the terminal — before it knew the new version would verify, start
  and take over; when any of that failed, the old version kept running and the recording
  was lost for nothing. A take now runs on until the moment the old version hands over,
  and only then is answered. That answer, and the answer of a recording export the update
  cancels, now reaches the client, and the export's unfinished folder is removed, before
  the old process exits (bounded at one second, and logged when it runs out).

- **Supervisor: a Bash box is judged under the shell startup it really runs with.** The
  rm circuit-breaker proof and the read-only rule read a command as zsh and bash run it
  with their default options and no user alias or function. Claude Code's Bash tool
  replays the person's own `~/.zshrc` first (its shell snapshot), and runs `.zshenv`,
  bash's `BASH_ENV` and any `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` or hook env script too. A `setopt
  globsubst` there makes `N='~'; rm -rf $N` remove the home directory (measured on
  Claude Code 2.1.284, which turns off only glob qualifiers). The supervisor now reads
  that startup from the worker's own Claude Code directory. Under `approve = "safe"`, an
  option the rules do not model (`globsubst`, `shwordsplit`, `nullglob`, `rcquotes`, …),
  or a startup it cannot read, sends every Bash box to a person, and an alias or
  function sends the boxes that may run it: a function `rm` however the line quotes
  `rm`, an alias `git` where `git` stands as a command (oh-my-zsh's `alias 5='cd -5'`
  does not stop `tail -n 5`). Each reason
  names the option, alias or file. At full power these boxes are still pressed, with the
  reason recorded as unproven.

- **A program in a split pane keeps its pane's size across an update.** When vim, less or
  htop ran in one pane of a split, the new build told it the whole window was its screen,
  and it redrew at twice its width into half the space until the window or the split was
  resized. The same wrong size stayed on the program when an update was rolled back. The
  program now gets its pane's size, and a rolled-back update puts each pane's size back.

- **A session open in two windows no longer costs the update its layout.** After Open
  Session in New Window, every update folded all windows into tabs of the first and closed
  every split and every Settings or document view. The layout now comes back whole, and the
  session shows in both windows again.

- **Scrolled-back reading survives output that arrives during an update.** A session that
  kept printing while the update ran came back scrolled to lines printed after it, not the
  ones being read. The view now returns to the same lines. And a session you type into,
  paste into or scroll while the update finishes is left where you put it: typing at the
  prompt could have the view jump up the screen partway through a command.

- **Keys typed into a window before an update finished stay in that window.** Clicking a
  window of the new build and typing while it was still getting ready could move the
  keyboard to another window partway through a command, so half the command ran in one shell
  and half in another. The window typed into now keeps the keyboard, including a window that
  was minimized before the update: it is no longer sent back to the Dock while you type in it.

- **An update that waited says why it waited.** When an automatic update stood down on
  its own (a busy machine missed the moment to switch, a video recording or a closed pane
  held it past its two minutes, every tab closed while the new version started), Messages
  said "you were typing" every time. The record now gives the reason the update actually
  stood down, and still says it tries again by itself.

- **A failed update is named for the version it tried.** If another aterm window
  downloaded a different version while an install was running and the install then
  failed, the failure was worded as "Couldn't install aterm v<the other version>", with
  Install now for bytes nobody had tried, or folded into that version's retry. It now
  says "Couldn't finish the update", the "aterm v<tried> is ready" row it was started
  from is taken down, and where installing the new download is up to you, its own
  "is ready" row with Install now comes up beside it.

- **An update-health warning no longer cancels an install that is still going.** A
  warning that arrived while the new version was starting (an overdue-update notice, the
  update checker's stall warning) used to end the install's glowing border and turn the
  Installing row into a failure, while the install carried on and finished. The row and
  the border now stay until the install itself ends.

- **"aterm updates work again" is recorded after an automatic update too.** When an
  update fixed a problem aterm had warned about ("Couldn't install updates"), the
  recovery was recorded only after an install you started, and only while the warning was
  still on screen. It is now recorded after an automatic update, and after the warning had
  already folded away.

- **A tab closing during an update no longer delays the next try by half an hour.** A
  shell that exited (or an ssh link that dropped) in the second between the freeze and
  the switch was counted as a failed update: the next automatic try waited 10 minutes,
  then 30, and each one used up part of the version's retry allowance. It is now treated
  the way the same exit a moment earlier always was, as the desk changing, and the update
  tries again within seconds.

- **An update held after its release was withdrawn says so, instead of re-checking
  forever.** When a build that had failed to install twice was then withdrawn from the
  channel, aterm could no longer read how many times that build had been launched, and
  checked again every 75 seconds with no end, while its notice still promised a retry in
  a day. After three checks that each looked at the installed copy afresh (a check that
  had nothing new to look at, on a busy machine, does not count) it now stops, holds the
  build for you to install from the Version menu, and says so; a newer release still
  installs by itself.

- **A live Claude upgrade is no longer frozen behind the supervisor's own "keep going".**
  A Claude Code that orchestrates all day reaches the upgrade only at the breaks of its
  own background work, and after the supervisor had typed its own continuation every break
  was held back until a true idle point came, which such an agent never reaches. Two tabs
  had no upgrade look for hours on 2026-09-28, one of them right after an Upgrade now. The
  supervisor now holds a break back only while its continuation has not been taken: once
  the agent is seen working on it, its next break is the upgrade's again, so the notice,
  the re-ask, the give-up and the next round all come.

- **A Claude Code that answered READY is no longer typed over by the supervisor.** After
  notices typed at breaks of the agent's work, the upgrade's own settle before the restart
  owned nothing: every wait before it (a person at the tab, the agent's answers without
  READY) had used up its looks, and a notice typed at a break started nothing over. The
  supervisor typed `keep going` one second after the READY and voided it. Every act of the
  upgrade's, at a break too, now starts that count over, and only the settle and drain
  waits it bounds count toward it, so the READY's settle is the upgrade's and the restart
  follows.

- **A notice aterm could not type is tried again, owns its point, and is told.** When the
  upgrade's notice was due and aterm's own screen fence refused it (the screen moved as it
  typed), the look owned nothing, so the supervisor's continuation took the point, and
  nothing counted the refusal. The notice is now tried up to three times within the same
  look, each try after the first only while nobody has typed in the tab since the look and
  no turn has started. A notice still refused keeps the point for three more looks, twenty
  seconds apart, before the supervisor may continue the agent; those looks are counted on
  their own, and an owner's word gives them back. Each refused look is counted, and after
  an hour and a half the owner is told that aterm could not type its notice, how often,
  and for how long (the band row, the tab's mark, and `refused=` on
  `aterm harness upgrade --status`), with Upgrade now offered. When Upgrade now is already
  in force, the row says that aterm's own typing is what fails and offers Not today and
  Skip version instead. Any word of the owner's starts the count over, so pressing Upgrade
  now there no longer brings the same row straight back.

- **An agent that said "not yet, my work still runs" is asked again when that work
  ends.** A Claude Code running long workflows answered every notice that it could not
  stop yet. The upgrade asked four times at breaks of the work, gave up, rested, and asked
  again, round after round, and the one moment the move could finish, the first idle
  point after the work with nothing left under the agent, went to the supervisor's
  `keep going`. That point is now the upgrade's: a round waiting for its answer asks again
  there at once, and a round resting after a give-up starts its next round and asks in the
  same look. Each end of the agent's work earns at most one such ask. If Claude's status
  still reads busy over the idle screen, that holds the ask back only until the usual
  half-hour re-ask, which then asks or gives up as it always does.

- **Claude upgrades stalled in several tabs share one row on the band.** Three tabs
  behind on the same Claude upgrade were three rows, which is all the band holds. They
  now stand in one row, "Couldn't upgrade Claude in 3 tabs yet", whose first line names
  the tabs, most behind first, and whose second says what its buttons do. Details keeps each tab's own words. Upgrade now,
  Not today and Skip version act on exactly the tabs the row listed that take that
  word, and each tab's menu still has its own words. A press is answered once a word
  is written, naming any tab it could not be written for; if none could be, the row
  says why and keeps its buttons. As tabs finish, the same row counts down; one tab
  left reads as its own row did. The row stays while a restart is under way, and it
  ends in words that say what happened: "Claude upgraded in 3 tabs" when they moved,
  or your word's answer when your word moved the last tab. A tab alone keeps its own
  row, and a stop, a refusal or a restart that sticks keeps its own row too, since
  each has a remedy of its own. A row you read or dismissed is not shown again, even
  after aterm restarts or updates, unless a tab it did not name joins or a tab moves on
  to a newer build; once its tabs stop stalling, the same stalls coming back are shown
  again.

- **A new upgrade round waiting on the agent's own work is a log record, not a
  warning.** When an agent had answered every notice of a round with "not yet, my work
  still runs", the round gave up and rested, and each new round's wait before its first
  notice put up a fresh warning row that went again a few minutes later. Until that
  notice goes, the new round now reads as the upgrade working, like the rounds around
  it. A notice aterm itself could not type is still told.
- **An agent upgrade held by a draft, a question box or a hold now says so.**
  When the upgrade had asked Claude Code to wind down and then found unsent text
  in its prompt, a box waiting for an answer, a login or a hold on the tab, it
  waited without asking again and without giving up, and it was filed as "still
  asking on its own", so nothing showed. Once the tab is six hours behind, the tab
  is now marked and Messages shows a row saying a person is what holds the move.
  A draft or box that passes quickly (you typing your next prompt, say) does not
  count; the hold must have stood for half an hour after the last ask.
- **A tab a day behind on its agent build is always shown.** An agent whose own
  work never ends (a background server, a `tail -f`, a watch loop) was asked,
  given up on, rested and asked again for days, all kept as log records with no
  tab mark, and pressing Upgrade now was taken back off the screen when the round
  gave up. A tab that has been behind for a day is now marked and gets a Messages
  row whatever its rounds are doing. A usage limit is the one exception: it ends
  by itself at its reset and stays a record until then.
- **The pause after repeated unanswered upgrade rounds is kept.** When an agent
  answered too late, after its work had already outlasted the round, the next
  round came two hours later however many rounds had gone unanswered, so the
  longer pauses meant to space out the asking never applied. The pause now keeps
  the length the repeated rounds earned.
- **One stale session file no longer stops every Claude upgrade.** An unreadable
  or out-of-date file in `~/.claude/sessions` left by a Claude Code that is no
  longer running made aterm wait on every Claude tab in the window, retried every
  minute with nothing shown. A file whose process is gone, or whose name is not a
  process id, is now ignored; a running process's unreadable file still makes the
  upgrade wait, as before.
- **A restart left mid-way by an update is finished or reported.** When aterm
  updated itself while it was restarting a Claude Code for an upgrade, the new
  aterm could stop looking at that tab: if the old Claude was still closing at
  that moment, or if the relaunch kept waiting for about five minutes, the tab was
  left at a bare shell while its row still promised the relaunch. The new aterm
  now looks again until the agent has closed, and a relaunch it cannot finish in
  time is named in the "Couldn't resume Claude" row. A later update that was
  started and abandoned no longer stops it either.
- **A crashed agent due to be relaunched during an update is relaunched.** If
  Claude Code crashed and aterm was waiting before relaunching it when aterm
  updated itself, the relaunch was dropped for good, and a "still trying" mark
  could stay on the tab. The new aterm now relaunches it, the old one does it
  itself if the update does not go through, and the mark is cleared once the
  relaunch is over. This also covers a crash in the moments while the update is
  getting ready. A crash in the last instant before the switch, after aterm has
  already saved the tabs for the new build, can still be missed.
- **A build that crash-looped stays out.** When an update fails to start three
  times, aterm puts the previous build back and never installs that exact build
  again. That record could be lost: the next download failure of any other build
  overwrote it, and a successful download erased it, so if the newer release was
  later withdrawn the bad build could be downloaded and installed again. A check
  that had started downloading the bad build just before it was put back could
  also finish and offer it once more. The record now has its own file that nothing
  else writes over, the download is refused if the build was put back meanwhile,
  and a copy some older aterm stages anyway is never installed.

- **A slow Mac no longer holds back a good update for a day.** When a check could
  not finish verifying a new build in time (a busy machine, a slow Gatekeeper
  check, a disk image that took too long to open), aterm treated the build as bad:
  it waited 15 minutes, then hours, up to a day before trying again, and after
  three such moments said the updates "download but will not verify". A check
  that merely ran out of time is now tried again at the next check, and only a
  real problem with the download counts against it. If it runs out of time at
  every check, aterm still says so after a while, in words that say the step
  could not finish rather than that the build is bad.

- **An aterm stopped in the middle of an update download is named.** If an aterm
  was paused (in a debugger, or with `kill -STOP`) while it prepared an update, or
  its download hung, every other aterm on the Mac waited two minutes at each
  check, gave up with "the next check reads what it staged", and never said
  anything more. aterm now tells a paused or stuck holder from one that is still
  working, records it in `aterm ctl update status` once two checks in a row find
  it so, and after a few checks says that another aterm is blocking the update.

- **No "Couldn't install updates" for a build that was withdrawn.** A build that
  crash-looped and was put back, one the publisher pulled, or one signed by a
  release machine that was later revoked, was reported an hour
  later as "waiting on this machine", again on every launch, until a newer release
  came out. It is no longer called waiting.

- **Unfinished update copies no longer pile up on disk.** When aterm was quit,
  force-quit or restarted while it copied a new build, or when a copy was stopped
  for running too long, the half-made copy stayed in a hidden folder beside the
  app (or in aterm's update folder) for good — one app-sized folder each time.
  Such leftovers are now removed a day later, once nothing can still be writing
  to them.

- **The "another aterm holds the update check" warning says what is true.** When
  another aterm is stuck holding the update check, the warning could be lost if
  aterm's own check had also stalled, and it was cleared with "aterm updates work
  again" as soon as a download started or aterm restarted its own check, while the
  other aterm was still stuck. The warning now stands on its own until the other
  aterm lets go.

- **An update with more than 62 tabs open lands again.** When the new build supports
  handing over more tabs than one message carries, and it had already been checked a
  few minutes before the update, aterm chose the new launch path for those tabs but
  forgot to tell the new build it could receive them in several parts. Every open
  terminal then froze for a moment, the handover failed, and the next try did the
  same. The new build is now told what the choice was made on, and the pause checks
  what the new build actually asked for before it freezes anything, so a mismatch
  gives up with every terminal still live. When the launch path falls back to the
  older way of starting the new build, tabs opened during the wait no longer fail
  that attempt for a limit the older way does not have.

- **An update that ran out of time preparing says so.** When the old build took
  longer than its few-second budget to write the handover files after the pause, the
  failure said "no successor dialed" and was counted as the new build refusing — though
  the new build had started and was waiting. It now says the time ran out in the old
  build, and it is counted as a timeout.

- **A new build that cannot take over your tabs no longer starts a blank terminal
  beside them.** When the new build received the tabs but then refused the handover as
  a whole (for example, the handover file named a different attempt), it went on
  starting as a fresh terminal: it used up the saved-session file and started a shell
  while the old build still held every tab, until the old build stopped it. It now
  exits at once, as it already did when only some checks failed, and the log says
  which check refused the handover. When the refusal was about the old build's
  handover files rather than the new build, the new build's exit asks the old build to
  try again later instead of marking the new build as broken.

- **A downloaded update that was withdrawn is no longer started.** When a release was
  pulled after aterm had already downloaded it, aterm still paused every terminal and
  started it, and the new build then refused to install itself and quit. The check
  before the pause now reads the same withdrawal floor the install does, so a
  withdrawn download is refused with every terminal still live — also when the
  download had passed its check a few minutes before it was withdrawn.

- **Many shell tabs with long command histories no longer block every update.**
  The handover file carries, for each tab, a record of the commands in the scrollback
  it hands over. With enough tabs and commands that file grew past the size the new
  build accepts, the new build refused the whole handover, and every later try did the
  same. aterm now leaves out the command records of the largest tabs until the file
  fits — their screens and scrollback still cross exactly; only jumping between those
  past commands is lost — and it never writes a file the new build would refuse.

- **Updating with a very large number of tabs no longer runs the new build out of
  files.** A new build started for an update got the system's default limit on open
  files, which is too low to receive a couple of hundred tabs; it then failed partway
  through taking them over, and the failure counted against the new build. It now
  raises its own limit before it asks for the tabs. Shells in tabs opened afterwards
  still get the system's usual limit, as they do in an aterm opened from the Dock.
- **`aterm doctor`'s `recovery:` row no longer says a killed run had no signal handler.**
  A run that ended with no crash signal and no exit path is listed as `killed (no crash
  signal, no exit path)`, the same words as the "aterm was stopped last time" line. It
  used to say `no signal handler`, which is wrong for the most common case: a `SIGTERM`,
  `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` does run a handler, the one that removes the control socket, its
  token and the `latest` alias before the process ends. Such a stop is still counted as
  killed, as before: it leaves its crash marker in place because only a quit or another
  clean exit removes it. Only the wording changed.

- **An API error is no longer missed in a tall window with a short conversation.** Claude
  Code draws its input box at the bottom of the window, so in a tall window a short
  conversation leaves a long blank stretch between the last thing it said and the box. The
  tab's state check read only the last 40 rows, and the error above that stretch fell just
  outside them: the tab said `idle` with no "can't reach the API", though the harness's own
  reader saw it. A run of four or more blank rows now counts as one row when choosing what
  to read, so the error stays in view. Ordinary conversations read exactly as before. A
  fresh Claude Code launch, whose banner sat above the same kind of gap, now reads as
  fresh too.
- **A Claude Code that is still retrying an API error is no longer read as idle when you
  have typed a draft.** While it retries, Claude Code shows `Can't reach the API server …
  · Retrying in 14s · attempt 6/10`, and typing into the box removes the `esc to interrupt`
  hint that had been the only thing marking it busy. The harness then read an idle session
  mid-retry and could treat the turn as ended. That retry line now counts as work in progress.
- **`/fast` pressed while Claude is working now reads Claude's answer.** Claude Code answers
  it with a notice beside the input box, above it or under it depending on the layout, and
  aterm looked only under it, so a refusal mid-turn was never seen and the light waited out
  its deadline. Both places are read now.
- **The `fast` light no longer runs into Claude Code's effort hint.** In auto mode Claude
  Code 2.1.284 shows `◐ medium · /effort` at the right end of its mode row, and a light
  drawn on that row sat flush against it (`/effort○ fast`). The lights are now in the
  rule under the input box, with a blank cell on each side of every light at every pane
  width, and Claude's row keeps its hint where Claude drew it.
- **An in-place update no longer garbles a sequence that was half-received when it
  happened.** The update can land between two reads of a program's output, and the new
  build used to start reading from scratch: the rest of a colour change printed as text
  (`6mX` instead of a red `X`), a character split across the reads showed as
  replacement marks, and a window title still arriving was lost. The half-received
  sequence now travels with the session and the new build finishes it. The rest of an
  image transfer that was cut off this way is now dropped quietly instead of printed as
  a screen of text. An update from an older build behaves as before.
- **A tab's history now says where an in-place update cut it.** A session's `timeline`,
  its `cast` recording and its `temporal` recording do not cross an update, and after one
  each simply started over, as if the session had begun then. Each now opens with the
  update: the `timeline`'s first row is `handoff carried=0 from_build=<n>`, the `cast`
  header carries an `aterm_handoff` note (and `cast frames` warns that its early frames
  lack the screen before it), and `temporal status` ends with `carried=0
  from_build=<n>`. Sessions that were never carried across an update read as before. This
  works from the first update into this version.
- **An in-place update keeps your place in the scrollback.** A tab you had scrolled back
  to read came back at the bottom after an update. The update now notes how far up you
  were and, once the tab's history has come across, scrolls back to the same place
  (never further than the history the tab holds). If you have already scrolled that tab
  yourself by then, it stays where you put it. The version before this one does not note
  the place, so this starts with the update after the one into this version.
- **A `video` recording running when aterm updates in place now gets an answer.** The
  recording died with the old version and `aterm ctl video` read a dropped connection,
  with no reason given. An automatic update now waits for a recording to finish, for at
  most 60 s (the longest recording `video` makes), and not at all once it has reached
  the point where it stops waiting for anything. When the update goes ahead with a
  recording still running, the recording is stopped first and its client is answered
  `ERR video: recording aborted: aterm is updating`; a recording still being written
  out is cancelled, and its client is told so. An update you start yourself does not
  wait.
- **A pane kept open with `--hold` keeps its final output across an in-place update.**
  When other tabs were still running, the pane whose command had finished came back as
  "not carried" and its output was gone. The update now carries that pane's last
  screen, and the new version shows it in the same place, read-only, as the finished
  pane it was: typing into it does nothing and closing it works as before. Links on
  that screen are not clickable after the update. If the screen cannot be carried
  (the update is short of time or space), the pane shows the "not carried" note as
  before. This starts with the update after the one into this version.

- **Pressing Upgrade now on a Claude upgrade that waits on its own work no longer
  looks like nothing happened.** The press answers its row, and half an hour later the
  tab's stall came back as a log record only, which took the answered row off the band
  with it: the word still stood, and nothing on screen said so. While your Upgrade now
  stands, that answer now stays on the band as a calm row saying what the move waits on
  and that it moves once that ends; with no word from you it stays a log record.
- **`cast` records a resize on the side of the output the terminal applied it on.** Output
  was timed when a background writer reached the recording, and a resize when the thread
  that resized reached it, so a resize could land after output the terminal had drawn
  after it, or before output drawn before it. On the alternate screen, where a shrink
  moves the rows, a replay (`cast frames`, `cast drift`) of such a recording shows a
  screen the tab never had. Each burst of output and each resize now carries its place
  in the terminal's own order, taken while the terminal applied it, and is recorded
  there; a burst a resize split in the middle is recorded as two.

- **With `temporal_recording` on, the recorder keeps a resize that ends at the size it
  started from.** A resize reached the recording only when the size differed from the
  last one recorded, so a flap between two reads was missing: an 80 → 79 → 80 column
  flap cuts the alternate screen's last column, and `temporal <tick>` rebuilt the screen
  with it still there. A flap that landed while the tab's reader was stopped (an update
  handoff that was rolled back, for one) was missed the same way: the next reader
  recorded only the size it found. The recorder now reads each resize from the
  terminal's own resize journal the next time the program writes output, and records it
  there, before that output; a new reader starts where the last one stopped. Until then
  the resize is not in the recording: `temporal status` counts such resizes as
  `pending_resizes=`, and a `temporal` replay at the recording's end adds
  `pending_resizes=<n>` to its header. The journal keeps 16 resizes, so more than 16
  before the next output cannot all be recorded: `temporal status` counts those as
  `lost_resizes=`.

- **Long coding sessions do less repeated work.** History search keeps its filter
  proportional to distinct text fragments, skips unchanged rows, and reserves memory
  within the configured retained-history limit. Claude Code's status and upgrade
  readers no longer allocate copies of tool payloads they do not use; transcript
  tail reads also remain bounded while the agent appends output.
- **Streamed code and screenshots avoid repeated allocations.** Text rendering
  reuses shaping plans for compatible tokens in a row, and CPU screenshots take
  ownership of the finished pixels without copying another full framebuffer.
- **Recordings stay bounded when output arrives in tiny pieces.** Cast recordings
  and live byte subscriptions now retain at most 65,536 events as well as enforcing
  their existing byte limit. Older events can be discarded sooner under this limit;
  cast truncation and subscription gaps continue to report the loss.
- **A windowed aterm now keeps App Nap off for as long as it runs.** On a Mac saturated
  by other work, a window went three hours without running at all. Its shells and agents
  kept going, but every `aterm ctl` failed with
  `Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 35)` and every relay client with "timed out
  waiting for the server". It came back 5 ms after the window server took an App Nap
  assertion on it, and aterm had never asked to be kept out of App Nap. The window now
  holds one user-initiated activity for its whole life
  (`NSActivityUserInitiatedAllowingIdleSystemSleep`, so the Mac can still sleep when
  idle) and records it in `aterm.log`. There is no setting for it, and `--headless` is
  unchanged. This removes App Nap's throttling; it does not stop a machine that busy
  from starving aterm.
- **The freeze watchdog now logs a stalled window's whole stack, and no longer blames
  the window for hours in which aterm was not running at all.** During those three hours,
  `aterm.log` cut the stalled main thread's stack off at frame 11, because one log line
  holds at most 1 KiB. When aterm came back, the watchdog said the main thread had been
  stuck for all 12138 seconds. The stack is now written as numbered parts
  (`MAIN-THREAD STALL stack: (part 1/3, captured at …)`), each small enough to keep, and
  each part says when the stack was captured. The watchdog now times its whole cycle
  rather than only its sleep, so a gap anywhere in it is caught, logged, and left out of
  the stall's length. The gap line compares the wall clock with the uptime clock, which
  stops during sleep, so it can say whether aterm was not scheduled (App Nap or a
  starved CPU) or the Mac was asleep. A sleep on its own is logged as one info line.
- **`aterm ctl` now says when aterm took the connection and never answered, instead of
  printing `Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 35)`.** During those three hours
  every `aterm ctl` call connected, waited out its deadline, and printed only the
  operating system's words, which read like a broken client. A deadline that runs out
  after the connect now reads `no reply from <socket> within <N>s (connected; the server
  did not answer) — the request timed out`, and the call still exits 124. The same line
  covers the `--stdin` payloads, `help <verb>`, `cast drift` and `aterm conn` (whose exit
  status is unchanged). A connect that fails keeps its `connect <path>: …` line, a full
  non-blocking stdout keeps the operating system's words, and the supervisor still counts
  the new line as a request that was never answered.
- **A control verb that needs a stuck main thread is now turned away at once, instead of
  waiting out its 30-second deadline.** Before that window stopped running, its main
  thread was stuck inside macOS's status-item setup, and the rest of aterm was still up.
  A verb that needs the main thread (`key`, `send`, `tab`, `image`, `window`, `settings`
  and the rest) could only be handed to a thread that could not answer, and held a
  control worker until its deadline ran out, although the watchdog's heartbeat already
  showed the thread was stuck. Such a verb now gets
  `ERR main thread stalled <N>s since <root>; retry` straight away, before anything is
  sent to the main thread, in two cases. Either the main thread has not moved for 5
