  seconds since it entered one of aterm's handlers, or a verb has already waited 5
  seconds on a main thread that left its idle wait and never came back. `<root>` is the
  handler the watchdog's log line names. An idle window is not stuck, so the first verb
  after a long idle, and any verb that arrives while it is answered, are let through.
  The bar is 5 seconds in every build, with no setting, and a dialog keeps its own
  refusal. The supervisor retries the new refusal the same way it retries
  `ERR control server busy`, including when a verb puts its own words first
  (`ERR input dispatch failed: main thread stalled …`).
- **The stall refusal and the `no reply` line above now report only what happened.**
  `settings set` hands its write to the config worker and is answered only when the
  write is done, which can take seconds on a busy disk. The refusal counted that verb as
  waiting on the main thread the whole time. So once such a write took 5 seconds on an
  otherwise quiet window, every other verb that needs the main thread got
  `ERR main thread stalled …; retry`, although the window was fine. A verb now counts
  only until the main thread takes it. A caller holding a scoped token that sent an
  input verb (`key`, `send`, `paste`, `mouse` and the rest) to its own front tab got
  `ERR denied` in place of the refusal, and the audit log recorded an authority failure
  that never happened. It now gets the same
  `ERR main thread stalled <N>s since <root>; retry` as every other verb, and the
  supervisor retries it. When an `aterm ctl` deadline runs out after the server has
  begun its answer, the line now reads `reply from <socket> stopped part-way: nothing
  more within <N>s …`, not that the server did not answer. It still exits 124.
  `aterm drive --help` and `aterm help drive` now list the stall refusal among the
  replies `--reconnect-s` retries.

- **Usage totals count a streamed message at its final size.** A subagent's reply is
  written to its transcript several times as it streams, its output growing from a
  first count of a few tokens to the final one, and the usage fold kept the first: it
  missed 93% of subagent output (measured over 1,527 subagent files). Each message now
  counts once, at its largest figures.

- **A limit reset that names its year is read.** Late in December Claude Code prints a
  weekly reset in the next year as `Jan 2, 2027 at 9am`; that did not parse, so the
  supervisor fell back to its back-off, the band showed no countdown and `harness
  limits` no reset. It parses now.

- **`approve = "safe"` no longer presses an rm breaker whose removal can reach outside
  scratch.** The rule that proves Claude Code's `Dangerous rm operation on possibly-empty
  variable path` box read the line as text, and pressed lines that remove `/etc` when
  they run: `D=$(mktemp -d); rm -rf "$D/etc"` (a `mktemp` that fails leaves `D` empty),
  zsh's `$=S` and `$S:h`, `$_`, `PWD` and the other names the shell keeps, `S=/etc
  export T=$S`, `echo hi < $~X` (zsh globs a builtin's redirect in the shell itself, and
  a glob qualifier in `X` can set a variable), and a symbolic link out of the scratch
  directory. It also pressed `A=S=5; printf %d A; rm -rf "$S/x"` and `printf -%d S=5;
  rm -rf "$S/x"`, where zsh sets `S=5` (it reads `A`'s value as arithmetic, and takes
  `-%d` as the format), the same through brace expansion (`printf {%d,A}` is `printf
  %d A`, `[ {-t,A} ]` is `[ -t A ]`) or a glob beside a file named `S=5` (`printf %d
  *`), and `echo hi {S}>/dev/null; rm -rf "$S/x"`, where zsh stores a descriptor's
  number in `S`, so the rm removed `5/x`, or a directory named for the descriptor's
  number, wherever the Bash tool's working directory was; and bash's `printf {-vS,%s}
  /etc; rm -rf "$S/x"`, which brace expansion makes `printf -vS %s /etc`, so the rm
  removed `/etc/x`. Each is now handed to you, naming why. A variable the line does
  not set itself is never proven: `rm -rf "$TMPDIR/x"` is yours, because the Bash tool's
  `$TMPDIR` need not be the supervisor's. Still pressed: literal paths and variables the
  line sets itself under a scratch root, as written and where their symbolic links lead
  on the disk — unless a later command may change the variable: a builtin that names it
  (`print -v S`, `stat -A S`, zsh's `echo hi {S}>file`, which stores a descriptor's
  number in `S`), a word zsh reads as arithmetic (`printf %d`, `printf -%d` — zsh's
  `printf` takes a `-` word other than `-v` as its format —, `[ -t`), a word the shell
  brace-expands or globs where such a command reads its words (one that starts with `/`
  expands to paths only, and is read as before; zsh's `EXTENDED_GLOB`, which a user's
  `setopt` carries into the Bash tool's shell, globs on `^`, `#` and `~` too, so `[ ^-vS
  ]` beside files `-t` and `S=5` is `[ -t S=5 ]`, and `rm -rf <scratch>/^x` removes every
  name there but `x` — both are yours now), or a word the rule cannot read — unquoted, or
  quoted but handed to a command other than a read-only program such as `echo`, `ls`,
  `grep`, `jq`, `sed` or `shasum` (a double-quoted word `printf` takes as data after a
  plainly written format with no numeric conversion, `printf '%s\n' "$x"`, is read as
  before); the reason names that command. The rest of the line must still be a read, and
  zsh arithmetic that can run a command is not one (below). Also pressed: a directory the line's own `mktemp -d` made — `"$D"`, or a path
  under it behind `&&`, `|| exit` or `${D:?}` with every `$D` double-quoted. The same
  holds under the retired `approve_all`, `read_outside_cwd` and `trust_dialog = false`;
  under the retired `rm_breaker = false` no rm is proven, a fresh `mktemp -d` directory
  included. The default (`approve = "all"`) presses every such box as before; its ledger
  row says `allow-once@v1` with the reason, and a proven one `rm-breaker@v3`.

- **The read-only check no longer takes zsh arithmetic that can run a command as a
  read.** zsh's arithmetic runs a command substitution inside an array subscript — from a
  quoted word, a variable's value or a file name a glob makes — and zsh evaluates as
  arithmetic `printf`'s arguments under a numeric format, the operand of `-t` in `test`,
  `[` and `[[`, the values of `export -i`, and a value assigned to one of its integer
  variables — the 23 zsh 5.9 evaluates, measured over all 298 names it declares or
  documents (`SECONDS`, `COLUMNS`, `ERRNO`, `ZLE_RPROMPT_INDENT`, …, and `DIRSTACKSIZE`,
  `REPORTTIME` and `REPORTMEMORY`, which it evaluates when it uses them: at a `cd`, when
  a forked job ends), and `MBEGIN` and `MEND`, which a matching `[[ … =~ … ]]` makes
  integer —, by assignment, as a `for` loop's variable or by `${NAME:=v}`. So `printf %d
  'path[$(cmd)]'`, `[ -t "$A" ]` with `A='path[$(cmd)]'`, `SECONDS='path[$(cmd)]'`, `for
  SECONDS in 'path[$(cmd)]'; do …` or `echo ${REPORTTIME:=A}; cat f | cat` ran `cmd`,
  and the check took each as a read: `approve = "safe"` pressed it on a Bash box, and
  beside a proven rm on the breaker. Such a word must now be a plain number (`printf
  '%d\n' 5`, `[ -t 1 ]`, `for SECONDS in 1 2` stay reads) wherever the check sees the
  arithmetic — inside a `${…}` operand and a here-document too (`${x:-$path[A]}`,
  `${x:-$[A]}`), behind zsh's flags (`$=A[A]`), on a special parameter (`$*[A]`,
  `"$#[A]"`, which also set a variable an rm beside it removed), and under a `printf`
  format that spells its `%` as a Unicode escape (a backslash, then `u0025`), which zsh
  decodes into a conversion before it reads the format (an escape that decodes to
  anything else, `printf '<check mark> %s\n' "$x"`, reads as before); `export
  -i`/`-E`/`-F` is not a read, nor is a `test`/`[` word the shell may brace-expand or
  glob into `-t` (under `EXTENDED_GLOB`, `^`, `#` and `~` glob too: `[ ^-vS ]`), nor a
  `printf` word before the format that may become `-v` the same way (bash's `printf
  {-vS,%s} /etc` assigns `S`), nor a `for` loop that sets `PATH` or another variable an
  assignment may not set.

- **The read-only check no longer takes a zsh glob qualifier that runs a command as a
  read.** zsh's `~` parameter flag globs a variable's value, and a glob qualifier in it —
  `(e:…:)`, `(+cmd)` — runs a command: `N='/(e:cmd:)'; echo $~N` (also `ls $~N`, `echo
  $^~N`) ran `cmd` and was a read, in every earlier version. A `$~` flag is no read now,
  inside a `${…}` operand too (`${x:-$~N}`), nor is an unquoted `(` inside a word (`echo
  "/"(e:cmd:)`, `echo $(print /)(e:cmd:)`), which zsh reads as a glob group or
  qualifier; a `(` that opens a subshell, `$((…))` or `<(…)` is judged as before.

- **The read-only check no longer takes a zsh assignment that picks the next program
  as a read.** zsh ties the array `path` to `PATH`, so `path=/tmp/x ls`, `path=/tmp/x;
  ls` and `for path in /tmp/x; do ls; done` ran `/tmp/x/ls` and were reads; so were
  `READNULLCMD=/tmp/x; < f` and `NULLCMD=/tmp/x; > /dev/null`, which run `/tmp/x`, and
  `module_path=/tmp/x; echo $terminfo`, which loads a library from `/tmp/x`. Every
  array zsh ties (`path`, `cdpath`, `fpath`, `manpath`, `module_path`, …) is now judged
  as its scalar, and `READNULLCMD`, `NULLCMD`, `MODULE_PATH` and `STTY` (run as code
  from a command's prefix on a terminal) are hazards like `PATH`: measured over every
  name zsh 5.9 declares or documents, none other runs or loads its value during a line
  of reads. Beside a proven rm, a command that only assigns was not judged at all, so
  `PAGER=/tmp/x; git log; rm -rf <scratch>/x` pressed; its assignments are judged now,
  and so is a default assignment (`echo ${READNULLCMD:=/tmp/x}; < f`, `${path=/tmp/x}`).
  `path=/bin ls` stays a read. A user's `setopt globsubst` in Claude Code's shell
  snapshot is still not seen (`docs/AUDIT-claude-harness-2026-09-23.md` §5).

- **An rm beside a `[ -n "$x" ]` is proven again.** Since the rm proof began reading
  arithmetic, a `[`/`test` with a double-quoted variable the line does not set made
  every variable unknown, so `S=<scratch>; [ -n "$x" ]; rm -rf "$S/x"`, `[ -d "$HOME" ]
  && rm -rf "$S/x"` and `[ -n "$1" ] && rm …` were handed to you, though they were
  pressed before. A quoted string or file operand of a one-, two- or three-word test is
  read as data again (measured in zsh 5.9 and bash 3.2: no value there assigns or runs
  anything). `-t`'s operand, which zsh evaluates as arithmetic, `-v`'s, whose subscript
  it evaluates, a word the shell may glob or brace-expand, `"$@"` (as many words as
  there are arguments: `[ "$@" ]` with the arguments `-t S=0` sets `S`), and a longer
  test still escalate; `[[` is yours as before.

- **`approve = "safe"` no longer presses an rm breaker whose line writes a file with a
  `mktemp` redirect.** The rest of an rm line is judged as a read, but the `mktemp`
  commands whose directory the proof follows, and the rm itself, were left out of it
  whole, redirects included, and the proof refused a redirect on the rm only. So
  `mktemp > ~/.zshrc; rm -rf <scratch>/x` (also `>>`, `2>`, `&>`, `1<>`, and `rm -rf
  <scratch>/x 2>/dev/null; mktemp > .git/HEAD`) was pressed, and the shell truncated the
  file; in every earlier version. Their redirects are judged now: `/dev/null` and a
  descriptor (`>&2`) pass, as everywhere else.

- **The read-only check no longer takes `sed -I`, a bash `${!NAME}` or a command after
  a zsh `}` or `]]` as a read.** macOS sed edits files in place under `-I` as under `-i`
  (`sed -I '' s/a/b/ f`, `sed -nI '' p f`, `xargs sed -I …`), but the check looked for a
  lowercase `i` only, so `approve = "safe"` pressed such a Bash box, beside a proven rm
  too. bash's `${!A}` expands the parameter `A`'s value names, subscript and all:
  `A='a[$(cmd)]'; echo "${!A}"` (also `${!A:-x}`, `${!A[0]}`, `[ -n "${!A}" ]`) ran `cmd`
  under bash 3.2 and was a read; an indirection is no read now, nor bash 4.4's
  `${NAME@OP}` (`@P` expands a value as a prompt; not measured here), while the
  listings `${!A[@]}` and `${!A*}` stay reads, as does `${!#}`, the last positional
  parameter. zsh runs a command written after a closing `}` or `]]` in the same list,
  and a `}` glued to the end of a word closes the group too: `{ ls } always { cmd }`,
  `if [[ -n a ]] cmd`, `if { ls } cmd` and `{ ls a} always { cmd }` ran `cmd`, which the
  check read as an argument of `ls` or `[[`; a word after a closing `}` or `]]` makes the
  line no read now. The group's own redirects do not (`{ ls }`, `{ ls } 2>/dev/null`,
  `[[ -f x ]] 2>/dev/null` and `[[ -n $x ]] && ls` stay reads), nor does a `}` on a line
  with no `{` (`echo } x`, which zsh refuses to parse). All three were in every earlier
  version; beside an rm the proof already refused the `${!A}` and the `{`.

- **A release can no longer leave Linux behind by accident, and the cutter builds Linux
  itself.** Every release from v0.86.0 through v0.93.0 shipped Mac-only, because leaving out
  `--linux-artifacts` silently made a Mac-only cut, so Linux installs never received an
  update. `ship cut` now refuses a real or rehearsal cut that names neither
  `--linux-artifacts` nor `--mac-only`, before it claims anything. And `--linux-worker
  ARCH=HOST:REPO` has the cutter build that architecture on a native Linux host over ssh,
  at the claim commit, in a throwaway worktree, and copy the result back for the usual
  provenance checks — no hand-carried handoff needed (docs/RELEASING.md, "The cutter can
  drive the workers itself").
- **A live upgrade no longer offers Upgrade now for a Claude that a question box holds.**
  A session found behind when its tab attached, or whose upgrade notice had just been
  typed, recorded no wait until the next look, and a look comes only at an idle screen or
  a break of the agent's own work. So a permission or question box, or a turn of hours,
  left the row reading "waiting on nothing": after six hours it was a warning with a tab
  mark whose Upgrade now could not move the session, and pressing it hid the row for half
  an hour before it came back. Such a row now reads Claude Code's own live status as its
  wait, never over a word a look recorded. A box reads "it asked a question and waits" and
  offers Not today and Skip version only. A background shell reads "its own work runs". A
  turn still running waits for its end (the waiting ladder's last rung), with no Upgrade now:
  nothing ends a turn for the upgrade. The window reads
  that status again whenever the tab's screen moves, so a box answered becomes the turn
  that follows it, not a question still waiting for the whole of that turn.
  `aterm harness upgrade --status` shows the same (`wait=not-idle:waiting`), with how long
  that status has stood.
- **An agent the upgrade stopped and has not yet told to carry on is shown.** When the
  upgrade abandons a notice it gave the agent (it gave up asking, voided a READY, was held
  by the owner's word, or its target changed), the agent is owed one line telling it to
  carry on. Until that line is typed, `aterm harness upgrade --status` carries `release=`,
  just before the line's last field `rung=`, with the reason (`gave-up`, `void`, `skipped`, `deferred`, `retargeted` or the stop's
  reason; `-` for none) and `--json` carries `release`. While the line's own gate holds it,
  the wait `release:<gate>` reads "it is owed the line telling it to carry on" on the
  band, and a round that gave up says the line is owed instead of only "it has not agreed
  to the move yet". Both are in `aterm harness --help` and `aterm help harness`. A line
  the upgrade dropped because it is no longer its to type (another process holds the
  conversation, or the agent took up newer direction) is no longer said to be owed: the
  gate's wait goes with it.
- **The upgrade ledger says when a restart under way is stuck.** A Claude Code whose
  shutdown hangs after the upgrade's SIGTERM, and a relaunched Claude Code that never
  becomes idle to be told to carry on, wait with no bound, and
  `aterm harness ledger upgrade` ended at `terminated` or `relaunched` for as long as they
  lasted while `--status` read `stuck`. Five minutes in, a sweep now writes one
  `stuck:exiting`, `stuck:exited` or `stuck:relaunched` row saying what it waits on. It
  is a note only: nothing is signalled, typed or failed for it, and a later sweep that
  finds the same wait writes nothing more.
- **A tab no longer says Claude needs approval long after the question was answered.**
  The Claude Code hooks aterm used to install marked a tab `claude needs approval: …`
  when Claude asked permission, and only those hooks could clear the mark. They were
  removed, so a mark they left stayed: it came back with every update, restore and
  crash recovery, and showed again whenever the harness cleared its own. A busy agent's
  tab read "Claude needs your permission" two days after its question was answered. Such a
  mark is now dropped when aterm restarts or updates, and the first update into this
  release clears any that still stand. A mark you set yourself with
  `meta set attention` still carries over, unless it begins with those same words.
- **The log says whether each "needs you" notification went out.** When a tab needed
  you, aterm decided whether to show a macOS notification (or not, because you were
  already looking, or because too many had just gone out), and wrote none of it down, so
  after a long wait nobody could tell from the log which notifications were ever shown.
  Each decision is now one line in aterm.log: queued (and how many it gathers up), not
  queued because you were looking or because of the rate limit, or refused by the
  notifier. The lines name the tab and the kind of wait, never the command or message,
  and a tab whose question flickers writes at most one "not queued" line every 20 seconds.
- **A shell that fails at start, or whose folder is gone, no longer disappears without a
  word.** An interactive shell that exits non-zero or crashes before its first prompt,
  within two seconds of starting, keeps its pane open with one line, such as `[zsh ended
  at start: exit 1]`, instead of closing its tab or quitting aterm. On macOS and Linux,
  a tab whose folder no longer exists opens in your home folder, and one message names
  the folder it could not find or open. `aterm ctl spawn cwd=` with such a folder is
  refused with `ERR no such folder <path>` or `ERR no access to folder <path>`, and the
  crash-restore message counts those panes, except one that ssh or another program held,
  whose folder may be on another machine. The Linux package stager says "no machine key"
  only on a box without one and shows gh's real error for a manifest it cannot fetch.
  The `--verbose` sandbox line no longer claims protections when `$HOME` does not
  resolve, and the paste prompt counts lone carriage returns. The merge gate's UNDER
  LOAD label no longer calls a type error a clock running out.
- **Menus, release scripts, gate output and the protocol docs say what is true.** The
  macOS menu bar checks and greys the same rows as the command palette, ⌘W's row reads
  "Close Pane" on a split tab, Help off macOS opens the public project page, and
  `--list-keybinds` lists every menu shortcut in the menu's words. The release and
  package-publishing scripts print remedies that work. The build and merge-contract
  gates print one line on a pass, fill in their fix commands, and aterm-nest reports a
  command that did not finish. The ctl man page, the operator brief and the
  introspection guide match the live protocol, and `aterm drive` takes its prompt
  pattern only from `--ready`: `aterm pkg doctor` flags a leftover `ATERM_DRIVE_READY`.
  After a crash, a pane that ran ssh opens in the default folder instead of reporting a
  remote folder as missing.
- **The control socket repairs itself when it stops taking connections, and `aterm ctl`
  says so in seconds instead of hanging for 15 minutes.** On 2026-09-25 an instance's
  control listener stopped accepting while the window kept working: thirteen connections
  sat in its queue, and every `aterm ctl` waited out its 15-minute deadline with no word.
  A watchdog thread now judges the listener; when it has not come back for three seconds,
  or connections stay queued with none taken, it binds a fresh socket at the same path
  (same token, owner-only) and new clients are served there. `aterm ctl metrics` reports
  it: `control_accepts`, `control_last_accept_age_ms`, `control_queue_pending`,
  `control_rebinds`, `control_rebind_failures`, `control_accept_errors` and
  `control_busy_replies`. `aterm ctl` now checks that the instance took its connection
  before it sends the request: with no answer within 10 seconds (or a shorter
  `--timeout`) it exits 2 with `no answer from <socket> within 10s: the instance took no
  request, so none was sent`, and says the two causes it cannot tell apart: a listener
  that is not taking connections, or a process that is not running (stopped, App Nap, a
  saturated machine). A supervising agent loop counts that as a request not served, as it
  did the old timeout. A busy instance's `ERR control server busy; retry` is reported as
  that, not as "Broken pipe". A forward to a child aterm (`@<sid>`) and a `dial` check the
  far end the same way before they relay. A client killed while it waits in `await`,
  `ready`, `wait`, `turn`, `await inbox`, `await consent` or `post --wait` gives its place
  on the socket back within about a fifth of a second, not when its timeout ends: while
  a socket caller waits, the wait wakes five times a second to check that it is still
  there. A `turn` whose caller dies after its text is typed still submits it, and
  `history` records it with `status=hangup`.

- **A slow moment no longer holds a healthy update for a day, or until you reinstall.**
  Before switching to a new version, aterm checks the signatures of the new copy and of
  the installed one, and each check has a time limit. On a busy Mac, or when Gatekeeper
  waited on a slow network, a check could run out of time. If it was the installed
  copy's check, aterm said that copy could not be updated, asked you to reinstall an app
  that was fine, and stopped updating automatically. Any other check that ran out of
  time, or another aterm holding the installer for more than 10 seconds, was counted as a
  fault in the new version: after two, the update waited a day. The same happened when
  the new version could not install for one of those reasons and quit. Now all of these
  count as a passing moment. aterm tries again by itself 10 minutes later, then less
  often. It keeps the downloaded update instead of discarding it, and never asks you to
  reinstall because of one. The Software Update page says "the new version could not be
  checked just then". A check that finishes and fails still stops the update and says
  why, as before.

- **An update no longer frees a halted session.** A session stopped with `hold` (by you,
  over the control socket, or by the fleet, including the halt aterm applies itself when
  its fabric connection is lost) was free again after every in-place update, with
  nothing said: the new version started its sessions without their halts, so an agent
  you had stopped could type again, sometimes minutes after you stopped it when the
  update was automatic. Now each halt, with its reason and who set it, comes across
  with its session and is back before the session can take a single command. A fleet
  halt is still lifted only by the fleet, and it stays in place while the fleet cannot
  be reached, as before. A halt set while the update is taking over now makes that
  attempt stand down, with every session left as it was, instead of being lost; an
  automatic update tries again later. A halt set in the last instant, after the update
  has compared the halts, waits for it instead: it is answered once the update has
  either landed (the connection closes, and the new version answers the retry) or stood
  down, and never with an OK the new version did not receive. This applies to updates
  from this version on; the update into this version carries no halts, because the
  version you are updating from does not write them.

- **A tab keeps its title across an update.** A title a program gave its tab (a
  terminal title, as vim, ssh or Claude Code set one), the icon name, and the titles a
  program saved to put back when it exits were all dropped by an in-place update: the
  tab showed its folder until the program set a title again, and quitting the program
  afterwards put back nothing. Now all three come across with the screen, cleaned the
  same way as when a program sets them. The update into this version already keeps the
  title each tab showed when it was last in front; the icon name and the saved titles
  come across from the next update on.

- **An update no longer takes a session away from its supervisor.** When a supervisor
  outside the window (such as `aterm-agent watch`, or a script using `meta set
  supervisor`) was looking after an agent's tab, the new version's own supervisor took
  the tab the moment an in-place update finished. The outside supervisor's next renewal
  was refused, and it was left only watching. Now a claim made with `ttl=` comes across
  with its session for the rest of its time, so its supervisor keeps the tab. For a tab
  whose claim cannot come across (one tied to its connection, or any claim when updating
  from an older version), aterm's own supervisor waits 45 seconds before it takes the
  tab, which gives the outside supervisor time to claim it again. Every attention
  request (`meta set attention owner=…`) now comes across too, so an escalation nobody
  has answered stays in the menu bar. Only the one without an owner came across before.
  A drive lease (`lease`) still does not come across; its holder acquires it again. The
  45-second wait helps from the update into this version. Claims and escalations come
  across from the next update on.

- **A zoomed font stays zoomed across an update.** If you had changed the text size with
  Cmd-= or Cmd--, an in-place update brought the window back at your configured size.
  The window was drawn with the zoomed number of rows and columns, so both the window and
  its text changed size. Now the zoom comes across, so text and window stay the same,
  and Cmd-0 still returns to the size you had before zooming. This applies to updates
  from this version on.

- **An update no longer drops agents aterm is bringing back.** After aterm stopped
  unexpectedly, or quit for a restart, it reopens your tabs and starts Claude again on
  its conversation in each tab that had it, and the reopened-layout message says so.
  An in-place update that landed while that was still under way dropped every agent
  not yet started: they never came back, and nothing said so. An update also left
  behind an agent restart of its own that was halfway done (the agent already ended,
  the line that starts it again not yet typed), so that tab stayed at its shell prompt.
  Now an automatic update waits while agents are still being brought back, for at most
  7 minutes from the first one, and says so: aterm's log notes when that wait starts and
  ends, and `aterm ctl update status` shows `apply_held=restored-agents` while it lasts.
  Past that, or when you update from the Version menu,
  the new version finishes starting the agents that were left, in the same tabs, and
  says which it could not bring back. It also finishes any agent restart the previous
  version left halfway. Finishing a halfway restart applies to the update into this
  version; the rest applies to updates from this version on.

- **A stopped aterm no longer stops update checks on the whole Mac.** Every aterm on a
  Mac checks for updates under one shared lock, so that only one of them checks at a
  time. An aterm that was stopped in the middle of a check (for example with ctrl-z in
  a terminal where it ran) kept that lock, and every other aterm waited for it for as
  long as it stayed stopped, with nothing said. Now an aterm that holds the lock marks it
  every few seconds while it is still working, a long download on a slow link included.
  When another aterm has held the lock through three checks in a row with no such mark,
  aterm checks without it, logs which process holds it, and shows a message that
  another aterm may be stopped or hung. The message goes away when that aterm lets go of
  the lock or works again. aterm also checks without the lock straight away when no
  aterm on the Mac has finished a check for about four hours and the one holding the
  lock shows no sign of working. An aterm of this version or later that is still
  downloading an update is never reported as stopped, however long the download takes,
  and a Mac waking from sleep no longer races the aterm that has just started checking.

- **On Linux, a copy you use only from the terminal keeps updating.** An update replaces
  the aterm file on disk, and the next aterm started from it has to confirm the new
  version works. Before this, only an aterm window could confirm it. A copy used only
  from the terminal installed one update and then waited for a window that never opened:
  it checked for nothing more, and a new version that did not work was never put back
  either. Now a terminal session started from the new file counts as a start too, and
  confirms the update once its shell prints its first output (or after 10 seconds).
  After three starts that never get that far, the next start puts the previous version
  back, as it did for windows. Several sessions started at the same moment (a terminal
  restoring its tabs, for example) no longer count as a failed update before one of them
  has had time to confirm it, and a version restarted over and over (a service that
  restarts every few seconds) is still put back, at its first start 20 seconds or more
  after the third. A terminal session confirms the update for the terminal only:
  windows still count their own starts after a session has confirmed it, from zero,
  until a window confirms it, so a version whose window does not open is put back even
  when you look into it by typing `aterm` in a terminal. One window that never opened
  (an `aterm` run with no terminal on a machine with no display, or a window closed at
  logout before it drew) no longer keeps your terminal sessions from confirming the
  update, and those sessions no longer count toward putting it back. The messages that asked for "an aterm window" now say the next
  aterm you start finishes the update. A copy that is already waiting from before this
  version cannot receive this fix by itself: start an aterm window from it once, or,
  where no window can open, run `aterm update rollback`, and the next release installs
  as usual.

- **On Linux, an update that cannot be undone no longer stops updates for good.** When a
  new version failed to start three times, aterm put the previous one back. But if the
  previous version was not allowed back (it was withdrawn, or the machine that signed it
  was revoked), aterm refused, and every later start, update check, install and `aterm
  update rollback` then waited on that update forever. Now aterm keeps the new version,
  says why the previous one could not come back, and installs the next release over it
  as usual. The same holds when the copy aterm kept of the previous version has changed
  on disk, and such a copy is never picked as the version a later update goes back to.

- **On Linux, a headless aterm no longer vouches for aterm windows after an update.** An
  `aterm --headless` instance (an agent harness, a service) counted as a window when an
  update was being tried, so once it had started, a new version whose windows crash was
  never put back. It now counts as a terminal session does, and only a window that opens
  shows that windows work.

- **On Linux, an update installed while aterm 0.98 is still running keeps its checks.**
  The aterm that installs an update keeps running the version before it, and 0.98 saves
  the whole update record without the fields it does not know. That dropped what a newer
  version records about its windows, so a version whose windows crash could stay
  installed for good. A record saved by 0.98 now reads as "the windows have not shown
  they work yet", and a window that works simply shows it again. A 0.98 save in the
  middle of several terminal tabs starting at once no longer makes the next of them put
  a healthy version back before any tab has shown its prompt.

- **On Linux, a later update no longer rolls back to a version whose window had
  crashed.** When a terminal session had confirmed a new version but one of its windows
  had since failed to open, the next release took that version as the one to go back
  to. Now it goes back to the version before it, as long as that version is still
  allowed back; when it is not (it was withdrawn, or its signer revoked), it goes back
  to the version it replaced, as before.

- **On Linux, old versions no longer pile up on disk.** Every update kept a full copy of
  the version it replaced, and none was ever removed. Now aterm keeps only the one copy
  it could still go back to, and removes it once it is no longer needed.

- **On Linux, update results are no longer shown as warnings.** Every window launch
  showed the latest update result ("Up to date", "aterm X is installed") as a warning,
  and a real failure later in the same launch was then not shown at all. Now only update
  checks that keep failing (three in a row) are shown, a changed reason is noted
  quietly, and the warning goes away once checks work again. Opening a window also no
  longer replaces the reason a failing check recorded with "aterm X is installed".

- **A logout, restart or shutdown is no longer cancelled by aterm after an update.** On
  macOS, a quit request (from the Dock, AppleScript, or a logout, restart or shutdown)
  that arrived in the few seconds while an updated aterm was taking over was set aside
  and never answered inside aterm. From then on that aterm refused every quit request of
  that kind: each later logout, restart or shutdown reported that aterm cancelled it,
  until aterm was quit from its own menu. Now a request that arrives in that moment is
  answered as cancelled right away, the same as macOS was already told, and the next
  one works as usual. A logout or restart that was cancelled this way, or cancelled by
  you, also no longer makes your next Quit keep your agents for the next start as if the
  system had quit aterm. This applies from the update into this version on.

- **The release process now checks that this version takes back everything 0.97 sends.**
  When 0.97 updates in place, it hands its open sessions to the new version, and it is
  0.97's own code that writes that handoff. The files 0.97 writes were already checked in;
  they now also cover the two ways a new version can ask 0.97 to carry less (the visible
  screen only, or a blank screen its program redraws), and the check now also reads the
  numbering, colours and shell-integration state that 0.95 and later send. The release
  process now runs that check itself, in the tree it builds, and refuses to release when
  it fails or when any required kind of desk is missing for the release being replaced.
  Each desk is required from the release that first writes it, so a desk added for a
  later release is never asked of an earlier one.

- **aterm no longer switches Codex's model on its own.** When Codex showed its
  "Approaching rate limits" box, the supervisor pressed its "Switch to gpt-6-luna" as if it
  were Claude Code's model-refusal pause: at 99% of the weekly window, and again at 1% twenty
  minutes after a usage reset, when the box was stale. Nothing read the switch back, so the
  session stayed on the cheaper model, and the supervisor kept typing `keep going` into it.
  Now the rule that answers Claude Code's refusal pause answers that pause alone — the
  box titled "Session paused" whose options are exactly its switch and "Edit prompt and
  retry…" — and still presses its switch while `[harness] model_fallback` is set. No other
  box's "Switch to …" is pressed by it. Codex's box is answered by its own
  rule (below), and Codex's "Continue with Luna Reserve" and "Continue with detected
  credentials" are no longer taken for a usage consent.

- **A Codex whose goal is running is no longer typed into.** Codex starts the next turn of
  its goal by itself within milliseconds of a turn's end, so a `keep going` typed there
  landed inside that turn as a steer. The supervisor now types no continuation while
  Codex's footer says its goal is being pursued. A goal that Codex's usage limit stopped is
  resumed with `/goal resume` once the limit resets.

- **A Codex thread that fell into a sandbox is no longer driven on.** When Codex's
  background server restarted itself, a thread launched with
  `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` came back in Codex's workspace sandbox and
  spent hours failing to commit or push. When every thread Codex has lately written in the
  session's folder runs sandboxed although the launch bypassed the sandbox, the supervisor
  types nothing into it and says once how to fix it: quit Codex and resume the thread with
  its launch flags. Each thread's sandbox is read from its own last turn record, read
  backward from the end of its log, so a long turn no longer hides the session's own thread
  and lets another thread in the folder decide. When the session's own thread is known —
  the thread lock its Codex holds open, or the thread it was resumed with — that thread
  alone decides, however long it has been idle; otherwise only threads written around the
  session's last work count, so a thread another tab wrote while this one sat waiting is
  none of its.

- **Two Codex screens are read correctly.** A usage limit followed by Codex's `Tip:` row
  now reads its reset time, so the wait lasts until the reset instead of about twenty
  minutes. A turn waiting on a background terminal, whose status row carries
  `· 1 background terminal running · …` after its Esc hint, now reads as busy.

- **A Codex upgrade no longer sits behind for hours in a goal-mode tab.** Codex 0.158.0 draws
  its input line with `»` instead of `›`. aterm did not recognise it as the input line, so
  nothing that acts at a quiet moment ran in that tab again: not the supervisor, not the
  upgrade, not `Upgrade now`. It is recognised now, and text aterm types there is guarded
  on the mark that is drawn. A Codex that is already current is still checked for pinning
  its background service (whose own updater restarted it mid-turn that morning), but at most
  once an hour, and never with a note, a mark or a hold on the tab's turns: that was a check
  at every turn one night.

- **An upgrade no longer claims it moves "at its next turn end".** A Codex working through a
  goal starts its next turn within a few milliseconds of the last, so that turn end never
  came. The words now say when the upgrade really moves. A Codex whose own conversation is
  still running a turn in its background service is not moved: quitting it then might stop
  the turn (Codex 0.158.0 carries a message saying so; when it is printed is not yet
  measured), so a goal keeps it where it is until the goal pauses. The same holds for the
  subagents a conversation starts: they run in the service where no screen shows them, and a
  turn of one is that tab's own work. A turn in another Codex session on the same service
  holds it only until aterm can tell that session is another tab's — which it never assumes
  while a goal is being pursued in this tab, since that goal's own next turn can run while
  the screen looks finished, nor for a subagent's turn, nor while that Codex is the
  service's only window — and is described neither as a goal to pause in this tab nor as
  surely another session's. The last look before quitting Codex checks the service again, so
  a turn that started a moment earlier still holds it. And a conversation that has finished
  is no longer taken for one still running because the last thing Codex wrote to its log is
  very long (a command's output, half a megabyte in the case measured, written after the
  turn ended): aterm reads the log back past it, up to 8 MiB, and only past that still
  assumes a turn may be running.

- **A Codex upgrade no longer stalls in a tab whose shell integration stopped working** (as
  after an aterm update). When its background service runs only that one conversation —
  with any subagents it started — and that Codex is its only window onto it, aterm now knows
  which conversation to resume without the shell's marks, and the relaunch line restores the
  marks as well.

- **`aterm help pkg` no longer points at a status row that is gone.** The fix for a tab
  from before an update (`. ~/.aterm/shell.d/00-atpkg.zsh`) was described as "the same
  line the window's status row says"; since 2026-09-22 the window records it only as an
  entry in `aterm ctl appstatus`. The page says so, and that sourcing the hook re-reads
  PATH, which also empties zsh's command hash, so a `claude` the shell had hashed to
  another copy is looked up again.

- **A Claude Code session at a usage limit continues by itself, and never buys usage
  credits there.** Claude Code waits out a limit on its own only when it resets within 24
  hours; a weekly limit stops at a "What do you want to do?" menu, which the window's
  supervisor did not know. The supervisor now reads that menu as its own kind and chooses
  "Wait here, then continue automatically" by its label, whatever `[harness] approve`
  says — never "Stop and wait", "Switch to usage credits", "Add funds", a plan upgrade or
  a limit reset. Full power had read "Switch to usage credits" as a model switch and, with
  `model_fallback` set (the default), would have pressed it; it now decides the menu
  first, and "Switch to usage credits" (any option that opens by naming usage credits) is
  a purchase it never presses on any box. A menu without the wait row goes to the menu
  bar; `[harness] limit_wait = false` hands the menu back to you.

- **After an update the menu bar names the version that is running.** A seamless update
  could leave the Version menu reading the old version with the update arrow (`v0.91.0 ⬆`
  over a running 0.92.0) until the window was clicked, because macOS kept showing the
  menu of the process that had quit. The outgoing process now titles the bar for its
  successor (plain `v<version>`, no arrow), the successor no longer asks to activate at
  launch, and a park that catches a terminal mid-sequence tries again on the same rung
  rather than climbing to a longer freeze. The outgoing build does the titling, so the
  update that installs this version can still show the old title; later updates do not.

- **An update's successor hands its claim only to the terminal it is replacing.** The
  launched successor checked only that the handoff rendezvous belonged to the same user
  before sending its one-time claim; it now also requires the kernel to name the
  listening process as the attested outgoing terminal, still alive, and exits before any
  window otherwise, leaving every session with the running terminal.

- **Saved connections stop calling their launch-nonce pin broken.** Settings and the config
  diagnostics said `expect_nonce` always refuses to dial and `sid` does nothing; the pin
  is enforced against the remote's session roster (since 2026-09-25), so only a `sid` set
  without `expect_nonce` is now reported (it is the one inert combination).

- **Kitty graphics no longer draws an image twice, keeps no leftovers, and leaves other
  protocols' images alone.** A `U=1` transmit (the way yazi and tmux-hosted tools draw)
  used to draw at the cursor as well as through its placeholders. It now draws only
  through the placeholders. Sending an image id again removes that image's old
  placements, and a Kitty delete no longer erases an iTerm2 or sixel image. On an `a=f`
  animation frame, `c=`, `r=` and `z=` are animation keys, so they no longer resize or
  reorder the frame, which keeps its image's layout. `a=a` now selects a frame with `c=`,
  as kitty's protocol says (it read `r=`, which names the frame whose timing changes), and
  the selected frame shows in every placement of the image, not only in its placeholders.

- **A failed command marks its tab, and `aterm ctl status` reports its exit code.** Under
  aterm's own shell integration the next prompt closes a finished command right behind the
  line that reports its exit, and the session status read only the block still open — so every
  command read as `outcome=none`, no failure ever put the red mark on its tab, and
  `subscribe … events` pushed `block-complete … exit=1` beside `status … outcome=none`. A
  prompt now reports the command it closed, and only that one: an empty Enter brings no
  older result back.

- **An AI tool's variable can no longer ride into a shell under a non-UTF-8 name.** A child
  shell (and the fabric bridge) never inherits `ANTHROPIC_*`, `CLAUDE*` and the other
  AI-tool and provisioning variables — but a variable whose NAME was not valid UTF-8
  skipped that check, so `ANTHROPIC_` followed by a stray byte was passed on. Such a name
  is now read by its lossy spelling, which keeps the prefix.

- **`cursor_trail = false` turns the typing-momentum glow off too.** The settings file has
  always said the effects master turns the glow off with everything else, but typing fast
  into a window with `cursor_trail = false` still lit the warm halo and the steady caret.
  The glow now follows the master (a trail style of `off` still keeps it, as before), and
  its Settings row says "Inactive · Cursor trail Off" while the master is off instead of
  looking checked and live. On Windows, where the cursor effects are off by default, this
  means the glow is off by default too until `cursor_trail = true` turns them on.

- **The Copy row, the release runbooks and AGENTS.md say what is true.** ⌘C and Edit ▸
  Copy copy from the tab-rename field even with nothing selected in the terminal. The
  release runbooks match the cutter, the atpkg republish runbook gives commands that
  work, and a sysroot-bundle pack given `UPLOAD=1` without its signing key refuses
  before packing. The release scripts' usage errors exit 2, the forge failure messages
  and the gate cells skip remedy give runnable commands, and AGENTS.md's commands,
  counts and alias names match the code.

- **The README and the install, update and key guides say what is true.** The README
  says what `--no-path` leaves alone, which command names aterm tabs reroute, which two
  macOS settings aterm changes by default and how to keep them, every `await` predicate,
  and the music-box typing sound. The Linux guide gives the install command and says
  `aterm update check` exits 0 when a release has no Linux build, and a terminal session
  can confirm a Linux update. The install and key-management guides match the live
  settings, buttons and publish commands. Release notes stop printing download sizes
  that had drifted, and a cut with no credentials profile is told which one to pass.

## Earlier releases

Sections before 0.100.0 were cut from this file on 2026-10-01: each release's
notes are its GitHub Release body, and git history has the file as it stood
(`git show 4cb786b1f:CHANGELOG.md`).
